At a glance this game looks part Visual Novel, part Princess Maker (Does this genre have a name? Raising simulator?). However, both are misleading.
From the Visual Novel side, while there is a very solid story, and quite a few secrets to uncover in multiple playthroughs, there are, ultimately, no diverging paths. The events always happen in the same order, and there are only a few cases where events from one week directly influence events in another.
As for the skill learning part, since skills are only used in skill tests, which only pop up for specific skills at specific moments, it is useless to try to build skills based on flavor, or for general use. You can't make choices based on all the skills you have, only based on specific, arbitrary ones. And since a decent skill level requires several weeks to build, you usually need to plan ahead for the incoming skill tests, and start training right on the first week.
What Long Live The Queen is, then, is a puzzle game. It requires putting a lot of thought into which skills to train in order to pass skill tests up ahead. It also requires some choice, since it's impossible to train fast enough to pass all skill tests. Additionally, Elodie's mood also needs to be considered, as it can help or prevent from training a skill. If you're looking for a brain workout with a good storyline, Long Live The Queen is the game for you.
Be aware that Long Live The Queen is very much a "wiki game". Since a large part of the game requires planning ahead for skill tests, which are rather arbitrary and offer no way of "predicting" which would come next, aside from having already played through the events once and seen which skill tests are needed. While this much can be done just by memorizing and multiple replays, since skill tests are shown, the exact level of the skill required is not clearly stated, and training it too much can harm training for other skills.
Additionally, while a recent patch adds a clear statement as to which skills are influenced by the current mood, other than memorization, or jotting down a table, there's no way to tell which mood you need in order to boost a certain skill which you wish to train. Since it can sometimes take several weeks and careful planning to change moods, not knowing which mood is needed may require repeating through those weeks several times. Hopefully, a future UI patch will correct this issue.
Overall, this game offers a great deal of replay value, even if you remain glued to the wiki, and have a complete "battle plan" before each play, simply due to the various ways in which you can deal with each week, and also the fact that you must always accept a less favorable result for some weeks in order to get a more favorable result for others.
Long Live The Queen. Survive 40 weeks and become the queen of Nova, or die horribly on your way to the throne.

text:
Recommending this game would imply that you actually get the masterpiece all those glowing 10/10 reviews promised you but sadly that is not the case. Pillars of Eternity is mediocre in every single relevant way. Every other known CRPG, be it modern or classic is better in at least one major aspect.
Firstly, the writers make the common mistake of trying to create a tolkienesque universe i.e. you are gonna need to learn a few new languages none of which feel authentic since they clearly were not conceived by a linguist of Tolkiens calibre. So what you get is a bunch of gibberish, containing a lot of "th"s, apostrophes, umlauts and the like. Even if the languages themselves were solid, their intriguing potential would still be squandered by Pillars' distinctly American voice acting.
Races are equally as bland and you can tell the designers were trying way too hard; you get your elves, humans and dwarves but thats the most basic array of races to base your characters on. That is why the artists had a big think and came up with their own intelligent beings. However, they are underdeveloped and superficial: what's an Aumaua? A seafaring ogre. What's an Orlan? Even hairier Halflings with long wolf ears. Not much more can be said about them. Godlikes, their versions of the Planetouched of D&D, are the most interesting creations but their background is not being utilised to any of its potential. They are obviously the rarest beings in the world, since they cannot procreate but I never felt like they were a big deal of any kind. Unlike the Planetouched, who are merely that, said to be touched by SOME outsider, Godlikes are literally said to be blessed by a major deity. Yet playing them is no different from playing a normal dude. Not even playing as the abomination that is the Death Godlike gets much of a reaction generally.
Combat is what CRPG combat has always been and I do not consider it important to the overall experience. It is a competent, completely functional system and it does its job.
Story on the other hand is what keeps you engaged in whatever you are doing and in this regard Pillars falls terribly flat. The premise is weak and the main conflict never evolves throughout the course of the plot. It starts off slow, never accelerates and then ends.
Sidequests are a mixed bag. The Endless Paths of Od Nua (think Halls of Undermountain, albeit with a clear end) are more engaging than the main quest and actually a microcosm of what it should have been: you start with a simple objective, finding the Master Below who lives below your Keep. On your descent through the ruins of what was once a very impressive basement you enter distinct areas, facing new challenges every level and learn new things about this Master Below. The quest develops organically and the plot thickens regularly. Other sidequests are mostly standard and I do not remember many of them.
Companions are relatively speaking the biggest strength of Pillars. While many of them lack complexity, their personalities keep you interested in them for the most part, which was enough for me to go through with their questlines, Durance's in particular; the guy is belligerent and keeps giving you♥♥♥♥♥♥for no good reason but precisely because of all that you want to know more about him and why he is the way he is. Having the best voice acting by far also helps, whereas the others range from "Ok" to "Hardly Trying" in that regard.
Locations are quite samey. With the exception of the aforementioned Paths of Od Nua, you will be seeing a lot meadows, forests and some castles. I get that this is in line with the pseudo-european setting of the game but that does not make it any less ordinary.
The main cities is where ludicrous amounts of money were left on the table so to speak. When you first enter Defiance Bay and see Copperlane for the first time, the city feels pretty huge with a lot to do in it. However you quickly realise that Copperlane is the location where most of the budget went. The districts of First Fires, Brackenbury and Ondra's Gift not only look and feel very similar to each other (with the latter being a minor exception, being the port district), they also have only about 2-4 relevant locations each.
Then you get to Twin Elms in the late-game and you realise that for that place they had 5 dollars and a ham sandwich left. It pales in comparison to Defiance Bay both in design and activities and it was clear that you were never supposed to spend much time there, since at that point only about 5-7 hours separate you from the ending.
I did play through the game cause I paid for the thing, I do not like wasting good money and I alawys give everything the benefit of the doubt. The story bored me to death but I kept waiting patiently for it to get good. When I realised that I had reached the third act and the stakes were still where they had been at the very beginning of the game, I rushed to the final boss, hoping against hope that at the last minute everything would turn out to have been worth it. Obviously it was not. The ending sequence and the last dungeon are hella lame: enemy encounters are a complete joke and the game tries to hit you with a mindblowing twist that has nothing to do with your character and also does not makes not a lick of sense. You beat the villain, then you win and all's good. I do not see how anyone would find this game's resolution satisfying.
If you are obsessed with CRPG and want to relive the old days of Bioware and Black Isle, buy Pillars of Eternity, if you must, on a good sale. Im talking 60% off at the least. To everyone else, play literally any other CRPG out there. Play any of the new Shadowruns. I would rather you buy Obsidian's own Tyranny, which, while having huge flaws of its own, has at least an original and interesting premise and universe to explore. Do a playthrough of the first Fallouts or Planescape: Torment if you just want the classics. Whatever you do, do not fall for the hype. Pillars of Eternity is not exceptional in any way.

I don't think this game needs any introducing, but I'm going to do this anyway:
Ultra Street Fighter IV is the newest in the series of 2D fighting games developed by Capcom, and this series is said to be one of those that coded the genre. I had some experience with Street Fighter II, so I can compare this to some of the older games.
First of all: despite the game having cell-shaded 3D graphics, it still sticks to the traditional 2D formula. You might call the graphics not incredible, but they're good enough that you can marvel at all the work in the background or character animations.
The gameplay is simple yet fun. All the characters have standard punches and kicks (in the light, medium and heavy varieties), as well as crouching and jumping versions of those. They can block, throw special attacks, use Supers or EX attacks if they get the Super bar high enough, or use Ultras which are fueled by the Revenge gauge that goes up by taking damage, making this a Comeback Mechanic. There are also throws, sped up / delayed wake-ups, Focus Attacks which block damage and guard break, and the new Red Focus Attack which is considered an EX attack (burns Super bar) but can soak up multiple hits (standard Focus Attack can stop only one). This adds to the options for combat and makes for a nice guessing game. Also, this game not being very combo-oriented as other ones (such as Guilty Gear or BlazBlue), it's well-suited for general casual play, as well as high-level play where players can pull off longer combos.
As of Ultra, the game has a gigantic roster of 44 fighters available to suit your playstyle, whether you like grappling characters with command grabs, mixup characters, or just want to stick to the standard Shoto Clone (Ryu, Ken etc.). Even the boss characters are more balanced towards general play, which is quite interesting.
On the music side, the tunes you hear in the game mostly aren't incredibly memorable, but they're catchy enough that you won't really get tired of listening to them over and over.
Overall, this game is a very solid title. Interesting and wide assortment of combat options, a lot of characters to choose from, and fantastic presentation, this game is great for both casuals and tourney-goers.

“Yo, this game is so sick”.
That is what I said about Ultra Street Fighter 4 after I KO’d one of my many online opponents by mercilessly throwing a beefy Metsu Hadoken right into his chest.

USF4 is, quite possibly, my favorite fighting game that exists to this very day.  This is a strong opinion that I have just given, but please allow me to explain why I feel this way, and why this game may interest you as well.
The characters.  USF4 boasts an IMPRESSIVE cast of fighters.  Fans of the older Street Fighter games will see just about all of the old characters they remember and love like Ryu, Chun Li, and Sagat, but the game also throws many new fighters into the mix as well. All together, USF4 offers 44 different fighters to play as.  Can you imagine having 44 different types of delicious pasta given to you at once? I would probably blow up from eating too much.
One of the ways that USF4 separates itself from other fighting games is by how accessible it is to fighting game newcomers.  Special move inputs are simple to perform, basic combos are not lengthy or technically demanding, and the pace of the game is much slower than other fighters like Marvel Vs. Capcom or King of Fighters.  This may sound bad for fighting game experts, but USF4 still manages to have a great deal of depth and can be very rewarding for those who put in the work and become godlike.
Be warned that this game does not offer much for the single player experience.  It comes with Arcade mode, Training mode, and a Trial mode.  Most players, though, will likely be spending their time playing online trying to become THE STRONGEST IN THE UNIVERSE.  Please keep in mind that many players have had problems with the online thus far. I, PERSONALLY, haven’t had much trouble.  Every now and then, I get a match that lags like a ravenous herd of chunky sea slugs swimming through a rich manure field, HOWEVER, most of the time it runs quite well and I dominate the opponent with my MLG decision making and cunning brilliance.
I would like to believe that Street Fighter is the face of fighting games, and luckily, it is also DOWNRIGHT SICK NASTY at what it does.  It’s got tons of memorable characters, stages, and music.  Good visuals and flashy attacks.  An online mode that works great (at least for me) and is very active.  It’s easy for newcomers to enjoy and deep enough for experts to play for hundreds of hours.  To put it simply, USF4 is just like a steaming plate of luxurious lasagna fritta that you never grow tired of.
I give Ultra street Fighter 4 a score of “Undisputed Champion of the Makuuchi Sumo Wrestling Division”. Thank you for reading this review.

Okay, I'm seeing a lot of negative reviews for Starbound...from people who've played the game for over 500 hours. Sorry, what?
I just discovered this game a couple days ago and just bought my own copy to support the developers. Let me first say, I knew about this game for a long time. I thought I wouldn't like it, so I didn't buy it. My fellow gamers who dislike pixelated graphics and two-dimensional gameplay as a rule will understand. And from what I read, it seemed like just another knockoff of Minecraft. It reminded me of Terraria, which I played for a few hours and couldn't get into.
But then I played this game. And oh man, I was wrong on SO many levels.
Starbound is, yes, like Minecraft. In space. With infinite planets. And fully explorable asteroid bodies. And moons. Everything from garden worlds to desert worlds to barren worlds to floating ore-filled rocks is open to you. And that's just the beginning.
You have a spaceship. It's customizable. You can upgrade it. You can get crewmates who upgrade your ship: mercenaries, incidental encounters, or colonists who are very happy with you being their landlord. (Oh yeah, you can establish fully customizable colonies anywhere with an atmosphere.) The spaceship has a teleportation function that can send you to any custom destination you want.
There is a plot. The plot is designed to introduce you to the functions of this staggeringly massive game one by one, and it also is fairly interesting, yet never gets in the way of your exploration. In fact, it encourages it.
Think you've got nothing to gain from exploring a supposedly uninteresting desert world in the middle of nowhere? Think again. Trudge around on the surface of that planet and you'll stumble across a heavily guarded Avian temple - with plenty of loot and unique items within. Mine below the surface and discover ancient ruins filled with treasure, and then use your archeologist's kit to extract the bones of ancient species from the nearby wall because
. Then make a base in said ancient ruins and chew through all the nearby ore. But keep digging and you'll discover the Hell-like underworld with a fitting number of disgusting creatures (and unique loot). Run back up to the surface and emerge in a massive tar pit brimming with oil. Take some for yourself and pop a flag down so you can come back if you need more.
Upgrade your character. Craft or find amazing sets of armor, and then put clothing on top of it to customize your character's look. Find the necessary components to upgrade your Matter Manipulator (essentially your pickaxe and placement tool, among other things) so it'll dig faster, suck up liquids, and punch through larger areas. Complete quests at the Outpost to gain abilities such as double jumping, dashing, and turning into a Metroid-like tiny sphere for those hard-to-reach areas. Craft a module that will allow you to survive indefinitely without an atmosphere, and then upgrade it to help you even more on your travels.
Oh yeah, you also can tame pretty much any animal and keep them as a pet. Seriously, why are you still reading this? There are dozens of other things in this game that I haven't even discovered, and dozens that I have but haven't touched on in this review. There is absolutely no reason to worry about getting your money's worth from this game when the average player plays 30-100 hours at minimum. Yes, all games have their time and I will eventually get tired of this game. But this is fifteen dollars well spent.

Let me preface this by saying that I've only just now completed this game on Easy and I'm working on the Original mode right now. I have not seen everything that the game has to offer. This is sort of a 'first impressions' review. If I have to alter the review or write a new one in the future, I will, but I'm pretty sure this covers most of what's going on.
This is a trial-and-error game. A 'ooh, what does this button do' kind of game. It's a learning process, and if you beat then entire game on the first try of your first time loading it, then you've just been insanely lucky and there's all that is to it. If you don't like repeating processes to improve your game, then you're not going to like this game at all.
I didn't find this game difficult. I didn't get anything correct on the first try, and I was stuck in that damn desert for hours, but nothing seemed difficult to me. And when Original is labeled as difficult, I expected Easy to be... About as hard as it was for me. If you jumped in on Original without understanding how things worked, then you're not gonna have a good time, but you should be able to pick up what's going on very quickly.
When the game was harsh and unforgiving, it felt like it was supposed to be harsh and unforgiving. I found myself speed-clicking through repeating cutscenes after losing a level(?) but that was the only time I ever felt annoyed with it, and I barely even felt it, then.
The graphics and animation are pretty solid. I mention below that a few things looked buggy for me, but I'm going to look for these things the next time I play to see if it's a problem or just something that happens (or is supposed to happen)? But overall things are really, really good. The sound and effects are well-placed, a little loud in some places, but 99% of the time they hit the nail on the head.
Now, this is where we enter spoiler territory.
Seriously, spoilers from here on out.
One of the problems I had with it was how abrupt the ending felt. It felt like I was just understanding what was going on, and then it was over without explaining it. We learn that Burden's experienced this world/timeline over and over (saves and reloads), but we never really learn why. It just is. The very ending, past the credits, might suggest to a wormhole or a rip in time, but we're kind of left hanging (probably to make room for a sequel), and there's this weird void of 'I don't get it' that lingers.
I can understand why people would think the story and characters are stale. Me, personally, I like the idea of a team doing what it needs to do, and even though the characters were a little generic, that's not a bad thing. All of their roles were made clear and you understood what needed to be done.
The characters of Xenolifer were... Eh. I understand that they were background, but at the very last scene, I had no idea who the people I was holding hostage were or why I should care. And I did my damndest to read and retain the information, but if I shot Claire's son... I mean, aside from it raising and lowering certain stats, I didn't have any reason for not doing it. I didn't have a reason for caring about these people other than the game telling me that I should.
I guess what I'm saying is that we didn't get a whole lot of Burden's background with that organization, and I kinda wanted it. The game has it's limitations, but I would have much rather preferred feeling for characters out of my own volition rather than the game telling me that I should care about them.
Those are really the only problems I have with the game, and they're minor. Some places seemed a little glitchy with the graphics, but I'm going to be playing it through again to see if it's a persisting problem or just a random one.
All in all, it's a good game, and in my opinion it was worth the time and money (I bought it on sale, but it's definitely worth the $10).
If I had to give it a grade:
Graphics: A
Story: B
Characters: B
Actual Gameplay: A
Tl;dr ... Good game dun good.

Dead Effect is the (unofficial) expansion pack to DOOM 3 released in 2014 to hold you over until the new DOOM gets released. If you were disappointed with Resurrection of Evil, this should make up for it.
In all seriousness, Dead Effect is a really neat game with a classic FPS feel, while bringing in a few modern FPS elements to the mix. It also incorporated a few horror elements to it, such as being very limited to how much you can run, a flashlight that actually takes some time to recharge, and a semi-limited amount of ammo to be collected. If DOOM, Dead Space, and F.E.A.R. had a threesome, this would be the baby. Although it is an awesome game, it's not something you'll play for 100's of hours, though I can sense some replayability in the game (I only beat the first few levels thus far).
Dead Effect isn't the best game ever made, but I had a good bit of fun with it. I would say that 6 hours of entertainment is definitely worth the 99 cents I paid for the game on sale.

This game isn't bad, by any stretch, but it isn't fun either ... in either a narrative or mechanistic fashion.  To the former, the things it tackles, like slavery, holding hostages, torture, are not easy ones, particularly when you're sometimes on the giving end of them, so it's not a light hearted romp.
But it's the mechanics that kills it.  While it doesn't always have numerical feedback as to how things are progressing (like what level of calmness / rebellion your hostages are at) which is something I actually appreciate ... it's sometimes unclear as to what particular 'gestures' mean.  Are they really anxious or just following orders?  The game lampshades this in the final act, showing that you have to go over and over and over again to understand HOW to play the game ... which isn't a bad thing in and of itself.
What IS bad is that it not only requires you to go through some sections again and again without skipping, some of the things just take FOREVER to accomplish ... the transitions could be snappier and the 'start from the beginning of the chapter' is unforgiving.  Further, even if you're just there for the narrative, the game doesn't give it out sequentially, but instead sometimes semi-randomly, so the point they're making varies ... and if you don't want to miss it, you have to read it all, which is sad because it gets repetitive as you have to restart over and over again to find the patterns to win.
If you can get this free or very cheap, it's an interesting few hours, but be prepared for some painful mechanics.

After only 20 hours played:
++++The game is REALLY easy to get into, and I mean reaallly easy to understand, it's a simpler but better version of Dayz!

+Vehicles are really easy "Arcade-ish" to drive which is good, not clunky like in other survival games.
+Realism/physics are good when running-jumping-climbing or shooting etc.
+Movement system (the gameplay is very responsive) BUT I would like some headbob when running.
+Mutants: the different zombies & the wild dogs/wolfs are AWESOME!
+Build your own base (you need to find different recipes though) or raid other bases!
+The hit registration is pretty good from my experience "playing on max 50-ping server"
+Performance: it really doesn't matter if you run low-med or high-very high settings on my setup I usually get a stable 120-FPS, performance may change 5-10fps, but in some weird corners on the map my fps goes down to 45, "it has only happened 2-3 times" and when I move 2 feet away my fps goes back up.
( My setup i7-6700k, GTX 1070 Strix, SSD, 16gb ram. )
-/+ Sound = mehhh on some weapons, and when you drive/sit in a car the sound is waaay to low from the engine (might been a bug for me I don't know)" but the storms/thunders are good, really 0rgasmic for the ears! the rain sounds good, only complaints are that some weapons sound very weird/weak & the car noise is to low when sitting inside of it. And as in most survival games you can speak with anyone in the close area via mic or text.
I know I know it's only early access but the game is fully functional and you'll find full servers 24/7 (EU)
And as usual you'll have a much better experience playing with a friend or friends, still its a very good solo game to try and survive in! GL & HF!

It's insane how much content they could fit in the game. Sure, the texture quality might not be the greatest (but take note that the game itself is from 2011) but the level design is TOP NOTCH. In some areas you just need to take a breather and take a look around. For example in Anor Londo, the view is gorgeous as the hints on the ground suggest.
This game has an incredible way to tell a story through the environment. You won't be bugged with long cutscenes of certain incidents, you'll just hear of them through the NPCs, like merchants.
The game creates an atmoshpere that you'll find hard to drag yourself out of. I myself found it difficult to stop thinking of the new areas I could find in the future, hours after closing the game. And so, the game kept luring me back in.
Sure. The game is difficult to someone jumping into the specific playstyle-genre for the first time. But still, after a lot of trial and error, beating a single boss fight after a half an hour learning its attack patterns, success feels rewarding.
In conclusion this game is a gem worth the praise it gets. I myself would rate it a solid 9/10 (would've given 10 if it wasn't for the clumsy pc port, which could've been improved a bit).

Similar in vein to the
of Japanese "life-sim" games released in the early 1990's,
tasks the player with planning the daily activities of a queen-in-waiting as she prepares to ascend to the throne of her realm. Time management and prioritization becomes key, as you have limited opportunities to train in certain disciplines that all raise skills. These skills play a crucial part in vignettes that determine the ultimate fate of your royal charge as she must contend with warring factions, political intrigue, assassination attempts, and more. Failure to meet skill requirements often have consequences on which of the myriad endings you will reach and can even lead - often - to your character's untimely demise. In fact, this game becomes something akin to a "Choose Your Own Adventure" novel in that you will, provided you don't use an online guide, have to play through the game multiple times and experiment with different training combinations just to survive through to the ending. This can be a point of frustration for many players, I'm sure, but the patient player will be rewarded with a surprisingly entertaining and, given the cutesy anime graphics, mature storyline.
this isn't, but nor is it a "magical girl" anime game; despite the "magical girl" costume that can be unlocked. Ahem.

I have spent a good part of 70 hours gaming State of Decay and even though I had some rough minutes getting used to the game starting off – I totally fell in love! This is despite I like to really live the character I play, because in State of Decay you play several characters. They get tired, hurt, die, and when that happens you really need to find someone else to switch to – the dyeing part is obvious though!
To me this game is a mix of The Last Stand: Dead Zone and Rebuild and then made into a big third person shooter. Roughly.
It has been made so you really feel the realism. Cars break down, but also carry things in its trunk. You need to scavenge food, materials, medic, ammo and fuel, so your base continually keeps running. Because yes, there is a base. You are to decide what to build and where. Save strangers and allies from distress. Fight hordes of zombies – and oh the zombies! They are hilarious. Have you ever gamed The Movies? The way they run, this is how some of the zombies run. I love it!
The AI, yeah it could differently be better and even though the game screams coop-multiplayer there are non and there will not be. Also I find it frustrating, that sometimes you sit with the feeling, that nobody but you are the one to really pull the plugs. Even though there are opportunities to get support, they really are only there to help you fight. So don't expect them to help more than that – not even at missions, which I missed a little to make it feel more realistic.
But I do look forward to a third State of Decay, meanwhile I warmly recommend this one. It’s worth the full cost if you ask me, despite the downsides.

I mean, I get that its a survival game, but you can literally be finding "new survivors" every time you finish doing something else.
The result is that you always have 2-3 things you can go do, PLUS helping with mini-missions (requests from current survivors).
If you leave the game from outside your home base, any vehicle you had with you is left where you were, while you get teleported home.
6/10.  Worth playing if you really like survival, but definitely not worth full price.

This is a fairly standard shooter with some quaint classic-era design elements to its credit that I find rather refreshing, especially after playing a lot of modern FPS titles.
There isn't anything new or innovative here.  You assume the role of one of two space marine meatheads (the stereotypical male space marine meathead or the stereotypical female space marine meathead, just to clarify) aboard an FTL ship in deep space woken from cryogenic status up to a ship full of zombies, and proceed through a succession of linear mission levels usually consisting of finding a few switches to power up elevators or unlock doors and shooting everything that moves with a standard (and I'd say woefully small) arsenal of weapons.  No platforming (you can't jump in the game: a thing I haven't seen in an FPS since Doom), no puzzle solving, nothing requiring anything much thought. Just go to room, shoot all the zombies, get a few generic instructions from the badly acted German accented scientist, rinse, wash, repeat.  No spoilers.
Along the way you find credits and gold bars to upgrade your arsenal, and a bunch of tablets containing various emails and communicaes left behind to attempt to flesh out the story and universe a bit more: you know, the same thing every sci-fi/horror themed FPS has done since System Shock.
Really, this is an amalgam of cliches from System Shock, Doom, and Dead Space cobbled together for no other purpose other than to give us a familiar setting that provides massive hordes of undead to spend several cathartic hours mowing down.
Go in with low expectations and you'll find a fun, competently put-together FPS.  Go in expecting more than that and you'll find yourself very disappointed.
For the $5 price tag I was plesently suprised. I am looking forword to the release of DE2. Its worth it as a fun jaunt and time killer.

Dark Souls gave me lots of pleasure and very unique experience.
At first I heard of this game on 9gag and decided to try. I played lots of RPGs and ARPGs. The last one I played was Skyrim. Oh boy, Dark Souls seemed to be very hard in comparison to Skyrim. Zero. You will need a gamepad, DSFix and other mods that you can find on nexus mods to make this purchase worthwhile on PC. The online isn't great nowadays, but if you manage to get some jolly cooperation, or get to invade or be invaded, you'll get some of this unique Souls experience.
First of all you have to understand that Dark Souls is more a puzzle game, than simple hack and slash. You need to read every clue you can find about the world and mechanics, because nothing is explained. Forget anything you knew about ARPG games. And don't be afraid to die - this is part of the gameplay. The game is about perseverance and overcoming the obstacles.
Second, understand the combat mechanics. This includes dodging, blocking, parrying and backstabbing. Also understand how weapon enhancement, ascension and stat scaling work - this is very important, because you need to level up your weapons as you level up your character.
Third, understand how your stats work. Resistance is absolutely useless. Str and Agl don't give a lot of damage boost if your weapon is not upgraded, so at the beginning consider investing in HP and Endurance. Watch for your weight limit, armor defense properties and poise that defines if your attacks can be interrupted. Match your equipment to your enemies’ weakness.
Fourth, don't sell or dispose your items, as a lot of them are hard to obtain and are available only once in a playthrough.
And the last one. Don't rush. Observe your enemies, observe your surroundings, observe the world. The plot is pretty solid, but you will probably miss it, because you need to piece together a lot of things - the intro, the dialogs (which are in old English), the item descriptions, the location you find these items at and the design of the enemies. There are no definite answers, so you have to use your imagination.
If you finished reading this review, you are probably ready to take on this masterpiece.

This is really by many standards a poorly made game, but the premise alone is SO original and fascinating that it's worth playing. It is loosely like the Japanese puzzle game Kakuro, but with negative values in the mix.
Here is how I would improve Energy Balance:
- The graphics feel disconnected. The number blocks look like they are made of primitive stone, versus the futuristic star background. I would change the block appearances.
- Make it CLEAR that the storyline dialogue can be skippable if you hit Space Bar (which makes a clickable "skip" button appear in the upper-right corner). I noticed this entirely by accident, and it takes way too long to display the text otherwise. Or just speed up the text and fade-in/-out character animations.
- Make it clear in the first level that any block can swap with any other block; you don't have to click only on adjacent blocks (which is a mistake I found myself doing at first until I tried otherwise).
- Add an optional sound effect per block click, and audio for the running text dialogue, like maybe a robotic mew sound for the cat. It's a bit odd to me that literally the only audio in the entire game is the music.
- Have the game remember your moves, to be able to undo moves. There is no "undo" button at all (although arguably this could be purposely omitted to make the game harder, which may float some players' boats).
- Have an option to
reset the music to a different track every time you leave game-window focus.
- Some of the tracks I think are not very well balanced, audio-wise (some are louder than others). It would be good if the audio could be balanced.
Anyway, here's a hint about the gameplay itself: it comes off as EXTREMELY tricky at first but the more you play through it (especially once you start beating levels 3-4 or so), it becomes easier as you understand how the number-swapping process works. You balance as many energy cells as you can, and then once you get stuck with the remaining 1-3, you carefully substitute, following the paths of other cells to find appropriately fitting values. It's extremely elating once you can really start figuring out levels without too much difficulty.
While I have read from other reviews that there are only 20 levels, the energy values change every single time you play, so the game is technically infinitely replayable, which is really cool for such an otherwise short game.
I really look forward to seeing this game on Android! That's where it deserves to be, but not really here on Steam. It'd rock on any touchscreen device.

Okay, I'm seeing a lot of negative reviews for Starbound...from people who've played the game for over 500 hours. Sorry, what?
I just discovered this game a couple days ago and just bought my own copy to support the developers. Let me first say, I knew about this game for a long time. I thought I wouldn't like it, so I didn't buy it. My fellow gamers who dislike pixelated graphics and two-dimensional gameplay as a rule will understand. And from what I read, it seemed like just another knockoff of Minecraft. It reminded me of Terraria, which I played for a few hours and couldn't get into.
But then I played this game. And oh man, I was wrong on SO many levels.
Starbound is, yes, like Minecraft. In space. With infinite planets. And fully explorable asteroid bodies. And moons. Everything from garden worlds to desert worlds to barren worlds to floating ore-filled rocks is open to you. And that's just the beginning.
You have a spaceship. It's customizable. You can upgrade it. You can get crewmates who upgrade your ship: mercenaries, incidental encounters, or colonists who are very happy with you being their landlord. (Oh yeah, you can establish fully customizable colonies anywhere with an atmosphere.) The spaceship has a teleportation function that can send you to any custom destination you want.
There is a plot. The plot is designed to introduce you to the functions of this staggeringly massive game one by one, and it also is fairly interesting, yet never gets in the way of your exploration. In fact, it encourages it.
Think you've got nothing to gain from exploring a supposedly uninteresting desert world in the middle of nowhere? Think again. Trudge around on the surface of that planet and you'll stumble across a heavily guarded Avian temple - with plenty of loot and unique items within. Mine below the surface and discover ancient ruins filled with treasure, and then use your archeologist's kit to extract the bones of ancient species from the nearby wall because
. Then make a base in said ancient ruins and chew through all the nearby ore. But keep digging and you'll discover the Hell-like underworld with a fitting number of disgusting creatures (and unique loot). Run back up to the surface and emerge in a massive tar pit brimming with oil. Take some for yourself and pop a flag down so you can come back if you need more.
Upgrade your character. Craft or find amazing sets of armor, and then put clothing on top of it to customize your character's look. Find the necessary components to upgrade your Matter Manipulator (essentially your pickaxe and placement tool, among other things) so it'll dig faster, suck up liquids, and punch through larger areas. Complete quests at the Outpost to gain abilities such as double jumping, dashing, and turning into a Metroid-like tiny sphere for those hard-to-reach areas. Craft a module that will allow you to survive indefinitely without an atmosphere, and then upgrade it to help you even more on your travels.
Oh yeah, you also can tame pretty much any animal and keep them as a pet. Seriously, why are you still reading this? There are dozens of other things in this game that I haven't even discovered, and dozens that I have but haven't touched on in this review. There is absolutely no reason to worry about getting your money's worth from this game when the average player plays 30-100 hours at minimum. Yes, all games have their time and I will eventually get tired of this game. But this is fifteen dollars well spent.

Just to preface this: I finished this game once so far, although most of my playtime has been off-steam.
So, PoE is pretty much old school CRPG incarnate. It's deep, it's complex. Compared to modern RPGs (looking at you, Bethesda and nowadays' Bioware) it's deliberately complicated. If you expect this game to be a Diablo-like Hack'n'Slasher you will get your face kicked in and probably be disappointed. It's just as technical as the old AD&D games - and then some.
The game's setting is pretty bleak, which might put some people off. It's not boring, it's not uninspired - far from it, actually. This is one of the more innovative universes in the modern RPG genre. But it's also a crappy, crappy world. Usually, there's not even a silver streak of hope to be seen on the horizon. The very first town you'll enter will pretty much greet you with a gallow tree with dozens of corpses dangling from its branches. This is purely subjective, but at times I found myself not wanting to play the game because the setting is just *so* downer.
The writing is top-notch, however. Most of the characters are pretty well written and have some interesting twists to their personality. Not all of them, mind you, but most. The quest-lines are engaging and make you want for more. There's usually no grinding involved and the MMO-style fetch quests are kept to a minimum. The game is very wordy to a point where it - positively - reminds me of good old Planescape: Torment.
A nice touch is that the general narrative (e.g. your party scaling a cliffside or trying to break through a dungeon wall) isn't presented in the usual dialogue box but in a very neat and well illustrated 'digital textbook' as I like to call it, which adds to the overall flair of PoE as a kind of interactive fantasy novel.
tl;dr: RECOMMENDED, if you're into old-school CRPGs like Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment or Icewind Dale and (best case) have some under your belt already.
NOT RECOMMENDED if you're into fast-paced action RPGs and are looking for a quick slash-and-loot affair.

This is an odd one, At first glance it seems to be an average kawaii visual novel game in the anime style, but once you break its surface, it’s a very entertaining, very cruel game. You play a princess named Elodie whose mother, The Queen of Nova, died. And you are to ascend to the throne. Unfortunatly it turns out that the cosmic forces that be, have it in for kawaii crown-princesses, and your job is to make sure she lives to see her coronation.
Gameplay is essentially, Elodie has moods, and moods give certain buffs or debuffs for certain skills that the player will select for Elodie to learn. The payoff is within the story scenes where events happen and depending on Elodie’s knowledge on a particular subject, there will be differing outcomes to a situation, quite a few of which can mean the difference between life and death. There are also certain outfits you can unlock which gives a boost to a particular skill.
Overall, I’d recommend it. It’s deceptively fun (and dark), has good enough replay value (Especially as you will die alot) and is relatively cheap.

Dark Souls is tough but fair.....most of the time. Though I could feel the blood boiling from within on occassion I couldn't stop playing. I couldn't let the game beat me. I knew that every challenge was beatable and when I finally got past a difficult area I felt elation unlike I've felt in a game in a long while. Seldom does my pulse quicken the way it does during the high points of this game. It's not for the faint of heart but for those up to the task this game will not dissapoint.
A few quick side notes though.
The game is playable with the Xbox 360 controller but there is a known issue where if you have multiple HID drivers in your Device Manager that the game, along with several older games, just won't recognize the controller. To bypass this irritating glitch disable all HID devices in Device Manager and then enable them one at a time until you find the one that matches the 360 controller. Once you do just enable that one and you're good to go. My issue stemmed from HID Wiimote devices that was creating a compatibility conflict.
The game world is well designed but isn't the most beautiful out there these days. However game worlds that are well designed tend to hold up well even if the details are lackluster years later. It's obviously not up to the standards of the later Souls Games but there are still stunning vistas, engaging labyrinths, and an overall good flow between the game's hub area and the branching paths leading out from it.
Combat is the true gem of this game. There's a lot to learn and much to tinker with considering your loadout, attributes, upgrades, ect... This part of the game kept driving me to test new equipment and strategies to figure out how best to tackle the hordes of Dark Souls. Incidentally much of the lore of Dark Souls is found through the equipment and item descriptions. Since the game does little ot expand the story cinematically be sure to read every description to get more out of the backstory. It is my one complaint really. Just a little more cinematics and backstory would have been welcome but I do understand that that is not what this game is about. Still, when the final credits rolled I was just a little unsatisfied with the story. There's always a tradeoff it seems.
Overall it was a great game and a must play for any action RPG fan or any hardcore gamer looking for a real challenge.

I don't normally write reviews for games, but I can't say enough about this game.  I don't want this to be 10 pages long so I'll try to be brief.
Like others have said, it's basically an interactive novel with platforming elements and mini-games.  The game mainly consists of running around talking to people and exploring the town.  There is no combat, there's not really even much in the way of puzzles.  Because of that, maybe the game isn't for everyone.  I personally love story driven games and lack of gameplay isn't a deal breaker for me if the story is good.
The dialog is probably some of the best I have experienced in a game.  I laughed out loud at several points and got emotional at others.  You really can't help caring about the characters, maybe even relating to them.  Even though they are cartoon animals, the characters are more real and fleshed out than in many novels I have read.  The main characters are 'young' and the dialog reflects that, but it isn't (IMO) done in an obnoxious or cliche way.
The game play admittedly isn't the greatest but it wasn't 'bad', and I like everything else about the game so much that it really didn't bother me.  Sometimes going through the motions of running around town did feel a little repetitive, but I was so interested in learning more about the people and the town that I didn't mind it.  I found myself wanting to interact with everyone whenever I got the chance so I wouldn't miss anything.  The only parts that I felt like I could do without were the dream sequences.  Still though... they had a nice creepy vibe, were visually awesome, and the music was good.
In general the music and appearance of the game are amazing.  The music really fits with the atmosphere of the game and was memorable.
The themes of the game I found pretty soul crushing, but that's not really a criticism.  Whenever I walk away from something like this and can't stop thinking about it, or I feel messed up over it for a while after, that's usually a sign that it was pretty well done I think.  It isn't that the game is just 'sad' or a downer in general.  It's got light/fun moments and heavy/real moments.  I think its more about the fact that its relatable and tackles subjects that do affect a lot of people.
A lot of people criticize the ending.  I'm not going to spoil anything, but I just think that... there's maybe more than one way to interpret things in this game.  Things are left kind of ambiguous, on purpose I think so that people will speculate and talk about it long after release.  This seems to be fairly common nowadays, and I personally don't mind it.  I for some reason like walking away wondering what this-or-that meant, and reading people's theories.
Over all it's an amazing game that will probably stick with me for a while.  I was sad that it ended, although it wasn't one of those games that left me feeling cheated because it wasn't long enough.  It felt like a respectable length, and you can't really experience everything in one play through so it has atleast some replayabillity.
I also played the 2 supplemental games which are very short but they expand on some aspects of the 'backstory' I guess you could say, so they are worth checking out if you are intrigued by the main game and want more.

When I stumbled upon this game I thought it would be a cute, quirky little game that I would beat in maybe 7 or 8 hours. I was both right and wrong.
Night in the Woods allows you to decide how much you want to do each day and gives you more control over the plot than most other games I've seen. One day you'll be running across town getting prepped for band practice and another you'll have spent over an hour talking to random people you were interested in on the street.
While some days will feel monotonous at times, the actual things you do each day can vary greatly, if you go looking for it. You’ll find yourself breaking into abandoned stores, flirting with clerks, and having to ask a friend to help your virus riddled laptop and not really be able to say that it was the weirdest thing you’ve done during the game. Each portion of each day has so many fun conversations and jokes packed in I found myself smiling for the majority of the game. However, the game isn’t a lighthearted tale of a young delinquent’s journey through life. Topics of loss, financial woes, mental disorders, and even the death of small towns and the middle class are brought up at various points. Though the game can be somber, it never felt depressing or preachy. It brings up these topics, not to try to educate you about them or offer solutions, but because these things are a part of everyday life for people.
The game is extremely replayable, as once you beat it you’ll come back to this page and see that there were things you missed. You’ll have to play twice anyway if you want to see the difference between the endings for the two potential besties you can have. Gregg, the energetic, lovable fox, who likes to throw lightbulbs and various other objects at you, as long as you have a baseball bat, and Bea, the snarky, but caring crocodile, who can play amazing drum tracks… on her computer. There are plenty of other people you meet in town and within the friend group who will honestly remind you of people you know and probably care about.
This game has so many events, activities, and interesting characters that the story has a tough time trying to stand out, but it is an interesting tale. You’ll be given clues as to the overall story around the beginning but will spend about 3-4 hours in game hanging out with family, townies and friends before you and the game remembers that little detail.
The downside of the game is the cast if you cannot stand millennials. Otherwise it is the lack of a save system, as you will want to replay the game but have to start from the very beginning after beating the game each time.
While Night in the Woods is single player, it is also fun to have friends go through the experience with you, both to bounce theories about the plot with each other and to be able to quote memorable moments with each other later. Playing Night in the Woods feels like hanging out with friends or just spending a lazy weekend hanging out in town, until the main plot arrives. Overall it is an enjoyable experience and I recommend it to anyone interested in story or character driven narratives. The first playthrough I took close to ten hours, but my second playthrough took 15 hours once I saw how much I had missed. Take your time with this game and enjoy your time in Possum Springs. This is a game where you’re going to want to make it last.
TLDR: Cool game, fun and replayable! Gregg Rules! OK!

There are a lot of really cool characters, who seem very human in their mannerisms. Third, the art style. The game is as beautiful visually as it is auditorially. There are no glitches I've found, and the images look great even at full resolution. The dream sequences deserve a special note here, as they are particularly mesmerizing to look at.
However, there are a few minor pitfalls in the game I think should be adressed.
One, there's the issue that the character's facial expressions are usually pretty lacking. In some extreme cases they change, but otherwise the faces of the characters don't change at all. Mae could be looking in another direction during a conversation, and a character could be making 'crying' noises, but show nothing on their face.
Two, there's Mae's personality. While she does get some explanation of why she's sometimes a total ***, she's still quite the fire-starter. Throughout almost every interaction you have with Bea, for instance, she puts her foot in her mouth in a spectacular way and pisses Bea off. She has a tendency to say the wrong thing at the wrong time, and that combined with a distinct lack of redeemable qualities until the end makes her seem kind of sociopathic, and kind of distant. Don't get me wrong, Mae's got really good reasons for being a total♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to everyone she meets, but it does get old kinda fast.
Third, please let some bits be replayable once you've gotten through them. Like the band minigame. I sucked at that, and I really don't want to have to play through the game again just to get better.
That's pretty much it.
All in all, buy the game. You won't regret it.

I guess the developer was on a kick regarding energy-themes in their games because the game title has absolutely nothing to do with the game play, even remotely.  The only viable tie-in is the aesthetic when you get a line to light up, as it looks like some energy is flowing, but that's pretty weak.  As for the game play itself, it's basically just a redesign on those arithmetic worksheets you sometimes got for extra credit back in elementary school.  You'd get a series of blank squares with numbers lined up and had to put in the correct math symbol to make the equation work.  For example: 7 _ 3 _ 4 = 17 would translate into 7X3-4=17
Quite similarly, in the game you have all of the numbers placed throughout the board with the total you need to reach at the end of each column or row.  All of them work on the basis of addition, you just have to switch numbers around until every single total works out correctly.  Clicking on one box will allow you to swap it with any other number on the board and you need to figure out what set-up makes all of the rows and columns work out.  One aspect that will make this annoying for people who just want to grind achievements quickly is how levels are slightly random.  The basic set-up will always be the same, but if you exit and come back to the same level, the numbers will be entirely different.  I don't know for sure if there is a certain pattern where you can always switch the same boxes the same way and it'll always generate the right answer or if it's all entirely random.  Unless it is that simple in design though you will have to legitimately play each stage on your own.
With such a straightforward design you would expect there to be several stages, but in total there were only 20.  My play time does demonstrate the honestly surprising difficulty in solving the puzzles, yet I genuinely don't think this is enough content for a game like this.  Straightforward, simple puzzles need a good base to feel like it's a full game and this simply falls short.  I would also mention an annoyance of mine was how long you'd have to wait for the stage select to load up, as each single level select button would slowly roll onto the screen instead of all of them spontaneously showing up quickly.
So, overall, I found the game play alright if you're someone like me who enjoys a simple math puzzle to kill some time.  However, with some minor development issues and such scant content, I can't say I recommend buying this game, especially since it's not really all that original or novel an idea and they did so little with the energy theme.

The gameplay is to come to mathematical equilibrium between connected rows and columns. Each end of the row and column has a number that you must equal from the direction it is facing.
This will take some seriously number crunching and note taking in the later levels. Too many movable parts, can’t rely on luck. Each level is randomly generated, no use for walkthrough or a guide.
The Music is probably the best part. The tracks are varied and they don’t loop on a level. You never get irritated hearing the same track. It can distract you when you are trying to think. You can toggle it off, though.
2.99 is a fair price for what the game offers, but recommend getting on a sale or bundle.

I stopped playing PoE after a rather major bug removed companions from my roster and duplicated others, and just generally prevented me from being able to change my party as I saw fit, something that was game-breaking for me. Worse yet was at the time when I looked for solutions, the only thing that helped was buying the 30€ DLC...
Recently, which was about a year after my predicament, I noticed a big update to the game, and figured that this would've fixed the bug so I took a gamble and restarted PoE from the beginning. FYI, it did fix it.
I finished the main game (no DLCs) in about 40h, which I guess is normal for a story focused RPG (though as a completionist I'm used to do playthroughs of 80h+).
The setting has a lot of interesting concepts which could've been more explored and expanded upon, but the story addresses them only superficially, and in typical Obsidian fashion, the ending seems a little rushed and anticlimatic.
I hoped that the companions would've been more relatable, interesting, and dynamic in their relationship with the main character and each other; I really wanted to love them, if not all then most of them, but unfortunately to me, Obsidian didn't live up to its reputation in this regard.
The combat, inventory and crafting are ok. I figure in the higher difficulties they require more managing and thus might be more interesting gameplay elements.
Dialogue is generally good and with a good variety of choices.
The environments are gorgeous, though speed mode and movement speed enhancers are kind of a must.
I definitely understand that where this game lacks, it's probably because it was necessary to create the setting first, and that takes a lot of work and time, and it took precedence to the plot and characters proper. Perhaps if the writers were solely focused on writing the story, that it would've been more polished. Perhaps that's why I hear only good things about the White March DLC. Perhaps the sequel will deliver it better.
But given the publisher's (Paradox) pricing politics (after 2 years it's still the same price point?? the DLC costs more than half the game?? bumping up the price before the Steam summer sale so that it seems the game has a bigger discount than in reality??), I'm not sure if a "perhaps" is worth it.

But unfortunately, I felt that the combat is incredibly bad. If you have several melee partymembers, don't think you can ever cast an aoe spell, since they will hit your partymembers too.
If you want to cast your spells or skills properly you have to pause every time you finish the previous action. Casting or setting skills every single second for every partymember isn't really fun either. On top of that, the fights are so visually cluttered that there's absolutely no way to tell what's going on exactly.
You can set your partymembers to AI combat, but that isn't all that great either. Sometimes they just don't do anything. And with the fact that some skills can only be cast once per rest (and your rests are pretty limited) AI combat just isn't viable for proper combat.
I also think there are too many mechanics. There are too many status effects and afflictions someone can have. There are too many abilities, too many stats, too many talents, and skills feel useless.
I'm a huge sucker for complex and difficult games, but this feels like it's complex to make it complex, not to make an interesting game.
Even on story mode I found the combat and mechanics too bad to recommend this game.

Synopsis:
My thoughts regarding Condition Zero are pretty much Identical to the original CS 1.6. This is basically due to both games sharing the same engine, with Condition Zero being different only in the texturing and meshing department. With CS 1.6 showing its age, Condition Zero might be a worth a squirt if your feeling nostalgic.
Basically once the game Is bought you have to two installation options, Counter Strike Condition Zero and Counter Strike Condition Zero: Deleted Scenes.
This is essentially the CS 1.6 variant of the game which allows for traditional CS 1.6 style online gameplay and a somewhat enjoyable mini campaign which spans across most of the original maps, where objectives are the same as multiplayer however you can build a team for each map with bots of varying skills with more powerful bots costing more resource which you will unlock as you complete the maps. This single player should be avoided since it offers no real value and you are much better off playing on servers with real players.
This installation covers the actual single player campaign for Condition Zero. Each theater consists of you playing as a different counter terrorist unit:
GIGN, GSG-9, SEAL Team 6, SAS and Spetsnaz
You in turn fight againest a variety of different terrorist factions:
Arctic Avengers, Elite Crew, Guerilla Warfare, Phoenix Connexion and Midwest Militia.
I rather enjoyed the single player campaign since it deployed a large variety of maps and global locations ranging from fetid jungles to war ravaged cities. Most missions have a pre deployment briefing but these just offer simple intel and not much else. Most missions range from hostage rescue, bomb disarmament to assassinations. In most respects the campaign is somewhat reminiscent to Call of Duty MW which often puts you in the boots of a different soldier serving under a different army.
In conclusion CS CZ is worth your time if you are a hardcore C.S 1.6 fan like myself. It is pretty much HD 1.6 with a enjoyable single player campaign.
Final Score: 85/100

First of all, it IS a great game. Really. You will enjoy it, find fewer bugs than most Early Access games but it has been out for so long with so little updates it's a shame. Your money is better elsewhere and this game doesn't deserve to be played in the state it is today.
This used to be a negative review talking about how some early access will never get updates or be released. While that seems to be something common it IS NOT the case with Stranded Deep. In my view, the devs were "stranded" after the re-write but that was a mistake: they are as active as ever and even better, they are listening to the community’s concerns!
ABOUT THE GAME: Does the deep sea gives you the creeps? Wait until you find the sharks. Beautiful waves, nice environment and awesome immersion makes Stranded Deep an unique experience with a fairly big map and a lot of new stuff to do. The craft system is even better than before and you can feel the realistic way you need to improvise so things can work properly, just like you should in an stranded situation.
ABOUT UPDATES: The game was huge. One day the devs decided to re-write part of it (a good part of it) and it got a little buggy. The game is now heading toward new features (you can check them in the game's page and forums) and that makes this one of the few "survival" early-access that are worthy of your attention.
CONCLUSION: This game deserves your money and you deserve the experience. Have patience as the game is developed and know the devs have their mind in the right place.

Unbelievably tedious and boring.
I have to admit, the atmosphere of this game is spot on. It does a good job of making you feel like you're under pressure and like every choice matters.
Unfortunately, that wears off after your first attempt at a level.
In Gods Will Be Watching, you're put into all kinds of bad situations, such as a hostage situation where you'll have to control all of the hostages and hack into a system to steal information while keeping the authorities at bay. You get all kinds of moral dilemmas, like your crewmembers breaking down mid-mission, forcing you to try and stabilize them emotionally, to hostages becoming panicked and making a suicidal dash for the door.
The only problem is the game's difficulty and repetitiveness. The game prides itself on being unforgivable and difficult, but that becomes the biggest flaw. Every time you fail, you'll have to start over from the very beginning, even if that reverts 10 minutes of progress. Every single time you die, you'll be forced to play the same part again, which will take another 5 or 10 minutes.
You've already gone through this situation before, though. The emotion and tension has worn off, so now it's just you clicking buttons and hoping that the game looks favorably upon you. And if you press the wrong button? Why, say goodbye to the last 10 minutes of progress you made. A hostage is freaking out while the authorities are getting closer? Well, there's no split-second moral decisions to be made now. You already know exactly what buttons to press in order to solve this dilemma, and any emotion or atmosphere the game tries to immerse you with is gone, because you know that you'll be going through this exact same situation again in about 10 minutes, after the RNG decides that you've ♥♥♥♥ed up.
Seriously, this game has an interesting atmosphere and story already, but I couldn't be bothered to finish it. Even on the easiest goddamn difficulty, it's just so mind-numbingly boring. I'd like to experience the story, but I'm hardly gonna pay attention to it when I'm bored out of my mind. It's essentially a meter-management simulator with a good story thrown around it. It's like a conversation with another character in a game. You speak with them and decide what you want to say, but if you say the wrong thing, you're forced back to the beginning. After that, you're just going through the same conversation you've already heard. You already know what to say up until the point when you ♥♥♥♥ed up, so now you're just waiting for the dialogue to finish so you can try again.
In summary: Gameplay is solid enough, atmosphere is pretty good. Lack of saves and extreme difficulty lead to extremely tedious repetitiveness, which makes the game pretty much unbearable for me.
I wanted to like this game, but no. Definitely not recommended.

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is an open world action-role playing video game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. You take control of a human protagonist named Talion who bonds with an ancient elven lord, Celebrimbor.
Having grown up reading Lord of the Rings, The Hobbit, The Silmarillion, as well as many other little side books from Tolkien and his son, this game was a dream come true for me from the get go. For those who aren't very knowledgable in LOTR lore, I strongly recommend reading at least the wiki on LOTR history (Silmarillion, etc) if you like Middle-Earth and want to expand it's story. It truly helps the immersion and puts you in a state of fan-girlness.
Movement is really well done. Sneaking over buildings, climbing and hanging on the side of walls Assasins Creed style, everything feels great, smooth and just works.
Anyways onto gameplay. Combat is really well done and comparable to the Batman series, it looks amazing and plays great. The combat in general is quite easy (making the game easier as well) but is just really satisfying. You will have 3 options for combat, either go in with your sword and slice through orcs and finish them with some execution finishing moves, stealth kill them through sneaking or keep your distance and snipe them with your bow.
There's been a lot of controversy about people claiming it's the next-gen combat system and that it's an advanced combat system, it's not. Don't be fooled. Sure it's very enjoyable and satisfying on how the combat system works, but it's very flawed. There's very little skill involved when you get the hang of combat. Spam attack until you see the right click button pop up regardless of swing time, spamming space bar makes you essentially invulnerable, hitting a certain number of hit streaks lets you insta-brand (recruit) or execute enemies again regardless of swing time, and you have a time slow ranged attack.
Don't get me wrong, I loved the combat, it's just not what everyone claims it to be. And yes, a lot of the combat I'm elaborating on is a little more end game based, but you can also do much of what I claimed at any point in the game.
For video on exactly what I mean, here's Destiny's take on Middle-Earth combat.
Pros:
+ Enviroment is well done. Looks great, Sounds great.
+ Exceptionally optimized. Don't be fearful of the requirements. I came across no bugs whatsoever.
+ Combat is satisfying, I had a blast destroying Orcs in so many ways
+ Story is great, typical good story-telling to be expected from Monolith and WB
+ Movement is really smooth and enjoyable to traverse Mordor
Cons:
- Combat is not what some people hype it up to be. Enjoyable, yes. Next-gen, no.
- Story can be finished quickly unless you take your time, I personally finished almost 100% at 24 hours of gameplay
- Last boss was a QTE
- Some forgettable supporting characters. Lack of characters as well tbh, and lack of in-depth details into what little characters are in the game
- Respawning of enemies in areas cleared prior happen almost immediately and is an immersion killer
- Game map (there are two sections, one opens later in the game) is small
- A bit too easy. Lack of a choice of skill level hurts replayability
TL;DR:
8/10
If Assassin's Creed, The Witcher, and Batman Arkham series had a 3 way baby in Mordor this would be it. Story is short but great, combat is enjoyable but a little too easy, movement is smooth, killing Orcs in many ways is super enjoyable. Gameplay was completed near 100% in 24 hours. If you're looking to get the game's sequel, Shadow of War, I strongly recommend  you play this first. Not the best game, but definite must buy if you're a fan of Tolkien's Middle-Earth.

A prime example of an interesting concept being squandered by rather bad execution. A game based around the Grimm fairy tales? I'm game, sign me up please. Haha, if only it were any good... There are 23 episodes which essentially boil down to 23 times the game does the same thing, over and over again. Plot: Take a fairy tale (not necessarily from the Grimm fairy tales too! ). Add tons of gore and violence. Make the language fouler. Make all the colors dark and bland. Poof, there's every single episode in the game. Or well, maybe not. I only played through 18 of them before I just got entirely sick of wasting time on this. Part of that is that when I tried to play episode 19, it crashed! Multiple times! So presumably it just flat-out doesn't work. I didn't even try any of them beyond that, which I shold probably be glad for.
So I've talked about how the premise was wasted with a lack of creativity beyond what a 12-year old would come up with. What about the gameplay? Well, each episode is 6 to 9 "levels" where you spend your time "darkening" the environment. This involves basically just... running around. Levels are either painfully easy and inevitably repetitive, or filled with the bad kind of 3D platforming I thought we agreed to get rid of 10-15 years ago.Walking on really thin platforms is a common theme. Some of the environments can get mildly creative but a lot of them feel like repeated scenes more often than not.
It just boils down to not being a very interesting game, with occasional bad level design. Maybe one day there will be a good game based around the Grimm fairy tails but this is not that game, what a shame.

There's two kinds of people who've played Pillars: one who wants to sing praises from the mountain tops, and one who shrugs and says it was too dry. Looks gorgeous, sounds nice, performance is shockingly bad still, and the DLC adds roughly 20 hours of the toughest combat, but has a middling story compared to vanilla.

Excellent game, running it with a 1080 Ti and every setting is maxed out, everything is so goddamn gorgeous. With a discord server full of friends this game is intense with shootouts, especially at night. Recently had a 30-45 minute standoff at the Airfield against another team, with emotions high and everyone tense. We lost the shootout but it was the most fun I've had in a game in what feels like years.
Here comes the criticism-
The progression is incredibly slow, and there's really not a huge threat of mutants in the game once you've got a melee weapon (hunter's knife is ideal) or a rifle/shotgun and some decent aim (one hit kill on headshots aside from brutes). Not only this, but looting slain mutants tends to be fruitless, and thus is just a waste of precious/rare ammo. Haven't ran into any violent wildlife (wolves) yet, so I can't comment on that, but every time I hear it I get nervous. Haven't really been able to progress much because of people who rather shoot-on-kill (and cheaters) than group up and progress together, but with a team of people it's so much better. Most of the bases in the game look awfully rag-tag so I'm going to guess the building process isn't very intuitive. Loot (especially useful loot) is hard to come by, and the storage management system is pretty lacking but you get used to it.
Here are some of my MAJOR gripes with the game
- Teaming system is NON EXISTANT, there's no way to accurately identify your allies. ESPECIALLY AT NIGHT.
- Cheating even on official servers isn't uncommon. People go invisible and melee you to death for fun. Infuriating.
- To add on to the above point, there isn't a proper way to identify nearby players, so you can't even report anybody...
- Fall damage is absolutely ridiculous. Jump 4 feet at full HP, immediately dead. Jump off a 25-30 ft cliff? Live with half of my health. Wtf? With how realistic the game tries to be, you actually think people die falling 4 ft off of a shed?
- Random spawn almost always places you near Brightmoor or Pinecrest, which means you spawn near the most densely populated areas, leaving you mostly incapable of looting the nearby areas for even food, meaning you blindly run north  to Haywood or other high-loot areas only to be picked off randomly and have to find your way back again. Can the game not spawn you only south? What was the thought process on this?
Overall, with friends, 8 or 9/10. Without friends, or just one friend, hard pass. This is definitely not the game for a solo player or just two people unless you purely like running around landscapes/purely playing for PvP shootouts and player hunting. Over time and with more experience I'll come back and review my rating to see if there's anything to remove or add.

It may not seem that i've played this game alot but, it's probably the best zombie survival game out there. Sure DayZ is pretty high up with its multiplayer fun but, if i had to choose, i'd buy State of Decay. Here's a list of the pros:
-Open World with a huge map and lots of places to explore.
-Runs fast on a lot of computers but, don't try to use your Dell laptop or anything, it's not THAT fast.
-The story is a great adventure all the way through.
-Scavenging makes it so you don't have to level up to get good stuff.
-Game is not glitchy so far from what i've seen. That's one of my strict things, if a game has glitches that change your gameplay, i will not play it.
And then there are cons:
-Game is really exciting at the start but as you progress, it gets a small bit repetitive.
-When your character dies, there is no getting them or their stuff back. But you have other people to play as.
-There is DLC but, at least they made their DLC fun. :P
So that's all i have to say. If you're looking for an open world zombie game that isn't DayZ, this is the right choice.

When does a game blur the lines between Kawaii Princess and hardcore simulation?  When you fire up this game, of course. Take care, it's harder to get her to the throne than you think.  While I would have liked some random elements in the game, otherwise you feel like you are on rails until you get to a choice that may or may not put you on a different path.

Probably the most accurate monarchy simulator ever made. The gameplay is extremely simple- you schedule Princess Elodie's classes in order to grind various stats in order to advance through a flow chart of possible events, with the goal of making it to the end alive. What makes the game really shine though is its extremely vast depth- there are loads of different events that can be triggered, and several possible ways to get through them, and how you get through those events can often affect other events later down the road. Replayability is impressive- it's highly unlikely for two playthroughs to ever be the same. The game is fiendishly difficult until you've played through it enough to know which pitfalls are coming and what skills you can use to avoid them, and pretty much every strategy you can think of is viable. The artwork is also very cute, the worldbuilding is pretty extensive, and the writing can get pretty clever. Also, Elodie will die. A lot. It's inevitable. But yeah, this game is really fun, surprisingly deep for what it is, and Elodie's subjects yelling "LONG LIVE THE QUEEN! LONG LIVE THE QUEEN! LONG LIVE THE QUEEN!" when you win is always satisfying, no matter how many times you've beaten it.
