Summary:
Casual Dead Space, but with bullet time instead of horror.
The Good:
- No bugs (at least, not for me). These devs know what they are doing from a programming standpoint.
- Nice graphics.
- Weapon upgrades are fun.
- Secrets to find in the game (Orbs, tablets, money) keep the player exploring - very Metroid, nice touch.
- Short. Doesn't outstay it's welcome (the reason I stopped playing Dead Island, it just draaaaaaagggged...)
- WAGNER. IT'S PARTY TIME!
- Gameplay. Those grenade zombies made me think about room positioning and you can use them against the other zombies if you are smart about it - definitely a bit of depth that kept me interested there. Bullet time isn't a get out of jail free card but rather an aid to aiming, which is all it should be.
The Bad:
- It looks like Dead Space, but it doesn't feel like it. No horror, no claustrophobia, no near-death experiences. This is only "bad" if that's what the developers were going for, but it's clear that the aesthetic is definitely "heavily inspired by" that game.
- More Plot? It plays like a casual zombie shooter and so lacks long term engagement, but then there's WAGNER and the lore tablets dotted around the place. I feel like the developer could have done a little more with the plot and made it more interesting. Compare it to, say, Dead Space 1 with the whole Marker thing and the gradual revelation of the source of the zombies, and there you have much better engagement
I think £3.99 is a fair price considering the enjoyment I got from it. Definitely worth it if it's on sale, you won't be dissapointed.

Part crossword, sudoku and deduction the puzzles in this game ramp up very quickly creating a jagged learning curve that may easily frustrated players.  Visuals are rather lackluster but the sound track helps make up for that small flaw.

Energy Balance takes a fine math puzzle and wraps it in some of the most pathetic graphics and in-game dialog ever created.  It's as if the designers actually sat in a room and said, "How can we make this even dumber?  Cool, let's do that!"  In addition, it has a really limited set of puzzles, and doesn't take very long to complete.  A rather disappointing affair.

I am a beginner in SF4 but have quite a few hours of SF2HDR under my belt. So far the things that make this game are the matchmaking, training modes and that there are quite a lot of people playing online.
Any online competitive game that has a decent ranking matchmaking system that is customisable for skill and ping is immediately going to get people playing. And SF4 does it very well. The only complaint I have is that there isn't more of an emphasis on a skill-per-character rank. It is already implemented in SF4, but it seems to rank mostly on the global points rather than the points for a particular character. Over all though, this is nearly as good as Star Craft 2. And in someways, actually better.
Being able to be waiting for an online game while being in the single player game is awesome too!
The downsides are mostly related to my gameplay tastes. I love games that are easy to play and hard to master. SF2HDR is pretty good for this. Unfortunately, SF4 brings back an execution barrier to entry which I don't enjoy. Gods WIll Be Watching opens with a bang. You select your difficulty, get a brief cutscene that raises more questions than it answers, and then the game hands you a gun and several hostages while the SWAT team beats down your door, leaving you only with the goal of surviving this nightmare.
And of course, you won't survive. You'll die horribly the first few times arount, the structure of the game practically requires it. Each level is a new time and resource management puzzle where the rules are complex and unforgiving, but fascinating to learn. Trial and error is sometimes a requirement, and a few levels pull curveballs, but so long as you think your way through things, you'll be able to make your way through it, as the solutions are more based in logic than chance. I've seen a few complaints about the RNG, but there are difficulty levels that minimize the RNG's impact, so it's all up to choice, and even then, there's only one instance I can think of in the whole game where it's truly up to chance.
For all the talk of dificulty, it's certainly possible to beat a level on your first try, as the framework is there (I've done it myself, whether through luck or skill, hell if I know), but even then, it's always an uphill battle, and you may have to take a very dark path in order to make ends meet. This is a game all about rationalizing your decisions, where you can betray your friends and murder innocents and in the end, the only ones who pass judgement are yourself and the gods.
This being said, the writing is phenominal. Towards the end, it starts to unravel a little, but the additional epilogue that has since been added re-ravels it quite well into a compelling, cohesive story. It should have been included in the original release, yes, but it's here now, so if you're reading this review, you're safe.
The only complaints I can truly levy against this game are that of the interface and the setback times. Several levels require managing resources and status levels, and provide you the means to see the exact values, but are a hassle to view. By the time I'm halfway through a level, I'm not going to be wasting every turn sifting through dialogue trees to get to the display window, and I shouldn't have to, as they're small displays that could have just stayed up in the corner of the screen. It's admittedly just a few clicks, but some of these levels get long, and a repetitive menu journey for a few numbers isn't fun for anyone. As well, if you die in a late stage, it can be a time consuming effort retracing your steps. There are only a few levels that this applies to, as most of them are simply balancing acts, but there are a few (chapters 2 and 5 in particular) where a lot of time is spent on things, and if you've been driven to dire circumstances, a single gamble can ruin everything and kick you back to the start.
These complaints aside though, I'd recommend everyone play this game. It's fun, beautiful, full of emotion, and not terribly demanding of your time or your wallet. You may learn some unfortunate truths about the things you'd be willing to do to achieve your goals, but hey, at least you didn't eat your friends in real life.

The world is dying, and all its great heroes are gone. Day after lightless day this place remains the same. There is agony here. We are cursed with immortality in a land that wants us dead, and we must suffer though it again and again, each time with some small piece of us stripped away. Between each breath the choice to either fight or fade is remade. Yet time is convoluted, and though we suffer alone, we suffer alone together. Lordran is home to all manner of creatures; many were human beings, but they lost the will to resist the dark – a legion of nameless hollows who surrendered their souls to the challenges now left to you. Welcome to Dark Souls.
This is the thinking person’s Action Role Playing Game. Tutorials are minimal, there is no world map, there are no quest markers, there is no pause button, and every decision is permanent on a single self-updating save file. Progress is made by resting at bonfires serving as checkpoints where players level their character, replenish spells and healing items, and sort their equipment. Resting at a bonfire revives all enemies, and dying sends you back to the last bonfire you rested at. Players level their character and purchase and upgrade items with souls earned by killing enemies. The bigger and baddy, the better the payoff. Die, and you lose them all but have one chance to reclaim them: reach the bloodstain your corpse left behind. Die again, and they’re lost permanently. But Dark Souls obeys its own rules; when you die, the fault is your own. For every great feat is a great reward and for every feckless blunder is a grueling punishment. However, death is not a punishment meant to frustrate or dishearten – it’s the game’s way of telling you to learn from your mistakes or try something new.
Dark Souls is also a game of choice. There are hundreds of weapons, armors, sorceries, pyromancies, miracles, consumables, and other items for you to mix and match to suit your play-style. Will you be a hammer, a razor, or a Swiss army knife? Will you expend resources to summon a stranger’s aid at the risk of falling prey to an invader, or will you brave the dark alone? Will you heed the ambiguous note left by a fellow player or trust your own judgment? Will you cross new thresholds and risk losing the souls you’ve earned, or rest at a bonfire to level up and restock healing items? Tact, decisiveness, creativity, forethought, versatility, risk and curiosity are rewarded in Dark Souls; if you are lacking in these virtues, the game will teach them to you whether you’d like it or not. Of course with every death the question is raised again: will you adapt to overcome the trials you face, or will you give up like the nameless hollows before you?
Along side its mechanics is a multi-layered narrative told with such subtlety and elegance that the unobservant and the disinterested can play to the end without ever knowing there is any narrative at all. They may never even realize the part they play in Lordran’s story. Lordran is more than a setting, however – it is a character in its own right. Environmental detail is as much of a storytelling tool as character dialog and item descriptions. There are no frivolous details, no insignificant one-dimensional characters, even the bosses have their place in the narrative. It’s up to you to uncover Lordran’s sad history, and to learn that of the characters you come by – the game itself never forces this on you. There is a sizable online community dedicated to deciphering Dark Souls’ lore, but there are gaps in the story – like pages missing from the annals of history. Some questions simply have no definitive answers.
Dark Souls creator and director Hidetaka Miyazaki has cultivated both one of the most respected games and one of the most dedicated player bases in the medium’s history. This is a game that hearkens back to famous titles like the original Super Mario and The Legend of Zelda while pushing games forward as a whole by way of level design, game mechanics and storytelling. Dark Souls holds a great many secrets and will make no effort to either show them to you or to get you to the end credits. A game completed, like a soul retained, is earned – and all the better for it.

Pros:
- The building character stats is interesting
- Unique random personalities is an entertaining idea
- Looting and missions are engaging
- Dispatching zombies has a very visceral quality to it that works well for the game.
- It's addicting.  I had fun.
Cons:
- Only a few combat skills can be upgraded on a character, everything else is at the mercy of RNG.
- Babysitting people who have temper tantrums constantly
- The story primarily gets told in random scraps if you happen to be lucky enough to be in the right place at the right time.
- As a result, the storyline army captain in particular seems almost bi-polar about "Today I neither like nor trust you" "Today I'm happy to be working with you and you're such a nice guy for saving those people" "Today I'm going to shoot at civilians for the crime of being in the area" "Today I'm willing to sacrifice my safety and my men to help people"  What... dafuq?
- Mission NPCs are virtually unkillable, but allies will perma-die depressingly easily
- Weapons degrade and cannot be repaired.  Don't get attached to anything (or anyone)

A true step up from the previous games in the FPS genre, Long Live the Queen excels over its competitors with immersive gun customization, endearing characters, and fun online multiplayer. LLtQ's action is like no game before it, combining Assassin's Creed-esque parkour physics with a Borderlands-esque level-up system. This is basically a choose your own adventure with a basic skills system attached to it. The concept is deceivingly simply, but the game itself is devilishly complicated. What impressed me the most is that even you quite frequently have to replay the same parts over and over (you can save games, but I found that quite often I would have to replay from the beginning in order to correct some minor error I had made), the game doesn't really become boring. The creative ways that they have you repeatedly die keeps it fun and interesting rather than (overly) frustrating.
I found that the biggest challenge I had with this game was letting the completionist in me go. I spent the first couple of hours constantly restarting the game as I watched skill check failures scroll across the screen. Letting go of the need to pass all of those checks, and focus only on what was important to completing the story forced me to step outside my normal gaming mentality.
Long Live The Queen manages to create a sense of time pressure despite being a turn based game. In that regard, it reminded me of
ability make you feel that every decision is critically important because you don't have the time to fix a mistake.
A significant part of the sense of pressure is the quality of the writing. Despite what could have been childish and overly campy, the story is surprisingly complex and I found myself connecting to this little anime princess and caring what happened to her.
Also like FTL, I find that I wish there was a free play mode with this game that allowed you to continue the story, building skills and encountering more random events after the initial story line.  I'd even happily take another well scripted year in the life of our new Queen as she deals with her kingdom.
Over all, this game is well worth the price if you are looking for a break from your usual gaming experience.

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is one of the more intriguing installments of Counter-Strike (Not including CS Neo, CS     Online, and CS Zexon Zombies) Its basically just a single player campaign for Counter-Strike and it shows this in two different fashtions. First there's Condition Zero where you go through Counter-Strikes multiplayer maps pairing up with a group of bots against other bots. The bots AI aren't the worst as they can be useful as depending on there cooperative abilitys, they'll alarm about any incoming enemys. But the bots aren't perfect like how enemie bots will take a couple of seconds that your right in front of them and that they should shoot. Each mission includes its own set of missions that are required to beat before completing the mission like kill a certain number of enemies, rescue a hostage, kill a certain number of enemies with a shotgun, and so on. This also includes multiplayer with the new maps and textures with it, but nowadays its rare to find at least two servers with a decent number of players. However getting the game on steam will give you the original Counter-Strike so its not a huge loss.
Then there's Deleted scenes, which was originally Ritual Entertainments idea for Condition Zero. The 18 missions are very Half-Life based with Counter-Strike theming and and assets. Each mission has you going through hoards of terrerosts that act like the military from Half-Life, and complete your objective to complete. The engine has been given some major improvements like enimies having special knockback deaths and high resolution textures. It does show some parts where the games not finished, but it's preety hard to notice. The voice acting can range from mildly cheesy, to chringeworthy with the rediculous accents. Overall, the difficulty can be preety challenging for newcomers, but pros of Counter-Strike shoulden't have much of a problem.
If you're a fan of booth Half-Life and Counter-Strike, then you should definatly check out Deleted scenes. And Condition Zero is also a great excuse to play Counter-Strike offline, but otherwise you should just play online with the newest installments.
Final Verdict:
Condition Zero: 7/10
Deleted Scenes: 8/10

While I really like number puzzles, they all have some sort of logical trick to them that you learn, and use to solve them.  You don't beat a Sudoku or a Kakuro with blind guessing, you have to eliminate the alternate possibilities until only one logical conclusion can be drawn...
This game doesn't do that.  At least, there's no logic underlying it that I've been able to find.  You really can't do anything but put together things that add up to possible answers, with no idea of whether you're screwing yourself over down the road. In short, it's blind guessing-and-checking until eventually you win, which defeats the purpose of a logic puzzle, since there's no real logic to it.
Reading the other reviews, even the people who were giving this positive reviews said it was easier to just keep quitting and retrying the puzzles (the numbers are rerandomized each time you start a level) until you get numbers that tend towards extremes to make the possible permutations easier.  Thanks to that, the game largely revolves around "brute force tactics" of just rerolling until you get good numbers, then trying every permutation until one fits.  It makes the game feel frustrating; Rather than like some puzzle you feel clever for solving, it's just something you beat your head against until the puzzle broke first.

Otherwise, basically sudoku crosswords.
Edit: I would like this a lot more if it had some more inbuilt tools for notes/number/combination tracking like Everyday Genius: SquareLogic (which I loved).

text:
I would describe this game as a cross between sudoku and crosswords. If this sounds interesting to you, read on!
_________________________
Energy Balance takes the standard minimalistic approach as other recent puzzle games do - light on explanations, yet simple in mechanics. The basic levels are also part of a vague story, which I found helped to break up the gameplay and give it a bit of a setting. Your spaceship is in trouble and you've got to fix all the components (engine, cloaking device, etc).
Levels consist of rows and columns of numbers - all linked together. The numbers in each row and column have to add up to the value specified at the end of the line of numbers. The object of the game is to select a number in a row (or column) that doesn't tally correctly, then switch it with a number that will help bring the tally closer to what is required. While this is all you can do, there is actually a lot to it at later levels, often requiring a great deal of thinking on your part.
Normal levels consist of single digits in the +8 to -8 range, but hardcore levels could possibly ask for rows/columns to tally +/-100. (Hardcore #2 was exceptionally hard for me, taking around 2 weeks before I finally got it.)
Various strategies can be employed to make number swaps work for you. A row that adds correctly, linked to a column that doesn't, may benefit from a swap of the number in the shared square with another from the row, effectively only altering the sum of numbers in the column... whereas a row out by -2 and another row out by +2 might better benefit from a direct swap from one to the other. You might find yourself more likely to be out by +1 though, and in only one spot, making swaps entirely useless.
Perhaps the most fun feature I discovered is that it is impossible to go online hoping to find a solution. Why? Because every time you quit without finishing a level, the numbers will randomise into a new puzzle when you go to try again.
So when you see someone has 100% achievements for this game, you can be pretty confident they earned it.
I digress though. I have mentioned normal and even hardcore levels, but while they are relatively few in number, they will take time to complete, and there are still further puzzles that are perhaps a bit less taxing and a bit more fun - a kind of reward for getting through hardcore. There is no story accompanying the hardcore or bonus puzzles, but they can still take time to complete, and fill out the game to make it worth its cost.
The accompanying puzzle music is surprisingly good - I found myself leaving it on more often than not. It has an outer-space feel to it that is enhanced by the background behind the puzzles - a moving, travelling-through-space backdrop that consists of stars passing you by, and a nebula in the distance. It is easy on the eye and doesn't detract from you trying to concentrate on your sums.
In short, it's a good game for anyone that likes puzzle games, the achievements aren't too difficult and it makes a nice break between larger games such as rpgs. It could benefit from additional puzzles, and perhaps an artwork gallery. 8/10

I wasn't sure I was a fan of survival games until I played Stranded Deep.
It's your basic survival game in a tropical island setting. Although it's still in development, Stranded Deep will manage to impress any survival fan. Not only does it has a fun crafting engine and an easy to use base-building system, but it also manages to balance performance and graphics in several ways. I can easily recommend this and say that's it's one of my new favorites.
- Beautiful tropical island setting, Impressive graphics
- Fun and easy Crafting, Rafting, and Base-Building system
- Explore shipwrecks. Find a shark. Kill a shark/Get killed by a shark
- Customizsble island-chain map when starting a new game
- Map Editor - Build your own island and place it in your game
- Devs are pretty OP. Game is fairly consistant with updates and devs are responsive in the forums.
- Really neat 'Spoiling' mechanic. Food goes bad. Raw food and salt water makes you sick.
- Bugs and glitches here and there. Nothing gamebreaking.
- Cannot break down base materials once they're built. You can destroy, but not recycle.
- Some of the keybindings and controls are a bit odd. Can be changed.
- I'm sick of coconuts
By the way, It is indeed a
. For those who know the film, you'll easily find a handful of things that Stranded Deep takes inspiration from.
These include:
- The intro
- You basicaly only eat coconuts, crabs, & fish
- Some of the tools look like the ones used in the film
- Some of the things you can build look fimiliar
- There's a 'DeadEx' package somewhere
- You can find Wilson "....WILSON!!!..oh thank god...Never again..."
Could use a bit more work, nothing much to complain about. This is just a beautiful game and rather peaceful to play...until you run into a shark that is.
Even if you aren't much of a survival fan, I would
recommend this game. I believe I bought this game on sale, but the price for this game is fair. This is one game where you definitely get your money's worth. Devs, keep up the incredible work!

Oh, my dark motherf***ing soul! 10/10
I've started my journey with Dark Souls 3. I tried playing it like 2-3 times and got killed almost instantly by the tutorial boss. For me it felt like an ordinary's game final boss in the first 10 mins of the game! But then I've watched some videos how people play it and understood that I was playing it completely wrong. Everything about this game is just pure game design genius! Gameplay is outstanding in it's depth. It's almost drowning you down in it's overlaying complexity and intuitivity (if you play on gamepad and use Dark Souls Wiki as your guide though). I mean it's pretty simple in many core parts - walking, jumping, fighting. But then you start playing it and understand that just dealing damage is not enough... Because the core of the game is an adventure with a loud Laugh/Love/Hate from developers. They are always around, laughing in the code) Constantly, and I mean constantly giving you fresh stuff to experience. Even though most of the time it means that you DIE again. It's hard and unforgiving but careless to some extent, as you can die as many times as you like and regain everything back (only until 2nd death though and not Humanity). Game is full of surprises.
And talking about surprises - for me Dark Souls is the best example of the perfect level design. At first you walk your way and levels feel pretty linear (meaning you won't be lost) but then you understand that these are not levels, but actually one big open-world area! It's all interconnected into one huge castle city and places around and most importantly under! It's the first game where they actually made me care to remember the game world visually rather than by the map or GTA style attached map markers. In here you will have to memorize certain areas, shortcuts and so on. But in the end you feel as you've actually experienced and studied this World. And what a feeling of relief to find a certain shortcut back Firelink Shrine or just a simple fire with a sword)
One thing to note though - I don't play games so often anymore, because most of the time I don't feel interested enough. Many titles are so easy today, that I always feel that gameplay is rather simple or easy that I almost play blind, or the World is way too limited, primitive, or the graphics, or something is often just not right for me. But with this game EVERY single point is just done right. If you are an experienced player looking for something more challenging and FUN - look no further DARK SOULS is the shiiiiiitt!
PS And by the way I don't want to say anything bad about Dark Souls 3 as for me it was the first Souls game and I loved it! But Dark Souls 1 is just better in every single way except for graphics. I play it and see that everything is similar to the third, but the map design is just classic, it's hard to overplay that.

This isn't difficult is what I thought, but that was only after I spent a lot of time practicing and grinding up my level. Dark Souls is a game that is notrious for being very difficult. It is, but you can learn to be good at the game.
This game is an Action Roleplaying Game, which takes you through a fascinating world filled with a lot of enemies. No enemy is a weakling. You can build characters that suit a variety of playstyles that take advantage of different aspects of the combat system whether it's the blocking, rolling, striking, or magic. Typically there are areas that you go through and bosses for all of them with their own unique fights. These fights are exciting, engaging, and excruciating if you're unprepared. I had a boss that took me countless tries to best. As you get further into the game you collect souls and level up. But, you'll never forget your two fast friends. The Estus and Bonfire.
The game has great atmosphere as evoked by the sound design, visuals, and your death-stained experience of the world. Designs of monsters, gears, and locales are all excellent. The setting is rather interesting, but it's show not tell more often than not. There are few friendly entities in this world, but there are some.
Gameplay revolves around combat and exploration. Combat has various components from blocking to evading. From melee to ranged attacks. Learning the system, then using strategy is essential. Once you get a hold of how to play, then it feels very satisfying. It is worth mentioning that you can cheese a lot of enemies if you can keep at a distance and shoot a whole lotta arrows.
There's a lot of content that lends itself to dozens of hours of play, but no text-rich narrative to follow.
Multiplayer comes in the form of many things like messages left behind, which deepen your experience of the game. You can also more directly interact by having people come to other games to help in boss battles or fighting each other. It is not a matchmaking system, but one that works somewhat indirectly in the game. So, it won't be the easiest thing if you want to play with friends in some way.
This game is best for those with patience and a love of high-stakes action. I highly suggest using a controller.
P.S. I haven't checked recently, but when I played the port to PC wasn't great by itself and needed an unofficial patch to make it work much better.

I'm going to try and make this review as unbiased as possible. That being said, Dark souls 1 is hands down my favorite game of all time. Between PC and Xbox I've logged well over 3,000 hours on this game.
I normally get bored with games ~the 200 hour mark. By then I've seen most of the content (in longer games) and have played it till I don't want to anymore. I keep coming back to dark souls though.
Now that I'm done being a fanboy, lets get down to the good stuff.
Dark souls is a game that teaches you, in a brutal way. People always try to sell it because of how 'Difficult' it is. A lot fail to mention how atmoshperic this game it. It makes you feel utterly alone. When you accomplish something, you actually feel like you've done something. You don't get that kind of feeling from games that hold your hand. You get rewarded for exploring - Hell, I still find things occasionally that I've never seen before.
When you start this game you'll likely die. A lot. Don't give up though - You've made it that far before and learned along the way. You're equipped with the knowlege and (hopefully) the skill to get your souls and humanity back. If you are really struggling, pop a humanity and hope to Gwyn there is a summon sign around (praise the sun).
The bosses on this game are memorable. I feel as if dark souls 2 and 3 lack this aspect. Yes, there are some good fights in those but can you truely name them all off the top of your head? I'm sure anyone that has finished dark souls 1 could repeat all the ones they fought along the way.
Now, here are the reasons I would say to buy...
-Amazing level design
-Great, challenging gameplay
-Doesn't hold your hand
-Promotes exploration
Any good review wouldn't be complete without some cons, however. Most of the cons I have are related to PvP. Some people play to win, thats just the way of the world. You can't avoid some of the generic builds (I'm looking at you Great Scythe)
-Some weapons have infinite stun locks in PvP (This can be avoided with a toggle parry/dodge but this can be hard to accomplish for some people)
-Backstabs (unlike in Dark souls 2 and 3) instantly lock you into the backstab animation.
(This one is not actually a 'game' issue but I would like to mention it)
-Parry spammers (easy to counter if you've played a while but can be annoying if learning PvP)
Overall, I highly recommend this game. If you have a friend to play with, you can easilly connect to others using the dark souls connection mod (DSCM for short). Would also recommend PvP watchdog as you can forcefully kick blantant hackers from your world (Note: This does not catch all hackers, just a majority of them)

8/10 - Infamous for its difficulty, Dark Souls is a satisfying medieval combat RPG that rewards tenacity, skill, and playing it smart.
+ Wide variety of weapons: Most of the weapons you find can be viable end-game if you upgrade them. There is little consensus in the community about what the "best" weapon is. Try them all out and find your own combat style. The way you battle various enemies will change based on your choice.
+ Story is told through world-building: You do not HAVE to talk to NPCs or read equipment descriptions, but they fill in so much of the Dark Souls universe that it is prone to draw you in to the background lore.
+ Did I mention satisfying combat?
- One of my few gripes about the game is the offensive sorcery spells. The melee combat in this game is so well perfected that most ranged combat feels rather bland in comparison. Just stick with melee, pyromancy, and support spells/miracles.
- Also, this is a game that is meant to be played with a controller. The mouse and keyboard controls stink and in-game GUI is only programed to show you the controller buttons. If you want to play with mouse and keyboard (I did), you will have to manually install some mods.
Finally, a quick tip for those interested: Play your first run with heavy armor and a good shield. Lock on to enemies and block their attacks while you learn their moves, see how they telegraph them, and develop a strategy on how to counter each move. Especially for bosses, learning how they operate before you attempt to kill them is essential for victory. Charging in blindly will most often just get you killed. After you have gotten a grip on the game, then shed that armor and become an untouchable acrobatic master!

GWBW is a game of many faces. On the surface it's a meter-management strategy game with many randomized factors in play. The story is a sci-fi thriller about leadership, sacrifice and rebellion (among other things).
Beneath the surface, there's a meta-story which constantly (and with subtlety) critiques itself and many other clichés in popular entertainment. If you have played Undertale, you might be more familiar with the idea of a meta-story: the player him/herself plays an important role in the game story (effectively breaking the 4th wall).
If you haven't played Undertale or don't have an understanding of meta-stories, then I would not recommend this game.
The gameplay is equally engaging as it is frustrating, but that is the whole point. The game mechanics serve more as a tool for narrative than for fun.
If you want a challenging and very narrative-driven game, then this is the game for you. This game tells many strong messages without even mentioning them, and that's what makes this game truly unique.
In my opinion it's an innovative masterpiece, pushing the boundaries of narrative-driven game design.

Ah, Nancy Drew...these games were my childhood. My younger brother and I would play these games over and over again when we were kids. I received two of them for my ninth birthday, and from then on, we were hooked on mystery solving! Our teamwork always made the gameplay shorter, but we always had so much fun together! When I told my brother that I had purchased another one, he was very excited and agreed to help me with this one. I'm currently a student at an all-women's college, and he's getting ready to go to college in September, so I figured it would be good to compare my school to the school in the game while teaching him some of the basics of college life. (Okay, this particular academy isn't really college, it's a boarding school, but still...)
Speaking of all female schools...there are some similarities between my college and the school in this game that are frightening. The most notable? "The Black Cat". At Agnes Scott College, there's a tradition called "Black Cat Week" in which the classes compete to show off school spirit. The junior class writes and performs a play; there's big dance; we decorate the campus grounds...in this game, however, the Black Cat is the alias the culprit goes by.
Anyway, how IS this game? Like most Nancy Drew games...it's great! There's an engaging story, lots of challenging puzzles...my brother and I were constantly guessing and second-guessing who the culprit was, and even when we thought we had it figured out, we were wrong!
There are a few notes that I took during gameplay: one of the NPCs, Rachel, seems to be unique in that when Nancy talks to her, she moves as Nancy speaks. The other NPCs remain motionless when Nancy delivers her lines during a conversation. I wonder why this is? Maybe the developers were testing out new animations for future games?
Overall, I'd have to give this game a solid A. It's got replay value (especially because of Steam Achievements!), a good story, challenging puzzles, and so much nostalgia if you grew up with the Nancy Drew games, like I did. Give it a go!

Whether, or not you believe in Deus-ex Machina; a superior force guiding you through life events in such ways that you question your own thoughts, not sure if they were your own; the way I ultimately got to purchasing Night in the Woods was out of pure serendipity. I personally have never heard of Infinite Fall, nor did I have a clue about NITW’s Kickstarter beforehand. Steam showed me this game on the day it got released (February 21, 2017), I saw the trailer (which oddly enough stirred up visions of Ralph Bakshi’s most notable works) and the Overwhelmingly Positive reception made something in me say “Shut up and take my money!” I am pleased to say…
Night in the Woods is not an action oriented game, even though it’s action packed. To call it a walking simulator would undermine all the other intricately placed mechanics in it that influence the pacing of the narrative. Perhaps the closest genre would be the adventure genre, however it works best when it mirrors the lives of a specific age range.
The music holds most of the immersion and aesthetic, along with the most shockingly honest dialogue I have ever had the pleasure of reading in a video game.
Alec Holowka’s music is haunting and melancholy, yet comforting. It gives the feeling of coming home to a place close to your heart, yet knowing that times are changing. Resistant to growing up, you cling to any memory of home you have left. “At the end of everything, hold onto anything.”
The maturity of this game comes from it’s story, showing peoples’ flaws, rather than telling us about them, however it’s characters hold back their true nature so adamantly, revealing it all when they have their backs to the wall. Yet all this drama works out because it reflects the player’s personal life through May, Gregg and Bea’s struggles of being young adults in a slowly dying town. By ten hours into Gregg’s storyline, (yes, I did the side quests as well) I broke down into tears, weeping like a baby and screaming like an animal (no pun intended) at 3am in my house. This game had the tenacity of giving me a reality check. And I fear I am not alone in this.
About the only weak part of the game is the supernatural Twin Peaks-esque mystery that is so sudden, thin, and anticlimactic, the only way to explain it’s existence is for advertising purposes since internal conflicts are much harder to sell to people in this day and age. Especially when it comes to video games.
A coming of age story works best when it talks directly to those of the same age as it’s protagonists, rather than expressing a point in someone’s life through imagery and vernacular that do nothing more than to show how out-of-touch the story is. Night in the Woods is a lesson in writing honest life stories in video game form, rather than focusing on external conflicts the way most games do.

is an interactive short story with Full Motion Video (FMV). It's short but worth playing through for its quirky laugh-out-loud humour alone.
A lot of people are suddenly behaving ferociously, attacking everyone who isn't afflicted on sight. You know, like in that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ M. Night Shyamalan movie,
. Or was it
? Never mind all that. You'd better check if your girlfriend is alright, hadn't you?
Gameplay consists of selecting dialogue options and coping with quick time events (QTE). I hate QTE but I'm an FMV afficionado so I had to try out
. It's safe to say the experience rekindled my hatred for QTE but nevertheless,
is definitely worth playing through at least once.
You can choose between four difficulty modes which determines the number of buttons you need to press simultaneously and how much time you get to press them. So it's up to you if you want to just experience the story or if you want agonizingly difficult QTE. On the hardest difficulty, you need to press up to three keys AND one of the mouse buttons at the same time within two seconds. That's physically impossible for us people who only have two hands instead of three. I'm sure it's a bit easier when you use a controller, as you can at least use both hands on one single peripheral but I for one didn't want to bother using a controller to play what's basically a visual novel.
The story is branching and some choices you make early in the game will affect later events and even the ending. It's a very short story so don't expect a lot of content. What you can expect is getting to see a lot of creativity that makes great use of an obviously low budget. The best part of
is its quirky, laugh-out-loud humour. I especially advise you to fail each and every QTE the first time, just to see what happens. Often you'll get to see funny stuff that way.
The acting is cheesy. That's the way it should be. Really, FMV traditionally requires cheesy acting because it just fits the medium perfectly, and even more so in the case of
because the whole game is a reference to cheesy B-movie horror.
The FMV is of top-notch quality. Man, if only the classic FMV games from earlier days could have supported movie-quality graphics like this…
If the youngsters among you want to have a quick impression of the FMV we had to look at in the old days, you can switch on '1994 Mode' from the game's menu. You'll immeditately see the photo on the main menu page converted to 1990s-style FMV graphics, and will most likely immediately switch back to 2017 mode.
The sound is sharp but some dialogue may still be lost on people whose native language is not English. They've got that covered: from the game's menu, you can enable subtitles in English, Spanish, Russian, Simplified Chinese or Italian. The game's menus are also available in these languages.
has 5 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
There are only 11 Steam Achievements but they are a varied bunch, and getting 100% completion is quite a challenge. All the achievements are missable. One achievement can only be unlocked if you bought the DLC. Several achievements require you to play through the game multiple times. The achievements granted for completing the game on the hardest difficutly settings, especially the one for not dying at all on the hardest difficulty mode, will prove extremely challenging to most players. As noted above, playing the game using a controller may be advisable if you're looking for 100% completion.

For those of us who have (mostly) fond memories of FMV games, Press X To Not Die will bring you an equal number of laughts and nostalgia. The game does not go far beyond the expectations of the genre, but what it does is done lovingly. This game is a labor of love, and shows in the amount of times I've replayed it.
There are plenty of areas they could improve though. The multi-button prompts are occassionally very hard to press and figure out, especially on a keyboard. For controllers, it only provides the Xbox style buttons, which was trouble for me and my Playstation style controlers (RIP Xbox 360 controller). The humor and acting is often cringy, and the game is WAY too dependent on pop culture and gaming references. The game is also very short, but this is an understandable, even welcome aspect.
Despite its flaws, this game is again, a labor of love. A bunch of friends filming scenes in their back yards, and piecing them together into an FMV game that is well aware of itself, and how these kinds of games can actually be fun.
If you ever enjoyed FMV games back in the day, you'll greatly enjoy this game. If you like humor games, or this sort of indie filming and gaming appeals, you will get a kick out of this game. Otherwise, it is probably not for you, but I still recommend you give it a try. If only so the developers can do more.

One of the most humbling experiences ever.
This game is one of those games that you have to commit to.  You can't just play it for a little while and come back to it later.  Once you start, you have to keep going.  I recently just got done with my first playthrough and wanted to share my thoughts on the game.  Were there more good moments than bad?  Absolutely yes.  But were there some noticable flaws in the game?  Also absolutely yes.  Let's get to it.
Let's start off with the bad:
-The PC port is terrible.  The textures are so low res and the game's capped at 30 FPS.  This issue is so big that it took a modder to fix it because FromSoft wouldn't.
-Sometimes the level design is a little wonky.  Best example of this is Demon Ruins/Lost Izalith.
-Difficulty spikes.  I mean I get it the game's supposed to be hard, but you'd think that it would at least curve evenly.
-Some of the boss designs are pretty bad.  Thankfully none of them are horrible with one exception. (if you've played the game you know which one)
-Armor stats don't even matter.
Now for the good:
+Level design is (mostly) top notch with Anor Londo, Undead Burg, and the final area being great examples.
+Some of the best bosses I've ever faced
+(Mostly) fair challenge
+Great, mostly implicit story
+Amazing soundtrack
+Praising the sun
+Everything else that isn't a negative (that isn't even sarcasm)
Please at the very least try this game.  It isn't for everyone that's for certain, but for those who love games like this, this is one of the best experiences you could ever spend money on.

American Mcgee's Grimm, an episodic series originally released for Gametap and made by American Mcgee an Spicy Hoarse, known for the Alice games and constantly cancelling Mcgee's Oz Projects. You play as the evil dwarf named Grimm, and his mission is to change cute and happy fairy tales into dark and twisted stories. The gameplay is very simple, running, jumping and occasionally butt stomping. The goal is to turn everything around you into a dark wasteland in order to progress with altering tales such as Little Red Riding Hood, A Christmas Carol, Pinnochio, Cinderella, Jack and the Banstalk, and many other tales. Each episode opens up with a cutscene to showcase the stories Light Theater with it's cute and cuddly characters, after completing each mission of an episode, you'll be able to watch the Dark Theater mode to see Grimm's version of the tale. Some episodes include power ups such as high jump, super butt stomp, flaming pee, and others. Each episode has a collection of Secret Tokens, collecting them al will unlock the Gallery and view both the light and dark versions of props and sets of each episode, too bad it doesn't show the character models. The only issue I had with this game is being stuck inbetween obsticales which can be annoying, there's only been a few times I had to leave the chapter and come back to it and not get stuck. The first episode if free to play to give people an idea on how the game is like, while the other episodes cost about 1 dollar each, as there are 23 Episodes total. This is more of a different game than most of Mcgee's titles, as this relies more on the artstyle and whitty dialouge with Grimm and the fairy tale creatures. It's also amazing that Roger L. Jackson voices every frikkin character in this game, even in the Mulan episode where he speaks in chinese gibbirish. The last event in the last episode, Snow White, is an epic and fitting end to the series. So if your in the mood for some more mature versions of classic fairy tales with it's simple gameplay, hilarous writting, and interesting art style, this game is worth a play for one of those slow days when you have nothing better to do. May all our stories end so well. Until next time.

When I was gifted this game as a present for Christmas, I was ecstatic. I'm a big fan of Princess Maker 2 and other similar games that are a mixture of raising sim and strategy. Sadly, after playing through enough to die in a variety of stupid ways, the game just sits untouched in my Steam library and probably will stay that way forever until I decide to just uninstall it out of pity.
The art in this game is quite nice. The game's premise and story are also both incredibly interesting and I found myself replaying just to see more of it, even after I was frustrated and ready to quit. Unfortunately, that's about all the good things I can say about Long Live the Queen. For a game with such pleasant art and story, the game mechanics just aren't up to par. Although it was advertised as strategic, the game is actually more about picking something at random and hoping you chose the right skills so that you won't accidentally die by chocolate, or a stray arrow, etc etc...(I will say, though, I did quite enjoy the way Elodie's mood affected the outcome of her classes. It felt like a nice touch.)
The only way to win (and by win I mean not die by something incredibly idiotic and actually get Elodie to adulthood) Long Live the Queen is to either follow a strict guide or just get lucky. I had thought that the game's mechanics would be similar to Princess Maker in that your choices help to shape Elodie and her future. Have her study magic? She'll become a magician. Study war strategy enough? She becomes a tyrant queen. That's...the complete opposite of what happens here. Unless you skipped out on studying something you were actually interested in to take a poisons class, or a swimming class, or an etiquette class, Elodie is going to fall victim to her own stupidity and end your game short. I'd probably even go so far as to say that if you actually try to rear Elodie in the way you find most interesting, you're setting yourself up for failure.
Would I recommend this game? No, not really. Not unless you feel like following a strict guide just to actually see the story and keep yourself from dying from the most inane of things after only playing for 30 minutes.

Excellent game. Somehow fun and harrowing at the same time.
Gods Will Be Watching aims (I think) to put you in the position where you can make monstrous decisions, but not 'in a split second of panic' like Walking Dead did; it gives you all the time in the world to choose to do something necessary, but positively atrocious. This way you get to dwell on the ramifications. Also in contrast, this time to Papers Please, only the Gods are watching. How you complete the objective is irrelevant to the game, and there's no 'second booth' assessing your mistakes or concessions. It's quicker to inject a lethal dose of a virus into a human patient to find if the antidote works, and sacrifice your men in the desert to cover more ground, but if you're as immersed as I was this won't be an easy decision.
Other reviewers will criticise the mechanics. Other reviewers are missing the point. Most moral choices are down to chance at the end of the day.
Long and the short of it is; I went in as a total pacifist and within ten minutes I was rationalising the knee-capping of tied up hostages.

Whether, or not you believe in Deus-ex Machina; a superior force guiding you through life events in such ways that you question your own thoughts, not sure if they were your own; the way I ultimately got to purchasing Night in the Woods was out of pure serendipity. I personally have never heard of Infinite Fall, nor did I have a clue about NITW’s Kickstarter beforehand. Steam showed me this game on the day it got released (February 21, 2017), I saw the trailer (which oddly enough stirred up visions of Ralph Bakshi’s most notable works) and the Overwhelmingly Positive reception made something in me say “Shut up and take my money!” I am pleased to say…
Night in the Woods is not an action oriented game, even though it’s action packed. To call it a walking simulator would undermine all the other intricately placed mechanics in it that influence the pacing of the narrative. Perhaps the closest genre would be the adventure genre, however it works best when it mirrors the lives of a specific age range.
The music holds most of the immersion and aesthetic, along with the most shockingly honest dialogue I have ever had the pleasure of reading in a video game.
Alec Holowka’s music is haunting and melancholy, yet comforting. It gives the feeling of coming home to a place close to your heart, yet knowing that times are changing. Resistant to growing up, you cling to any memory of home you have left. “At the end of everything, hold onto anything.”
The maturity of this game comes from it’s story, showing peoples’ flaws, rather than telling us about them, however it’s characters hold back their true nature so adamantly, revealing it all when they have their backs to the wall. Yet all this drama works out because it reflects the player’s personal life through May, Gregg and Bea’s struggles of being young adults in a slowly dying town. By ten hours into Gregg’s storyline, (yes, I did the side quests as well) I broke down into tears, weeping like a baby and screaming like an animal (no pun intended) at 3am in my house. This game had the tenacity of giving me a reality check. And I fear I am not alone in this.
About the only weak part of the game is the supernatural Twin Peaks-esque mystery that is so sudden, thin, and anticlimactic, the only way to explain it’s existence is for advertising purposes since internal conflicts are much harder to sell to people in this day and age. Especially when it comes to video games.
A coming of age story works best when it talks directly to those of the same age as it’s protagonists, rather than expressing a point in someone’s life through imagery and vernacular that do nothing more than to show how out-of-touch the story is. Night in the Woods is a lesson in writing honest life stories in video game form, rather than focusing on external conflicts the way most games do.

Fans of the original game will find OMD2 mostly enjoyable. The gameplay mechanics are identical, but there are lots of new traps, weapons and avatar buffs, all of which have several upgrades to select. There are also a couple of new orc types. The result is even more tactical depth and playing style diversity. Story mode seems a bit short compared to OMD1, but replayability is extended by the game type called Endless, where the objective is to survive as many waves as possible before you get overrun. And then there's coop mode, but this isn't necessarily a good thing. Some of the maps seem to be specifically designed for two players, with far too many orcs coming from too many directions for one player to cover all at once. This makes some maps frustrating to play, even after hours of grinding Endless for enough skulls to fully upgrade your traps. I don't mind difficult games, but OMD2 at times simply feels unfair to solo players. Overall though OMD2 is still worth playing.

Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Once upon a time, on another game service far away, there lived a little episodic game series called American McGee's Grimm. It hailed from the once cheerful and joyous kindgom of Gametappington. The Kingdom of Gametappington however was overcome with a blight, and chaos soon took over, when the original king was slain, and the kingdom was soon taken over by the evil king Metaboli. Metaboli ruled with an iron fist, and took all the fun and cheer away from the once joyous kingdom of Gametappington. And with that, Grimm was locked away, soon to be long forgotten.
Well one day, a kingdom on the other side of the world, known as the kingdom of Steamtopia, ruled by our mighty lord Gaben, began amassing an army of indie titles under the recruitment orders of Sir Greenlight of Steamptopia. Grimm of the kingdom of Gametappington had escaped the clutches of the evil king Metaboli, and fled clear across the globe. Along his voyage to freedom, he worked for various traders to seek employment. But he had one goal in mind. Steamtopia. So he continued his trek to Steamtopia, seeking refuge as his endgame. And one day, he arrived at the gates. But he had to prove himsewlf worthy first. Sir Greenlight of Steamtopia saw potential in this little episodic trooper, and gave it a chance. But he let the citizens of Steamtopia decide its fate, much like all of its other soldiers of the Greenlight army. The citizens of Steamtopia liked this new Grimm. They welcomed him in with open arms. And henceforth it is with great pleasure to announce the forever citizenship of Greenlight Knight Grimm of Steamtopia!
Grimm is an episodic game series, much like another Gametap original you all know as Sam & Max Season 1, which has made it's way to Steam. It's a pretty nifty little title. Simple, yet adorably gruesome if that makes any sense. Each episode, which is covered over 3 seasons, with 23 episodes in total, starts out cute and innocent enough, but ends with some sadistic retellings of beloved tales from the brothers Grimm.
It is definitely a game intended for kids. But I would not go as far as saying little kids. there is blood, and there is gore. But it is no worse than what you may see on an episode of The Simpsons Treehouse of Horror, or any regular episode of Family Guy. But parents beware, you may want to check out the game first before letting any little ones play it. That said, it can still be enjoyable for adults. It does have some decent humor even we can enjoy.
The gameplay is simple. You control a warped and twisted version of Grimm, who is fed up with how cute the fairy tale stories have become, and he wants to give them a good kick in the rear with a dark and disgusting makeover. So each episode has Grimm walking around, jumping, and stomping chaos into everything. As he corrupts more of the area, his dark-o-meter fills up, and the more bars he gets, the wider the radius of his corruption becomes. There are some characters who will be immune to the dark corruption, but as more bars get filled, even they succumb to the darkness. But before they succumb, they can erase the darkness with their own small radius, as they walk around. But they are more of a small bother than a real threat, and can be easily worked around.
There is not really much challenge in any of the levels, and each episode can be beaten in roughly 30 to 45 minutes tops, even taking your time. With 23 episodes in total, that is not too bad of a full gameplay length. But don't expect any huge leaps in gameplay with each episode. It's pretty much, walk around, corrupt, and butt stomp! That said, this game is more for the humorous story retellings than anything else.
Each episode starts with a short cinematic showing the cute version of the fairytale, and ends with the newly improved dark and twisted version. You'll find retellings of such faiytales as Red Riding Hood, Cinderella, Pinnochio, Snow White, and more.
All in all, worth the $9.99

This game is a "Grimm" reminder of how fairy tales used to be.
Each episode concentrates on one fairy tale, introducing the episode with the modern saccharine version, and then you take control of Grimm a dwarf with the powers of darkness that must turn the tales back into their original darker form.
The gameplay is slightly similar to Katamari, at the start you can only convert small items into dark items as your darkness grows, you move faster and jump farther and your "area of influence" grows too.
Many of the fairy tale villagers will try to clean up Grimm's mess unless stunned or attacked by dark villagers or dark forest dwellers.
The controls aren't perfect many times you will die due to the slippery controls, but the game is never so demanding that it should really matter that much.

I see in the comments that people arn't allowed to play the game without the DLC. That's stupid of the developers to do, but I say this in response; why don't you have the DLC? The best of the state of decay gameplay come from the Breakdown DLC, because every level gets increasingly difficult. Especially when it comes to resource management between your dwindiling number of survivors. (Lifeline was nothing special, just a shame they didn't make it an addon to the original map, so you could continue the campaign with the same characters)
The thing that really dissapointed me in this game was the map size and character interaction. Basically this is how the game goes. You start off as one character; Marcus (Watchdogs 2 lmao), and most of us decide he'll be our go-to/favorite character right off the back. You then find some other people whom you never interact with again unless you swap to their character to either give your favorite characters a break, or to go kill them to save on resources.
The missions that do involve character involvment are basically the same run-of-the-mill traits to them. Basically get a notifcation to talk to a character or look for them. Tell them they are important, and then they tell you a generic story with the same named people mentioned from different characters. (now that really grinds my gears) they have all these unique characters, but they seem to all have the same backstories. In ordder to improve on their next title, Dead Labs needs to impliment more unique character backstories, and maybe even a set of backstories for each character so that there are multiple personalities to each character on a different playthrough (or level on Breakdown).
So I mentioned Map size being lacking in the last paragraph, and what I mean by that is; there are only 2 towns. And from my understanding one 'town' isn't really a town because it's lacking all the aspects a town has (hopsital, police station, fire department etc.) So that just means there is only 1 town in this game on this map. Now shouldn't a group survival game the involves the vital mechanic of scavenging for supplies, have more than just 1 town? Realistically with a group of 5 people with the size of the town in the game, they could easily clear out all the usefull supplies within a couple real time hours (because the game is based in real time, except the day/night cycle. What I'm getting to, is that this is the type of game that needs more places to explore, with their DLC being more maps that continue along the same storyline.
TL:DR  Game is ok, but they could have done better, and the dev's didnt deliver on some of their promises, but... It's still fun to play for about 100 hours.

State of Decay starts out very promising. Setting up a base, dealing with group dynamics, scavenging for ammo, dealing with hordes, and having your characters die permanently is all great stuff. It's great until you realize how easily handed hordes are, how little effort it takes to deal with a group (none, really), how abundant ammo and other resources are, and how easy it is to keep characters alive (eventually you'll have so many skilled characters it doesn't matter if you lose one once in awhile, anyway).
And you'll realize all of this within a couple of hours.
Which means there's not much to the game except the story missions. Which is bad news, because the story missions suck and the story sucks. Nor are the core game mechanics anything interesting. The promise of the game comes from all the aforementioned stuff, which amounts to a big pile of fluffy zombie flavored nothing.
I didn't hate the time I spent with State of Decay, but I didn't love it, aside from a couple of hours at the start. It was a decent way to waste 15 hours when I didn't have anything better to play. But by the time the game was done I was excited it was over just so I could stop playing State of Decay and do something, anything else.

This is Long Live The Queen, the exciting Novel/Choose Your Own Adventure game.
In this game, you play as Elodie, a crown princess that is about to come to rule. The game is composed mainly on choices the player makes.  Every in-game week, you select what skills you wish to study, studying a skill increases Elodie's knowledge in that range.  The skills range from court manners to horse caring to military strategy, and later to magic.  The game has a somewhat strategic twist to it, because events in the plot can be effected by Elodie's knowledge in specific skills.  The game allows you to "fiddle" with Elodie's emotions that allow you to increase or decrease the results of your studies.  Your choices will either lead Elodie to her queenly rule, or to her utter demise.  Though it can be frustrating when the lovable princess dies, you learn from your mistakes and prepares you for the future.  Plus, you can use that anger as motivation to make better choices in your next save file.
I have to note that the game plays out more like a digital graphic novel rather than a full-fledged game.  But if you're a fan of games with interesting stories, shocking twists, interesting characters, and the ability to shape the plot with the single act of skipping a history lesson, I suggest you pick this game up.
A, must, play

You can screw this up so royally (ha-ha) that you actually start a civil war and *everyone* wants you dead. So you're trying to make the peasants happy, the nobles, keep the foreigners at bay, and keep everything together as an inexperience (apparently) uneducated princess. You will die. A lot probably.
The game itself is short (40 weeks, which is basically 40 turns), but it's going to feel longer and you are going to die before you get there over and over. So you're probably going to have to replay at least 4 or 5 times. The paranoia factor is very high and sweaty palms are the norm for decision making (even when it's just deciding whether or not to accept invitations to birthday parties).

Tldr; Story is bad, if you like luck based management resource games then you'll like this.  Game is pretty.
I will preface this by saying that I don't enjoy luck based games, especially those that punish the player almost purely on luck.  I do enjoy narrative games though, and for that reason I have played this game on narrative mode.
I enjoy this game conceptually.  The themes of circular time, heavy social issues, and tough survival elements makes this game interesting.  However, I don't think the game came through on many of its ideas and in general, could use a lot of work.
The narrative is awful.  I played through the entire story including the epilogue so that I might understand the story more thoroughly. All of the characters had the same type of speech, and all in all it felt like every character was the same person, which is a sign of poor writing.  The writing was superfluous and flowery with no real meaning behind the words.  The emphasis on depth and the urgency of the each scenario wasn't reflected in the writing.
The main character has points where he just jumps into these auto-fellatious monologues which is to say,  I didn't enjoy at all. I felt the overall philosophical message the writer was trying to communicate was flawed. Unfortunately,  the writing projects depth, but is unable to deliver. I didn't care for Burden, or the biblical and pseudo victorian-esque naming of his character.
The narrative then in turn suffers from the main game mechanics in which there are several scenarios where you depend on luck and management of resources in a survival situation.  If this is your type of thing, then go for it; I did not enjoy this.  Even if this is a game mechanic is intended by the developers as what they were aiming for, it doesn't make it a good mechanic.  The high failure rate coupled with the fact the survival portions of the games need so much time to complete is awful.  This is most prominent in chapter 3.  I played it on narrative mode, so I didn't have to restart as many times however, it quickly became frustrating and that frustration takes away from the narrative in a way that I became more focused on completing the objective than the characters who can easily die.  This is tedious, and I understand they were probably going for a Dark Souls thing (I liked Dark Souls a lot), but the mechanics come off as cumbersome and don't encourage exploration or different tactics as the choice of tactics are limited anyway.
Further, it doesn't actually matter if the characters die because of spoilers. Again, there is a narrative reason for this but I felt that it cheapened the story.

Whether, or not you believe in Deus-ex Machina; a superior force guiding you through life events in such ways that you question your own thoughts, not sure if they were your own; the way I ultimately got to purchasing Night in the Woods was out of pure serendipity. I personally have never heard of Infinite Fall, nor did I have a clue about NITW’s Kickstarter beforehand. Steam showed me this game on the day it got released (February 21, 2017), I saw the trailer (which oddly enough stirred up visions of Ralph Bakshi’s most notable works) and the Overwhelmingly Positive reception made something in me say “Shut up and take my money!” I am pleased to say…
Night in the Woods is not an action oriented game, even though it’s action packed. To call it a walking simulator would undermine all the other intricately placed mechanics in it that influence the pacing of the narrative. Perhaps the closest genre would be the adventure genre, however it works best when it mirrors the lives of a specific age range.
The music holds most of the immersion and aesthetic, along with the most shockingly honest dialogue I have ever had the pleasure of reading in a video game.
Alec Holowka’s music is haunting and melancholy, yet comforting. It gives the feeling of coming home to a place close to your heart, yet knowing that times are changing. Resistant to growing up, you cling to any memory of home you have left. “At the end of everything, hold onto anything.”
The maturity of this game comes from it’s story, showing peoples’ flaws, rather than telling us about them, however it’s characters hold back their true nature so adamantly, revealing it all when they have their backs to the wall. Yet all this drama works out because it reflects the player’s personal life through May, Gregg and Bea’s struggles of being young adults in a slowly dying town. By ten hours into Gregg’s storyline, (yes, I did the side quests as well) I broke down into tears, weeping like a baby and screaming like an animal (no pun intended) at 3am in my house. This game had the tenacity of giving me a reality check. And I fear I am not alone in this.
About the only weak part of the game is the supernatural Twin Peaks-esque mystery that is so sudden, thin, and anticlimactic, the only way to explain it’s existence is for advertising purposes since internal conflicts are much harder to sell to people in this day and age. Especially when it comes to video games.
A coming of age story works best when it talks directly to those of the same age as it’s protagonists, rather than expressing a point in someone’s life through imagery and vernacular that do nothing more than to show how out-of-touch the story is. Night in the Woods is a lesson in writing honest life stories in video game form, rather than focusing on external conflicts the way most games do.

**Composite Score: 9.125/10**
If you enjoyed the first game, you'll definitely enjoy the second. If you have fun with tower defense games which incorporate FPS elements, you'll enjoy this too.
This game launched at $15 for a single copy or $25 for two. Or, if you got it during the Steam sale, $12.50/$22.50. That's really inexpensive for this quality of game. I definitely recommend picking it up at these prices f you're into this game genre.
**Entertainment Value: 10/10** Solid excitement mixed with charming humor. I really enjoyed playing solo. Co-operative play really depends on who you're playing with and dealing with network/tech issues. My partner had some microphone and XBOX controller issues, so we had to deal with tech problems at the start. But, after we got those sorted, we had a good time roasting, slicing, and crushing waves of orcs.
**Graphics: 9/10** The Vision engine still delivers as good of a product as it did in OMD!. On my SLI GTX 570 setup, I get solid graphics performance and appearance. Anti-aliasing and Anisotropic Filtering are both great. No artifacting at all. Only reason this doesn't get a 10 is that the traps often don't mesh perfectly with the surroundings. And, coins sometimes get lost behind walls.
**Sound: 9/10** Solid sound like the first game. Music is lively and entertaining. The surround system works. The orcs still tell silly lines, and now that dwarves have been added, they enhance the humor too. I give this game a 9 instead of the standard 8, because the dialog and music enhance the experience better than most other low-budget games of this style.
**Design and Gameplay: 9/10** Gameplay has been tweaked since OMD!. There are more weapons, trinkets, and a new female character, the sorceress. There are new monsters. There are other ways to play such as ENDLESS and Co-op. Also, the way players can upgrade traps and items is distinctly different from the first game.... somewhat more like an RPG than before. Otherwise though, it's still build traps and use your character's powers to defeat the waves of mosters before they exit the map.
**Game Length: 9/10** Given the game's low price and its incorporated multiplayer mode, don't think too harshly about it taking me less than three hours to complete the first half of the campaign on War Mage (normal) difficulty. I'm not done with the second half yet, but I've spent a couple of hours doing and redoing the next few maps. Also, I've spent many more hours playing through ENDLESS maps, going for high-scores, and playing through the classic maps using the new trap upgrades and weapons. Therefore, I'm quite happy with the game's length.

♥ Who doesn't love Nancy Drew?
The dialogue, the graphics, and the events stay very true to the Nancy Drew series. There are puzzles, there's mystery, and there's bits and pieces of easter eggs spread through out the game.
I appreciate how they stay true to the spirit of Nancy Drew - there's never a vulgar word, graphic content, and it never forgets who she is.
♥ The graphics are better than the older titles.
There are some Nancy Drew games that feature more dated, clumsy graphics and a clunky inventory/clicking system. However Warnings at Waverly Academy is one of the updated games, thankfully without the awkward, clay like people animations and overly sized arrows.
♥ I enjoyed the mini games.
Usually when I play Nancy Drew games, I don't pay too much attention to the mini games, seeing as I'm more focused on solving a mystery or two. With Warnings at Waverly Academy, I actually enjoyed playing them, something I was pleased with! If you want to expand your play time, this is a great way to do so.
✘ The puzzles.
If I have to do that science puzzle again, I will quit. Uninstall steam, done...
If you want challenging puzzles, this one has it, in full! They just weren't quite to my taste, blarg because the rewards for solving the puzzles weren't there.
✘ The characters were blah.
I don't think this is a failure as a Nancy Drew title, however I don't think it's the best it could be, not even close. In the The White Wolf of Icicle Creek all the AI drew me in - they were interesting, unique, and I still remember them years later. However with Waverly, they just didn't feel "real" to me, nor did I feel like their personalities showed through as best as they could with their dialogue and the ways she would interact with them.
✘ The ending felt ....off.
One thing I appreciate about Nancy Drew games is the fact that the endings tie the game together, pulling in the obvious with the small, hidden hints that you may have missed story wise. There's usually a twist and a turn with a nice seasoning on top. This I found utterly lacking with Warnings at Waverly Academy.
Overall if you're intent on playing every Nancy Drew game, this is worth playing. However if you are new to Nancy Drew games or only wish to play the best ones, avoid Waverly Academy.

I say this with genuine affection: "Dead Effect" is basically a schlockier version of "Doom 3."  Like D3, it takes place on a space station that has been overrun with Space Zombies. You, the Grizzled Space Marine, must stop them with your Space Guns and Space Grenades. There is much KERPLOWing and KERPLOOPing as zombie parts fly, and explosive things go KABOOM. Along the way, you pick up PDAs which tell the story of the Dumb Scientists who started the whole mess. Eventually you face off against The Big Bad Guy, and then... it just kinda ends.
The main difference between "Dead Effect" and D3 (other than the former's much shorter runtime) is the nature of the combat. In D3, you were faced with a steady trickle of monsters that would pop out of nowhere and attack from a distance with pistols, fireballs, etc. By contrast, "Dead Effect" basically repeats one combat scenario over and over again:
1. You open a door
2. You see a group of 20 slow-moving zombies start shuffling toward you
3. You pick out the one zombie holding a grenade and shoot him first (optional, but recommended)
4. You walk backwards and pump shotgun blasts at the rest as they stumble uselessly in your direction, since they aren't capable of ranged attacks
5. You celebrate victory
I'm really not exaggerating; that's pretty much the whole game. Personally, I found this to be quite fun in a mindless B-movie kind of way. But I could see how others could hate it with full justification.
TL;DR: it's a boilerplate zombie shooter in space with repetitive combat. I found it to be oddly charming and competently made, and perfectly satisfactory as cheap fun. Others may (and do) hate it, and I don't begrudge them that. To each their own.

American McGee's Grimm is a game that was previously released in weekly segments. Every week, a new episode of this game would come out. Now, all 23 episodes are on steam in one big bundle.
You play as Grimm, a person who's clearly never been in a shower, who despises fairy tales. So he goes around to random fairy tales to make them darker and nastier. The gameplay mainly stays consistent through all the episodes. There's some platforming, which is usually pretty easy. The main focus of the game is to turn everything into dark stuff, by simply walking up to it. It's simple, and will get repetitive playing all of it. I played the first episode and already I could feel the repetition setting in. At least the gameplay is pretty fun, though.

This is American McGee's Grimm, and Happily Ever After ends now!

As Grimm, you will transform the classic tales of Little Red Riding Hood, Cinderella, Jack and the Beanstalk, and more of your favorites into darkly twisted Grimm versions of themselves in 23 episodes. Each episode is a complete, standalone experience and the episodes can be played in any order.
