Pillars of Eternity:
Pre-Review note: To all the idiots crying about Paradox increasing prices before the beginning of the Steam Summer Sale 2017, you do realise there are a plethora of other websites offering the game at a far cheaper price, right?  I did not buy my copy from Steam. Besides, 18 USD for the game and 15 USD for both expansions is not bad...Use your brain and search for the best sales if that is such an issue for you.
With that out of the way, I must say this game is incredible. I've been playing for a little over 50 hours at the moment and it's great fun.
+ The combat is very smart and tactical, giving you a nice challenge even on normal difficulty. You'll need to combine aoe spell disables, healing, buffs and aoe damage, position your party members appropriately, use potions, summoning and just about every advantage you have to overcome difficult foes. Pausing the game every micro second to issue commands, reform ranks and try and gain the upper hand in a fight is critical.
+ The main story is pretty interesting, teasing you with more and more information about your purpose and goals as you progress. I won't summarise it here due to spoilers, but you'll just need to trust me when I say it's great. The side quests are equally rewarding, providing exploration and tough decision making.
+ Pillars of Eternity cleverly uses attributes like intellect, dexterity, resolve, might and so forth in dialogue to give you unique opportunities to complete quests. If you're dextrous enough you can snatch a piece of a valuable artifact from a man right before his eyes. If you have high might, you can often intimidate others into backing down or relinquishing goods. But beware, how you treat locals can affect your reputation as well.
+ The skills system is also solid. You'll want to balance your party so that you have specialists in  multiple fields, some for mechanics to disarm traps and unlock doors, while others can focus on stealth to sneak up on enemies or survival to gain combat perks.
+ The game's world is beautifully drawn by artists. While it may not be fully 3D (you can't rotate the screen because the pictures are essentially 2D drawings), it doesn't really matter. You'll still find it's fun to adventure in.
- One aspect of the game which left me annoyed was the lack of explanation on faction alignment in Defiance Bay (one of the town's you'll visit). There's no real warning that accepting a specific quest from one faction will cause you to ally with them and hence, oppose the others.
Any attempt at doing so by the characters is hidden behind innuendo.
, says one character. Yeah, NOT obvious that i'm going to be completely locked out from rival faction quests by accepting this one. No fix for this by Obsidian, so poor game design in this regard. It's problematic because it breaks my immersion and doesn't allow me to follow the faction I wish. There needs to be a solid warning screen so players are aware of the gravity of their decision - a point of no return.
I also found my impression of particular people and consequently, my choices regarding them were sometimes influenced through deception, which irritated me. As an example, I met a young man in the Catacombs of Defiance Bay who claimed he participated in a bar fight with a crucible knight, knocking him to the ground. The man claimed the Crucible Knights would want him to hang for it and so he seeked refuge beneath the city. This was only half the story and at the time I wasn't aware - so I decided to pay the man 300 copper for safe passage out of Defiance Bay. Later I learnt that this was not merely a bar fight, because the Crucible Knight involved actually died from the injury he sustained. If I had known this initially, it might have changed my decision with how to deal with the man. Again, poor game design. Luckily these encounters are infrequent.
Overall Score: 9/10

Starbound is a fun game and when I first played it, I was so hooked at playing it to relieve my stress from work. But as I progress through the story and all the side quests, I got bored of it a little bit since some quests are rather repetitive while you explore other planets.
Would I still recommend it? Yeah sure...it is still fun to play. But if you'll easily get bored of the side quests and how the story progressed, this game might not be for you.

Starbound had a lot of promise, and a lot of potential. Sadly it squandered both. The game's movement system is janky and floaty, which becomes very unfun when you have enemies that move at about five times the speed of your character and can demolish you in two or three hits. Effectively guns are the only even remotely viable option, spitting in the face of anyone who wants a different playstyle, and the various races have no effect other than mild cosmetic flair, while the overall game plays like a bad europlatformer, quite likely seen as a good thing through the rose-tinted nostalgia of the developers vision.
The boss fights are basically slug-fests in which you have neither the damage output nor the damage-absorbtion to compete with the enemies, with which you are locked in a small enclosed space with little room to maneuver and few options other than "Get hit and die, come back and do it again". The tech-skills offer a slight improvement but the timings on the dodges and jumps are still so wonky and unfun that mastering them feels like a game of chance rather than developing any kind of actual skill.
The game seemed like it was going in a nicer direction for a bit but then several of the updates basically rolled back the playstyle content to what it was originally, again spitting in the faces of anyone who wants to play something other than a gunrunning shootmans in this supposed sandbox. In addition to this the planets all feel very same-y and the quests simultaneously manage to take up all your time -and- be boring somehow.
I wish I could reccommend this game. I wanted so badly for Starbound to be good.... but it's not. And it only gets worse with time.

NOTE: I do reviews of game script because everyone does Steam general-reviews. In my opinion, for things that aren't writing oriented, the art's great, the gameplay can get repetitive but the gameplay's not focused on so it's more forgivable than in most games. Anyway:
This is a weak recommendation but I suppose it's a recommendation if the concept of a writing-focused slice-of-life character study with horror elements appeals to you. If that doesn't sound fun to you, do not pick it up because it's not even really the greatest version of such a game.
Very quickly:
Pros: Occasionally funny, engaging moments of character drama, great pacing for first half.
Cons: Occasionally cringe-y, begins to drag about half-way in, something of an anti-climax and...
There's nothing wrong with having an unlikeable main character. Plenty of stories have done it. If we want to call to mind the spectre of other hipster-media, my very first thought is Scott Pilgrim, a lazy mid-twenties manchild who complains about his life ad infinitum, mistreats the people in his life and expects the world to be handed to him on a platter.
Scott Pilgrim was a good character, but a bad person. Mae Borowski of Night In The Woods is a bad person and a bad character.
The thing that separates Scott Pilgrim and Mae Borowski is not the ways in which they are bad. Mae is a selfish, unlikable, stunted, obnoxious leech whose bad qualities extend far, far past
In many way, Mar Borowski is a less bad character than Scott Pilgrim, at the very least she understands when she's royally ♥♥♥♥ed something up.
The difference is not an internal one. I'm not asking for a different character. I'm asking for a different world. The world must react realistically to any character, good or bad. Scott Pilgrim literally had the♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of him for being such a little manbaby and his friends routinely understood when he was being a selfish prick and refused to engage him.
Mae Borowski is a character who verbally mistreats her friends, blows up at people for no discernable reason, melts down at the slightest provocation, constantly asks for favors while giving nothing in return, has no ambition to even a humble amount of independence, leeches off of others and offers nothing of any value to anyone in return whether it be emotional, physical, financial, spiritual or any other measurement of value. She's a worthless human being whose only redeeming quality seems to be a modicum of self-awareness regarding her own inherent lack of any redeeming quality.
Yet every character treats her like she saved their puppy from a fire. It's genuinely infuriating when, after the story comes alive during a character's rational and angered response to Mae's insufferable and immature attitude, Mae is forgiven immediately afterward to allow for the story to continue and for Mae to consistently dodge any real repercussion for her disgusting behavior. At least four times in my playthrough, I was forced to endure a character going back on a firey and relateable outburst of frustration with Mae only for them to make up because Mae apologizes with no sincere attention to change her ♥♥♥♥♥♥ behavior.
I'm reminded of Lightning from Final Fantasy XIII who would have been a perfectly servicable character if someone, anyone, would just step up and tell her that she was acting like a snobby, disaffected ♥♥♥♥♥ who's better than everyone around her.
Is it a deal breaker?
It's close. It's really close. But Mae's horrible personality is, for the most part, treated naturally and doesn't choke out all of the game's good qualities. Underneath the skin of this insufferable brat is an intriguing story of a group of characters whose future stretches out in front of them in the form of a crappy town that none of its inhabitants can escape from, and how death can feel so close when you can see your future so clearly.
As I said above, the ending's anti-climactic, there's certainly some fat on this story and a good number of the jokes don't totally connect (even if they weren't intended to be funny but rather illustrate friendships, I am still, unfortunately, forced to read them).
If none of that dissuades you, giant and bulbous criticisms though they may be, then I recommend Night In The Woods.

I got State of Decay with both DLC packs when it was on sale over a month ago and I must say, it is a great game considering it was made by a smaller game studio. I loved several things about this game, but also hated some parts of it. Review below!
THINGS I LOVE:
1. The Open World. There is a linear storyline but you aren't forced into playing it. Almost every building you encounter is explorable and has cabinets and such that have to be searched in order to obtain supplies.
2. Bases. Your home base is where you'll return supplies you've scavenged. You can build your base to include commodities such as more sleeping space, a garden for more food upkeep, a library, a workshop, etc. Certain combinations of things you build in your base will be beneficial to you ingame. For example, you can upgrade your garden to a greenhouse and if you have a survivor who is good at farming, you will have more rations of food per day. This concept is probably one of my most favorite of the game because you can clearly see how much thought was put into it. You can also move home bases, which you will end up doing as you progress through the story.
3. Weapons. There are a variety of melee weapons and guns in the game that can be obtained and used by your survivors. You'll see early on that melee weapons are the best way to go because guns make noise even if there is a silencer on them, and noise will attract zombies. Weapons, if overused, will break, which I think was a pretty cool mechanic that the Devs put in to encourage players to play other survivors. Also, to add to that, if you play a survivor for too long, he/she will get tired and will receive penalties to their max stamina. Again, a way to encourage players to play other survivors.
4. Outposts. Outposts are essentially a small safe zone where you can resupply if needed. They save A LOT of time and are a life saver if you're in need of supplies such as meds to keep your health and stamina alive and well. They also are equipped with traps that destroy passing hordes of zombies. If you use your outposts wisely, you can create a shield of protection from zombie hordes that will make your life much easier.
5. Zombies. In my honest opinion, the game is at perfect difficulty for me, although that will differ depending on how you like to play your games. Normal zombies are easy to defeat with melee weapons or guns. However, it is easy to get overwhelmed by them if you are by yourself. There are other types of zombies, called "freaks", similar to special zombies in the L4D series. They are much harder to defeat and require a certain degree of strategy in order to defeat them. I learned early on not to mess with juggernaut zombies in melee combat... Besides types of zombies, a cool mechanic that I enjoyed in the game was the fact that zombies get attracted to noise. This means that it's difficult to really go anywhere in a car without having to fight zombies. Whenever you break through a door, a window, fire a gun, etc. zombies will show up.
THINGS I DIDN'T LIKE:
1. Glitches. Although this game was a lot of fun, it is quite glitchy at times. Don't expect it to be a highly polished game if that's what you're in to.
2. AI. I really hope AI gets improved with this game eventually. It is terrible. Both zombies and survivors. Just horrendous.
3. Repetitive buildings. Despite almost every building being explorable, it does get repetitive after a while. Searchable cabinets, cupboards, desks, etc. become predictable. The items you recover also become predictable. Kinda wish they would switch things up a bit somehow.
4. Car handling. This is more of a personal preference. The car handling in this game is really arcade-like, which I don't really like. But like I said, it's preference. When I first started playing, I could barely handle a car without veering off the road and hitting something.
5. Repetitive events. After a while, random events that Lily brings up over the radio get boring because you know exactly how to complete them. Sure, the first time you play these random events will be loads of fun and a new experience, but again, they just get boring.
And there you have it. My pros and cons list of State of Decay. Overall, I think it's a great game with LOADS of potential. Undead Labs has announced that they see a bright future for the game, so I'm not too worried about Devs not improving it. In conclusion, It's definitely a fun game with loads of features, but will unfortunately get repetitive at times.

"This is like any normal zombie shooter, just this time your in space. Plus zombies can throw grenades at you!"
Watch my review here:
It has zombies. They like to eat...

What starts as a pretty simple, zombie beat-em-up game quickly turns into a challenging game that needs you to build the toughest group of survivors in order to succeed. The core game will likely gobble up hours in just scavenging and hoping to not get torn in half by a big 'un. Play the DLCs too,  and you gain in effect a brand new game and a sandbox, 'no bull' version of the core game.
Melee mechanics are very solid, with dodging and attacks both being fairly responsive and effective even when faced with a 1 v 5 scenario. Stamina, which powers these movements, be it defensive or offensive, can drain quickly on lower-leveled characters, and even faster when one puts the effort in to ensure a downed zombie stays down for good. This can lead to frustrating moments where a character becomes too exhausted to fight far too soon, and if one hasn't packed any snacks or didn't think to eat one before entering combat, then the chances of coming out of a big fight unscathed are slim.
Stamina aside, the game provides a long list of items to aid lucky survivors in either evading, battling, or downright eradicating the zombie threat. A variety of harmless noisemakers can help lure zombies away from a goldmine of loot - or safe passage - or can help lure them into a killzone. Improvised incendiaries and explosives make for quick dealings against hordes, but come at the cost of attracting nearby zombies. And a good collection of firearms and melee tools help cater to the kind of character you want to build. One can create a bruiser character that wields a sledgehammer to devasting effect, or build a silent urban ninja that can creep in and get supplies without making a sound.
Vehicles play a prominent role in not only making the map smaller, but also providing space to cart your loot home. Car doors can be utilised to smack zombies, and damaged vehicles can be parked up and repaired overnight - provided a workshop has been built.
Without going into much detail, one of the meatiest parts of the game is its emphasis on building a community of survivors. As already discussed, the characters you build are crucial to everyone's survival, but so is building a base that can protect them. Making effective use of free space is important, because not every home base can build every facility, and every facility provides useful buffs that can make the game much easier. Of course, these facilities cannot appear from nothing, so one must go out into danger to gather the materials and supplies needed to build them. Can't have the rewards with taking the risks first, right?
All in all, after having played all but Lifeline (which is next on my playlist), State of Decay of a highly addicting game that will reward you for keeping your survivors alive. They stronger they become, the more abilities they unlock, and therefore the more specialised you can make each survivor. But the game will also throw harder challenges along the way to test your survivor and you. One wrong move can very easily get a full-stat character killed - with no way to ever bring them back. It is this constant danger that makes the risk all the more exciting, and the rewards all the more sweeter.

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Dead Effect is a first person shooter port that takes place on a ship where some sort of disaster has occurred, and all the occupants have been afflicted with a virus; zombies in space, what more could you ask for?  Well, for starters.....
Content for the game is wide and filling time wise. One option that is offered separate from the campaign is that once you have completed a mission, it unlocks and you have the option to replay it if it was one you enjoyed, or one you wanted to improve upon. I like that they have this option, as you don't have to play through the entire game again just to replay that one mission. The lighting and effects of the game are reminiscent of DOOM 3, and do a good job of adding to the tense atmosphere needed for a horror FPS game. The voice acting is poor and overdone, and actually takes away from that horror feel although.
There is a large variety of weapons available, but you are only able to take 3 into the game at a time, and there are rules to which three; (you can't put an assault rifle in your handgun slot, and you can't take an assault rifle and a shotgun but no grenades, for example). While the weapons have the right heavy feel and sound good, having a cap of three weapons undermines the large variety of weapons that are offered. You can always have a little of personal discretion or preference in your choice, but you will also be shoe-horned into using certain types of weapons as they all feel ruffly the same meaning some will be much better for wider encounters.
Character upgrades are very limited; basically health regeneration. The weapons can be upgraded, for the most part by purchasing them with the in game money. The money system did transfer over well to PC, and is relatively balanced. What I found to be unbalance, however, was the difficulty settings. I normally play a game on the hard to hardcore setting, but in this game I found myself being one-shot by monsters on the easy setting, unless I adjusted the Gamma settings to make the rooms brighter. (Doing that however, took away from the atmosphere and immersion into the game). The easy difficulty setting plays and feels like it is the hard setting. This ties into the money aspect of the game as well, because when you die mid level, you have to use your hard won currency to revive yourself, and the further you get into the game, the more credits it costs to revive.
Playing it on the easiest difficulty and being one-shot by enemies that you cannot see, and then spending your money that should be spent on upgrades on reviving your character instead, makes you feel that you are never progressing with your character. I go into more detail on this topic in my video review, which I encourage you to watch if you want more exploration on the reasons why.
The multitude of irritants throughout this game including the difficulty levels, the weapons limitations, the difficult to follow story and the lack of character upgrades all add up to making this a game an unbalanced time annoy-er that I cannot recommend.

Starbound crafts a wonderful universe that makes you really want to love it, but then goes and puts all of that on the other side of a series of terrible walls and pits.
Even with above the recommended system requirements, you're risking a game that runs at an unpredictable framerate, some days deciding to rarely go above 15, other days staying above 30 even at the worst of times, and this is made worse when you're in multiplayer. To make that worse, the performance issues were practically nonexistant while the game was still in early access, and only became an issue with the 1.0 release of the game, with further updates doing little to nothing to alleviate this, only adding more mechanics that worsen the performance.
One of Starbound's best features is the sense of exploration as you begin to explore the first world, then the first solar system, then the whole galaxy. But this wonder is quickly stripped away when you realize that practically every planet of the same type will be functionally identical, featuring the same biomes and often even the same pre-generated mini-dungeons, making extended periods of exporation quickly run dry on content as you encounter the same structures for the 23rd time. This could have been alleviated with the quest system, but instead any randomly generated quest follows one of about a dozen different variants, most of which you will encounter in the first village you find, and any non-randomly generated quest is either so generic that you could do it on nearly any planet in the game(get a certain set of armor that you already want to get anyway, make item x and bring it to me, etc) or will be a major story or boss quest that teleports you directly to a pregenerated dungeon rather than challenging you to explore the galaxy and actually go there yourself.
As cool as upgrading your ship is, it ends up too small to function as any sort of large scale multiplayer hub(if you can get multiplayer to run at a decent framerate), and serves no benefit to your travels around the galaxy other than more closets to put boxes full of random crap you collect. Your ship is also rendered useless in the mid-to-late game as you get the ability to make teleporters and set one up on each type of planet so you can go gathering whatever you need without spending a drop of your ship's fuel. The ability to hire crew for your ship also seems like something quite interesting, but quickly runs dry as only a couple of the already small pool of crew roles turn out to be useful as anything more than someone to act as decor on your ship.
Overall, Starbound has the spark of a wonderful and hugely enjoyable universe, but lacks the variety for a sandbox's longevity in favor of simpler gameplay, but then ruins that gameplay by both missing one of the most enjoyable elements of it, as well as not being able to perform at a stable framerate.

Long Live the Queen is not your typical Visual Novel RPG. Rather, I like to refer to it more as a "spoiled-teenage-dress up-monarchy simulator," but in a surprisingly fun and addictive way. Elodie is a 14 year old princess who you must guide over a 40 week in-game period on the road to her coronation ceremony to become Queen once she reaches her 15th birthday. Only problem is...almost everyone else in the other kingdoms wants to see her fail or die before the 40 weeks have passed.
Essentially, each playthrough is inherently unique based on the classes you have Elodie take to progress her skills each week; The classes you assign Elodie and the story's plot progress at a week by week level instead of a day by day format. The amount of progress she makes in each skill every week will depend upon her mood that week and which two skills you decide she should learn at that time (morning and evening class schedule). In order to change her mood from week to week, you must choose certain paths to take in the game, pass or fail in-game events, and/or vary her evening plans each week. Her progress in certain skills and the choices you make each week can mean the difference between life and death for Elodie. One of the beautiful, albeit frustrating, features of the game is that there is no way to make Elodie good at everything. There is a system that almost forces you to actively think through each decision you make, which adds to the complexity of the story and gameplay overall.
There is a plethora of ways to win and multiple endings as well, many of which have Elodie dying before the coronation ceremony, but every ending is based upon the decisions you made throughout the game 'til that endpoint. However, there are many events that are locked-in which you cannot avoid; this is one of the negative aspects of the game in my opinion as it makes the story seem more linear in progression and not as dynamic. Despite all of this, if Elodie manages to survive to the end she will always be crowned Queen... but what kind of Queen you become, what kind of Kingdom you create in the future, and how you get there exactly depends on your stats and decisions. I cannot reiterate this wonderful facet of decision-making in the game enough (if you cannot tell). Also, the game allows you to see your entire runthrough and the choices you made via textlog whenever you reach an endpoint should you want a recap or printoff of it in detail.
In conclusion, I recommend this game only to players who like visual novels, who are persistent, and are not easily discouraged or rage at their failures, because you WILL fall short in this game numerous times I assure you. Some people have used guides in the past even due to its difficulty to give you an idea of what to expect if you buy it. However, I submit that if you are dedicated to the plot, enjoy struggles only to try again to better yourself, and have plenty of time to put into the game, then you will most likely enjoy it. I know there are mixed feelings about the game, and I have displayed some of those feelings within this review. As such, I give Long Live the Queen a Solid 7.5 or 8 out of 10. While it is very difficult, lengthy, and possesses a somewhat linear plot, the game also has a great story, challenging decision-making aspects, and adaptive gameplay mechanics. Plus, it is always fun to dress her up in various new clothes based on her skill sets. So if you do choose to grab this game, I say to get it while it is on steam sale. Good luck, and hopefully you won't die. Regardless, of if you do-- LONG LIVE THE QUEEN!

It is really hard to decide if this is a game I should recommend to people or not because it is such a niche game. While the game can drag on forever sometimes it also makes you really feel something if you stay for the ride.
Gods will be Watching is a survival- and recourse management game. You will be put in all sorts of situations where your survival will need sacrifice in one way or the other and you will have to choose between bad or worse. The problem for some people will be that these situations can drag on for a long time and require a lot of trail and error, but they also become extremely tense and rewarding.
In between chapters there is a text heavy and quite philosophical storyline, taking place in a dirty futuristic, intergalactical setting, which was intriguing for me, but might put some people off. While asking lots of big questions, the storyline is not very deep, but charming nontheless.
I would recommend this game to people who want to feel something and know they have patience. If you just want to "get on with it" this game is not for you.

Night In The Woods is the best game I've played in a while.
I judge games on their ability to make me feel, And I felt a LOT during this game...
I am 20 years old. To me, this perfectly captured what it's like to be in this "millennial" decade. Of growing up in a messed up world, trying to survive, trying to be different. Just ... living.
I don't leave reviews very often, but this is an exceptional game and I need people to know it.
My cousin introduced it to me, and a few days later I caved and bought it full price because I was dying to play. I began playing a few hours each day and I never once regretted the $20 purchase.
Score: 15/10
Reasons it is amazing to me:
-You're rewarded for exploring. I LOVE exploring in games, and in this game, there are many hidden corners to explore, and conversations to have. You slowly learn new information about each character over time.
-It's an ongoing adventure that progresses on a day-by-day basis. You move throughout the year, watching the seasons change and getting to learn new aspects of the characters each day.
-The characters a beautiful and dynamic. Each had their own special personality, and they are so relatable. To me, the main character, Mae, represents the average 20 year old. She lives a fairly "normal" life with both her parents in a nice neighborhood. She's relatable, yet has her own personality. There's a side to her, that we as the player are not even aware of. She's hiding something, a dark side, the reason she left college. What happened in her past.
Then you meet her friends and the neighbors in town, each with their own unique stories.
-IT HAS MINIGAMES. like every day in the game you can play some sort of mini game with the friends. Going to Mall with Bea, smashing cars with Gregg, PLAYING BASS HERO WITH AWESOME SONGS
-the Music
-The dreams (+the dream music)
-dream music is the best
-The Journal with the drawings in it
-It is my life. It's so relatable to real life and becoming an adult
---
DO NOT play if:
-you don't like repetitive scenery
-you don't like long dialogues and character interactions
-you don't care much for artsy styles and music (it is a large focus of the game)

The latest iteration of the Street Fighter franchise.
Since the transition to Steamworks, online play has been plagued by inconsistent network perfomance.
The latest update brought Omega mode, a selectable character mode in versus and endless games, bringing new moves and different properties to the whole cast. It was released to keep SFIV fresh while waiting for the next installment, Street Fighter 5.
Omega is hit and miss. Some characters completely changed compared to their "vanilla" counterparts, other got some welkcome (or unwelcome) additions. It's all but balanced, but I don't think that was the main aim for this mode.
Be aware though, for newcomers this game can be brutal. The largest part of the userbase are players with years of experience. It's a game with a pretty steep learning curve, as a newcomer, be prepared to get utterly destroyed the first week or even months. Because of that, even the games' online matchmaking is off at times. As a newcomer, you'll face off against players whose skill is way beyond yours.
Sure, there are trials to get to know the characters and their possible combo's, but a lot of those combo's are of the flashy, but not so useful kind.
As a beginner, it's more useful to learn spacing and how to punish, coupled with some basic combo's you'll be sure to land when the need arises.
So my best advice is find to find some players at the same level as you or slightly above. It will keep the saltyness levels manageable, and won't make you quit the game after a week.

TL;DR, stealth is simplistic, combat is slow, and the game is unclear with what's important. Sauron's Army mechanic interesting and underutilized. Focus on the story mission and be as stealthy and efficient as possible and the game should be a lot of fun, but otherwise it can turn into a slog.
Those unfamiliar with the Batman Arkham games should skip to paragraph 2. For those who are familiar with those titles, Shadow of Mordor feels very much like Batman: Arkham City, set in Lord of the Rings. This impression is strongest at the start of the game, and gradually lessens as the more advanced mechanics of the game are revealed. It uses the same combo/finisher/counter system seen in those games, and you eventually unlock a 'dagger-throw combo' that acts very similarly to the batarangs of the Arkham games. Unfortunately, the mechanics can feel at-odds with the setting; it makes little sense for Tallion (the main character) to slash into an uruk with a two-handed sword repeatedly without crippling or killing them. The only explanation for the general lack of lethality in combat seems to be, 'because Batman has to punch people a few times to knock them down, and this game is like that game.' To make matters worse, the player is often confronted with very large numbers of enemies - which could be very challenging even if (perhaps especially if) the weapons had a more realistic level of lethality or reach to them (Tallion actually has less reach with his sword than Batman did with his unarmed attacks), but instead the player must whittle the enemies down - or, more likely, rely heavily on the instant-killing bow and instant-kill takedown maneuvers heavily, which turns combat into a series of slow-motion cutscenes rather than an interactive experience. While there's a definite sense of tactics, the combat system isn't as free-flowing or intense as Batman's, feels at-odds with the setting, and certainly isn't up to the level of challenge or diversity seen in Arkham Knight. Add to that that the stealth is far more simplistic, since there aren't any gadgets or interactive hiding spots, and you might think this game is a poor knockoff of those games; don't be fooled, because the real value of this game lay entirely elsewhere.
Overall, the game's biggest flaws are in the area of conveyance; it seems like you are set loose on an open-world map to do whatever you want, and you're presented with the Sauron's Army interface very early on, which allows you to see the Warchiefs who lead the army, and the Captains who serve under them (and sometimes act as their bodyguards). Furthermore, by gaining Intel from certain uruks (called 'worms') or documents, you can learn their strengths and weaknesses, making it easier to defeat them.
The first few story missions emphasize this aspect of the game, giving the impression that the game developers want the player to interact with the captains and warchiefs significantly; indeed, most of the game's unique features come from this system, including such things as captains remembering their previous interactions with you and holding grudges, or fighting among themselves when you're not around. It's entirely possible to accidentally stumble across a pair of captains, have a wild beast show up, and one of the captains flee in terror while the other flies into a mindless rage and fights the creature to the death, giving you ample tactical opportunities to slay both. Captains can be so unique and diverse that the game can often feel like Assassin's Creed, as the player analyzes their potential foes and finds ways to interact with them that put them at a huge disadvantage - or simply uses the free-climbing system to navigate to a perfect spot and take them down with a diving stab from above.
Unfortunately, this is precisely the opposite of what the game requires you to do. Slaying all of the captains of Sauron's Army is actually impossible, as new ones will show up periodically to replace the fallen (especially if you die, but even if you do not). Instead, the player must continue completing story missions until the game reveals that your goal is to slay the warchiefs, who do not get replaced periodically as captains do. After doing so, the story will take the player to an entirely new area, with five new warchiefs, and this time the story will ask you to turn all five to your side - either by turning the warchiefs themselves, or by turning their captains and politically maneuvering the captains into replacing them.
This second area, with its emphasis on turning uruks to your side and interacting more directly with Sauron's Army, is where the game really comes into its own (though assassinating the warchiefs in the previous region can be fairly engaging as well), but it's very easy to run afoul of the exact same problem; the game presents that the best way to turn a warchief is to turn one of their captains and maneuver them into replacing them, but the fastest way is actually to confront the warchief directly and ignore the captains entirely. Your turned forces will aid you later in the game, but only the warchiefs; the game entirely disregards how much you might have weakened Sauron's army by disposing of captains, and captains you've turned will be entirely forgotten by the game during the ending sequence.
In other words, this is an open-world game with a very linear story, which is presented as optional to pursue whenever you wish, but is not; you really must pursue the story as soon as possible to make your open-world actions meaningful, and only certain open-world actions have any real impact on advancing the game. This is a frustrating situation for players, as the game essentially gives you meaningless freedom; you can choose to either do what needs to be done, or 'waste time' interacting with the most interesting and detailed aspect of the entire game. Combined with a combat system that seems not to know what it wants to do with itself - constantly plagued by slow-motion sequences and cinematic kill-cams despite the fact that you tend to fight as many as dozens of enemies at once, meaning the player spends more time watching fights than participating in them - and the game can be off-putting to those unaware of its draws and flaws.
I recommend getting the game (especially with how cheap it is on sale), because it tells an interesting story (though Tallion, the main character, occasionally feels off-putting in his behavior early on; he gets over it before the end), presents some very interesting mechanics, and will generally create memorable and positive experiences for a player before they get through it. I highly suggest avoiding combat as much as possible throughout (the game will force you into enough big fights before it's all over that you will get sick of them), focusing on the story missions as strictly as possible, and generally playing with the mindset of a stealthy assassin and infiltrator rather than a superhero. If played in that fashion, I believe the negatives of the game will be minimized while the best aspects are highlighted. Oh, and though the game never tells you this, you can fast-travel from anywhere on the worldmap, directly to any tower you have visited; it makes things substantially quicker.

Overall, I can definitely recommend the game and I'm not disappointed in having purchased it.

Condition Zero comes with 2 modules:
- Provides a slightly different MP experience to that of CS1.6, mostly graphical changes with a few gameplay changes. Also has a player vs. bots singleplayer mode, which is essentially just multiplayer with bots instead of humans, but with added objectives to make it a bit more difficult.
- A scripted single player campaign similar to something you'd see in Quake or Unreal Tournament.
For simplicity's sake I'll go over the changes CZ introduces, just keep in mind this isn't something I've thoroughly researched or anything of the sort, just what I know from playing multiple versions of CS for around a decade now. If you don't know the core gameplay of Counter Strike to understand these changes... well then go buy 1.6 and then consider picking up CZ.
Outside of the additions I mentioned at the beginning of the review, that's really the extent of the changes. Mostly all visual changes.
So the question is... do these changes warrant a purchase? Not in the slightest. For various reasons, if you're buying this for multiplayer, you're better off just playing 1.6.
In my eyes, the only reason to pick up CZ is for the Deleted Scenes. However I don't believe Deleted Scenes is actually worth the $10 CZ goes for.
Basically the campaign is a collection of missions with no overarching story or really anything of interest in the way of plot. They are all linear. They take place in different locales around the world. They are all played on the CT side, although the factions will differ. They offer a very small amount of puzzle solving. They have boss fights. They have forced stealth sections.

Starbound is a fun game and when I first played it, I was so hooked at playing it to relieve my stress from work. But as I progress through the story and all the side quests, I got bored of it a little bit since some quests are rather repetitive while you explore other planets.
Would I still recommend it? Yeah sure...it is still fun to play. But if you'll easily get bored of the side quests and how the story progressed, this game might not be for you.

Starbound had a lot of promise, and a lot of potential. Sadly it squandered both. The game's movement system is janky and floaty, which becomes very unfun when you have enemies that move at about five times the speed of your character and can demolish you in two or three hits. Effectively guns are the only even remotely viable option, spitting in the face of anyone who wants a different playstyle, and the various races have no effect other than mild cosmetic flair, while the overall game plays like a bad europlatformer, quite likely seen as a good thing through the rose-tinted nostalgia of the developers vision.
The boss fights are basically slug-fests in which you have neither the damage output nor the damage-absorbtion to compete with the enemies, with which you are locked in a small enclosed space with little room to maneuver and few options other than "Get hit and die, come back and do it again". The tech-skills offer a slight improvement but the timings on the dodges and jumps are still so wonky and unfun that mastering them feels like a game of chance rather than developing any kind of actual skill.
The game seemed like it was going in a nicer direction for a bit but then several of the updates basically rolled back the playstyle content to what it was originally, again spitting in the faces of anyone who wants to play something other than a gunrunning shootmans in this supposed sandbox. In addition to this the planets all feel very same-y and the quests simultaneously manage to take up all your time -and- be boring somehow.
I wish I could reccommend this game. I wanted so badly for Starbound to be good.... but it's not. And it only gets worse with time.

This game is fun. It's also dark, and some people of a certain religious or moral persuasion really won't like it. There's a reason for the darkness and moral ambiguity, though, which I'll expand on later.
You play a character named Grimm, whose mission is to restore the 21st century versions of fairy tales to their original medieval purpose. This involves removing as much pink and shiny “niceness” as possible, and replacing it with darkness and corruption. That said, the whole thing is handled in a fairly humorous manner.
The graphics are not spectacular, and the game play is not demanding. It is, however, very funny, and I'm enjoying it a lot.
If I have a gripe, it's that the game doesn't even attempt to address the censorship of the sexual content of the old fairy stories. On the one hand, given the current moral panic over the effects of computer games, I can understand. But on the other hand, isn't it just that censorship that the game seeks to address?
Anyway, it's an enjoyable game, and very thought provoking.
I apologise for this next section. It started as a review, but became an essay. I'm concerned that some people who have written about this game don't understand the history or purpose behind it.
The stories we now know as “fairy tales” were largely based on folk tales current in 16th and 17th century Europe. The stories, however, are in many cases much older. They captured people's imagination, and were passed down orally from generation to generation, because they performed a valuable teaching function. They warned people of the dangers out there. They were not originally intended for children, and many of them explore extremely violent, sexual and disturbing themes.
For instance, the oldest known version of “Sleeping Beauty” is “Sole, Luna, e Talia” recorded by Giambattista Basile, published in 1634. In this story, the handsome prince does not kiss Beauty to wake her. Instead, he rapes her while she's unconscious, and then departs, apparently without a thought. Leaving her still comatose, but now also pregnant with twins.
In the original version of “Red Riding Hood”, there's no granny, no cottage, and no huntsman. There's just a little girl, alone in the forest, and a wolf. And it kills her, and eats her. She doesn't get rescued, there's no happy ending, she's dead.
19th century writers such as the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen recounted many of these stories. But, in keeping with the moral code of their time, completely removed the sexual references, and greatly toned down the violence. Even so, this sanitisation was nowhere near enough for 20th century moralists. Disney is an easy target here, but Disney are far from alone in further Bowdlerising the stories to the point where they're fluffy, happy, and completely inoffensive. The problem is that the modern versions of these stories are also totally meaningless, and devoid of any of the original teaching. “And they all lived happily ever after” is a modern lie. It's not true now, and in 1600 no-one would have been stupid enough to say it.
That's what American McGee is getting at here – these stories were originally extremely nasty, but deliberately so. They were intended to teach lessons about a violent, dangerous and untrustworthy world. In censoring them to suit modern sensibilities, they have been completely stripped of their original power and purpose.
While being pretty basic on the gameplay side of things, it's the style and storytelling that really makes it compelling.

I'm a big fan of the type of games and don't get me wrong, I'm not bashing the game or say it isn't entertaining (I'll probably play it again, once the bitterness of dying because I don't own a dog while being the equivalent of an archmage subsides).
The thing is, when I pick up a game like this one I expect to have fun discovering the multiple endings it contains, not trying my hardest not to die and then find out which ending I end up with.
I understand the concept of the game is to "live different lives, learning from last time's demise", but when I actually played it just felt like a game of memorization; the story is kind of generic and there doesn't exist much foreshadowing in it.
There should be something in the narrative that tells me certain skills might be necessary in the future, but instead it's just a game of trial and error, which becomes tiring after a number of playthroughs.
My biggest gripe is that most events happen out of the blue, and as the story progresses they need bigger and bigger skill checks. The problem with this is that if you neglected said skill (or group of) you're toast; you were practically dead 10 turns ago, but you just have to keep playing until the game decides to kill you.
Seeing the tweaks that have been made to the game, I believe that something could be done to help the gameplay without straying from the concept of the game. I picked up LLTQ for $2.50 or $5 during a sale and am essentially done with it after about 5 hours’ worth of play. It’s surprisingly enjoyable but I can’t recommend it because it’s too short and weighed down by an overly complex skill system that will only appeal to a very niche market.
First of all, I give it extra points for the amount of effort that went into all the different story options & skill choices. Critics say it’s too linear but that’s not entirely true. Having the same events occur at the same point in the story allows you to strategically plan how to overcome challenges. If random events were procedurally generated each time you played, you would only be able to survive by dumb luck. Also, you can unlock extra dialogue choices, outfits and hidden events depending on which skills you develop and actions you take.
It is fun to fail at a skill check, possibly die, then replay and build your character differently and overcome a story obstacle. However, the further into the story an event occurs, the further you need to backwards plan for it. This gets complicated due to the labyrinthine way the story events snake together with learning skills & plotting mood adjustments (different moods give bonuses & penalties to learning different skills) and the only way to get around it is to write down some notes about which events occur at which times. While I appreciate all of the multiple endings and achievements available, unlocking those would require way more effort than most people would be willing to spend. The game does give you an option to export a text log of story events, but it doesn’t include any information about skill checks so it’s not nearly as useful as it could be.
I was still having a pretty good time despite the flaws because I liked the story, but just when I felt like things were getting interesting, it ended. You only need to survive through 40 turns or so to win, and those turns go by blazingly fast when you already know which choices you’re going to make.
LLTQ gets an A for effort but I simply can’t advise anyone to buy it unless the thought of manually charting out every story event, skill point expenditure & mood adjustment through trial & error appeals to you. It will keep you amused for a few hours and you’ll have no need to ever go back to it.

This is a very hard game to review under Steam's system of recommended versus not recommended. Even though I have it set to not recommended, I plan on continuing to play this game extensively. I also think it's a very well made game with extremely tight balance. Yes, even Dan is playable in this game (though still not great, by design).
If you're a fighting game enthusiast, then odds are you already own this game. If you don't, and you really are into fighting games, then get it. I fully recommend it, just be aware that this game is much slower paced than most 2d fighters. Combos tend to be short and difficult to execute, as opposed to being long and fairly easy. Other than that, there's nothing here that should be out of the ordinary to you.
For everyone else... this is not a game you can simply pick up and begin playing. The single player content is as bare bones as could be, providing a training mode, a short arcade mode, and then a series of trials for every character. I'll get to the trials in a moment.
Quite simply, this game does not teach you anything. It does not delicately introduce you to its mechanics and help you learn. If you want to play this game, you must dedicate yourself to it or else you're basically throwing your money away. I've played a lot of fighting games, especially in the Soul Calibur, Smash and Marvel vs Capcom series, and this game is the single most prohibitavely difficult game to begin playing of any of them. The trials I mentioned, while they do help you learn some things about your chosen character, there's nothing in the game that teaches you about the core fundamentals of how to play it.
At this point, I've spent more time practicing, studying (using online research, as again there's not much here that will teach you on its own) and learning this game than any other I've ever played. That includes things traditionally considered hard to learn, such as MOBAs like Dota 2. In fact I'd probably guess I've spent as much time with this game trying to learn it as I spent with the majority of the college classes I took when I was still in school. I am not exaggerating in the slightest. And after all that, I still lose the vast majority of the time, despite the fact I have fairly good win percentages in other fighting games. Or at the least, not as crushingly awful as my current 15ish to 120ish win:loss ratio.
You're also probably going to want to buy a specialized controller for it, like a Madkatz Fightpad or an arcade stick (and good arcade sticks cost as much as some tablets, keep in mind). You can play it with a keyboard or a regular controller, and there are a small number of really good keyboard warriors, but I think it's generally accepted that these methods are harder than playing with a stick or a specialized fightpad controller.
And that's really why I have to set this game as not recommended, despite the fact I love it. It's entirely unacceptable that I am currently almost 70 hours played after doing online research since the game does almost nothing to teach you anything itself, and I still barely understand what's going on. At this point I'm just continuing to play it because I'm just starting to reach the point where I don't feel completely lost and overwhelmed, but the satisfaction I get out of it is about the same as if I had just booted up my Wii U and played Smash Brothers instead, a game which is far more accessable.
If you have a true commitment to learning this game, and you don't mind getting utterly crushed for an extensive amount of time and buying extra peripherals just to play it, then go ahead and get it. Also, pick Guile or Ryu for the first little while, as those characters are made to help new players learn the game while still being powerful at high skill levels. Pick Ryu if you like quarter circle characters, or Guile if you like charge characters... and if you don't know what a charge character is, look it up, because the game won't tell you. For everyone else, save your money and look elsewhere. You will just get frustrated and feel like you wasted your time.

This game, I feel, is leaps and bounds ahead of DayZ. With the basebuilding, crafting, difficulty of mutants, I find it a lot of fun. I truly love DayZ, and yes, Miscreated isn't being developed on a brand new engine, but I can almost promise you that if you like DayZ, you'll love this game.

So far, i like this game. i like the survival aspect of it all. i like having to scavenge for gear, and decide whether i should keep one gun with 5 bullets, or another gun with 4. i like having to keep an eye on my thirst, and hunger levels, and hope that i can find more cans of pears, or dog food before it gets too low. i like running away from mutants, and roving bands of players alike because i've spent hours finding what's in my inventory, and i don't want to lose it. i like building a small wooden shack to use as a base of operations. i like creating a clan of friends to play with together.
i don't like being limited to one small, and one large storage crate per plot of land, shared by everyone in the clan. In what post-apocalyptic setting would a survivor *not* hoard food, or ammo? If you were only hungry enough to eat one can of dog food, but there were three more on the shelf, would you just leave them there hoping nobody else would come along and pick them up? No. You'd grab them and stick them in your stash for later. Would you leave a pile of shotgun shells behind a bar, or would you take them and save them for later?
Items not in use are not rendered. Whether it's in your backpack, or a storage crate at your base, storage is handled by a database. One entry, or a hundred aren't going to make much of a difference if your servers are configured properly.
Item decay is another gripe i have. If i want to go on vacation for a week, you might as well give all your stuff to another player. Yes, you can extend the decay time by making your base larger, but why? If you don't want to build a fortress, you shouldn't be penalized for it.
Yes, it's early access. Yes, it's still in development. i get all of that. But without being able to store your hard earned finds, in a base that will still be there after a week of inactivity. i like the game. It's a hell of a lot better than others like it (*cough* DayZ *cough*). i still recommend it. i just hope storage, and base decay gets better in the future.

Overall Rating 7.5/10
The Good
There are extremely limited expositions, and pretty much nails the 'show don't tell' aspect. Mae and the personalities she meets along the way become the strongest driving factor of the experience. You are rewarded for digging more into the story and to explore in general. Story-telling is charming, funny and manages to deliver a relatable and perhaps contemporary, message. The backgrounds in this game are absolutely stunning, while accompanied by soundtracks that are not too far behind in terms of helping to contribute to the mood of the game. Gameplay is enriched by usage of mostly platform mechanics, and creative mini-games spread throughout.
The Bad
The game is worth less than the sum of its parts. The plot writing fell apart near the final stages of the story. The climax did not live up to the build-up. Questions central to main plot were not satisfactorily addressed and the game ends abruptly. Gameplay also becomes repetitive and a second playthrough isn't a tempting option for the most part.
The End

This game is like my new addiction.  I asked some friends who owned the game what it was about, and they all recommended it.  Therefore, I tried it out.  During my first play-through, I was a little disappointed.....but then I got addicted after dying the first time.  Your first few play-throughs will be dedicated to beating the game (which you will most likely not do your first few play times).  After you beat the game, then comes the real challenge: finding all the deaths and achievements.  Yes, this is a game where the ending is boring, and the stuff in-between is what you want.
This game is both entertaining and frustrating.  Every choice you make influences the gameplay, and I'm amazed by how many possibilities there are.  I know I still haven't found them all.  As you play more of the game, you learn what choices can help or hurt you, but it's the things you never think of that may get you achievements.  Some of the achievements are super easy, but others are super hard to achieve.  You can have the princess all set-up to do well on one scenario, but find out later that a choice you made earlier in the game caused you to completely skip that scenario.  It keeps the game interesting, and it will get you hooked.
What are the downsides to this game?  Well, it can get very, very repetitive.  You can skip certain dialogues, but that only speeds things up a little.  When you are trying to get to a scenario in week 35, it takes forever to get to that point because you have to play through each week.  Yes, you can save right before that scenario and go back to it in case something goes wrong, but you want to make sure you have the correct classes and mood.  That can take a while to build-up when you start at the beginning of the game.  The save files help sometimes, but you may end up with so many saved games that you forget what is what even if you name them.  There are sooo many pieces to the game that need to be right that it's not really worth saving a game all the time.
Is it worth the $10?  To me, I think it's worth a little less.  I really wanted this game, so I waited until it was on sale half off.  It was worth that price, but I do think the full price is a little much.  If they expanded on the game, it may be.  It's one of those games that's fun to play at first, but once you figure everything out, the game will lose most of the fun aspect.  However, I can guarantee it will take a ton of gameplay to earn all acheivements if you aren't cheating.  35 hours of gameplay later, and I still have 1 death, 2 epilogues, and 4 acheivements to find.

A western visual novel about a young princess' arduous survival until coronation. Don't let the cutesy design fool you - it is only there to hide a dark and complex world where everyone wants you dead or in their bed.
Pros
* Surprisingly mature themes, including wars, assassinations, political conspiracies, human sacrifices and forbidden romances
* Replayability as long as you are curious and savvy enough with your skill checks. The main plot won't change but a whole lot of side plots will open up
* The sprites are beautifully drawn and the characters are compelling if you manage to dig in their little secrets
Cons
* You will die a lot and most of the time it will be unfair. There's really no room for failings and you will need to gauge carefully your training in each of the 40 weeks until the end of the story, which is relatively linear so each death will feel frustrating
* It's really a game of mathematics and planning after learning from your errors rather than a RPG, which will catch a lot of people unaware of what they actually bought
Read some tips before starting and remember you can skip already read dialogs. Be prepared to rule the world or die trying!

The screenshots and videos on the Steam page highlight a beautiful world with crafting, spear fishing, building, etc... Which this game does have all those things.

I could go on for a good while about what's wrong with this game, and it's currently my first and only ever refunded game. I highly recommend avoiding this game at all costs during it's early access phase.
Once the game is finished and properly made, it has promise to be absolutely outstanding.  But as it is currently, I wouldn't even play this if it were free.

Starbound is a fun game and when I first played it, I was so hooked at playing it to relieve my stress from work. But as I progress through the story and all the side quests, I got bored of it a little bit since some quests are rather repetitive while you explore other planets.
Would I still recommend it? Yeah sure...it is still fun to play. But if you'll easily get bored of the side quests and how the story progressed, this game might not be for you.

Starbound had a lot of promise, and a lot of potential. Sadly it squandered both. The game's movement system is janky and floaty, which becomes very unfun when you have enemies that move at about five times the speed of your character and can demolish you in two or three hits. Effectively guns are the only even remotely viable option, spitting in the face of anyone who wants a different playstyle, and the various races have no effect other than mild cosmetic flair, while the overall game plays like a bad europlatformer, quite likely seen as a good thing through the rose-tinted nostalgia of the developers vision.
The boss fights are basically slug-fests in which you have neither the damage output nor the damage-absorbtion to compete with the enemies, with which you are locked in a small enclosed space with little room to maneuver and few options other than "Get hit and die, come back and do it again". The tech-skills offer a slight improvement but the timings on the dodges and jumps are still so wonky and unfun that mastering them feels like a game of chance rather than developing any kind of actual skill.
The game seemed like it was going in a nicer direction for a bit but then several of the updates basically rolled back the playstyle content to what it was originally, again spitting in the faces of anyone who wants to play something other than a gunrunning shootmans in this supposed sandbox. In addition to this the planets all feel very same-y and the quests simultaneously manage to take up all your time -and- be boring somehow.
I wish I could reccommend this game. I wanted so badly for Starbound to be good.... but it's not. And it only gets worse with time.

Overall Rating 7.5/10
The Good
There are extremely limited expositions, and pretty much nails the 'show don't tell' aspect. Mae and the personalities she meets along the way become the strongest driving factor of the experience. You are rewarded for digging more into the story and to explore in general. Story-telling is charming, funny and manages to deliver a relatable and perhaps contemporary, message. The backgrounds in this game are absolutely stunning, while accompanied by soundtracks that are not too far behind in terms of helping to contribute to the mood of the game. Gameplay is enriched by usage of mostly platform mechanics, and creative mini-games spread throughout.
The Bad
The game is worth less than the sum of its parts. The plot writing fell apart near the final stages of the story. The climax did not live up to the build-up. Questions central to main plot were not satisfactorily addressed and the game ends abruptly. Gameplay also becomes repetitive and a second playthrough isn't a tempting option for the most part.
The End

I've got a superhero I've created who would get into this better then I, so I just channel him when playing.

Your mission in the game is to walk around the level 'infecting' (restoring?) evil back into the story from what it has become *Over time so many Grimm stories have became kid-friendly politically correct fairytales*. An incredibly well put-together game, with refreshing dialogue, music, graphics, and mystery. The story is very fleshed out and there is a lot of information packed into such a tiny game. Many people complain about the length; some even saying it took them 20 minutes to beat. Well if it took you 20 minutes you're FAR from experiencing the full game. I exhausted almost all dialogue options, and searched everything around the house, made my decision thoughtfully on who to kill, and it took me a little under 2 hours. I don't believe game length matters as long as it was the CORRECT length. Now, while Postmortem DID end a bit early, the length was fairly well established and the game ended when it should have, more or less.
The characters have rich and thought-out stories and have realistic responses and what you say seems to matter. I would've liked more options and more people, though as far as a dialogue-driven game goes, Postmortem does what it sets out to do very well. Postmortem has incredible potential and I hope to see a sequel in the near future. I wouldn't be upset if they released DLC (fairly priced, of course) which consisted of other houses and events with the same premise: just more scenarios.
It was very enjoyable to play through and listen to each character's story and that's saying a lot because I don't usually enjoy games like this, and lately my attention span has been getting shorter and shorter, so it's rare a game captures my attention for this long nowadays. But alas, Postmortem did, and for good reason, it's a great game and if you take your time playing through it and actually make a thoughtful decision, there can be a good amount of impact and intensity to it which makes it a good experience overall.
I recommend buying this game if you like murder mysteries (even though it's somewhat backwards since you're the one doing the killing), dialogue and story-driven games, rich characters, charming graphics and soundtrack, and an engaging story overall. I would also recommend waiting until it goes on sale if you're worried about the length of it, as $6.99 is a bit much for a 2 hour game for some people.

There is a bloody conflict between Newagers, who care little for history and culture, and Oldagers, who wish to remain set in the traditional ways. You are Death, and are assigned to a fundraising party held to benefit (although the term is applied loosely) a school that was recently vandalized. Guests come from all walks of life, and have their own political beliefs and emotional attachments. Everyone there plays a role in the hostilities, and it is your job to select one who must die -- thus sending events hurtling in a particular direction.
You could simply approach anyone, tap them on the shoulder, and that's that. However, the real meat of this game is to investigate each room, ask many questions about events and each attendee, and maybe even sneak a peek at some hidden items. At the end, take a look at your journal and select the one who will have the greatest impact (for better or for worse). Once the deed is done, a series of news articles will pop up and show you the fruits of your labour. You'll also have a brief, albeit rather pointless, scene with your target. After this, you can compare your choices to others, much like in the Telltale adventure games.
Okay, let's get the bad out of the way first.
1) The resolution options are limited.
2) There's a distracting amount of screen tearing.
3) The controls are fiddly.
4) There seems to be an average of one spelling mistake every sentence.
5) Once you've exhausted the 20 or so dialogue options for every character, and there aren't many of them, the game essentially ends. Well, unless you want to stand around and listen to the snippets of classical music that make up Postmortem's soundtrack.
6) The political beliefs are fairly simplistic (e.g. foreigners are bad, women don't deserve rights, capitalism is awesome, etc.) and aren't as nuanced, or blended as I'd like.
So what's good about it?
1) There aren't many games like this. A locked room... er, make that a locked apartment mystery, with no real right or wrong answer.
2) A hefty amount of backstory and information links the characters together, be it psychologically, socially, emotionally, etc. A fair amount of thought went into all this.
3) It doesn't overstay its welcome. As I mention in Neg.6, there isn't much to do after talking to the people, so you can make your decision rather quickly -- perhaps in 45-60 minutes should you examine every nook and cranny, and draw out every last line of dialogue.
I do wish there had been a few more locations. I read a review mentioning attending a protest, maybe also visiting the host's factory, and so forth. Then again, I believe this would only expose some weaknesses in the game's foundation. Nonetheless, with more and/or stronger writers (and an editor!), I think this could work, and work well.
Is Postmortem a great game? No, but it's definitely not a bad one. It has a strong premise, and good parts, but is brought down by its linearity and lack of polish. Nonetheless, it can be found on sale often, and at a steep discount, it's an experience I would recommend.
Just know what you're getting into first.

Long Live The Queen is a game that features trial and error, logical thinking and strategy.
To win, Elodie must survive to her coronation, but there are a lot of dangers on the way. Every week, you can pick two classes to let Elodie study on, varying from social skills to combat experience.
An important factor is Elodie's mood: It's hard to be social when you're depressed, but that's a good opportunity to learn more about something cheerful, like singing. Each weekend you can let Elodie do an activity that affects her mood (while the story may also affect it a little, such as a snake scaring Elodie). When skilled enough in a certain area, such as for example Military, Elodie can unlock a Military outfit that boosts said skill a little.
As stated, strategy will be involved as Elodie's skills heavily affects how the story plays out. For example, there is a part where Elodie is given a box of chocolate that is poisoned. Depending on certain skills, Elodie will either know it is poisoned, or she will have the patience to leave it for later (in which a steward steals it, leading to his death). Lacking any of these, means you aren't even given the option to not eat the chocolate as Elodie will be too eager to feel the sweet taste of soon-to-be-death.
This is why it is also a bunch of trial-and-error: Your first time playing, you're not going to know what's coming at you; eventually you'll slowly progress and remember what events are coming ahead in which you can plan stratetic mood alterings to help you level up the skills needed to pass the events.
It's a very calm and fun game that I can recommend to people who want something really simple.
Not recommended for the faint of heart who can't read about Elodie dying in many different ways...

One of the best survival games I've played so far. No zombies or mosters. Just you, mother nature and sharks! ... yes sharks!
You survive a plane crash and end up in a big ocean full of islands. You have your watch, which is able to track your vital signs, and some basic stuff. You take the raft from the plane and find the nearest island. Finally with your feet on land, it hits you! You need to survive and that's not going to happen if you don't take action right away. So start planning. Find food, water and materials to build your island paradise.
Your only enemy is you and nature.
As you explore the islands, you'll find wrecks of ships and planes. Explore them and go treasure hunting. Not real treasure, gold is of no use on a deserted island. You'll find useful stuff like water bottles, axes and engine parts.
Build your house, traps for catching fish and learn how to survive using just that what you can find. It's an intens game.
Buy this if you like survival games. This is early access but it's really good and fun. One of the best early access survival games out there.

Biggest reason for my negative review is incoming, with MAJOR SPOILER ALERT IF YOU CONTINUE READING.
So. Yeah it was an alright story. Alright. Not great, not amazing, not compelling, it was alright. And then at the end they went and poopoo'd on your parade by taking the literary suicide copout of "It was all just a dream."  ... It wasn't a dream, but every time you die in game your character ACTUALLY dies canonically in the story. Your death is PART of the story, restarting is PART of the story.  Because the main character is stuck in a time loop.
Ever see that movie with Tom Cruise where he gets infected by some alien thing and resets to a save point every time he dies?  Don't. It's bad.   But that's basically what's happening here.
The main character has to relive every event between point A and point B every time he dies, always starting at A.
At the "end" of the game you jump in a black hole and go back in time and also infect yourself with... some sort of.. timey wimey disease that was really not elaborated on at all.
so the end of the game is just a "it was all just a dream/recurrence" copout. Your decisions in the game have no impact whatsoever, no matter what you do the main character is going to go through the exact same sequence of events over and over, sometimes dying earlier (like when you were struggling on first mission) sometimes making it to the end of the full circuit (like when you beat the game and jump in the wormhole.)
In summation, the story uses a literary tool which equates to "and it was all just a dream" at the very end of the story. This invalidates the story. The story is about 85% of the selling point of this "game" (I'd argue it's more of a choose your own adventure story than a game) ...   So the ending invalidates 85% of this "game" entirely.
$10 for a story that is invalidated by its ending.  I'm really glad I got this one on sale. I don't understand how it got such positive reviews.

Gods will be watching is a pretty novel hybrid between an adventure and strategy game.
Essentially the gameplay puts you into a tough situation, where you have to deal several pressing concerns by giving out orders to your companions, which may bring you closer to resolution but may also result in their death. It's a game of tough decisions. Ultimately it is possible to save everyone but it will often require practice, planning and a bit of luck to pull off. Speaking of luck, the game has a degree of RNG that ensures that you are never certain that everything will go according to plan, however you are usually given tools to avoid risking too much as well. This is however still something that can put people off, so the developer was kind enough to add a 'puzzle mode' which reduces the effect of RNG. The game is still however pretty difficult, expect to fail a few times till you get through it. The game does come with an 'easy' mode that makes the challenges noticeably easier to overcome, but there's a reason the developer states that the game should be played on normal and I also feel it ruins the experience to go 'puzzle mode' or 'easy mode'.
In the end I recommend it provided you're not put off by the difficulty, particularly if making tough decisions is your thing.

A brilliant piece of narative driven game design. An interactive thriller indeed.
Mechanically it is a point-and-click algorithm finding simulator, but make no mistake- it is almost a true rpg by the sheer force of role playing it stimulates you to do. The trick is the difficulty of the game- 90% of your play time you are battling against the overwhelming odds, trying to figure out the best way to beat a chapter.
That means two things: firstly, that it's never a dull moment, you are constantly hooked to see how the situation reacts to your actions, and secondly: it contributes to never ending tencsion, wich in turn bonds you and the protagonists, adding weight to the decisions.
The writing feels a bit off at the beginning, with somewhat heavy exposition, but quickly picks up, as the story progresses.
In conclusion- a bold and uncompromising experiment, a true "game" and a definite "must try" for everyone who considers himself a gamer
