State of Decay is by far, and I truly do mean by far, the best Zombie/Apocolyptic game I've ever played. If I had to describe the game mechanics put simply, it's a mixture of Sims & GTA with zombies. I can't even begin to explain the thrill of being thrown into a simulation of a zombie outbreak such as what Undead Labs has blissfully crafted. What I can confidently say though, is that if State of Decay were to have been introduced multiplayer compatibility, it would have easily obtained much more recognition. Even more so to cast a shadow on popular runner up games like DayZ.
Now, don't get me wrong, I'm not describing SoD as a masterpiece among video games, it surely has it's fair share of bugs and other kinks. Though it managed to do what more popular titles (of the same genre) such as `Dead Island`, `Left 4 Dead`, `The Last of Us`, & `Dead Rising`, did not. SoD allowed players true open world freedom. By this, I mean players are not bound to a specific story line per se.
Players can roam the vast environment offered to them to do as they please. Want to run over zombies? Go for it. Want to spend your day hacking and slashing, battering brains and flesh all over the place like a madman? Go for it. Want to scavange for supplies to keep your group members alive and kicking? Go for it. Want to build an unpenetrable zombie-proof fortress? Have at it.
I'll end this review with the following statement,
If you haven't tried this game as of yet, do so, and I guarantee it will blow your favorite zombie game out of the water.

8/10 - Damien Hunt, The New Sherlock Holmes?!
When I found this game I was pretty excited. I love visual novels and this one is a little more interactive than others. This game includes (3) episodes that take about an hour each. You can achieve multiple endings and catch different suspects as you see fit.
You play as Damien Hunt, a junior police detective from the Crownstown Police Department. Typically, all new detectives are paired with a veteran but for the first time, due to circumstances beyond control, you are paired with another rookie. Everyone claims the city is  now safe and peaceful so the new arrangement is fine...but will these two newcomers find out otherwise?
You will collect evidence, interrogate witnesses and suspects, travel around the city visiting more than 15 locations and piece together everything in an effort to apprehend criminals that are secretly plaguing the city. My only complaint is that the hotspots are often difficult to identify and this makes triggering future events frustrating at times. Please note you may need to click the same objects more than once, for different information.
Overall, I would definitely pay $5 if you like visual novels. This one won’t be put in the epic category but provides a really fun experience!

Very well-written game. Immediate impression: Very short, technically one level, about 2 hours unless you rush in and do whatever with little regard for writing; no action, just choices; rather interesting characters and a cool concept.
Yes, I did not stutter-- this game is super short. You're in a mansion and you're talking to about 7 people about this and that, and you choose one person to die. That's really it. Except there's a good amount of reading involved. So if you hate reading and character development, then steer clear. Otherwise, welcome to literacy!
The developers did a great job of making the conversations... conversational. Like many RPGs of our time, the tendency is to give the player only a few options. In Postmortem's case, the only times I felt limited were when I needed to make a solid choice on a morality issue. Yes, you're death, but you yourself are playing. And what kind of topics are discussed in Postmortem? Politics and morality. Ah yes. They cleverly change the official titles of the left and right wing into something more general, but all the ideals are there. Between talking to the characters, we're given insight into several 'current issues', such as xenophobia, feminism, big corporate buyouts, and apparently a bit of gay rights (I somehow got that involved in the end game).
I liken the moral choices to that of the Walking Dead game by Telltale. A lot of times, you the player must draw from your own perspective and answer as you would, if you were in that same situation. Unless of course you're roleplaying as something specific. No matter how you play the game, you get to see how your choice affects that world, as well as what little actions you've done while playing (did you gossip about someone or snoop a little, for example).
These games are always refreshing to play occasionally. And should you feel like spending a bit of time with a choose-your-own adventure that makes you question your own political/moral standpoint, Postmortem will be a great game for you. Simple and easy to play, but sometimes tricky in the choices you make.
For the record, I played as close to middle-of-the-road as possible, and the ending actually kind of reflected that. Awesome~

I played this game multiplayer with mods (frackin universe) and had a lot of fun. It's very fun to explore and see new planets, creatures, and loot. I really like the open world approach that lets you choose your own pace without punishing you.
However, the base game is a complete mess. There are essential and basic features missing, such as knowing distance, inventory sorting, and basic item stacking. The campaign is boring and repetitive. It consists of "Go here, scan this. Go there, fight this." and that's it. Without the help of mods, digging and collecting resources is as tedious and boring as it gets. The amount of upgrades to do basic functions without wasting hours digging several blocks at a time is absurd. By far, the worst thing about this game is the performance. The game locks to 60fps, but you're lucky if you get that most of the time. Some planets bring your fps down to a crippling 7fps, other planets force you to wait for sections to load if you are going too fast. For a 2D game that is unacceptable. I have had times when the game just runs slow for no reason in dense npc areas.
I recommend this game ONLY if you play with mods, friends, or love to grind endlessly for the fun of grinding.

Ignore the fact I only have 27 hours on this, I recently bought this version and haven't had much time to play it.
Regardless, I love this game. No, not just this game, all of these games. In total, I have played this game, dark souls 2, and 3 for well over 500 hours. Only that was on Xbox, not here. But why did I play it so much?
•it forces you to pay attention to your environment
•the combat feels good and is very rewarding to those who are patient enough to wait for an opening
•the bosses are USUALLY fair (I'm looking at you bed of chaos) and when you beat them it's one of the best feelings in the world
•it has TONS of different play-styles. For example, three different sets of spells (fire,magic,and miracles.) and maybe 7 or so different weapon types, with every weapon (about) in each type being a little different)
•unlike most RPGs this game is VERY complicated and will feel a little overwhelming at first. Honestly, you should try to get as far as you can without wikis but I along with most other people had to use them at one point or another.
•not to mention that while you can sometimes feel as if where you are is WAY to hard, usually you just need to either go somewhere else for now or look at it through a different set of eyes.
Now. This game isn't all sunshine and smiles. There are a few MAJOR downsides to this game
-multiplayer kinda sucks for PVE... your summon can't heal themselves so usually you either waste healing items getting them to full health or don't heal them at all when you heal yourself.
-you NEED a mod called DSfix. It's easy to put in and I almost made this a positive because honestly the game looks, runs,-and is overall better with DSfix.
-you don't NEED a controller but if you don't use one... say goodbye to winning any multiplayer for a long time and say hello to no progress until you are used to using the controls with a keyboard. My opinion, just go spend like 10-20 bucks on a Xbox 360 controller.
-if you do want to do multiplayer there's a plus and a minus
+it is much quicker and more consistent than on the consoles (granted this was tested with someone on the same wifi at the same house so your experience may differ
-you can't do it at all without a mod. Don't remember the name so just look up dark souls multiplayer mod and you should get it (I'd recommend looking on the dark souls nexus)
So... that's my opinion of these wonderful games. I haven't even touched how deep the lore is or a multitude of other things but my fingers are starting to hurt soooooo...
TL:DR... This is the beginner to an amazingly deep and complex set of games and if you are willing to look past all the bad parts then you have found yourself a gem. But... I've gotta say. If you want good pvp... then play the second one. This one and the third one have AMAZING PVE but the pvp seems to fall short of fun sometimes

I wrote a review for this game back when it was in early access. It's still good, still fixed a lot of things I didn't like with Terraria. I'd still recommend it, but not as much because of these three major gripes I have with this game:
1) There's basically no need or benefit from building bases or colonies on planets. Yeah, they recently added farm animals, but that's about it. Everything you need you can get from the outpost, and the colonists you invite are just generic vendors save for an achivement you get for attacting ten special colonists. Yes, I know it's a game about space, but give us reasons to mark planets as our favorites, or more to do on them than just loot the surface, mine the ore, and then leave. Your ship is important, yes, and it's great that you can customize it to any way you see fit. But if you're going to give us these vast and diverse planets, give us more reasons to colonize them!
2) Building aforementioned useless colonies the way the player wants to is kind of hard when it comes to being creative. This also applies for when the players want to build anything in general. A lot of blocks people enjoy using for building have to be cheated in with admin commands. There should be ways to craft them! Maybe some kind of special crafting tool that specializes in blocks?
3) Multiplayer. The game is really unoptimized overall, but especially so in terms of this. So unless you have a fully dedicated server you can basically go screw yourself if you just want to play with one or two friends. A lot of people play this game to play with friends, and a lot of people don't want to go to a dedicated server filled with strangers for that. Some people do, and that's fine, but please make simple multiplayer not require an entire dedicated server just to play with a couple of friends. Even in singleplayer the game is very likely to crap itself because of things out of your control.

I bought this game back in the 2015 summer sale ( back when the sales were actually good ) and as you can see, I have a lot of experience with this game. I advice most people to ignore the negative reviews where people only have less than 3 hours as that is not enough time to form a real opinion on this game, also because some of the reviews are misleading and just r******d. I personally really enjoy this game, the game leans heavily on PVP for the moment as the game lacks proper survival that games such as DayZ have, more survival features are being added in the future though. Loot in this game is very different to most other survival games. Loot has set spawns in each house and other buildings for guns, ammo, food and water. But nothing ever spawns in the same place twice. Base building is in the game and at the moment, is very basic and isn't great. It uses a freeform system instead of the snaping into place system you would see in games like Rust. Recipes, or Blueprints are required to build and craft the more advanced parts and it can become a bit of a choir to find the right one that you require. Raiding someones base is also way to easy, all you need is an axe and you can chop one of the walls down within 10 minutes and you're in. The only way to keep your base safe is to either plan it out properIy, or have your base floating in the sky. Thankfully the devs are working on a fix for this as the floating bases at the moment can really break the immersion. I have not bothered with base building in the game for awhile now as the devs say they plan an overhaul for the whole thing. Guns fights and combat in the game are extremely satisfying and tense and can really get your heart pumping, guns sound and feel great to use and nothing feels better than wiping out a squad or taking down a geared guy. Melee combat needs work though and is only really useful for taking out mutants. There are 5 different types of mutants in the game, The brute, a two headed dog, The spike mutant, creepy looking one and the normalish looking one. 4 of those deal out roughly the same amount of damage with the Brute being able to take huge chunks of your health off if you get to close to it. A headshot with drop all of them but the brute, he requires a bit more firepower. The world of Miscreated is beautiful one, easily the best looking survival game there is, lush, dense forests and nice looking towns with detailed interiors make the world look and feel realistic. I missed out on a few other things such as being able to kill and take the meat of animals like Deers, Wolfs and Pigs so you can cook them over the fire. Also being able to split and swap out ammo with other mags. So while there are negitives, I do recommend this game to people who enjoy survival games and some good PVP. The game will continue to get better over time with the devs releasing monthly patches to improve the game with new content and bug fixes.

Counter Strike Condition Zero is the sequel to the original Counter Strike and now it includes a Single Player Campaign, so let's take a look shall we ?
When I mentioned that this game has a single player campaign, I didn't mean a story mode. The single player campaign is a very short bundle of missions where you have few objectives during each missions. Like rescue hostages, defuse bombs and take out terrorists with a specific weapon.
The missions are incredibly short and you can finish all 12 within 2 hours.
The AI will make the hostage missions a living hell. Once the round starts the AI are on the hunt to find any enemy player on the field and will not help you so don't expect any help from the AI. Getting a hostage to a drop off, before your team kills the entire enemy team.
The gameplay is not much different from the original Counter Strike so don't expect a major change.
Now for the feature everyone cares. THE MULTIPLAYER. It's almost completely dead. I had trouble finding a match and when I did get into a full lobby match, I felt bored and it's not as good as the original Counter Strike.
This game is not good, but it's not horrible either. The campaign is short and not worth the money and the multiplayer is slowly dying out. In the end only get this if you're a hardcore fan, otherwise get any other game in the franchise.
Final Rating:
6/10 - Okay

Despite having been a gamer since the 1970's "Stranded Deep" represents a lot of gaming firsts for me. It's the first "Early Access" title I've devoted serious time to. It's the first "survival" game I've played. It's one of the few games I've played that didn't have a stronger element of combat or some way to "win"; in a game like "The Sims" there was a clear "win" that isn't currently present in Stranded Deep. And my experience with Stranded Deep hasn't suffered because of any of these things.
On the whole I'd just say that Stranded Deep is a title that sucks you in. You never know what's lying on that island on the horizon until you build a raft and go check it out. You never know what piece of equipment you might find on that wrecked ship just off the shore of your current sanctuary. Will it hold a pair of flippers that will make swimming easier? Is there a bunch of tires chained to the submerged hull that you can use to make a raft? Does it hold the final part you need to make a boat motor? You won't know until you swim down and look. And that's where the "sucks you in" part comes into play. Does that island off in the distance have a bunch of sunken ships littering the sea around it's shores? You won't know until you go see for yourself.
Does Stranded Deep have problems? It sure does but even though I'm fairly new to Early Access I realize that most of the problems the game has mainly stem from it's status as an EA title more than for any other reason. So far the game has a lot to offer in a more "cerebral" experience than I'm used to and that's pretty cool. This is one EA title I'm eagerly waiting for to get a full release because while it has a fun factor in its current state I have a feeling when its completed it'll be a solid title.

I was a backer of this project on Indiegogo back in 2013, and while the final product is not
what I was expecting (i.e.
), I really,
love it.
I think Gods' has been underappreciated and unfairly reviewed simply because it poorly manages our expectations. I want to emphasise that
. You don't walk around freely, examine things, pick up or combine items. There's no inventory. There's no traditional adventure game puzzles. Again, it's not an adventure game. It's just not.
Most chapters are just one "room" with a clear objective, and you must manage the people and resources in that scene carefully to survive until the objective is achieved. The interface is minimalist: You don't get direct control of your character. Clicking a person or object in the scene brings up a context menu with a list of choices. Typical choices are conversational, issuing orders or performing an action. The "puzzle" aspect comes from failure. Each chapter, you have to figure out how these actions affect the variables and only then can you develop a strategy to balance and exploit them. Because you can fail before even trying all possible actions, you'll probably fail at least once per chapter.
The reason I think it's called an adventure game (a classification I strongly reject), besides superficially presenting as one, is it's a highly narrative experience, played out primarily through conversational in-game cutscenes leading into each chapter.


Some of the first PC games I played, around 25 years ago had this magical and mysterious air about them. They seemed so creative and imaginative and just so... out of nowhere. I don't really get that feeling these days, but I got it from Gods Will Be Watching. By chapter 5, I was totally sold, and after completion, I couldn't stop thinking about it for days. That's why I'm proud to have supported this game, and have featured it on my Steam profile ever since.
While it's far from perfect and I can completely understand why some people even go so far as to loathe it, to me, Gods' is an absolute treasure and is close to my heart. This has nothing to do with nostalgia and everything to do with artistic merit. There are many better designed games but somehow they're just not as memorable.

+ The price isn't high, which is one of the only reasons I picked this up initially.
Neutal
+/- Enemies pick up in number rather quickly on some levels, for some maybe too quickly
+/- 10 levels, not a lot for now but enough
+/- Match times are short, in 30 minutes I've played 5-6 of the 10 maps to completion
+/- More resolution options, no 1920x1080 yet, but I'm sure it's on it's way
+/- More variation in the Enemies, while they all are pretty much the same thing, visually there is a variation of at least 5 different "Knights". A good step in the right direction.
+/- Only one special ability, to summon 2 extra troops
Cons
----- No information on your upgrades/abilities, while you can guess/assume, you really shouldn't have to.
--- There is no tutorial.
-- There's no way to track your progression and there are no locked levels so there's no real sense of achievement or buildup.
- Some of the music duing the levels, while reflecting the art style is repetitive, some sound like a 5 second loop, others are more fleshed out luckily (The first two stages are the worst sounding)
- The SFX sounds aren't that great, they do their job but also run the risk of starting to sound annoying like some of the music.
I for one can't recommend this game at its current stage, but hopefully that will change within a few updates. Because as of right now, it doesn't bring anything new, different or better to the table. But don't put it out of your mind completely, just check back on it in a week or so and see if the reviews change at all, as the game is in early access and should grow to become something better over time.

I finished Night in the Woods for the first time and I am already on my second playthrough to get the rest of the achievements. First, I must thank my friend who gifted me this amazing game (which i eyed from the beggining when it was released on steam) and secondly I must thank everyone that contributed in creating it. It helped me get through an emotionally hard time this week.
Onto deeper thoughts:
- Visually I love the art style of the game, beautiful color palettes all around, really vibrant and radiating of happiness (and in some cases mystery or horror).
- The soundtrack is very well crafted and synced with the events and the switch from one song to another is almost undiscernable and very smooth, withouth breaking the immersion.
- Immersion! This game pulls you in it's world right from the beggining. The characters, dialogue, story, visual arrangement and soundtrack placement are so well done you forget you're playing a game.
Some cons:
- Even if you take your time to explore every corner of the game, listen to all the characters and what they have to say and complete all the events in 1 playthrough, the game (for me) felt too short, and I in general hate it when games end and the immersion is finally broken.
- They could have extended the play-time by adding more chapters until the end of the games so you could complete all events in just 1 playthrough rather than more.
- As someone who is playing the game a second time, I wish the game would have a mechanic where it would be slightly different, such as the dialogue options are changed or some events, as the game knows you finished it once. Or just have multiple endings ?
- If you are bad at games such as Guitar Hero it will be absolutely terrifyingly hard to 100% the game since the Maestro achievement will be near impossible to get, considering how hard the songs are to play. Wish the devs could add levels of difficulty to it that you can select.
But in the end the pros outweight the cons (which are more my selfish desires) and I would totally reccommend this game to any friend of mine that likes such types of story-driven adventures.
Thank you devs and thank you to the kickstarter contributors for making such a great game.

I hope (even if it amy take a really long time, which i have) that we may see in the far future a possible continuation of this adventure, where many of our unaswered questions amy find peace.
P.S. Mae rulz! I love all the different expressions she has the ability to portray and she is such an interesting and story-rich character that you will deffinitely fall in love with!

The indie scene is more prominent than ever boasting a diverse selection of games that often serve as bite sized reprieves from major triple A releases. While the indie scene isn't immune from uninspired copy and paste designs, there have been a string of recent releases that depart from traditional game design in a major way, challenging what we think of as games. One of the more overlooked releases that fits into this growing segment of games is Postmortem: One Must Die which tries to test players by forcing them to make a single decision that promises to have far reaching consequences. While major releases have tried to accomplish this same goal on a large scale, most have come up short. Does Postmortem's smaller and more focused scope deliver more satisfying results?

Playing as an agent of death, it's your duty to take the life of one person from a fund raising gala in a fictitious turn of the century setting on the cusp of an industrial revolution. The nation is split with conservatives that believe in upholding tradition at the expense of progress for women and greater economic development. Meanwhile progressives are riding a wave of industrial prosperity at the expense of  their workers. Both sides have admirable qualities and some absolutely abhorrent qualities which quickly muddies the line between noble and contemptible. Unbound creations has expertly balanced the qualities of each side of the conflict to tear gamers and make who they choose to snuff out a real struggle. Your potential targets rage from an influential member of the media to a young, idealistic student. Each person leans strongly in one direction and by thoroughly exploring the dialog tree you might find that your conversations with these characters may have quite an impact on them in the future...

Gameplay in Postmortem simply involves wandering around in an isometric world slathered in Victorian decor, scavenging details from news articles strewn about and talking to the patrons of the gala. Each character has a lengthy dialog tree that will allow you to acquaint yourself with them as well as current events. A wide variety of responses and questions are available and not asking questions can also have an impact on how the events play out. Dialog is generally well written but it can be a bit too purpose driven. Postmortem never creates the illusion that you are just another patron making small conversation, your pointed questions make each interaction feel like an interrogation rather than a conversation. The blatant agenda to your questions never allows the characters to show you who they are, they merely share what they perceive themselves to be.

Your interactions with the gala patrons ultimately culminate in your character deciding who should meet their end. Once your decision has been made, a series of newspaper articles show the results of your involvement at the Gala. It's not the most invigorating way to see the consequences of your actions unfold but there may be a few surprises for some players to uncover based on your actions. Also, a link to detailed player stats is viewable upon completing a play through to show how your behavior compares to other Post Mortem players. A thorough playthrough exploring all of the dialog options will take in the neighborhood of an hour and subsequent playthroughs will take less time. It doesn't take long to figure out what dialog has what impact so many players may not want to take the time to explore every possibility. The beauty of Postmortem however is that you are not required to buy it to enjoy the core experience. By purchasing the game, players are given an extra character to chat with as well as wallpapers, concept art and some behind the scenes development materials.

Like its triple A predecessors, Postmortem falls short of delivering a wholly satisfying choice based narrative. That is not to say that it isn't a worthwhile experience however, it's morally ambiguous world and intelligent and fresh setting remain engaging and some of the conclusions are engaging and surprising. It's brevity makes it easy to pick up sporadically and enjoy. I for one hope that Postmortem is simply an amuse-bouche, tantalizing our pallets for something a bit larger and scope and more accomplished in execution from Unbound Creations.

It's difficult for me to write a negative review of this game because it tries very hard to be the kind of game that I enjoy: interesting and original. The following are reasons why this game fell short of that mark.
1. Very poor sprite animations. Distractingly hideous.
2. An abundance of grammatical and spelling errors.
3. Meaningless conversation choices.
4. Lazy variation of endings, despite being the selling point of this game.
A few good surprises were had though.
1. The ending (nothing more than a collection of news clippings) is altered by more than your choice of victim. Your conversations with the dinner guests can convince them to do certain things which affect the ending.
2. The history of the world is well realized.
3. No hand holding. You are thrown into the world and left to experiment. The game doesn't make it particularly obvious how to get the ending you want. Killing the guy you dislike the most might actually result in a bigger "villain" rising to power. Going to places you're not supposed to might get you in trouble.
4. You're free to make tough moral decisions. All of the characters are likable and hatable in the same breath. The game doesn't bludgeon you with a preachy message, nor does it bore you with a simple tale of good guy vs. bad guy.
At its total, this game would look great on the drawing board. There are many areas of this game that make the player excited with the possibilities, but it doesn't feel like a completed game. As a free flash game (or demo) this game would be acceptable, but at 7 dollars I can't recommend this to anyone, even the most hardcore of text-based fans.

I love games about agonizing, complicated choices, a'la The Walking Dead. Unlike the aforementioned, however, the choices here really matter.

I don't know why, but when I launch this game.. I can't leave it until hours upon hours of playing it. I've only had this game for about five days; however, I've played more than what I usually do in one game in just one day. I've been trying to stay away from this game so I can actually play other games I've bought, but this game somehow brings me back to it.
I've noticed that when people first start out playing this game, they have asked many questions. The one I hear a lot is about the cars. When you watch the trailer for this game, you see a lot of cars but when you launch the game, you hardly see none. Just a little friendly reminder, that's because in this game, it doesn't just hand you a car. You have to work for it. Just like everything else in the game which is something I really enjoy. Surviving at first is difficult, but after you can get nicely geared up, it's nothing but an adventure from there on out.
Building bases, pvping, killing things, exploring the map, and trying to learn where the ♥♥♥♥ you are when you spawn in is so much fun. Since I've played this game a nice amount, I've started to learn the map like the back of my hand; however I still have trouble. I don't mind it, especially since I love the idea of adventure. Also, this game is beautiful. Sometimes I'll just stand at the top of a mountain and just look out at how beautiful I find this game to be.
Although, like any other game, there are some things I feel can be different about the game. My main problem sometimes is trying to load into a server. Sometimes it will take me just a few minutes, while other times I might have to wait about 10 to 15 minutes. This wasn't that big of a problem until a lot of people started to play the game here recently. Another thing I have a complaint about is the cars. Like I said before, you have to work to get a car running, but sometimes it's still hard to find a car to fix up. I feel like it would be nice if they adding in some more cars. I don't mind walking to where I want to go sometimes, but others, it would be so so so helpful if I could just jump into a car and go to where I need to go. It's not that big of a problem, but like I said, it would be helpful sometimes.
I don't have that many problems with the game other than those two flaws I found. So, if you're one who loves adventure, working hard to survive, and some action whenever you feel up to it, I highly recommend this game to you. Yes, the game has been in early access since October 30, 2014.. but trust me, this game is worth the money. (Especially if you get it now while the summer sale is going on...)

6/10 "Runs better than DayZ"
This is a DayZ clone that really brings nothing new to the table.
I've got a lot of time on DayZ, the DayZ mod, H1Z1, and the various Arma 3 mods such as Breaking Point and Exile, so I'd say I am a tad familiar with these games, let's talk about the gameplay.
Gameplay is the same as EVERY OTHER DayZ clone. Find food and water, find gun, shoot other people. That's all these games ever provide in terms of gameplay. It's mostly to just go around killing people, to be honest. I've played with groups before, and we are generally bored with base building and looting at this point, we just want a gun to shoot people. Also, the gunplay is terrible. You move slow with your gun raised, and if you are in third person it takes you a full second to get to your iron sights, which is very poor. I'd at least add a type of crosshair when you're in third person, so you can at least try to shoot back without having to aim. It took me about an hour to get a gun, and when I got it, I ended up having to fight with people almost immediately, since there is only two REAL spots to get military loot (Haywood and the Airfield). Scavenging in general is pretty much the same, the inventory system is nothing new, that's generally what this game is, to be honest, nothing NEW. It's the same crap we've been shoveled for the last 10 years since the original DayZ mod for Arma 2.
There are some positives, however...
The community didn't seem super aggressive, I met several people in the non-military areas and they didn't immediately try to kill me. So that was pretty nice, I guess.
The game runs very well compared to the other DayZ clones, including DayZ itself. I was getting a steady 60fps and I only had one framerate drop.
Animations are fluid, smooth, and everything looks nice.
Mutants are pretty sporadic, and aren't impossible to kill, nor instant death type encounters. Not too many of them and not too little.
Overall, it's just another DayZ clone. Maybe in 5 years the game will have some interesting game mechanics and be a bit of fun, but I cannot recommend this to another person in it's current state. And if it follows the route of DayZ (which it will), it will not be finished anytime soon.

I have owned Starbound since way before the 1.0 release but did not play it much if at all then. As a result, I can't compare it to the previous version but I can say now that it is a great game with many features to offer. The game itself plays very much like terraria but the thing that I love about it is that it really makes you feel like you're in a big universe you can travel around. There are endless amounts of planets, many different types of planets, and now with the 1.3 update includes a crap ton of places to visit other than planets. Also, the game extends very far into the "tech" world of progression. Not only can you just play to survive and build a massive base / civilization on a planet but you can also work to upgrade your ship and travel around the galaxy to new and hostile places. After the 1.0 update, the game is now even complimented with a cool story line and scripted missions that you can travel to but it is by no means necessary. I think that the 1.0 release trailer that is on the steam page gives a good idea of what you can do in the game but overall I enjoy the gameplay very much. As of the 1.3 update, there are some really great and interesting features that I feel add a lot more to do in the game. So far after 1.0 there have been procedurally generated dungeons / bosses you can do with friends, an entirely revamped space, space stations, enemy AI ships, friendly AI ships, traders you can encounter in space, mechs to customize and improve, and fishing to do if you really get bored. Overall I highly recommend this game to anyone and is honestly probably one of the most immersive games I have ever played. You really feel like you are part of a full universe of people and are your very own character in it. If you got this far, 10/10 with rice.

Dead Effect is one of those "it is what it is" games.  In Dead Effect you get guns, ammo and bullet time.  In return you use guns, ammo and bullet time to knock the stuffin' out of zombies in ridiculous, cartoon-y splatters of blood, guts and brains.  You will do this over and over again as you collect money to upgrade equipment, find tablets to flesh out the backstory and enjoy some of the cheesiest, most poorly acted voice-overs since the beginning of time.  Don't let my smart-alecky sentences chase you away.  I had alot of fun playing this and am already at work on a new game plus with the intention of enjoying the other modes shortly after.  The game basically is a B movie splatter-fest combining Doom, Dead Space and Resident Evil.  It's not nearly as good as any of those games but it doesn't need to be.  It does what it does well enough and is plenty entertaining, especially for the low price tag.
The game is deliciously simple and after stomping through Volgarr, Betrayer, Deadlight and several other games that required some thought, strategy and timing, it was fun to turn off my brain entirely for this one.  As a hard as nails space marine, you're way too tough to jump, think crouching is for fools and can't ran worth a crap due to your heavy space suit.  None of that really matters as you blunder from one point to the next pressing a few buttons (barely disguised as mission objects) while blasting every single zombie in your path with shotguns, assault rifles, magnums, pistols and more.  It's not very difficult, although the grenade zombie is a pest but as long as you have cash you can pick up right where you fell in a heap by paying to revive.  Dying's not much of a problem anyways because the levels are fairly short and really once you've got a few guns at your disposal, you'll shred everything like paper.
Having a new game plus to carry over your gear and earn more cash to buy those elusive, extra expensive guns was a great idea and the weapons themselves are satisfying to shoot.  By no means is this blaster-o-rama without its flaws.  The graphics for the zombies, guns and splatter FX are all pretty solid but the levels are mostly a bland set of corridors, walkways and other similar areas.  It doesn't detract too much from the score (and as an old school gamer I don't give a hoot about graphics really) but don't expect to get any twisted scenery to match the dire situation your'e fighting your way through.  Since zombies are the opponent du jour, it was cool to see some varied types;  chainsaw wielders, spitters, grenade tossers, armored zombies, etc., yet none of them really pose much of a challenge.  You might die a few times at first while figuring out how to manage their numbers, but again, once you have the tiniest modicum of strategy and beefed up guns, they go down like paper planes in a tornado.
While not a major problem, the controls will sometimes get you in a bit of trouble as they can be touchy and have you staring at the nearest vacant wall instead of the revenants you need unleash hot fury upon.  Another slightly irritating aspect is that other than the chainsaw, there is no melee combat.  In close quarters you've got the electric arm, shotgun or saw...but that's it.  It would have been sweet if you could carry more of your levelled up guns around, or swap out a few of the things they make you carry for other guns.  The grenades weren't overly useful at all.
There's really only two bosses in the game (three total if you count the second encounter with the first one), but they are so easy I'd practically bet you 50 bucks that you won't die while fighting them.  Aside from very early on you're never in that much trouble, so those looking for a white-knuckle, bullets to bedlam challenge, you're barking up the wrong corpse.  This is seriously exactly what you need if you're just looking to shoot thousands of bullets, drop mobs of the undead and really only tax the trigger finger.  Nothing more/nothing less...  It was honestly alot of fun, if not something you have to have (depending on your tastes).  I will certainly play Dead Effect 2 and it'd be a hoot to see this with some multi-player options.  I'll make a list of pros and cons for you, and then please excuse me, I have more zombies needin' taught some manners!
Pros:
-Fun arsenal of weapons that are a blast to shoot and upgrade
-Satisfying, old school combat
-Enough secrets, modes and extras to encourage additional playthroughs
-Mobs of zombies are a hoot to pummel
-Easy to pick and up play
Cons
-After a few skirmishes there's virtually no challenge
-Upgrades are awesome, but also render you darn near invincible
-Putrid boss fights that are far too easy
-Controls can be a bit touchy and oversensitive
-Few more levels wouldn't hurt
-Other than the chainsaw, there's no melee combat or close quarters hand defense
-It would have been nice to be able to carry more than 2 weapons at a time or at least swap out the electric arm, or grenades for another gun
This is a budget game that does things right.  Unlike the semi-horrid Land of the Dead, this is a zombie smashing romp that's worth taking.  It's far, far, far from perfect but if you know what you're getting and that's what you wanted, you'll have some fun!
Rating:  7/10

Before posting my review, I would like to start out by saying I believe that this game should be played on
, as it preserves the essence of the game which I will attempt to capture in the review.
This game really feels like this medium's 'great literature'.  It's not the most enjoyable experience out there in terms of gameplay, but it sure is a treat for the mind.  It somewhat reminds me of Lord of The Flies: I did not enjoy reading the actual book because the story infuriated me, however, I really appreciated the underlying themes and messages the book carries.  Gods Will be Watching is similar to LoTF in this aspect.
Players control Sgt. Burden as he tries to keep himself and his team alive through 7 (there's also a free DLC chapter) brutally difficult scenarios.  Players will try, fail, and try again only to fail once more due to the heavy reliance on the RNG.  One might then begin to wonder if their choices even mean anything - up to 40 minutes of work can be wiped out by a single event that's not even within their control.  It creates this very tense environment, knowing that one is doing their best, yet is still not in control of their own fate: that privilage belongs to the Gods, who are indeed watching you.
This raises an important question: 'why would anyone want to play a game where they aren't in full control of their destiny?', and, at least in my interpretation, is the point.  This game isn't about the gameplay, but the overall experience.  Once one accepts that failure is inevitable in this game, one can plan around it.  Each failure will come with a lesson, thus increasing the odds of success on subsequent runs.  Once players accept and embrace the nature of the RNG will the game truly shine because then they will have fully grasped everything the game has to offer.  Failure in this game should not be a maddening experience, nay, it should be an enlightening one, even when it occurs through no fault of the player.
One might even wonder about the choices presented in the game, and of their significance; one might even begin to see the parallels drawn between the game and real life in this vast, possibly infinite, expanse of space we call home.  On a scale the size of the Universe, does anything anywhere even matter?
The entire game, from it's RNG elements, to its abundance of failure, to its minimalistic nature, to everything else, constitute a carefully woven lesson in
, one that is retread and enforced in the game's finale, which brings every component and set peice together and wraps it up into a neat knot.  Every question posed by the game and even questions the player has about the game are brought to the fore and resolved in the finale - questions such as 'did my choices really matter?', 'why do I keep ending up wandering the desert when I fail?', and 'why are people who died in a previous chapter alive in the next?' are probably among the most important ones resolved.
In the face of such abundant failure, even the most difficult choices become mundane, almost routine, throughout the millions of attemts at becoming the legend that is Sgt. Burden.
The one (free) DLC chapter emphasises the game's main points: it takes the ending and adds on a meta-ending to it, which carries the same themes as the original ending, and builds upon them, thus driving the fateful point home once and for all with tremendous force.  One important thing to note however, and I really want to emphasize this, is that
.  The resource management gameplay aspect is simply a medium through which the developers convey their story.
A friend recently mentioned to me that the game shares many parallels to the Myth of Sisyphus, and that given the situation presented in the DLC chapter, it seems to have served as inspiration or as a guiding foundation for this game.  I am definitely inclined to believe this is true, and its article on Wikipedia can explain Existential Nihilism/Absurdism much better than I can.
Before I conclude, I would like to pose a question to the reader, one that is best saved for after  all 8 chapters of the game have been completed.

Gods Will Be Watching is a game with a fantastic design aesthetic but a poor gameplay loop. Ultimately the game is a 'stress simulator', each 'level' is a crisis situation where you have a number of choices open to you, each relying on a variety of factors that are strained as you progress until either failure or a (most often Pyrrhic) victory.
Whilst there are a number of difficulty settings that alter how tricky the task will be, ultimately I found they felt like unengaging number-crunching exercises after a few failed attempts at each mission. You begin to game the system, rather than going on instinct. In one mission, it may work out better to kill a comrade in order to preserve supplies for the rest of the group, but instead of feeling like a weighty and meaningful decision, it instead feels like removing a resource-draining column on a spreadsheet. On top of this, the level of frustration rises when some of these scenarios take so long to complete and can often fall apart at the last moment. This leads to you trying the scenario again, often repeating most of what you did the previous time, with a few tweaks to your 'logic spreadsheet' in the hopes it works.
Whilst this game may seem entertaining to some, I think most will find it repetitive, awkward and frustrating. A fantastic artistic aesthetic with questionable design.

I finished Night in the Woods for the first time and I am already on my second playthrough to get the rest of the achievements. First, I must thank my friend who gifted me this amazing game (which i eyed from the beggining when it was released on steam) and secondly I must thank everyone that contributed in creating it. It helped me get through an emotionally hard time this week.
Onto deeper thoughts:
- Visually I love the art style of the game, beautiful color palettes all around, really vibrant and radiating of happiness (and in some cases mystery or horror).
- The soundtrack is very well crafted and synced with the events and the switch from one song to another is almost undiscernable and very smooth, withouth breaking the immersion.
- Immersion! This game pulls you in it's world right from the beggining. The characters, dialogue, story, visual arrangement and soundtrack placement are so well done you forget you're playing a game.
Some cons:
- Even if you take your time to explore every corner of the game, listen to all the characters and what they have to say and complete all the events in 1 playthrough, the game (for me) felt too short, and I in general hate it when games end and the immersion is finally broken.
- They could have extended the play-time by adding more chapters until the end of the games so you could complete all events in just 1 playthrough rather than more.
- As someone who is playing the game a second time, I wish the game would have a mechanic where it would be slightly different, such as the dialogue options are changed or some events, as the game knows you finished it once. Or just have multiple endings ?
- If you are bad at games such as Guitar Hero it will be absolutely terrifyingly hard to 100% the game since the Maestro achievement will be near impossible to get, considering how hard the songs are to play. Wish the devs could add levels of difficulty to it that you can select.
But in the end the pros outweight the cons (which are more my selfish desires) and I would totally reccommend this game to any friend of mine that likes such types of story-driven adventures.
Thank you devs and thank you to the kickstarter contributors for making such a great game.

I hope (even if it amy take a really long time, which i have) that we may see in the far future a possible continuation of this adventure, where many of our unaswered questions amy find peace.

This is a strange title, because at times it's almost more of a detective/choose-your-own-adventure book than a game. Yes, you play it, but the majority of that game play involves walking around, reading notes and papers, making decisions, referring to your journal, and talking to people.
In fact, I should point out that you'll be doing a LOT of talking. If you normally dislike lots of dialogue (which is mostly silent, so no voice actors beyond a word or two every so often) then don't get this game. Fortunately, you don't have to remember every little detail as vitally important information is automatically written down in your journal.
The story is you're a novice reaper (okay, get "Don't Fear the Reaper" out of your system before you continue reading) on your first assignment. You're told that ONE person must die at the gala you're attending. Admittedly, it's a very small gala, since there's only about six people there.
What happens next is you read various notes and newspapers (and even open some safes and unlock doors, if you manage to get the right keys) and talk to each of the six individuals there. Every single person will have varying views on the shakey political situation going on and have something to say -- both bad and good -- about other people there.
None of the attendees are "innocent" in that each one has their own faults. One man is very sexist and thinks women shouldn't enter the workforce, while at the same time wants more rights for male workers. Likewise, one woman has some very feminist views (as in equality, not male bashing), but is extremely anti-immigrant and wants "those people" out of her country.  There's also poor vs rich issues and arguments about whether violence means are justified to change current conditions.
In other words, everything discussed in the game is a reflection of real life, both past and present. What's interesting about that is you have the chance to agree with them and further encourage their current point of view or argue a counterpoint, sometimes changing their mind.
Once you make your decision about who to kill, you'll see the reports detailing the aftermath. All of your actions -- who you decided to kill and what you discussed with the survivors -- play a role in shaping the future social and political climate.
There are some negative points, however. The game uses a somewhat primitive sprite-based 2D isometric graphical style, which for some reason or another, randomly experiences slowdown while walking. The resolutions offered are also limited.
There's virtually no mouse support other than clicking on menu buttons, so almost everything is controlled via the keyboard. That wouldn't be so bad if the controls didn't feel clunky.
There are numerous grammar and spelling issues in the dialogue. The font used is also small and the letters appear squished together, which makes reading sometimes a chore. That's a huge black mark against the game considering you'll spend more time reading than not. I will admit that I played this on a laptop with a screen resolution of 1366x768, so the font may be easier to read with larger screens and higher resolutions.
As far as I know, there's no way to save your game. Granted, the game isn't terribly long, but if you want to see all the outcomes, you'll have to talk to everyone each time you play and some dialogue trees can be very long. So while you could immediately go and kill different people right from the start, you wouldn't have affected anything (other than murdering someone) without talking to everyone first.
Post Mortem: One Must Die (Extended Cut) is  currently $6.99 USD on Steam or offered at varying prices on the developer's website. The regular version (which lacks numerous extras, including a new character) is also available for FREE by the developer at

You play as a reaper, you must pick one person to die from those attending. The developers have released this as a DRM free game on their website in its non 'extended' version - and unfortunately should have stayed as such. It has potential to be a sort of 'cluedo played as death' game; if it was expanded throughout several scenarios. As it stands however it's just too short and simplistic to be considered a full game.

Dead Effect is a first person shooter set in space, much like the deadspace series. You awaken from a Hybernation Pod to find the ship badly damaged and the crew seemingly dead by what appear to be zombified crew members. So far in the short hour I've played I found the game to be fun, if not predictable so far. Each level you complete gives you a review of how well you done with the option of replaying it. Hidden orbs and stashes are located on each level, and you pick up various weapons as you navigate through the ship. The credits you obtain while exploring can be used at the end of each level to purchase upgrades, new weapons and more. I look forward to seeing where the game goes with the story, as I only completed the first level and then replayed it for good measure. Playing on Hell mode does not seem to present much more of a challenge than most games on normal, but that could always change as you progress further along. All in all it is a fun game and it was relatively cheap making it a good buy.

I make no exaggeration when I say that this game changed me. I have trouble looking at other games without seeing them through the blood-tinted glasses that is Dark Souls. The game isn't as difficult as people claim but it will test your resolve. It will force you to rethink your own strategy at times and may even lead to a rage-quit or two. But when you pick up the pieces of your shattered controller and mourn the loss of your souls, you'll know it was nobody's fault but your own. You’ll try again with more patience and experience (the real-life kind, not the in-game kind) than you had before and you’ll learn. And it's those bitter losses that make the victories taste that much sweeter.
Dark Souls never holds your hand. It gently nudges you through the opening level and then lets you free in a surprisingly dense and complex open world that somehow manages to seem huge and small at the same time. This is also how Dark Souls tells its story. You are given a nudge—a prophecy—and then left to find your own path. There are entire areas of the game I missed during my first playthrough and some more areas I missed on my second. Each new area, each new NPC, and each new item, giving you a clue to this world and the poor, tragic souls who live there. The method of storytelling in Dark Souls has made the expositional dialogue of other games seem outright cringey.
I won’t say this is the best game I’ve ever played, but it has certainly had one of the biggest impacts on me and how I view games, storytelling, worldbuilding, and life in general.

The moment the game launches a vague, almost ethereal noise like gently blowing wind in a vast expanse accompanies the logos, and then your ears are treated to some of the best title music anything has had in the past decade. It's jazzy, it's despondent, it gives a sense of nihilism and rebellion all at once, while climbing to be a bit faster and even hopeful near the middle of the song. All of this in only the first three and a half minutes of a three volume, six and a half hour long soundtrack. It's a good sign, to be sure.
Constantly the music complements the atmosphere of the scene it plays to, slowly dropping out during tense conversations, shifting to new tracks based on the weather, where you are, when in the story you are, and who you're with. Listen closely to the music in the trailers for tracks that perfectly encompass the breadth of the game from start to finish in barely over a minute. Enjoy the way the music blends with environmental noises to further immerse you in the world, echoing slightly in tunnels and adding extra instruments to the track when in-game musicians are nearby. Due to these details, this game is best played with a headset as opposed to external speakers.
Alec Holowka has done an exceptional job with this music, which includes the soundtrack for the game within the game dubbed Demontower, as well as all the tracks for the two supplemental games that I also highly recommend. I listen to all of it in a partially shuffled format that mostly retains chronological order at my leisure because I'm a sucker for seamlessly blended genres.
You'll be ridin' the chariot looking at this game. From the album art to Mae's journal doodles it's all fun to gander at. There's a lot about the art style that I can't talk about without spoiling the game's meta narrative, so I'll tell you how it reinforces everything else later and focus on the broad strokes here.
Vivid colors and crisp shapes really bring out the Autumn feel, tasteful contrast accentuating every angle and detail on both the characters and the environments. differences in lighting between scenes help to set the mood, and the way lighting sources are distinguished pairs with other small details to draw you in to the world depicted onscreen. Characters kick up leaves and twigs in some places, your presence can frighten squirrels and birds if you move too quickly, fireflies dance around lamps at night, and the sounds of your steps match perfectly with the ground you're seeing. These may seem like a small feats in isolation, but when these details are spot on throughout the entire game it adds a bit of magic to the game.
Then there's the animation, from the walking and running cycles of each character to the way the fur on their arms sways with small gestures during closeups, it's all spectacular. The occasional blinks, ear twitches, and expression shifts add even more to love about these artsy graphics that deftly sidestep common trends and the uncanny valley with stylish and lively anthropomorphic animals.
Do you want to play a platformer, dungeon crawler, puzzle game, runner, or rhythm game? How about a game where you dodge bottles and smash lightbulbs? One of those weirdly difficult sniping games with a shaky camera? Something that simulates you and friend trying to stab each other in the hand? Well, I guess you could play this. Night in the Woods is
all of those things, but that isn't really
.
Night in the Woods juggles these gameplay elements as stylishly as it does narrative themes and musical influences, using them to enhance the experience and the plot. Some stuff is rather difficult, or even completely insane, while most sequences aren't too challenging, but it always
, and because of context rather than shallow scores or leaderboards. You'll want to play a song well because you want Mae to make a good returning impression on her old friends. You'll try to reach new areas and solve puzzles to learn more about Possum Springs. Talking about the rest would be spoiler city, but you get the idea.
I've been playing highly competitive video games since a very young age, and it get's exhausting. After punching my billionth demon in DOOM I start to wonder what the point even is. To reach 22nd place on a leaderboard nobody cares about? Bleh. With Night in the Woods I can enjoy a motivation that transcends all that, which brings us to the next Pillar.
So here's what you know from the very beginning: you're a bundle of shapes that vaguely forms a cat-person. After a couple minutes you learn that Mae is her name and she's certainly not you. Unlike the route typical immersive games take with their blank slate, vanilla protagonists, Mae is a massively complex and intriguing character in her own right, and she carries the plot forward as much as you do.
Strangely enough, this game doesn't seem to advertise that your choices matter, because a lot of the time they don't. In other games with dialogue options as expansive as those in Night in the Woods there would be all manner of buzz surrounding how much "agency" the player has, but by avoiding trying to trick players into thinking pointless choices actually matter the game can focus on making some key choices impact the final sequence. Furthermore, where you go, what you do, and who you spend your time with will determine how much dialogue pops up later and what is said. Even the things that objectively don't matter can matter
because of the context and character development.
There are boatloads of perfectly timed content and foreshadowing hidden away in optional/missable encounters and environmental details. Even the expressions characters are wearing as you approach convey a lot, since they are almost always in a standard state by default. Any variation is immediately noticeable, and this pairs with the writing to make everything feel more real. My recommendation is that you find everyone you can everywhere you can and do all of the optional hangouts. The fact that you can miss out is a part of the meta narrative, but not missing out ruins nothing and adds to the surface narrative.
This is yet another win for the writing, as the conversations between characters do the most to make them feel tangible and realistic. More than that the way they talk matches their age and the zeitgeist of our time. This game takes place in 2017, and it actually feels that way. It's refreshing to stumble upon a game that succeeds at being set in current times, since using historical settings is so much easier to execute and market.
Not only do the characters come to life through their words, but also how they say them. There's no voice acting save for a few grunts and huffs, so text tells the story. It can have a particular color for certain characters, and the game hides some important characters by just giving them standard white in spite of their importance. Sometimes the font is subtly larger to show steadily growing agitation and loudness. Other times it slithers on a particular word to show it was said with a sleazy, hateable tone. Other times Mae will flip out and start yelling like a maniac, her letters jittering around in her speech bubble.
Combine the mutability of the text with expression changes, Mae huffing at the right time, and characters raising their arms or even flailing them around depending on the circumstances and you've got some truly memorable characters. They're unique, they're fun, and you'll legitimately care about them.

Night in the Woods, in short, is awesome. The environment, writing, and situations are all extremely immersive and I thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough of it, especially in the last two parts.
Story and Characters:
Our story follows Mae, a recent college dropout that's returning to her 'boring' (NOTICE THE QUOTES) hometown, Possum Springs, to live at home again. After being forgotten at a bus stop by her parents, Mae begins her journey around Possum Springs revisiting old friends and rekindling some other relationships. The main supporting cast features Gregg (an impulsive and energetic fox/dog/not sure), his boyfriend Angus (a soft-spoken an level-headed bear), and Bea (a reptilian edgelord that you come to love). Some creepy things start happening around town and Mae begins having some introspective supernatural experiences which I won't spoil for you! And from that point, the story of the game takes off. I wish my post-college life at home was as exciting as this (ya know, without all the mental anguish and creepy happenings).
Gameplay:
Most of your time in Night in the Woods is spent exploring. Running, jumping, and dialogue between the townsfolk and friends are the main playing points of the game. There's a few rhythm game-esque sections during the group's band practice, a mini game on Mae's laptop, and a few other neat mechanics. The focus of the game is its narrative and, frankly, whatever gameplay is here is perfect for the experience. Certain choices you make will have you go on adventures moreso with Gregg & Angus or Bea. I've only completed my first playthrough of the game and look forward to my next when I'll spend more time with the two lovebirds. I loved the sheer amount of natural character development that Bea goes through while you spend time with her though. Time spent with the characters in this game is where the game shines.
TL:DR
Just buy it. It's worth it at full price and I've never loved a complete cast of characters like I do with this game. Connecting constellations and reminiscing on childhood memories with Angus, smashing sh*t with Gregg while he throws glass bottles at your face, and going on car rides with Bea were worth every minute and every penny. I think it's impossible not to be charmed by this gameworld. Germ is cool too.

So I bought this game on a whim, after a LoL streamer I was watching at the time made a big fuss over it. The overly cutesy outward appearance made me question my decision at first, expecting it to be one of those "games aimed at girls" with appearances taking precedence over actual content. Thankfully, I was wrong.
So, what is this game then? In essence, it's a mix of visual novel and "breeding simulator". The game consists of ~40 week long storyline. Each week you choose what the main character, Elodie, will study in morning and evening, while during the weekend Elodie has the option of visiting one of several places, some of which are unlocked by reaching certain skill tresholds. Most of these locations affect her current Mood. The rate at which Elodie learns the varying skills in the game depends on her current Mood (range of eight emotions, including Angry, Pressured and Cheerful) as well as how advanced she already is both in the general subject as well as the greater aspect. For example, let's say Elodie is already well-versed in all aspects of Intrigue as well as both Novan and World History. Both her general aptitude with Intellectual matters as well as her aptitude in history makes it a breeze to learn Foreign Affairs, also found under History.
In addition to deciding what Elodie wants to learn every week and visiting a location, every week progresses the story of the game, facing Elodie with both challenges of every day life as well as the responsibilities of being the queen-to-be. These challenges come in form of events with Skill Checks. For example an inventor has requested an audience to seek funding for his invention. If Elodie has the required skills to understand how beneficial this invention could prove, she has the option of either giving the funding needed or dismissing the inventor. On the other hand, lacking the skills required Elodie automatically dismisses the inventor, scoffing at the invention.
These skill checks have varying degree of importance. Some checks don't affect the game, only providing extra info to the player. Others either subtly or obviously change the story. Some affect Elodie's mood or unlock an area to visit during the weekend. Finally there are literally game-ending checks that lead to one of the numerous (over a dozen) Dead Ends the game has to offer.
One important thing to know is that there are no dice rolls or other random things in this game. You either fail the check or succeed based on your skill level, although some checks also have the possibility of partial success. Partial successes are mainly used when you face a series of checks in a row. As an example, you get attacked: failing to react means you die. Partial success means you have less time to react and as such the following check will be harder, while full success means easier follow-up check.
The story itself is partially branching: the game always starts the same and always leads to the same final challenge: while the story does branch depending on your choices, the branching "merely" affects how your Elodie shapes out to be, how ready your kingdom and your Elodie are to meet the final challenge and what options are available to you to deal with it. There are several very different ways to deal with the final challenge, although more ways would have been welcome in my humble opinion.
Which leads to my general opinion of the game:
Goods:
+ Interesting story with plenty of unexpected turns, some of which you might completely miss on first playthrough because your skills are either too low (or too high!) to see them.
+ Plenty of ways to get the good ending, as well as over a dozen bad ends to find, giving the game more replayablity.
+ Dialogue is mostly well written. It flows surprisingly well even when there is some monologue added/missing depending on your skills.
+ Lots of hidden stuff you only find by really going for them.
Bad:
- Aesthetics are a bit on the overly "girly" side for my taste.
- Music gets repetitive. The track is decent, but the game would have benefited from having a broader music score.
- Too many skills with 1-2 uses in the entire game, some of them hidden in branches of the story you may not even find unless purposefully gunning for them.
- Combined with the above, many skills have a threshold after which there is little to no point in raising them, since vast majority of the skill checks do not require full 100% in a skill.

It's a really fun game, and quite addicting to see where the story changes, but you're going to be hand in hand with the Trial-and-Error twins the entire run through, and would probably be saving constantly to avoid any choice you didn't want

Long Live The Queen is an indie visual novel sporting the anime art style with the choice and decision system of a political intrigue game.
You play as Elodie, a 14-year-old princess who is to be crowned Queen of Nova. Play the game of politics where assassinations and threats of death are a daily occurrence. Be a skilled diplomat, a military leader, a powerful sorcerer or a little bit of all in your road to the throne.
+ Art Style: -(This is subjective) Having the anime look will have the "you either love it or hate it" effect from people. Some people like it, some people don't. I personally like it.
+ Planning Ahead/Consequence System: -This game does require the player to plan in advance by having a massive amount of attributes and skills that can be learned and mastered in a very limited way. Different players will have different skill sets depending on how they play through the game. Thinking ahead is a necessity to stay alive.
+ Mood System: -You can only advance your skills through tutoring and schooling, unfortunately however, how well you level up and progress is dependent entirely on your character's mood. (example: Anger = Gives bonus to lessons with regards to Military and Weapon Expertise but has corresponding penalties to Royal Demeanor and Expression.)
+ Good Difficulty: -Easy enough to learn but hard to master. I takes at least 2-3 playthroughs to get a general feel of the game but multiple playthroughs are recommended. This game requires experimentation and attention to detail to effectively win.
- Way too short: -I finished this game under 5 hours in my original gameplay (including deaths, and restarts). This game is suffering from the same flaw as I saw on Recettear since the main campaign is just too short. I think the developers could have added more complexity in the game as well as extend the campaign past your coronation period. It would have been nice to continue playing as the "Queen" after said coronation.
- Events not Random: -Though some events are triggered only by specific skills you possess at that time, all events relating to the main quest are virtually the same. This actually encourages the player to learn from his mistakes and try not to do it the next time around. Note that deaths in this game are instant game overs.
- Not as Deep as I thought it would be: -I expected a level of political intrigue including empire management, army management, family and court management, but unfortunately this game only delivers the basics of those.
GOOD BUT NOT FOR EVERYONE. I personally am satisfied with the game so I'm going to RECOMMEND it.
Patience is a very important consideration if you are planning on buying this game. If you're the type who doesn’t want to do a lot of thinking and just want a casual experience, this game is not for you. If you're the type of gamer who likes life-sims, visual novels and enjoy choosing your own adventure, then this is game deserves your attention.

A fantastic fighting game that upholds the proud tradition of decades of Street Fighter excellence, with absolutely unplayable online multiplayer mired by incessant lag and dropped connections.  If you're considering upgrading from Super Street Fighter IV, look forward to content ported from another Capcom fighter.
Street Fighter IV takes place after SFII but before SFIII, but you don't care about that.  You're here for Ultra Street Fighter IV's 40+ characters and the robust systems you've heard so much about.  You've got the Super Combo gauge, which you can use all at once in a devatstating move, or consume piecemeal with enhanced special moves (like an EX fireball that hits twice).  You've got Focus Attacks, which let you absorb a hit and let rip with your own counterattack or reposition yourself with a dash.  You've got Ultra Combos, which are powered by the Revenge Gauge that fills as you get hurt.
Of course, if you're new to everything, the game has lots to catch you up.  In addition to the standard freeform training mode, there's Trials, where the game tells you various moves and combos your character is capable of.  It could definitely use some polish (it'd be nice to see how they expect you to perform some of these, since some aren't inherently obvious and some actually require you to push the training dummy to the corner), but it's a start.  The single-player content hits the bare essentials and little else.
The real star is the online multiplayer, connecting you with fighters the world over!  Or, it would, if the connection was any good.  Even the online menus are plagued with heinous lag spikes, which is to say nothing of the matches themselves.  Even a little lag can be a death sentence in a fast-paced fighting game which essentially requires your constant input, and USFIV's lag can last for whole seconds.  Of course, this all assumes your connection isn't randomly dropped to begin with.  The experience combines to create an incredibly dull experience with a dwindling community, with most of the serious players jumping ship for the superior netcode of the console versions.
"Super Street Fighter IV" is also out there, but Ultra is an upgrade which brings some minor tweaks, new characters, and new stages.  With one exception, the characters and stages have been ported from Capcom's previous bomb, Street Fighter x Tekken.  The exception is a Cammy reskin which, admittedly, plays a lot differently from the character she looks like, but this is all being listed for the sake of completeness to help inform your purchasing decision.
All in all, Ultra Street Fighter IV is a rock-solid fighting game that has earned its longtime fame and frequent appearances in international gaming tournaments.  The PC port, however, has a lot of fixes it needs before it can be competitive.
