stratO is a game that I feel needs some advice given before even starting this review. There are a few strategies online for stratO (even by the developer) mentioning a few different tactics, but I have to admit that one tactic rises above the rest. That strategy is to pick one set of controls (like the left and right air brakes) and while not trying to fly through rings, just get used to what those specific controls do to the plane. Just focus on those buttons while trying to avoid the giant blocks. That’s it; rinse and repeat for additional controls. This should help the learning curve. It’s weird and feels pointless, but it does work.
That said, I was frustrated with the controls since I couldn’t configure them the way I wanted to, that and there seemed to be a lot of buttons. Changing the controls wasn’t exactly straightforward, but I eventually did figure it out. Instead of getting used to what the developer had set up, I was trying to set up controls that the game refused to let me use. I was trying to assign two different controls to the joysticks and while it would work on the control setup screen, it wouldn’t work in-game. Eventually I gave up and just used what I was given and I then got used to it and the 100 rings in a row achievement. I feel I could have done this a little easier with my idea, but you can only do so much.
There is no tutorial and point to the game just yet. Well “point” may be the wrong word. I think maybe “reason” would be the better word. Why am I flying here? Why are there random blocks jumping up in front of me? What’s with the rings? Why would I want to continuously fly through them? Is it just for the achievements? The short answer is that stratO is a game that the developer seemed to want to create around his control scheme. Figure out the controls to the best of your abilities and enjoy trying to get all the achievements. It can actually be quite relaxing once you figure out enough of the controls to not hit things.
The developer is also adding a new mode to the game named Salvo. It’s almost the same game currently but with a gun attached to your plane that automatically fires. I’m assuming that you’re just supposed shoot the blocks. This feels like an easier mode than the regular mode and can almost act as a bit of a tutorial. I’d almost recommend playing Salvo mode first. I’m sure that there will be more to this, but as it stands, it’s good enough since he’s still creating it.
Score: Gewd.
While there’s not much going on in stratO and you can see the developer is working on this and adding more to the game and that’s no small feat. stratO is a smooth experience and if you can get a combo going with some good flying the music rewards you and makes the experience all that much better. While I am not completely enjoy the controls, it’s not something that can’t be overcome like some other games I’ve played. It took me a bit to get completely into this game, but in the end I can say that I enjoyed my experience. I can’t say its got a lot to make you want to come back unless you’re an achievement hunter. Maybe when the Salvo mode gets fleshed out we might have something a bit more to solidify the foundation and possibly help me get the one achievement I tried hard to get: “I DO WHAT I WANT”.

Obsidian does an excellent job of birthing a Baldur's Gate 1/Icewind Dale 1 hybrid.  Oozing with atmosphere and down-to-Earth authenticity, Pillars of Eternity is a vibrant walk down memory lane for any avid Infinity game fans.  Superlative music, fantastic voice acting and great art design all culminate in an wonderful example of a master-crafted isometric WRPG.  Couple the daunting game villain with item crafting/enhancing, detailed keep building and branching quests/storylines and you have a lasting winner.  The game doesn't always impress however, as the rules system is far less intuitive than traditional D20 fare, spells/abilities often bore and the atheist story overtones fall flat towards the end.  While the game doesn't hit the plotting, design or characterization highs of Planescape Torment or Baldur's Gate 2, Pillars of Eternity still sets a fantastic foundation for future development.
Recommended.

Still amazing, I hope we see more from the developer!

My stratO experience is one of the more unique experiences with a steam game.
I started out confused and frustrated. I went to the forums and complained about the lack of tutorial and how confusing the controls were.
One of the forum moderators added me almost instantly, walked me through some of the basics, watched a broadcast of me playing, and then had me watch a broadcast of him playing. After that, I kind of knew what was goin on, but still felt lost.
Then the developer himself got on the forums and posted a 22 minute comprehensive tutorial. I watched the whole thing and after my next flight I got my first achievement.
1.3 hours of gameplay later, after all of that, I still feel like a complete n00b, and am still very lost as to what I'm doing when playing, but I'm starting to figure it out little by little.
And, with each little bit I figure out, I'm more and more impressed by how groundbreaking this game is.
I am going to recommend this game, but with the warning that if you're not ready to go through a serious amount of learning just to figure out the basics, this might not be worth your time.
However, if you're craving something new and insanely challenging, buy this now.
Also, I'd like to point out that the dev and moderator who helped me are two of the nicest and most patient people I've come across on Steam, and should get a medal just for dealing with crazy people like me :)

This is one of my favorite Nancy Drew games that I can remember playing. It's terrifying and interesting and I loved it.
Plot: Super scary stuff happens around the hotel you're staying in. I am a big baby and actually screamed at a few points. There's also some complex family drama going on that needs to be sorted out. It's very well done like most Nancy Drew games are.
Minigames: Okay, I could make bento boxes for literally days. Years, maybe. Adorable animal-shaped sandwiches in a puzzle game. Yes please. And nonograms. I did not know nonograms existed but now I am obsessed. (There is also Sudoku and another number game that is horribly difficult and I didn't last very long.) At one point, you have to write your name with a calligraphy brush. Having taken a Japanese class, let me tell you, this is already hard as heck. Trying to do it with a mouse is even worse. Survive that minigame, though, and the rest is awesome.
Puzzles: There were a few puzzles I needed to google the answers for because the game set them up strangely. Like walk aruond the garden a hundred times and you never see a thing, but after you know about the puzzle, click in a verrrrry specific spot and suddenly you can find new stuff. Also plenty of codes to break, timed puzzles with death looming, etc.
Exploring/Snooping: You get to shoo people from their places and investigate! It's great. This one (similar to the Waverly Academy game) has a time mechanic where you must wake up in the middle of the night to snoop around while everyone is sleeping. You get to visit different areas of Japan, play pachinko, etc. This game gives you a lot of freedom to run around and do things, and I enjoyed that.
Characters: One thing I liked about this game from the others is that several of the characters completely shut you down when you are snooping. In some of them, they open up so easily "oh hey you completed a minor puzzle for me. Awesome. Let me tell you my entire life story." This one made you work for it. There's also a cute romantic subplot with two characters off-screen, and the handyman at the hotel is adorable and fun.
All around, this is one of the better Nancy Drew games. Definitely give it a play if you like the series. :)

One of my favorite puzzle games.
It's far from perfect, gameplay-wise. It's more about survival and resource management than it is about puzzles. It's broken up into several different chapters, each with a different goal and overall mechanics, but usually with the same general idea of "get as many people to survive for x amount of time", and it does a very good job of that (with the exception of one or two chapters which were honestly just a pain).
However, the reason why I absolutely love this game is because of its storytelling. There are a lot of themes of sacrifice and many difficult choices, often with unique and creative setups. Unfortunately, I feel like giving any specific examples would be too much of a spoiler because this game is absolutely unpredictable. One level you'll be withstanding torture, the next you'll be searching for the cure for a vaccine. Yet it all somehow manages to flow with a strange sort of brutal and intense pacing that will have you wondering what will happen to the characters next.
Unfortunately, the ending could be a turn-off for a lot of people. Without spoiling anything, it gets VERY meta and kind of pretentious, akin to that of BioShock Infinite. However, while Infinite's ending had subtly built itself up over the course of the game, GWBW kind of just brings it in out of nowhere. That said, the way they do it is still VERY interesting and completely unique, so it is at least memorable.
The game is also very replayable, as there are a number of different approaches you can take to get through each chapter, and if you fulfill certain requirements you can even unlock concept art and additional background information on the characters.
It's far from perfect, particularly one or two chapters which feel completely luck-based, and the ending doesn't entirely seem to fit what the rest of the narrative was building to, but it still has an incredible story and the majority of the game is well worth playing.

This game has what looks like a neat story, but two really major problems.
Narratively, the lack of choice is not only annoying in and of itself, but extremely poorly-executed. This becomes evident early on in the game where, as an example, a character has a chance of dying, but if they do, they show up again in the next chapter like nothing happened at all. The game literally retcons a character's death. There is an explanation given later on (timelines, Groundhog Day), but it feels lazy and unsatisfying.
The other problem is that it's deliberately difficult in a way that isn't fun. Unless you're on narrative mode, if you get through any scene on the first try, it's by sheer luck. Randomness has a high chance of wrecking you, and even with minimal random elements, most of the puzzles require a few deaths and restarts before you have a handle on how things work.
The game has a deliberate theme of helplessness and futility that carries over to the mechanics, which seems intentional. As a concept it's interesting, but "let's make a game that's unpleasant to play" is a self-defeating thing that exists only for the artistic statement. And I cannot recommend you spend money on that.

There aren't many games that keep me hooked like Shadow of Mordor.
Let's start with the combat. Shadow of Mordor brings a not-so-new-but-still-fun-to-play combat system à la Assassin's Creed. You got counters, you got executions. The regular deal. The executions are pretty damn satisfying though, as they look really sick.
You can upgrade you character with new abilities, and these abilities make sure that encounters with Uruk are never boring. As you progress, you keep learning new stuff. No battle I fought was ever boring.
The graphics are pretty good. The OST is astonishing (it's hella epic when you encounter a random captain and they chant their name through the background music. Amazing). The voice acting is also done really well, the characters are all very convincing.
I think the best feature of Shadow of Mordor is probably the Nemesis system. It's an innovative, interesting mechanic put in the game to keep the game from being a generic brawler/beat 'em up game. Toying around and playing with it is very fun. That, on top of the fact that it really fits into the storyline and game. The way captains react to your actions and behaviour makes everything very personal, and just really cool. "OY, MAN SWINE"
Maybe the only con I could think of is that when you got all the upgrades you want, there is no real point in the side missions. I was satisfied with my 'build' pretty quickly, so I had no real need to do those side missions as the main missions already gave me enough currency/exp. I only did those side missions in the beginning of my playthrough, but after that barely.
Stealth also leaves some to be desired. Or maybe it's just me and Uruk really are that stupid.
tl;dr: excellent beat 'em up game that not only just delivers fun combat. Good story, good music, good voice acting, good mechanics, just good game.

I loved this game. But it took me until the second time around.
My first playthrough, immediately after starting the game and while moving to the very first quest objective, I came across an Uruk who had a name and said some dialogue. I did not realize it at the time, but this was a captain.
What I also could not have realized at the time was the method the game generates abilities for captains. And by the insanely unlikely odds of RNG, that captain happened to be invulnerable to everything. As in, he was invulnerable to stealth, ranged, could not be vaulted over, continuously regenerated health, and could not be damaged by combat finishers. Having JUST started the game (but considering myself a veteran of games like Batman and AC) I lacked certain abilities or strategies that may have helped me defeat this captain, and all I knew was that EVERYTHING I did, he countered. I hit the right buttons and he would throw me around and choke me to death. The fight went on and on and on until I finally was thrown down for trying to vault him one too many times, and I was killed.
I totally flew into a rage. Screamed to my friend about how stupid the game was and went off on a tangent about how if it was a disc instead of a download I'd have whipped it against the wall... But begrudgingly admitted it had seemed like a good game for the 55 seconds I had played up until meeting said invulnerable captain.
TL DR; THIS GAME CAN BE VERY FRUSTRATING, ESPECIALLY IF YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU'RE DOING OR DON'T UNDERSTAND THE NEMESIS SYSTEM.
That being said...
This is the best, most fluid, enjoyable combat system of any I have ever played. Unlike batman which felt clumsy when trying to counter, the game feels responsive to the moves you make. Unlike AC the executions, finishers and various ways to kill Uruk and Orcs still has not begun to feel repetitive. What's more, each execution feels extremely rewarding, as it can be somewhat difficult to get an Uruk into a position to be executed without either landing a number of well executed blows without being hit, or stunning them and having the time to execute them. When enemies are knocked down and give you the chance to finish, it can be challenging to find a reprieve from combat with the other nearby enemies long enough to finish a downed foe. But unlike batman the character will drop whatever they are doing to block or parry if you hit the button, meaning you were almost never locked into an animation that would get you hit or killed.
The nemesis system itself was a tremendous ammount of fun, adding a layer of meaning to the game that most other games miss out on. Most games either ignore player death all together or punish it so ridiculously it can take the fun out of trying again (Looking at you, dark souls) but this game will promote the nameless grunt who shot the arrow or threw the spear or thrust the sword and killed you, they will often challenge other captains and will make comments about your previous battles. Also, oftentimes enemy captains are killed but not decapitated, and so some back with horrific scars or armor plates over the spot you last killed them, such as a blow to the head or scars on the chest. Another thing is that even after hundreds of slain captains, warchiefs, and uruk, they still feel unique. The body types and expressions of the uruk, their armor and pretty much everything about them, combined with the nemesis system remembering their combat history with you, makes you feel like each captain is an individual. It feels as though the game is playing the game with you as another entity or player, in the sense you are against the nemesis system and both of you operate inside the game world, but the game remembers when you die, remembers when you quit, remembers when you killed an enemy and how. It's by far my favourite part of the game and a major selling feature on the sequel I haven't tried yet. And collecting intel on enemies to plan out how to work around their abilities and strenghts/weaknesses has always felt meaningful (in the sense it is important to how I play) and yet never feels like a chore. After all, you can always go into combat blind and see what happens =P
At present I have just ventured into the second act, a second area that is completely different from the first, where you go from volcanic mordor wasteland to cliffs and greenery and the like. The game has opened up even more now, to include 'branding' enemy uruk and bending them to my will, allowing me to lead hoardes of Uruk against their kin in very meaningful feeling battles. I could go on and on and on about this game, it has easily rocketed to the top of my favourites list alongside games like AC Black Flag, Sleeping Dogs, and Witcher 3. The story is short and easily relatable, giving you just enough urgency to progress the story at a reasonable pace. The experience and point gain has also been consistently reasonable, allowing me to enjoy the cool unlockable skills without much grinding.
All in all I would reccomend this game to anybody who enjoys hack and slash third person combat games. My feelings on this game are mixed. It has beautiful graphics. It has sophisticated, smooth-running mechanics (many of which even make sense). It doesn't crash (at least it never has for me). And it has a lot of great ideas. It's really endeavored to be a kind of "spiritual successor" to past classic iso-RPGs, such as Baldur's Gate; and it does a decent job of this, at least in the combat aspect. The game is very polished and definitely professional quality.
Why then don't I recommend it? I simply didn't find it fun.
To me, the appeal of games in this vein lies in the story and the characters. I found the story to be very bland and uninteresting, which was made worse by the cast of incredibly bland and uninteresting characters. After meeting and traveling with all the recruitable NPCs in the game, and finding not a single one that I actually liked, I eventually settled on creating my own custom party - which basically means trading meaningless and pointless dialog for no dialog at all.
One of the most annoying things I encountered was that the vast majority of in-game "characters" cannot actually be interacted with in any meaningful way. I understand, these are meant as a tribute to backers and supporters and such; but they actually make the game very annoying for us players. No, I don't want to reach out and touch their soul and read some totally random, meaningless fanfic... ughh... I wish there was an option to just remove them from the game. Although... that would make it seem very, very empty, since there are so few *real* characters to interact with.
If none of this bothers you, by all means check it out. It's not a horrible game. I was on the fence about recommending it; but eventually decided to give it the thumbs up because the developers did create a high-quality product.

As of writing this review this game is reviewed as mostly negative, not because of gameplay, story, or anything about the actual experience. Rather, it is mostly negative because of the price, which i don't support in the slightest.
This review is going to be about the game itself, which i highly reccomend, and not the raised price due to the upcoming steam summer sales.
This game is great, one of the best story games i've ever had the experience of going through, or started in the time of the review. The game feels very DnD esque, the usual character creation: pick race, sex, class, and attribute rolls. Much like DnD your character's class and attribute roll specifically effect how events turn out in game. for instance, catching someone you're climbing up a wall with if your dex is high enough.
now, this game feels very... slow, i guess. it's basically the best game you'll ever read. If you enjoy expansive lore, deep and well written dialogue between all characters, in your party and village NPCs, this game is for you. It requires A LOT of reading, and if you're not into reading multiple paragraphs of dialogue throughout basically every interaction, then i would reccomend to stay away, unless you want to adopt a summer reading project.
The gameplay is interesting, at points it will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ making you rethink about your party's positioning, attacks, etc... and at others it will make you feel like it's a bit too easy. You feel really good when figuring out puzzles, which is great as most RPGs seem to have lackluster and bland counterparts. The race of your character effects gameplay a bit, some of it being a niche novelty used rarely, if not ever, this being most noticable with the godlike race, where they can't wear helmets but, you can light torches with your head, this being basically only used in some puzzles, but hey, it's something. The combat in this game is slow, but methodical, you need to know how to rearrange your party in certain combat situations, freezing time constantly to switch and focus targets. This game can be brutal, especially for new players who have never played games such as baldur's gate and others like it.
This game should be played, especially if you enjoy DnD and RPGs. I definitely reccomend this game to anyone who has time to spend reading paragraphs of enjoyable and well written dialogue, even if the combat seems a bit... slow. This is definitely something you should pick up, if only the stupid devs/publishers would stop raising the price of it.

Oh man, what to say about StratO. I honestly wasn't sure if I was going to like it, I've been a fan of the developers streams for a while but wasn't sure if this was quite my cup of tea.
The game seems brutally difficult at first, but upon a few trail and error attempts and reviewing the controls, I found myself becoming more and more accustomed to the gameplay. Within the first twenty minutes I was coasting off of walls and blasting through rings at lightning speed!
The gameplay get's very intense, as you scrape by buildings at blazing speeds you'll hear gusting winds as the camera shakes vigorously giving you that feeling as if you're an ace pilot in a big budget action film! It makes the game's learning curve SO worth it!
The biggest plus for me however, is the game seems to adapt to any style of play. If you're looking to collect rings as fast as you can, scoring multiple bullseyes while preforming skill chains will phase the player into what is known as "B-side", were rings scored will award double the points but it's significantly harder in the process. However if you're looking for something more laid back and chill, you can traverse the map at a laid back pace and still remain competitive against other players.
There is no ineffective way to play this game, and that's probably the game's strongest feature. Some have stated that this game is anti casual. I'd argue the opposite. Once you take the time to learn the controls and physics of StratO, it's very easy to log in, play it for ten minutes, and go back to your work space feeling completely satisfied!
Gameplay: 5/5 - Difficult to learn at first, but after a while it all starts to make sense. The physics are incredible!
Graphics:   4/5 - Simple but effective. Nothing looks awkward or out of place. The lighting in some of the later maps is beautiful!
Soundtrack: 4/5 - Clever use of game mechanics that change the in game music while rocket boosting make it hard to resist muting the music for something else. The in game music, particularly the "default" map track which is most commonly used is great! It's not too fancy and fits the atmosphere well. My only complaint is there needs to be more music tracks for the game to swap through as you get into the later maps.
Story: not applicable - It's an arcadey game, what'd you expect?

Resident Evil 0: Inventory Management and Bakctracking Simulator is...
Still a pretty good game despite its flaws. Like the joke title implies, you're going to be doing a LOT of backtracking to pick up items you were forced to drop to be able to pick up important items; there are no magic item boxes like in the other classic RE titles. Sometimes you'll die on the way back there, too, since enemies are sometimes difficult to kill, ammo is scarce, and healing items scarcer still (not to mention it's pretty easy to get in the orange Caution or Danger zone, especially as Rebecca). Still, the scarcity oddly adds to the experience since you'll need to be smart about using resources.
Other than those things- with the only real "complaint" being inventory management- RE0 is a fun game that leaves you feeling satisfied once you beat it or even advance to a new part of the game after killing a boss or solving a puzzle. I personally enjoyed the game, at least, and well enough to recommend it and to advise ignoring any complaints about it being too hard and tedious. It's suitably challenging. This is also coming from someone who hasn't played any of the classic RE titles for nearly a decade, meaning you don't have to be all too familiar with the style of the classic games to get the hang of things.

Man oh man, this game is a special kind of special. Now I was going to make a really predictable joke about the graphics and all, but I still have a bit of self respect left. Instead, I will simply tell you why should you buy this wonderful piece of gaming satire.
Press X to Read Review
So, you wake up to find almost everyone in the city insane and killing each other, and as you see your best friend being murdered right in front of you, you brush it off and go find your girlfriend, Hoes before Bros am I right? And so you venture in this epic journey of action, violence, and love to save your girlfriend and escape this madness.
Well, I can't get really much into the story without giving slight but meaningful spoilers, so I'll leave you guys with that, and move on to gameplay. Just know, that the whole story and concept are absolutely hilarious and very well done.
This game is just like one of those interactive movies from the 80s, where you react by pressing a button and your actions determine what happens in the game, stuff like THREADING THE THIN LINE BETWEEN LIFE AND DEATH and other, more meaningful stuff, like deciding if you are going to creep on your girlfriend showering.
There's also plenty of replay value, due to some choices the game have you make, so that's a plus.
The game is basically a glorified QTE scene, but don't veer your eyes away just yet, it is all really well done, and there is a lot of effort put in by the actors and the director.
The games graphics are amazing, they're just like real life (HAHA FUNNY JOKE. Dammit, I just lost the rest of self respect I had.), but seriously, everything is just beautifully shot and amazingly creative, the developers did a wonderful job at filming, all the locations are amazing, the actors are pretty good, there are barely any cringy moments, and you can see how much effort they put into this game, also, all the neat editing tricks they've used are a sight to see. It is all filmed with a GoPro, and it is just wonderful. (Insert more praise here)
The music is also fantastic, it has a really serious tone to it, but that just adds to the satire.
The game has really nifty extras, like a death gallery and behind the scenes pictures, which shows how much effort and fun the developers had. Also the game has a wonderful DLC which is the prototype they've made prior to filming, which will definitively get you to laugh. Also it's only a dollar.
Overall, this game is worth it for two reasons, it is a wonderful piece of gaming satire, and it is hilarious, also 3$. You really should buy it, you are definitively going to get plenty of laughs while playing and a lot of replayability, so even more laughs. Pick this one up, you won't regret it!

Don't mind me, just rewriting my review because I was tired when I made my last one.
So, I'm going to be upfront with this and say I don't think Starbound is a bad game. I just don't think it's very good.
Right. I'm going to list it's problems.
I'm not listing the good points, because all the good stuff can be found in other games. If you like Starbound and are skimming through the down votes then you should go find something better to do.
For a game about exploring the infinite vastness of space, it also does a great job of showing just how empty in boring it is. The only interactions you have with space is travelling through it, and exploring lone, tiny asteroids. The only challenge with space is fuel, which becomes obsolete the moment you get the crew member who raises fuel efficiency to 100%.
The game boast randomly generated weapons, planets, dungeons, and monsters. But the problem with this is that if you don't include enough variety, everything ends up the same. There are very few differences in weapons aside from their appearance, name, and whether it's a gun, melee weapon, or staff. All the planets are also near identical, just painted different colours and with different set-pieces and mini biomes. Dungeons have little variety in their layout. and last, the monsters. Oh, the monsters. As far as the randomly generated monsters go, well...
There are 3 of them. There are randomly generated walkers, flyers, and swimmers. While two walkers may look different, once agroed and they all behave exactly the same.
There are also randomly generated side quests, but don't bother to much with them. There are really only a few. Escort missions, make food, deliver package, blah blah blah.
There are so many different, multi stage food recipes, and they are all useless. While some may recover more hunger than others and give you a short buff, shooting a bunch of stuff and cooking the meat is the most efficient use of your time. The devs added a coooking log to try ans encurage you to cook lots of different foods, but it's still not worth your time.
There's not much to say about them. They are the mest source of ore in the game and are filled with villagers that will freak out and attack you if the volcanic planet they live on happens to have an ember shower that burns down their buildings.
Why go into a cave if all the ore and weapons you'll ever need are available on the surface? Same goes for fuel.
On moons and some planets, meteor showers occur. The meteors fall fast enough as to be hard to avoid, and one shot you regardless of armour and health. "Oooh, but that's realistic" someone once said. Sure, but realism doesn't always make for good game mechanics. The few times I died was to meteors which would kill me because I didn't play with the game zoomed super far out and had no idea they were coming. Yes, I am salty. Shut up.
Valcanic planets also have en ember shower event which destroys logicically flammable blocks. I'm fine with this. However, my suspension of disbelief breaks when I find a wooden village built on the planet's surface. And whenever a furniture item breaks due to the fire, the guards all become hostile.
Also on moons is a spooky space ghost that also one shots you. I've never been killed by it, but it's still annoying. It's best never to venture inside a moon, and to just run along the outside gathering all the fuel readily available on the surface, and then beam away. Also, fuel becomes pretty pointless, as I said, when you get that crew member that removes the requirement for fuel

Classic FPS that hearkens the days of monster closets, b grade cinema story line and voice acting and a world limited by arbitrary obstacles and corridors. If you are me and were a big fan of FPS in the 90's I say give this a chance, you just wax poetic and shed a tear in retrospect of simpler times...shall I say purer times? This is Doom 3 lite, Dead Effect doesn't innovate at all nor does it provide a deep gamelay experience . What it does provide is tight controls, excellent graphics, non stop action, great audio and real care that went into level design, however old school or derivative it may be.
For old school FPS fans like myself there is a lot of fun to be had here, for the price this is a great value.

Overall, I can only say that Dead Effect, in all of its derivative and "Mockbuster"-esque glory, really is a game made for me and my very specific FPS tastes. I like zombie gore, I like mad scientists, I like this System Shock/Dead Space/Doom 3 type of setting where all hell breaks loose on a spaceship or space station, and I like straight forward corridor shooters where my mouse finger does all the work while my brain gets to shut down. Your personal mileage may vary, especially if you're looking for a slightly more sophisticated (or original) experience, but I'm a simple man of simple pleasures, and I've had quite a lot of fun with this.

State of Decay is a great game with an engaging story line (see last line for the one major flaw in the game).  It is not open ended (without the DLC) and plays more like most open world mission based games like GTA but with some RPG aspects for building characters up.  The game relies very little on building your character.  My ratings for the game would be:
Gameplay 8 out of 10:
Controls are easy to use, movement and driving vehicles is easy.  Unlike most RPG driven games you receive nothing for killing zombies other than staying alive which means that because your not getting money or equipment drops out of zombies, you are driven to use stealth when possible.  In fact your supplies (ammo) dwindle and your equipment eventually breaks with usage, so killing zombies randomly is a form of attrition on your base forcing you to do extra supply runs and those runs do not produce tons of resources so expect to do a lot of work if you decide to go on a zombie killing spree.  Base game is mission based and if you have played GTA or Driver or any open world games you will find the gameplay and movement/interaction to be familiar.
Graphics 8 out of 10:
Nothing special, exactly what you would expect out of this style game.  Playing at low settings will not affect the game that much for you compared to max resolution.
Storyline 9 out of 10:
Fun storyline that reminds you of The Walking Dead, missions are not just random all the time and usually pertain to the backstory of each character.
NOTE:  Over all it is a fun game BUT expect gameplay and the storyline to become victim to repetitiveness to a point of becoming a tad tiresome.  DLC may change this from what I see, but I have not purchased them to confirm this.

I got this during a sale and despite playing it 4 years later after release it still a nice game if you haven't played it yet, I've played all Splinter Cell games to date, my favorite being Splinter Cell: Double Agent.
Compared to Splinter Cell: Conviction, which was too combat and narrative oriented (similar how Hitman: Absolution departed from the series, but came back closer with the latest Hitman)... this one similarly moves closer to what the series was, although not quite the same. It combines aspects from the original Splinter Cell game style and the Conviction game style. Gadgets are back, although a lot more limited compared to the old games, stealthy missions are back, the classic splinter cell black suits are back, but still retains the continuous personal narrative focus and action-oriented game style that Conviction introduced.
Compared to the older games though, it's still a bit fast paced, but generally you'll feel like Sam is a much more badass then ever before. in the old games, being discovered is generally a death sentence, aiming is hard, and there's not much hand to hand combat, this Sam Fisher can fight and shoot, just like in Conviction, but hides and disappears just as good as he was in the older games.
Despite using the very old Unreal Engine 2(It's a heavily modified version), it still looks good, the only thing that looks bad is the character faces, they look so plastic and unrealistic. The Graphics in general though still looks modern enough and could pass even as a 2017 game. I wished they at least used Unreal Engine 3 though(which is already even surpassed by Unreal Engine 4)
The game has plenty of content, aside from the main campaign missions, there's plenty of side missions from each of Sam's allies/friends, and there's also a coop and online multiplier game modes as well.
The game is not that polished. while the Animations look smooth and fluid and the executions are nice and well made, there are quite some noticeable bugs, animations does not blend well when interacting with other entities, like when using kill-moves, you'd see characters 'snapping' to each other, ragdolls and physics are a bit off, with bodies suddenly flying, guns suddenly floating in the air. This deserves a mention as this is already 4 years after release date.
Controls are also weird, it takes a while to get used to it, it's not well-designed, but it is a passable set up. I hated that they ditched Michael Ironside for a new actor, it just sounded weird. I got used to it after beating the game though, and after watching old Splinter Cell videos, hearing Michael Ironside now sounded weird.
I would say though that despite these. it's still an enjoyable experience. and would recommend getting it on a sale if you're a fan of Splinter Cell or even a newcomer of the series looking for some stealth-action games similar to Hitman or Metal Gear.
Score: 8.3/10

As of writing this review this game is reviewed as mostly negative, not because of gameplay, story, or anything about the actual experience. Rather, it is mostly negative because of the price, which i don't support in the slightest.
This review is going to be about the game itself, which i highly reccomend, and not the raised price due to the upcoming steam summer sales.
This game is great, one of the best story games i've ever had the experience of going through, or started in the time of the review. The game feels very DnD esque, the usual character creation: pick race, sex, class, and attribute rolls. Much like DnD your character's class and attribute roll specifically effect how events turn out in game. for instance, catching someone you're climbing up a wall with if your dex is high enough.
now, this game feels very... slow, i guess. it's basically the best game you'll ever read. If you enjoy expansive lore, deep and well written dialogue between all characters, in your party and village NPCs, this game is for you. It requires A LOT of reading, and if you're not into reading multiple paragraphs of dialogue throughout basically every interaction, then i would reccomend to stay away, unless you want to adopt a summer reading project.
The gameplay is interesting, at points it will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ making you rethink about your party's positioning, attacks, etc... and at others it will make you feel like it's a bit too easy. You feel really good when figuring out puzzles, which is great as most RPGs seem to have lackluster and bland counterparts. The race of your character effects gameplay a bit, some of it being a niche novelty used rarely, if not ever, this being most noticable with the godlike race, where they can't wear helmets but, you can light torches with your head, this being basically only used in some puzzles, but hey, it's something. The combat in this game is slow, but methodical, you need to know how to rearrange your party in certain combat situations, freezing time constantly to switch and focus targets. This game can be brutal, especially for new players who have never played games such as baldur's gate and others like it.
This game should be played, especially if you enjoy DnD and RPGs. I definitely reccomend this game to anyone who has time to spend reading paragraphs of enjoyable and well written dialogue, even if the combat seems a bit... slow. This is definitely something you should pick up, if only the stupid devs/publishers would stop raising the price of it.

This review will make ample comparison to Terraria, such comparisons are of course inevitable given the nature of the two games. If this triggers you, feel free to hit that downvote button and move along.
Where to begin? Starbound is a game of plenty. In short, it's a monumentally successful sub $20 purchase simply as a value proposition. There's a lot of game here and I'd just be a liar if I said it wasn't worth the asking price on its own merits.
But so much of what Starbound does, has been done better in Terraria. Both games are good in their own right, and often for different reasons, but there's a very clear advantage here that Terraria has over Starbound. That being that Terraria understands its sandbox nature more than Starbound understands its own. Starbound attempts to leash you with some ham-fisted "Story" which actually only serves to illustrate how transparent the core exploration gameplay loop is with its linear progression of tiered planets.
This tiered system is probably the root of all of Starbounds design issues as an open-world sandbox game. Despite having a (Theoretically) infinite universe to explore, the game plays out in an incredibly linear fashion up until you've vanquished the big bad. It's almost as if the "Story" itself should be considered simply a tutorial. However, this ends up leaving a good chunk of the universe and planet diversity redundant. What's more, is the "Story" Pushes the player artificially through this tiered system which violates (At least in my opinion, but this whole review is my opinion so whatever) the underlying core of discovery and exploration. Terraria on the other hand, hides almost an identical loop of advancing through material tiers simply by what it DOES NOT do. That is, it doesn't tell you a damn thing. It lets you discover things on your own. It trusts the player to investigate new things when they acquire new tools such as double jump, hookshot or flight capability. This organic processes of discovery and advancement is probably (I think definitively) Terraria's biggest strength over Starbound.
Now what does Starbound do that's unequivically better than Terraria? Quests. Terraria really has none, And while most of Starbound's quests are throwaway, one in particular stands out as an exemplar of how to design a quest in such a game. The Hylotl Museum quest line which has you search (With no real direction given) for artifacts in order to add to the collection. Now, if that sounds familiar to Starbound players in more ways than one, it's because it's almost literally the exact same setup as the main quest, without some nonesensical "Story" thrown in there for forced narrative urgency. Organic emergent gameplay is the greatest ally of the Open-World design. When you're creating a sandbox, it's better to let the player fill in as many blanks as possible while just pushing them in a certain direction with context.
That's my assessment on some of the more subtle design running under the game, as for more of the objective and technical strengths and/or weaknesses, those are easy.

I''ve been playing the Nancy Drew games since the very first, Secrets Can Kill. They are always delightfully fun. I've noticed the following things since I started playing these games. As more of these games are released, the puzzles are becoming a bit harder, but the games themselves are shorter.
Shadow at Water's Edge was no different in this respect. If I sat down and really played it, I could have completed it in less than a day, easy. However, like the other games, certain events are triggered by being in a certain place at the right time, or by doing something else first. In this title in particular, those triggers were a little harder to find.  In addition, I didn't exactly understand the point of grading the students' homework in Nancy's schoolteacher role, other than perhaps getting a trophy for it at the end. It seemed like a pointless little thing to do.
This is the first foray into the actual "horror" genre for Nancy Drew Team, if one does not count "The Curse of Blackmoor Manor," and they did pretty well with it, highlighting all the points of  "typical" Japanese ghost-- watery footprints, trying to come at you through a mirror, locking you in a room, etc. The puzzles were, at times, a little challenging, but completable. The voice acting was perfect, as usual, and I actually really enjoyed the Bento making minigame. [Although, I personally would have preferred it to be actual sushi instead.] Overall, I would recommend this game to lovers of mystery games, search and find/point and click games, and adventure games.

I have a confession to make: I play every Tonguc Bodur game. I'm addicted. They're always Unreal asset flips, they are almost all the same (there's a cave sequence, dodgy narration, surrealistic lighting, alcohol references, statue-turning puzzles, and vague nonsensical metaphors in just about every one), and I just can't help myself but to play them all at least once.
Nephise disappoints in a new-and-improved spin on Dan Pinchbeck's formula, though. It's a walking simulator where you barely even go anywhere, and it's a narration vehicle with nearly no narration. What it does have is a frustratingly dumb puzzle, a few shiny assets, and all the Tonguc Bodur tropes I have grown to know and love.
You play as Nephise, a woman who loves getting drunk and getting 100% achievements on Steam. She <spoiler>falls into a drunken stupor and dreams that she does a boring puzzle, explores a cave, kills a man, and drinks more</spoiler> I MEAN spends the night at an inn and then has to do an extremely tedious puzzle.
Here's where I give Bodur some credit for striking out in a bold new direction--there is more interaction than normal in this iteration of the TB phenomenon. You have to solve some riddles and collect ten (count 'em, ten) orbs that glow bright red in a totally white environment. But the puzzle sucks. You have to orient the statues in certain directions based on riddles you hear out of nowhere, but not the whole statue! If you do that, you will consistently find that it doesn't matter how closely you pay attention to the riddles, you will be sorely frustrated. This is because you must orient the statues so that their FACES point in certain directions, not the statue as a whole. I feel as though this is Tonguc Bodur's way of saying "Nah-nah nah-nah boo-boo, I am smarter than you!" It's deeply appreciated.
If that weren't bad enough, you play as Warwick "Nephise" Davis and thus you walk at the speed of lint, so moving around the (rather small stock) map is a chore. Meanwhile, repetitive harp music and surprisingly crisp but repetitive crunchy snowy footsteps drill a jagged hole into your brain.
TL;DR: This game means nothing. It brings almost no original content to the gaming scene. The narrator barely did anything and was of basically no importance from a stylistic perspective. Bodur does the things he always does only with even less effort (because, honestly, he normally arranges his stock assets with thought and care). If you know how the statues work you will finish this game in five minutes.

Alright. My journey through Tonguc's catalog continues. My current stop is at Nephise, a charming little tale that can realistically be told in about 15 minutes, but with which you could easily spend an hour simply taking in the sights.
At it's heart, Nephise is the whimsical, lighthearted tale of a young orb hunter named Nephise, who enjoys a nice brew, gets some sleep, and then goes on an orb hunting adventure. Her exploits could potentially be the stuff of legends! For the purposes of this tale however, she really is starting off on what could be the road to legend.
While quite simple, the story in Nephise is effective and amusing, and as such marks a bit of a departure from the more somber topic matters covered in the Drizzlepath series. While it isn't a fully realized story, I also don't feel it is necessary within the confines of this game. Perhaps if the series is explored in greater depth though, this will become more explicit in its conveyance. Nephise Begins is next on my list, so maybe things are even more fleshed out there.
7.5 out of 10
The gameplay in Nephise is not so dissimilar to previous titles from Tonguc, but does actually rely more on puzzles and less on actual exploration. This is driven home by the small environs crafted for the game, which really just entails a small snowy forest area near an inn, and a brief subterranean system below. There is really just one primary puzzle, but it was pretty clever in design and relies on you doing what you should be doing when playing a walking simulator: taking in and observing your surroundings. If you do so, the puzzle will be pretty obvious in design. If not, you may be wandering back and forth for a little while trying to get it just right.
Now, Nephise is an orb hunter, so you will be advised to embrace the role and find the orbs lying about the forest. There are ten in total, glowing red and pretty easy to find. My advice is: when you feel like you have found all of the ones you can, progress the story. You will find the remaining hidden orbs by doing so. Does this have an actual impact on the story? Not that I can tell. However, why not dive into the role presented, right?
As far as functionality, this is once again another example of seamless programming. No technical issues whatsoever.
9 out of 10
As always, Tonguc's use of the Unreal engine is exemplary. This is a snow covered and beautiful world on the surface, with some interesting formations and a rad looking wolf. Once you go underground, the world really becomes stunning and somewhat different than I have seen before in a game. Really a unique and awesome looking experience. Also, the Inn itself, which functions as your intro story spot, looks quite rustic and nice.
10 out of 10
The audio in Nephise is pretty limited overall. That doesn't mean it doesn't sound great. It is simply limited in scope, which is consistent with the game itself, as it is very focused with limited scope overall. I thought the musical score was nice, and the old lady narrating sounded believable and fun all at once.
9 out of 10
I thought Nephise was a charming experience with a sense of fun and whimsy that I didn't expect going in. I quite enjoyed it as the first entry into Tonguc's second series of games. I am very interested to see what will happen next.
8.875 out of 10, which of course rounded up will be 8.9 out of 10. I definitely recommend this if you want a peaceful and charming experience.

There are two playable character, male and female, each with different starting guns.
The plot is paper thing, the zombies are the standard fare, the animation can be a little akward and the between mission menu is kinda janky (not reading mouse clicks right).
All of this said, I've been wanting a game like this for a while. A proper, switch off shooter with not pretending about what it is. Stupid, dumb fun. There is even a simple rpg-lite system with cash and gold to collect in game (which smells kinda micro-transactiony but thankfully there is none of that; would have killed this game) for between missions where you can buy new weapons and upgrade existing ones.
Easy to recomend for this price.

I was a huge fan of Resident Evil back in the day, especially the first one.
While some old games can be re-released and be a reminder of how good things truly used to be, these older REs with the fixed camera style are coming apart at the seams.  The main reason this and REmake got so much attention is because they had great graphics and sound for their time, especially for the GCN.  Take that away, they're both really tedious, broken puzzle games with poor combat and clunky movement.
Regardless of control scheme, it still controls like garbage most of the time.  An unfortunate trademark of this style of RE.
The visual upgrade may have some redone textures here and there, but the vast majority of it was just taking existing assets and upscaling the resolution.
All the inventory management gets old fast.  It's just plain tedious.  An expanded carry capacity option would have really alleviated things.
The AI buddy system got a lot of flak in its day from hardcore RE fans for taking away from the survival-horror element, but it really doesn't do much but add more senseless micromanaging to the game.
The hookshot is a huge troll maneuver from Capcom - you either take up two blocks carrying it with you almost the entire game to use it way later after its first use, or you drop it to make room and then have to run all the way back to fetch it when you do finally need to reuse it.  That's right - no item boxes with special teleporting powers.  You want to make space, you drop something, and it stays there for if/when you come back for it later.  This was when some gamers were making a lot of noise demanding more "realism" from their games, and in almost all cases we ended up with more tedious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like this to sate that audience.  Better take notes of where you dropped your♥♥♥♥♥♥..
RE0 has a terrible story.  Even by RE standards, all of which is throwaway now that people know none of them are really linked and info in one game gets retconned out later.  Skip the cutscenes.
There is only one good line in this entire game, and it's because of how absolutely abysmal it is: "Aaa!  Billy."

After playing 4,5,6 and 7 over the past decade it is a breath of fresh air to play a classic Resident Evil title again. I never owned a gamecube (like the vast majority of people) so I never got to experience 0 or the remake, and I have to say they are fantastic. I knew 1 enough from playing the original to have an idea of what I was doing but 0 is completely blind and so far it is hard! After the train (which felt like the tutorial level sort of thing) I have a knife and 2 bullets!
This is the first Resident Evil I have seen that so far feels like survival. Of course you can bait out zombie attacks and run past them but I've always been a killer, and usually you're provided with just enough ammo to kill everything in 1,2,3 and CV, but it doesn't feel like that is the case in 0. The puzzles are quite intuitive for once and the 2 character system works far better than I thought it would of, this game honestly just makes it sting knowing that 5 could of been an incredible game had it been more like 4 and had the character system 0 has. I do love playing as Rebecca as she is one of the better characters in the series, but she has never seen that much screen time. Seeing her again in 0 and recently in Vendetta (CGI Movie) gives me hope that she and Barry (Rev2) will make a return to the series in the future.
If you're a fan you owe it to yourself and the community to get this along with Remake, there are still many Resident Evil titles that are missing from Steam, including the Xbox 360/Ps3 remaster of Code Veronica that is currently lost in time and nowhere to be found for most users. Though it doesn't seem like there are that many people interested in Remake or 0 on Steam which is tragic, Capcom may not bother to give us any of the older titles now.
I hope Revelations 3 or Resident Evil 8 go back to this style of gameplay. 5 was uninspired and the turning point for the series derpy descent into machine gun madness, and 7 is too extreme of a step backwards in terms of gameplay and perspective, with awful monsters and enemies as well as an uninteresting and empty plot which adds nothing to the universe.

The other resident evil game that for a long time was only on the Gamecube just like the remade original and I always found it a shame that they were never made available to a wider audience until years later. And when it did finally come over in HD form it was an absolute treat and is every bit as good as the RE remake also in HD. The visuals are amazing, you have the horror, the atmosphere, the environments, the enemies, Rebecca as a stand-out character and certainly not weak or vunerable as you might perceive from the original game. It looks grim but knows when and where to make things look better or to stand out, add in achievements and modes and quite a lot of replay value such as finding all keys or trying to do the entire game without a single save allowed. Yes most of the DLC is costume based and you should only get them on discount, however I have no issue with adding choice or variety to the game and it helps to keep things fresh, especially if your going for another run to hunt down that one achievement your really after.
Overall this game is worth your time and money, the core resident evil mechanics you know and love are all here and I would pick this over RE7 anyday regardless of how RE7 changed the formula.
Recommended and approved, your horror gaming experience is pretty safe here.

Exploring space with friends have never been so much fun! Welcome to Starbound a sidescrolling space exploration game developed by Chucklefish, and exploration is where this game excels, exploring space feels natural with a multitude of different planets of different tiers to explore and minibiomes unique to each one it definitely feels like exploring space. The combat is nothing special but its fine, it fits the game to the letter and is simple... which I think is for the best, the music is phenomenal ranging from a magnificent orchestral classical style all the way to a techno funky style. The character creation is simple and but makes it feel you are unique to compared the NPCs and each race is distinct each with its own culture inspired by real life cultures like Aztec, Feudal Japan (and modern), Tribal, Middle Ages, Authoritarian High Tech Sci-FI, Uh Human? I don't really know what the collective name for all of future humankinds culture is... (okay I looked it up the offical Starbound wiki lists it as "Modern"), and the Wild West! The GUI is not doing the game any favors but its simplestic design and easy use kind of makes up for it. But this game does not just inhale air and fart out rainbows and daisys, Starting with survival mode which makes you drop items on death, but only some of them you drop food, crafting supplies, and healing items, this would not be a pain for the first two but droping healing items and anything that makes it more of a pain to get back to said items in the first place is not something I would consider a good idea (this problem increases ten-fold when you die underground when monsters spawn on your way down and you get screwed cause you can't heal and you end up dead again), and a particularly fun storyline is masked behind pain in the♥♥♥♥♥scaning "barriers" which are missions where you have to scan objects from one of the races until you scan enough "importent" objects so you can finally gain access your kick♥♥♥♥♥dungeon and even more amazing boss fight. Going solo is a fun experience once and a while but the game really shines in multiplayer when you load in and all of your fellow universal explorers team up to take on the many worlds. Starbound is a fairly solid experience that is best played with friends alongside you, so get going! Team up and take on the universe!

I've *almost* got 100 hours in the game, that includes main-game, DLC and lots of end-game content.
Having played Baldur's Gate 1&2, as well as Planescape Torment after this game (currently on Divinity: Original Sin EE with a friend), you can see that I've played/am playing a lot of CRPGS. I really enjoy the style, and as a game master, it inspires my campaigns and let's me live out what being a PC could be like.
Pillars of Eternity 2 is on the way soon, and the kickstarter has been backed and I can't wait.
Pros:
- Great Soundtrack
- Fitting, stunning graphics
- old-school freedom
- more plot than Baldur's Gate, or at least, one that'll interest more people
Cons:
- combat can get tedious in the late-game and DLC, but that's standard for this genre
- "breaking the game" in an old-school way, or rather, thinking outside the box doesn't work often
9/10, fans of the genre or of the studio should definitely check this game out, it's a love-letter to old-school RPGs, like La La Land was a love-letter to the musicals of old times.

Even though this game is pretty janky compared to From's more recent titles, I'd still strongly recommend playing this game. I'd even say you should play this one first because the next games build upon DS1's theme of cycles and struggles. The aesethetics are amazing, they're often imitated but never duplicated in other games. The game play is very open ended and the different areas can be tackled in any order, although certain areas are locked until you complete certain story events. Some of the best items can be obtained very early in the game if the player explores the  more dangerous areas instead of going to the  undead burg first. The catch is that if you die in these areas you stand to lose a lot of your souls, which are used to power up your character. The bosses are fantastics, although not all are created equal.
The jankiness shows up in PVP and elsewhere. As it is right now, the pvp is still fairly active, which is pretty noteworthy given the game's age. However it straight up does not work without using Wulf's Connectivity mod (google it). The pvp still has it's fair share of cheaters who make their character invincible and able to curse your character, leaving them locked at half health. Curses can be cured but there are only two ways that exist to do so. There isn't much you can do to combat a cheater other than making them fall since most of the time they still take fall damage. The pvp is relatively unbalanced but I still enjoy it when I can find a player to connect with.
The game's controls are another common gripe. This game REQUIRES a controller (xbox or ps3 if you install scptoolkit) because the keyboard controls are awful and difficult to manage. The graphics are very muddy but can be fixed with texture mods by using dsfix. Dsfix is 100% necessary even if you don't want to mod your game. Some areas of the game are rushed. The demon ruins/lost Izalith are just not finished. Poor bosses, graphics, and design, it's just a shame.
Still one of my favorite games. The game has lead to the creation of many memes, so if you like those that's nice.

Nephise may just as well be Tonguç Bodur’s shortest creation, yet it still bares the developer’s mark of distinction. Just as its lengthier predecessors, Nephise is both abstract and relaxing. A journey which represents something entirely different, depending on what the players perceive or desire it to be. Having played through all of Tonguç’s games so far, I can safely assure you that each and every one of them, has a distinct and fascinating tale, just waiting to be discovered. You will only need patience and an inclination towards walking simulators.
Just as in the prequel (Nephise Begins), the titular heroine is silent and unseen. Playing from a first person perspective, sure you might say that it’s hard to get a glimpse of the female protagonist (since video game mirrors are notoriously difficult to implement, or don’t match the themes), yet most of the titles in the Drizzlepath series showed the mysterious heroes, at least at the end of each game. So I’ll just have to trust the female narrator when she describes Nephise as a “young orb collector”. In Begins she was more interested in collecting mushrooms and animal skulls, by the way.
In fact, collecting orbs in this title seems more of a secondary objective. Your main goal is to escape a strangely enclosed snowy forest by discovering four statues and tilting them in a certain position. So that is indeed involving some environmental puzzles. If in Nephise Begins, players had to convince a giant fox to stop blocking  an escape path, now we have a giant wolf who’s blocking a cave entrance. Finding and collecting all ten orbs present in-game, will unlock a Steam Achievement.
Powered by Unreal Engine 4 as with the large majority of Bodur’s previous projects. It looks gorgeous when maxed out, but I cannot undertand what makes the Nephise games harder to render in 4K resolution and decent frame rate, than any of the Drizzlepath games. Both Begins and now Nephise, forced me to run them in 2K resolution and even then, I had frame rate dips as low as 45, at times. Must be UE4 confirming to me once again that eye candy alone ≠ gameplay stability or fun factor. Unity can look almost as good as Unreal or CryEngine without any pretentious side effects or frame rate instability. Kona and Narcosis are just two examples of the beauty which be achieved on the Unity Engine, if a dev team spends enough time with it.
You can finish Nephise in less than an hour, but I took my sweet time and snapped quite a few screenshots. The snow-covered woodland reminded me of both Skyrim and Tonguç’s Bottle. The cave exploration (spelunking) seems to be the one element which is prevalent across all of the developer’s titles. Can’t blame him. Even abtract games deserve some consistency, since there can’t be only dreams and nightmares involved in the creation process. Overall, I was pleased by what I saw and even at 2K, Nephise looks great and runs decently, with no glitches, bugs or crashes.
The already mentioned narrator is interrupted from time to time by some instrumental songs which had a medieval vibe to them. Those reminded me dearly of the Stronghold series, for some reason. It was pleasant, no matter how brief the overall experience might be. Some more character context would have been appreciated though and I’m almost missing that strange poetry from the Drizzlepath trilogy.
No type of progress saving options. This really annoyed me once I noticed that I missed collecting an orb in the cave section and couldn’t reach it again. I actually restarted the game just to pick up that one troublesome orb and receive its Achievement. I’m not even hunting for these on Steam, but I couldn’t miss the chance to unlock all three “cheevos” in Nephise. They’re low-effort, as long as you “keep the eyes on the prize” and not wander around constantly looking for screenshot opportunities. OCD is a terrible thing, kids. Almost as bad as booze and Nephise can really confirm this. Play the game until you reach its conclusion and you’ll understand.
Being easy to complete and reach even its secondary goals, you cannot complain that this walking simulator bored you to tears. Sure, you won’t get to blast anything or kill zombies/nazis/aliens/dinosaurs/etc, but you should have known that before you purchased Nephise or the other titles in this particular abstract collection. You walk, stop, stare, reflect, or do whatever you want. You don’t have to collect the orbs in Nephise, just like you weren’t forced to collect the mushrooms in Nephise Begins. Though, playing Nephise after its prequel, I have to wonder what were those shrooms exactly? Another unsolved mystery. At least until the next Bodur game shall be released on Steam.  I sincerely hope it shall take longer to finish.
Like them or not, purely abstract titles are here to stay. Steam and the indie development scene go hand in hand (despite the occasional “mishap”). You won’t find big devs or publishers willing to take risks in the direction of a game that can represent something or nothing, depending on who’s playing it. So be aware that Nephise may disappoint you, if you’re looking for precise answers or concrete action. But you can’t really argue with its price tag. You get far more than what you’re paying, of that I’m certain. Along with Trading Cards and Achievements. Go for it!
+ Abstract experience.
+ Gorgeous graphics and sounds.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Brief and with no replay value.
- Abstract experience.

At the end of the day Nephise is a perfectly fine Walking Simulator that's rather short, but if you like the genre enough and want something quick to play (and I mean quick, can be beaten in less than 30 minutes on your first try - quicker beyond that), then Nephise may hit the spot for players looking for that kind of experience. The scenery is rather pretty, though due to the tedious task of walking around collecting orbs and rotating statues, it can come off as a little boring. I'd personally wait for a sale, but I don't necessarily think the $1.99 asking price is particularly bad either, despite what others have been saying.
I like to support Indie devs as much as I can, and I personally really like Walking Sims as they're relaxing to me and a nice change of pace from the usual craziness in more mainstream titles, but, to me, a great Walking Sim should be accompanied by a great narrative as well. Since there's not much in the gameplay area typically with this genre, the story is where they should excel at most. Nephise doesn't really do much here either, though I got a good laugh from the end (which I believe, and hope, was the intention). If there was a sideways hand I much rather give it that, but I'll give it a thumbs up instead since by no means did I hate or dislike it, warranting a thumbs down. Just know, even if you're a fan of the genre, this really won't be for everyone.

From my brief 2 hours of playtime. I would have to recommend this game if you have friends to play it with. That’s not to say it’s not enjoyable solo, but to gain the full experience of the game you should. Of course, since I only had 2 hours of playtime that means I didn’t experience any bugs, I did experience only one random disconnect from a server but other than that nothing major. Gameplay wise, it is much like Dayz (though I have not played that game) in that you spawn randomly on that map and then must search for supplies to survive. There is base building in the game, though you do have to craft a “wooden sign” to claim land and then you can build. Combat in the game is simple as it has two weapon categories, Range and Melee. I was killed three times, twice by another player and once by a mutant. There are no “zombies” in this game, more of “mutants”, and animals. Wolves are apparently in-game as I did hear them crying in the woods. There are also some peaceful animals like chickens, rats, and pigs. Items are plentiful and easy to find so surviving is easy. Overall, again I only have 2 hours of playtime and would recommend this game if you’re into multiplayer survival games. It can be done solo but for the full experience again it should be done with others.

OK, quick PROS/CONS review:
PROS:
-Solid zombie experience, sound mechanics works just fine
-Decent size map, with well designed details
-Good looking game, well ported
-Satisfying combat
-Good price for what you get (specially if it's on sale)
-DLCs give good replayability, Lifeline brings a new urban map
-Tons of different weapons
-Dozens of different characters to play with, some of them randomly generated
-Well developed survivor community mechanics
-An easy fight can go south very quickly, making it more immersive
CONS:
-After about 50% of the main game, "standard zombie story" becomes "weak and poor zombie story"
-Some loading issues in specific areas, dangerous specially while driving
-GUI/commands scream "controller" and focuses on multiuse keys
-The camera tends to be quite uncomfortable in tight spaces, and when aiming in CQC
-Driving experience is barely sufficient (some cars have ridiculous handling/behaviour)
-Zombie animations sometimes bug with the terrain or obstacles
-Looks a little dated despite the use of Cry Engine 3
-After some hours, it can get repetitive. I found starting from scratch to be more entertaining than late endgame
-The other survivors' AI can be stupid quite often, getting themselves chewed on with ease
Minor stuff I complain about and might not be so important for you:
-Unrealistic/cartoonish looks for some of you out there (they're ok, but...)
-Lack of easily visible explanations for advanced controls (ie combos)
-Almost half of the mechanics aren't explained anywhere (ie outpost resources and their costs)
-Zombies sometimes spawn right behind you following the sound mechanics, but the place was just clear...
-Cars can make things all too easy sometimes, killing bunch of zombies in one go
-Lack of hard-to-reach places, special points of interest, "secrets", etc
-Unsatisfying main storyline ending, at least in my opinion

This review will make ample comparison to Terraria, such comparisons are of course inevitable given the nature of the two games. If this triggers you, feel free to hit that downvote button and move along.
Where to begin? Starbound is a game of plenty. In short, it's a monumentally successful sub $20 purchase simply as a value proposition. There's a lot of game here and I'd just be a liar if I said it wasn't worth the asking price on its own merits.
But so much of what Starbound does, has been done better in Terraria. Both games are good in their own right, and often for different reasons, but there's a very clear advantage here that Terraria has over Starbound. That being that Terraria understands its sandbox nature more than Starbound understands its own. Starbound attempts to leash you with some ham-fisted "Story" which actually only serves to illustrate how transparent the core exploration gameplay loop is with its linear progression of tiered planets.
This tiered system is probably the root of all of Starbounds design issues as an open-world sandbox game. Despite having a (Theoretically) infinite universe to explore, the game plays out in an incredibly linear fashion up until you've vanquished the big bad. It's almost as if the "Story" itself should be considered simply a tutorial. However, this ends up leaving a good chunk of the universe and planet diversity redundant. What's more, is the "Story" Pushes the player artificially through this tiered system which violates (At least in my opinion, but this whole review is my opinion so whatever) the underlying core of discovery and exploration. Terraria on the other hand, hides almost an identical loop of advancing through material tiers simply by what it DOES NOT do. That is, it doesn't tell you a damn thing. It lets you discover things on your own. It trusts the player to investigate new things when they acquire new tools such as double jump, hookshot or flight capability. This organic processes of discovery and advancement is probably (I think definitively) Terraria's biggest strength over Starbound.
Now what does Starbound do that's unequivically better than Terraria? Quests. Terraria really has none, And while most of Starbound's quests are throwaway, one in particular stands out as an exemplar of how to design a quest in such a game. The Hylotl Museum quest line which has you search (With no real direction given) for artifacts in order to add to the collection. Now, if that sounds familiar to Starbound players in more ways than one, it's because it's almost literally the exact same setup as the main quest, without some nonesensical "Story" thrown in there for forced narrative urgency. Organic emergent gameplay is the greatest ally of the Open-World design. When you're creating a sandbox, it's better to let the player fill in as many blanks as possible while just pushing them in a certain direction with context.
That's my assessment on some of the more subtle design running under the game, as for more of the objective and technical strengths and/or weaknesses, those are easy.

Starbound is a fun Sci Fi adventure with the gameplay style of Terraria. It is made by the same developers so it makes sense. It feels like an episode of Star Trek but you control what happens; the massive nerd in me loves that.
-Gameplay
So as I already said, the gameplay is similar to Terraria; a side scrolling adventure. With slight differences. Due to the Sci fi theme you are not limited to one planet, like in Terraria. Therefore you are given a permanent base; which takes the form of your ship. Which you can use to travel to a plethora of planets with different biomes. That have different animals and generated civilizations and dungeons. There’s also a hub with vendors and quests. I’ll go through each of these individually in more detail.
Firstly the ship. So after the beginning mission
You start with a broken ship that you have to fix, the first quest takes you through how to do just that. After you’ve fixed the ship you can treat it like a house. You can place any placeable items in it if you have the space. To get a bigger ship you can upgrade the ship via the outpost. As you upgrade your ship you can recruit more crew members which give you advantages. For example a engineer can make the ship more fuel efficient. Up to the point where you don’t need to use fuel anymore. Medics can be used to heal you on your adventures and much more. The ship can then be used to travel to various different planets once you’ve got the fuel.
Now the planets in Starbound. There are various types of planets; each requiring something additional to your character to survive on them. For instance you need a heating EPP to survive on a Frozen Planet. The different planets and moons contain different resources which you need to craft different gear. The harder the planet is; the resources on that planet can be used to craft better gear for example.
The Hub world. The outpost. This is where you go to further the main story. As well as to visit vendors and other stuff. Otherwise there’s not much more to say.
Finally the Civilization and Dungeons. So on every planet, at least everyone I’ve seen, there are either generated Dungeons or Civilizations. The Dungeons require you to battle your way through enemies to the end where you can get cool loot and can potentially find furniture for your ship. The Civilizations are filled with NPCs; some of which are Guards, Merchants or normal townspeople. Some of the townspeople offer quests. Once you’ve completed their quest chain there’s the possibility of them becoming available to recruit.
-Music
One of the many items you can find in game are musical instruments which you can use to play a range of music. If you are playing with other people you can combine instruments and play a song in unison as a band.
As a side note there is a lot of workshop content available for this game, so if you’ve completed it you can find more things to do. Or you can just spice up the base game to suit your tastes
To conclude if you are into Sci Fi and want to play the adventures yourself I would recommend this game indefinitely.
