Alright, review time again.
I've played over 100 hours of this up until today.
The saddest part is that I didn't really pick it up until 2017.
Rebirth was gifted to me by a former friend, in 2014, when it first came out. I played 25 minutes of it, died a few times and never touched it again.
Until January 2017, I put like 17 hours into it and then stopped until recently.
The entirety of August I practically did nothing else than playing Isaac.
The game is hard to get into, but it is damn cool.
The pixelated artstyle and overall topdown rogue-like look might deter some, but you really have to try it out.
It is very unforgiving at first and still will be after a long while of playing.
I get sweaty hands all the time wheb trying to complete a run.
Because if your life bar is deplenished, it's over. No checkpoints or anything like that.
You controll Isaac, a small naked boy who tried to escape his mother by leaping into a secret entrance to the basement underneath his rug. His mother, being motivated by a deity, had to present the ultimate offering to it, by slitting Isaac's throat.
As you go forwards you encounter all sorts of weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ living feces, moving rotten pieces of meat, versions of Isaac himself but without eyes and so on. Also, you are able to find items that help you increase your main source of defense and damage: Your own tears. Alright there, that's a bit ♥♥♥♥ed up.
Every floor will have a specific set of rooms. One item room each floor, up until the boss (which is Mom, very surprisingly, haha), a shop where you can buy goods with found money, a sacrifice room and a curse room. Each floor also has two secret rooms only openable by a well-placed bomb at one of the walls.
At the end of the floor is always a boss, which is a much stronger enemy type than the ones you encounter in the rest of the floor. After defeating it, you'll get an item for free.
After beating mom in the Depths, it is not over, however. Beat her a second time and you'll be able to enter her womb (wtf). At the end of the two womb stages, you'll fight Mom's Heart, which is essentially the final boss.
But wait! Did you really think it would end there? Nah man.
Beat the Heart 11 times and you can go down to Sheol (essentially the hell), where you'll fight Satan. So it is getting totally non-sensical now.
If you do some things right, you can also go upwards into the Cathedral, in which the boss is YOURSELF. You have to fight Isaac. Nice.
There is even more, because you can go even further after beating Satan or Isaac.
But whatever, let's focus on other things for now.
The gameplay is dodging and aiming projectiles. Practically nothing more. Dodging is really hard, and definetely a skill you should learn. Some enemies are downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, i.e. spiders, which crawl around in a very irritating manner, making them very unpredictable.
Luckily there arr some very strong items to help you in Isaac, but that is of course all rng based. You'll never know what you'll find, which makes the replay factor immense. Strong synergies can be a GG for you, but if you find worthless crap like Butter bean or the poop then you are pretty ♥♥♥♥ed. Some of the best items are unlocked fairly late, like beating Satan with a specific character (which you can also unlock).
What made me lose interest in the long run is how grind-heavy this all is. Pretty much every serious isaac player is an achievement hunter, who aims to complete all of 'em. It's too much and too frustrating to get the 100%, because some of them are downright impossible without putting at least 500 hours in.
After 100 hours you have seen everything, and the new item you unlocked isnt going to help there, because maybe you won't even find it once in the next 50 hours.
The soundtrack gets old really fast, it isn't my taste, so I used the original soundtrack through a mod, which helped.
To really have fun with this game, buy the dlcs in a sale, they provide tons of new content for a washed up player such as me.
Or, install the fan modification "Antibirth" which surpasses dlc and the normal game in every way.
So:
No for me, Yes for the general public. I can recommend this game to anyone who likes grinding and rouge like dungeon crawlers.

The big difference here is allowing the player to control two characters which works as a double edge sword.  While it does allow for some well crafted puzzles having the extra pair of hands unfortunately cuts a lot of tension from the game. This is also hampered by the fact that  Resident Evil 0 ensures there is  constantly enough ammo  for both characters,  removing  the dilemma of having to choose your fights wisely. Though a far cry from the best, Resident Evil 0 is by no means the worst . Definitely worth playing if  you're a fan of the old style, but be sure to have some reservations.

The unsung hero of the Resident evil series. It added unique features like dropping items anywhere, item mixing while picking up said item and lastly two playable characters. Its a prequel to the original resident evil/remake and as a prequel it gets the job done. Although you'll wonder why Rebecca is soo tame In RE1 after going through all thats happened in this game. Billy is cool character aesthetically but he functions the same as Chris Redfield from the first game, they take more damage then their partner, only difference is that Billy cant mix herbs and can carry more and Chris is the opposite. Billy is one off character and never appeared in any RE squel game since. And Rebecca is just a delicate flower , PRO TIP: give Billy's handgun to Rebecca and vice versa it helps offset her weak health.
This is a remaster and its very well made, I had no issues running it and it includes a wesker mode a very overpowered game mode where Billy is replaced by the fan favorite Albert Wesker(Code Veronica,RE5) with eye laser that can penatrate bosses with ease. This game mode along with bonus character costumes are exclusive to this new remaster. Its well worth it as the game holds after all these years. Mechanically its classic Resident evil, nothing over the top except for weskers eye laser in that game mode. Prerendered background are a lost art that i wish would make a comeback in mainstream gaming, The backgrounds and location in these RE games really capture your attention an add to the experience, they are beautiful, erie and foreboding.
The only issues this game faces is the one it introduces, dropping items can be a godsend but also causes more added backtracking but this holds true only for maybe the first playthroughs as most likely you'll know which items to drop prior to doing anything in later playhtroughs. In terms of actual survival horror its there and this the earliest of the partner system that would be later used in modern RE games, its just this game has it in the classic RE setting thus making atmosphere less scare and more tense as there is no reviving partners or checkpoints if one character dies its over, I'd say RE0 is underrated as it brung good features to the classic RE formula but the game came too late with those features and was released a year later after the excellent RE1 remake which was lauded a survival horror masterpiece. A tough a act to follow honestly.

RE0 was advertised with the slogan "BEFORE THE MANSION, BEFORE THE DISASTER, EVIL WAS BORN" which made the game have air of mystery and excitement, it did succeed in explaining the origins and the cause and effect of corparate greed but it felt short and rushed and then turns into another cliche stop the bad guy plot because its what RE has been from the beginning and why try to mix up the plot?
There is one thing RE0 does well. Makes you appreciate the good RE games - such as REmake - even more.

If you're a fan of the traditional RE survivor horror games before Capcom decided to change the formula for 4-6,then you'll enjoy RE0. As a RE fan since the original I was disappointed with the RE games after RECV,I tried the games after that but it really didn't grow on me like the PS1/2 games.
Good
Classic RE atmosphere & tension.Welcome to the world of survival horror.....
Returning enemies like the Hunter,new ones like the Eliminator or the dreaded Leech Zombies.You know when there's one nearby as the music changes into something more sinister...also when they explode & you're close it's game over.
Good old inventory management is back,your characters each get 6 slots to carry stuff.
Plenty of unlockables to get like Leech Hunter or Wesker Mode.
It doesn't contain any quicktime events,silly action sequences or mutiple boss stages that get boring.
Amusing charcter voice acting & dialogue.  My favourite quote- James  Marcus "You are trespassing & I'm very territorial"releaseses some Eliminators followed by an evil laugh.
The character zapping system,switch between Rebecca & Billy or team up to survive.
Bad
There is the problem with slowdown due to the resolution being locked,luckily this can get fixed very easily so that you can play at a stable 30 fps or higher depending on your PC specs.
Without a storage chest you'll need to drop items in an area to collect later,this can get very tedious running back & forth when moving to a new area.Thankfully you can backtrack to most areas until the final part of the game. Best thing to do is drop items in a save room to avoid the chance of being attacked while picking things up.
I felt there were too many puzzles that required the zapping system,don't get me wrong I enjoyed trying to work out puzzles but this game seemed to have lots more puzzles than the others.

+World is small enough that you don't get lost, and has enough to do that you don't get bored.
+The game does a really good job of making you feel alone in hostile territory - I really like how the ubiquitous viewpoint towers are also pretty much the only safe-zones in the game.
+The sheer number of enemies you have to fight makes the combat more challenging than, say, the Arkham games.
+Bosses have specific weaknesses that you can learn and exploit, making them interesting challenges.
Cons:
-Main story is kind of boring
-Main characters are REALLY boring
-Doesn't do anything about the racist undertones that have been with LotR since the beginning, as you murder hundreds upon hundreds of another race because they're inherently evil or something.
-Certain abilities are withheld unless you play the story missions, which I, for one, tend to take a while to get around to while I'm busy killing that one goddamn chieftan who keeps wrecking me.
-...That's about it, actually. I mean, those first two are pretty big issues, but there really isn't much to complain about on the gameplay front.

I remember taking the time to tell all of my friends about how cool I thought MUGEN was, any character you wanted, so many choices, blah blah. And them shooting me down hard, Oh man, MUGEN is a fight simulator bro, it will never amount to more than that... Yet as far as AI is concerned, there are clear resemblences to both.
At least in the middle of the generation, you could watch characters throw whiffs and gauge how they felt about fighting, and occasionally you'll get stuck with the distance perfect ai that seemed to punish you for trying anything short of isolating their tyranny. This game seems to tickle that point, and whets itself on the same MUGEN imbalances that make you feel like any grappler is God tier and Ryu is insurmountably better than ken, all the while feeling like Street fighter 2 all over again.
What do you mean by that? I mean the same ol, oh boy here's ryu, goodbye high score, or I just failed to ground seth so... Yeah. There are CLEAR cuts in ai and it hurts this game in ways only MUGEN fans could ever begin to understand. Nothing breaks the accuracy of a score than having an upset character exist after a solid line of boring crouch turtles who shouldn't even fight like that at all. Easily put, You can set this game on hardest and not notice until you see characters like Honda and Vega finally feel like attacking now, and Ryu actually knows other moves, and he seems like he can't help but combo into everything. If only all champions of each character could get together and build a solid AI that wouldn't seem exclusive to a challenge... I'd be happy, and also inclined to lock myself into training against it.
This game is the bitter taste of choice. One ultra or both. You want to use both? good luck depending on it having the killing power like it used to. Though I highly recommend you use it just for that, so you don't depend on it. Looks like you have to be within an inch of your life to use it, or successfully eat attacks with your focus. So depending on how you can use that, your ultra level may seem easier to obtain.
WELL THEN WHY IN THE WORLD DO YOU RECOMMEND IT!?
For starters, It's the only fighting game I know with character mods that don't have to be nudes or color swaps. So if you can harass someone to change a character for you, or search long enough, you will find something cool.
Next, I think capcom knows that their ai is useless for anything but rage, seriously, where else would focus attacks be extremely useful in pinning someone down? someone will tap you twice and you'll be eating moves, in my opinion the AI is only good for one thing, Spanking jumpers into misery for using a tactic any old time gamer has used since Megaman and Castlevania.... Jump lag reset. If akuma still had that CvS2 Air chop super they would probably not hesitate at all to burn you with that move for even being in the air when he's stocked... So them adding in options such as online training is really nobile of them to do.
Then... It's rated the best fighting game of all time! What does that mean? ask activision I don't know... Pick it up just because I guess. But another selling point is that it gives you all the arcade edition costumes. so just take off another 15 dollars of what you think it's worth. In my opinion it's a medium jab to everyone who decided to just upgrade, and a warm welcome to the newcomers. Mixed emotions on that, as newcomers are literally getting the game for an upgrade cost if they can appreciate the dlc. Which I do. Besides, You need the dlc If you want character slots to install the mods to.
Also, no more crying about how your character got nerfed and you wish they still let you use them, because allegedly you'll be able to roll back and apparently can when it comes to this game. I don't use certain words because I've never actually bothered building a combo with this game, I can make a few hits work, but since there is no real juggle I just keep it simple.
It's a completely new experience. Though to be honest almost all of them were, the jump from 2 to 3. The alpha series, etc. I still prefer alpha to this as a street fighter game, however, If they can polish the AI enough to where I can't cross my fingers through a difficulty and only count on seth to be an upset to my score... This game could end up being a real deal online and off, because it seems for now online is the only real thing that counts, as the highest rated reviews toil of people unhappy with the online system.
Regardless... 20$ On gamersgate Right now... Cross your fingers for the dlc outfits going on sale like I am, and happy fighting. It's worth owning, And it adds a new standard to fighting games it actually bothers to support in it's own stubborn... Same game tweaked tricks kind of way...

Yesterday was my first experience with the game. This is how it went.
I woke up on a road,  with some clothes and a flashlight. I saw a town up ahead and I start moving in. I find a baseball bat and drink some water out of a toilet. I get a change of clothes, and then I hear some guys outside. When I go to investigate, they have a group of 3 people. I ask if I can hang with them and they said sure.
After a bit more gearing up, I had plenty of food and drink, and a .22 rifle with 4 shots. We started heading up the road, to a place that sounded almost mystical when they said "Hayward". Another guy joins our party and we start heading up the road. We reach some scaffolding near a bridge and start looting. We find some shotguns, some ammo, some food, and that one of our party members has died, either from falling or from starvation. Up until this point we were all communicating through ingame/direct chat, so we had no clue what happened to him. We soon join a Discord server together.
We continue up the road and find Hayward and go in. The city itself looks absolutely stunning, something that looked like it belonged in The Last Of Us. We go into the underground parking garage, and it was so atmospheric and just. Everything was so cool down there. We leave and head towards some scaffolding next to the Police Station. We start making our way up when one of our remaining party members gets bear trapped and killed. Two to three men are upstairs, fully geared and with traps set all over the place. They slowly pick us off until we're all dead.
Later, we're split up with new respawns. I'm at an airstrip with one of the group members, and they're very far inland. It's turning night and we start searching buildings. In the corner of an office building in one of the hangars is a fully geared guy. My friend immediately throws his hands up, but I take a revolver and shoot him. I take his gear and leave some for my friend, he must have been AFK or something. We start moving towards the rest of our group when we spot a flashlight in a military tent. I fire two rounds and see his body drop, then we go and loot him.
Much, much later, we group up and meet another guy, who says he's got a boat and he'll take us to Hayward. We become quick friends with him and he takes us to Hayward. Another group member just got back though, so he will need to take another trip to get him. Once we're dropped off, we wait a bit until he tells us he was ambushed by 5 guys, fully geared. They killed him and took the boat, and he said they're heading towards us.
We quickly take position. I'm station on top of a ridge with another group member maybe 100 feet ahead, and the other is on the shoreline hidden in the trees. We see the boat coming, wait for it to get in all of our sights, and start lighting it up. They veer off and try to get to the shore, but our group member was already there, and he finishes them off. They all died and we got their gear. Some more stuff happened afterwards, but it was much less interesting.
That was my first day on the game. Do I recommend it? Yes of course. It's what DayZ wishes it could be.
TL;DR we ambushed some guys who were in a boat and killed them as revenge for killing our friend. Get this game immediately.

Some minor flaws in lack of attention to detail - spelling errors, occasional graphics bugs, but nothing that I feel spoils the game.
Enough difficulty that you can't just sail through, but not so difficult that you give up. For the price it's definitely worth it.

Gods will be watching may just be my favorite story-driven indie game of the past few years, and it's 75% off this week with a newly added free dlc, so I'd certainly suggest anyone interested to consider picking it up now.
The game features point and click gameplay where your goal of each chapter is to usually survive under harsh conditions with limited resources. It's all about efficient time and resource management, with hazards and dangers thrown in to cause hiccups in your plans. An enjoyment of micro-management is somewhat key, which can discourage some players. The game puts a focus on making hard decisions such as sacrificing lives for the sake of others (i.e. cannibalism of friends and hostage control and such). However, you are never "penalized" for decisions and losses made in the game, which has upset people in the past, you may see sacrificed characters in later chapters.
It's up to the player to gauge their satisfation with their performance if they believed certain sacrifices weren't necessary.
The story invokes sci-fi and
themes that really get your noggin pondering. I was certainly a bit bewildered and amazed my first playthrough.
Oh also, the music and art (in-game and unlockable) is amazing. Ch. 3 is practically my favorite in every way. I still replay it here and there.

Pre-ordering this game back then was a mistake. Since I had a bit of time to spare these past few days, I thought why not pick this game up from where I had left it years ago? I liked the simplistic yet detailed text-based narration and dialogue system. I was hooked the first few fours and would have loved to have completed the game but for one major flaw; the combat.
It is very repetitive and frustrating. Most physical attacks barely do any damage unless you focus all your party members on isolated targets and majority of spells and buffs are reset upon rest instead of after each encounter. To rest, you need to either visit an inn or use one of the limited camping supplies you are able to carry on the road. But the one thing that really irked the hell out of me was the role endurance and health played. When you engage in combat encounters, it is more logical to expect health to be the factor determining your per-encounter survival and endurance for how many encounters you can engage in before the need for rest. But here, the developers decided to swap the roles as if trying to formulate something different. If a party member runs out of endurance during encounters, unless other members are able to restore endurance for allies, they are unable to continue fighting till said encounter is resolved. This means that my tank with 600HP but 120 END is basically useless once the latter is reduced to zero, making survival an unecessary challenge for the other party members. You also cannot pre-buff before encounters to try and compensate for this stupid mechanism as most buffs last barely enough time to be fully utilised.
I am very disappointed in how this game turned out. I wish I had done my research adequately before investing in this game. I strongly suggest you do the same.

Note that while I own both Expansions, at this point, I have only completed the main campaign.
Playing Baldur's Gate was a turning point in my Vidya life. I was a console kid, and BG1 basically turned me on to the potential of PC gaming. I still play BG every now and then. Pillars of Eternity is not Baldur's Gate. It takes obvious inspiration from the classic Infinity Engine games, but it is absolutely its own thing. The combat and skill system are great. BG had a combat system that was basically "Buff, Cast, Tank, Complete". Pillars changes enough about the combat to require strategy, which is actually an improvement in my eyes. I did not like the combat at first, but as the game went on, I liked it more and more.
The story is pretty deep, though it took frustratingly longer than I had hoped to learn certain names and invented words for things that have common English equivalents. I get it, but sometimes I wanted a ghost to be called a ghost. Some of the story seems confusing and muddled, but I suppose that if I were to play through again, things would be more clear. I just don't know if I have another 100 hours to put into another playthrough.
Someday I will get to the White March content, and probably update this, but I guess in short, if you like RPGs with strategic combat, and especially Infinity Engine stuff, you should at least give it a try.

Takes me back to the days of Neverwinter Nights and Icewind Dale. So much nostalgia.
I spent a good 40 hours on the main campaign, with a lot of side quests along the way. The presentation and story progression are excellent. But the real highlight is the writing. It is astonishingly good., way better than many novels that pander as fantasy classics.
Make no mistake, this game is hard. On Normal mode, some fights are unfair while others are impossible to win. You need to master the mechanics of your group. Thankfully, the game's intuitive interface makes team management a real pleasure.
Some annoyances exist though such as the long and arduous travel between maps for quest completion. Some folks like that sort of immersion but I would pass it if I could. Also, there is no real incentive to certain mechanics such as Stealth. I found the straightforward mechanics of "face and fight" do yield more reliable results.
But let none of these minor complaints bother you. Pillars of Eternity is a breath of fresh air. After so many years, a true RPG has risen which honors its predecessors. I can't wait to see what Obsidian will do with the sequel.
Highly recommended.

Pros: Immersive writing, characters, and world. Some of the best RPG writing I've ever seen. Great ways to customize your character, and many different playstyles and talents to choose from. The graphics are nice for what they are, and exploring was enjoyable. The fact your choices matter was well done, and one of the better instances I've seen this used in a game.
Cons: I felt the combat was pretty lackluster. While I've played Baldur's Gate, etc, I think this is an outdated throwback included for nostalgia's sake, and not because it's a well designed system. You essentially get a few, very limited abilities, and autoattack the majority of the time. (As melee) The combat just feels very chaotic, and your healer can just get instantly gibbed if you get a string of bad luck, at which point you're screwed.
Overall, I'd give it a 7/10, and would reccomend picking it up on sale.

The vanilla aka regular version of the game comes like a lesson learned from Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, but still frozen in time. The same outdated looks, some of the same old flaws, and the same approach to roleplaying quests with lots of monster butchering anyway.
The improvements balance the first statements in several ways, still one has to love this style, and the remaining and overdue flaws, to really enjoy this overpriced relic from a finally overcome era of programmers.
The game has a nice start approach, as it allows story mode (easy combat) for the roleplayer just as much, as brutal no-game-saving hack & slash orgies for those who prefer that kind of 'roleplaying'.
Characters can be customized in quite atmospheric ways, culture and your personal player choices can round-up a character, or condemn him or her into mediocrity and reload!
Skills have been crippled-down to a lacking assortment. No dialogue skills and the fact that searching has to be clicked by activating stealth-mode are a notch weird.
Character classes are ill-balanced, as certain concepts have been skipped away. While I do not mind wizards in full platemail and swinging ANY weapon it still looks, as if one more programmer couldn't help it but cheat-together his favorite mix on expense of all us 'oh so unimportant customers'... The lack of limits by class really makes classes like fighter or barbarian a kinda superfluous, as the healing-spell paladin can equal them and usually does.
Companions are so limited (not even one full assortment per player class available) that it spoils MUCH of the story. To balance that every inn (and your later stronghold) allow to create your own NPC companions, as you may need some to survive AND operate your stronghold at maximum efficiency.
Beyond that the game is living proof that 'Torment - Tides of Numenera' is even more outdated and ill-programmed. ;-)
Community reacted, and STEAM, Nexus, and MODDB all had several helpful mods and tweaks for this game. From alternate voices to dual wielding a firearm along with another weapon or torch to portraits and stuff... Thanks for that!

(This review discusses technical aspects of the remaster. The original game is about an 8/10 and a must play for RE fans.)
A good port/remaster for the most part. Capcom re rendered all backgrounds, something I did not expect after the upscale job they did with REmake's backgrounds. Everything looks nice and crisp. 3D models, lights, and effects also got a boost, and the game runs at 60+ fps. Performance is good and no crashes.
My main complaint would be the widescreen mode; with the exception of the actual gameplay sequences, everything is rendered in true widescreen where you see more to the sides. Cutscenes, menus, loading and puzzle screens all show more in widescreen. Gameplay sections were rendered in the original 4:3 aspect, and in widescreen mode they are blown up to fill the screen, then the camera pans while you move the characters, making you see less. Everything feels close and claustrophobic, like playing a FPS with a reduced FOV. Why make the most important part in 4:3 and do a pan and scan when you have the source material available? I can't find a reasonable explanation. You're still getting a huge visual upgrade if you're playing in 4:3 mode, but the remaster had more potential in this area.
Another point would be the controls. The original game had certain actions bound to one key, for example shoot, action and confirm were one button. The remaster splits these up, adding a new layer of frustration. Sometimes you can confirm using space, others you have to use enter or a left click. Rebinding controls is also tricky and required finding a solution online.
No substantial improvement was done to gameplay. A few examples:
As a port, performance is good and the game is stable. As a remaster the visual upgrade alone warrants a revisit, and you get a few goodies too. This had potential to be a more refined experience, but we have to make do with what we got.
What can I say, just play it if you enjoy fighting games and want to keep up in the incrowd such as the FGC, Hit me up if you have it of course.

I just finished playing the Resident Evil HD Remaster, so I figured it would be a great time to give the prequel, Resident Evil 0 HD Remaster, a go. One game is not objectively better than the other. However, I found myself enjoying 0 better than 1. I think most people have opposite feelings on the matter, but I just liked far more things better here.
First off, let's talk about the battle between camera and controls. I have no qualms with the "tank controls" or any of that. This version has a nice new control scheme you can use , along with customizable controls, which allow you to go downward when you push down, left when you press left, etc., unlike the Gamecube releases of these games. However, the RE1 HD Remaster also gives you the new directional controls. The big difference between 1 and 0, is that there are less wacky camera angle changes, in my opinion, and almost none where you will get killed or seriously hurt as a result of this. In RE1, however, this was a massive annoyance to me. I liked this far better in 0.
Second, I found the dialog to be better. Although the lines are often cheesy and dumb, in my opinion, there's more charming stupid dialog than the HD Remaster of RE1. The Playstation version of RE1 had some magnificently cheesy material, while the Gamecube version, unfortunately, was played pretty seriously, and I found the performances to be really dry in it. With 0, the campy, cheesy dialog isn't superb, but it's got enough cornball delivery from people actually trying and putting emotion into their lines that I could get into it.
Third, the character interaction blew that of 1 out of the water for me. Rebecca and Billy are your two playable characters in RE0, and I felt that their interactions with one another as the story progressed, was head and shoulders above anything Chris and Rebecca, or Jill and Barry shared in RE1. I was more interested in them, and if they'd been more popular, I would've liked to see them again in subsequent games. I didn't like Rebecca at all in RE1, but after RE0, I loved her. The writing/directing made her far more likable for me, and Billy was pretty decent. I certainly liked him more than Chris as he is represented in dialog and cutscenes, etc., in RE1.
Fourth, doors are clearly marked by what has them locked. If you're a mega-RE1 veteran, you know which doors the sword key, armor key, etc. open. However, imagine that you don't know and aren't using a walkthrough. The game tells you which key you need when you interact with the door...but your map isn't marked with an icon, and if you just look at a door, it's impossible to tell which key you need unless you are trying to open it.
In RE0, however, most doors are very memorably marked when you look at them, so you know what type of lock it is. Orange door with flames etched on it? Fire key. Blue door with watery squiggles or some such on it? Water key. Doors with no knob and a clock above them? Solve a clock puzzle. The map isn't marked, but the visual cues on the actual doors themselves in-game make it so much easier for more people to be able to remember which door needs what thing done to open it. I loved this, and found wandering around trying every single door in RE1 each time I got a new key to be tiring and boring.
Fifth, I found this game's "active" story to be far more engaging than the original. A lot of folks probably disagree because nostalgia blinds them, or they might genuinely like something better about the first game's plot. For me, there wasn't really any plot. What I'm referring to by "active" story is the events and things we witness in the game, either real-time or in cutscenes, including flashbacks. In RE1, almost no plot developments ever occurr. RE0 isn't exactly amazing in that department, but outside of background information you read in notes in RE1 (which I do love and think are a lot better than RE0's notes),
RE1's plot is "split up in mansion, Wesker and <Name> are gone, encounter other survivor and help or get helped, obvious bad guy is obvious, self destruct time, escape hopefully with <Name>, your team member from the beginning and possibly another survivor. RE0 could be simplified, of course, but flashback stuff, things between two villains, dialog and events including Billy and Rebecca...I felt like a lot more happened here, plot-wise. Stuff happened in RE1, but not much of it was story that you witness, and I'm a fan of well-told
Alright, so with the good out of the way, though, I do want to address things I found to be
enjoyable for me in RE0. I just said I liked the story better than RE1. That's true, but I do have one issue with it: conflicting information. Rebecca appears in RE1 as a total wuss. However, by the end of RE0, she's pretty badass. With this being a prequel, there's no way Chris should have to save her. I had so many magnum rounds in her pockets at the end of 0 that she should be able to kill Hunters for days and days. She sure wouldn't sit back and let Chris do all the work, realizing he could use a hand.
Something happens in the ending of RE0 which characters would have seen or heard the aftermath of in RE1. Also, a villain reveals the identity of one of his evil proteges near the end of RE1, yet Rebecca never shares this information with Chris in RE0 when she absolutely would tell him this name and what is going on for obvious reasons. I'm sure there are various other continuity errors/issues in the lot.
Next up, the inventory is a mixed bag. There are no item boxes in RE0. Instead of dumping items in an item box and pulling whatever items back out at any other item box in a safe room, you can drop your items anywhere. There are seemingly random maximum numbers of items you can drop per room, but yes, you can ditch stuff almost anyone. On the one hand, it's cool to be able to make your own personal treasure trove of healing items, guns, ammo, etc., but on the other hand, you might find yourself without an item you need, and it's on the opposite end of the game. Although this was annoying having to run back and forth so much, I found it less annoying than doing laps back and forth from kerosine containers to "killed' zombies in RE1. That got so old for me. One big plus, though, is that you control two characters, so you technically have 12 slots for items, which is a lot moe forgiving than the 6-8 in RE1.
Let's see...lastly, the game has an androgynous villain who laughs about doing evil things, speaks a bit pretentiously, has long hair, and wears white robes. I thought he was very cliche in appearance and personality, and he made the game less interesting to me. Oh, and opera randomly plays while he's being evil, because of course it does. At no point did I ever find him scary, cunning, interesting, shocking, cool, formidable (as a wits-matching/evil plan kinda guy, I mean), relatable, or even pitiable. I did not like him and felt bad for the game when he was on-screen, because he was one of the few things I didn't like about it.
Although I've brought up a few things I didn't like about the game, I overall enjoyed it quite a bit; more than RE1, even. For me, the dialog, character interactions/line delivery, less wonky camera angles, the doors having obvious requirements to unlockthem, visible based on the door's appearance itself, and other features made this a good gaming experience for me. If you like older Resident Evil games, it's certainly worth checking out.

I don't normally write long reviews, but I'm loving this game too much to just give it a snarky or funny comment. This game has turned out to be more fun than I ever anticipated. You play as an ever-growing (or ever-dwindling) group of average people trying to survive a...wait for it...zombie apocalypse. You're probably thinking how you're ready for the zombie craze to end. But it won't. The idea of humanity being forcefully pulled from their lives like a fish fished out of the sea and left on the boat's deck to flop aroung and ungracefully gasp for air as they fight for their lives is all too appealing. And this game seems to deliver the goods for an entertaining and challening zombie survival game.
What makes it fun/exciting/worthy of this long review?
First of all, it's open world, and you get to ride in cars and run over zombie hordes. Sometimes a zombie will get stuck on the hood of your car. That's always fun. But I digress.
You can switch between the available playable characters whenever you want for the most part, but the idea is that as you play with one character for an extended period of time, that character gets tired and weak. A tired character suffers penalties to their stamina, for example, so they aren't the best to use to go scavenging the town. That's when you swap out for a well rested character so the tired or sick characters can regain their strength. Each playable character has to go through their own "level up" process, too. And if your character dies, or if one of the playable characters die even when they aren't your active character, they really die. There is no respawn, so the urgency for planning your supply runs and missions definitely exists.
Not only are your survivors important, but you also need to build up your defenses for your current home base. This includes scavanging the city for supplies and materials, building new areas within your base, or creating outposts to increase your claim on the land. Once your base is at population capacity or you've depleated all resources for the area in which you are located, it's time to pack up and find a new base.
There are also missions for you to complete. This includes helping survivors who may then join your ranks, fighting rival groups, or trading supplies with others. A lot of these missions are time sensitive. So if your fellow survivor is in a jam, you better go save their skin before it's too late...unless, of course, you want them dead. But then your reputation with your group may suffer...which brings me to my last point.
You have a reputation with your group, and your group has an overall morale meter. Generally speaking, if your morale is low, your group probably isn't too happy with you. So you need to constantly do things to improve your base, your rep, and your group's morale. The happier your group, the better their performance. And if you steal from your group's general supplies and never replenish it, don't expect them to like you or take you seriously...because they won't.
Basically, just play the damn game. It's really fun, and it offers a new take to the gameplay of a "typical" zombie game. If you can catch it on sale, it's a must buy. But I honestly think this game is worth it at it's regular price. Now go buy the game already!

The first hours of this game were promising - the initial areas are dense with quests, secrets and enemies, the difficulty of battles high enough to make them enjoyable, and not punishing, and the mechanics innovative enough to make getting good at it a pleasant diversion. However, the favorable impression wears thin in the later stages, when you're swimming in unspendable cash, have more HPs than God and are able to instakill any unit of the enemy army, while resurrecting all your own fallen units. In addition, the latter parts are railroaded to hell and gone (also, markedly uglier than the initial areas). The ending itself is as enigmatic, as it is uninspired.
In short - 5 hours of relative fun (for a non-exacting TBS fan) in a 15-hour package full of ugly padding. Can't be recommended with a clear conscience.

Get it on sale if you must, but don't let the pretty graphics and promise of compelling story fool you. This is easily one of the most frustrating and confusing games I have played in a long while, even in "Narrative Mode," which is supposedly the easiest setting. I tried to give it a fair chance and still intend to finish it, but after wandering around a labyrinthian desert for over 2 hours with no progress, I just don't care enough. And while I'm sure the story starts tying together the further you get, it starts off as a confusing mess of unexplained science fiction jargon while you struggle to figure out exactly what the hell you're supposed to be doing in order to complete the chapter. Characters die and go missing as frequently as you let them, but that doesn't seem to matter since they reappear in subsequent chapters with no explanation as to why. If it weren't for a static visual effect on the dead characters, I would have thought it's a bug.
Gameplay-wise, it's very reminiscent of Oregon Trail. Most of the missions seem to revolve around managing time and resources to keep as many of your crew alive as possible (not that it matters). The bulk of the game involves asking one character about the status of the other characters via drop-down dialog boxes and making decisions based on that, then repeating.
But if you've been looking for a game that accurately simulates all the fun of aimlessly wandering around a desert, then knock yourself out.

I was on the fence about buying this game for quite a while, but I'm glad that I did! It consists of seven vignettes each of which is a game in itself. All involve making tough choices based on observation of other characters (the pixel-art graphics are surprisingly expressive!) and the amount of risk that you're willing to take.  I completed the game on original difficulty, generally needing only 3-4 attempts at each chapter, but easier difficulty levels are also available (though completing a chapter on the first attempts won't be anywhere near the satisfying achievement that it is on original difficulty!) Overall, the game drew me in with its art style, interesting setting and excellent music, and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone looking for an engaging challenge.

A super tough and stylized game about making tough decisions for the good of the team. Everyone can die but you.
Pros:
•Very atmospheric and beautiful pixel art, a good example is the desert/canyon level.
•You go to a variety of places, doing a variety of tasks. No two levels are similar.
•Choices for easier difficulties, though discouraged. They even added a choice to remove all random elements, in response to complaints.
•When they say difficult decisions they mean it, they hold up on that part.
•Shows a neat little graph-like thing of all the decisions you made, and what percent of other players made those decisions.
Important Notes:
•The game does not save to the steam cloud; I played half the game when I stayed at my cousin's house for the week, and when I got home none of it was uploaded. This may have changed, if its important to you, look a little more into it.
•The game occasionally makes you take out a pen and a sheet of paper, which in my opinion made it a little more interesting, but some may not like that.
•The second level is a level about choosing how you receive torture. This level is one of the hardest, and truly affected me for about half an hour after each session of trying to beat it. Very dark stuff.
Cons:
•If a crew member dies in one mission, they magically reappear in the next. I understand why, but they could have come up with some stupid excuse other than just *BAM* he's back and was never gone.
•Can get somewhat tedious, often you get into a cycle of doing the same exact things.
•Crashed once for me, erased some of my progress.
6/10: For all that it is and however hard it tried, wasn't as gripping as some other games. It does supply what it advertises.

This game is (simply put) awesome.
It's a point-and-click moral puzzle and it's really difficult and unforgiving most of the time, but you just can't stop playing it. Well I wasn't able to stop at least. I played and tried to beat this game and after around 13 hours in one single gaming session I did it. I was at the end and my eyes hurt like crazy. But the feeling in the end was pretty damn good.
In every scenario you need to manage different factors with limited time or resources and try to keep everything under control or you'll lose. And you'll lose often. Start the scenario new. Lose again. But the game still kept me entertained all the time.
✓ really challenging scenarios
✓ intense and engaging
✓ great art style (if you like pixel art)
✓ good story
✓ awesome soundtrack
✓ pixel art gore!
✓ no checkpoints (I like that you need to begin the scenario again. The only checkpoints are between the different scenarios.)
✖ sometimes too luck-dependent
✖ sometimes really frustrating
✖ no checkpoints (you can't save the game during a scenario; for some that might be a problem)
If you don't want it to be too nerve-wrecking I would recommend playing it on the difficulty level "original light" which is easier than the "original" game. But it's still pretty difficult.
I probably wouldn't recommend it if you're easily frustrated, looking for an easy-to-beat game or don't want to "waste" too much time on one game. If you like intense games that are extremely challenging and don't mind the luck factor (and if you like pixel art): this game is for you.

I decided to pick up this title a couple days ago and I decided I wasn't going to review it or anything until I finished it. I went into the game avoiding spoilers as much as possible and it ended up being worth it.
The game is a heavily story/narrative-based adventure title with a heavy emphasis on the main character of Mae Borowski and going through Possum Springs interacting with her friends and other people and objects in town along the way. Various characters have their own story arcs and they're all well developed throughout especially depending on which choices you make and which of her friends to hang out with in particular. The story is generally well fleshed out, and there were a number of times where I felt like I could relate to the characters especially Mae. A lot of things struck a cord with me as a milennial and I felt very invested in what was going on and once I finished it now I want to play it again just to experience things again and discover whatever else this game has to offer in terms of story and endings.
Overall, I'd say It's a very thought provoking game that won't take you too long to beat but has enough to keep you going and it will most likely be a game I revisit in the future. I can't say it's a game for "everyone" per se, but for those who love story-based games and titles like Undertale and whatnot then this game's most likely going to be up your alley.

If you're just getting into this game, don't do it alone - get some friends to tag along.
The majority of the playerbase are veterans of the Street Fighter scene and are happy to eat up new players.
It's difficult to input special moves correctly with a controller and impossible to play with keyboard/mouse
You'll want to invest in a joystick...it'll still take a long time to get the inputs consistent, though
It feels almost like a guessing game at times, but you can tip the scales in your favour if you can recognize patterns in the other player's gameplay
The game engine demands dedication.
It's sometimes difficult to simply land a special move on its own, but you aren't going to win much if you don't learn to string moves together (forming a combo) at a timing that's sometimes as tight as 1/60th of a second.
Enter at your own risk.
EDIT
After playing for awhile, I'd like to point out that combos with a margin of error of only 1/60th of a second are far and few between
You can go far without that sort of thing, but know these combos do exist

First up, my congrats to Capcom for managing to successfully port a GameCube game to Steam! Maybe you learned something from your♥♥♥♥♥♥house RE1 port? Then again, I sincerely hope not, since you've never taken the time to go back and fix that one for the numerous punters for whom it STILL DOES NOT WORK. But let's let bygones be bygones, eh? It was only a few hours of my life which I'll never get back, vainly testing it out on multiple machines. And what's a few hours, out of a whole lifetime? Useless turds.
Secondly, I'm giving this game a pretty decent score, but please understand this score comes with reservations. The game has dated somewhat, and was never the very, very best of the RE games in the first place. They've also done such a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job of updating things like menus and mechanics that I'm not sure how much I can recommend this to anyone who didn't play it the first time 'round.
Put it this way: if you're new to not only this but any other old-school, fixed-camera-angle survival horror games, this definitely isn't the place to start. Its mechanics were tricky even back when, what with all the pedantic partner-swapping and ruthless inventory antics, and it's become even less forgiving with time. But for those who have fond if slightly frustrated memories of playing this on the G-Cube...welcome home. You know what to expect.
The partner-swapping thing, once you get used to it, was actually one of the niftiest things about the game when it first came out. In short, you have to swap frequently between the cute-but-mousy Rebecca Chambers and the surly-but-sexy Billy Coen in order to successfully solve various puzzles, perform specific tasks, etc. They'll get constantly separated, have to closely co-operate, fight side-by-side whenever possible...you name it, this game gets pretty good mileage out of the partner premise. It's more than just a gimmick, in other words; it's absolutely integral to story and gameplay. That said, it also has its irritations, but...I'll leave it up to you to find those out for yourself. Wouldn't wanna spoil ALL your fun.
Another area where this game excels is atmosphere. Like any great horror game, it has fantastic locations, memorable monsters, and there's no denying that the spiffy new graphics look...well, pretty darned spiffy. I just can't warn the unwary enough about the game's overall difficulty and awkwardness, especially early on.
You want resource management? Boy, do we have your resource management. The opening couple of hours on the train will test your resource management skills like few games before or since, believe me. You're a better gamer than yours truly if you can manage to procure and/or productively use every item on offer without constantly dropping things and backtracking for them later. For two certifiably butt-kickin' characters, they sure don't seem to be able to carry a lot of stuff between 'em. Useless ♥♥♥♥ers.
I still love this game, but a part of me hates it, too. The score below is biased and mostly aimed at veterans, as I've already noted. For everyone else, the risk is yours. Don't say I didn't warn you.
Verdict: 8.5/10 (9 for the game, minus 0.5 for the lazy port).

This is a good HD remaster of the last classic style Resident Evil game. The game is just lacking something compared to the series’ highlights. I would recommend RE HD over this. Lasts about 10 hours for a full playthrough.
Firstly the port / remaster is really good. The higher resolution allow you to see all the detail of the backgrounds and 3D models. So if you’re just looking for nostalgia this is a great update to the original game.
This game was originally released in 2002 and at this point the series had been having a release virtually every year from 1996. So it’s fair to say that the gameplay was beginning to feel about as fresh as one of it’s decomposing enemies.
In an attempt to invigorate the formula you now control 2 characters who you can swap between with a button press. This introduces some clever new puzzles where you must use the characters together or parts where you split up and pass each other items with handily placed dumb waiters.
It also introduces some problems. Inventory space feels even more limited than other RE games. Larger weapons take 2 out of 6 slots and only Rebecca may mix herbs and chemicals. Meaning that you have to constantly fiddle with the inventory screen which just becomes tedious.
The partner AI is another annoyance. It can be managed with a menu but it will do it’s best to irritate. Such as when it gets in your way and when it doesn’t follow you through doors.
This game also suffers from the syndrome of having enemies off screen in the same room really often. It can be scary to not known where enemies are but you are constantly auto aiming and firing at stuff you cannot see and then listening to hear if they fall down.
The gameplay is never bad and if you can look past the flaws this has some good puzzles and good (but not inspiring) levels. It just lacks something and has some annoyances compared to the best RE games.

The vanilla aka regular version of the game comes like a lesson learned from Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, but still frozen in time. The same outdated looks, some of the same old flaws, and the same approach to roleplaying quests with lots of monster butchering anyway.
The improvements balance the first statements in several ways, still one has to love this style, and the remaining and overdue flaws, to really enjoy this overpriced relic from a finally overcome era of programmers.
The game has a nice start approach, as it allows story mode (easy combat) for the roleplayer just as much, as brutal no-game-saving hack & slash orgies for those who prefer that kind of 'roleplaying'.
Characters can be customized in quite atmospheric ways, culture and your personal player choices can round-up a character, or condemn him or her into mediocrity and reload!
Skills have been crippled-down to a lacking assortment. No dialogue skills and the fact that searching has to be clicked by activating stealth-mode are a notch weird.
Character classes are ill-balanced, as certain concepts have been skipped away. While I do not mind wizards in full platemail and swinging ANY weapon it still looks, as if one more programmer couldn't help it but cheat-together his favorite mix on expense of all us 'oh so unimportant customers'... The lack of limits by class really makes classes like fighter or barbarian a kinda superfluous, as the healing-spell paladin can equal them and usually does.
Companions are so limited (not even one full assortment per player class available) that it spoils MUCH of the story. To balance that every inn (and your later stronghold) allow to create your own NPC companions, as you may need some to survive AND operate your stronghold at maximum efficiency.
Beyond that the game is living proof that 'Torment - Tides of Numenera' is even more outdated and ill-programmed. ;-)
Community reacted, and STEAM, Nexus, and MODDB all had several helpful mods and tweaks for this game. From alternate voices to dual wielding a firearm along with another weapon or torch to portraits and stuff... Thanks for that!

It's a little late in this game's lifespan for me to be leaving a review, but I see new people trying it out every day, so I'll go ahead and let my voice be heard. I'm just going to start out by saying I absolutely love this game. No exaggeration, I'd say it's probably in my top 15 games out right now. I have yet to encounter a game that, in my opinion, has such immersive roleplaying elements, while still delivering on gameplay and combat mechanics. There are a lot of nay-sayers when it comes to Pillars, but if you really give it a chance, there's so much to love.
I'll start with character creation. I think any hardcore RPG fan would agree that one of the most enticing and sometimes most important parts of an RPG is the character creation. And let me tell you, the options are endless. For those of you who haven't already done research on this game, there are six races to choose from, each of which has anywhere from two to four sub-races, most of which have their own unique powers (the human race is the only one to lack in unique sub-race powers - though it still has sub-races). On top of that, there are 11 classes. If you're counting, that presents you with 165 options based on race and class ALONE. Now add to that six countries you can be born in, dozens of backgrounds, and hundreds of spells. I have never encountered a game like Pillars, where I truly feel like I can make whatever character I want.
Once you make it into the game, it really feels like your choices matter. There are hundreds of dialogue options, some only available to certain classes and races, some only available to people of a certain reputation, and the list goes on. Talk about roleplaying; this game lets you be who you want to and approach the story the way you want to. Not to mention a world FULL of exciting and unique lore. In most games I can never make it through all the little books and scrolls you find, giving you backstory on the world. In Pillars of Eternity I can't WAIT to find another book to read.
Also, to any prospective buyers who have read reviews stating this game pushes you to a certain play-style, ignore those reviews. Anyone who thinks you HAVE to go on endless killing sprees in this game, or that you MUST have a six-person party, hasn't figured out the intricacies of this game. Will it be harder to play solo? Yes. Is avoiding combat, and staying stealthy a challenge? Absolutely. But the beauty of this game is that it gives you those options while trying to stay as realistic as it can. If you play on solo it will be harder - a LOT harder - but journeying out into a world full of monsters alone would be much harder than going with a group. Combat only gains you so much experience, and after a while, facing the same foes yields you no more benefits. But the great thing is, you can decide, based on what kind of character you've created, if fighting for the sake of combat makes sense still, or if your hero would rather stick to the shadows, avoiding a needless confrontation.
Buy this game. Buy the expansion. There's no other experience like it.

One of the best games I've ever played.
The writing is the most obvious strong suit. The main plot is well thought-out, and the side missions are an excellent blend of serious/engaging and frivolous/simple. The characters are varied, consistent, vibrant, deep, understandable, and engaging. I think I will struggle to find a game with writing this good or better.
The audio is surprisingly great. The music is fitting, well-balanced, and evocative, though of course much of it repeats fairly often (I think there are only two or three battle tracks, for example). The voice acting is just phenomenal on all fronts, with some performances that are probably even better than they need to be.
Visually, it's simple but well-executed. The painted pieces are gorgeous, including the character portraits, and all of the locations are very believable and well-designed. Effects are clear and consistent, and character models actually change based on what they're wearing (something many RPGs, especially isometric, lack).
The gameplay is solid, though companion AI can at times be slightly annoying. It was never a massive issue, though. The classes feel well-balanced, though perhaps more cracks show through at higher difficulties. There are enough interesting options and mechanics to make multiple playthroughs likely quite satisfying, especially with the absolutely brilliant Disposition system in conversations.
Cannot recommend this game enough.

Dead Effect is alright. Somewhat enjoyable even. The controls are useable and the atmosphere is pretty good. Some game systems make the experience frustrating, but if you go into the game not expecting much, it's reasonably enjoyable.
It's got some decent zombie shooting, with hordes of zombies that actually feel somewhat threatening, even if they are actually easy to take out. Not many weapons, but at least it's got a little variety in there with the upgrades system and the weapons actually feel different.
It's nice that there is room for exploration, some little areas that are off the beaten path to check out for collectibles and supplies. This doesn't amount to much if you don't care for collectibles, and once you realize that supply gathering is pointless because you won't run out of ammo unless you spray like mad the exploration is easily not done.
The voice acting is hilarious! I love how the scientist on the comms link has the most stereotypical stupid accent. It's too bad there was basically no audio design because the voices are really hard to hear over the sounds of creaking metal and vents spewing what looks like toxic gas (which doesn't even hurt you to my surprise). It's even worse when the zombies are moaning, because then there's something more than the atmosphere dampening the voice over the comms link.
However, the store and upgrades system in the game isn't very good. It is pulled straight of out a mobile system, and that makes for a poor shopping experience with a mouse. You've got to drag your mouse around like you're using your fingertips to browse the store. This can be lived with, there isn't very much scrolling you will have to do in the few times you need to access the store.
What is unforgiveable is the fact that death leads to a very expensive continue or a full restart of the level. This wouldn't be so bad because the enemies are pretty easy to handle except for the grenade zombie. They can destroy you with a single lob of a grenade, so that means you have to take them out first. The only problem is that identifying them through the hordes of other zombies and the haze of darkness along with a low power flashlight that doesn't shine far is very difficult.
The game isn't all that difficult, but it is made frustrating with some lacking game systems to make the experience more enjoyable. It has some good points; Dead Effect has the most hilarious budget voice acting I have heard. However, as long as you don't expect a grand experience from this game, you'll have a little fun,

The best way to enjoy Dead Effect is to play it slightly drunk.. :) At first, it was exactly what i expected from a budget shooter. But it has some nice points and over time I grew to like it. Soundtrack is ok, The story line has "B" written all over it, but halfway through the game they come up with pretty elegant excuse for it (if you bother with collecting the PDAs), but still there are too many clichés. It has a very Doom3-like feel to it and, surprisingly, sometimes it can give you a nice scare.
It also borrowed ideas from other games as well (Mass Effect 2 hacking anyone?), but not in a offensive way. Voice acting is cheesy, but again, it was meant to be (obvious excuse on the devs part, I know) and if you are a bit tipsy it is actually fun. Obviously there are some problems as well. Guns feel wrong and secondary aim is just rubbish, which is a very low point in FPS. There are only few types of enemies (granade ones are really OP) and in the end of the story mode you are left with "Boy, that escalated quickly" feeling, but then you see the credits and you have to give credit where it's due ;). Nice game for such a small team.
Would I recommend this for 5Euros (and in my case much less)? Hell yeah!
BTW: After first start i realized that Dead Effect actually comes from my country, but subtitles are not correct at all, Czechs beware, It is better to play in English. :)

This is a game that completely surprised me. I normally hate zombie games, and I really was very skeptical about this one. But I decided to give it a try because it was a singleplayer game (I hate multiplayer), and it was on sale during the steam summer sale. Anyways, the best way I can describe this game is to call it a combination of Fallout 3 like scavenging and exploration, with Saints Row The Third like controls. Basically, your goal is to build up a shelter that you and your crew live in. You need to explore the countryside looking for useful supplies that your shelter needs while hiding from or fighting several zombies. As you do this, you are expected to complete story and optional side missions. You cannot create a custom character. Instead, you find new recruits, and if they are friendly enough, you can play as them. You switch to different characters when your current character gets too tired. All in all, I would give this game a 9/10 for gameplay alone (weak story, though). I was surprised when I saw that I put 30 hours into this game in less than a week! That was NOT expected.

I was so very hopeful for this game. Let me preface this by saying the art is wonderful, the music is great, the story is dark and full of meaningful undertones, and the characters are lively and interesting despite never hearing a word from them.
NOW sadly the gameplay has nothing to do with actual choice. It's an absolute crapshoot to play the game as the developers intended it on original mode because the choices you make are almost entirely RNG based off of luck almost completely. Would it feel like an acomplishment if I were to complete the game on original mode? sure, but I have no desire to do so, and that would require the game not giving me a god damn aneurysm within the first two chapters. The game boils down to some sort of resource managing skills or making an attempt to gauge a character's state of being and give your best guess at how they would react to which choices you have. In the second chapter you're being tortured and you get to choose in between torture sessions whether you'd like a medkit, painkillers, or intel brought to you for the next torture session, which would be a really cool little bit IF IT DIDN'T REQUIRE 20 CYCLES OF THAT TO MOVE ON. Oh, and if you die on day 10 or so, you have to start completely over from, thus elongating your game time spent flicking through almost entirely identical dialogue instead of playing the game and actually furthering the story. Absolute trial and error, you're really just praying the odds are in your favor.
For example I played through the first chapter on original difficulty and every time I died (which was a lot of times) the game gave me the little rundown of my choices and told me I had a balanced approach. Managing hostages, an assault, and hack progress/security requires some balance and in finally achieving the balance, instead of being rewarded I'm greeted with another death thanks to some dumb luck, until my balanced approach worked, I'm guessing because the game pitied me.
In the games defense though it does have the cool bits where your decisions are shown at the end of each chapter and how they size up to every other player reacted to the situation and the decisions they made, which is ♥♥♥♥ing cool. Now don't get me wrong I love games that punish the player and have a harsh learning curve, Binding of Isaac, the Souls games, Rogue Legacy etc. but all of those games can be mastered. Skill can be developed to further progress your time to beat and so on. Where Gods Will Be Watching loses me is in the random chance and luck required in order to advance. Instead of allowing its players to progress in the story with penalties for the mistakes they made, which would truly change how the game is played and how the story unfolds (which would be extremely helpful considering a point and click game is centered so heavily on story), it restricts the player to ensuring each chapter ends with a very linear story progression (in my experience, keep in mind I haven't beaten it) that can only be achieved through frustrating luck and trial and error.
Sadly, I wouldn't recommend this game, but boy do I wish I could because it's fun to look at, the story is captivating and it has some good stuff going for it, all of which are ruined by chance serving as a gameplay factor.

"Gods Will Be Watching" is a simple point and click micromanagement game that revolves around making tough choices as Sgt. Burden (wink wink) who will have to decide on how to survive 6 dangerous scenarios. The gameplay is entirely micromanagement: you have a group of factors that need attention, and only so much time/actions/resources you can have to use to prevent things from spiraling out of control. On top of which lies a factor of chance, as actions are accompanied with varying levels of benefits with a chance of failure. It has a dark tone and is repetitive, and the gameplay forces you to make some ethical decisions if you fail to make the most flawless ones. The repetition works very well to project a feeling of the monotony and struggle of surviving without resources. It is similar to “Papers Please” in style and in that they both are repetitive, dark, and have morale choices; but its primary difference is while "Papers Please" evolves in difficulty, the micromanagement completely changes in the levels of "Gods Will Be Watching".
The visuals are an abstract form of pixel, and everything is iconic, which allows the player to imagine how characters look in terms of detailing, which inherently creates a greater investment of emotions tied to each character. The music is repetitive and consistent, and it works in great effect especially as the gameplay deals a lot with straining time and resources, giving a sense of struggle and inevitable doom.
The biggest flaw of the game is the writing. It is not poor but it’s not great, especially the conversations held by the characters feel like they are all the same person. No one in this game has a unique personality, in fact many of the characters have the same dialogue lines when interacting with them. The uniqueness each character receives is from their appearance and their abilities alone, you simply could not tell the characters apart without describing their occupation, look, and purpose. For example, at the beginning of the game, Sgt. Burden holds four people hostage, and when you want to calm them down, he says a line about how their crying reminds him of his dear sister; which makes sense when he talks to the female hostage but it doesn't make sense when he is talking to the fat bloke. Some of the scenes just don’t make sense, and I will continue if you don’t mind the spoiler. If you do mind just take my word and blink over my example.

The E.C.U.K. has been tracking the leader of the Xenolifer, Liam for a while now and has demanded that Sgt. Burden kill him due to his maniacal hijacking of a super weapon (the virus) which Sgt. Burden helped him get in the first place. Sgt Burden, being the idealist he is, vehemently disagrees stating that this act will make Liam a martyr and spark a war, which shows how smart Sgt. Burden is for helping him get the weapon of mass destruction in the first place, and how much he knows about making good choices for the greater good. The E.C.U.K. declares that he is bound by his obligations and in not killing Liam soon that he will become a traitor, later Burden gets caught and tortured and days later is finally saved by the E.C.U.K. who then decides to take him back anyway after branding him a traitor. Furthermore they fail to recognize the leader, Liam lying a few feet away from Burden, which would be tantamount to a US soldier in the Middle East failing to recognize Bin Laden in 2008.
On original difficulty this game is actually very difficult, with many hidden parameters that you will not understand without playing the scenario a few times around. While the difficulty is not a bad thing, the frequency of hidden parameters demonstrating the game’s lack of instruction and intuition is more detrimental than creative. For example, in the beginning part of the game you can shoot the guards and the hostages will panic, this is a good use of intuitive and creative gameplay. After apologizing to Jack, and having Jack lose the ability to shoot the guards is a demonstration of detrimental lack of information, which I found would force me to restart.
Despite these flaws, I felt a strong sense of will in trying to beat Day 2, which led me to staying up till 5 AM. I must really feel an investment to the game if I am willing to go to such lengths in playing it in both plot and gameplay. I would recommend it to people who like plot driven gameplay, as well as gamers who are comfortable playing more abstract indie games similar to “Papers Please”.

I really like the concept, I like the art style, I like the theme, but the problem is that the game is unbelievably dishonest in the challenges it proposes. It presents you with a risk management scenario and have you devise a plan to crack it. Then midway through it changes the rules just because, and you fail. Even though you fulfilled the original goals. Sometimes it makes narrative sense - even if it's infuriating gameplay wise - but later on the game doesn't even bother to keep the pretense. At one point you're tasked with researching an antidote in 24 hours or everyone dies. It consists of cracking a 3 digit code out of a possible 5, your scientists inform you, and managing a myriad resources to meet that deadline. You devise a plan to meet that deadline. You meet it. Then your scientists inform you they "forgot to mention", you actually have to crack a second 4 digit number in the remaining time. Of course you don't make it in time and have to restart, now with your prescient knowledge of how the game intends to cheat you this time. Please. If you're gonna ♥♥♥♥ me like that, at least provide a believable, sensible reason other than "the scientists forgot to tell you, their lives on the line and everything". The interface doesn't even help. One of the subjects you can theoretically test antidotes on is a dog, and naturally you wonder if that's a viable option. The option to inject him with the experimental vaccine is there in the menu. The scientists are in the room with you. You should be able to ask them about that, correct? You can't. So you go and inject it anyway, and then when you try to analyze his blood, nothing happens. No message, nothing (other than a very helpful "woof". Yeah, that answers everything I needed to know). In short, the game isn't fair, and it appears to actually take pride in how infuriatingly cheap it is.

First time I feel compelled to make a negative review... so that's saying something I guess. This game has some great visuals, but it doesn't redeem the amount of frustration you'll experience in the "gameplay", the trailer is misleading which is unforgiveable and I feel burned because of it, but I actually feel even more burned over the fact that I wasted 8 hours on this with the hope that it'd get better than over the money I spent on it.
The first level was okay, but after that the 'gameplay' relies too much RNG, not in the good way Darkest Dungeon implemented it either (where adequate preparation can soften the impact of the RNG, as well as the fact that Darkest Dungeon seems fair in it's own morbid way because the enemy can get ♥♥♥♥ed over by RNG just as much as you can), and unlike Darkest Dungeon the RNG here doesn't add to the replay value, after you finish a scenario here all you remember is what a painful experience you had to endure... and in Gods Will Be Watching the RNG is on the forefront, and often the deciding factor on winning a scenario is pure luck. You'll also get a lot of scenarios here that require you to gamble with an 85% chance of losing the gamble, and if you lose a scenario you lose 30-45 minutes of progress.
Overall, you feel like you're in a RNG casino, and instead of playing with money you're playing with time that you can be using to play something better with more depth to the gameplay. GwbW left such an awful taste in my mouth that it's hard playing anything where you see characters from a sideview with pixelated graphics.
