Played this a good while ago from a CD, but it wouldn't run on W7. I'm happy that steam made a compatible version.
Don't expect anything fancy in the technical sense - graphics weren't awesome even when the game was new and there's no voice acting, but it doesn't matter. The game is pretty stable, I found just one bug: a big guy sends you to find a key, but you already have it by the time you talk. Talking to him again later will crash the game. Also, the auto-save feature is not always hepful: it's supposed to save before a battle, at the point when you can choose not to attack, but sometimes, it saved right in the first turn of the battle. And choosing your battles is essential, especially at the beginning.
You - the king od Airath - get betrayed by your court mageand hit with a spell that should kill you. It only breaks your armor, though, and deposits you somewhere far away, in a land called Oganthar, alone and unarmed. Oganthar doesn't have a king, the lands are divided between seven Lords (six, actually, plus one Lady). And since you can't return home in your current state, you decide to unite Oganthar and raise an army to take back your lands.
Easier said then done - you have a handful of hitpoints and hit about as hard as a peasant (the weakest unit in the game). You get some cash to hire an arrmy, but money is not really the limiting factor. Your Authority is. That's a stat, almost like a currency, which you need to command troops. Unlike King's bounty, here every unit takes up a bit. Also, units are not available for hire in infinite Numbers, so you need to optimize a bit. You also get XP and level up fairly often (lvl 50+ at the end), so don't worry, you'll get more than the initial six peasants. You can inprove your physical damage, but there's no point playing as a fighter. You still need to move around the battlefield to hit someone and you only hit one enemy with your sword. With a spell, you can kill a whole stack at once, so you'll end up leveling your magical power.
Stacks work differently than most turn-based fights. You have space for ten stacks in your army (one of them being you, so nine, really), each with max ten units. "Units" come in all shapes and sizes - humans (melee and shooters), animals, undead, giants. Yes, you can have giants in your army. Yes, they are as awesome as it sounds. In actual combat, you don't see stacks like in HOMAM, you see each individual unit - but you control the stacks. You fight on a hex grid and your (and enemy) units are smart enough to go for the most kills. So, if your archers do 50 damage each and the enemy monsters have 51 hitpoints, your nine archers will kill four monsters and heavily wound a fifth one, rather than wounding ten monsters and leave them standing. All units have a Speed stat, which determines hw far they can move on a turn, but also how soon they attack. Killing the faster enemies will make your life easier and if you do it right, you can kill all oposition before they get a chance to do anything.
The beginning is a bit frustrating - you are pretty much too weak for any battle, so you have to pick your fights carefully.  The game ends if you are killed and since you have no armor, that can happen very easily. Some early quests give you some extra units beyond your Authority limit, so you can get something done. And when you get organized, you;ll find the game is pretty well balanced. By the time you find tougher enemies, you can also hire more and tougher units. And when you finish uniting Oganthar and turn homewards with your army of Furies, Dragonslayers and Knights of the Sun, you feel pretty invincible. Don't worry, you'll be proven wrong, soon enough.
The story is nothing to write home about, but also not terrible. The whole game took me about 13 hours to finished and I think I'll come back.

A (now, in 2017) classic Resident Evil title that is a must play for anyone, including myself, who sometimes misses the original gameplay elements that brought this series to life. I'm talking locked crappy camera angles and tank controls, yeah baby! I was gifted this recently and decided to play through it again, despite my last playthrough being on the original Gamecube version. So much nostalgia from growing up. For this review, it's noted I played on Hard mode with classic tank controls (Original). I'm adding a couple sub categories in my rating for this game.
Voice Acting: 2/10 - It's awful. I remember liking it more when I was younger.
Story: 7/10 - Despite the lackluster voice work, the story is actually pretty good. It takes place before the mansion incident that occurs in Resident Evil 1, and Resident Evil Remake (HD). Billy is a solid character who comes off as a smarter-than-your-average-jock, and Rebecca is fresh legs Mcgee out on her first assignment. She's green and weak af, but will mix herbs to save your life. Again though, and it has to be said, the voice acting ties directly into the story, and brings it down quite a bit. -4
The ending scene for this game is quite touching. +1
Sound/Music: 10/10 - Fan-♥♥♥♥ing-tastic. Weapon sounds have weight to them, the blood gurgling effects make you nauseous, and the music provides each setting with the perfect Ambiance. Rarely will I give a 10/10, and I may be a bit biased, but this game's sound effects and music really seal the deal.
Graphics: 9/10 - Yes, a 9. Here is why. I absolutely LOVE how great the pre-rendered backgrounds fit in with the character models. Each and every environment looks great, despite not rendering in real-time, and the characters models, especially for it's time (2002), are polished and fit compositionally well with the said environments. There is so much detail had in each area. I'm well aware that the HD remake took out the pixelation from the original release, and made the colors look better. Despite that, this is a game that has and will continue to visually age well into the future. Well done.
CGI cutscenes still look like♥♥♥♥♥ -1
Gameplay: 7/10 - Gameplay hinges upon a glorified room escape algorithm. You'll find one item that'll get you into one room, then another that will get you into the next room, all while trying to survive against the game's many enemies and obstacles, the most notorious being the camera angles. -2
Annoying text after every load that attempts to sound ominous but really just wastes time and comes off as annoying. -1
Overall: 8.5/10 - Visually, it holds up. Sound/Music quality is better than a large portion of today's games. Gameplay is acceptable. Story is acceptable. Do you enjoy classic survival horror and haven't played this yet? Grab it. It's a good-un.

While Resident Evil Zero (RE0) is an amazing addition to the franchise; it's not without it's flaws...just like every other game.
You control two characters: Rebecca Chambers and Billy Coen. By working the characters together, you get around certain puzzles; for example: Billy is the only character with the strength to move boxes; Rebecca is the only character to combine herbs (etc etc).
The graphics, the gameplay, the controls - are all sound. The game keeps you engaged and thinking by throwing puzzles for you to beat either by yourself or by combining the skills of Rebecca and Billy.
However, with no item boxes to store or stock-up on recovery items or ammunition; you're forced to store your items on the ground and backtrack to retrieve them. Backtracking is a major player in RE0; especially when controlling either character or switching between. Just like with the original Resident Evil games (RE1, RE2, RE3) - when you save and then die; you get returned to the main menu and spend the next few minutes reaching where you were last.
For any Resident Evil fan or survivial horror fan; this game will satisify your needs. It's a classic, fun example of what Resident Evil used to be and should be! Bring on the RE2 and RE3 remakes (with no changes, just updated GFX)!

I absolutely loved this game. Even with multiple playthroughs trying to get all of the accomplishments, I am still delighted by the story change subtleties that arise with different actions. I willingly go back again and again to play this game in vain attempt to get all of the in story achievements. While I am normally not a fan of strategy games, I enjoyed exploring different story pathways and strategizing to get different events. The artwork is fantastic. My only critique is having to start at zero for each skill at the start of each game. Let's be real, if she was a princess, she would have been in lessions since birth, so a randomized starting skill set would have made the start more interesting and more realistic.

Now here is a refreshing break from the standard. If you can get over the cutesy anime look, you'll find a rather fun text adventure about the 40 weeks before your coronation into queenhood. Mechanically this is a skill optimisation game. Every week you train two of your massive set of skills. Depending on your current mood, you get bonuses or penalties. Then the event of the week happens, the game checks for a certain level in required skills and you possibly make some choices. After that, you can use the weekend for one activity, which manipulates your mood levels.
The story and setting are quite interesting, the writing is good and finding out all the ways to die, endings and achievements is fun. The things that irked me were that the game does not show all the numbers and variables under its hood, which is very frustrating to keep track of yourself. It also does not tell me how difficult the skill checks are, which hurts repeat playthroughs. And finally, while the art is great, the overall graphics are sketchy and lack polish. And the user interface is sub-par.
In summary: Not flawless, but very fun.

This was my first time playing an isometric RPG, so I played on the easiest difficulty setting. That said,
+ The story was rich and incredibly detailed. Everyone had a story to tell, the world seemed full and complex and lived-in. There were many ways to solve quests and respond to questions, not just on a "good or evil" scale, but you could show mercy, deal harsh justice, be clever, be cruel, etc. in your interactions with others. I found myself truly thinking about the consequences of my actions and the questions the game raises: what role should gods play in our lives? What is a soul worth? Is the progression of science worth any cost, or should some knowledge be kept secret? My colorful and well-written party members each had their own opinion on these issues.
+ The combat is very complicated if you have never played this kind of RPG or Dungeons & Dragons style game, but there were many hints and tips through which I slowly learned how to best proceed through combat. Like D&D, setting up your character is exhausting and confusing. Each of the standard categories (strength, intelligence, dexterity, etc.) affect your combat in some way, and there are multiple ways to attack a foe (such as slash/pierce/crush, but also attacking them physically vs. mentally and so on). On easier difficulty settings, you can slowly get the hang of these and build up to bigger baddies towards the end of the game.
- On my admittedly old laptop, even with the settings tweaked, some of the gameplay itself was a bit laggy and slow. Loading screens sometimes took a while, and sometimes it took several clicks for the game to register a dialogue option. At one point the game itself failed to recognize my save file, and luckily googling found a solution, but apparently this has been an issue for many other users.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to people looking to play a high fantasy book that is well-written and nicely blends animations and drawings with your imagination.

Dead Effect is BadFly Interactive's first game. As such, I think a little slack is deserved. It was designed by a small team with a focus on mobile functionality. As such, the gameplay is a little stiff and knunky. However, it's easy to get used to with a little practice.
Dead Effect's campaign is rather short, but features new game+ and time and wave based survival modes to supplement that. You take on the role of a male or female super soldier trying to figure out why everything on your space ship went to hell while you took a cryo-nap. Helping you along this journey is the only other survivor you know of, Dr. Wagner. The basic plot is reletively predictable, but is a bucket of fun either way. Especially with the wide variety of weapons at your disposal.
Dead Effect was supposed to feature a co-op mode, however, BadFly bit of more than they could chew with that feature and the idea has since been scrapped for Dead Effect. An honest mistake that has been apologized for a number of times already. Dead Effect 2 is in the works and co-op is being kept in mind for debut.
All in all for the developer's first game, it's a bit rough around the edges, but more than worth the $5 price tag.

OK I just finished the game. Let's get this over with.
Story:
To sum it up, Mordor is a closeted homosexual living inside a wall with his wife and son. After the wall gets attacked by zombies, he must fight hordes of black people and defeat Satan with the help of his ghost boyfriend.
OK the story SUCKS. BUT
The black men are great, and I wish they gave the captains more relevance. There was this guy named Forza Horizon who kept killing me and taunting me and came back after I ''killed'' him. The captains actually had a lot of personality, and I would have been happier if I was up against Forza Horizon in the story a bit more. I hated his guts, but I supported him with his affairs with other captains. It was amazing and actually felt like an adventure.
Gameplay-Stealth: Well, the AI is horridly idiotic. They won't see you even if you are in front of them, and if they see you you can just run at them and kill them before they call their buddies. Also, the game doesn't even let you be stealthy at times, and doesn't have that much freedom.
Gameplay-Combat: The game features the standard combat of Batman and Assassins Creed games. In my opinion this♥♥♥♥♥♥has to end, I hate this system. I used the classic Video Game Explosive Barrels™ a lot, because I simply didn't want to fight them for hours, spamming clicks and sometimes right clicks. The enemies commit ♥♥♥♥ing cellular mitosis, and they just don't stop coming. Don't even get me started on ''boss fights'', which were just glorified quick time events.
World: The world of MESOM simply feels plastic. It is just the same sidequests copied and pasted. The world around you is dead and mostly consists of ruins and empty lands. It's an okay game. Since its on sale a lot and really cheap its a nobrainer to get it and play around with it  a bit.
You can expect it to be like an Assassins Creed within a changing world.
That is actually quite inventive and new to this game; The world actually changes and you change it. When you take out a powerful Orc another one will take his place in time. If you get killed by one they will increase in power and maybe even rank up. So some enemies you will meet a few times. Also they change location on the map depending on their rank. Since you are deep in enemy territory you see lots of patrols or groups of orcs that just do whatever pleases them. The story is not one of Tolkiens but feels like fan fiction. It is okay and suits the genre.
I felt that after a bit I pretty much discovered a lot there is to the gameplay. The gameplay is innovative and has some new elements to it but after a while it feels like more of the same. The leveling tree is fun and you know which perks to pick and which perks to pick later - but it won't change gameplay that much.
Controlls are sometimes a bit off. Climbing was a bit of a pain for me. Sometimes you just dont know if you can climb a wall, or you want to grab a specific ledge but the game doesnt agree with you and lets you hold on to the other five ledges that you dont want first.
Combat is fun but "basic". Each boss has weaknesses and streangths, depending on how high their rank is. Some can only be damaged by specific actions and the game rewards you if you get intel on a boss and then use it to your adventage. This is rewarding. Not rewarding are bosses that call insanely huge groups of orcs to help them. They all call some but a few bosses just call the entirety of Mordor to their side and you will stand as the odd one out in a group of 30 enemies trying to dodge parry and kill the boss with very limited attacks.
The combat doesn't allow for many actions. First its a bit overwhelming how many actions you can do in a fight and then there are actually just a handfull and on tough bosses only one works. Same as with ledges it sometimes is a pain to get this specific attack working. Combat in DarkSouls is a lot more intricate and entertaining.
Lore and NPCs are fun to interact with. Its fun to hear orcs talking about their plans or their battle stories. The cutscenes are well done and progress the story nicely. There are no quicktime events and the game feels fluid. You dont get interrupted by cutscenes during gameplay, yet you get enough cutscenes to make this game feel a bit cinematic.
Its a solid mediocre game for most players that I can recommend playing. I have no special interest in this game but I imagine if one thing totally sparked me about this game I would even say its an excellent game.

This is not your average adventure game. Through out all of the missions there is an easier way of doing things and there is the morally right way of doing things. In simple terms if you have less people you dont need to spend extra resourses on them. What makes this game worth playing is the challenges that it has for the levels. Most adventure games are hard because at some point you end up playing a losing game of "guess what the developer is thinking" in order to progress. Okay, okay, I'll write a real review. Might be a bit haphazard since I just finished the game like 20 minutes ago and it's 2am, but whatever.
Let's get a few quick things out there first:
Mechanics are standard point-and-click, not much to say about it. The only method of control you have is your mouse. That's it. It's a point-and-click game.
Graphics are absolutely phenomenal, in my opinion. The art is gorgeous. I will admit the font used is difficult for me, PERSONALLY, to read, but others may not have a hard time with it like I did. I ended up getting used to it but it was still a bit of a pain and that's my only real complaint.
Now to the meatier stuff. Gods Will Be Watching is a relatively short game - I finished it in five hours, though I will admit I was on the easiest difficulty and therefore failed probably a hell of a lot less than I might've if I were playing on a harder difficulty. Point is, I got five hours out of it, which I felt was fulfilling. I didn't feel the game was lacking.
"u failed a bunch on the easiest difficulty git gud" Yeah, yeah, I suck at video games, whatever. The thing is ... this game kind of wants you to fail. That sounds horrible, but it's honestly part of the experience of playing the game. The difficulty selection even tells you the harder settings are going to be punishing and tells you that YOU WILL FAIL. It doesn't matter how good you are at video games, you're going to fail at least once, and seeing how difficult the easiest difficulty mode was, I hope you like screaming at your computer.
Like, there's no beating around the bush, it's a stressful game. I came out of it angry and stressed out. I was stressed out and irritable through the entire experience. If you want a nice relaxing game, this is not it. This is a game to get mad at. This is a game that you play when you decide you hate yourself and want God to punish you for your sins.
It's unfair and stressful and punishing and I loved it. This game makes a mechanic and a story out of failing and I love it. To put it as simply as possible, the game is pretty much about failing. It's about failure. It's about learning from your mistakes and doing your best in a world that wants you to fail. That's about as much as I can say without getting into SPOILERS.
Now, honestly, the story might be a bit hard to follow at first, because it doesn't really tell you anything. You have to do a lot of filling in of the blanks as you go. The game tells you so much about the world and the characters without really telling you anything at all and it's done super well.
The game is written in a way that if a character you've known for five minutes dies, it's enough to evoke such a strong enough emotional reaction from you that you immediately want to restart just so you can fix it (and you can restart a level whenever you want, you CAN get your ideal conclusion).
In my opinion, GWBW is one of the best games I've played this year. It won't be everyone's cup of tea, especially not with the whole "HAVE FUN WANTING TO GNAW YOUR ARMS OFF, PLAYER" thing, but I urge everyone to try this beautiful little gem out.

I'd just like to say, this game is kind of your run-of-the-mill survival game, but not in a bad way... It's actually a good thing because, the way they did it is fairly user friendly (once you get an idea on how to play it), and it's also fun. Searching for items in every house in a neighborhood is a bit monotonous after a while, yes, but it makes it easier when there's not say, other players or enemy NPC characters trying to kill you... And for this being Early Access, there's still time for improvements, so the "generic survival game" thing shouldn't detour you from buying it.
Pros:
-Pretty game. The game is REALLY good looking. With it being built in the most recent version of the Cry Engine, it runs on a nice version of DirectX.
-Controls are responsive. This is a problem with most survival games like this (for example, the free game called "Aftermath") with the controls that is, poorly done, to say the least... They don't usually control well, and feel really sticky, but this game feels like the controls were designed specially to work in a more fluid fashion.
-Fairly optimized. For a large open game like this (and being Early Access on Steam), this is well optimized. I run this game at minimum graphics on a laptop with a 1.8 GHz AMD A6 processor, 6 GB of usable RAM, and a 1 GB of VRAM (Video), and the game runs at a mostly smooth 25 FPS (for a laptop like mine, that's not bad).
-Good building system. I had not really played long enough to get myself enough wood to build a base, but from what I saw from the video I found this game on, it has a fairly good building system... Like I said, I didn't use it myself, so I'm not going to comment further, but from what I've seen, it's good.
-Multiple cameras. Not too amazing, but it is kind of cool to have different view angles...
Cons:
-Lacks functionality? Not really, but from my experience this kind of missed a bit. I thought there'd be some form of hunting, but I didn't find one animal the entire time I played.
-Occasional frame drops. As said before, the game is EA (Early Access), so that's not really unexpected, but it is a problem at times.
-LONG load times. It took me about an hour to start up the game after choosing a server. Once in the game it has FPS issues from loading in map areas when starting.
-There's nothing to find half the time. Cupboards are made of wood right? Why can't you break them for wood? You see an entire bed sheet? Oh, no, there's no cloth there! You're a moron! Bed sheets made of cloth? Nope... This in my opinion, is kind of a problem...
Suggestions:
-Single player. Controversial suggestion I know but I think that would be a great thing to add because, people like myself don't always play online and would like to I don't know, cheat for items like infinite wood to just walk around and build a really big base without worrying about being banned... Just think about it developers. Or, you could add a sort of Sandbox mode where you can build whatever you want.
Conclusion:
Not a bad game! It was definitely worth the $10 I spent on it (through the Steam Summer Sale). And if this is on sale still, you should definitely get it. All else fails, you can get a refund, and spend it on something else, but at least give this a shot...

I finished this in a 9 hours setting so I guess I was hooked? Not exactly sure. Yes I really loved the art style, the soundtrack and the writing, but I'm not sure if I would recommend it to people other than those interested in unique storytelling.
It's sort of a visual novel, or the non-action parts of a Persona game. The loop is you starting a day, going around and talking to people then comitting to spending the rest of the day with one of your friends, then coming home to sleep and reapat the process. You find out a lot of peoples backstory which is very interesting.
What I did not like that much about the process was that it takes quite a bit to reach those people. Since you don't exactly know what you're looking for and if you like to check every corner it does get a bit tedious. I think this is mostly the reason as to why Mae is allowed to jump. It gives you something to do during that traversal.
This game like Gone Home is relying on a specific aspects of American culture, which as an outsider makes it harder to relate. I could relate to some of the struggels, but a lot of Mae's interactions are not player controlled and is used to characterize her as the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the group. This is refreshing, but I wonder how well this sits with people.
I wonder how this game was made, because the main plot is based Southern Gothic ideas, but the characterization that result from the situtations seem so real in some cases, they sort of conflict with supernatural aspect of this story.
Can realistic behavior and supernatural themes coexist? Yes they can, but I'm not exactly sure they were working together. The supernatural aspect of the story is overshadowed by the struggles of a shrinking rural American town.
Mae's struggle in that regard becomes the low point of the game to me. While it is briefly interesting, it takes the place of a story of how a real person would deal with being a returning college drop out. The game takes a long time to introduce the mystery as well. I just don't think it added much to the story except to be a convenient way to excuse some of Mae's behavior and postpone her growth which left me unsatisfied. In thinking about it, you could make the argument that the horror that has taken roots in her town is a metaphor other real world factors that are just as looming and uncaring and that her refusal to accept it is the start of her growth, but it is just unsatisfying compared to her friends' sidestories.
Overall though it is a great package, I think 15 euros would have been a better price, but I think this game is important. Not only because of the Southern Gothic vibes, but because it is an interesting example of how to do a visual novel style game. I'm not saying they struck gold, but we can see how certain gameplay decisions affect our enjoyment of this type of game. Constant interactivity because of walking and chosing replies is good, but then traversal could have been sped up because at a certain point you know all of the town and certain canned animations repeat. Some of the minigames like band practice are good, but not being able to repeat these sections seem counterintuitive to what "band practice" is supposed to be. The nightmare sequences are a nice stark contrast from the real world, but they are a too formulaic and do not add much to the story. Maybe a more combat focused horde mode with a bat would have made it feel like struggle to fight off something. Maybe a more visually grotesque platforming challenge would have been better suite. As it stands I just find four dudes over and over and they play a song. The melanchoy works mostly the first time and the sequences lose meaning once you realise their formula.
All in all recommended for people looking for unique storytelling and visuals in their game, but don't expect the package to be cohesive and it's actual gameplay to be as interesting.

Right, so imagine this:
You are a young guy/girl, you grew up in a small town, which rarely sees sucess, you however, beat the odds and get out of the town and go to school.
Soon however, you have problems. School isn't what you've imagined, being independent is rough, being responsible is impossible, you make mistakes.
Soon, you're back home, in the small town, living with parents who were so proud of you only several months ago...
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the plot of "Night in the woods", and a reality for many college aged kids. Why talk about reality when disucssing a videogame? Because if this situation seems familiar, this WILL hit home.
Now, for some people, this will be rough. You get in arguements, you get dressed down, you get in trouble, you say/do regrettable things. So what is the appeal?
The characters/dialogue.
Simply put, this game has some of the most human characters ever in a video game. Everyone has flaws, everyone has character arks, everyone has their own personality/sense of humor, some of which may take some getting used too.
Some people you will like, some you may hate. You may even hate yourself, but at the end of the day, every college dropout has hated themelves at some point.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So why buy this game? If you like decent platforming, fun minigames, and dialogue you can relate to (and laugh at!!!), this game is for you. It's a story of making the best out of a bad situation. One that many people have dealt with, and will instantly relate too.

Long Live the Queen is a visual novel roleplaying game mixed with a death simulation. Yes, you read that right.
In LLtQ you play as Princess Elodie, whose mother, the queen, has just died. As the regent you are handed the reigns of authority and must manage your kingdom successfully in the 40 weeks until your coronation as queen.
Your day to day activities in LLtQ revolve around managing your moods, taking classes (with bonuses or penalties depending on your mood), and making decisions in a personal and royal capacity. Throughout the story you'll be making countless dozens of skill checks against your knowledge and abilities.
Some of these skill checks are trivial, but most are important. Many of these checks are survival tests, like a check to dodge an arrow (fail and you take an arrow to the stomach), followed by a check for battlefield medicine (fail and you bleed out). Others open up or lock you into plot alternatives, almost all of which will eventually lead to further survival tests.
Yes, in Long Live the Queen you'll be dying. Over and over. You'll be poisoned, drowned, run through with swords, burned to a crisp, eaten by monsters, and have your brains splattered across the floor.
And that's where the magic of this game lives. Beneath its cute anime novel roleplaying exterior is a soul of hardcore planning mechanics that tempers that cuteness in a forge of brutality. Every tragic death will motivate you to plan better, choose better, and fight better to get that adorable princess on the throne on her 15th birthday.
LLtQ was a wonderful surprise and one that I can easily recommend. It scratched the itch created by Academagia (a far, far deeper simulation that I heartily recommend) and far surpassed the fun, yet shallow and lackluster, experience of Magical Diary.

So... This is kinda painful to admit. I really want to like this game. The gameplay is good, the maps are great, the graphics are amazing, and there just aren't enough high reflex dogfight games these days. But I just can't recommend this. The main problem is how shallow the gameplay feels. I've looked at a couple guides and found that the game throws almost all of its challenge into refining the use of what few moves you have at your disposal. That means mastering a jet mode, hover mode, aiming, dodging, and... that's it.
The gameplay is fun, but it is severely lacking in depth.
Most vehicle based combat games will add depth by allowing players to customize their vehicle or choose from a line up to suit their preferences and add complexity; you need to know how to play, but you also have to learn how others play.
Strike Vector does not do this(or at least not very much). Customization comes down to which weapon you use, what special ability you have, and what stat you want an incredibly minor boost to. You can customize your craft's engines, cockpit and paintjob, but they don't actually effect gameplay in any way.
The weapons all handle differently enough that you can tell the difference, but they simply fit into one of 4 playstyles:
Hit and run
Pursuit
Dueling
And camping(which only actually works with the sniper laser)
Next, the specials: probably the most interesting part of the game. The specials are nicely varied and each have their own use;
there's one that deploys a healing field that heals everyone in range regardless of who used it
a seeker mine that can be placed around corners to surprise enemies
a minefield to deter persuers
a damage field centered on your craft that melts people that get too close
an EMP to disorient enemies
a crazy speed boost for quick escapes
and a super shield which renders you invulnerable for a short time
And finally, there's the passive buffs(of which you can only equip one at a time):
Take a bit less damage from enemies
Move a little faster in jet mode
Move a little faster in hover mode
Be able to zoom in more while aiming(no that isn't just part of the sniper weapon)
Be harder to see on radar
As you can see, they're far from interesting.
While I definitely enjoyed my time in the game, and while I did have the thought "okay, one more round," it almost always actually meant "one more round" instead of "five more rounds" like in other games. The gameplay is fun, but just not deep enough to grab me for more than an hour.
Finding a match is also a problem because while you can play against bots, actual players will have to join the community discord server and hop on when someone announces a meetup due to how few players there actually are. This game is on life support and the devs don't seem to be adding anything more to it; so as much as I would love to recommend it, there simply isn't enough to this game for it to be worth purchasing.

Straightforward FPS killing zombies in space.

Good price, good graphics and great gameplay.
Great purchase.

Let's get the bad stuff out of the way first.  Your character glides around like he's on rails, he can't sprint for more than three seconds per minute without getting puffed, the voice acting and dialogue is arguably ill-advised (like a second-rate Duke Nukem or Serious Sam being guided around by the maddest "mad Nazi scientist" stereotype this side of Auschwitz), and there's an ever-so-slightly questionable save system which requires you to complete a whole level before said save occurs (though you can spend your hard-earned dollars on NOT having to go all the way back to the start of the mission...money you COULD be spending on new weapons and upgrades once you've completed the mission, but oh well)!
One should furthermore be prepared for some of the WORST excuses for "quick-time" events in the history of video gaming (and that's surely gotta be sayin' somethin').  Oh, and no matter how much you turn down the music, you STILL can't hear what your mad nazi scientist friend is saying to you half the time, not least of all because he usually picks the exact moment that a lot of noisy action is happening in which to tell you what you're supposed to be doing next...

Apart from the above, the graphics are rather nice (i.e. make for nice screenshots, even if they don't look so flash when you're actually MOVING), the gameplay is by-and-largely "fun", and it's always kinda nice and refreshing to see old-school WALKING zombies every once in a while.  Which isn't to say that this doesn't take ANY influence from more recent "running zombie"/"infected"-type games...I mean, what post-Left 4 Dead zombie game would be complete without a fat, Boomer-ish zombie who spits or vomits at you?  So originality is certainly NOT this game's strongest point, but at least it can't be accused of being pretentious (or even remotely ambitious in any way, shape or form, for that matter).

On the whole, not too bad a game at all if you've already played all the Dead Space games and the hundreds of frankly superior first-person shooters also available on Steam.  And I guess the price tag is pretty reasonable, if you're swayed by such things (I had my copy gifted by an over-generous friend, so no complaints from me at that end, hahaha).

Dying in this game is absolutely fine; don't let that put you off the game; it's an essential mechanic in the game's design!!

I personally am not too fond of the magic builds in this game because I find them a bit OP; I guess that's the games idea of an "easy mode" since there is no difficulty selection (another thing that I love about the game; difficulty is almost self-selected by the way that you choose to play the game).
The only problem with the game is that unless you use the DSFix mod it performs very poorly. It would be fantastic if From Software would address these issues.

Being one the lesser known properties from Sierra catalog, Quest for Glory often gets omitted from the countless top lists of classics to play and quite unjustifiably so. The series features some of best storytelling, witty humor and gameplay Sierra has ever created. Blending classic adventure gameplay with class system and progression akin to classic rpg's allows QFG to offer nearly unprecented (for point&click game) replay value, where games puzzles vary depending on the class chosen at the beginning of playthrough. As with most games, Quest for Glory isn't without its faults. Some activities like navigating throughmazes may feel needlessly tedious. Limited combat skill set, may make the combat somewhat repetetive in later stages.
PROS:
excellent writing and witty humor
rich and detailed world
unique setting for each installment in series
3 unique classes allow for 3 unique playthoroughs
ability to carry over between games.
high replay value
CONS:
some tasks may feel tedious by today's standards.
Combat can be repetetive if taken in large doses.
Occasionally less than obvious copy protection requiring information from game's manual.

This is actually a love letter for the developers.
Following the launch of Quest for Glory 4 in 1993, the series got canceled. Fans immediately deluged Sierra with petitions and in 1998 the last entry in the Quest for Glory franchise came out (Dragon's Fire).
After some time playing the hell out of the fifth and final entry back in the day, I ran into a text file inside the game's folder called Special.txt. It said:
"
...
Well, this is it.  Your long wait is finally over.
This is the final episode of Quest for Glory.
We'd like you to plan to finish Quest for Glory 5 on your own, without any hints.
It might be frustrating but just savor the game. It'll be over sooner than you wish.
Don't let anyone spoil things for you.
Once you finish, you'll have wonderful memories of the journey.
We'll miss you...
Thanks for everything.
Lori, Corey, and the QFG5 Team.
"
When I got this on Steam, the first thing I did was open the QfG5's folder to search for that text file, and to my delight it was there. I was only a kid the first time I read this and it seems like it happened yesterday.
It was never frustrating and although it does have an ending, it will never be over for me. I never stopped playing QfG and I never will. I do have wonferful memories and if I close my eyes for just a second while listening to Silmaria's tune, I can travel back in time.
This is the most beautiful and meaningful universe I have ever had the pleasure of exploring.
These are the best games I have ever played.
Lori, Corey and the QFG5 Team;
You've given me a journey for life. A place I can visit anytime I want and remember who I was and everything I held dear.
Thank YOU for everything and I hope you get to read this one day.

I finished this in a 9 hours setting so I guess I was hooked? Not exactly sure. Yes I really loved the art style, the soundtrack and the writing, but I'm not sure if I would recommend it to people other than those interested in unique storytelling.
It's sort of a visual novel, or the non-action parts of a Persona game. The loop is you starting a day, going around and talking to people then comitting to spending the rest of the day with one of your friends, then coming home to sleep and reapat the process. You find out a lot of peoples backstory which is very interesting.
What I did not like that much about the process was that it takes quite a bit to reach those people. Since you don't exactly know what you're looking for and if you like to check every corner it does get a bit tedious. I think this is mostly the reason as to why Mae is allowed to jump. It gives you something to do during that traversal.
This game like Gone Home is relying on a specific aspects of American culture, which as an outsider makes it harder to relate. I could relate to some of the struggels, but a lot of Mae's interactions are not player controlled and is used to characterize her as the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the group. This is refreshing, but I wonder how well this sits with people.
I wonder how this game was made, because the main plot is based Southern Gothic ideas, but the characterization that result from the situtations seem so real in some cases, they sort of conflict with supernatural aspect of this story.
Can realistic behavior and supernatural themes coexist? Yes they can, but I'm not exactly sure they were working together. The supernatural aspect of the story is overshadowed by the struggles of a shrinking rural American town.
Mae's struggle in that regard becomes the low point of the game to me. While it is briefly interesting, it takes the place of a story of how a real person would deal with being a returning college drop out. The game takes a long time to introduce the mystery as well. I just don't think it added much to the story except to be a convenient way to excuse some of Mae's behavior and postpone her growth which left me unsatisfied. In thinking about it, you could make the argument that the horror that has taken roots in her town is a metaphor other real world factors that are just as looming and uncaring and that her refusal to accept it is the start of her growth, but it is just unsatisfying compared to her friends' sidestories.
Overall though it is a great package, I think 15 euros would have been a better price, but I think this game is important. Not only because of the Southern Gothic vibes, but because it is an interesting example of how to do a visual novel style game. I'm not saying they struck gold, but we can see how certain gameplay decisions affect our enjoyment of this type of game. Constant interactivity because of walking and chosing replies is good, but then traversal could have been sped up because at a certain point you know all of the town and certain canned animations repeat. Some of the minigames like band practice are good, but not being able to repeat these sections seem counterintuitive to what "band practice" is supposed to be. The nightmare sequences are a nice stark contrast from the real world, but they are a too formulaic and do not add much to the story. Maybe a more combat focused horde mode with a bat would have made it feel like struggle to fight off something. Maybe a more visually grotesque platforming challenge would have been better suite. As it stands I just find four dudes over and over and they play a song. The melanchoy works mostly the first time and the sequences lose meaning once you realise their formula.
All in all recommended for people looking for unique storytelling and visuals in their game, but don't expect the package to be cohesive and it's actual gameplay to be as interesting.

Right, so imagine this:
You are a young guy/girl, you grew up in a small town, which rarely sees sucess, you however, beat the odds and get out of the town and go to school.
Soon however, you have problems. School isn't what you've imagined, being independent is rough, being responsible is impossible, you make mistakes.
Soon, you're back home, in the small town, living with parents who were so proud of you only several months ago...
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the plot of "Night in the woods", and a reality for many college aged kids. Why talk about reality when disucssing a videogame? Because if this situation seems familiar, this WILL hit home.
Now, for some people, this will be rough. You get in arguements, you get dressed down, you get in trouble, you say/do regrettable things. So what is the appeal?
The characters/dialogue.
Simply put, this game has some of the most human characters ever in a video game. Everyone has flaws, everyone has character arks, everyone has their own personality/sense of humor, some of which may take some getting used too.
Some people you will like, some you may hate. You may even hate yourself, but at the end of the day, every college dropout has hated themelves at some point.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So why buy this game? If you like decent platforming, fun minigames, and dialogue you can relate to (and laugh at!!!), this game is for you. It's a story of making the best out of a bad situation. One that many people have dealt with, and will instantly relate too.

I've never really played a game like this before. You are a pretty pretty princess in a not-so-pretty world filled with death and destruction at every corner. You have no skills, so you must train everything. You get to train 2 things per week (or the same thing twice) and how effective the training is depends on your mood. The remainder of the week is spent between doing an activity (that allows you to adjust your mood via increments) and game-events. These events almost all have a test where the game checks your level in a skill versus the minimum level required to pass the test. If you fully pass the test, you get 1 outcome, if you semi-pass (not enough levels to full-pass, but halfway there) then you get a 2nd outcome, and if you fail you get a third outcome. A continuing series of these game-events eventually results in your being crowned queen or, more likely, dying a horrible death. The charm of the game comes from the branching story line. Sometimes the best outcome actually is a semi-pass, or even a fail. The frustration of the game comes from not knowing what the cutoffs are. For example, there was a section of the game where a naval battle occurred. Accordingly, I anticipated that I might need to train swimming (in addition to naval battle theory, etc). As expected, my princess fell into the water. Unfortunately, knowing swimming to level 40 (out of 100) apparently wasn't enough to tread water until rescued by another ship, and I drowned. So apparently I need to be Michael Phelps to survive falling into the water admist my own naval armada? Also, once you beat the game, the only reason to continue playing is to experience all the other forms of death. Sure, you could try to win in a different manner (maybe be kinder? maybe less murderous?) but the game seems to want to teach you that being anything less than a murderous, scheming, bloodthirsty princess means you'll end up dead. So in all of your following playthroughs, if you're trying not to die, you're going to default to murder, scheming, and bloodthirst. Not that being those things isn't fun as all hell....

What should have been an engaging, great RPG instead turns out to be a tedious, monotonous, repetitive, nonsensical waste of time.   So much of this game is based on flawed premise.
You don't get experience for killing enemies after the first couple times you encounter an enemy type, but the game is FULL of pointless battles.
Combat is literally 90% of this game, and yet it's not something that you actually get rewarded for. Enemies are often immune to half of your attacks, have better ability to hit you and absorb damage than any of your characters are ever capable of. You are ALWAYS outnumbered in every encounter.
Roleplaying  encounters are often based on skill checks with no prior indication of what might or might not work.
Traps just appear in random places with no indicators of why they'd be there, or how you'd ever know to search for them. They're literally often just random lines on the ground, forcing you to constantly be in search mode(which makes you move at a snail's pace).
The game suffers from some of the worst AI pathing I've ever seen, often resulting in your characters getting stuck, or moving in random directions.  I've had characters literally run in the opposite direction of where I clicked.
The sound assets keep bugging and clicking in strange ways. Voices often change volume at random.
The system of restricting resting is deeply flawed, because not only do your entire party have to rest if a single character gets too low on health, but you also get heavily penalized for not playing perfectly(again, making combat the emphasis of the game, but not rewarding for it).  Many abilities can only be used so many times per rest, but in nonsensical ways that aren't in line with the power of the ability.
Basically everything about this game except it's story and lore is a mess.  I've tried so many different ways of playing, and the only way that's really effective is to CONSTANTLY pause and micro-manage every single attack and movement every second.  And not because it's more tactical to do so, but simply a requirement to avoid the idiotic AI and pathing from forcing you to reload due to a failed combat.
I can not in good conscience  recommend this game to anyone.  Go buy and play Tyranny instead. It's a better game, for less money.

There are few games that have come out in the past decade I could describe as being magical.  It’s not something I attribute because it’s a successful Kickstarter project with undeserved praise, rather that this game takes the design philosophies of two decades ago, polishes its gameplay and storyline, and makes a game that is greater than the sum of its predecessors. The result is a game that not only shows the devotion of fans who wanted the genre to return but also a vast richness in world design that few games can ever dream of.
This level of polish is something I think cynical reviewers may overlook because of the many derivative elements you will find from Black Isle Studios (and BioWare): Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale and Planescape Torment.  While originality is important—and by no means is PoE lacking its own ideas—the thing that is always more important is the execution of an idea, and PoE is living proof that an imitation can be a sincere form of flattery but also become the next crowning pillar of excellence.

As previously mentioned, PoE goes to great lengths to masquerade all its complexities from its past. The most obvious comparison is the style of gameplay as you can play with a six-party team of adventurers in an isometric world. Various monsters are also obviously rebranded from D&D like the Xaurip (Kobolds), Vithrack (Mind-Flayers) and, my favorite, Vampyres. Even the mechanics of classes and leveling up takes a lot of inspiration from D&D’s ruleset with player expression in their choices (mainly for combat).
Perhaps the subtlest of all deviations is how Obsidian has reworked the implementation of THAC0.  If you have played these games, then the concept is familiar enough; however, if you have not played them like when I first started, the idea is that it represents the player’s ineptness at the start and becomes the player’s greatest show of growth overtime. In BG, this number factored in various other statistics that alienated most players from ever finishing the game; in PoE, they rebranded it into something simpler to understand and more complex to affect, Accuracy.
Accuracy is the sole component that determines the difficulty of this game. It not only determines the chance/skill to hit and the damage output, but it also acts as the player’s ineptness as this number adds up over every level to help drive the player’s growth. If you balance this number along with Damage Reduction and Recovery Speed from armor, then you have understood the most important details of this game.
This system is much easier for newcomers, myself included, to understand how to become better at the game as almost all skills, passives, class-unlocks, etc. are related back to Accuracy. There are various unlocks, spells, potions, food, etc. to achieve the best result that it helps not only make each character feel distinct but also helps the player roleplay. Even when it comes to the game’s unique usage of difficulty where it modifies the number/quality of your encounters, except for Path of the Damned which modifies them only slightly, mastering the game is a far easier and rewarding challenge.
Speaking of roleplaying, the amount of dialogue options taken from PT—mainly five to six various tones but always a yes, no or kill option—the quest-opportunities, the reputation system, and the way companions work for this game lends immense replayability value. Backgrounds—species, history, classes, and even character sheets—also add in little moments that will make each playthrough distinct in small, though over time grand, effects.
In brief, RPGs by their very nature make numbers behold beauty in their simplicity, and this game’s implementation of statistics and of player expression is as beautiful as Einstein’s theories of relativity. This facet alone would make this game nearly flawless; however, the storytelling and world are also the richest parts from this game to explore.
Before I delve into discussing the narrative, there are two things I want to say. One, I will avoid spoilers by discussing its themes as well as how the structure works (for companions and the story), so nothing I say will diminish experiencing it for yourself. Second, I chose that word for a reason as it is something this game and Tyranny excel in handling: Agnosticism.
Agnosticism has nothing to do with beliefs but how one knows the world. This theme is integral to the storyline of PoE by how it handles exposing you to the viewpoints of gods through writings from people and even the viewpoints of other gods from both sides. For most of the game, as well as DLC, you are indirectly learning much from the world by comparing both sides of their stories and parsing out the truth from the misconceptions. Twenty hours into the game and I was already comparing the teachings of Abydon to the ways of Wael as well as their end-goals, and the story is richer as a result. Even if you do not care about reading the texts of lore, the exposure from the quests and various factions/places in the world will make you stop and question what is accepted as truth.
If you have played Morrowind, then you will be familiar with this style of a plot-structure. The result is that most of the quests are indistinguishable from the main-plot as it’s all tightly woven together, and unlike modern BioWare, there are no major plot-points to emphasize urgency. This is seen in how companion quests are often simple questlines with tangential stories that delve into the lore. As a matter of replayability, this structure is superior because it doesn’t force the player to do something specific, though people may find that many end too soon or have a vague/lacking ending. And when you reach that final decision in the game, the consequences and ramifications of your actions show up a la Fallout: New Vegas.
If games want to emphasize linear storytelling, PoE is how they should be handled, emphasizing lore with the plot through replayability, and this game is by far the best in that category. Not everyone may enjoy its structure, and, admittedly, the antagonist has the grandeur of Irenicus but suffers a small presence like Sarevok from BG, so the story itself isn’t flawless. It’s the usage of a game to tell that story which embodies its grandness.
None of this is to say that the game doesn’t have its faults.
The gameplay requires a lot of micromanaging of party-members on Path of the Damned as well as being intimidating at first. Some encounters are obviously meant for higher-levels that you will only know after trying them. If you prefer more non-combat options for RPGs, then this game may disappoint you in forced encounters—you typically can avoid the more difficult side quests or make them easier to handle. Also, the main game itself is a 40 to 75 hour storyline that may dissuade some people, though the mechanical complexity and leveling-up system keep you retained. Lastly, the stronghold system is half-baked with a surplus of gold always being at your disposal and some enemies/effects are rather ridiculous like paralysis from Shades.
For every one of these issues, however, there are always a work-around, and after 70 hours of Path of the Damned—including the high-level alterations—I was never forced to use consumables for buffs if I managed my party efficiently. This level of challenge is something few games can handle correctly without ruining the fun as it makes all the surplus consumables to help you on repeated playthroughs to overcome a challenge you once found insurmountable.
The only criticism I think is undeniable is if you don’t like reading you won’t like this game. And if you read this much of a review and found the game interesting from what I’ve shared thus far, I think you’ll love it in spite of all the stupid Engwithian names you will learn.
We are once again in the goldan age of RPGs thanks to Obsidian and Larian Studios. Thank you.

Dark Souls 1 is probably the best game I have ever played on the PC platform. It is expertly crafted in that the game doesn't hold hands with you, but makes you learn the inner workings through the level design. And this is truly where Dark Souls shines. Each area in Dark Souls connects to others in such a compact way that it is spatially synced to the overworld. The player will find shortcuts which will lead back to a previous area they found. Not to mention the nonlinear path that a player can take. Once you finish the tutorial, you already have the choice of going two ways, and if you picked up the Master Key, you can even take a third path. If you're itching for some epic boss battles, Dark Souls has nothing but the best. Unfortunately, a negative side of this version on Steam is that it is not optimized well at all, and this could be a make or break for many people who are wanting to play this game. Other than that, this game is fantastic.

Alright, review time again.
I've played over 100 hours of this up until today.
The saddest part is that I didn't really pick it up until 2017.
Rebirth was gifted to me by a former friend, in 2014, when it first came out. I played 25 minutes of it, died a few times and never touched it again.
Until January 2017, I put like 17 hours into it and then stopped until recently.
The entirety of August I practically did nothing else than playing Isaac.
The game is hard to get into, but it is damn cool.
The pixelated artstyle and overall topdown rogue-like look might deter some, but you really have to try it out.
It is very unforgiving at first and still will be after a long while of playing.
I get sweaty hands all the time wheb trying to complete a run.
Because if your life bar is deplenished, it's over. No checkpoints or anything like that.
You controll Isaac, a small naked boy who tried to escape his mother by leaping into a secret entrance to the basement underneath his rug. His mother, being motivated by a deity, had to present the ultimate offering to it, by slitting Isaac's throat.
As you go forwards you encounter all sorts of weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ living feces, moving rotten pieces of meat, versions of Isaac himself but without eyes and so on. Also, you are able to find items that help you increase your main source of defense and damage: Your own tears. Alright there, that's a bit ♥♥♥♥ed up.
Every floor will have a specific set of rooms. One item room each floor, up until the boss (which is Mom, very surprisingly, haha), a shop where you can buy goods with found money, a sacrifice room and a curse room. Each floor also has two secret rooms only openable by a well-placed bomb at one of the walls.
At the end of the floor is always a boss, which is a much stronger enemy type than the ones you encounter in the rest of the floor. After defeating it, you'll get an item for free.
After beating mom in the Depths, it is not over, however. Beat her a second time and you'll be able to enter her womb (wtf). At the end of the two womb stages, you'll fight Mom's Heart, which is essentially the final boss.
But wait! Did you really think it would end there? Nah man.
Beat the Heart 11 times and you can go down to Sheol (essentially the hell), where you'll fight Satan. So it is getting totally non-sensical now.
If you do some things right, you can also go upwards into the Cathedral, in which the boss is YOURSELF. You have to fight Isaac. Nice.
There is even more, because you can go even further after beating Satan or Isaac.
But whatever, let's focus on other things for now.
The gameplay is dodging and aiming projectiles. Practically nothing more. Dodging is really hard, and definetely a skill you should learn. Some enemies are downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, i.e. spiders, which crawl around in a very irritating manner, making them very unpredictable.
Luckily there arr some very strong items to help you in Isaac, but that is of course all rng based. You'll never know what you'll find, which makes the replay factor immense. Strong synergies can be a GG for you, but if you find worthless crap like Butter bean or the poop then you are pretty ♥♥♥♥ed. Some of the best items are unlocked fairly late, like beating Satan with a specific character (which you can also unlock).
What made me lose interest in the long run is how grind-heavy this all is. Pretty much every serious isaac player is an achievement hunter, who aims to complete all of 'em. It's too much and too frustrating to get the 100%, because some of them are downright impossible without putting at least 500 hours in.
After 100 hours you have seen everything, and the new item you unlocked isnt going to help there, because maybe you won't even find it once in the next 50 hours.
The soundtrack gets old really fast, it isn't my taste, so I used the original soundtrack through a mod, which helped.
To really have fun with this game, buy the dlcs in a sale, they provide tons of new content for a washed up player such as me.
Or, install the fan modification "Antibirth" which surpasses dlc and the normal game in every way.
So:
No for me, Yes for the general public. I can recommend this game to anyone who likes grinding and rouge like dungeon crawlers.

Disclaimer: At time of writing. Steam will point out I have no hours logged in this game. This is because I already owned these games from another source and had my fix before this came out. When I saw a Steam version, I couldn't resist re-purchasing it for Steam. I cannot properly endorse the STEAM version of this for performance or stability; the gameplay, however, still compelled me to review a game which I love dearly and believe deserves more attention.
But really, no reviews for this collection yet? Really?  Alright, let's give this a shot.
Quest for Glory is a game series from Sierra, famed creators of Space Quest and King's Quest from days of yore. Unlike it's more popular kin, QfG is an Adventure story game with Action/RPG elements throughout. What does that mean, exactly?  If you've ever played the other games of Sierra's creation, you know what an Adventure game is; you are presented with a challenge or obstacle, and must overcome it with your wits and a plethora of knick-knacks you've collected along the way. Remember that shard of glass you picked up 2 hours ago? Time to use it to cut that rope around your legs! Hope you found the strange bottle, you need it to get around the guards.
I could say Sierra's games are the grandfather of Telltale's games, if that's something you're more familiar with. It's a bit of a stretch, but they give me the same feeling as Sierra's games. But I digress.
The Action/RPG elements are what set this game apart from the rest. You create your character much like a Dungeons and Dragons character, spending points to increase your strength, dexterity, spellcasting potential, as well as various skills you may use in combat or puzzle-solving. This gives nearly every challenge in the game a plethora of ways to be solved. Your character skills rank up through use, allowing you to spread out your advancement and grind them up or to play more with a more linear focus on your existing strengths. You'll find yourself wondering if the best way to get that bird nest down is to throw a rock at it, to climb the tree and get it, or to find a spell to collect it for you.  When you enter a hidden goblin camp, you hope your sword and shield are up to the task, or surprise some of them with thrown daggers or a magic assault. And whatever you do, don't sleep outside the town at night. The Night Gaunt gets ya.
Perhaps the most innovative part of these games to me, and something I wouldn't see again until Mass Effect, is that your character is carried forward through each game. You don't remake your character and start from scratch or play a different hero. The hero you create is the central character of the entire arc, and once you finish a game your character file is saved for use in the next installment. Your skill ups, your gold, your equipment, nearly all of it carries forward. Some things are changed or removed and your skills lowered to a degree to allow new progression, but it was an incredible moment to me when my character moved to a new land, ready to learn new tricks.
That being said, this is a collection of old, old games. I write this review with nostalgia gripping my heart, painfully aware that this game probably hasn't aged well and may not be fun for all audiences.  The graphics are downright painful if you don't enjoy the pixel-art aesthetic, Quest for Glory 2 needs to be played with a walk-through (nobody has time for the maze-city navigation anymore!), and games like Skyrim can arguably do what this does but better. "Better" is subjective, naturally, and all I can do in this review is suggest people try it. Steam offers refunds these days, and I do suggest that anyone who is curious gives it a shot. Boot up each game quickly to make sure they run smoothly, and just dive in.

I have lost count of the amount of times I've placed something, only to pull it down and attempt to re-place it several times before I was satisfied with its position.
Why also can I not place an item on uneven terrain? An example would be a platform. Four posts, any of which could be buried in the ground upon placement or "sawed off" to suit the terrain. And if I were to place another right next to one, instead of it lining up to a flat surface the next one would end up much higher than the one originally placed. So if you were fortunate to be able to place say, four platforms it would somewhat resemble a BMX track with massive gaps between them. Good luck getting four sides of gap free walls on that mess.
Storage. Oh storage. I understand that you want to grab a hold of our nuts and limit the amount of gear that we can posess to minimise the amount of alphas who could hold a monopoly on a server, but give us server owners the right to select an option for ourselves in the config file.
Official servers are a different matter but we are paying a ridiculous amount of money to rent a server that we have no real say over what we can provide our players. I don't care about weather settings or the other inane and menial options, I want control over more important options.
Vehicles. Why TF is a vehicle disappearing after 48 hours of no login? I want to be able to spend a weekend with my family or go on holiday for more than two days without coming back to a base with no transport as it de-spawned. And while I'm on the subject, why limit the amount of vehicles on the server?
Those with vehicles are smiling with their toes tapping, while others who come in once the vehicles are claimed have no transport whatsoever. If those holding vehicles crash and burn, their chances of finding a replacement are slim to none. Give us more vehicles to locate, or does the reasoning behind this come down to the storage strangle debate.
The main gripes I get are for lack of vehicles and storage, and these people stop playing the game altogether.
PVP and PVE. I whitelisted my server as I had in the description no KOS or base raiding. Well, we had a bunch of !%@#s come in and start KOS and base raiding. It's impossible to scroll through and find the people responsible so I can place them on the ban list because the damage logs are ridiculously long.
If I state no KOS or base raiding then I should be able to configure my server in that manner. Cast your mind back to the paragraph on storage about more options, I should be able to flag this for no player or structure damage. Some people enjoy playing PVP, others do not and when they work for months to build something up on a PVE server, only to lose it while they sleep, on holiday or are are work is unacceptable.
Carrying dynamics. Okay, let me get this right. I can place two wheels in the pockets of my T-shirt, but I can't place 20 rounds of .357 in the same spot?
I have a bus that will hold X amount of people (unsure of the capacity), but I can't place more than ten pieces of paper (guides) in the inventory of the bus, but I can carry ?20 people.
Why can't a fully loaded backpack with, for example - ten cans of soda - be placed in the tray of a pickup? If I were to go camping I could place ten loaded backpacks, a tent, sleeping bags, and a whole bunch of other gear in the vehicle and have room to spare.
Here it should again come down to the server configs of the renter, and again the storage strangle debate.
Glitches. Too many to name but believe me whan I say they are numerous. Loot being half buried in whatever it's supposed to be sitting on (making half the loot next to impossible to find), mutants attacking and damaging through walls, vehicles flying into the air on a flat section of road, DC's, blank screens, black squares on screens where the rendering bugs out, Items dropped falling through the ground into a black hole of non-existance (dropping something for someone else to pick up is a hit and miss affair), falling under the terrain (My son was walking at the airfield and disappeared under the terrain, he literally swam to the ocean side under the land mass and popped up) the list goes on. Yeah, I know - "It's still in alpha".
Servers. Here's the kicker. Why do you have such a monopoly on who can provide the server? i3D are the only providers at present who we can rent off, and at the price that's being charged for a server that we can't configure to suit our preferences is nothing short of robbery. Oh yeah, I can go and shove it if I don't like it, go play another game, I also understand that. But this is why there is so much talk about there being kickbacks for exclusivity.
If I want to host this game on a personal server I can't, if I want to play this game by myself on my PC lone wolf style I can't, nor can I shop around for a better deal to save a bit of money on a game that just doesn't quite hit the mark at the present moment in time.
In conclusion, I like the game but I see it heading in a uncertain direction at the moment, and that's what's holding me back. I want to say it's a good game to play but the statements above lend weight to the descision that I've made that I will see the rental of the server until the next payment is due, then it's game over. I have seen many servers disappear over the time I've played which prompted me to rent one, but I understand why people give up and stop paying.
I could just join the masses and play on another server but, will I be fortunate enough to find a vehicle? Will some griefer rob my base or KOS on a PVE server while I sleep? Will that server give up as a bad investment, just as I will be doing? Too many unanswerable questions that make me say that it's not worth playing the game.

This used to be my favourite game when i was a child. I bought it after beatin Warcraft 3, and loved it a lot. I also replayed it a few times and enjoyed it every time. About a year ago i tried to play Kings bounty, but enjoyed it a lot less than this game. Maybe it's nostalgia, but i really love that in this game every unit is separate, when in KB it's just one unit with the number. It makes it a lot more fun for me.
This game may have bad graphics, but does this even matter? It's best part is the fighting system. It's not too long, so i didn't get bored with figths, which are, by the way, pretty different each time. If you played KB, you should know what i'm talking about. In Ascension it also matters how many units you put into one cell. It may be 1 weak soldier, which can be a bait, or a group of them. In the second scenario the group is more likely the distract the enemy, they can even protect more important units with their own bodies, which you couldn't do in KB, but the also can be destroyed by one hit of the wizard, while putting them into separate groups makes it longer to take them all down.
The rpg part is not very developed, this is true. There is no skill tree or anything like that. But if you choose to be a wizrd, which is a wise choise, you definatly will enjoy finding new spells, like triple fireballs or distraction. Most of them can be bought learned from wizards in towns, but some, like fast travel spell, are hidden on the map. However, if you want the game to be more challanging, make your hero a warrior and don't learn spells.
The world is divided into three continents. The land of humans, the land of orcs and barbariabs and the land of demons. Each of them is full of characters, secrets and side quests. It's really interesting to explore in ths game. If you do, you may find a worthy treasure.
Side quests in this game are rather small, but more interesting, than just "kill-bring" ones. There are such quests as drinking competiton, detective quest. In most of those you can express your will. For example, in the detective quest you can either punish the criminal you find, or take his money + keep  him available as a merchant.
There are also several items in this game, which cost a lot, A LOT of money. You'll have to complete some side quests in order to buy them. Those are armour, rings etc. Funny thing: you won't be able to buy some items. Merchants will tell you that they are no use for you. They are actually useful for a main caracter of the sequel, which is sadly not on steam. Those items are easter eggs of some sort.
I found the plot interesting. The final battle is pretty epic. Plus there are some interestings parts of the main quests, in which you, for example, will have to get rid of all your weapons and armour, your whole army too, and dress as a monk in order to enter a city, taken over by a demon. Hten you'll have to fight him without all things you left behind. If you're a wizard - it's difficult. If you're a warrior - good luck.
The in-game journal is done decently. It doesn't say "kill 10 rats, dragonborn". The notes in it always fit the atmosphere, and, if you read them, may contain useful hints.
I definatly recommend this game.
