: If you like Assassin's Creed games you will probably like Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor. It's like Assassin's Creed but with less down time and you have super powers that you gain as you level. The world is based around the use of both fast paced stealth gameplay and combat alike and feels streamlined for exactly that.
(I have completed everything that the main story has to offer in around 45 hours of playing)
- The gameplay for Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is Arkham style like most other WB games where there is little true depth to the combat but it does not make it any less fun. You are rewarded for killing Uruks in more creative ways by getting more xp, and with the xp you get skills that are used to help kill uruks. It's a cycle that works well because every skill point you obtain is used to help get even more skill points.
- The captain system is what you will be playing with for the majority of the game due to the fact that it is required for the main game and is fun to play with regardless. You can either kill the captains or brand them, and by branding them you force them to help you in different ways, whether it be killing other captains in your place or giving you information to help you kill them yourself.
- The rune system is a RNG based system that gives you runes for killing captains, the mini-bosses of the game. The runes then give unique attributes to either your sword, bow, or dagger. They are varied in such a way that you can create a semi-unique style of play suited for yourself. Not only do they add more varied gameplay but they encourage the player to explore with the captain system and kill more difficult captains in hopes of a greater reward.
- Stealth gameplay works well when you work quickly and with deadly effeciency, the second that you have to slow down though there is a lot of down time while waiting for the Uruk AI to move where you want it to. Once you get some level ups you can obtain skills that allow you to kill faster both in and out of stealth. You also get upgrades to your bow which help in dispatching large amounts of enemies quickly.
- The movement system is great 80% of the time but the other 20% is what sticks with you. The game sets you up with a bundle of skills which make traversing the map a breeze, such as the shadow strike ability which lets you teleport and knock down an enemy for two arrows, or the fact that while climbing you leap incredible distances upward to reduce the down time while climbing (think the grapling hook from Assassin's Creed Syndicate but more immersive). This helps while climbing the towers of light (yes ubisoft towers) to make them quick and easy. In addition you get access to multiple creatures that you can use to help you roam the map very quickly. The 20% of the time is incredibly painful to play with though. It suffers from the issue that Assassin's Creed has where sometimes the player character just won't go where you want or need them to go, or just jumping off a ledge. For the missions that require the player to remain undetected this is insanely frustrating and almost drove me to stop playing the game for a short time, as I would want the character to continue moving along an edge but it would instead jump down into a group of enemies, failing the mission instantly. Sometimes I would be trying to run away along an edge from a captain I couldn't take on at the time but the character would stop moving entirely, causing death.
- The story for Shadow of Mordor is mostly good, it bounces around between different characters fairly quickly which is upsetting because of the unique persnoalities that they came up with. They do help this by keeping them around in the DLC which you get with the season pass. The story follows Talion who has been denied death by a curse after watching his family die and is now linked with a wraith. The wraith lends Talion his power in an effort to learn of his lost past as Talion helps the human resistance. Despite using two very cliche motives being amnesia and revenge the game does it well.
- The music is mainly orchestral and fits the setting well but towards the end of the game I noticed I was hearing the same music over and over again. This won't be a large problem for people who focus on the main story because of it's length, but for anyone who completes all of the busywork you may find yourself listening to the same track.
: 7/10
Story - 6/10
General Gameplay - 8/10
Music - 7/10
- The game is really entertaining but is a typical open world game and struggles from regular open world problems like having a giant checklist of seemingly endless things to do. The checklist only really got boring when the game required that you not be detected. Other than those moments the combat is incredibly fun and killing Uruk doesn't get boring easily (which is good considering that is what makes up almost all of the gameplay. The story could be better but isn't boring at any point and creates a few moments of intensity. The music gets repetative after a long time playing it which isn't a huge problem. The biggest issue I had with Shadow of Mordor was that the movement can be extremely clunky at points. Overall a good game and well worth your time.

Dying in this game is absolutely fine; don't let that put you off the game; it's an essential mechanic in the game's design!!

I personally am not too fond of the magic builds in this game because I find them a bit OP; I guess that's the games idea of an "easy mode" since there is no difficulty selection (another thing that I love about the game; difficulty is almost self-selected by the way that you choose to play the game).
The only problem with the game is that unless you use the DSFix mod it performs very poorly. It would be fantastic if From Software would address these issues.

Considering it's a tablet port, the controls feel fluid and precise (although the sight on the most expensive assault rifle sways horribly when you move your mouse), the zombies are well animated, the weapons are literally "This gun is far better than this gun. Use this.", and when you get the minigun, you've practically won the game.
It looks good, there are plenty of secrets to find,  the music seems a little out of place at times, but the sound design is rather well done. They've done a good job of making sure you know you're on a broken down, abandoned, zombie filled spaceship, with the hisses of broken oxygen tanks and hoses, the gargling and moaning zombies are easy to locate due to the fact that, even with just speakers, you can hear exactly how far they are from you, AND where they're likely located.
For £3.99, I genuinely cannot complain. It's very reminiscent of games like Rise of the Triad, Painkiller, and in survival mode, maybe even Serious Sam, gameplay-wise.  I just got nearly two hours of non-stop fun out of it, but I will say this..
If you're looking for a perfectly polished, difficult, long, drawn out experience, this isn't the game for you.
If you want a few hours of mindless zombie slaying with some quite decent story (albeit grammatically incorrect, at times) told through the dialogue over the communicator you're wearing, and through text-based PDA logs (a-la Doom 3 without them actually being read out to you) that you find throughout the game (some are hidden fairly well, so check EVERYWHERE in the room you're in before moving on to the next one! Counter-Strike: Condition Zero is basically 'just' a slightly improved version of Counter-Strike 1.6.
If you happen to be unfamiliar with the CS games series, the concept of the idea is simple.
Players play against eachother in online matches, choosing to play either a terrorist or a counter terrorist. The team that completes their objective or eliminates the opposing team wins.
Counter-Strike is a fairly old game, built on the Half-Life engine, that became extremely popular years ago and is one of the best known shooter games (series) ever made, alongside eg. Unreal Tournament, Doom, Call of Duty and other such classics. And thanks to a large community, there is a huge amount of custom content available for these games. As long as you have some people to play with, it's hard to get bored in the world of Counter-Strike. And Condition Zero is no exception to this.
What most people familiar with the series can tell you is that while CZ is a decent game, it is highly underrated compared to both older and newer installments. Why is this? Well there may be several reasons, but the easiest way to put it is this: it's the middle child of CS games.
CS purists will prefer to play the original Counter-Strike, versions 1.5 and 1.6. And the newer games draw a big crowd because they're flashier and fancier. Since Condition Zero is situated in between the older 1.6 and Counter-Strike: Source (which started using the new Source engine), it doesn't get much of the attention it deserves, in my opinion. However, I can tell you that it is definitely a game worth playing if you're into slightly older shooting games.
--------------------
More information...
-=Gameplay=-
Q: How is it played?
A: After joining a server, you have four options. You can join one of two teams, you can let the game decide for you which team you'll join or you can spectate the game, basically existing as a ghost, watching others play. You can play as a counter-terrorist operative or as a terrorist. The moment you spawn (when a new round starts, or within seconds of a round starting) you're able to open a menu that allows you to buy weapons, protection and various equipment. If the round has not yet started, you are unable to move. If you picked a team seconds after the round started, you will instantly be able to move. Everyone spawns with a basic pistol and a little bit of money. Once you're able to move, your goal is to move out of the spawn area and attempt to complete any of your objectives to earn more money and to win the round. When the round is over, everyone respawns in the same area as last round and the game is repeated. If you died, you'll start over with your gear, otherwise you keep what you had before. You will keep playing rounds until the server changes to a different map (level), usually after 20 minutes. There are a couple of standard game types, determined not by server options but by the type of map that is being played. The three main types are bomb defusal, hostage rescue and assassination. There are other types, but those are only featured in custom maps. Completing just ONE of the listed objectives will win a team the round and earn additional money for all of it's members.
*Bomb defusal
-Terrorists must plant a bomb in one of two possible bomb sites and make sure it explodes. (the team still wins if the bomb explodes while all it's members are dead)
-Terrorists must kill all counter-terrorists.
-Counter-terrorists have to kill all terrorists.
-Counter-terrorists must defuse the bomb if it is planted. (the team still wins if all CT players are killed after the bomb has been defused)
*Hostage rescue
-Terrorists must stay alive and keep the counter-terrorists from rescuing all living hostages.
-Terrorists have to kill all the counter-terrorists.
-Counter-terrorists have to rescue all the living hostages.
-Counter-terrorists have to kill all the terrorists.
*Assassination
-Terrorists must keep the VIP from the rescue zone while staying alive themselves.
-Terrorists have to kill the VIP.
-Counter-terrorists have to kill all the terrorists.
-Counter-terrorists have to get the VIP player (picked at random) to the rescue zone within a specific time limit.
-=Experience=-
CZ is an old game. It runs on an old engine. It looks, feels and sounds old. Quite simply, if you can't stand anything but HD graphics, realistic water effects, decent ragdoll physics and other such things, this is not the game for you. That said, there's enough to keep it interesting. Weapons all sound and behave differently and it takes practice to get good with each (type). The maps are diverse enough in types of environment. It's worth mentioning that in a game like this, the maps are relatively small, forcing players into confrontation to keep the game going at a decent pace. Because the action is usually fast and intense, you will usually be too distracted to really notice what your surroundings sound or look like. For some interesting experiences, try a few custom maps! Made by members of the community, you'll find the craziest levels. Themed ones, maps based on popular films or tv series and just insane maps that seem to be all over the place. Shake things up by customising your game and trying out new things.
-=Technical, controls, etc.=-
Again, CZ is a fairly old game. As long as you can get the game started, you're not going to have issues with this. It's pretty stable and even if you do suffer a bug or error, you will easily find a solution for it through Google, thanks to the large amount of players who have played this and other CS/HL games over the years.
It's extremely small compared to modern games and will take up very little space, even if you start adding custom content to it and customising it further. For anyone with a normal internet connection you can download this game very quickly.
Controls are what you're used to in PC shooters. Pretty intuitive and unsurprising. Thankfully, if there's anything that is not working how you want it to, you can change it. Controls can be changed in the options menu and if there's anything not listed in there, you can always find a way to fix it by using the developers console. This may sound complicated if you're a casual PC user/gamer, but again, the community has made sure that there's enough information for you to figure things out without spending a lot of time doing research and basically missing out on actually playing and enjoying the game.
Besides regular user controls, there are also enough options and commands by default for server owners (you, if you're hosting a game) to keep control of the match. These can be expanded upon greatly by installing an administrative modification on your game (server) and again, there's enough information for anyone with limited computer knowledge to succeed in this endeavour.
Pro's:
-Basically an improved Counter-Strike 1.6
-Extremely and easily customisable with a lot of custom content available
-Easy to learn, hard to master
-Features working bots (not brilliant ones in gameplay, though) and the game can "learn" custom maps and make waypoint files for the CZ bots automatically. They work in multiplayer too
-Comes with Deleted Scenes, separate game on the same engine that has you playing a proper SP campaign, going across the world to stop terrorist activity in scripted missions.
Cons:
-Highly underrated and not well known, will not have as much players as other CS games (best played with friends)
-Somewhat pricey, unless you're planning on playing it a lot, despite the content available and given with just the game itself

Before I review the actual game, I want to start by saying that I came real close to demanding a refund. I was having the issue everyone else is having. You need to register the game on Uplay. Fine. Problem is the game can't connect to Uplay, effectively making the game 100% impossible to even start up. Luckily I did find a work around. By doing this, the game is now fully playable, but what a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If you're going to force Uplay down everyone's throats, fine. But in the future make sure it actually ♥♥♥♥ing works. That said, I'm still thumbing this game up, because I'm reviewing the game, and not this stupid Uplay ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.



Now onto the actual game review. OG Splinter Cell was the only SC game I'd played until now. I played through it on the Gamecube way back, and enjoyed it a lot. I was expecting this to play a lot like that and was pleasantly surprised to learn just how much it changed for the better.



You have full customization of your character. There are 3 skill trees that level based on how you go about clearing missions. You can customize your armor, your weapons, what gadgets you bring and even how they behave. You even have a sort of hub word in the form of a plane. You can upgrade your plane to unlock new upgrades for your character and extra things to do in missions.

Again, the gadget customization. The distraction camera was my favorite gadget in the old game. You could shoot it at a wall and make noises with it to draw guards near and then gas them. Sadly missions always gave you specific gadgets to a mission and you didn't always get the distraction camera. Here, not only can you bring the camera with you on any mission, but you can fully customize it to give off flashes to blind enemies, or even make them explode.

The world is linear, but very open. There's lots of different paths you can take, some being better for different play styles.

There is a cover system where you can stealthily snap to the environment and move silently between nearby props to work your way closer to the enemy. Controlling this system took some getting used to, but makes stealth a lot of fun.

There's lots of optional objectives to do in missions. For example, the crew on your plane can mark wanted men for you. You can sneak up on them, tie them up, and tag them to be taken into custody and receive a bonus. Certain upgrades for your plane can actually allow for more side missions like this to become available. This is a nice little way to add some replayability to the missions.

You can play the game however you want, and the game will reward you based on your choices. As said before, there's 3 different skill trees: Ghost, panther, and assault. How you go about dealing with obstacles will earn you points in each tree, and nothing is restricting you to a tree. You can silently cut a guards throat, then run in guns blazing on a group of enemies in the same mission and gain points in each skill tree.



If you're willing to put up with the Uplay crap to get this game working, it's definitely worth it once you get past the stupid stuff. Thumbs down to Uplay, but thumbs up to this solid game.

There are literally areas in levels that you cannot go into unless you have a parter, so there are areas that I will never see. But in addition to that, this game managed to make a fun series frustrating by the simple mistake of making the save system checkpoint based instead of based off manual saving. That only works in Arkham style games because they save roughly every minute and a half even if you don't complete an objective, and because those games aren't primarily stealth based. Having to redo an enire section (or entire side mission because those are meant to be coop and for some reason have no checkpoints even in single player), because you were seen, isn't fun.
It pains me to say that I wouldn't recommend this game, because the level design is neat, the story isn't bad, and I do think that it had potential once. But I bought Splinter Cell Chaos Theory right before this, and after coming from that game to this one, it just isn't a comparison. All the little problems add up to make me say:
Go play any one of the Dishonored, Deus Ex, original Thief trilogy, or old Splinter Cell games instead of this one. You'll have more fun, and they're cheaper.

What doesn't kill you makes you stronger. When I was a kid, Space Quest and King's Quest were my jam. I completed them all multiple times and adored these series, even though if I were to play them for the first time today, I would likely be pretty put off by them due to there ruthlessness of the games, and their lack of characters and plot that I care about to any extent. Since I dealt with them back in the day, and despite their abusive, start-the-entire-game-over-if-you-missed-one-item nature, I persevered and enjoy the games even today.
Quest for Glory is a series I never played as a kid, even though it is 3 years
than the Space Quest series. That said, since I grew up and did battle with Space Quest's ruthless oldschool nature when that was simply the way of things, I got used to those games and enjoyed them. So here I am, a child of the '80s, playing a late '80s game for the first time, and having about as good a time as I expected to have, which is to say not a good time at all. If I'd played it as a kid, I probably would have spent days wandering around town looking for items and things to do, and trying all the different stats to figure out which stats do what, going to book stores at the mall with my parents, hoping with all my heart to find a strategy guide to make it a little further if I got utterly stuck, and I would have still liked the game.
The present day version of me, however, is spoiled rotten. There are plenty of good and bad games coming out in the present, but they are typically far more streamlined. This comes down to a matter of player preference. Do you like your games to try to make you smile and tell an interesting story, or do you like your games to try desperately to kill you? I am not being a smart♥♥♥♥♥ here. Neither camp of people is "right" or "wrong;" it just comes down to what you like. I enjoyed the harder games in the '80s because that's pretty much all there was! I had to make due. As a shopper of today, however, I have choices, and can avoid abusive games.
With that in mind, I cannot get into Quest for Glory. It is a weird marriage between point-and-click adventure and RPG, which throws starting stat and class selection at you with no in-game tool-tips when the game absolutely could have them if they wanted to bother (mouse-overs or click to inspect), and the combat has a stamina meter which kills you from exhauston if you run out. I fought two goblins and died after my second swing at the second goblin. My HP was nearly full...my stamina ran out. Of course, the game only gave me a warning that I should rest one click before I died. =/
If you played this way back when and didn't hate it, you'll probably love it now. However, if you never played it, this could be a tough series to get into. I think the pure adventure (no RPG mechanics) of King's Quest and Space Quest would make them easier for someone to get into now, but it's still a crapshoot.

I love Obsidian, but I think this is their weakest entry I've played. I was looking for a high character building RPG with good mechanics, and a nice story when I bought it on day one at full price. I played for quite a bit, then realised the combat just wasn't what I was looking for, or the story. I suggest Tyranny instead: Much better presentation and weighty, focused combat.
You design a character before you're introduced to the story, ensuring your first playthrough will make no sense at all. So, you're running around with this character who makes very little sense being in this situation, and then you pick up people who make even less sense hanging out with you. Granted, this is an Obsidian game and your companions will react a little differently depending on what you do. But you can also have created party members, who are a whole lot more creative than the game's selection
. Naturally, you'll want to have the people you can make, but they have no story at all to them. A bit of a mistep, I think, because you're playing as a player created character, player party members are in the game, but they can't think of a way to add some flavor to them, but saddle you with some cliche dudes who seem like they're there simply as a nod to Baldur's Gate. And all the Kickstarter generated content is really jarring, like you see a big cool knight, you talk to him, and hes got this 7 paragraph spread of amatuer writing by someone who paid money to have their story featured. Or you click a plaque on the wall, and there's a bunch of depressing memorials to real life people. That last part is kind of nice, but it takes you out of the game. Otherwise, the story has it's high points at the start, which you will get tired of if you have the inclination to make more than one character. Then it drops from one tail-chasing plot to another completely different one, and it's really hard to keep track of what's happening in addition to 5 hour plots that are actually side quests. UNSKIPPABLE OPENING where everything can only be done one way is not earning it any points. Also, there's a lot of write-ups on the game's places and races, and this is some fun reading, but at no time does the game world feel immersive over just a collection of unconnected generic fantasy stories.
As for the gameplay, the combat feels really floaty and unimpressive. The game looks gorgeous, but it also looks like an oil painting, and with limited armor sets and such, it's easy for your SIX PARTY MEMBERS to blend in to the background in and out of combat. I emphasize six party members, because to me that's way too many. I can keep track of the 4 parties with 16 members in The Last Remnant better than the blurr of six people with maybe one action skill between them (for non-casters) plowing through enemies. And the combat just gives too little feedback: There's very little flourish executed by individual party members, spells and contacts don't seem to have any weight to them; and there's usually too much happening on the screen to pay attention to all of it without pausing. I don't like to pause, so fights in the game are usually just "we killed them right away" or "they killed us right away, reload" and not much in-between. Maybe I'm playing it wrong and shouldn't max out my part so fast? But I've found small parties boring in this title. As far as character building goes, there's a lot of classes, but leveling is slow and not much happens in terms of power gains between levels. It reminds me more of Ultima Online than a modern scheme; just selecting a new spell here and there, pumping an attribute.
As many times as I've gone back and tried to play it again over years, it just doesn't do it for me. Maybe you'll like this if you're into Baldur's Gate and other games like that, and you don't mind all the camp of the Kickstarter back-patting. I'm sure I could like this format with the right presentation, but it just comes off as amatuerish. I was a bit taken in by the showering of praise leading up to the release of this title, and I'm sure plenty of others will also be taken by the Steam reviews. I'd say it's worth $10-20, though, just for the character creation and opening story elements. 30 hours of playtime isn't bad at all, even if I didn't enjoy some of it.

AN OLD SCHOOL CRPG'ER, WHO WASNT THAT MUCH INTO BALDUR'S GATE..
I'm gonna be honest here, I've had this game for a year or so...
Played 30 hours and put it aside.
So what am I doing here, why more than 30 hours, and why do I like this one if I diden't like BG ( good question)?!
1. Its the world; this isn't D&D, this isn't Forgotten realms, Dark Sun...etc etc..everything were used to when playing an Infinity engine game..no magic missles, no sleep, and no 18/00 + chars, maxed out and doing max damage..the skills and stats are way different, your never gonna heal up your party after each fight unless they never get hit, or you just rest all together ( yep, resting is an important mechanic that you're just gonna have to play the game to figure it out).
2. The wide and verying char classes; if I actually got into this part like it deserves, there probably wouldent be enough room, plus you guys would get cheated of the chance to slogg through this part yourselves (which is why we play good old rpg's in the first place, so there) suffice it to say, its dam good, its refreshing, and if you even remotly enjoy  actually role playing your chars, you're gonna have fun...you will be hooked, and remember, this aint D&D so time to relearn EVERYTHNG you were expecting, and GET A FREAKING DRUID, AND A HEALER ( they call them preists) because YOU WILL GET CHARMED, AND TURNED TO STONE..etc etc..with your awesome godlike fighter, who is only good at hitting things (go figure).
3. the graffics; I honestly don't remember BG looking this good.
Now I know this is a new game and all, they have the new "updated" BG, but this game looks damn pretty, sneaking through the hollowed halls of long forgotten temples as the torchlight flickers, watching the shadows waning in the twillight hunkerd down in a cops of trees awaiting the silver moonlight strands as the fireflies flutter about (because SOME OF US prefer to hunt at night). Everything looks just fine here, and some of the special abilities (usually being used against you) look fantastic, and will scare the living #### out of you when they go off.
4 DRAGON'S.
5. the writting and quests;.....oh man....I'm not gonna start..some of the decissions you have to make, but since you can do multiple playthroughs (and you will want to, this the good part). I can already tell my next playthrough is going to be completely different and I have yet to reach the second chapter..the choices...all this stuff right here should be enough of an endorsment, but if you're into instant gratitude, or charging through the story like some kinda super linguest, YOU ARE GOING TO MISS ALOT. This isnt the type of game you blaze through..turn off quest markers and give yourself a challenge, this is a thinking mans game, rarely are there straight foreward quests where you're just killing point B for point A..but you can if you want too I soppose.
6. the world.....yeah...its that good..
7. OH YEAH, THE SOUNDTRACK; So this game has a full orchestral soundtrack, its got the moody stuff, its got the happy stuff, and its got some of the best encounter music in any game. No lie folks (and I'm suprised more people don't point this out), look it up on YouTube. Everytime you have a fight (if you like orchestral soundtracks), its freakin bad a##, wether you live or die.
Its not constant in the "real world", but when it slips in and out it really does set the mood. It is quite capable, and draws you in if you like that kinda thing (which if you like D&D and you're looking at this game, I'm gonna say "yeah, you do"). this to me is important in this kinda game, and should be noted (I'm thinking if John Williams did a D&D movie right after The Empire Strikes Back, this is what it would sound like, so props to whoever did it), so good music-CHECK !
So the only real con I have found so far is sometimes the pathfinding seems kinda lost (only durring fights oddly enough). perhaps its because I'm trying to fit an 8ft tall chanter between my godlike fighter and my supple paladin ( I don't know, I have to playtest this further) but it comes up when your guys arent "forming that line" like you told them to, dosn't happend much (twice so far for me) but it was near doorways, or otherwise tight spaces so like I said "I have to check this out for myself".
Thats pretty much it...if you like taking your time, and figuring out all this cool stuff, looking at little dudes whacking forest trolls phantoms and demons or other dudes, with a deep tactical system, with spells swords and all that stuff, great writing, really pretty world..etc...etc..and theres dragons so yeah...I can recomend it..

Full disclosure, I played these games as a kid, so there's going to be an inherent bias compelling me to hit the "recommend button". With that said, I will give this the thumbs up with some caveats - these games haven't aged all that well.
The biggest issue they have is the combat. Combat hit detection either doesn't run as well on modern computers in spite of Dosbox tweaking, or it was never good. Given that these games were sort of the firsts that attempted what the did though this is sort of excusable - not to mention that the main draw of these games ISN'T the combat - the combat is just kind of a blight on the overall gameplay.
The normal gameplay is King's Quest or Space Quest Sierra style adventure gaming except with a twist. Death doesn't come as abruptly as it does in a typical King's Quest game, but it happens. Whether you like Sierra's style is up to you - just make sure you save often. The big twist to the Sierra style is that you can pick from 3 different classes that all have variant ways to approach each puzzle - which is genius for the genre. You can even allocate your stats at the beginning of the game to create a hybrid class, letting you choose puzzle solutions as you see fit.
Which brings me to the second biggest issue about these game's age - The "level up" system. The game expects you to use certain skills to solve puzzles, but since there are stats, if you don't have the appropriate level of skill it's time to grind! Grinding is so incredibly tedious that it would ruin the game if it were more necessary to complete it. Thankfully the stats aren't a huge issue until the 5th game.
A blessing and a bane of this series is the ability to import your character into the next game, carrying all of your stats forward. However, you're usually just better off starting a new character unless you've spent half an hour or an hour each game just clicking on random things to get your stats up, since your stats will probably be higher just starting with a premade. Nothing changes in the story from importing, with the exception of being able to play a special class in QFG3 and 4 - but that class is lame anyway because it's focused on combat, which I have already mentioned sucks (But it does have a cool exclusive quest in the 4th game.) My recommendation is to not bother importing in general, or to see how far you can get without grinding. But maybe you like grinding - I sure don't.
I wouldn't say that any of the games are skippable until the 5th one, but some are definitely better than others.
QUEST FOR GLORY 1 - A great starting point for the series and filled to the brim with all of the charm that made people fall in love with this series back in the day. The VGA remake is expertly crafted and while very short by today's standards is still a fun little romp down retro lane. While the characters improve immensely in QFG4, there's still a lot of fun to be had from the writing here.
QUEST FOR GLORY 2 - Maybe the most epic of the series, and has some of the best moments, but it also tried to play with the day/night system of the game making events happen only on certain days. The problem is that the game doesn't have enough content to keep you occupied every day you're playing, so you might find yourself sleeping for an entire playthrough once you already know what all the puzzle solutions are (And since this game has a class system, you will probably find yourself playing this more than once if you care.) There's a great remake available on the Internet but it doesn't really solve this particular issue and it's my biggest complaint about the game. Otherwise it has some of the most memorable parts of the series.
QUEST FOR GLORY 3 - Would be good, but this game feels like it's something EA pushed out for a deadline. It's full of glitches and problems, and overall feels unfinished. The story is basically on rails with even fewer sidequest options than QFG2. The poor thief has only one house to steal from and that's required to beat the game. The Wizard just has one simple quest that takes him to the same place the other three classes go to... I dunno. I like the African setting, I just feel like the game is broken in some way.
QUEST FOR GLORY 4 - The pinnacle of the series. After playing the first three games, this game feels like such a leap in production values and writing it's hard not to be impressed by the progress the series makes. It employs excellent voice acting to bring character to the NPCs that he series has never seen before. And the Combat... Still sucks... But at least they make an attempt to improve it! In my opinion playing the series and ending off with QFG4 is totally worth it - even if it has some 90s adventure game puzzles that make you go "Huh... Why??"
QUEST FOR GLORY 5 - I didn't actually play this one as a kid, so I went into it completely blind and... it's so bad I couldn't finish it. This game drains me. It's not fun to play or explore the game's world. They improved the combat by making it click to win like Diablo or something, but then they filled the game with it so that every class has to deal with monsters. Plus, they took the charming animated artstyle of QFG4 and made it look just plain bad. Someday I might get around to finishing this one to give it a proper review, but I feel no motivation to do so. It's an awful end to an otherwise great series.
Collection score overall: 3.5 out of 5

I picked this up the instant I realized it was released. I was a fan of the Strike Vector but despite that, I didn't play it all that much. I loved the basic gameplay of it but in the end I felt it lacked depth, and the player base died off quick as well.
I didn't read up on EX at all when I bought it. I went in totally blind, hoping for a real sequel with added depth and variety.
Unfortunately, EX is more of a remake of some sort. It's quite weird to be honest. They added a single player of some description but beyond that, there isn't much extra to it. They updated the visuals, removed the ability to equip two different main weapons and strangely, they remade the controls. The controls really threw me off. It's like they reveresed the logic of them. Standing still is now the default mode. You have to press extra buttons to go forward. I don't agree with this way at all, but I did eventually get used to it. And I rebound some buttons to make more sense to me, personally (I got it from a post from the actual devs... ). I really think this is a case of fixing something that wasn't broken. The old controls were tight as hell. They are forcing you to rethink it. It's possible and not a deal breaker maybe. Just...weird.
The single player has a very cringeworthy dialogue and throw-away story with scenarios with bots. I didn't hold my interest for many minutes. That was not what I got Strike Vector for and not what I wanted out of EX.
You can also play Skirmish with bots, and if that is what you wanted from Strike Vector, here you go. Perfect. But to me it feels pointless.
Multiplayer seem dead on arrival. I would have played at least a couple more hours just to experience the SV gameplay again, if only there were players active. I never see anyone playing the times I've gone online to check. It might be different for your time zone or whatever, but to see nobody playing a completely new game is unusual to me. Even a small game tend to have SOME people playing at all hours of the day at least. Even in servers with poor ping in relation to me.
In the end, I can't recommend this. Core gameplay is largely the same as SV, which is good. But I wish they made a proper sequel and not some kind of reimagining/remake/expansion thing. I'm quite confused by why they did this.

GWBW is no telltale game, you won't follow a linear path and have to choose every now and then who dies and who lives.
In this game, from the get go you are free to approach (nearly) every scenario the way you want, and granted, Gods Will Be Watching is often more about ressource management, dealing with unexpected small accidents and learning from your mistakes than making moral choices, but this moral aspect is still definitely present in the game, but in more subtle ways than in other games where that focus is entirely on giving you precise choices in precise situations.
And that's what everyone should know before buying this game: it's not about being thrown into a situation and picking which choice you think is right; it's about putting YOURSELF in a situation and having to get out of it by yourself with nothing but your brain and wits and, to some people's despair, luck (though good planning can greatly help you make it through poor luck runs).
Gods Will Be Watching is a game that not everyone will enjoy, but its characters, story, soundtrack and visuals are all VERY solid and i always felt proud for finishing a mission knowing what i did was all me, the good and the bad.

What is Long Live The Queen?
- A text-based choose-your-own-adventure style RPG.
What I liked about Long Live The Queen:
- Decently-long (1-2hr) branching story with many different possible endings.
- Large number of interesting skills which affect the story in surprising ways.
- Mood-management system adds satisfying level of complexity to training via boosts and negative modifiers.
- Visual feedback system for skillchecks helps hint at storyline branches and missed opportunities, ehancing replayability.
What I didn't like about Long Live The Queen:
- Game events proceed in the same sequence each time and only branch based on player actions - more randomization might have been fun.
- Hidden skillcheck levels and complex multi-tier skillchecks for certain encounters leads to a lot of trial-and-error to find successful combinations.
- The precise effects of the mood system on the skills bonuses must either be learned by trial-and-error or through the help of a third-party wiki/guide.
- Art and sound assets are fairly limited - a few characters do not even have profile pictures.
- The character art is highly anime-stylized - it would have been nice to see a wider range of facial characteristics to help differentiate characters from one another.
Overall:
I enjoyed the game enough to play it through several times. At first it felt fun to try different skill combinations and choose different story paths. However, eventually trial-and-error tedium took away some of the fun and I found myself resorting to using a wiki to figure out how to get the results I wanted. It would have been nice if the game gave the player more information, such as the skill levels required to pass certain checks and the precise effects of different moods. As a budget title this game is worthwhile, but be warned that it can also be frustrating.

This game rocks, but can be tiresome if you play it too long. Every day in this game is packed with new dialouge and new things to interact with, that I rushed through a lot of it on my first playthrough. I wish I had taken more breaks because I couldn't absorb the amount of new information that I was finding. On my second playthrough, I deliberatly limited myself to play one day in game before I went to bed. That way I could thourghly explore Possum Springs, and see everything I wanted to see.
The game's visuals and audio are almost flawless. The game plays smoothly, every environment looks polished, and the music sets the mood perfectly throughout the game. I came across one bug where part of Mae's body was in front of some fog that covered the rest of her body, but that was the only imersion breaking glitch I came across.
The dialouge is well written, but I had some issues with it. There are some grammatical errors that disrupted the flow of my reading. Some characters, like Mae's teacher, spoke in broken english, which forced me to read slower. Anyone whose read Jim's dialouge in "Huck Finn" might understand what I'm talking about. In games, I'm used to simple dialouge that I can just speed read to get the jist of conversations, but I can't do that in this game. However, when I played my 2nd time, I had an easier time understanding every character's dialouge.
I appreciated the wide variety of characters I could talk to. You could talk to a preacher, a homeless guy, a musician, a poet, and many others. Thanks to including a diverse set of characters, the game can cover a lot of themes like religion, coming of age, etc.
The gameplay usually fits the context of the narrative. When Mae has to shoplift, you take control of Mae's hand. When Mae builds a robot, you get to assemble it yourself. Gameplay helps amplify those mundane actions, and helps immerse you in the world. Also there is a rougelite game included that's actually pretty challenging.
Overall, A Night In The Woods was worth my time.  Some day, I plan on playing it a third and final time to experience the rest of what this game has to offer.

This is not my usual game to play. I had eventually gotten it on a whim between games and I was very pleasantly surprised at my own reaction.
I’m not exactly an avid gamer and I don’t intend to review any technical aspect of the game. The controls are simple, and that’s perfectly okay; the goal in this game isn’t to test your abilities. Night in the Woods is story that you get to experience and to that end the simplified controls allows you to focus on what is going on and not be distracted on how to get there. The visuals are also simple, but with stylistic integrity that reflects the care that was taken into making this game. Even with such fundamentally basic graphic design it manages to be beautiful and properly evoke the appropriate emotion in each scene. I have never found myself doing as many screen captures during a game as this one; so many scenes struck such a chord I wanted to see and feel them again later.
The story itself is engrossing and personal. I found myself caring about the characters and about the choices I made. I have only played through once but there are many paths to the end of the story to take and I’m looking forward to seeing what else could have been if I had made once choice instead of another, or if I had said one thing instead of something else. The greatest care I have seen the creators take in this game has been in the storytelling. The dialog gracefully swings between fun then poignant, serious then playful. Without digressing into the nitty gritty of it, the story is told from the perspective of a 20 year old young lady. Those of us who can still recall what that period in our lives was like will empathise with the character and their perspective throughout  the story.
This game is worth playing. I should more accurately state that this story is worth experiencing. The developers deserve a lot of credit for the creativity and dedication to detail that they displayed in creating this experience for us. I recommend it wholeheartedly.

Night in the Woods is one of the experiences you did like to go through and through again, just with no background memory.
It captures and masters one of the many elements I miss in many story-written games. The fleshed out personality and dialogue you have with all characters. You can interact to everybody multiple times, on a new day even more. It's like a little city full of people ready to tell their story what they did last night or 20 years ago. If it's tiring, you can skip the dialogue and go straight to the main story back. The protagonist's friends didn't see Mae in the long run. How they speak and hang out together is sweet to watch. The writing is shockingly relatable and describes problems many have to face in their daily life without us realising it.
The art style, being held that simple, is astounding well put together and very detailed which gives the whole game an extra flavour of personality.  The soundtrack is solid. It represents the situation and scenery very fitting.
The only thing I would criticise is the first part of the story. It stretches out a little with no real goal the player can look forward to. RPS did a really good job summarizing it than I could do better.

A lot of users have explained the good and bad of the base game, but I'd like to add in a review for the two DLCs, Breakdown and Lifeline.  I already poured in more than 20 hours into Breakdown alone just because it was designed as an infinite sandbox mode with increasing difficulties.  I have the characteristics of a completionist, so the long hours into the $6.99 DLC is self-explanatory as all Breakdown delivers is the sandbox mode many players have asked for.  All the scavenging and zombie destruction without any plot at all.  There's a leaderboard to encourage players to try and break into the top 100, 50, 10, whatever, but since there are methods to take advantage gathering points I lost all motivation to try and progress.  There's the incentive to unlock hero characters based on unlocking achievements, but I wasn't motivated enough to keep playing the game.
Lifeline, on the other hand, is what I would call a truly different game mode because it's more action and planning ahead vs. trying to get by.  Zombies will periodically attack your military base between the free times of saving civilians and soldiers.  The core gameplay is still the same with the scavenging, combat, and facility management, but you don't have to worry about resources as long as you can maintain a high influence count.  To my understanding, there is a basic plot with the army trying to find a cure to the zombie outbreak.  There's a leaderboard in Lifeline as well, but I feel more motivated to play through to the end and get a high score.

An average zombie apocalypse game. Not reccommended due to a lot of frustrating elements. It can be considered as a "community simulator". Read on if you like, this is a long review. Or skip to the end to see the short "TL;DR" version.
This game consists of permadeath (not a bad element), scavenging constantly, doing chores for everybody else in a bad manner (who the hell tries to make somebody happier by being rude?), automatic off-game progression (more on that soon below), bad AI, no variety and very linear gameplay/storyline.
It is not exactly survival, nor sandbox, as survival elements aren't challenging and the only real way to die is through unavoidable (most of the time) combat, or unfair glitches. It is not sandbox due to how the world is set, and there's no real variety into things you have to do: search a house, kill the zombies, scavenge, repeat until your character gets tired which lowers your stamina and then return to your base, to then switch to another survivor and repeat the process. Unless you're going to do a mission, but it's still very linear on that.
If you're actually reading this looking for something positive about this game, then these are the only pros I can mention:
- The world is decently big.
- Characters only really talk through voice, so there are little text dialogs. Although the Voice Acting is a bit lazy.
- Regular zombies do present a threat, but unfortunately due to bad design.
- It's a little addicting. Until you find out how this game breaks into nothingness due to the automatic progression.
- Soundtracks are okay.
Now for the worst parts of this game: The AI, automatic off-game progression, the Juggernaut (special zombie) and unfair glitches.
:
The AI for this game is
. If I had to rate it a number within 1 to 10, I'd rate it 2/10. This is because of the following reasons:
- Zombies are able to outrun you anytime they like, wether it's daytime or night (time/light doesn't matter), making running away a non-viable option for surviving combat.
- Survivor NPCs can decide to be OVERPOWERED, or straight out dumb at the most inappropiate times: A survivor can sometimes go up to a zombie and snap it's neck, exploding it's head in the process, somehow. Or a survivor can be stuck kicking a zombie repeatedly and forever, until you go up to the zombie to attempt to kill it and THEN they'll kill the zombie. Or well, you could need a survivor to not mess up while fighting something like a Juggernaut (more on that special zombie soon below), but they end up letting the zombie kill them.
- Survivor NPCs don't know how to avoid a zombie horde, grabbing it's attention and dying in the process IF you don't go help them.
- The pathfinding overral is crappy.
:
This is a mechanic that is in little games for a reason. This mechanic consists of letting the game world progress on it's own while you're not playing the game. Changes take place as soon as you load your game, and it'll compare the exact time you stopped playing and it'll take the current time, and then speed up the world with that time difference. After 3 days, the changes are smaller.
Now, are you assuming this is a nice feature and concept? Well, it sounds like it is, but it isn't. Atleast, it wasn't executed properly for this game. The problem with this feature for this game is that the game becomes unplayable after a certain amount of time. Look at my logged hours as playtime. It took me approximatelly 20 hours of playtime before the game started being straight out unplayable due to lack of resources WHICH were wasted by the survivors at my base while I was either at university, sleeping, eating or
.
Survivors use up Building Materials like if it was food, except there's the Food resource. And food is EVERYWHERE. The world is
with food, but your survivors use it very, very slowly, not to mention there's so much food that you'll be leaving it behind constantly. You need building materials if you want to move out into a new base, which is necessary later in the game due to where you're living might be out of resources by then, but your survivors waste it
in less than a day. Overral, this whole mechanic BREAKS your playthrough after enough time. You have to rush the storyline missions if you want it to not "break" on you.
:
A Juggernaut is a special zombie in this game, out of a total of 4 special zombies, the other 3 being: Screamers, Ferals and SWAT zombies. They're all balanced (although Ferals can be annoying sometimes too). But that is not the case for Juggernauts.
Have you played Left 4 Dead 2? If you did, think of the Juggernaut as the Tank in L4D2. Now mix that with a Charger's speed. And now mix that with a Witch's power, health and overral danger. Unthinkable, right? Well, this game has that huge mix-up: the Juggernaut. Also called Big Un in-game.
If you did not play Left 4 Dead 2, just think of a fat and tall zombie that can charge at you at insane speeds and simply kill you with ease.
Why is this zombie unbalanced? It's because of one of the attacks in it's moveset, consisting of:
*A grab, which goes into 1 of 2 forms.
- 1st Form: The zombie grabs it's victim and bites it, doing normal damage and then throwing the victim to the ground.
- 2nd Form: The zombie grabs it's victim and then... *Spoiler text: do not read if you have a weak stomach.*
Confronting this zombie most likely means you or a Survivor NPC dying before the battle ends.
:
Now, I'm just going to name *one* glitch that really messed up my entire playthrough. First things first, I was going up a radio tower in order to survey the area to search for important things, all good. Then I proceed to go to the ladder to go back down, but then the worst possible thing happens: My character RUNS OFF the edge and dies off the fall. I would have been okay dying due to careless-ness and that kind of stuff, but my very first death in the game was because of a really bad glitch. After that, it became a necessity to crouch and slowly approach the ladder before going down the tower, making it look like all of my survivors suffer from fear of heights and are scared of falling off the edge. Like my first character did.
TL;DR: This game is below average, and very unbalanced. It's storyline is linear and there is no actual sandbox feeling and survival just depends on your skill or luck. The AI is really bad and the special zombie called Juggernaut can kill atleast one of your survivors very easily and inevitably. The glitches in this game are really frustrating, to the point it can ruin your entire playthrough. Buy at your own
.

is an astonishing role playing game featuring the classic, old-school gameplay. The story begins in The Eastern Reach, a region suffering from wars, poverty and, as it turns out, the Waidwen's Legacy - a disease refering to children born without souls. The majority believes that the ones responsible for this illness are animancers - people who study and experiment with souls, there are also some who claim the Waidwen's Legacy is a punishment from gods. Find out for yourself what the truth is!
If you have ever played games like
,
or
, you'll recognise the gameplay. It's an isometric game in which you control a party of up to 6 characters. Most of the possible companions can be easily found in the diverse, semi-open (travelling is allowed only between certain locations) universe your main character ventures through, whilst accomplishing challenging tasks. Due to nature of the real time combat, it is crucial to think strategically and use enemies' weak points to your advantage.
provides one of the best plots I have ever experienced in a role playing game. Every element of the world is thought through and advancment of main story is slow enough to do interesting and original side quests. Furthermore, most of the decisions you take during your adventure influence how other characters percieve you. For example, if you choose to use brutal, barbarian force and threaten people to achieve your goal, you will get the "Aggresive'" trait, whereas when you are friendly, kind and generous, you are likely to get the "Benevolent" trait. Estimated play time with most of quests done but without DLCs' content is about 50 hours.
Wonderful, oldschool graphics alongside with gorgeous music create unique atmosphere encouraging you to venture further and further, to explore every nook and cranny. Harmonious, orchestral music acommpanies you while admiring varied, beautiful locations made by extremely skilled artists. And a simplistic and intuitive user interface fits perfectly, making the whole experience unbelievably pleasant.
Another amazing aspect of
is a fortress - later in the game you are given an old, ruined castle which can be rebuilt to gain special bonuses. Apart from being a badass shelter it gives the possibility to take prisoners or interact with occasionaly visting guests. It also provides special tasks which can give fame, powerful items and money. In addition, it lets you manage companions. When you need room for a new person, simply leave the other character in the stronghold - brilliant!
Despite over 50 hours of the gameplay
simply lacks diversity in a few aspects. First of all, combat is extremely repetitive and most of enemies are copies of the same creature but with changed colours or statistics. Furthermore, classes have no specialisations, which results in an arguably low variety of party setups. Also, most of items are very similar to each other both visually and mechanically, especially the ones found in shops. Overall, low variety isn't a major problem, but leaves a feeling that something is missing in the game.
took some ideas from here and there and created its own, unique combat system. To begin with, I have to admit that the endurance & injuries system and the enemies' weaknesses are really well done. In particular the fact that once a character is knocked down, he recevies penalty to some statistics untill the next rest and after every combat he automatically revives himself (unless he was knocked down several times and died).
Sadly, other mechanics leave a lot to be desired and could be easily improved. Firstly, there are almost no actions which can be taken before the battle and there is no time to take them while fighting. Potions, protective spells and special abilities are only enabled in combat mode. Imagine a companion being flanked by 5 enemies trying to drink a potion while being constantly interrupted by them - a waste of time and, in most cases, the life of the character.
There are also stealth and disengage mechanics. The second one indicates that when a companion tries to run away from the enemy focusing him, he receives instant damage. The problem is, he's likely to be further followed by that enemy. Wouldn't it be smart to hide then? Well, no - because of how the stealth works. You just can't hide from enemies in combat, probably because developers didn't want the player to "cheat" with the endurance system described above. So why not make that system a little bit different? For example characters knocked down only being able to be revived by other party members - that would be a much better out-of-combat mechanic.
In this paragraph I've decided to place some aspects which were too small to be included as distinct parts.
•
extremely resembles
/
series - in spells, locations and mechanics. To see minor differences check out
comment, made by
on
. In my opinion it's pretty accurate.
• The developers included a commentatory of the game, describing the process of creating certain locations or events. This can be turned on in options if you would like to listen to them while venturing forth.
• The game traded some important RPG elements for easier gameplay, such as infinite stash or no items' weight. That's why for all players experienced whith this type of game I would recommend using at least hard difficulty.
To conclude,
is a magnificent example of an old-school role playing game. Congratulations to developers for their success in creating great adventure experience and providing hours of fun. I'm looking forward to playing the upcoming sequel of the series and I hope the negative aspects will be less noticable in future creations of
studio. I strongly recommend this game to anybody looking for intense gameplay, and especially to people who never tried any isometric cRPG before.

Resident Evil 0 was in development hell since around the mid 90's, where it was planned for an N64 release but constantly delayed due to issues in storage inherent with 64MB cartridges. The game's development was moved onto the NGC and  finally saw release in 2002, and in 2016 an HD Remaster was brought out which fortunately made its way to PC. Let's get one thing out of the way: this is a true HD Remaster; you can easily google comparison shots. Short story: this isn't just upscaling-it really does look much better than the previous version. Reason being that they pre-render shots for these classic RE titles, and the assets they had beforehand were actually really high quality and 'downscaled' to Gamecube hardware. So here we're getting a bit more of how it originally looked before being filtered down.
I start with a bit of a history lesson for some context: this is basically old Capcom. This is an RE title from the same Capcom that was at its zenith in the late 90's to mid 2000's. If you enjoyed the RE titles pre-4 (not that 4 was bad or anything) then this is more of the same in similar quality. This game was born in a specific time-period whereby quality was of a particular level.
RE0, as you may have guessed, is a prologue to RE1. It's plot concerns the same cast of characters within Racoon City, and if you like your RE lore you'll enjoy this, albeit there's nothing incredible nor is there a huge revelation here. Rebecca is the star here, along with Billy, an escaped convict. Can't say I'm particularly satisfied with the plot since there was no underground lab as there was in RE1, or family members turned into monsters. There's nothing particularly gripping in the plot, and it all seems to end rather abruptly, but it still holds well as a stand-alone tale. Just don't expect anything amazing.
The game itself is more of what you'd expect: pre-rendered backgrounds and fixed camera angles with, lets face it, god-awful combat. There's nothing worse than moving back a bit and the camera angle switching because of it. RE has never been a series known for its combat, the challenge is in exploring the map and solving puzzles. The tension is in the cinematic camera angles and not knowing whether the next room has an enemy. The fun is in managing your inventory space and running low on ammo. But the fun in RE titles and its are of specialization has never been in its shooting mechanics. Luckily, the game has a button assigned for auto targetting-one push and you automatically target an enemy on the screen. This saves the whole thing: you don't have to worry about losing your target and being impeded in any way by the fixed angles. You get to keep a unique feature and alleviate its short-comings-problem solved.
The partner system is unique and changes things up a bit; ultimately your partner character is really just more storage slots for items when you're together, but you are often seperated and have to work things out until you can meet up once more. It's different, it's not ground-breaking, but it adds some interest to an otherwise similar approach to the formula. You can also drop items on the floor and return to pick them up; gone are those magic boxes that store all of your items. Personally I'm not for it, since you wind up having to backtrack if you leave something important far behind (protip: always keep the grappling hook nearby until you activate the cable car). You wind up leaving items in save rooms anyway so I'm not for it, but it does allow you to just drop an item then and there if you need to pick something else up. It's an interesting idea, but one that needs a bit more refining.
All in all I can't complain; this is from classic Capcom and it shows. It also shows that this is a prologue game that doesn't build too much, but this is also from Capcom's peak so even that is fantastic. Strongly recommended if you loved old RE. Waiting on remakes of RE2 and RE3, Capcom.

Makes a startlingly good first impression, and it's pretty good value for your money. If your value your time more than your money, though, I can't recommend Dead Effect. Everything about it is perfectly serviceable, and kind of impressive for what appears to be a budget game, but it doesn't do anything particularly well. There's a lot to it - a story mode (complete with some of the most endearingly bad voice-acting I've ever heard), different survival modes, and a decent variety of weapons/equipment you can unlock with in-game currency that you grind out in the various modes.
Basically, for everything that Dead Effect does, there's another game that does that thing better. Dead Space, Killing Floor, maybe Doom? All of those are going to be more rewarding. Dead Effect is mediocre in the purest sense of the word - it's not bad, but it's not good, either.
SUMMARY: Good value for your money, but your time would be better spent elsewhere.

At first glance, Dead Effect looks like it has a little something new to offer.. Once getting into it, you realise you were lied to.
Being a formerly free-to-play mobile game, (Personally believe it should have stayed that way), the only major thing I can give it credit for is that it doesn't really look like it.
The plot leaves a lot to be desired with the usual zombie story-line of 'wake up in zombie apocalypse', except they thought of a nice new little twist of putting it in space on some space station or space ship, this really isn't explained. After first having stepped out of your cryo-chamber you are handed a stun-gun straight off the bat shredding any chance of the decently eerie and 'horror-ish' element developing.
I might add that you are also infected! Can I get an 'Uh Huh' from my Resident Evil (Movie) fans out there?
That aside you continue on your merry way to find more to add to your arsenal of over-powered typical zombie/shooter game weapons. Another complaint lies with the fact that in every single description of these weapons, the words 'destructive' and 'accurate' are tossed about like it's special or something. Weapons are generally designed to be both of those things, throwing those words into every single description does not make your weapon stand out from anything else, it just ends up being repetitive and quite frankly irritating, like the rest of the game.
Following through the repetitive dark corridors, waves of zombies, a 'special' suit, diary entries, detached guiding voices which happen to pop out of nowhere, slow motions bullet time and the cherry on the cake is the even more un-original names for the two characters you are given to choose from - Jane Grey - (Might as well be Jane Doe) and Gunnar Davis… I was half expecting a tower defence segment to be tossed in with the rest of the re-hashed, overly used un-original and typical ideas.
This game I swear just picked up a book of "How to design a zombie game using almost every cliche".
They even manage to stuff up the sounds for the female character, her dialog is female but all the voice effects for eg. grunting, panting, groaning, are male. This merely adds onto the quite poor voice acting which could have been completely over-looked as it had decent sound effects for the weapons, decent graphics, zombie models and a semi-storyline. Something that doesn't seem to be that common in zombie games now, as a lot seem to lean towards the; point A to point B, survive zombie waves rinse and repeat kind of thing.
One final thing that bothers me immensely is the sodding music. Basically; -Take Inception noise, put on repeat, make super loud and.. Done!- No, no, no, no... No.
I really did have hopes for this game, but for anything more than a dollar or two, I wouldn't really waste your time on this little number as it's the usual drenched up, repetitive and just downright annoying game-play with the only challenges being - Having the effort to play through it entirely, and dealing with the 'boss' zombies (Basically a Boomer from Left 4 Dead 1&2) hurling bombs at you when you have no jumping ability and nothing but dark, dank corridors to navigate around.

I liked it. It was exactly as the reviews said, far too easy, after a few days to finish the campaign I couldn't be bothered to do the DLC. It has all the problems of both Skyrim and Batman: Arkham Asylum. The last boss is one of the worst in any game because the game mechanics aren't suited to boss fights. The lore is ropey because Tolkein is ropey (check out "Epic Pooh" by William Gibson). The background music is random ponderous orchestra. And I'm sick of playing any game with orcs and health points. But it has a fun game mechanic that is executed really really tightly. For example, when you finish taking over an orc's brain you sort of boot them over onto the floor; do this on top of a building and the orc will fall off the building - the little animation sequence isn't just window-dressing, the game keeps track of where the booted orc is. But there is one main reason above all others I played it to the end and had fun...
Cockney orcs!
It sounded just like when I was little, really took me back. You go to London now, that accent is gone because we've all left apart from the OAPs. After 20-30 hours of listening to orcs bantering (which they do constantly), the recorded voiceover lines had only repeated a handful of times - the game must have thousands of them. Often they are absolutely splendid.
Tolkein was criticised for racism, he said in a letter that orcs look like "the least-lovely Mongol types". Well, now they're originally from Putney. They play an escapist fantasy where no amount of liberal elite, matriarchial, new-age mumbo-jumbo spouting elves can relocate us all to other counties and steal all the school places. In another 50 years, Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor is all that'll be left of us. Tourists to London will rotate old bus tickets to "find the memory point", but our sense of humour and our dropped aitches will be forever preserved in over 1000 lines of orc voiceover. "What we need is some rain and lightnin'. Then those pinkskins'd 'ave somethin' to cry about. (Uvver than the torture and starvation.)"
Buy it on sale and don't bother with the sidequests. Or the ending.

I was really excited to play this game. I thought the original Gods Will Be Watching - an experimental flash game featured online - was a brilliant little invention that inspired feelings of care and responsibility in the collection of pixelized figures you were meant to save. The idea that Sergeant Burden - the character you play - had a lifetime of making difficult decisions in a lifetime of leadership and servitude made for a potentially amazing game.
Unfortunately, the game I imagined turned out to be better than the game that was gifted to me.
Instead, the scenarios are tied together with an overwrought, uninteresting plot and cast of characters. The dialogue, which was merely serviceable in the original, fails in the attempt to carry the action from one plot point to the next. In its attempt to impose a story and a plot, Gods Will Be Watching loses a great deal of what made it interesting - the ability of a player to impose meaning on his or her own experience. (A great example being in games like Half-Life, where the player does not speak - allowing players to fill in the blanks with their own reactions.)
I wanted a game that presented me difficult situations devoid of context. I wanted to imagine a Sergeant Burden that would have lived this life, instead of being told who exactly I was playing. Maybe that was too much to ask, artisticly, but I think the game developer put too much of his own ideas in when he got his big break.
Also, the torture part is just too much for me. I don't enjoy playing through it. I accepted the "standard" difficulty and it is just an utterly punishing segment. Maybe it succeeded in its intention, but after hours of attempts I just gave up. It killed my interest in wanting to progress further.

The graphics may look frilly, but it's nice to look at it for long times - considering that you'll spend most of your game time looking at the skill-review screen to decide what to learn. The concept is good, and so is the plot; pretty much everyone could be planning your death, and most of the time you won't even know what you will be facing. The storyline also manages to surprise with sudden twists, so every skill may come handy.  I have already achieved two different endings, but I'll definetly play more to discover new ones.
Moreover, after dying many times, you kinda feel good for the main character when finally you get to the ending xD I figure that once familiar with the mechanics and once used to save and load at specific points of the story, breaking through the endings is surely easier, but that's not a downside, actually.

This game rocks, but can be tiresome if you play it too long. Every day in this game is packed with new dialouge and new things to interact with, that I rushed through a lot of it on my first playthrough. I wish I had taken more breaks because I couldn't absorb the amount of new information that I was finding. On my second playthrough, I deliberatly limited myself to play one day in game before I went to bed. That way I could thourghly explore Possum Springs, and see everything I wanted to see.
The game's visuals and audio are almost flawless. The game plays smoothly, every environment looks polished, and the music sets the mood perfectly throughout the game. I came across one bug where part of Mae's body was in front of some fog that covered the rest of her body, but that was the only imersion breaking glitch I came across.
The dialouge is well written, but I had some issues with it. There are some grammatical errors that disrupted the flow of my reading. Some characters, like Mae's teacher, spoke in broken english, which forced me to read slower. Anyone whose read Jim's dialouge in "Huck Finn" might understand what I'm talking about. In games, I'm used to simple dialouge that I can just speed read to get the jist of conversations, but I can't do that in this game. However, when I played my 2nd time, I had an easier time understanding every character's dialouge.
I appreciated the wide variety of characters I could talk to. You could talk to a preacher, a homeless guy, a musician, a poet, and many others. Thanks to including a diverse set of characters, the game can cover a lot of themes like religion, coming of age, etc.
The gameplay usually fits the context of the narrative. When Mae has to shoplift, you take control of Mae's hand. When Mae builds a robot, you get to assemble it yourself. Gameplay helps amplify those mundane actions, and helps immerse you in the world. Also there is a rougelite game included that's actually pretty challenging.
Overall, A Night In The Woods was worth my time.  Some day, I plan on playing it a third and final time to experience the rest of what this game has to offer.

This is not my usual game to play. I had eventually gotten it on a whim between games and I was very pleasantly surprised at my own reaction.
I’m not exactly an avid gamer and I don’t intend to review any technical aspect of the game. The controls are simple, and that’s perfectly okay; the goal in this game isn’t to test your abilities. Night in the Woods is story that you get to experience and to that end the simplified controls allows you to focus on what is going on and not be distracted on how to get there. The visuals are also simple, but with stylistic integrity that reflects the care that was taken into making this game. Even with such fundamentally basic graphic design it manages to be beautiful and properly evoke the appropriate emotion in each scene. I have never found myself doing as many screen captures during a game as this one; so many scenes struck such a chord I wanted to see and feel them again later.
The story itself is engrossing and personal. I found myself caring about the characters and about the choices I made. I have only played through once but there are many paths to the end of the story to take and I’m looking forward to seeing what else could have been if I had made once choice instead of another, or if I had said one thing instead of something else. The greatest care I have seen the creators take in this game has been in the storytelling. The dialog gracefully swings between fun then poignant, serious then playful. Without digressing into the nitty gritty of it, the story is told from the perspective of a 20 year old young lady. Those of us who can still recall what that period in our lives was like will empathise with the character and their perspective throughout  the story.
This game is worth playing. I should more accurately state that this story is worth experiencing. The developers deserve a lot of credit for the creativity and dedication to detail that they displayed in creating this experience for us. I recommend it wholeheartedly.

Night in the Woods is one of the experiences you did like to go through and through again, just with no background memory.

"I think here the aimlessness, the lack of a sense of direction, or understanding about where it might be going, is a lot of the point. It reflects Mae’s state of mind, if being a lot less erratic and haphazard than in her head."
