Flix the Flea is the first game that I have permanently removed from my Game Library....
It’s one thing a game being simple; look at Tetris, a game widely regarded as one of the greatest games of all time. However, Tetris’ simple gameplay belies difficulty scaling, amazing music and an addictive streak that borders on brutal. Flix the Flea has none of these things and is essentially an 8 bit game dressed up to look appealing and run more smoothly (Bugaboo the Flea, which in fairness the developer freely discusses). I admit, watching the gameplay videos I almost feel a pang of regret no longer having access to the game. But then I remember.....I remember the jumping mechanic (I really wish Flix could walk a little), the unappealing objective of jumping to the top of the levels, and the slightly bizarre miniature pterodactyl. Because that’s essentially the long and the short of it, charge jump, pray you land ok, repeat. It’d be wonderful to elucidate on other features or challenges (yes you can collect things, no it doesn’t make the game more fun), but that’s basically it.
If the idea of holding down one key or another to charge a jump sounds infinitely repeatable, fun and challenging then this is the game for you. Otherwise, if you’re looking at owning a Psychotic Software game, then pick the other one (Power Up), which is a lot more fun.
I'd probably have enjoyed it more if it was called Flix the Pea though...
Not worth your time.

If you've not played Dark Souls, chances are you're missing out on one of the best gaming experiences of your life. From its satisfying combat mechanics, to its uniquely interesting world, to the subtle way the really quite deep storyline is implemented and coexists with the gameplay, Dark Souls is as much an experience as it is a game.
It's no secret that Dark Souls is known to be very difficult, a fact that probably deters more people than it attracts. As much as I enjoy the level of challenge the game presents, it's not as monstrously hard as many seem to believe. A big part of what makes the game difficult is the fact that it doesn't hold your hand. There's still room for error, as I can't think of a single boss fight where one small mistake is sure to be the end of you. That being said, yes, it's harder than most games that are being released today, but unless you can't enjoy a game where mashing your attack button is almost always the answer to any given situation, chances are you'll get a lot out of Dark Souls.
I'm personally not a big fan of the game's PvP elements, largely thanks to the fact that if you're invaded, it's probably going to be by someone who has a character specifically prepared for it, whereas you probably won't. It's never been a massive issue however, and if you really want it gone you can always play the game in offline mode.
Another thing to note is that the game isn't well suited to play with keyboard and mouse, so a controller is basically a must if you're to get a good experience out of the game.
At the end of the day, I'd recommend this game to just about everyone, and if they complain it's too hard, I'd recommend it some more. I'm a little bit jealous of everyone who have their first playthrough of Dark Souls still ahead of them.

Most arcady flying combat simulators are dull. Not this one.
One of the biggest advantages of Strike Vector is that you fly across all kinds of debris, corridors or tight corners, surrounded by beautiful cyberpunk scenery. It’s never an empty space. When you get inside the cockpit of a vector it immediately becomes apparent how agile it is. You can dodge shots, change directions instantly and unleash a barrage of death on anyone that gets in your way. Vector is a sci-fi interceptor  of the future.
Original Strike Vector got it’s needed reboot for many reasons. Mainly because of incredibly high difficulty ceiling. Developers made an effort to split the playerbase based on their skill levels, as well as incorporating bots to make sure servers always have opponents to fight. Some game mechanics were reworked for controller support and now you can actually play this game from the couch.
It doesn’t get any easier than this. Strike Vector EX is still a brutal shooting experience where you will get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked, unless you’re willing to learn. Fortunately this game has one of the best fan communities on the market. People that shoot you out of the sky faster than you can spit are delightful to chat to, will give you hints and even cut some slack, if you’re new. Join Strike Vector Discord, and you will see how dedicated this community is. One of the biggest strengths of this game, is people who play it, and if you’ll devote some time into learning the basics, you’ll see how important that is.

But to all the people having issues with Uplay and not being able to even launch the game, this is what I did. Manually downloaded the Uplay client outside of Steam. Run it in windows 7 compatibility mode, and as administrator. Install and then log into your Uplay account. Go to Steam, right click the game, view CD key and click copy to clipboard. Go back to the Uplay client and click the key icon on the top right side. CTRL+V to paste your key and click activate. is one of my top video game picks of 2014. It is a turn-based "point-and-click moral puzzler" set against a futuristic sci-fi / bioterrorism setting. I just finished it (rare for me to actually finish a game these days), clocking in at around 13 hours. It is great and you should play it and here's why.
Firstly, what is this game about? It's hard to describe what genre it is in. UI-wise, it's a point-and-click puzzler, but it doesn't work like normal puzzle games. It's divided into six scenarios, and each has totally different mechanics. You give orders to your guys, and each order typically takes some unit of time, so you have to prioritize which actions to take (although some scenarios let you do actions in parallel). Do you execute a hostage to keep the others in line? Do you free a hostage in exchange for more time? It essentially comes down to juggling a set of variables, and if any of them drops below a threshold, you die. There are always a couple of different valid approaches to each problem.
For example, in the first scenario, you take hostages while your team attempts to hack into a research station. You're barricaded in and the police are slowly marching in. You need to keep the hostages in line (calm so they don't make a run for it, but not too calm that they try to take you down), negotiate to keep the police a safe distance away, increase your hacking rate, and keep your hacker from being locked out of the system. Fail to attend to any of these duties for too long, and you're hosed.
This game is very hard. You'll often try each scenario a dozen or more times before you finally succeed. (It has easy mode settings, but it begs you not to use them or you'll spoil the fun.) And that's the whole fun of it: experimenting with the various controls in each scenario and learning the mechanics by observing the results. After a few scenarios, you'll have a general sense for how to be good at
, but you won't have a clue how to tackle the next scenario. There's also a strong luck component involved, and this is important: you can't win just by memorizing a sequence of actions or by trial and error. You must understand the mechanics so well that you can maximize your probability of success. Once you've "cracked" a scenario, you can beat the random number generator and can win it in 2 or 3 tries. (In this sense, the game feels a bit like
.)
The 8-bit graphics are 8-bit style are drawn and animated nicely; the music is splendid. The story is epic and well worth following (though it is extremely complicated and involves reading huge walls of text). It also features extremely graphic violence, as well as some bad gender stereotyping (the few women in the game are all "nurturing" type characters). The tough question for me is: is the game really about moral choices? On the one hand, you can just treat each scenario as an optimization problem, with each character being just a resource to be used up. But it's also hard not to feel an attachment to the characters and want to keep them all alive. The one critical flaw in the moral choices is that
. That tends to devalue the characters' lives in each scenario. But I'll admit, it would be pretty hard to design a story so dynamic when most characters can potentially die on most missions.
is, at its core, a deeply mechanics-based game that rewards experimentation, observation, and understanding. You can play the original "survival" prototype
, but be aware that this version is severely unpolished compared to the final game (the prototype scenario is in the final game and much improved). And remember... GODS WILL BE WATCHING!

I don't have a way of knowing an exact number, but if I had to guess, I'd say at least 40 to 50% of Steam users will absolutely hate this game.
Some people are calling it a visual novel and honestly... it's really not. Visual novels are marked by a very distinct style of play (the typical POV directly conversing with characters) as well as (9 times out of 10) branching storylines. Night in the Woods contains neither that play style nor a branching story. There are choices you can make as to what scenes you will see, but ultimately the main story is, to my knowledge, completely linear.
Honestly, to that end it's hard for me to call Night in the Woods a "game" per se. "An experience" sounds about as pretentious a term as they come, but it's hard for me to decide what else to call it. There are platforming elements, but they aren't really the main driving force of the game.
What IS the main driving force of the game, is its story and visuals. And oh my god, this is one of the prettiest games I've ever seen. The art style might not appeal to everyone. There are those who will not care for it. Those people can suck it. I'm sorry; everyone's entitled to their opinion, but I'm not budging on this one. Night in the Woods is a fantastically gorgeous game and I will hear no argument to the contrary.
As for the story... well, it's a mixed bag. For my money, I loved the story. I found the overal experience very, VERY relatable and even felt close to tears at some points of it (I'm a softy; bite me). That said, there are those who have pointed out that the entire game is written in a certain style and... well yes. While the characters themselves are distinctive and have individual personalities, there are times in the game where it feels almost like it's one person talking to him/herself. But in spite of that, the heart and soul of the game manages to brightly shine through and it's a funny, enjoyable, and heartfelt experience.
For me, this game is an easy 4.5/5. Not perfect, but more than worth the money. I'm the kind of person who will probably play through it again at some point. But it's not going to be for everyone. If you're unsure, wait for it to go on sale. Otherwise, I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

FYI this is my first review on Steam.
TL;DR - it's surpisingly amazing, don't shun it becase it's a zombie survival game. It doesn't represent the DayZ side of the genre, it represents what it should have been.
Honestly, this game was one of the most surprising purchases I have ever made on Steam, and especially within early access.
Of course it is yet another zombie survival game in early access, but so many things about this game makes it so much more than that, and there are some things you can't pinpoint as to why that is.
But there are some things you can pinpoint, and here they are:
- The world in this game is so fully realised. DayZ doesn't even close to the atmosphere the environement and surroundings give off in this game. You really feel like you're in a lived in, overgrown and desicrated post-apocalyptic island. The Cities are vast, the countriside is beautiful, yet all of it has this sad and alluring aura because it feels and looks like a place people actually lived in.
- This game has enough depth in it to be interesting and realistic, yet it doesn't throw you into the deep end with it. These complex mechanics and interesting details are there for you to discover, but not necessary. The game is well balanced, you will find food and drink easily, and you will find yourself a weapon with relative ease. This for me is what DayZ is missing. This game manages to nail that accessibility mixed with complexity without scaring off the player or just being too damn hard.
- My player interaction has been fantastic. The community is great so far, having met a number of friendly players and a number of bandits. There's a good mix here, and what I LOVE, is the whistle feature, where you can whistle as an emote to other players. It's made some really interesting events, and I've used it to lure out bandits before.
- The game runs like a DREAM. For an early access game it is extremely impressive, with no difference in framerate if i'm in the biggest cities or an open field. It's always buttery smooth.
Any problems with the game?
- the only thing that bugs me at the moment is that the footstep sounds are a little off, sometimes you'll think there is someone walking right next to you when there's no one there, it's led to some serious paranoria.
I could go on and on. But honestly I have had more fun in the 7 hours that flew by in this so far than I did in the 40 odd hours I spent jogging around searching for one can of beans in DayZ. For me, this game is what zombie survival games should be like, and I think it's worth giving it a shot, because this doesn't represent the tired genre at all, and it deserves a chance.
One last thing, if you want an example of the kind of atmosphere i'm talking about, here's a story: I was in the largest city at night for the first time, thunderstruck by the size of the buildings and the density of it. I found a hotel that I wondered into, because there were lights coming from it and a loud noise. This was the first time i'd seen electricity running in the game. So I wondered in and discovered a player had turned on the generator operting the lights of the building, and the elavator was working. So I took the elavator up to the 9th floor, checking corners and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ myself thinking i was about to get jumped on. I cleared the 9th floor and thought it was odd that no one was there. All of a sudden the lights shut off, and I was plunged into literal pitch black; someone had turned off the generator.. I whipped out my torch and flickered it on and off to see where i was without drawing too much attention. ... I got out alive in the end, but needed new trousers and underwear...
Good game :)

Okay, yeah, you know what, there's a massive issue when you prefer Games for Windows Live...
Okay sure, it's a fun fighting game for all players, young, old, beginner or master and it's easy to learn with a different variety of characters, costumes, colours, stages and moves... But what's not fun is getting absolutely destroyed because of the online of this game.
Steam has completely ruined online for this game, it jitters constantly which slows the game down and makes it literally impossible to do a special move, but then what happens? It's A-Okay! Finally the lag is over!.... For 5 seconds then proceeds to jitter more, I don't know if this is just the netcode, my internet connection (which is perfect, I have no issues on any other version on this game), or my computer (which is a beast and runs anything I make it run on the highest graphics possible) but it's seriously broken, like, actually broken.
On the other hand, some say that the netcode is fine with no issues, but these people who have told me that the netcode is fine have over 40mbps download and 10mbps upload speeds (no surprise there is there.) So what about the people who can't get fibre optic connectivity? We just can't play, at all.
Games for Windows Live was a GODSEND compared to this broken hunk of junk, GFWL is active on multiple games *cough* Street Fighter x Tekken *cough* UMK3 *cough* so why can't we bring it back? It was infinitely better than this, sure we sometimes got some problems with connections, but that was mainly down to a persons internet speeds and connectivity, NOT broken netcode... I seriously pray for Games for Windows Live to make a return, at least that worked correctly!
In conclusion, I recommend it for people who want a fun OFFLINE fighting game, or for people who want to practice without the need of a console, but unless you have very fast internet speeds, I wouldn't recommend investing time going into Ranked Mode.
TL;DR: Broken netcode, not fun, dropping combos, fun game offline for the whole family, praying for GFWL to come back, not recommended online, recommended for offline use.

Years before Elder Scrolls would take the adventure/rpg world by storm, and right smack in the middle of the point-and-click adventure boom, Heroe's Quest (Quest for Glory 1) was released.  Decades later I still think fondly of my time spent in its world, and the discovery of my love for the rpg genre in a time when I often had to chose between puzzle or action games.
While the focus is more on exploration, problem solving, and story-telling, the rpg component augments these aspects.  Depending on the class you play as, obstacles may be overcome in different ways. This not on contributes to the immersion but also to the way the story is told.
One of the coolest features of the series as a whole, is the ability to save your character after you complete a game and import them into the next.

Full disclosure... This review is instigated and inspired by the 2016 Steam Awards.
There I was going through my library of hundreds and hundreds of games taking this whole Awards thing far too seriously and quickly realising that the only games worthy of any accolades are all very very old.
The modern gaming era has given us some awesome graphics, cool animations and plenty of mindless distraction; but no depth, no character and no real engagement.
Whenever I start to drift away from gaming, whenever my interest wanes and I forget why I ever enjoyed it in the first place there are a few games I go back to. Those classic games that serve to reinspire, reinvigorate and remind me why I game. Of all the classics I own none has been more revisited than Quest for Glory or "Heroes Quest" as I know it.
To this day after so many play throughs I still laugh at all the jokes, my heart still pumps a little harder as I infiltrate the bandit stronghold and I still spend hours upon hours maxing my stats for the umpteenth time.
There is also one other thing I do each time I replay this wonderful game and that is to wonder at its ongoing appeal and each time as easy as it would be to chalk it up to nostalgia I am forced to realise it is so much more than that. The world of this game which on the surface can seem childish even silly is so deeply and completely fleshed out that the characters though in a very literal sense caricatures have greater life and depth than those sprawled on the pages of many acclaimed novels I have read. The world itself though it borrows heavily from many a source is put together so perfectly and joyfully that it quickly becomes real to me and the freedom of its gameplay never even once detracts from that suspension of disbelief. This game has a truly extraordinary and unique heart that you cannot help but feel and embrace flaws and all.
I honestly could easily write essay upon essay at just what this game and the stories this series tells do right but I do not need to. This is not a game where I feel any need whatsoever to convince other to love because I know that anyone who plays this game cannot help but come to love it and so all I will say is this… Play it.
P.S. Steam Awards are back again, nominated for the The “No Apologies” Award 2017

Resident Evil 0 may feel like just a standalone expansion pack to RE1, but its rich, detailed levels, pseudo co-op mechanics, and more combat-oriented approach will provide plenty of challenge and entertainment for any classic survival horror fan, despite its lack of proper story.
Since Resident Evil 0 was created alongside the Resident Evil 1 REmake—even using the same engine—many players consider it the younger sibling of the more famous and mature title. In a sense, they are right, but RE0 is still a good game with some memorable moments that can stand on its own.
RE0 stars one of the most unjustly underused characters from the old games, Rebecca Chambers, and crams an entire day’s worth of excitement into her life that preceded the events of RE1. She ends up as the involuntarily partner of a fugitive, Billy Coen, which in this game translates to a strange single-player co-op mechanic, where we can control either characters at any time, while the computer takes over the other. Although one would think that having two inventories helps in a survival horror, item management is actually even more tedious than in any other old RE, chiefly because of the lack of item boxes (you have to drop items to the ground, leading to quite some backtracking).
Probably the main reason for RE0’s small fame is that it has some gameplay issues. For example, the new enemy types are bland: they are usually just large animals or leeches. On the other hand, players have to face nearly twice as much of them as in RE1.
This enemy density tries to hide the shortcomings of the story: our protagonists essentially never meet anyone and the plot mostly boils down to them going through a set of beautifully rendered stages (the starting luxury train is quite iconic) until they meet an end boss. Sure, there is actually a bit more going on, but in the end, this is probably RE0’s biggest downfall.

I don't mind a zombie game every now and then. I, like most gamers, am getting fairly tired of the trope, but when a game promises a new approach to mob-style survival horror (especially at such low prices), I'll give it a shot. I'm a huge fan of Killing Floor, and so when I read reviews that this mirrored the gameplay (and with the 70% off), I grabbed it on a whim.
Dead Effect starts with your character awakening from a cryo sleep on a space station. Much of the story is revealed through found tablets with various notes (nothing new here), and the seemingly endless corridors of the space station, while showcasing limited assets, adds to the feel of being "trapped" while you play. The zombies are zombies. Some crawl legless, some are in biohazard suits, and other various types add to the Killing Floor vibe. There's always plenty of enemies around, and being overwhelmed is as easy as missing a crucial reload. Grenades, special suit-based AOE attacks, and bullet-time modes make combat interesting and fast-paced, despite the slow hordes lumbering towards you.
There are several different game modes apart from the campaign. Guns in the campaign are given early and often, and ammo (if you explore) is scarce, but easy enough to manage. Aforementioned suit-powers deliver devastating AOE attacks, used for those 'surround' moments. There are gripes, of course; Your character cannot jump, can only sprint for a few meters before tiring, the HUD isn't incredibly easy to understand at first, and the upgrade menu for after missions is extremely buggy for a final release game.
All in all, it's a good little game, ESPECIALLY for the low price. A lot of hard work certainly went into it, and if you're into games like Killing Floor, Left 4 Dead, and any other mob-based zombie game (of which there are hundreds), this will be a good addition.

Pros:
*AI is smart, it has a good line of site and when it sees you it will start to come after you. If you get to close and it can't see you it will start attacking you.
*AI helps other AI - if one zombie sees you, all zombies in the room your in and any ones close to a door to that room your in, will come after you.

Cons:
*Character Development - The only backstory you get to the two characters you can select, is literally almost just one sentence, and that's it, I have no reason to want to play as the character I play as aside from their abilities or their weapons.

*Weapons - You can only have two types as a character unless you pay in-game currency to get say, a shotgun for the male character for example. I mean, its not all that bad but I'd rather save my money and spend upgrades on the weapons I already do own.
Ok now, I did get this for 1.49 because it was on sale, and the original price was 4.99 so I should stop ranting now. Well, have fun everyone, and happy gaming! :3

When I purchased this game, I was not expecting much. The graphics are decent, satisfying sound effects (lots of splats and gory, juicey sounds when heads explode), and an easy system to learn. As with many shooter games, do not play this for the story. It is fairly cliche' and the voice acting is pretty terrible. I actually thought it brought a sense of comic relief. In terms of the environment, this game is similar to DOOM 3, except with more satisfying kills and you do not need to holster your gun to hold up a flashlight! However, this game is not nearly as creepy as DOOM 3. If you are looking for a scary/horror game, spend your cash on Dead Space or Outlast.
Some negatives are the relative shortness of the story, the ease that one obtains money (you can get the best weapons within an hour if you play survival or biohazard), and some janky aspects of the controls. Sprinting slightly zooms in the view that could mess with your head, there is no jump option, and crouching just makes you feel like the midget version of arnold schwarzenegger. However, the most aggrivating thing is not having any form of melee attack. This is substituted with an electric glove that needs to be recharged after every use. Granted, the game is not very difficult if you are used to first person shooters, so you will likely not need a melee option.
This game will not fulfill all of your first person shooter fantasies unfortunately. However, it is well worth the $1.49 that I spent on it. If you see it on sale, snatch it. It will provide several gore-filled hours of senseless violence and entertainment.
As a side note, this game has the best credits. It lasted perhaps 8 seconds.

This game makes quite an expansive addition to the original Strike Vector title that only featured online multiplayer, this time around , coupled with a campaign mode, plus offline skirmish to play against bots until you feel ready to jump into the meat grinder (online mode).  Still, Strike Vector EX is one of the fastest third person/first person shooters of this "dumbed down" generation of the fps market.
Sure, the game feels somewhat dumbed down itself with the weapon loadouts now forcing all players to have one type of weapon for both arms of the jet now (which was the meta to begin with in the original game) but they all feel like they have more of a punch now.   You should feel encouraged to use other weapons instead of focusing on one gun.  my favorite is the shotguns now, Puts Gears of War to shame with the close quarters combat at 400 + mph in this game.  It's insanely fun.
another fair warning: You're always gonna run into other pilots who are better than you (even I got trashed for a bit) but you can still shoot them out of the sky if you just try hard enough, which is part of what this game is all about!   It's a solid shooter all around, fast paced, competitive---all right here.   I wish more people would just stop feeling so fragile about video games these days and just play the damn game.  like if you're not scoring kills left and right like you would in something like Call of Duty or some other mainstream shooter, then don't worry about, you're learning how to play an insanely fast paced shooter.
As it always should be, game on folks!
welp, don't worry about not having played Vanilla Strike Vector.   Here's a few things to chew on..
+Single player modes now availble to help you get to know how to play the game.  Do an offline skirmish with bots too.  There's also some challenge missions in the single player campaign once you see the stadium levels.   I'll say this: there's one mission where you have to escape a whole facility before the place goes up in flames.   Feels like F-Zero GX from the gamecube.
+Kebs now have a purpose!  It's in-game currency that you win from online matches, so save them up so you can buy things like cosmetic parts for your vector, concept art that helped create this game, all from the command center button---NO, ♥♥♥♥ Pay2Win ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, just play the damn game and win kebs, they're yours.   permanantly if you want but you can use them to pimp out your vector.
+Weapons and perks, abilities, and mods configs are now simplified.  Just pick what you want to spawn with, fly out, and go tear it up.  no need to figure out what's a good combination anymore <<  balance issues happened in the old SV I think, some were great, some weren't. I used to run Swarm rockets and miniguns, feels like the generic starship set up, but extremly weak.
+ now you can plug a controller into your usb port and play the game just fine.  Just know that the keyboard and mouse setup will always outplay the game controller any damn day of the year.
not everyone agrees with this weapon loadouot change but it's whatever at this point.  game's fun.  it's all that it matters.  Hardly any negative things to say about this title, so....that says quite alot.  SV EX has defintely inproved from the last game alright, and I hope the game continues to grow from this point on.
and another thing: I'll say it again from my other review:
It was a thing on the back of a cover for a ps2/gamecube game called "Robotech: Battlecry" which was based on an anime show about a special technology called "Veritech" which is a fighter jet that transformed into a walking tank and a hybrid of both and they used these machines to fight of some militaristic humanoid giant invasion forces wanting to take over earth.
so in SV EX?  change between 2 flight modes while in combat, or you die.

This game has promise. I didn't play much, but found the experience so unrewarding that I almost feel like I'd be suffering if I were to pick it up again and had no desire to use a guide.
After a lengthy intro you are dumped in this hostage taking situation. You're given almost no cues. Stuff just happens. It is a trial and error type affair, but that's just not fun. Clicking different things and getting no feedback just doesn't do anything for me. You have a guy stood at a box watching the guards, but no feedback from him. You have to prompt him but for what? You give him orders but you get no feedback on what said orders have accomplished. Either the guards come or they don't, I guess. Then you get to try again. It's all a bit... "figure out this scenario... but we won't give you hints."
After losing 5 or 6 times I quickly decided this game wasn't for me. It's not the losing - hell, one of my favourite games is 'Iter Vehemens ad Necem' - but the lack of any clues or useful feedback on the gameplay. I think the issue is, if they were to include that kind of thing then the game would be over too quickly because the scenarios probably boil down to quite simplistic number games of cat and mouse. So they extend the gameplay by making you guess until you hit the right combination to survive the scenario. I guess that's no fun for me.

This game.... I'm not a huge fan of games that go out of their way to kill the player, yet I find this game so much fun. I've played through 5 games so far, died every time. Yes, it's frustrating and I rarely play more than one game per sitting, but with a break between sessions this game is quite addicting. As many others have stated it is quick to pick up but there's a lot going on behind the scenes and I know I haven't even scratched the surface of what this game has to offer.

Decisions. You must make them. And in this game, said decisions could lead to your ultimate demise. Darn. Luckily the save button is there, because you will be dying. A LOT. SO MUCH DEATH. But you'll learn from these mistakes, survive the next time, then die again. Why? Because this game doesn't like you. It doesn't want to be your friend. It wants you to die. And die you shall. But allow me to actually explain the game. Here, you step into the shoes of a princess soon about to become queen. You must prepare for this though. So every week you take classes. History, swordmanship, magical lore, etc. Each of these classes better help you understand (and survive) situations getting betwen you and the crown. And mos likely, you will not take the right ones, and end up dying. But with each death, you learn a little more, that will help you your next attempt. WHich will be a few days after raging on dying for the 42nd time.

The biggest mistake I made playing LLTQ was thinking "how do I get the perfect ending?" but really, there is no perfect ending.  You will most likely die on your first play through, but that is the fun of the game.  It can be a bit tedious and fickle, so use of the save slots helps immensely.  Once you know which skill checks you need to pass in order to stay alive, you can experiment with moods, classes and conversation choices.  Unlocking one skill check and a simple conversation may send you on an entirely different adventure than the last ten or twenty playthroughs.  It's not for everyone, but I definitely thought it was worth the $4.99 I paid for it during the holiday sales.  Also, Elodie's Lumen Madoka-esque outfit made my inner magical girl very happy <3.

Watching this game develop has been awesome, and it's not even done yet! If you've played games like Terraria, you'll know what to expect in terms of movement and combat. Then, add in:
And those are just features that set it apart from other similar games. The features are very accessible, and the committed playerbase has put together a fairly expansive wiki to explain anything not obvious. Be warned, a large part of this game is exploring, salvaging, building, and collecting. Relative to other games in the genre, it's not repetitive at all, but the whole genre tends to be repetitive compared to other games. Instead of spending hours mining, you'll spend hours searching for that one last piece of a cosmetic set that you like, or one of the end-game weapons that looks cool. If you absolutely hate the whole side-scrolling, block-mining RPG genre, I wouldn't expect this to change your mind, but I would reccomend it to anyone who likes this sort of thing, and anyone with an open mind.

Starbound is a very enjoyable and quite expansive Sandbox/Adventure game with both single-player and multiplayer modes.
In Starbound, you start out on a planet where you need to gather resources to fix your spaceship in order to explore further. Eventually, you'll be free to fly anywhere you'd like, and there are a ton of different planet biomes and places to see. There so much to explore! Each planet and star system will have a vast array of planet types, terrain colors, ore, creatures, and structures, and the planets in Starbound are procedurally generated, so as you're playing as different characters, likely no galaxy will be the same as another.
There are seven races in Starbound: The Humans, the Avians, the Floran, the Glitch, the Hylotl, and the Novakids. Each race has different armor sets, decor, furniture, and spaceship differences. As you explore planets, you will likely find structures of a certain race's theme, finding NPCs of that race and seeing their unique styles and appearances. You will also come across lore for each of these races, and their backstories, throughout the game. Each of the races seems to be inspired real-life cultures around the world, for example, the Glitch and their Medieval-themed motif, and the Florans with their primitive, prehistoric-type furniture and clothing. The variation in these items is quite pleasing, and fun to explore.
Starbound's crafting, resource collection, and building can be quite satisfying, as well, and there are all kinds of blocks, furniture items, decorations, costumes, and objects that you can use to flesh out your structures, homes, bases, and any kinds of buildings that you make.
Starbound is also a mod-friendly game, and it has all kinds of awesome mods on the Workshop, and on the Chucklefish forums alike. Everything from more technology, more items, more furniture, more player colors, and all kinds of things!
Starbound's visuals and soundtrack are very nice, as well, and its lighting and the different effects on different types of planets make the variation of each area all the more charming. The sound ambiance in Starbound is also quite immersive as well, and there are plenty of nice details in the environments and in the game.
I would recommend Starbound to anyone and everyone who loves RPG adventure games, and sandbox games! It can be such a joy to play and so much fun, and it also has multiplayer, so that you can share your adventure with your friends. I have no complaints about the game, and I think it's a pleasure to play! ^.^

I played this game immediately after REmake, which is a truly stellar game that has stood the test of time. It doesn't provide the incredible artistic experience of Silent Hill (in fact, the writing is laughableb-movie hilarity), but the gameplay and level design embody survival horror better than any other game I've played. It's deeply atmospheric and very punishing.
My main complaint with the REmake was that it gets too easy in the 2nd half on the highest difficulty. Then RE0 came along and had me begging for that. This game is for masochists only. The early RE formula is already unfair - tension is created through fixed camera angles, claustrophobic hallways, a scarcity of ammo and medical supplies, fixed save points where you have to use save items... this game compounds that by having 2 characters you have to keep alive and some nearly indestructible enemies (even after you get the heavy weaponry that made the first game easier).
I very nearly didn't play the rest of the game after experiencing the opening sequence. Many here have stated that the train is the best part of the game, but to me it's the exact opposite. Yes, it's the most novel environment, but that whole sequence is marred by frequent incredibly cheesy cutscenes which ruin any sense of atmosphere, largely thanks to the banter between the two insufferable main characters.
Thankfully, after you escape the train, the cutscenes become far less frequent. Don't expect to gain any insight into the later RE titles from this prequel, as the story is mercifully very scant - it only exists to justify the game's existence, and it barely accomplishes that. Don't think about it too hard, and don't expect it to make sense.
The environments from here on out are basically a re-imagining of the original games, but with higher difficulty and two characters. The bulk of the game is a training facility which looks a whole lot like a mansion, which is followed by an underground lab which mostly looks nothing like a lab (though I hear the lab in this game is actually modelled after the lab from RE2, which I haven't played). Tack on an extra section at the end for novelty and good measure....
The mansion is much smaller than that of the original game (though the basement is larger), and frankly it's a bit of a pale imitation - while the graphics look flashier than REmake overall, the camera angles aren't as artistic and it never feels quite as isolated and distubing as the original while controlling two characters (which require a somewhat wider field of view to fit, eliminating some of that claustrophobia).
But the gameplay more than makes up for that by being much harder. It took me exactly 20hrs to beat this game, which is the same amount of time it took to beat REmake - only my final in-game time on REmake was nearly 10hrs, while this one didn't even reach 6hrs 40min. I spent 2/3 of my time in this game dying and retrying. This game will make you feel very intense anxiety, even beyond the original, and it never gets all that much easier (the final boss is quite difficult this time, as it's even quite resistent to the Magnum - I used up all my ammo and had to carefully run around and take it down with a pistol).
The scarcity of healing items is even more punishing this time around, since you have two characters to keep alive. At any given time, one of them will be dying. Ammo for the shotgun and grenade launcher is even more scarce than in the original, meaning you're basically going to be trying to survive with a pistol (as ammo for that is quite scarce). Except you basically can't kill the game's hardest enemies (abominations, leech zombies) with a pistol without getting killed.
Ink ribbons (for saving the game) are much more common this time around, but I didn't find myself using them more often - mainly because saving would involve backtracking through dangerous areas. The one attempt to make things easier didn't end up helping.
Many have complained about the inventory system, but it didn't strike me as being much worse. Let's be honest - not being able to drop things and having magically interconnected boxes was goofy. I only found myself backtracking marginally more here, and I'm sure it doesn't compare to playing the original on Survival Mode (where boxes are not interconnected). Perhaps this is because I was playing on hard, so there were less items available period. Yes, this frequently turns into 'inventory management: the game' just in terms of figuring out which character needs which item, but the inventory isn't much worse than the standard early RE fare. Heck, you even have twice the space with two characters!
Many have also complained that you can send the wrong character to the wrong place and die. Yes, this game is all about trial and error, and if you keep enough backup saves (which is essential in early RE games anyway), you'll be fine. There's never a point at which you can lose toooo much progress if you save regularly enough and don't always overwrite your saves.
Despite disputing those complaints, I still can't recommend this game to anyone except masochistic completionists who wish the already difficult original game was harder. Objectively, this game is poorly written, the story makes no sense and the main villain is cheesy and random, the environments are recycled, the enemies are unfairly difficult (bat boss fight where it's impossible to aim at the boss thanks to a swarm of tiny bats anyone?), and the mechanics make it that you'll spend half the time in this game moving items back and forth between the two characters, watching door animations, and dying. I enjoyed my time in it quite a lot, to be honest, but I uninstalled it as quickly as I could when I was finished and will certainly never be revisiting it again - it's simply too cruel. If you really want more REmake, just play it again and then wait for REmake2.
The extra modes don't add much - Leech Hunter is basically a survival mode where you try to collect 100 items in the mansion without dying (so, virtually impossible - don't even bother), while Wesker mode is basically a humorous god mode - I can't really see a reason to play the full game with it, though it's moderately entertaining for a few minutes.

One cannot accuse the makers of the Resident Evil games of recycling the formula, even if they do recycle their games for newer generations (which I am in total support). These changes are not always greeted with approval.
Overall, one could say, that all Resident Evil Games are about two characters in some form or in another, whether it is through direct co-op, alternative play through or simultaneous controlling of both, as is here the case. Having twice that many inventory spaces across two characters should in theory makes things easier, but how Capcom made the game it actually causes a ton of backtracking and item transportation as there are no storage boxes. Instead we can drop the items on the floor. This is closer to reality, then the “item teleportation boxes” but it is the reason for a lot of time wasting.

If you have never played the older RE games, then I don't think this would be enjoyable for you.
After playing Resident Evil 7, I was delighted to learn that there were two remastered classic Resident Evil games available. I have been a Resident Evil fan since playing RE2 back in 1998. This is one of the few REs that I have yet to play so I was delighted to learn that it had been remastered early last year. I have realized that the gameplay mechanics from the older series has not aged well.
Cons:
- Fixed camera angles. Although this has always been an issue with the older RE games, it seems to be a lot worst in this one. There are several miniboss battles that take place in hallways which have camera angles that only focus on the player. This makes the player have to rely solely on audio and the autolock system which brings me to my next point.
- Autolock system. The autolocking system in this game is terrible. The character often choose to lock onto random enemies rather than the closest threat. This was especially annoying during the church bat battle.
- Lack of item boxes. I like the ability to leave items on the ground instead of having to backtrack to an item box. This does become an annoyance when I want to transport a major weapon to another area. Although meant to decrease backtracking, the lack of item boxes actually made me have to backtrack even more.
- Story. The story in this RE is one of the weaker ones in my opinion. The mad scientist who dresses like an anime wizard was just lame.
Pros:
- Buddy system. Each RE has had some sort of gimick. RE0's is the buddy system. I liked how a lot of puzzles required use of both characters and I liked the ability to exchange items.
- Puzzles: Most of the puzzles were interesting. However, some of the puzzles were not completely logical. Case in point: the prey puzzle in the training facility. All of the clues seem to indicate that you light the fires in the order from the weakest animal to the strongest, yet the actual answer was completely counter intuitive (a wolf is lower than a horse in the food chain?).

It was immersive, dark. The combat was pretty mediocre. The storyline was cheesy. Billy Gives it one thumb up. Get it if you are interested in the RE storyline. But if you want a genuinely fun game this isnt it.

A great prequel to RE series, maybe even better than RE1. Setting is pretty much the same as in RE1. With the exception of (really cool) train sequence at the beginning, you will again find yourself in a villa and underground labs, BUT they are completely different now, with new puzzles, new (and really tough) enemy types and a lot of bossfights.
RE0 is also much, MUCH harder game than RE1, and pretty much harder than even the rest of the RE series. Even on normal difficulty you will find much less ammo, medkits and herbs, and encounter much more enemies, so be prepared for a real survival. You will die a lot of times.
Gameplay stayed the same, except now you control two charaters at the same time. And since crates to store items are not present this time, you will spend a lot of time in inventory managing items between your characters. Inventory management could definitely been more user friendly, but you will get used to it after an hour or two.
Story in RE games was always mediocre, and it's the same in RE0. But it's flow is much better than in RE1, much more things are happening and revealing the story behind T virus and characters behind it was interesting.
All in all it's a great game. If you loved RE1-3, you will also love this one. And now let's hope that waiting on RE Code Veronica and RE2 Remakes won't be too long.

Really interesting oldschool twist in day of modern RPGs that are concentrated mostly on action. Pillars of Eternity gives player lot of locations to explore in world that can be from time to time really interesting and from time to time just pure cliche. But that doesn't matter, that is actually what I've signed up for. The combat system works pretty well and skills can be quite interesting. You have to learn how to make skills of every character cooperate with others in your party and also figure out what is the best strategy for different enemies. It can get pretty boring over time but that's just sign you should take some time off from playing.
Side quests have real consequences just like conversations. But some of those are just little bit boring if you spend lot of time running around a city, talking to bunch of people and waiting for long loading screens to load different parts of map.
Some of the party members have really interesting backstories, or personalities and some are just plain boring and some you would just love to punch in the face (I'm looking at you chanter Kana!).
Overall this isometric RPG certainly isn't everyones cup of tea but it certainly is for all those who enjoy exploration, conversations, combat that needs little bit of thinking and stories.
PS. After you play this game on easy you'll wonder if someone actually defeated it on one of the hardest settings. If such person exists it must be either insane or masochist.

Combat in this game seems to be very reliant on cheese. On vetran difficulty enemies seem to swarm your party like Zerglings and I win engagements either by steam rolling lower level enemies or by having Eger block a door way while everyone else from shoots from behind him.
Maybe I'm not playing the game right. I might be fighting enemies that are meant for higher level characters because engagements seem either too easy or too difficult. I've reached the last level of "The Endless Path" in the middle of act 1 and found that I have to "cheese it to win it" in many engagements.
For the most part I will aggro enemy pods in this game the same way I would do in XCOM then lead them into traps and ambush and choke points. Many times I'll try to lure single enemies out from an impossible large groups then kill them one by one - otherwise, if I charge in I'll get surrounded and wiped in seconds! It really really feels like cheese is the only way to deal with combat. Low level enemies on the otherhand are walkovers where you don't need to use spells or abilities because they can't damage you at all!
This is a personal opinion but combat feels like a chore to get onto the next map. There's not much in the way of tactics unless you consider cheese a tactic.
As for the plot... I'm not sure if there is any. I'm not motivated to resolve the story at all. I've awakened as a watcher because there was this guy and a storm and a fancy machine... Okay, from where I'm standing that seems a lot less important than pillaging loot from every container in the world.
In all, I appreaciate the heavy mechanics under the hood and expansive background building that has gone into this game, however I feel POE didn't mash this together in the way that older classics like Baldurs Gate 2 did, and compared to more modern games, Shadow Run: Dragon Fall and Hong Kong had far more personality and emotional depth.

Date: 2/3/16
Review Number: 8
Game: Stranded Deep
From (Creator Publisher): Beam Team Games
Played On: Laptop (In-Home Streaming)
Steam Price as of Review: $14.99
Total Time played: 60 minutes
Review:
I was surprised when a review of another open world survival game came up on the wheel of misfortune so quickly after my last one, but I couldn't say that I was unhappy that I got to play Stranded Deep by Beam Team Games.  I have been in possession of this game for some number of months, and had admittedly played it for quite a while, then I had put it away when the Forest took my attention away from it for a while.  Now that it was back, however, I was eager to reinstall and get the game running again to experience the hopelessness of a Castaway-style adventure, only with the volleyball as a green coconut, and the name Wilson being replaced by Aidan.
It was when I installed and started the game, though that I realized that the game I was putting myself into was vastly different from the original early-access game I had come to know and love some months ago.  Looking over the reviews it appears that a relatively short while ago, but after I put the game down for a time, they went ahead and completely recreated the game in a new engine.  Now while this is not necessarily a bad thing, and I certainly think the new version is beautiful, it appears that this recreation meant a lot of the features and the tightness of the gameplay aspects I enjoyed are yet to be re-implemented in favor of a few new systems that seem a bit of a hodgepodge of features gleaned from other successful games.
That being said, I certainly think there were some improvements.  The graphics have improved without any significant detriment to performance, and some of the odd physics bugs I would normally see such as suspended items and the like are no longer there.  The crafting system is a little bit more intuitive, if horrifically incomplete so far, and parts and pieces can be assembled directly from the menus instead of having to place all the items on the ground to get the hammer to handle it.  Even the harvesting seems a bit easier, if changed, though differentiating between driftwood and not driftwood got a bit annoying, especially when it came to inventory management.
All in all, I feel like this has (and indeed always had) the solid foundation of a good game, and they had done an excellent job of building a solid game, then threw it all away to make it better.  However, it feels like it’s not quite where it was.  Hopefully, time will remedy this, and as they have proven before they can make a good game, I am cautiously optimistic about it.
Game’s Fate: Kept around to play occasionally.  If they start restoring a lot of the features I miss, I may replace RUST with this
Buy/No Buy: This one is a keeper, if anything for the promise, but if you already have a survival game or two, you may want to delay the purchase a bit and continue to entertain yourself with them.  Buy.

Reminiscent of text based games from long ago, Long Live the Queen is a very entertaining strategy game.
You control the heir to the throne before coming of age and game-play consists of choosing which skills to develop before your coronation next year.  Many different events will happen as time progresses and depending on what skills you chose to focus on, you will either open up new story paths or in some cases even end up dead.  There are many different ways to die, some very unexpected.
Replay value comes from going back and trying to see the different endings (or the different ways to die – yep, I’m still working on that achievement), or even the different story options.  You can save any time you want and the game also includes an auto-save so  you can go back some to try different strategies.  Many times though you will want to start over again fresh, picking different skills just to see what happens.

If you prefer action based or shooter type games, look elsewhere.  If you like anime style artwork and unforgiving strategy you will not be disappointed.

A very quick disclaimer: I finished the main game in order to stop the community from using the argument "git gud" that they seem to love to spam to anyone that doesn't sing praise to these games, hence my time with the game.
Now onto the review itself: Dark Souls is one of the most unfriendly and unfair games you'll ever play if you decide to give it a go. There's two main factors for this:
1. Trial and error gameplay: granted, everything in life is trial and error, but this games will always, and I mean always, keep throwing new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t parts your way in order to make sure that you die and lose progress. No matter how good you are, no matter how much skill you have, no matter how much of the game you've done before, the game will throw something to kill you that's unfair. Whether its enemies that inflict you with a incredibly dangerous and annoying status effect that persists through dead, or suddenly invisible floor while walking through ice where a mistep will instant kill you. This kind of design seriously gets tiring after a while and it just gets worse by the next point.
2. Long stretches where there is no checkpoints: This particular problem is at its worse when you are trying to get through a boss fight, and everytime you die you are sent back quite a bit, sometimes a full level entirely (I'm looking at you Sen's Fortress), This is quite enfuriating as it gives me no chance to learn at a good pace how to beat the bosses. Out of 3 hours I spent fighting a boss over and over again at one point, more than 80% of that time was just the trip to try reach him again, making for a incredibly frustrating time.
This is without mentioning the amount of secrets all over the place. Some of them completely optional, some of them mandatory, and some of them optional but might as well be mandatory by how essential they can be to not have a bad time. Making this game not only a game where you need A LOT of patience to get through, but half the stuff will require a guide to even figure out. This is just not good design at all.
Now, Its not all bad, I will now quickly give some praise to some aspects that the game does very well:
1. The Combat itself although clunky at times, feels very rewarding and makes for great battles whether with normal enemies or with bosses, quite enjoyable when you get the hang of it.
2. The atmosphere of the game is supreme, Its not my cup of tea as I dislike dark places in general but the sense of dread this game provokes is something that most horror games wish they could imitate, the world itself and the lore is very interesting, props to the developers for craftting such a nice world.
3. The middle level of the game, Anor Londor, felt like a ray of hope, this was the one part of the game that I really enjoyed from beggining to end even with the incredibly hard boss.
But bear in mind that in order to enjoy these positives I just mentioned, you will have to go through a lot of punishment before you can get any enjoyment. The unfair difficulty is just not fun most of the time. When I finally defeated the final boss of the game and got one of the two endings, I didn't feel happyness/achivement, I felt relief of finally ending a nightmare.
Final word: I do not recommend this game to almost anyone except gamers that really want a wall to bang their head agaisn't. Maybe the future games are friendlier or maybe I played the game wrong (I went for a DEX BUILD), but in the end it was more frustration and desperation than fun.

This collection is great. They are old school adventure RPG games. My favorite as far as the art style is QoG 4. This was the first game series to allow you to import your character from one game to the next.  They are packed with humor, fun puzzles, and unholy monsters.

The Quest For Glory Collection is a convenient way to purchase and play 4 of the best games I have ever played. Is that statement tainted with some nostalgia? Probably. However, I can assure you that I have played the series a number of times throughout my life. That is quite rare for me.
The key to the longevity of my enjoyment of Quest for Glory is its balance between humour, creative storytelling, and emotional weight. Not every moment of the game is laugh out loud funny, but many are. Tropes of heroic adventures are used, but often subverted when doing so serves a greater purpose. Emotional connection to memorable locations and characters is slowly ramped up until the finale act of each game requires true heroism on the part of the characters.
While the graphics of the game in no way hold up to the modern capabilities of computers, that is not necessary for a series so steeped in its own well though out mythology. The storytelling of Quest For Glory is wonderful and entertaining, and in the end that is what we seek when we play games. We wish to be entertained.

Oh my goodness, these games are my childhood. When I saw that the humble bundle for September was Sierra classics like Quest for Glory and King's Quest, I immediately bought it. These games are fun, have great replay value, and they are challenging. The art work is fun and the writing is clever. The games were developed by a husband and wife and consistently have the same quality across the whole story. My favorite game in the series has to be Quest for Glory IV: Shadows of Darkness. The darker tone of that game, combined with the depth of the story really put it over the top for me. The soundtrack is pretty great too despite the first four games being all synthetic. The fifth game in the series has a live-recorded orchestrated soundtrack and was in fact the first video game to ever do so.
The games are sometimes a little buggy, but there are patches for that, and I would recommend playing the AGV Interactive fan remake of the second game instead of the one in the collection.

The end is here. Life as you knew it has gone to hell after the mother of all zombie outbreaks. Now you and the few scattered survivors must band together to survive. Switch back and forth between several player characters, you’ll travel across the multi-town desert region recruiting new survivors, searching vacated shops and houses for supplies, and managing relationships with the people you encounter. Every choice matters.

I've surprised myself at how many hours I've sunk into this game, the core story is nothing special but as there is much to learn I considered it more of an extended tutorial. Since then I've picked up the Breakdown DLC which is a sandbox mode in which you spawn a random hero and do your best to survive, and this is strangely addictive!
You start by finding a base and from there you head out to find supplies, recruit randomly generated survivors and build up your base. In Breakdown there is only one goal, to survive long enough to find and an RV and escape. The RV can only seat 6 (+1 non-playable character) so you'll need to put some consideration into who you take with you. With each escape you find yourself back in square 1 with your team and supplies and an increased difficulty level, so before long you'll encounter larger and more aggressive hordes and more special zombies.
Breakdown keeps me interested in achievement hunting as each level offers a handful of challenges such as kill 100 zombies with blades or 400 with a car door. Upon meeting these requirements you'll receive an escort quest that will earn you a special hero character. These characters usually start with maxed out stats in one or more areas, useful skills such as medic or mechanic and occasionally bring radio commands such as calling in an airstrike or vehicle delivery. Heroes aren't always better than your average survivor but its defintely worth putting thought into who you want on your dream team; ideally you want to characters that each serve multiple functions and max them out in different areas.
As the levels progress and you flesh your team out your going to max your skills in each area, which is good as you'll need a solid team. The gameplay is usually managable but the tide can turn quickly under certain circumstances and it only takes one slip -- forgetting to bring food, crashing your vehicle in the wilderness or simply getting cocky -- and you've lost that maxed out mechanic/cook/shotgunner you've spent the last 20 hours levelling! And levelling an untrained replacement character on a higher level is not so easy.
All in all I found this to be a great, if repetitive, game that is reminiscent of Dead Rising. There're definitely bugs but the overall experience was enjoyable, but more so for the sandbox than the mediocre story. What's more this game has potential for a great deal of improvement in the future and I'd love to see a State of Decay 2 with drop in Co-Op, item crafting and randomly generated maps for Breakdown.

This game isn't for everyone for sure. It takes a point and click adventure and boils it down to its very essence and then introduced more failure (alternatively, say 'small adventure game with a heavy resource management component' either one should give you an idea). The mechanics are quite simple, but the game is tough as nails.
It's not perfect, and I can understand a lot of the complaints that people have, but I really loved playing this game, and I thought it had a hell of an ending. I streamed it, and so I felt a bit corny reading some of the dialogue, but that aside I found the story quite engaging. I also loved how the developer integrated the fact you're likely to behave in an 'unrealistic' (ie. overly risky) fashion into the story itself.
Don't try it if you won't enjoy something simple, and please don't cheat yourself out of the satisfaction of beating it on the classic mode. Provided you have the patience and interest in doing these two things, I give this game a strong recommendation, and find it well deserving of much more than the 'mixed' review it currently gets.

Gods Will Be Watching is not the game that is advertised to you. A lot of people seem to have similar complaints, but I'll try to keep this relatively condensed.
What you are promised/expecting:
A point-and-click adventure game, filled with moral dilemmas, something that will make you "feel bad" - as PC Gamer says in the little blurb given on Steam. This sounds fun, it sounds like a game that has a solid story, and very interesting psychological/ethical questions accompanying it.
What you get:
Perhaps the only quote that is really accurate is "There's no good or evil, just decisions, with only you and the gods as a judge to your actions." While this quote was probably meant to make the reader think "I'll be in such dire situations that any action can be justified!" What it comes to mean is that the game is a monotonous disaster, and none of your choices are really evil or good, by the end of the game you're going through the motions. The game is comprised of several ball-breaking puzzles, and there is certainly some incentive to make moral decisions at first. However, it quickly becomes clear that there are very few options, by the end you don't care if you're shooting the civilian, or calming them, it's whatever you have to do to get to the next level. Why? Because you've seen all of this dialogue and these situations over and over again. The game is at its worst when you are killed half a dozen times, and you have to read through the same dialogue time and time again.

The Metacritic score for this game is extremely misleading and may cause some users to miss out on what is perhaps the most visceral game I have played this year.
Learning to appreciate Gods Will Be Watching means overcoming some barriers.  The first such barrier will inevitably be the graphics.  For someone such as myself who was raised on sprite based games this retro graphic style is part of the allure but I know for others (such as my child) the gut reaction is "the graphics of that game suck!"  What you, the skeptical buyer needs to understand is that the graphics of this game are an aestetic and artistic choice.  Yes, this game could easily have been created utilizing modern 3d graphics and it probably would have still been fun.  The graphic style complements the entire game themetic:  do more with less.  The entire game you struggle to do as much as you can with extremely limited resources.  This theme can be read as the theme of the game in general, the game designers endeavoured to accomplish as much as they could with as little as possible.  We will return to this argument later.
Related to this first barrier is the second obstacle the player must overcome:  one of the most steep and unforgiving learning curves of any game I have played in perhaps a decade.  In a way this difficulty is appropriating the difficulty of older sprite based games before the invention of quicksaves and quickloads.  Not all of the complaints of the difficulty are without merit though.  I found the pacing of this difficulty somewhat random.  Instead of starting off difficult and ending up super difficult, near impossible levels are followed by relative walks-in-the-parks.  I think some better planning in this regard by the developers could have lead to a better recepection of the game.  That said,  I think the difficulty  of the game, like the sprite-based graphics is an artistic choice.   Ostensibly it is a love-letter to mind-blowingly difficult rogue-like games of yesteryear.  It is important to understand though that the difficulty of the game is supposed to be a mirror of the morally difficult situations you find yourself in in each level.  The threat of making a bad decision is made more visceral when you understand that you may be very close to having wasted nearly an hour of your time for nothing.
If, you are willing to perservere past these barriers, an extremely rich and rewarding experience awaits.  The game draws inspiration from such varied sources as Quentin Tarantino's Reservoir Dogs, the film Edge of Tomorrow, The Dark Tower series, as well as the entire encyclopedia of Science-Fiction tropes.  The two things this game does better than many others out there is tension and meta-gaming comentary.
I'll try to keep this spoiler free but I must give kudos to the developers for showing how flat sprites can build tension.  In one level a torturer decides which device he is going to use that day.  His blocky sprite hands moves slowly from potential weapon to potential weapon and though you cannot really make out anything, you can envision it.  Even the way he slowly takes a sprite based drag from his sprite based cigarette builds a whole much greater than its constituent parts.  Ultimately, this game wags a shaming finger at AAA games who have access to million dollar CGI video and high end 3d graphics but who produce products empty and soul-less.
As I mentioned before this game seems to be speaking not only to its industry but to those who consume it.  The main characters name is "Burden" connoting not only his in-game responsibility but also how he functions as a work-horse for you, the player.  The character of Burden slowly becomes aware that there is something awry in his decision making process and that problem is *you*, the player.  The titular "watching gods" are not some fictional deities, but you, the player meddling and interferring in the gaming world.  The game asks the player to not be a detached meddling god but to invest in the characters emotionally.  The game provides a compelling world (via excellent sound, story, and yes, graphics) and asks you to simply try.
And based upon the metacritic score, many players seem unwilling to do so.  They would rather quickload up their quicksave and blow the heads off of people wearing turbans and then teabag them with special American flag boxers they purchased as a DLC.  The developers of this game have recognized a sort of illness in this industry and like Burden and his cohorts have attempted to make a remedy for it.  Ultimately, the choice of whether to take that cure (and purchase this game) is yours.
Choose wisely.

I played this game when it was still an indie prototype from a game jam.  And it kicked my♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing hard.  I was frustrated, but I was also intrigued.  Punishing gameplay can be intentional and can often bely a fascinating enigma of a game.  Just ask any Dead/Dark Souls fans.
I am writing this review to counter the many negative reviews I have seen of this game.  Anyone who has reviewed this game negatively has no ♥♥♥♥ing idea what they are talking about.  However, that is largely due to the fact that the game didn't start out with the multiple difficulties it has now.  Many reviewers played it when only the "Original" difficulty existed when the game is infuriatingly difficult for all but the most hardcore (which I am most empathetically not).
I guess I was fortunate to not have time to get around to playing the game until the "Mercy Update" came out.  I had been following the game since I saw and played the game jam prototype.  In the prototype I barely made it 7 days without everything going to hell (The prototype was what became Chapter 4).  When I tried the commercial version on Original Light I was done before I was halfway to the Chapter 1 goal.  I had to play on Puzzle Mode Light.  LIGHT.  I am not an inexperienced gamer and I might have made it through on Puzzle Mode but considering how many times Chapter 5 kicked my♥♥♥♥♥I know I should not be so arrogant to think so.
Simply put, anyone who complains about the difficulty (ESPECIALLY after they added the other difficulties) has no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what they are talking about.
THE POINT of the game is the difficulty.  It is the base DNA that was present even in the nascent prototype.  The difficulty MUST be high.  The entire point of the game is moral ambiguity and hard decisions.  How can a game force you to feel these things if the difficulty is not cranked up?  How can a game force you to choose between running out of food (which would cause characters with low morale to commit suicide) and killing the least useful member of your troop so that the others would survive, without making the "save everyone" option almost impossible?
But the Mercy Update fixes that.  Because the multitude of difficulties added makes this game accessible for players of all levels of masochism.  And that is a good thing.
Because the story is a masterpiece.  A complex tale of gray areas, branching pathways, personal discoveries, and hard choices.  The music is masterful in its creation of an atmosphere. The gameplay combines adventure game style branching pathways with the tense resource management of a thriller strategy game.  You will be surprised how tense this game will make you.
But most importantly, at least to a player such as myself, this game fulfills my criteria for "Games As Art".
Many games can be considered art, but for me, the true pinnacles of the media embrace message and metaphor in a way no other medium can: through gameplay.
I can't say much else about it due to spoilers, but the game embraces its branching pathways, gray areas, and hard moral choices into it's core story to create a metaphor about the hard choices we make through life.  When the gameplay and story intersect to become a metaphor unto themselves is when games truly become the sublime.
This game is EASILY one of the best games of 2014.  Many of us just needed the lower difficulties to see that.  Don't be so arrogant that you feel you can't play it on the lower difficulties.  The INTENT of the game is to be punishing and inspire HARD CHOICES.  It's fine if you can't handle that but if you dismiss this game out of frustration you are robbing yourself of one of the few experiences of a truly inspired piece of interactive software.

If you are looking for a RPG in the same style as the classics, look no further. This game brings back memories of Baldurs Gate and Icewind Dale, and it definitely delivers the same high level of quality and immersion as those games.
The setting is well designed, and you have a lot of lore to dig into if that is your thing. At no point does the game force you to do so, so you have a lot of freedom. The stories are good, and you are rewarded mostly from completing quests as opposed to hacking and slahing your way through the game. This enables you to better roleplay your character, as opposed to having to slay mobs for XP, which can sometimes be a problem in RPGs.
Expect to invest a lot of hours into this game if you plan to complete it. This can be good or bad I guess, depending on what you are looking for. The main plot can be completed in about 50 hours, but to get the full experience, it is recommended to study a bit away from the game - what does each stat do (there is a lot of them), what about conditions, class mechanics, spells and so on. It is quite detailed and rich.
There's some problems with the game you should be aware of:
- Tanky characters often fail to hold aggro
- The ending seems a bit rushed compared to the rest of the game

Just a Rehash of the original Strike Vector. I can't reccomend this title in its current state due to clunky menus (with console buttons used for menu navigation that can't be turned off), and massive connection issues (when hosts leave the session it closes the server, and you lose any progress you made in that match. It's 2017!!! Where is host migration?). It seems to me not much quality control was done, the functionality of the online play feels very dated. If you still enjoy the gameplay this can be an enjoyable experience, but you'll be frustrated at how buggy the experience feels as a whole.

To owners of the original, this is the same game as Strike Vector, it's just repackaged for consoles. The maps, weapons, specials, ship customization, etc. are all the same, besides LMG being removed and vector painting highly simplified.
They gave it a clunky console interface and reduced loadout complexity by letting you only wield one weapon instead of two. They also made collisions in jet mode much more sympathetic. These changes are presumably to make the game easier to control on the console release but they lower the depth and skill ceiling. The interior view of the cockpit in first person mode was also removed for some reason. Besides balance tweaks, the additions are 64bit support, bots and ranked matchmaking.
Why are they selling it as a new game? It doesn't amount to anything more than a bad patch. Something they stopped releasing for the original less than a year after release. Considering this was packaged as a new release specifically to sell on consoles, the decision to relist it on Steam as a new game as opposed to an update was just a scummy cash grab.
They should have just released Strike Vector as freeware (or implement LAN sharing) after it was abandoned - so a long lasting community could be allowed to exist around the otherwise dead game - instead of trying to milk the corpse.
