For all its visual prowess this game is about as penetratable as a petrified nun lodged at the bottom of a swimming pool filled with concrete. "Difficult" as a word doesn't quite do this game justice as a description. It is simply the most difficult game I have ever played to the point where I have to assume that any levels following the initial first level; a hostage siege, simply don't exist, as I have never seen them, and I resign myself to the fact that I will never see them. The first level's setting however is quite apt inasmuch that it is a mirror to my own experience in futility suffered through being held hostage by this game.
The developer gives indication that the game is in fact "their's" and not "ours" as players, this is given away by the fact that there are two game modes "Original - as it was meant to be played", and "Lite - a lesser difficulty". In that it tells you that a lighter game mode was seen as beneath the grand vision of the auteur developer. This is the risk you play when purchasing Indie games. The game experience is at the cost of the deveoper's vision, when in fact the two should be achieved in unison.
I also could accept that the issue regarding difficulty may lie with my ability, yes, were it not for the fact that I've played pretty much every games console and micro computer in existence, right from casette based games you programmed yourself to cartridges and discs and never in all that time of completing games to a completionist level, have I encountered a game as staggeringly difficult as this. On "Lite Mode" it simply is just 25% too difficult for any invested player to achieve, makes me wonder if the game saw a gamer based focus group at any stage during its development.
However the graphics are bang on the mark and so was that developing story from what I could gather. As an investment I could hardly recommend it however purely based on time and money invested versus progression, as I have so far played 1.4 hours and still have not progressed past the first level. Which is a new first for me, and it seriously makes me want to reassess wether I should keep this installed on my machine just occupying useful space.
In essance I really desperately want to like it, but how can you like something that at a base and fundamental gameplay level simply and stubbornly refuses to comply.

Rarely have I experienced a game that is by turns so engrossing and yet also frustrating as
.
These designers at
undeniably share the vision I've always had for the ideal zombie apocalypse survival RPG.  For all the potential this game offers however, it falls a bit short of perfection due in part to limited optimization for PC, minor design flaws and a hundred little moments that will have you doing /facepalm.
The primary features like base building & upkeep, character progression and the constant need to scavenge while fending off hordes are highly engaging.  The dynamic mission system, the relationship system for playable and NPC survivors and the decent pacing of the story guarantee that you'll always have more to do than time to do it in.  Decisions like 24/7 near-real time progression and permanent character deaths enhance immersion and tension.
Gameplay goes back and forth between pursuit of the main quest line and addressing challenges to your (and others) survival.  Smart choices and hustle are rewarded with a secure base and (relatively speaking) happy community while poor ones are compounded by a variety of repercussions.  Combat is fun once you develop skills enough to unlock handy special abilities and acquire some slightly higher quality weaponry.
State of Decay is a PC port, and in short it feels and looks like what it is.  The combination of features here is awesome but I'm left wanting more depth, quality and variety in them.  They should also do a careful pass of the experience from start to finish for convenience and user interface.  I'd also like to see a more robust story, more unique survivors with their own side quests, a vast improvement of zombie AI/pathing and an effort to balance special zombies a bit more.  In other words, bring all of the people and zombies to life more convincingly.
This game is destined to divide players into:
1) A hardcore group who want a higher level of difficulty and realism and,
2) A more general group of zombie and RPG fans who get riled up over that first death and the coming to grips with permanent loss of a useful character (who you're emotionally attached to, to boot).
I highly recommend State of Decay to any genre fan.  Temper your expectations reasonably and you will be thrilled with this fun game; I loved it.  I have not yet tried the
or
DLC's but reportedly the former provides a satisfying level of difficulty from the getgo and in the end a serious challenge.  Any sequel to this has huge potential and I will be keeping an eye on the future developments by Undead Labs.  Any successor
a Cooperative mode.  Demands it.

A triple-A game that is actually innovative? Can it be? Yes.
But first, I have to say... the game's storyline is fairly underwhelming. I felt NO investment in Talion's character, or his motivations. Secondary characters are arguably more memorable, but in a few cases, their fates are up in the air. The wraith, in my opinion, is the most interesting character, but said interest is a result of pre-existing lore, not any character development in the storyline.
The gameplay basics are fairly straightforward: Assassin's Creed platforming with Arkham combat. And as those games have shown, these mechanics work well. In fact, Shadow of Mordor would be considered derivative without its main and best feature: the Nemesis system.
The Nemesis system, in essence, adds distinctive traits to the Uruk Captain and Warchief mini-bosses scattered throughout the world. Each Uruk has a random name and personality; examples include generic bloodlust, creepy silence with teeth-chomping, arrogance, and even POETRY. Yes, I have encountered an Uruk poet.
These uruks also have unique combos of combat traits that change how you fight them, including health regeneration, orc summons, special combat moves, immunity to your special combat moves, or fears and hatreds. This results in emergent gameplay, where the player can forge their own experiences.
I could detail my own experience with the Nemesis system, but you are better off with just buying the game and making your own experience, your own Nemesis. Forge your own story.

I waited a lot before writing this review because this awesome game is cursed by a really bad netcode implementation, I thought the issues could be fixed but since after 2 months the situation is almost the same I think things are going to remain like that forever. Anyway, let's start with everything else, we will get there eventually.
The game is, as was SSFIV AE, one of the best fighting games ever made. The roster is huge and the gameplay of each character is unique (shotos share similarities ofc). Usually with a huge roster tier list gets crazy but in Ultra Street Fighter IV there are almost no impossible match-ups.
Graphics are really nice and on PC you can customize even more game's graphic settings, music is really good (character bgm are better than stage bgm IMHO, but that's just for me) and SFX/announcer are part of what makes the game street fighter.
Now let's talk about the netcode implementation. When you buy a fighting game you're not supposed to play alone by design.
In 2000 you wouldn't expect the game to have any online mode implementation and you'd have struggled to search players at your level (it involved moving around your country a lot) to learn the game and eventually enjoy yourself.
In 2014 you expect your game to be fully playable online since 30~40 ms ping values are totally bearable (it's more or less 2 game frames that should even be mitigated by the netcode). Sadly this is not the case.
The netcode is bad and so the "mitigation" is completely missing (at least it feels like that) meaning that if you play with low ping values (let's say <40ms) outside ranked, the game plays fine, otherwise you will experience totally unplayable games.
To recap, gameplay 10 (wouldn't make major changes), graphic 9 (it's old but on PC you can enhance it), music/SFX 9 (totally enjoyable), netcode 2 (well, read above)

Post-Netcode Fix of April 9/March 30, 2015:
Great game. Easily one of the best fighting games around. SF4 plays like a sped up, modernized version of SF2, with some additional mechanics. As a bonus, it's 3D on a 2D plane, done *right*, with 2D fighter gameplay.
The netcode--now that it's been fixed(See the whole sordid scandal below. Despite making a very good game, Capcom has not treated its fans very well...)--is excellent, and you can play people hundreds of miles away with minimal lag. (Assuming actual internet issues aren't present.)
Pre-Netcode Fix Review:
======
Great game. Worst implementation of multiplayer I've played in over a decade. Don't touch this with a long pole unless you're planning on playing offline only.
Incessant lag due to the network implementation blocking the game thread when responding to matchmaking pings, both in the menu(Random 2-second pauses while navigating any multiplayer-aware menus.) and during actual gameplay. General sluggishness and lack of responsiveness during online games(Often feels like you're playing with a half second delay on anything you do, plus inputs are randomly dropped.), and network connection rating icons that don't display accurate information(Poorly-rated connections are often good(Bearing in mind the entire game's network performance is awful. "Good" is very relative.), while good-rated connections are often awful. Plus it takes several seconds for the game to decide how to rate most players' connections while matchmaking, usually extended by several more multi-second freezes of the game.).
Additionally, the game's developers have gone from a very good working multiplayer implementation, back in late May/early June 2014, to completely breaking it with the above-mentioned technical problems, to promising a patch to correct issues that did nothing, to deploying a beta patch to correct issues that did a LITTLE bit, to promising another patch to correct issues, that also did nothing.
Additionally, looking at the release notes of the various patches in spring/summer/fall 2014, it's painfully clear that the current development team Capcom has allocated to the game is incompetent and has zero ability to develop software beyond changing variable values.
All this while Capcom public relations personnel post soothing promises of fixing things soon, once the outcry from the playerbase reaches the level of thousands of complaints.
Is it playable, in light of these technical and mismanagement issues? Kinda.
Is it enjoyable, in light of these technical and mismanagement issues? No.
No one in their right mind should spend a dime on this game.

SVEX is a reworked and expanded version of Strike Vector in the unreal 4 engine. Should you pick up this "new" game?
I think so, because there is simply NOTHING like Strike Vector out there right now. Flying Mech / 6DOF/ Space Shooter / Jet combat junkies get attracted to this game, but its actually more like Quake style FPS in space, highly maneuverable super fast paced and better played with a mouse and keyboard. As a cult game, you just have to allow some of its quirks and glitches and experience it for what it is. I think it's a must play even for owners of the first SV and I really hope to enjoy some renewed multiplayer activity. Make sure to join the community discord channel!
longer review below:
I'm an owner of the original strike vector who tested the SVEX open beta and then bought the game at the 50% temporary discount for owners of the original.
Here are some of the pros and cons of SVEX as a revised and updated version of the original game. Overall I think this game is worth the purchase even for owners of the original who might have preferred EX as a free upgrade instead of a 5.99 discounted new product.
First, here are the main positive differences between SV and SVEX:
+ rebuilt on Unreal Engine 4 (previously UE3) fpr PS4 and now ported to PC (yes it's a "port" with tweaks, more on that below)
+ new solo campaign with a story and voice acted characters (pretty short but fun and cheesy like a dreamcast era action arcade game vibe. also each mission is timed so there is replay value to speedrun them)
+ reworked (simplified) gameplay mechanics. Most notably: Weapon loadouts are the same for left and right guns, and they fire together.  It's much harder to die from crashing into walls than the original but still possible(a major reason newbies gave up on the original), speed boost rings also no longer have a crash-able surface around them. Finally theres some additional control options such as the ability to hold a key to trigger fast mode, which makes things feel WAY more fluid on its own.
+ AI Players integrated seamlessly into multiplayer. Lack of bots was a big reason why the first SV died, and now they populate empty servers automatically and get replaced as real players join. you can also play practice skirmishes against bots for those who arent interested in multiplayer. They are pretty well done and the higher level AI can be a nice challenge.
+ new multiplayer maps (theyre in the works if not currently available)
+ steam achievements
+ new crosshairs (small detail, but made a big difference in comfort for me to have a + reticle instead of a circle).
there are a lot of other design changes not mentioned here too.
Now some cons of SVEX:
- it's a console port, so some console port woes exist. notably: netcode built for 60fps (can be unlocked  but with possible glitches in multiplayer. 144fps feels great otherwise); interface is designed for console so youll see console button prompts alongside keys; in first person mode the weapon models are cut off too soon at higher FOVs (hopefully theyll add an option to turn weapon models off).
- it's NOT a sequel. Make no mistake this is an expanded form of the original game. Whether you think it's worth the price as an owner of the original is up to you. If you havent played the original, definitely get this version as it's got much more content. The only reason to play the old version would be to retain some of the details of the game mechanics that made it particularly brutally hard.
- Until people set up more dedicated servers, many of the multiplayer servers are P2P which among other things means that when the host leaves the server gets shut down. Hopefully more dedis will get put up soon, since right now when the host ragequits, everyone gets kicked

I'm going to be brutally honest.
Strike Vector EX is virtually the same game as Strike Vector with tweaks to make it easier for new players and harder for vets to crush said new players, all with a shiny new coat of paint. Yeah, the graphics are better. There are bots now, and they definitely add a lot of replayability. But don't kid yourself. This game isn't anything more than a v1.5, with much of the game dumbed down. Its... not really worth it if you're a veteran. I'd like to emphasize, however, that this is all
+ Bots. Adds a lot of replayability and great for training your skills.
+ Quickmatching based on skill level.
+ Skill level tiers that prevent lower skill players from being crushed by higher skill players. However, fragments the already small community.
+ New music unique for each stage, which is quite good.
+ Optimization for controller play, and they can keep up with keyboard-mouse players.
\ Time trial challenges. Campaign is, in many ways, reskinned challenges with a plot tacked on top.
\ Balancing. Its much easier to kill with many weapons, and be killed by anybody. Many passives and active abilities have been buffed.
\ Items. Its harder to heal overall, even though its easier to pick up many items.
\ Much more forgiving with collision detection.
\ Vector painting has been dramatically simplified; you can only pick from a preset number of colors.
\ Gravity no longer sucks, in fact its a beautiful map and no-gravity mechanics have been tweaked to be less wonky.
- LMG. Considered too weak in the face of the Gatling Gun.
- Dual wielding. You can no longer fire either side of the vector weapons separately.
Disclosure, this was from the alpha, but nothing you see here is absent from the current game. You might level up slower though.
The devs don't advertise this game, so it doesn't get exposure. I have my doubts that the community is going to last long, probably shorter than Strike Vector.

This was tough choice to vote down or up as I did enjoy small partsof the game, but due to a lot of poor design choices & annoying game mechanics I recommend you spend your time & money on other more enjoyable games.
* Fun weapon types which can have interesting secondary fire modes (the first time you discover them)
* Multiple levels of crafting stations & ship upgrades to encourage you to explore other planets
* Some of the unique main quests or outpost quests along with the portal challenges found underground are fun & challenging (the first time you discover them)
* Copy, paste & repeat weapon types - once you have found one type of weapon you are going to see a lot more of them throughout your playthrough
* Copy, paste & repeat enemies - fairly limited re-skinned enemy types, with the same attack patterns
* Copy, paste & repeat dungeons / portal challenges - it's interesting the first time you find a unique NPC village or challenge, however you quickly realise that after you've seen it once, you are going to see pretty much the same thing on every planet you go to
* I found the difficulty levels to be fairly frustrating- the food system was more of an annoyance than a challenge - forcing you to stop whatever you are doing to quell the irritating beeping for another 5 minutes.
The game was also very easy to complete as I played the vast majority of it in solo mode & I didn't need to craft the top end gier or potions, food etc to complete it & ultimately it felt a bit of a let down when I completed it
* Main quests - part good, part bad - the game generally requires you to do one mission to scan items of a certain race, which first involves finding that civilization.  This can be extremely frustrating (they aren't always on the planet type they point you towards in the quest description & with virtually no information as to where abouts to find them on that planet type, sometimes you can be looking for hours unless you look it up online).  Once you do find them you simply left click on everything in sight with your scanning tool to fill up an arbitary meter bar before returning back to the quest giver (and you may need to visit multiple planets of the same copy paste world types to fill up this meter) - I realise this is to encourage you to check out new planets or their creations, but it just isn't fun & you will need to do this at least 3 or 4 times in the main quest line for different races which seems like extremely lazy game creation to me.  Once you managed to get these scanning quests completed they unlock the actual dungeons & unique instances in the main quest were actually enjoyable.
Tutorial / tooltips - the game does a very poor job of explaining the in game mechanics to the player, for example the first tedious main quest requires you to scan objects of a certain race on a certain planet type - but good luck working out how the travel system works, with-out sheer luck of clicking use on everything & hoping that it is correct - with no in-game explainations or help on these matters it is another frustration - and these are fairly early on in the game!
The fact that most of the tool tips do not actually display the real damage certain items do, or what benefits you get for eating certain foods or what certain items do is also infuriating.
A game with some interesting concepts, some well made unique dungeon instances &challenges but some extremely poor design choices, copy paste worlds, enemies, & weapons makes for a disapointing experience.
If you do decide you are going to purchase this game I would highly recommend that you play it with friends & also use some of the quality of life mods available on the workshop, such as the ability to stack food, storage container options, food tooltip descriptions etc.

Flix the Flea is a two button platformer where we play as some kind of mutant flea that snuck on-board into a space shuttle and is brought to space. If you were to skip the opening you would have no way of knowing you are in space as there are pterodactyls, bats and even trees. Granted it does take place in caves but why mention we are in space then? Nothing really makes sense which is not a bad thing but you see all this game has to offer in the first mission. Each level feels very similar even though they are visually different. There is a life system and if you lose all of them it is back to the beginning of the game.
The only way to lose your life is if you touch a  pterodactyl that flies around the stage. It is a lot easier said than done as the screen is far too zoomed in and everytime you jump you will have no idea what lies ahead.  Most of the time that leads to you following down all the way to the bottom since pterodactyls do have a huge arrow pointing at their location when near that also makes a highly annoying warning alert. But it is not uncommon to land directly on top of one and die. There is a shield powerup that allows you to take up to two hits which comes in handy.
Jumping itself is pretty simple and works well enough. As said before there are only two buttons. One to jump to the left and one to jump to the right. The longer you hold down a button the further and higher you jump. It works well enough when the game is not demanding precise platforming but it does feel like a lot of trial and error as you can't really see where you are heading until you take the jump and get a better feel for the level. Bugs and stars both litter the stages for you to collect and add to your highscore but I don't believe it adds lives once you reach enough. Though I did not bother collecting most and may be wrong.
Which brings me to my main problem with the game. It can only be played in a tiny window with no way to increase it's size or play in fullscreen. That may not be matter to some people but I find it worth mentioning as I personally can not stand playing in a window. There are no graphic options which doesn't really matter much since this game is not demanding at all. Graphically it is not a bad or good looking game. It is acceptable and does the job. There is no way to rebind the keys which may bother some as the default keys are left arrow and right arrow. Flix the Flea is really lacking in any options and is as bare-bones as they get.
Unfortunately the music in this game doesn't fare any better than the rest of it. It is mediocre but the main issue is that it is very short and loops over and over again with no option to turn it off. It is one song throughout the whole game which will be burned into your consciousness by the end of it. The jumping and bug crunching sound effects sound fine but the pterodactyl's screech is obnoxious. Repetition sets in fast due to all these factors and Flix the Flea doesn't do anything to remedy that issue in later levels. Instead it focuses more on precise platforming which just don't work well with the way you move in this game.
The novelty of only using two buttons is a good one but executed poorly. It is a very low budget game made by one person but I'm afraid I still can't recommend it. There is just very little fun to be found here and your time could be better spent elsewhere. Slamming into walls while trying to jump to the exit can be entertaining for a while though it quickly loses it's fun when the levels start to demand more precision. The only reason to play this game is if you got it through a bundle and want to collect it's trading cards. Which is actually broken and no cards can drop during the time of this review. It's kind of a shame to slam down such an obscure game but it simply isn't worth a recommendation.

The Quest for Glory series is one of my favorite game series of all time. I have put so many hours into these games, I have lost count. These games mix classic point-and-click (for the first 2 games, text parser) adventure with RPG action... and it mixes them beautifully. These games make me feel happy everytime I play them making them perfect for relaxation games.
The soundtrack for these games are very amospheric and filled with calming and memorable melodies. My favorite part in most Sierra adventures is their tongue-in-cheek humor, and these games have tons of those moments which I absolutely love, always referencing that there is a player controlling the character while also throwing in references from other Sierra titles every now and then. You can tell the makers of this series had fun.
One feature I love from these games, and I wish other game series had this, is if you max out your character in one game, you can carry it over to the next, inventory included! It really makes you want to grind your character in one game, then progress to the next playing a total badass while he takes on any monster the game throws at him whilst still building your character for the next. Rinse and repeat. So satisfying!
These games have lots of replayablility mainly because when you create a character, you have to choose a class: Fighter, Magic User, or Thief. Each puzzle has a different solution depending on which class you choose. Plus, there are areas in the game a particular class can only have access to. There is also a hidden class that you can achieve for in Quest for Glory 2 which is the Paladin class which grants you some special magic spells and a better sword. Since Quest for Glory allows you to carry over your character into all of the games in the series, the Paladin gives you access to some additional quests in later games that the other classes can't.
My a favorite games of the series are QFG2, QFG4, and QFG1. All the games in the series are great, but these 3 define the series for me and make me come back for more each time.
Buy these games, you will not regret it!

Quest for Glory 3: Wages of War and Quest for Glory 4: Shadows of Darkness changed my life.  No joke.
I think I was twelve or so when I was handed a used Win95 machine and a bunch of programs.  Two of them were the floppies for QfG3 and QfG4.  Also had the Famous Adventurer's Guide and other items.  These were the two games I would play over and over.  They changed how I view games from then on.  Every RPG I run at the table is, in some way, inspired by the design of Quest for Glory.
The open ended puzzles that cater to individual classes, yet allow multiclass characters to work.  The embracing tropes, but then going onto mess with them.  The silly NPCs and references sitting along side Big Adventure.  Exotic locals.  The writing of the game.  Razzle Dazzle Root Beer.  These are the things I try to include in all my games.
I don't know which was my favorite.  QfG4 is fully voiced, with an incredible performance by John Rhys-Davies that immerses you in the lite-horror themed world.  He sells every word and I cannot imagine that game without his voice threatening you with doom if you dare use that item somewhere you shouldn't.  "That wouldn't be a good idea" has never sounded so menacing.  I have no idea why he wasn't nabbed by every video game since.  QfG4 was also a buggy mess back in the day, and would crash frequently due to it relying on processor timings that were not future proofed.
QfG3 is also great.  If it had John Rhys-Davies giving me dire warnings of the Awful Waffle Walker, it would be Best Game.  I was in an alpha for an expansion to an MMO that was African themed.  I mentioned that it reminded me of QfG3.  A dev immediately started talking to me about the game.  We pulled in one of the environmental artists into the conversation.  I recall we also dragged the chief animator into it, and tried to convince them to replace centaurs with liontaurs.
I love these games so much.  I had the original floppies for 3 & 4.  I found a stash of unopened boxes of the original collection hiding in a store that shouldn't even be selling games.  I bought them all, kept two incase the first broke, and sold the rest for $80 a pop.  First thing I did when I finally got internet at home was buy QfGV from Amazon, even though I didn't get a computer that could run it right until later.  I bought the collection the moment it was on GoG, and now again on Steam.  I did extensive experiments regarding sound cards and sound card emulators when setting up the games.  (Roland MT-32 is best)  I've had the same avatar since Steam launched, that of the QfG3 cover.  I use the names from these games whenever I need a character name in an MMO.  I use the Hero's March as a ringtone.  I bought this collection JUST to post this review.  That is how important these games are to me.
These games, man.  Best Sierra ever produced in my opinion.
(Heads up.  Quest for Glory II: Trial by Fire is text parser interface.  There in a complete fan made VGA remake of it that you should play if the text parser is a stumbling block.)
I hereby nominate this game for the Changed My Life Award.

I have played the Quest for Glory series for over 20 years now.  After 20 years of playing the series, I still start each game with the same sense of fun I started with.  This series is well told, with an entire world, lore, characters, magic and strategies to learn. I remember this game like my oldest, dearest friend. I'd come home, and my friend will be there waiting for me. There'd be tales of great adventurers, none quite like the other; the warrior and his mighty sword and strength; the wizard's cunning and secret society hidden among the swirling sands of Shapier; and the thief whose shadow is all that is seen. These are tales long since forgotten, and it's good to see them back again.
This game does one thing that I've not seen be mainstream or ever (or at lest very seldomly) done. You can save your endgame character (with all the buffed up stats) from the first game and import that character to the sequel. You can begin your new adventure with a familiar character and be a thief/warrior/magic user in a new world with new stuff to do and learn. You don't just play an adventurer. You ARE the adventurer.
I can't recommend this game enough. If Steam had an icon for two thumbs up, I'd click. Then, I'd ask for another button that has 20,000 thumbs up and it still wouldn't be enough. It's only $10. Buy it. Play it with the wonder of being brought to a new world. You'll love it.
UPDATE: November 10, 2016
I see a lot of people are having trouble with importing characters. Here's how to do it:
In order to import characters, save the imported character file to the "C:\" drive. Now, it won't actually be in your real C: drive. However, saving to the game's C:\ drive places it in the same folder as the game.
For example, if you beat QFG1 and save your imported character to C:\, the import file should be located in your \steamapps\ folder in the QFG1 folder.
Now, to load an imported character, you copy and paste the import file to the main folder of the next game. In other words, save your QFG1 import file in the QFG2 folder. Then, when you're importing a character, look for the file in QFG2's "C:\" drive.

Many of my fondest video game memories are of the Quest for Glory series.  My elementary school friends and I would work together to solve the games' puzzles and understand the intricacies of the game mechanics. Whenever a new entry into the series came out, we'd each stay up really late, if not all night, playing it, so that when we met up at school later we could share our experiences.  Man, those were the days.
I got a real hit of nostalgia when I loaded up Quest for Glory 1 just now and saw the classic Sierra logo pop up along with its theme song.  I don't think I can express how much I'm looking forward to playing through these games again.

I played this series to death in the '90s, and I'm looking forward to working my way through it again. It was very satisfying to carry my character through all 5 games, as the savegame import feature was revolutionary at the time.
These games have a wonderful blend of adventure, witty jokes, and clever game design. I'd highly recommend them to anyone, especially the third and fourth games in the series.

For all its visual prowess this game is about as penetratable as a petrified nun lodged at the bottom of a swimming pool filled with concrete. "Difficult" as a word doesn't quite do this game justice as a description. It is simply the most difficult game I have ever played to the point where I have to assume that any levels following the initial first level; a hostage siege, simply don't exist, as I have never seen them, and I resign myself to the fact that I will never see them. The first level's setting however is quite apt inasmuch that it is a mirror to my own experience in futility suffered through being held hostage by this game.
The developer gives indication that the game is in fact "their's" and not "ours" as players, this is given away by the fact that there are two game modes "Original - as it was meant to be played", and "Lite - a lesser difficulty". In that it tells you that a lighter game mode was seen as beneath the grand vision of the auteur developer. This is the risk you play when purchasing Indie games. The game experience is at the cost of the deveoper's vision, when in fact the two should be achieved in unison.
I also could accept that the issue regarding difficulty may lie with my ability, yes, were it not for the fact that I've played pretty much every games console and micro computer in existence, right from casette based games you programmed yourself to cartridges and discs and never in all that time of completing games to a completionist level, have I encountered a game as staggeringly difficult as this. On "Lite Mode" it simply is just 25% too difficult for any invested player to achieve, makes me wonder if the game saw a gamer based focus group at any stage during its development.
However the graphics are bang on the mark and so was that developing story from what I could gather. As an investment I could hardly recommend it however purely based on time and money invested versus progression, as I have so far played 1.4 hours and still have not progressed past the first level. Princess Simulation Simulator 2014 is hands down the best game I have ever played in my hundreds of thousands of eons of life on this earth. It is a complex look into the life of a young princess, caught up in a political maelstrom which only YOU can guide her through. You will need to think realistically about the life of a princess, and the skills she will need to succeed in the political world, while also balancing her mood. You should be wary of all manner of things, ranging from assassination attempts, to social or political faux-pas', both of which can cut short your political career.
The protagonist has a likeable personality, (for a fourteen year old) and a myriad of different outfits to choose from, each of which give specific boosts to a certain field of skills. The addition of these outfits make the protagonist feel like a real person, as real people also change their clothes to suit their vocations.
On a socio-political level, Princess Simulation Simulator 2014 could drastically improve the quality of life for any aspiring politician, or even just as a human being. The skill descriptions provide real world advice on how to improve, and generally are very helpful. I would recommend this game to any person who is the heir or heiress to a large fortune or amount of political power, as it is a very realistic look at the various challenges you might face. Furthermore, anyone looking to expand their wardrobe or fashion sense should play this game, as the outfits that the protagonist changes between are a breath of fresh air, and would surely go over well in any social gathering.
I rate this game a total of seven stars out of seven, with an additional nine ghost points, to boot! The gameplay is fast paced and exciting, with never a dull moment to be seen. The dialogue is stellar, and I must emphasize that each of the writers of this game should be given the Nobel Peace Prize for their amazing work. However, the game misses out on the elusive tenth ghost point because I do not wish to appear to have been bought out by the developers of the game in order to give it a perfect review.

Long Live the Queen is a surprisingly engrossing visual novel type experience.  With a surprising number of endings and a well-written story I can readily encourage anyone who enjoys visual novels to give this one a try.
The game covers the year until our protagonist's coronation ceremony, and while there are many different endings make no mistake, living until that coronation is by no means a guarentee.  With assassins, betrayals by nobility, wars, and duels both magical and non-magical there are many ways to meet an untimley end.  This game even brings with it a more literal meaning to "death by chocolate."  Each week you choose two topics to be tutored in, which is how you gain skills in the game.  You will have a bonus or penalty to how much you learn based on your mood plus you'll learn skills you already have many points in more quickly.  Then you'll choose how to spend your weekend which will affect your mood.  Each week there is also an event.  What happens in each event is not only affected by your previous choices, but by your skill levels.  By default you can see the skill checks that the game is making, and it can be rather disheartening to see several failed checks pass by (or sometimes worse, a single one followed by a death), but it gives you some idea what you're missing and helps you plan what you'd like to be able to do differently on later playthroughs.
A lot of the intrigue can be a little hard to keep up with, but you can see the effort that went into the game's story with more and more attempts.  Studying up and your history and domestic and foriegn affairs will provide insight in the flavor text of the skill increases, but will also give the protagonist more insight and options in dealing with them.  Quickly it becomes clear that each betrayal, each rebellion, and everyone's feelings about you are actually justified and their characters actually have consistency.  On a first playthrough someone's actions can seem like a cheap plot twist, but only on another attempt do you have the right combination of skills and make the right choices to learn you actually could have seen it coming.
And make no mistake, you will play this game several times.  Even should you live to your coronation a single playthrough will only take a few hours, depending on how fast you read.  But there are several times the length of one attempt worth of hidden treasures that are fully worth digging for.
Long Live the Queen is a game with heart and genuine emotional involvment.  If you have any interest in the genre you owe it to yourself to give this a try.

Dark Souls is definitely one of those old classics that anyone with enough patience to deal with anything that isn't up to the modern stand should give a shot. The controls are rather poor, and poorly optimized to pc, you definitely want to play this with a controller. I tend to use the steam controller and enjoy that greatly but of course it's the players preference. Aside from these control issues and the occasional bad camera angle *cough* capra demon *cough*, It's a wonderful and challenging game with plenty of opportunity to explore a world riddled with deep and highly subjective lore. I'd certainly recommend this to anyone who can put up with the aforementioned issues but loves a good challenge and/or a good story. If you've played other games by From Softwware and are trying to delve more into the Dark Souls series and are trying to decide what in particular to buy, I'd say this is probably the best game for people who haven't played a Souls game before. There's a wide variety of things you can do right after you leave the 'tutorial' area, and it's start is a good balance between 2's rather bland tutorial and 3's rather punishing tutorial. If you're looking for more challenge and exploration, you'd probably want to go with 2 instead. After 2's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tutorial area there are already a couple ways to progress that are fun and challenging, and there are some new game mechanics in it that while they are very punishing to new players, they can be a rewarding challenge to veterans, like reducing max health after each death. If you're coming here straight out of Bloodborne or just want to♥♥♥♥♥♥around with other friends that are already familiar with the series, you definitely want to get 3. Through Bloodborne, From learned a lot more about game design and they put all their new ideas into grand improvement of 3. Additionally the password matchmaking system in 3 allows you to play with your friends easier and remove any soul level restrictions.

I first played this game because someone gave me it, knowing that I wouldn't want it. I accepted the gift and played it anyway out of curiosity. I played it completely blind save for a few friends giving me tips here and there, and I ended up quickly hating this game. Fast forward almost a year from that point, and I picked it up again on account of someone doubting that I could beat it, and so I played it. I deleted my old save file, since I jokingly picked the Depraved class on my first playthrough. I started a new file, picking the super obvious best class (knight), giving my character a terrible blonde bowl haircut, and set him as the smiling black dude. I was set.
I got to where I was in my previous playthrough in absolutely no time at all, noting how much obviously easier the game was when actually using a class, and I continued from there, still running the game completely blind. I got stuck, so I looked some♥♥♥♥♥♥up because I just couldn't find where to go and didn't feel like wasting more time than needed. Looking through the guide, I found that I looked over a dimly lit ladder about 4 or 5 times, so I climbed on while continuously using the guide since I found out that I missed some pretty essential stuff. This continued pretty far into the game, and I gawked at how many essential things were locked away without any possible sign of said essential thing actually even being in the game. This is what this game got wrong, but also got right.
In my point of view, hiding things (very, very well, mind you) that are 100% required to complete the game is automatically a red flag in my brain in terms of the quality of a video game. I've played many MANY games like this in the past, considering I collect vintage games as a hobby, and it's extremely rare that I actually enjoy any game that does this on my first playthrough. However, to many people out there that don't share that same hobby, I can see why they might see something like this being implemented as something special, unique or additive to its difficulty. I kept asking myself, "why would a game like this insist on using a retired method used by age-old games to simply drag out the play time of their game?" Well, it took me until the very end of the game to find the answer: this method is used as a metaphor of a sort. It's much more of an artistic stance than it is meant for the enjoyment of the gamer.
As I said previously, I continuously used the guide for my playthrough, yet as I moved along through the game, it felt as if the guide started to become less and less effective. Over time, less things surprised me, hidden paths became more noticable, traps were laughably easy to avoid, and enemies became nothing more but fodder to my blade. I mainly stopped using the guide after a while, and the world of Dark Souls became more and more familiar to me as time went on. It's like I could see everything for the first time. It's like I was becoming something much larger than this world I once was indefinitely confused by. It was almost as if I've become ruler of it.
Then, I played the DLC area. The bosses absolutely destroyed me for the most part, and this strange world I was taken to looked so much more friendly than the one I left, yet it ultimately was much more harsh. It pushed my buttons like no other area in Dark Souls did, and I actually began to enjoy myself. I continued onwards, slaying the last few bosses that were in my way with relative ease. Alas, the final battle between Gwyn and I was near. Warping to Firelink Shrine for the final time, I took note of the dwindling numbers of the residents here. This place almost felt eerie due to the missing presence of so many I once lounged about to talk to. I shurgged, returned to the Lordvessel, and placed the souls of those I've conquered in it.
I moved forward, and into the bright staircase below. I caught a glimpse of a familiar Black Knight figure moving slowly in the distance. "Just another enemy to kill," I thought to myself. I walked up, shield at the ready for its assault, but as I walked closer, it never attacked and instead proceeded to move across, paying no attention to me. Still assuming it was an enemy and merely bugged, I lunged at it, only for my sword to go straight through it. It was an image of an enemy; a ghost. There was no satisfaction in this. It was an enemy that had already lost. One last surprise. I shrugged this off as well, and proceeded down into the now very familiar castle from the DLC area. This castle seemed much more comfortable to me than the castle from the past, as I now understand it to be. I continued, slaughtering the rest of Gwyn's dwindling army. I was at his gate almost immediately: no real struggle. Not like the castle from long ago. I waltzed into Gwyn's dirty, unkempt chamber and fairly easily took his life. It was the end of the game, but I didn't feel any sense of accomplishment at all. It was as if I had just hunted down an old, wounded wolf. I ended the game; no big, final hoorah to send the player off. Only a short, lifeless cutscene showing you that you've succeeded.
That's where I understood this game. It's not just a game, it's meant to be taken much deeper than that. You become the game. This isn't a difficult game by any means, because it's no longer a difficult place that you were thrust into: not like in the DLC where the land was once full of creatures that have yet to succumb to time. The land, and its inhabitants, of Dark Souls are tired, and were already beaten far before you came there. The only thing holding you back from the ending was a handful of cheap tricks and a long path.
Dark Souls is meant to mould you into something this land hasn't seen in many, many years. Nothing is tougher than you: only you are. As long as you are willing to play this game all the way to the end, you will always see the final boss, because the final boss is you. This is why you aren't anywhere near punished by death comparatively to anyone else. This is why you can use these bonfires in ways nobody else can. This is why you become the single most mobile being in the land with the Lordvessel. This is why you can kill anything without even thinking about it by the end of the game. This is why Gwyn no longer uses his bonfire. This is why you decide the fate of the rest of the world. This is why I have grown to love this game.
Dark Souls has some really good things going for it, and it makes it somewhat addicting, however it also has some glaring flaws due to the way it goes about establishing its own artistic value. This is a fantastic game, but it could easily do without the Simon's Quest-esque trickery.

What a great survival horror experience this was, despite being my second time playing the game, after the original!
Storywise being the first game in the main series, Resident Evil 0 boasts great horror atmosphere and graphics (enhanced in the remaster), spooky music, tense sequences and nice puzzle moments that really make you use your head, always in style with what Capcom has done with this franchise so far.
The addition of the partner system was also nice, since your inventory is very limited in space, so you had to make best use of both characters (Billy and Rebecca) in order to make it, by exploiting each character's unique features.
The zombies and monsters were plenty and with great variety and the same applies to the bosses.
I really appreciated the newly added Wesker mode too (not present in the original game), with which you can play as the series' main antagonist Albert Wesker (duh) and use some more unique (and badass) features for such character, though it was more of a glorified Billy skin (with some words and cool moves), than the character interacting himself.
The story was ok, nothing extraordinary and a bit cheesy at times, but in line with the other games of the series and with enough twists... after all, as I wrote, the atmosphere, music and puzzles more than make up for it!
Lastly, if I had to complain about one and only thing in this great game, that would be... DOORS! Infinite numbers of them, which equal infinite loading times for very small environments, but oh well, guess I can't be too picky since the game is more than a decade old and also since, like it or not, it's a distinguished trait of the first Resident Evil games (in a way it adds some charm to the atmosphere too).
That will be all for now then, and remember... shoot them in the head!

A good classic RE game with one rather big drawback: just about everything it does is handled better in Resident Evil 1. It has some good puzzles, the environments are fun to explore and figure out. But overall, the level design is more straightforward than RE1, the absence of Crimson Heads makes traversal less interesting, storyline is cheesier than your typical RE storyline (which usually contains a high quantity of cheese), item management can be a chore without item boxes, and voice acting and writing is worse than RE1. I still recommend the game, just don't go in with extremely high expectations.
Remaster-wise, it actually surpasses RE1 Remaster by quite a lot. Like RE1 Remaster, it features some new outfits, it has a new rendering engine which makes characters look a lot better, but the biggest difference is that they were able to re-render all the backgrounds. Seeing real-time rendered characters with high resolution pre-rendered backgrounds gives the game a very distinct, cool look. The only thing I personally don't like with the new graphics is that they re-designed Rebecca's face, and she ended up looking much worse. Thankfully, there are mods to fix that.
One thing I find baffling is that they decided to leave in the door animations without any option to skip them. They were originally implemented to mask loading times, but that no longer applies, so you end up looking at doors slowly opening for several hours throughout a playthrough. If you ever get tired of them, I suggest heading over to steam guides and installing a mod for skipping the door animations.

Disclaimer: The following game was played and reviewed without the use of nostalgia glasses.
I never owned a Gamecube or a Playstaton 3. I had a Playstation 2. It was there that I discovered the fun survival horror of Resident Evil. I played and beat the original and had beaten Resident Evil 2 many times over 15 years ago. Fond memories.  The series went on without me and I watched the series change. Back in the day when the Resident Evil remake was done, I was excited to see the game get a serious facelift, but I had no way of playing it. Then I learned about Resident Evil 0 and I became mildly curious. An origin story....could be promising. I am so happy that a lot of the RE games have made their way to the PC, enabling me to play the entries that were inaccessible. With the announcement and now release of RE7, I decided it was time to go through the series, see where it all started and watch the mutation of one of the best survival horror franchises.
For those who love the classic adventure slant of the Resident Evil franchise, this is a must play. When it come to Resident Evil, I will probably always prefer the third person perspective. The tension is high as you never know what is around the corner, until you round the corner. The use of puzzles to advance rather than gunning everything down was wonderful territory to revisit. I enjoyed the herbs, the files, the typewriters, and those famous doors, stairs, and ladders loading screens. But this game is much more than paying homage to the familiar elements of the series. Its a wonderful blend of the old and the new, for me at least.
Chris and Jill....Claire and Leon....and now, Rebecca and Billy. While in previous entries where you had to play two separate campaigns to get a feel for each character, we have two people helping each other in one campaign, and it works out really well. Rebecca may not be a master of unlocking, but she knows how to mix herbs which makes her a strong asset to Billy Coen who is the muscle of the two. The two start a wary alliance but by the end of the game they have come to each others rescue multiple times and have formed a strong bond. There will be times that they have to split up to achieve goals and progress through the game. You can easily switch between the two and choose a Team setting or have one of them go by themselves. On Team setting, the AI Billy or Rebecca has your back, and is very good at covering for you. This served as a strength and weakness for this game. As I controlled Rebecca, it was hard to get scared because I had Billy following and covering with a shotgun. But when circumstances forced Rebecca away from Billy....thats when I would freak. She's a medic. She can shoot a gun, but she does not have the muscle that Joey has. I was always happy when the two met up again.
Now how does this story fit as an origin story? I think pretty well. In the bounds of the Resident Evil universe it makes sense. Those who have played RE1 and RE2 will probably understand the character relationships better and will enjoy the familiar faces.
The survival horror aspect is a mixed bag. First off, there are some new monsters that will make you want to run rather than stay and fight. However, I found myself not getting scared so much since I had Rebecca and Billy together so much. My biggest anxiety was my very limited inventory. Rebecca and Billy have very different inventory needs (she is recovery items and small guns and he is the heavy hitter) but the same amount of slots. What I wouldn't have given for those wonderful classic storage bins!! It would have been nice to find a little side pack to add a little more inventory space, but oh well. Instead you have to drop items and pick up others. On the plus side, when you look at the map, you can see all the items you dropped and where they are, so you can go back and retrieve them. Whats annoying is that when you find a puzzle related item, you don't know if you should pick it up or not because the puzzle might not show up for a while. You don't know how long to run around with the grenade launcher or shotgun because it is RE and big baddies can show up at any moment. It really is the scariest part of the game...what do I take with me!?
The game is beautiful. I never saw the original so I can't compare but oh my goodness it is gorgeous in a survival horror kind of way. The controls have two options: the more modern controls or the original. I found myself at home with either, since I prefer the birds eye view. The soundtrack is also very RE. The voice acting was perfect. Rebecca is spunky, strong, resilient, and a great healer. Joey won me over with his entrance and it made me very sad to watch him walk into the sunset. I hope to see him again.
As I finished RE0, I knew another playthrough would be in the future. This game has the feel of a classic RE game with the beautiful modern graphics. Rebecca Chambers is currently high on my favorite RE characters list, and I look forward to seeing her again in Resident Evil as I play as Chris for the first time.

Gods Will Be Watching attempts to straddle several horses, among them being punishing difficulty, making morally ambiguous choices, puzzle-solving, vignetted storytelling, and so many more that wind up stretching it too thin to be enjoyable.
Due to your sweaty-palmed fate you've spent the last 20-60 minutes crafting (in this instance, let alone the last few hours you've spent on the game in previous chapters) coming down to a dice roll, having to restart it over and over saps the impact from the story at hand. From reading further reviews and watching lets plays (I admit it, for help and guidance), the worst part of this draining experience is that if you've somehow managed to haphazardly grope your way through a level, sacrificing life and limb, your choices wind up not mattering at all in the tail end of the game.
After your sixth try at a level, it turns into a monotonous gray slop you have to somehow make sure you do not muck up at before you get to where you mucked up at last, and then either continue your so far 'proven' method of beating the level, or riding it out to failure oncemore.
No amount of 'the end explains all of the retconning' or 'git gud lol u suck' will justify this game's existence in my game library. I'm fairly sure I could hand a zoo full of monkeys a typewriter and then have the local crack fiend outside the gas station edit the monkeys' work into a text-based adventure game (with illustrations) off of dice rolls where he attempts to break one of my fingers and shitcans my progress every time he disagrees with me for cheaper than this game.
TL;DR voxel art point and click attempts to capitalize on the developing niche market of 'cuckold gaming', where you pay however much money to Gaben to be repeatedly destroyed for things that are and are not your fault; if you do not enjoy this game, you are a scrub who cannot appreciate art and needs to 'git gud'.

The Dark Souls series is famous for its gloomy atmosphere, the creative, sometimes grotesque, but always impressive art style and its very intense combat system. The player has to concentrate constantly, as almost every mistake might be punishable by death. In comparison to Dark Souls II, Dark Souls is a bit more welcoming to beginners because deaths do not cause the maximum health to decrease here ("hollowing"), so that the same nasty boss can be taken on without that additional disadvantage. For me, this was a frustrating turn-off in DS2, and I enjoy DS1 more. Also, unlimited enemy respawns in DS1 make farming and upgrading easier than in DS2, a significant factor for starters who prefer a lower difficulty.
However, it is still crucial to study the game in order to advance. You need to know how stronger enemies and bosses can be beaten, either by your own observation or by watching tutorials. And you have to optimize your stats, at least as a new player, in order to gain some wiggle room for the inevitable mistakes. Basically, by optimizing your stats, you determine the difficulty of your game: Running around naked with a dagger and without levelling up is one of the highest "difficulty settings". If you want to have an easier first run, you watch tutorials and read wikis in order to
- find the best locations to farm souls (= xp points and currency) in repeated killing sprees and subsequent zone resets (=enemy respawns) at a Bonfire
- understand how the basic stats determine secondary stats (e.g. strength and physical damage, or encumbrance and roll speed)
- get tips how to upgrade both your character and your weapons and armour
- learn where to find or buy pieces of equipment that suit your playstyle and match each other.
One example for matching equipment at the beginning of the game would be:
- Zweihänder, a heavy and slow weapon that deals high damage and gives you a good chance to stagger enemies, but consumes a lot of stamina with each attack
- Grass Crest Shield, a special item that boosts your stamina regeneration even when worn on your back, while two-handing your weapon
- Elite Knight Armour, which is relatively heavy, but gives good defence values and poise, enabling you to take hits from quicker enemies while you build up your slow two-handed attack without being staggered or killed
- Havel's Ring, a magical ring that increases your load capacity, meaning that you can still run and dodge roll relatively fast despite of heavy equipment
This example should give you an idea how complex building a character can be, as there are so many interacting factors to consider.
Due to the number of equippable items and viable strategies, all the DS games invite players to try out different combinations and find out what suits their taste most - not only regarding tactics and weapon movement sets that "feel good", but also the looks of your hero (the internet created the term "Fashion Souls" for a reason).

The tagline of this game should read "Your choices don't matter."
I never seen a game that is so anti-choice, it literally embodies it into the story and makes it part of the gameplay. And smugly claims "That is how its supposed to be". So basically a game where the makers admit is designed poorly, and forego immersion for the least interesting part of the story.
It starts on the wrong foot by having the first level be the hardest one, because nothing like a bad first impression.
On the second level we are shown their stellar QA, where if your buddy dies he still keeps talking during the scenes. And surprise! It doesn't matter because the story continues as if nothing happened to him.
The third level is the better designed one, but still none of your choices get carried over, removing any challenge from it due to lack of any real consequences.
In the fourth level I had 3 people of my crew die, and that only made the level easier. allowing me to I click wherever halfway through.
The fourth level almost seemed like it involved some tactics, but then you realize there is only one proper way to play it, and it becomes busywork.
I liked the idea of the fifth level initially, but that all went alway when I finished it by just guessing the password codes, which I wasnt expecting the game to let me.
And then comes the final battle, the ultimate middle finger to the concept of choices, where the final boss just telegraphs his moves and you have to select the proper counter move. The last attack will always result in a kick animation regardless of what you had to click.
You are given one last "choice" that matters very very little, mostly for the stats shown at the end of every chapter.
At the end it is explained why nothing gets carried over, even though it just as easily could have been used to explain branching story lines.
Its a terrible shame, because this game has lots of interesting concepts (and all with poor executions) and I really liked the art-style. It would have lots of potential if the whole concept didn't revolve around removing the most important aspect that makes a game worth playing: meaningful choices.

Full review:
Many of you may just look at Long Live the Queen and pass it off as some “girly anime game”. I too thought that the game looked a bit silly, but I was surprised by just how enjoyable it is. It’s almost a masterpiece, which is not something I’d say too easily.
Long Live the Queen is essentially a visual/interactive novel, but it goes a lot more in-depth in terms of interactivity that most visual novels do. You’re tasked with getting the main character, Elodie, to her coronation as Queen of Nova without getting killed. Although the game seems incredibly childish, it’s actually quite morbid. There are several deaths that Elodie can run into, with my first one being an arrow to the side, of which my “battlefield medicine” skill was not high enough for me to survive the incident.
The other half of the game, aside from making good choices, is made up of skills. Elodie can learn a variety of skills. It’s actually a bit overwhelming, the amount of different skills that can be learned. Every week, you have the choice of choosing two classes to take during that specific week, with each skill having its own class. Each of these skills is a part of a group of skills, which is a part of another group of skills. For example, the “Social” skill tree is made up of three skills: Royal Demeanor, Conversation, and Expression. Each of these breaks down even further, into three “sub-skills”. Expression breaks down into: “Decoration”, “Instrument”, and “Voice”. The four major categories for skills are: Social, Intellectual, Physical, and Mystical.
During the development of the game’s story, you’ll encounter various “skill checks” during the dialogue portions of the story. Passing a skill check is always good, as it progresses the story in a positive way (and can help prevent your death). Failing a skill check usually does not matter too much, but in some scenarios, failing a skill check can actually cause your death.
There’s also another major aspect to this game, that being Elodie’s mood. Her mood changes based on what happens during the storyline of the game and the choice you make at the end of the week as to what Elodie will do during the weekend. There are four sets of moods in the game, with two different emotions in each: Afraid — Angry, Depressed — Cheerful, Yielding — Willful, and Lonely — Pressured. Whichever mood is dominant determines the skill bonuses for that specific week (each “turn” in the game is another week). Each mood gives a bonus and a penalty to certain skills. The “depressed” mood gives a bonus to expression and animal handling, but a penalty to royal demeanor, conversation, and athletics, with all other skills remaining neutral. This can be used to greatly improve any of Elodie’s skills, depending on her mood that week.
Long Live the Queen was a very, very fun experience. If I had to criticize the game, I’d note that the player has no idea which moods correspond to which skills in terms of bonuses and penalties (until you have that specific mood), so the use of a wiki is almost essential. I prefer to go at it and learn myself, but I could understand one using a wiki to avoid getting penalties when attending classes. Also, unless you use a wiki, you’ll have no idea when a certain skill will be required anytime during the story. You may get the hang of it after playing the game for an extended period of time though. Highly recommended!

This was tough choice to vote down or up as I did enjoy small partsof the game, but due to a lot of poor design choices & annoying game mechanics I recommend you spend your time & money on other more enjoyable games.
* Fun weapon types which can have interesting secondary fire modes (the first time you discover them)
* Multiple levels of crafting stations & ship upgrades to encourage you to explore other planets
* Some of the unique main quests or outpost quests along with the portal challenges found underground are fun & challenging (the first time you discover them)
* Copy, paste & repeat weapon types - once you have found one type of weapon you are going to see a lot more of them throughout your playthrough
* Copy, paste & repeat enemies - fairly limited re-skinned enemy types, with the same attack patterns
* Copy, paste & repeat dungeons / portal challenges - it's interesting the first time you find a unique NPC village or challenge, however you quickly realise that after you've seen it once, you are going to see pretty much the same thing on every planet you go to
* I found the difficulty levels to be fairly frustrating- the food system was more of an annoyance than a challenge - forcing you to stop whatever you are doing to quell the irritating beeping for another 5 minutes.
The game was also very easy to complete as I played the vast majority of it in solo mode & I didn't need to craft the top end gier or potions, food etc to complete it & ultimately it felt a bit of a let down when I completed it
* Main quests - part good, part bad - the game generally requires you to do one mission to scan items of a certain race, which first involves finding that civilization.  This can be extremely frustrating (they aren't always on the planet type they point you towards in the quest description & with virtually no information as to where abouts to find them on that planet type, sometimes you can be looking for hours unless you look it up online).  Once you do find them you simply left click on everything in sight with your scanning tool to fill up an arbitary meter bar before returning back to the quest giver (and you may need to visit multiple planets of the same copy paste world types to fill up this meter) - I realise this is to encourage you to check out new planets or their creations, but it just isn't fun & you will need to do this at least 3 or 4 times in the main quest line for different races which seems like extremely lazy game creation to me.  Once you managed to get these scanning quests completed they unlock the actual dungeons & unique instances in the main quest were actually enjoyable.
Tutorial / tooltips - the game does a very poor job of explaining the in game mechanics to the player, for example the first tedious main quest requires you to scan objects of a certain race on a certain planet type - but good luck working out how the travel system works, with-out sheer luck of clicking use on everything & hoping that it is correct - with no in-game explainations or help on these matters it is another frustration - and these are fairly early on in the game!
The fact that most of the tool tips do not actually display the real damage certain items do, or what benefits you get for eating certain foods or what certain items do is also infuriating.
A game with some interesting concepts, some well made unique dungeon instances &challenges but some extremely poor design choices, copy paste worlds, enemies, & weapons makes for a disapointing experience.
If you do decide you are going to purchase this game I would highly recommend that you play it with friends & also use some of the quality of life mods available on the workshop, such as the ability to stack food, storage container options, food tooltip descriptions etc.

How do you imagine the perfect zombie apocalypse game? For me it's storyline from The Last of Us, characters and dialogues from Telltale's The Walking Dead, weapon crafting and time expiring events from Dead Rising, many side quests from Dead Island (ignore the one where the drunk guy asks you for alcohol), the real survival from Project Zomboid, horror mood from Resident Evil, open world from most of them and the multiplayer combining the best from Left 4 Dead and DayZ.
State of Decay ads to that managing your own base and group of survivors. Game draws you in its world very quickly and is very addictive. There is always something more to do in it. But it lacks a good story and multiplayer. I can stand no multiplayer in it, but the good plot? Not so easy.
What i mean is not that the game has no storyline at all. It has, but after a few missions the story of your survivor crew breaks off and you have to witness boring stories of army and some other groups. Most of people that joins your crew is generated randomly. They have no personality so it is hard to become acquainted with them. Death in State of Decay is permanent and hurts very bad, but it would hurt even more if you would knew these people.
State of Decay is not an ultimate zombie survival game but it's really, really close. So i recommend it to all of you looking for a good zombie apocalypse game. Developers - Undead Labs have a name that obliges and they are already making their new game so I keep my fingers crossed.
