Press X to Not Die, is a throwback to the classic quicktime event full motion video games like Dragons Lair, Space Ace, and Braindead 13. FMV is a genre of games where the player would be given a choice to perform an action, or die. Pressing the button for a choice didn’t assure living either, you had to make the right choice, or else your character would still die. Think of the genre as a video version of a choose your own adventure book, that is linear, and a second play through is rarely ever needed.
So now that you know what you would get into with purchasing PXTND generally, how is the game itself? (TLDR at the bottom) I guess to start, the game is linear for most playthroughs, with very little variety on how the game changes based on your decisions. There are 20+ ways to die, and its fairly easy to get through the whole game. The gameplay is as such, watch the video, until the game prompts you to press a button, or a character asks you a question. If you fail to press the right button, more often than not you die, and go back approximately 20 seconds to try again. The answers you give do not seem to seem to change anything for the most part, and that’s the game. I finished it once, and to be honest, there wasn’t a reason to play again for the following reasons:
This is a game that lacks inspiration. Reviving a dead genre is normally done with a goal in mind, a new twist on the same old story; PXTND is not it. The story is more or less first person Dawn of the Dead, the story of how it happens is generic military scheme, and the spoken jokes are outdated pop culture references. Farmville, Twilight, Hunger games, and angry birds are the references, 4 in total that I found, and when they were not out of place (the Twilight reference was just shoehorned in), it became weirdly pretentious (accepting angry bird players, but hating on Farmville…). There were 2 visual gags that made me laugh, if you play the game you will spot them, but overall if someone is trying to sell this game to you as comedy, you will be disappointed. The few jokes are counteracted by the bad acting, which you have to sit through to get through the game.
To start about the bad acting, the game informs me in the extra’s menu that the reason why the acting is bad is because it is purposefully trying to do a callback to bad B movie acting. That is just a lie; when I hear bad B movie acting, I think of overacting, I think of overactive screams, out of place expressions, I think of campy out of place moments and over the top reactions. Don’t let the trailer fool you, the first character Matt nailed B movie. He gives a great intro, lets you know how to play the game, gets shanked, and then lets you know he forgot to press X, ♥♥♥♥ING METAL! That intro, and the fact the game was on sale, is why I purchased the game. For the rest of PXTND the acting past the intro takes a nosedive, the zombies all are doing an impersonation of DOTD zombies, and really don’t bring anything. Again, its college art movie, not B movie, so they lack direction to look like anything other than people pretending to be a zombie/crazed person. Don’t let someone sell you the line that looking like a highschooler filming their first youtube video is what they were going for. It wasn’t funny bad, it was unprepared mess. The biggest problem is the girlfriend in the games acting.
The majority of the game, the only person giving dialogue is your girlfriend. While the zombies in the game try to kill you, she tries to kill the game. No expressions outside of line reading, no emotion, not inflection, just reading the lines. A paper plate on a stick would have been preferred. She brought nothing, and while she is supposed to be the sarcastic death relief (oh you died because…) that didn’t happen. I think the writer was imagining a crazy, spunky girl as he was writing her character, and didn’t envision that someone who looks as stiff as a board through the whole game would be the choice for the lead.
This is the sort of game that reminds me to be wary of the indie community. This just isn’t good, and the people that are adamant that this is the second coming, I think just want to be part of something. It lacks wit, it is using outdated jokes, its pacing is crap, its death scenes are without humor or irony, its 1 liners are out of place, the acting is bad, and not in the fun MST3K way, and the bulk of its jokes are just pop culture references. The game ends with letting you know there is already a planned sequel, but if this was the dream project of someone to revive the FMV genre, and it lacks all of the charms that made those games great, then why would you buy an into an episodic game series that doesn’t seem to have a direction other than making a movie on their Go Pro and taking your money. This could have been shot in a day, written in a day, and programed in a day. This isn’t a passion project, it’s a small developer banking off of the indie community♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves to proclaim how cool they are for playing such a unique pile of crap, that only true Scottsmen get its comedy.
TLDR;
Bad, unfunny acting; Spoken jokes are all pop culture references; Story is the definition of generic; Story is pandering to how Meta gamers are... without irony; No replay-ability; Completely devoid of inspiration; Short (less than 30 minutes), with planned future episodes; Overall a black mark on the already stained FMV genre.

Dark Souls 1 is a hardcore RPG game, that was developed by FromSoftware and published by Namco Bandai Games. It has a refined combat system, decent graphics based on the time of its release, and rewarding gameplay.
I did not complete Dark Souls 1, but after purchasing the game I was determined that I would complete the game as I could prove to myself that I wasn't a noob when it came to this genre. After a days worth of hours sacraficed into this game, I still didn't believe that I would be able to complete the game, and the motivation to keep playing died due to its minimalistic story telling, and the shear difficulty of this game. Before you all try to murder me in a more savage way than any Dark Souls boss did, I would like to justify myself.
Sure this game is fantastic, and people that enjoy a strategic and punishing combat system will love the hell out of this game. Despite it being released in 2011, its graphics aren't outdated to any extent all thanks to DSfix.
The combat mechanics are some of the best that I have ever seen playing a game. You have to be strategic when it comes to battle, otherwise your a gonner, and you will remain a gonner unless you reflect on your combat methods, and try to find the most appropriate way to attack your enemy. Every enemy in this game has a unique fighting style, making every battle enjoyable until you die of course, as you then have to trek back across the badass world of Dark Souls fighting the same badass creatures that you had already spent excessive time slaughtering.
The sound effects of the game are decent, and the soundtrack is immersive and makes battling your foes that more intense.
The games combat and graphics were enough to keep me satisfied with the game for a reasonable amount of time, but the unforgiving difficulty ruined my experience entirely. Sure, this game was designed to be difficult, and the majority of people that have played this game have completed it, after many attempts and alot of dedication. I however don't have the fuse of these hardcore Dark souls warriors, and got fed up of retracing my footsteps only to get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me on a silver platter by the same creature that had KO'ed me previously.
I know, i've dissapointed the Dark Souls community by giving up so soon, but I would recommend this game to anyone who was questioning whether to buy it or not, as the experience that I had may have been irritating, but this was made acceptable by the rewarding feeling of defeating a boss after hours of dedication and the vast amount of customization that you can do to your character. I understand that this game was created to be difficult and to put the players skills to the test, and its very effective in doing so and has shaped the whole Dark Souls series, I just simply am not built to praise the sun.
I would have personally preferred the game if their was a saving function which would get rid of all the heartbreak when you die, but of course that would ruin the whole concept of Dark Souls.
Overall I loved the game, but the game didn't love me the same way.

A heck of an achievement for a zombie game, it almost gets it perfect - Almost.
This is a third person view game with some of the shoot em up of Left for Dead mixed with some of the story and social aspect of Walking Dead.   I prefer it much more to the heavily scripted Walking Dead.   Even though this game has scripting in it, it will give you missions in a random fashion.  It also has some of the social aspects of Walking Dead (kicking someone out of the group, someone gets mad, patching things up, needing certain supplies etc).
Did I mention you can climb in a truck and mow zombies down by running them over?  And, you will likely do this alot!
Although the developers should be applauded, it certainly isn't a perfect game.  The next section is where I complain......
The Biggest issue I have with the game is the zombies.  They are everywhere.  This isn't a big city you are in, it's in the country and there seems to be zombies like every 100 feet!  And, they never seem to disappear.  It doesn't really matter how many you mow down because another group seems to replace them - Almost Out Of Thin Air.
To make this more realistic, the developers need to have a set number or zombies in an area + have a regeneration rate that would be much lower than what is currently in the game.  There are not ENOUGH PEOPLE in a rural area to support the number of regeneration zombies in this game.  If you want to have huge wandering hordes that would be acceptable and a more realistic way to bring more into town.    The player would also naturally encounter more zombies, as they moved into other areas with zombies.
So, it's a really cool game with a big glaring plot hole that needs to be fixed.
UPDATE:  Lifeline.  While a cool idea,  Lifeline continues some of the glitches of the original game.
The vehicles have a very strange physics model which can make them overturn if they run over so much as an oily rag.   My truck got stuck on a tent and started Hoving.  I have seen the zombies walk through fences.   Zombies can appear suddenly out of thin air.  The player character has an annoying tendency to slide while stopping as if on Roller Blades.  NPCs leave unexpectedly and for no reason while on a mission with you and can then be seen running down the highway being chased by Zombies!
Still, they are on the right track.  They just need less drivable vehicles, less zombies and more story.

Hey, so yeah. Right up front, I've spent a couple hours messing around with this game and I'm pretty dissapointed.  I'm a huge fan of the zombie/survival genre, and this game definitely hits the nail on the head for this niche.  However, the gameplay is sub-par at best.  The potential is there, for sure, it's just lacking in so many areas.  Combat is clunky, character movement is clunky, the same 2 (maybe?) animations are used in combat.  You don't feel any sense of accomplishment when you off a zed (what they're referred to in the game).  It's more like meh, ok who's next? I'm assuming combat wasn't the main focus of the developers, but it's a zombie game, obviously a huge part of it is getting creative with how you smash skulls you know? Okay trying to refocus my thoughts.  Another core aspect of this game is the GTA-esque open world, where you're free to explore, upgrade your home base with different structures, search for resources and weapons, and ultimately complete the missions that drive the story along.  While this was a fresh and innovative look at the zombie/survival genre gameplay, I again find it lacking in many ways.  First and foremost, it's absolutely boring after about 20 minutes.  It's the same deal everytime; go to a house or shack, break in, kill a couple zombies, search in the boxes, find a resource, either grab it yourself or call in runners from your home base to come grab it.  Over and over and over again, the same old boring story.  Second, although the developers boast that you will be immersed into a community of survivors, this just does not happen.  The NPCs are dumber than a box of rocks.  They do nothing to help out unless you drive them to do it, they interfere in combat, again it's just plain boring.  Third, the cutscenes (dunno if that's what the developers were going for?) are lame and again boring, stale, dull, whatever you want to call it.  Fourth, the missions are the same 3 or 4 missions over and over again.  Meet up with this group of people to trade, go see what the army's doing, clear out an infestation, go get resources.  SAME OLD BORING STORY.  I could go on and on about how lame this game has been, but I'm going to stop and offer my two lame cents on how this game could be better.
-Fix the combat guys.  Seriously. I hit a zombie with a pipe and it's like I'm transported back to COD1, hitting germans with my entrenching tool.  I mean, how you can release a game like this after "The Last of Us" with your combat system is a tragedy.
-Give some life to your NPC survivors.  Have them work on stuff at home base, give them customizable gear, give them a personality, have them move around, rush to the gates when the guard is shooting, get a little creative for gods sake.
-The missions. I understand you sort of hemmed yourself in with the style of the game, but if you're gonna have missions at all in a game like this, you have to make them interesting.  Give a little life to the missions and this game gets a little better.
-Home base.  I come back to it and the only thing I feel is "okay, no zombies, I can look at my journal and see what else I can do?" IF you would have made home base more like a home (things you can work on, crafting, customization, interactions with characters, again creativity?) it would totally turn around how I feel about this game.
-The feels.  I want to come back to home base after a fight, or a foraging gone wrong, and feel it in the way the characters react and respond. How bout a little blood spatter on their clothes? sullen expressions or demeanor? Anything to make me feel like we're all that's left and we're trying to survive.
TL/DR: Good idea, lacking in so many areas.  Played it for a couple hours over the last few days and I don't think I even want to play anymore.  I started this review wanting to give props to the developers for making a style of game like this happen, but after really stewing over all the ways it falls short, I can't help but be super dissapointed in its execution.  Here's hoping another developer comes along and saves this style of game in the future.

So, what makes a game a great game?
Unless you're the first to create something never-seen-before with an earth-shattering-gameplay, you're living with a legacy. Your best option then is to live up with player's expectations of the genre, plus surprise them with one truly good and well executed idea to deliver a great experience.
In Dead Effect, you are shooting zombies in a spacecraft. That's it. Many titles comes to mind like Doom, Dead Space and such. And for a reason. It seems that most of these games tropes has been collaged in this game, but with no to little inspiration. The level design is repetitive, the zombies aren't that exciting, and the storyline has a smell of deja-vu.
But let's say Dead Effect uses these fairly known genre elements to lay a great core mechanic on top of it? If only.
First, your character moves a little too slowly (it glides actually since there is no footstep sounds), and can run just a few meters since he's apparently an heavy smoker. He also cannot jump so I suspect he or she's overweight too.
Your character can carry two weapons, that are predefined for most of the story campaign : pistol + rifle or revolver + shotgun. But since all the weapons are suboptimal at first, and have a atrociously long reload time, you die often - or walk back all the corridors just to be safe.
To make things worse, Dead Effect does not feature a save game or checkpoint system, forcing you to restart the whole mission even if you die a couple of seconds before the end. You're in to grind your way to the next level, and it really feels like a chore.
If you want a better weapon, don't try to pick one, you'll have to upgrade yours or buy one during the intermission - explaining why you are collecting money while trying to escape.
And here is the fatal flaw of the game. In my opinion, either :
- you design and balance each weapon to provide player with variety, uniqueness and consistency (like Doom, Half Life, Fear, etc);
- you can buy upgrades or upgraded version of your weapons in a marketplace (like Borderlands, Bioshock) to add the thrill of finding a badass one - at least for a couple of hours;
- you can upgrade your weapons & gear using "spare parts" found in the world (like Dead Space, Shadowgrounds Survivor) to add the thrill of making tough choices.
But I personnaly find using a "pay as you go to upgrade your gear" too artificial and really non-immersive, especially when you're supposed to be alone, cut from civilization.
I know that Dead Effect is a port from a iOS game, and uses micro-payements. But that's not an excuse for bad or inadequate game design. For the PC version you pay upfront, so, in way, you're supposed to see none of the monetization elements.
So, if you really like to shoot zombies, endless corridors and flat storyline, you can give this game a shot. A piece of advice : upgrade only your best weapon and be cautious of the grenadier zombies.

This is one of the rare EA games that actually uses EA as it should. The devs did not dump a early Alpha monstrosity onto Steam in order to get more funding for it, no. Rather, this is somewhere around a late Alpha, early Beta stage where the game is playable and pretty well fleshed out already but needs tweaks.
Visually, it is for the most part excellent. There are some issues with glare and over reflectiveness (which the devs have promised to work on) but everything is vibrant where it should be and dull where it should be. It does very much look like a space ship. It also is very well optimized. I experienced no jitters or lag whatsoever with everything maxed. It's not a particularly cutting edge engine, but it does the job well.
I had a good time exploring the initial mission. You got juuust enough extra information to piece together what was going on, although I do wish there was an internal "wiki" of sorts. The characters knew what this semi-mystical Stardrop was, but the player is never told.
All in all, this game shows much potential and for an EA game, it is very far along on its development path. It's clear the devs know what they are doing when putting together an exploration/adventure game. I look forward to seeing where it will go in the future.

Since I haven’t reviewed a fully fledged HOG (hidden object game) since Darkarta, I decided to dedicate several hours to this fascinating genre and write about it. Runaway Express Mystery has been around Steam for a few years already, yet it flew under my radar until several days ago. Developer Icarus Games has released two other Hidden Object Games for the platform but sadly they went off the grid since 2014. Judging their projects at a superficial first glance, I doubt they couldn’t have provided Steam players with more quality, narrative-driven experiences.
Amanda Waters is a caring mother for her two children and in 1996 she decided to take the youngsters to a train exhibition in a vaguely discussed location, which I’ll presume it must Paris since one of the main themes present also in the title is a fictional namesake to the Orient Express. I’m referring to this Runaway Express, naturally. It seems to have followed the same historic railway itinerary of Paris to Istanbul in a luxurious environment, all amenities included. Ours is a supernatural tale, of course and the female protagonist has to save her boy and girl from a sinister entity that has kidnapped them aboard the doomed train. Without spoiling anything, that trip will involve solving quite a few murder mysteries since the Runaway’s few lingering passagers cannot leave the train before finding their solace and subsequent, eternal rest.
Can’t recall the last time I didn’t play a HOG that involved ghosts or the undead, but you won’t read any complaints from me. The story has sufficient original ideas, to offer a pleasant gamplay involving novelty. If you figured out my own nickname here on Steam, you’d understand that mystery fiction and crime novels in particular, are of great interest to me. So no, Runaway Express Mystery is not a reimagining of Agatha Chriestie’s “Murder on the Orient Express”. It doesn’t have to be, since it already has set pieces and characters which shall take our heroine to several locations and back in time. Budapest itself, is rarely featured in games. Sure it was a backdrop to Hitman (Agent 47 & Contracts), but it never receives as much “screen time” as Paris.
It’s hard to find conclusive data on the graphics engine in HOGs, since most use proprietary versions. I won’t bother with that, yet I have to stress out that I was surprised by Runaway Express Mystery’s default video settings. You can't fiddle with them at all, but you don’t have to. It automatically scales to your monitor’s native resolution and playing it at 4K, I honestly didn’t expect it to go so smoothly. I never understood why some of its genre counterparts never got the memo that 1080p isn’t the threshold any longer, but at least Runaway didn’t lock me into 1366x768 like Darkarta did. I know that this game type is meant to be enjoyed even on a budget laptop, but devs need to take into account all potential players and systems. PC gaming will never be “one-size-fits-all”.
So the game runs smoothly, it scales flawlessly and for a 2D engine and assets, it plays nicely with motion and shadow animations in order to offer the illusion of 3D on occasion. I never witnessed a bug, crash or even frame rate issues. Speaking of which, no vsync option has been implemented and the Steam Overlay reported crazy FPS numbers such as 900 more often than not. Since no rapid movement is present in-game, no screen tearing will be observable either. A rare case in which 60 or 1000fps really makes no difference. The backgrounds are gorgeous, I always like HOGs for their inherent attention to even the smallest details. They couldn’t be otherwise since the genre relies heavily on player intuition and predilection towards clicking everywhere.
Runaway Express Mystery and its so far immaculate image begins to show some stains when you’re listening more closely. The soundtrack was fine, if a bit low-key. My gripe was with the voice acting which can best be described as “hit and miss”. Sure, Amanda sounds convincing enough, but most of the train’s mysterious passagers lack the depth and enthusiasm one would expect from professional voice actors. So what do we have? And old man’s voice that was lent to at least three distinct characters (TES IV Oblivion style), a singer with a clearly faux Southern belle accent and the worst transgression of them all, a British lord that sounds as authentic as Kevin Costner in 1991’s Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves. Yes, the kind of posh English you’d be yelling at a hot dog vendor in New Jersey.
At least Runaway didn’t disappoint from its gameplay perspective. It managed to mix the titular hidden object sections with challenging puzzles and evidence search. The corroboration of multiple facts on panels that would lead to a final suspect, was most pleasing. Good detective work, from a single mom whose professional background is never revealed. Of course, it’s the players that do the hard work, but for the sake of argument and some good ol’ suspension of disbelief, let’s concede that Amanda Waters will go to any lengths in order to save her children. As any mother should, no doubt. Apart from the train’s many compartments, both Paris and Budapest are well featured with several streets and addresses to visit in each case. I almost wish the trip would have ended in Istanbul though. If you’re gonna showcase a fictional Orient Express, at least “finish the job” and the journey.
If the puzzles will ever seem either too difficult or time consuming, you can freely skip them. I could have probably shaved off an hour of gameplay, but where’s the fun in skipping the one element that defines such titles? Nothing is insurmountable in Runaway Express Mystery, provided you pay close attention to even minor details. If all else fails, a hint button is also available and it vaguely alludes to whatever point of interest will further the story. Yes, it’s fairly linear, but I’ve yet to find a truly open-ended adventure game in which puzzle solving and character interaction has a profound impact on the overall narrative through freedom of choice. Some titles mask that flaw better than others, but even Telltale’s creations ultimately lead players down several predetermined paths while only offering the illusion of choice.
Just by the fact that it scales to whatever resolution your PC’s running on, this game deserves a closer look. Couple that with a captivating tale which combines the supernatural with murder mysteries and you have a formula for HOG success. Runaway Express Mystery would have benefitted from some proper voice acting, but even as it presents itself now,  I’ll consider that a flaw which should deter no one from giving it a try. Who knows, perhaps you’ll enjoy the game and genre even if you had no previous interest or experience in this type of gameplay. My own interactions with the genre began in 2005 with “Agatha Christie: And Then There Were None”. I’ll always return to such titles, no matter how often I’ll be in the mood for them.

A HOG-lite adventure game from Icarus Games, Runaway Express Mystery fails to take any chances and introduces nothing new to the genre. Having said that, it is very polished with strong voice acting, sound, visuals, and the story is good enough to maintain your interest.
Pros.
Not many HO scenes and those that are there are more to do with finding objects that interact with other objects so that you can get a final object that is story related.
There's a map with fast travel and actions required.
Other than one stereotyped character, the voice acting was very good.
The story progression was strong and each chapter overlapped bringing a nice conclusion that wrapped up most of the loose ends.
Cons.
The game was relatively short at just over 2 hours for me.
Same tired old storyline of "missing relatives due to supernatural elements."
Very few puzzles and those that exist weren't particularly difficult.
Overall, the game is well presented and above average for the Hidden Object Adventure genre, but is more on the adventure side than the HO side with very few HO scenes and puzzles. The story is engaging enough to keep you interested and if you like or are interested in the genre, then Runaway Express Mystery is worth checking out, but it is about half as long as similar games, so try to pick it up at a discount.

There's a bathroom area where you only pick up one item and poof, that's it. Nothing else, no HO scene, no mini-games, nothing. Just pick up one (1) object. It was odd. Would be a waste to ask an artist to create this entire background for that one single purpose of clicking something in a half second and leaving forever. As someone who works with graphics, this is way too sad, haha! (Please pay your art department well!)
PROS:
> Crime-solving! You get to solve 3 different murder cases and you gather evidence and make conclusions (think of AM's Enigmatis series)
> Bright colorful sceneries of 1920's Europe! There were lots of areas! Pretty chocful!
> Kudos to the design team for making so many bits of papers and receipts, bits and bobs. Always appreciate people who try to use immersive typography! (Drink when you see generic fonts in HO games, you'd lose...)
> Fast-travel maps!
CONS:
> Somewhat weak character models haha! I guess this would double as a comment about weak characters (what was the purpose of some of them? They only delivered one (1) piece of information and that's their entire role).
> The minigame with the engineer broke my brain! I can't math at 4am!
> A loose hitbox! I found myself accidentally moving/leaving areas or looking at the wrong spot because the hitting space might be too wide. Often times, even though I've collected all the items available, the spot can still open up. It's confusing because I thought I haven't collected everything.
Overall, good job! I was really surprised. I didn't actually think this was a detective game, so really that was fun for me. I love anything "investigative". I look forward to more games from Icarus Games if ever, as I noticed this game was made in 2014. Definitely recommend for people who prefer mini-games over HO scenes in HOGs.

Runaway Express Mystery is more of a casual adventure game than a hidden object one, which will offer a few hours of fun for anyone who likes a good murder mystery or three.
I think technically we can classify Runaway Express Mystery as a hidden object game, although it only offers some silhouette-based scenes and no conventional puzzles whatsoever. These scenes are pleasantly fun, but it is obvious they were just a marginally important element during game development.
This game is more of a casual level, point ‘n’ click, supernatural crime-solving adventure. It doesn’t start like that, it uses the most basic hidden object premises instead: a mother’s children disappear and she tries to find them. To do so, she must solve three murder cases, all of which are connected to the train the kids went missing on.
All three stories take place in different cities to offer some nice sceneries, and despite being featured in a casual game, the writing is pretty impressive: it is easy to get lost in the adventure and investigation, so this small little gem created by a small Czech studio is more than worth its price.

A well-intentioned but failed effort to innovate on the casual point-and-click adventure formula.
The idea is that you are detective who finds clues to solve mysteries. Cool! Unfortunately, there is no real gameplay to it. You just keep finding new objects to add to your “solution” board, and they are always immediately added to the right place. So the mystery will just solve itself.
Worse, the classical aspects are handled poorly. Hidden-object scenes involve you using detective tools to find objects, but you just need to click with these tools all over the screen until you find the fingerprints and blood stains. Puzzles are poorly explained: I've played these games for years, and yet was stumped with what exactly I was supposed to do in some puzzles.
The graphics are good, but the voice acting is horrendous: it seems that just two actors were employed to do all the voices. Honestly, I don't blame them for doing such a poor job considering the ridiculous script. The story tries hard to be clever, but in the end is an insultingly insipid variation on the theme of “mother trying to save her children.” Only this time the mother doesn't seem to care very much at all.
Skip this one.

is a decent HOG title and one of the earliest games coming from the relatively small Czech developer, Icarus Games. The game presents an interesting and well detailed supernatural storyline, ending up with a couple loose ends, convenient for developing future installation as series.
Amanda Waters is a mother of two young children, visiting the nearby antique train exhibition to see Runaway Express, a famous locomotive hailing from early 1900s. It's all fun and games until the appearance of a mysterious engineer and the train taking off with Amanda's children on board! Determined to find her children, Amanda catches the train in last minute. From thereon, she'll meet many strange passengers on the train - long dead and lost in time. If she is to find her children, she should solve their mysteries and shed light into their stories first. With each new clues she gathers, Amanda gets closer to saving her children. Can she solve the dangerous mystery of Runaway Express, revealing the dreadful affair of its last journey and return her children home safely?
As you can once again observe, a loved one in danger + a supernatural mystery dynamic never fails in HOGs. This game is no different, aside the remarkably irritable personality of our protagonist. Amanda seems to be immune to fear or surprise, and amazingly fixated on finding her children only. She is a mother first and foremost, okay. But she embarks on a train, meeting corpses and travelling back in time for God's sake! She keeps walking around, reprimanding living corpses (!) and demanding explanations about the whereabouts of her children from them! It's amazing to watch her reactions and listen to her comments. This whole eerie setting has literally no effect on her. Once she is declared that the only way to save her children would be solving the mystery, she gets into the investigation yet keeps challenging the rules, looking for shortcuts all the way. The mystery itself doesn't concern the mother of the year. Talk about one track mind. Imagine your mother reprimanding Frankenstein's monster - that is Amanda Waters for you. Now that would be hilarious.
Visuals are beautiful, and the atmosphere is appropriately rustic. Background artist knew what he was doing. Character designs are well done too. Talking animations of characters are a bit clumsy, but they have impressive facial mimics and body gestures. All characters are voice acted with clean cut accents. Listening to Evelyn's heavy Aussie accent was cute, for example.
The main attraction of the game is the investigation process for each new case about various passengers you meet. You walk around, gather clues about their pasts and try to solve their murders a century after their demise. You are expected to arrange your clues on a crime board, explaining the course of events. There are not many HOG scenes, but the ones that we have are short and easy to manage. Puzzles are mostly innovative and interesting. The train is huge - with a couple of visited stations along the way - and backtracking may become an issue if you are not playing in casual difficulty, but the map has a teleport function at least.
The ending was a bit anticlimactic, I won't lie. The mystery of the train is revealed alright - with a nicely arranged inter-relevant background story, but the nature of the engineer is not explained at all. It is hinted that this won't be the last time we'll be facing him as our enemy. Over all,
is a good casual game for you to spare 3-4 hours and explore a nice story. Hit it when you'd feel like having a light reading on the mystery department. Enjoy!

Pros:
- Excellent story and engaging setting
- Interesting and story-rich companions.
- Customizable characters and interesting zones.
Cons:
- Combat is unbelievably slow and complicated.
- Long sections of dull, repetitive content that are required to get to the good bits.
- Arbitrary gating of story choices and resolutions behind other, less interesting content.
- The "Nevermind-factor"
Review:
All of the pieces are there for PoE to be a smash hit, but for some reason it just doesnt quite come together.
The main story is impressive and engrossing. However, I often find myself slowed to a crawl by tedious sidechores - Sidechores that you are almost required to do if you want to be powerfull enough to even survive the next leg of the story.
I am not just speaking of sidequests, whose quality varies from pretty good to absolutely atrocious, but also of story-less and repetitive content such as bounty hunts and..URGH..The Endless Depths of Cad Nua. A dungeon crawl that is so long it could be its own standalone game, but it is mind-numbingly repetitive, as are many of the "dungeon" segments in PoE. They are long, tedious, punish any attempt to get through them faster with traps and obstructions, and offer no fun at all. This is further hampered by an overly complicated and very punishing combat system that makes even small skirmishes a long slog to get through.
In addition, the "perfect" resolution to story quests often requires you to do other quests first. Sometimes to insane levels. For example: To resolve a critical battle in the ideal manner, you first need to completely finish the 2 expansion packs before you can proceed.
The end result is that I cannot for the life of me motivate myself to keep playing through the game - For every good segment, I feel like I need to grind through mountains of repetitive and dull content if I want to finish the story my way. And I just dont want to do that. It requires so much effort and time to carve through the boring sections that on every attempt I end up throwing my arms into the air and saying: "You know what, Pillars of Eternity? Nevermind. Just -nevermind-."
PoE is the "Nevermind factor" made real.

Combat is the weakest part of the game and if you want to enjoy the story, quests, and characters I suggest you to play in easy or story mode just so that you can finish combat quickly. But I have to say there are couple of boss fights that are really enjoyable, but only a couple unfortunately.
There is also the stronghold mechanic, on paper it sounds really nice but as you play the game you can easily notice that the devs couldnt finish their plans for it on time. With patches it got some nice upgrades and sidequests, but its still not complete.

As someone living in a small town with a bunch of delinquient friends, I could see aspects of myself and the people I know in the characters. Of course, this isn't a pre-requisite to enjoying the game - anyone dealing with a mental illness, be it their own or someone they love, can find someone and something to relate to in this world.
I strongly encourage anyone that's on the fence about this title to just pull the trigger and enjoy it, before Tumblr and other fan communities spoil everything of note for you.

This is essentially a visual novel with much more personal interaction in the flow of events, allowing for a lot more immersion as you explore to find clues to the city, your friends, and Mae. Literally nothing is given to you straightforward, you piece it together from Mae's thoughts and interactions gradually. It rewards lots of exploration every day, but isn't in a rush to get where it's going. If you want an organic story about flawed people with a spice of the possibly supernatural, give it a try. It has enough choices for two playthroughs, with the second one likely including a google to find everything you missed.

Well worth the play. The tag "story rich" should be particularly noted as it's more of an interactive story than a game. There are certain moments that require certain moments of puzzle solving or platforming to progress, and certain encounters or secrets can effect events later on, but there aren't any kind of fail states. The major appeal is very fascinating and relatable story and characters. There are minor continuity errors here and there, but nothing game breaking. I feel like there's possibilities for a sequel, and I hope there will be one, but there may not be. Philosophically, the ending still works even as a stand alone game.

Made by fans for fans.
If you are new to the series, then this is a must buy.
If you've played the old versions of the game, then you have already bought Ultra.
If you're thinking "this is a new version of an old game", then you probably haven't played SF4 ever and you're just an internet troll .The definitive version of the game. There really isn't any competition when it comes to deep, involved fighting mechanics. You aren't drowned in a quandary of different systems and minutia. Everything simply works.
The balance is also razor thin. The worst characters (when looking at a 10 point match up tier list) are only 20% below the best. The same can't be said for pretty much any fighting game aside from SF2. Using MVC3 as an example, the best character is actually close to 250% better than the worst (on a match up based tier list).
You also don't have to sit there and watch the other person play while your character is endlessly juggled for half the match. Combos are there but they are swift and succinct. No more 15-20 second long combos of MVC3 and King of Fighters 13.
The character variety is amazing. The inputs are tight and responsive while also demanding that you learn your character. There is no dial-a-combo system, so mistakes are still risky but not as risky as Street Fighter X Tekken where stray jabs lead to full out dial-a-combos.
If you are new to fighting games this is absolutely, positively a 10. If you have the older versions of Street Fighter 4 then this is a 9, seeing as how you've tread this ground before.

The most balanced fighting game you could ever own, Ultra Street Fighter IV stands as the king of fighters. I'm not one for reviewing games but I wanted to throw in my two cents to encourage you that if you are interested in playing a fighting game, this should be your first if not only choice. While Street Fighter was first born in 1987 and the title may seem like they have rehashed the game overtime, this is definitely not so. Each character has their own unique attributes, strengths, weaknesses, and believe it or not, playstyle. Just like with any game, there is a so called tier-list based off their number of favorable matchups against other characters but for the most part, anyone can win. It is not as up to date graphically but if you appreciate the cartoon/cell shaded style graphics that gives it much more of a fantasy look, it's great. Beautiful soundtrack, sound effects during fights, and add-on content with crazy costumes for characters gives you personality during your fight.
The biggest turn off that you may expereince in any fighting game is that you instantly go on-line and expect results. The problem is in a fighting game, being hopeful and mashing buttons just does not bring results (think of grinding in MMOs). While anything can happen in a match, the greatest feeling is learning the ins and outs of the fighting system where combos are difficult enough that when mastered give you a trule feeling of levling up in your gameplay but are not long stretched out button cominations such as Tekken which I myself never was fond of. Online/Offline training mode as well as trials give you the opportunity to grow and develop your timing, spacing of moves, see damage statistics as well as observe your input data to see why the special move you are trying to do is not happening.
When it comes to fighting, Street Fighter is very straight forward, with three different levels of punches/kicks, ranging from the lighter faster jab or kick all the way to the stronger but slower hook or roundhouse. While it seems so simple, every character has completely different frame data (meaning that moves do completely different damages and come out faster or slower, some making a character vulnerable to being hit if blocked). This includes characters like Ryu and Ken who everyone knows and thinks they are so similar. While most think that all that is needed to be done is throw Hadoukens or mash special moves to win, this is just not the case. In this generation of gaming, it is crucial that you fight with your mind. Not being able to defend yourself results in very fast knockouts. What I love personally about this is that since every character is different, you start to learn which characters are aggressive, defensive, controling certain spaces, etc. This aids in creating a unqiue experience with every character you play.
The community for this game itself is very focused on the growth of players though just like any game, you will have trollers. It's inevitable. Great replay channel usage (download and upload as well as linking to Youtube.) Split-screen play as well which is a rare commodity in this day and age.
The only downside about Street Fighter is that on PC (While I wouldn't consider it a precise downside but for those that don't do reserach, it will be), playing online optimized will require to setup your PC in a specific way. The game is made to run at 60FPS for second without too much enhancement. Failing to run it properly will keep you from being able to perform combos correctly which of how frame precise button presses are (though this is with just about any fighting game). The preferred method of running the game includes the following settings:
- Enable v-sync and triple buffering for Ultra Street Fighter IV in your nVidia Control Panel or ATI Control Center (This fixes screen tearing and allows a 60fps without over-smoothing the game to cause issues with button presses
- In-game run whatever resolution you can comfortably and disable V-Sync in game, and put Frame Rate to "Fixed."
By doing this, it will be running close to if not mimicing the arcade version in terms of fluency.
With achievements, difficult to master, great online experience, and depth, this is THE fighting game you will not want to pass up.
PROS
-------------
+Replay value
+Character Roster  (44 Characters)
+Character creativity / uniqueness
+Controls
+Online community
+Gameplay Depth / Mechanics
+Soundtrack
+Graphically beautiful
CONS
_________
- PC version not as optimized as console. Requires tweaking for the best experience.

I can't recommend Long Live the Queen enough. You play as the princess of a kingdom during the year before she ascends to the throne, and you have to survive long enough to get her there. It's essentially a text-based RPG at it's core: you level up different skills every week and as you progress through the game you're met with different checks of those skills. (For example, you can't retrieve an item from the royal treasury without a high enough 'Presence' to intimidate the guards).
The art is beautiful, the story and worldbuilding are very good, and it has a very good amount of replayability due to all the various different endings you can get and ways in which you can get there.

The game has the exact same scripted actions happen each time through the game, and it doesn't allow you alot of wiggle room in what stats you should max. If you wanted your Princess to be a strong, skilled swordfighter but lacking in manners, you'll fail checks that otherwise you'd have needed to win the game.
It's not a terrible game by any stretch, it's just way too short and linear for the price, and most of the fun the game has is quickly diminished by dying over and over until you figure out an optimimum stat build.

This game is unbelievably fun. I picked it up solely based on a recommendation from a friend during a summer sale.
It is pretty challenging (as I'm sure you've heard) and some sections of the game are downright punishing. To echo everybody else, the satisfaction you get from overcoming a challenge in this game is amazing. You will die many times, and some sections you may get stuck on for hours, so it isn't really a game for casual players. Before long you will get the hang of the combat and you will struggle less, but then out of nowhere you can still die to some easy enemy because you were not paying attention or were overconfident.
What I like
- The layout of the world is cool
- The boss fights are challenging (as is the game in general)
- Large variety of weapons
- The factions in-game are cool, and there are a few options
- The combat is really fun
- There are connectivity mods available to make it easier to join up with a friend
What I don't like
- It can be difficult to come back to the game after a break, since there is no journal or anything to let you know what you've already done/what you were trying to do when you last played
- If you aren't playing a lot you might as well not try PvP because many people have extremely refined PvP builds and hundreds of hours of PvP experience (you will be easily destroyed)
- Even with the mods sometimes it can be difficult to join co-op with a friend
- To join a friend they must have not yet beaten the boss in the area you wish to join them
Neutral
- The game gives you very little direction (it gives cryptic hints that are few and far between)
At this point Dark souls 2 and 3 are out (which are also amazing games) but this one is still worth a try, especially if you haven't yet tried the others.

If you're like me, Gamespot and Metacritic are my resources to get game reviews.  I rarely buy games that get below a 70% rating with either of these reviewers.  That being said, I bought this game despite the 64/100 on metacritic, I played it not knowing what to expect, and thankfully, I really enjoyed it.
As many of the other reviewers will tell you, this game is not for everyone.  I purchased it because I loved Hotline Miami and seeing the previews for this game I was drawn to the brutal violence and artistic style.  It's a very challanging game, and it forces you to pick up on little trends and nuances during the gameplay if you want to win.
To explain further, this game requires patience. Just as you start getting really mad because you're getting your tail handed to you, you realize that something you're failing in isn't just RNG, it's something you just haven't been paying attention to.  Sure there are parts that are randomized (which you can disable if you want), but the changing factors with each restart keep you on your toes.
The story is interesting enough to follow and it actually kind of makes you look at the way you play ruthless games such as this one that force you to die or fail over and over again in order to discover a solution.  Things you do will make you feel bad, they'll make you feel like you could have done more, and they certainly make you feel helpless.
Bottom line, you feel like you're in a Cormac McCarthy novel.  Despiration, violence, and death on death on death.  Love it.
Play it for yourself, but with one stipulation: DO NOT LOOK UP WALK-THROUGHS.  FIGURE IT OUT BY DOING!

The time is ticking, lives are in your hands, and your decisions dictate who lives, who dies.  Your choices may not be the most popular, or the most moral, but they may be the most logical.  Only you and the Gods will be watching.
is a 2D point-and-click adventure regarding the trials and tribulations of Sgt. Burden, an agent of E.C.U.K., the Everdusk Company for the Universe Knowledge, tasked to be undercover in the group Xenolifer to learn about the origins and wherewithal of the Medusea Virus.  Throughout the game, Sgt. Burden is tasked with hard-fought decisions: from which hostages to trade or to kill, to which partner will receive the lethal dose for the sake of a cure.  These choices that
gives you are never clear cut or easy to do, most will have a negative aspect in the short-term but are necessary in the long run to the success of finishing the said mission.  It’s a haunting feeling knowing you may have to kill an important partner to complete a mission because he can take an antidote test better than your other crew, and those uncomfortable feelings are easily worth the price of admission.  It’s hard to come by games nowadays that can make you squirm in your seat because you know what you have to do, but you most certainly do not want to do them.
boasts a retro style that really breathes a lot of life into the scenery.  Even with the disadvantage of having very little specific details in the characters and backgrounds,
does a fantastic job painting a beautiful picture of open worlds and claustrophobic corridors catering to the difficult tasks at hand.  The music that accompanies the brooding situations highlights and builds accordingly to the situations, sinking into your brain and not letting go, making every decision you take even heavier and intense than the last.
Though
is an impactful and thought-provoking game, it’s not a terribly long experience.  Gods Will Be Watching at the most will take you around 7-8 hours on its difficult “Original” mode, with specific tasks to beating each level netting you awards like concept art and illustrations.
does add different styles to its chapters: Puzzle Mode removes most of the random number generating puzzles and makes the chapters built on a pattern that can be cracked, while Narrative Mode allows an easier run-through of the game allowing one to indulge in the story more so the complex issues that arise from it.  But ultimately once you’ve finished
, the tense atmosphere of not knowing what’ll happen next get lost during your second and third play through.
Even though
is a short, difficult experience, it is an experience that should be recognized and indulged.  The moral choices and brooding atmosphere sucks you in and doesn’t let go, giving the player an uncomfortable, tense, and thrilling rollercoaster of a ride, even if it’s only good for one go around.

This isn't a laid-back adventure that some people are used to. It's a gritty survival game in the point n' click format. That said, it is a story-driven experience that gives context to the challenge, trial-and-error, consequences, and the prices you pay to reach your goals. It's all about managing your resources and paying attention to other people's morale and actions. The game actually lets you know how your decisions work, it just requires more of reading between the lines and paying attention to what's been said. The Original difficulty throws in chance, so I recommend Puzzle Mode to keep a consistent challenge.
The story of Sgt. Burden's mission to keep his teammates alive and face terrorist group Xenolifer is one that requires more thought. It's not accessible for anyone who wants a simple plot, let alone a straight-forward explanation to some of its, to avoid spoilers, more avant-garde direction with the narrative contextualizing the game mechanics of choices and consequences. I was close to accusing Gods Will Be Watching for a plot-hole or two, but finishing the game and letting the story marinate in my mind made it much more acceptable and logical.
Gods Will Be Watching is not intended to be a simple and light-hearted experience. I would go as far and say this is the point n' click equivalent of The Last Of Us, Dark Souls, and Metal Gear Solid 2, in terms of inaccessible but rewarding narratives.

Very short but well done Hidden Object game about a mother trying to rescue her children kidnapped by the ghost of a cursed train's engineer. The main character will have to solve some murder cases to help the ghosts of the train's passengers, visiting Paris and Budapest to gather clues and analyzing crime scenes. No achievements and some backtracking is needed but gathering clues and solving the HO scenes using detective tools is very interesting.

The story starts off as cheesy, you're on a train, searching for your kidnapped kids, you soon realize that the train is bizarre and something is off... I won't spoil ^^
The game is really well done, I really liked the graphics and the good music, the story is very well told too. The dialogues are fully voiced and it's rather well done. The characters are nice, the locations are beautiful and varied. Original thing: the evidence board, a special game mode where you piece up a story by collecting evidences, very cool. You have 3 cases to solve and you'll find blood stains, pictures, letters, etc. As far as HOG scenes, there's only the silhouette type where you have outlines of items to find, some helping you to find others etc. Pretty classic gameplay but it's very well done. You also have a forensic variant where forensic tools are also used to find some of the items (black powder for the fingerprints, flashlight to check dark places, etc). There's some mini games, really well done too.
It was short - 4 hours but I'm pretty fast with HOGs, so add an hour for a leisure playthrough. The short time length is also due to not having classic HOG scenes with lists of items.
Big up for this game, it's very good and should not be missed by any HOG fan!

Game breaking glitch. (sigh, so sad)  In all good conscious I can not recommend this game, unless the developers fix this game stopper.  (There is a game fix listed in the discussions for good game hackers, unlike me who messed up my game so badly I had to erase everything and start over anyway.)  Also unsure if it is my computer or the game but there are severely lagging areas.  When Amanda first jumps on the train, and the background graphics are moving, everything lags severely.  This lagging occurs anytime Amanda is outside the train while the train is moving.
This glitch is avoidable so here it is where the glitch occurs for the intrepid or the just down right obstinate like me.  The glitch occurs in Budapest as soon as the gamer opens the bank safe.  Before you do anything, or even move, click on the vault and the gamer should get a photograph.  If you do not get the photograph for criminal evidence you have encountered the glitch.  Please understand this photograph occurs in the third segment of the game, and more then halfway through that segment.  So play this game at your risk.
Other then this the gameplay is unique and interesting.
Story: Amanda Waters (is the name the game automatically gives the gamer but the name is changeable) has brought her children, Peggy and Jimmy, to a train exposition.  The arrival of the train the Runaway Express is the highlight of the exposition.  While her children are on board they are not allowed to leave by a person in an iron mask and the train starts to leave the station.  Amanda jumps on board to rescue/save her children.  On the way she encounters three different crimes and must solve each one.
Gameplay:  A fair mix of Hidden Object finds and point and click gaming.  The Hidden Object finds, however, are not the usual list word finds.  The Hidden Object scenes are a combination of three different types of finds.  The first find type is the criminal investigation.  The gamer is given a magnifying glass, fingerprint power, a squirt bottle for finding blood stains and a flashlight for dark areas.  When using the magnifying glass and flashlight the game will state whether they are needed or not.  Finding blood stains is fairly easy as a find, since the game scene goes darker and the stains can be seen if looked for.  Otherwise just spray all over the scene like one has to do with the fingerprint powder until all of them are found.
The second type of find is silhouettes.  Find the object and click on it, easy enough.  Which leds directly to the third type of find, interactive.  If the silhouette picture stays this indicates that the item needs to be used somewhere in the scene.  Overall the Hidden Objects are not overly challenging, but not especially easy either.  They are a nice change of pace from the usual list finds.
Puzzles: The few actual puzzles (not counting the point and click obstacles) are brain twisters.  Before my game glitched I encountered two quite worthy of the time and effort I put into solving them.  I would have to call them master puzzles since they are between the segments of the game or between major points in the game.
I really would recommend this game if it were not for the game breaking glitch.  (I would even recommend it despite the lagging, though I would warn everyone about that.)  Too bad.  I wish I knew how to contact the developers so I could tell them about the glitch so possibly they would fix it.  That way I could change this "thumbs down" to a "thumbs up".

State of Decay provides a well made, open world Zombie Suvival experince, of quality and brilliance that few "Zombie Survival" games tend to offer. The Mix of Action RPG, Base building, and over all open world survival gameplay gives an ambitious quota to fill. Though State of Decay even only From the Vanilla Story mode succeds in most if not all these aspects. With only minor complaints with some, confusing side missions, bugs, and annoying reptitive voiceovers.
"State Of Decay's" story takes place in Turnbull Valley, TX (I assumed a psudeonym for a real area.) In which you are thrust into the lives of several surviors who must interact with local squatters, the military, police forces and so on. The story is not specfic in said overall arch, but more events and minor charecter devlopments. The goal is to survive and escape the valley with whatever help you can suffice from the locals and supplies from descarted areas.
Turnbull valley is full of interesting and unique landmarks and locations that help it stay interesting over your trek through the game. It really feels like a proper country area of the United States fairly untouched by city life. With mid 50's styles local attractions set up like the Bronto Gas Station.  Set up wise Turbull Valley reminds me of the county in Swery's Deadly Premontion. In fact I really often get reminded of Deadly Premontion when driving around out collecting things, due to their similar gameplay.
The gameplay varies in several different ways:
The Action RPG elements come from combat gained skills in a sort of beat'em up/ third person shooter ala Resident Evil Shooting. The combat can get very crowded and it's very easy to get over whelmed if not with an ally or if you are ill experinced. Stealth can be employed while on foot, and weapons vary from melee, guns, and items. All Acuired throught yor adventure
Base building and mangement involves building new faciilities for supplies and food and shelter. Such as Workshops, Farms, Bunkhouses,etc. Supplies are collected and traded with supply chests and outposts to protect and keep watch of an overall area. Giving base building and making sure you have enough outposts a important major goal next to most other priorities.
The Open world exploration is involves scouring buidlings and lookign for vantage points to survey the lay of the land for buidlings, zombies and other curiosties. Surveying helps clear up whats in the are so exploration is slightly easier, and outposts can be set up.
The Last and minor gameplay mechanic would be driving, Driving works fine for what it is, but you can easily ran into things and often wreck up your car easily if you are not careful.
Oddly enough and it's most likley intentional Vehicular Combat is the best way to dispatch Undead foes in SOD (except for the largest vareity of zombies Juggernauts) As it almsot always kills them immeditaly. I found my self constantly finishing missions and escaping by hopping in a car and going maximum overdrive on the hordes. Good or bad driving is sorta clunky.
Missions:
Missions consist of several types.
Helping a ally, Hunting a Zombie, trading, clearing infestations, and story missions.
All of these have minor variations. Most missions will get reptitive after a few times, but story missions help mix things up to add more depth to the gameplay. While It'd be nice if there was more minor story missions or overally different types the Storymode Delivers.
Overall the gameplay is very fun and slightly clunky in soem areas, but imagine GTA with Zombies Aesthetics.
Now onto the video and sound.
If you're not a fan of bloom effects and heavy shadows like me you might dislike the graphics. Though the game does look amazing in of it's self and has an overall sepia tone to the game and purpleish hues at night. It's very atmospheric and feels bizzare and creepy. The feeling of not knowing whats ahead really emiantes at night.
The Graphics are great, but not for people who dislike bloom.
Audio,
The Soundtrack consists of several differnt event themes such as for horde attacks and Home base music.
As well as road music and so on. It's a vey nice mix of slow guitar that gives a melocholy down on the ranch feel.
The voice actings good with some only minor complaints with the infamous line "you know, some stuff" when supplies are delivered to home base. Good all around.
Controls
SOD was orgianlly made for consoles and this shows, with it's driving and running. It's not easy to learn at first and as i used keyboard things felt clunky due to some of the keybindings used. The worst thing to ever happen to me was having a charecter fall to their dead from a cell tower since i moved to fast to the ladder. I was really bugged by it, but later learned later to move slower near ladders. The controls are dfeinatly a minor but needed hurdle, but it plays like most openworld games overall in it's controls; just in third person.
Who will like this:
If you love The Walking Dead, Survival Games, Resident Evil, GTA, or you want a refined take on the Zombies survival.
In Conclusion
State of Decay shines for it's Gameplay and exploration features, It's not really a signle genre it's more like a Role Playing game made proper into a video game. It's a mix of minor mechanics from different genres and turns them into an awesome smoothie of gaming.
I really enjoyed iState of Decay and felt wanting more as I finished the game in a day, I've only thus far played the orgrinal story mode so I have yet more to come. I'm eager to knwo what happens next!!
I can't wait to play the DLC and hope that it improves upon the already addictive and awesome gameplay.

I like the premise - a salvage and rescue crew, unconcerned with the politics and intrigue of Space-Opera empires. Here, you're doing small, personal things against the backdrop of the galaxy - and that vastness serves to make them feel all the more important, and all the more yours. There's not much to go on just yet, but I got an optimistic feel from the game - although it might just be me. The thing the characters found the creepiest, I found noble and inspiring, so take that with a grain of salt. The developer of STARDROP has stated that in the form it is in right now, it's about 35% done - suggesting a game with a total length somewhere between 6 and 8 hours - maybe more, depending on the depth and challenge put into the subsequent chapters.  Personally, I'm happy to give the developer a few meals' worth of groceries or a few days' worth of utilities with my payment to see through the rest of it.
PROS:
- A reasonably-priced, mechanically-consistent independent adventure game.

Pros:
- Excellent story and engaging setting
- Interesting and story-rich companions.
- Customizable characters and interesting zones.
Cons:
- Combat is unbelievably slow and complicated.
- Long sections of dull, repetitive content that are required to get to the good bits.
- Arbitrary gating of story choices and resolutions behind other, less interesting content.
- The "Nevermind-factor"
Review:
All of the pieces are there for PoE to be a smash hit, but for some reason it just doesnt quite come together.
The main story is impressive and engrossing. However, I often find myself slowed to a crawl by tedious sidechores - Sidechores that you are almost required to do if you want to be powerfull enough to even survive the next leg of the story.
I am not just speaking of sidequests, whose quality varies from pretty good to absolutely atrocious, but also of story-less and repetitive content such as bounty hunts and..URGH..The Endless Depths of Cad Nua. A dungeon crawl that is so long it could be its own standalone game, but it is mind-numbingly repetitive, as are many of the "dungeon" segments in PoE. They are long, tedious, punish any attempt to get through them faster with traps and obstructions, and offer no fun at all. This is further hampered by an overly complicated and very punishing combat system that makes even small skirmishes a long slog to get through.
In addition, the "perfect" resolution to story quests often requires you to do other quests first. Sometimes to insane levels. For example: To resolve a critical battle in the ideal manner, you first need to completely finish the 2 expansion packs before you can proceed.
The end result is that I cannot for the life of me motivate myself to keep playing through the game - For every good segment, I feel like I need to grind through mountains of repetitive and dull content if I want to finish the story my way. And I just dont want to do that. It requires so much effort and time to carve through the boring sections that on every attempt I end up throwing my arms into the air and saying: "You know what, Pillars of Eternity? Nevermind. Just -nevermind-."
PoE is the "Nevermind factor" made real.

State of Decay is a third-person zombie apocalypse survival game developed by Undead Labs and published by Microsoft. State of Decay is a single player only game.
State of Decay gameplay is quite deep, but somewhat repetitive at certain point. At the start of the game, you play as two main characters, Marcus Campbell and Ed Jones as they are ambushed by the living dead. Then you will have a home base where you and other survivors making a stand against the undead. From there, the sandbox play begins. Your home base is where you and your others survivors live, obviously, and it needs supplies to survive. You need to hunt and raid outside to get supplies like foods, medicines, building materials, ammunitions, weapons or fuels. Your home base can also be improved, you can build a workshop, garden, sleeping area and more as long as your home base has the space for them. You can move out from your current home base and find a new bigger or better one too. When you're out there hunting, you may find some neighboring survivors or survivors who may want to join you in your home base. You will also find some driveable civilian vehicles which can also be used as cargo for your scavenged supplies for you to bring home. Your home base will sometimes attacked by approaching zombie hordes. You will need to set up some outpost to defend against these living dead hordes. Outpost will also create a small safe zone outside your home for you to take shelter.
In State of Decay, survivors can become tired, injured or sick. When that happen to survivors you currently play, better get home and switch to another survivors. Yes, you can switch characters when you have become friends with them. If a survivor gets tired, his/her max stamina will decrease, same goes when he/she is injured. Survivors will also gain some experience and skill as you play with them, such as cardio, wits (ability to search faster but quiet), fighting, shooting and more. But beware if your survivors is killed, their death is permanent. Survivors can be equipped with melee or firearms, whichever you prefer, but melee weapons will gets damaged over time and will be destroyed if not repaired. Firearms can also gets damaged and if not repaired, will become jammed but not destroyed.
Graphics of State of Decay is great, looks good, but not one of those next generation thing. Using CryEngine 3, State of Decay does have good environment view, lightning, good textures, physics and effects. Characters animations are great, when dodging zombies, attacking with melee, it's good. Blood and gore effects are also present in this game, in fact, you can see your survivors getting torn in 2 pieces by the zombies.
State of Decay performance is good, but can use more optimization. At maximum setting, the game sometimes but rarely stutters which can ruin your aim when using a gun. Aiming a gun also seems clumsy and quite hard. Otherwise the performance is good and fine.
If you're looking for more friendly zombie apocalypse game, then State of Decay is for you, since the game is single player only, you won't find yourself get shot from the back by somebody when you just spawn in the game. With deep gameplay mechanics, State of Decay can entertain you for many hours. I recommend this.
Rating 9/10

Note my opinions here are based on the First Build of early access after playing through the content 1 day after EA launched. Views may change as development progresses.
I dont normally review early access titles as they often go through so many changes during the EA process. However the current content in this title is already polished to a very high level that I feel it is worth bringing to peoples attention. I spent about 5 hours playing through this on my twitch stream today going over the current content.
The mechanics inside the initial ship you get to explore are quite simple yet provides such a great atmosphere. The environments are clean and simple to look at however the ambient sounds and lighting just makes everything feel right. There are a couple of areas where the lighting is a little overpowering but this is something the developer already stated he is working on while I was streaming the game (thanks a bunch to Joure for hanging out and answering questions). The attention to detail is great which follows through already to a generous set of options including 5 seperate volume sliders which is something I feel ALL narrative games should have. The voice acting of the main characters is done to a professional level with a believable friendship between these characters.
The game has no combat and is purely intended to be a narrative exploration experience. With this in mind it works very well. I am very much looking forward to additional chapters being added during the early access process and for the low entry price I recommend this title to anyone into sci-fi driven narrative experiences. I really feel like this could turn out to be something very special.
The game definitely has very high potential.

Long Live the Queen is a RPG on rails, stripped of almost everything but the character sheet. All events are scripted and will play out the same way on each play though. Your "choices" can take you down a slightly different path where skill checks will vary.
The challenge in this game is in documenting the various skill checks that come up as a result of the choice tree. Once you know what skills you need for a certain ending you just need to replay the game to get your skills up to the minimum level to pass the various checks.
The anime style art work didn't help the game, but a least it was consistent. But if you like seeing a cartoon 15 year old girl who is drawn like she's 12, and acts like shes 10, dress up in skimpy outfits, this game might be for you.
TL;DR: RPG with only the character sheet; get your perv on.

LLTQ is basically Crusader Kings 2 politics, depth and events (insane amount of intrigue and backstabbing) with manga/kawaii flair and an overdose of Dark Souls thrown into the mix (difficulty, lots and lots of deaths, mature theme and the game rewarding the player for patience and careful planning).  The game offers an insane amount of gameplay depth as well, the storyline differs massively depending on the choices you make and the way you educate your character.
Don't be fooled by the cute and "child-friendly" looks of the game, it contains mature themes and has more in common with Game of Thrones than your cute kawaii run-of-the-mill visual novel.
Highly recommended.  Buy it, otherwise you'll seriously miss out.

Press X To Not Die is a game I first saw on YouTube. I thought it would be an interesting experience. So I bought it and I'm glad I did.
This game is kinda like a tribute to those old FMV video games from the early to mid '90s like Wing Commander 3 and Night Trap. I've personally never played those kinds of games, so seeing a video game done in this way was very new to me.
I recommend you play this game on Normal difficulty because the higher ones expect you to press about four buttons in three seconds. Unless you are going for achievements of course.
It's a very short game, but satisfying in many ways. The acting is pretty cheesy which I enjoy personally. The menus feel really well done which surprised me even.
And yes this game is just quicktime events basically, but one that made me laugh through a lot of it. This game has a strange sense of humor from referring to M. Night Shyamalan to FarmVille. But it does work. I greatly appreciate the use of Kevin MacLeod music by the way, it actually fits nicely here.
Overall, this is a very fun and cheap indie game that I recommend if you just want to be entertained. It doesn't have the same level of substance as most indies I've played, but it is to become a classic in the future!
