This game could have been amazing, but it lost its way a long time ago. If you're hoping it's REmake's underrated sister game, or a gripping chapter in the olden "pre-4" Resident Evil lore, you're gonna be disappointed.
RE0 uses REmake's engine, so most of the core classic RE gameplay tenets remain in place. You direct your protagonist through a series of pre-rendered environments with tank controls, stockpiling and managing the necessary resources to deal with assorted spooky foes while snooping through people's journals and solving mid-90's adventure game style puzzles. It's a survival horror game.  It's an aesthetically pleasing one, too, and the HD Remaster in particular showcases this beautifully. However improbable, Billy and Rebecca duckwalking along the roofs of the Ecliptic Express under torrential rain is a memorable image.
The first real problems are the bloat Capcom introduced to the old formula. Starting around ten minutes into the game, you're controlling (and swapping between) two different characters. That's two different health pools, two different arsenals, and potentially two different geographical positions you're now tasked with managing (whichever character you're not currently playing as is a bot). This lends itself to two major "innovations" in the scenario writing--situations where Rebecca is in danger and Billy has to save her, and partner puzzles. Partner puzzles can be further split into two (2) main types:
1. Character A pushes a button/pulls a lever, Character B grabs an otherwise inaccessible item.
2. Character A and B push two different buttons/pull two different levers simultaneously.
There are some (obnoxious) outliers in the third act, but that's the gist of it. It's less exciting than it sounds.
All that's just going about the game's "action." The department where RE0 starts really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the bed, gameplay wise, is inventory management. In prior Resident Evils, you were given 6-8 (by which I mean "8 in all but half of the first game") slots of inventory space to house the hodge podge of pilfered firearms, eccentric knick knacks, and medicinal herbs you'd collected on the fly. Anything more than that would have to be stored in item boxes (or chests, or ottomans whatever). There were maybe around 10 or so item boxes throughout the game depending on how big the given game world was (usually found paired with a typewriter for saving and sometimes complete with soothing music), and they were all universal. Which is to say, you could put a chess-themed buttplug in an item box in Raccoon City's police station, and later retrieve it from an item box in William Birkin's lab. For all intents and purposes, this system worked fine. It was kind of annoying when you'd come across something you wanted with a full inventory and have to either backtrack or maybe waste a healing item, and gaming rags used to ♥♥♥♥♥ endlessly about not being able to just drop things on the floor, but it wasn't that big of a deal.
But for the sake of...I'm not sure exactly what, I guess "innovation," Capcom decided that change was in order. In November of 2002, GamePro-Writer-From-1998's most perverse desires were finally made manifest: RE protagonists could now leave♥♥♥♥♥♥lying on the ground indefinitely, and come back for it later. This intoxicating power, however, came with a hefty price: the magic item boxes.
That wasn't the only caveat, either. For one, Rebecca and Billy only have six inventory slots to their name apiece. For context, the only RE protag to have that few before this was RE1 Chris. Everyone else started out with eight, and in 2, 3, and CODE: Veronica, they could eventually upgrade to ten. No such upgrades exist in RE0. For another thing, RE0 was also sort of the first baby step into RE4's gridspace intentory system, to disastrous effect. What I mean by this is that in most classic RE games, one item=one slot. Improbable, since it implies a rocket launcher is as bulky as a key, but it's a video game. ♥♥♥♥ off. RE2 made some exceptions to this--unlockable "infinite ammo" weapons, or any weapons that had infinite ammo counterparts, took up two slots. This amounted to three guns: the Gatling gun, the rocket launcher, and the SMG. One of those only shows up in a normal campaign at the very end, and another doesn't show up at all except as an unlockable.
In RE0, every weapon I can recall except the knife, pistol, magnum, and Molotov cocktail takes up two slots. The grenade launcher, the shotgun, the second shotgun that only holds a max of two ♥♥♥♥ing shells anyway--everything. So does the "Hookshot," which is a stylized new take on staircases you get to see whenever Rebecca finds a hole in the ceiling.
What this means is that you're even more strapped for space than RE has ever made you before. I'm not sure what the dev team's "vision" was or what they thought would come of this, but what it amounts to is you're just gonna use whichever character you like least as a pack mule and leave all your♥♥♥♥♥♥on the floor of two or three adjacent rooms. Combine all this with the longest, most drawn-out door opening screens in the franchise's history, and the game becomes a slogging chore of an experience, and probably the single source of all the franchise fatigue that set the stage for RE4 to diddle the gaming world's butt. FluffyQuack's doorskip mod is a mandatory fixture.
Not only are the aspects of the old formula that could be construed as tedium stretched to such proportions they can't ♥♥♥♥ing help but be exactly that, but the "action"/"horror"/"INCIDENT" parts, the payoff, are almost as dull as the Research Center's creative "brown and dark brown and tan" color palette. The enemies are unimpressive. The series' mainstay zombies, zombie Dobermans, zombie crows, cattle-sized tarantulas, and Hunters are back, and I think that's cool and good. Who're the new faces?
Giant frogs, giant crickets, zombie monkeys, and leeches.
Fantastic. What about bosses?
A big scorpion, a big centipede, a big bat, the end boss from the first game but with Down's and Parkinson's, and
LEECHES
LLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLELELELELEELELELELELEELELEELCH LEECH EERLCH LEEBALEEBLE LEECH REECH GREECH LEECH CLFLGG
DWWWWWWWOOOOOOOOOONNNNNNNNNNGGGGGGGG
(Yeah don't you worry we'll get to the story in a sec)
So the new enemies are all either lame or outright stupid, the fetch quests are all boring and uninspired, and to top it off, a number of puzzles are copypasted from other RE games--the piano from RE1 and the voltage meter from RE2 are the first examples that come to mind, the latter with the same exact solution and everything. Every aspect of the formula has either been tampered with and ultimately broken, or just half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Is there anything I actually liked?
Well, REmake had a really good artstyle, and RE0 is cut from the same cloth. Probably why so many people remember it as a good game. Like I said before, the train sequence is absolutely gorgeous. Marcus' old school kinda gives me a headache after an hour, but the outdoor areas are gloriously chilly and muggy and the game does make an (infuriatingly brief) trip to Birkin's lab from RE2 for some fanservice and desperately needed cool tones. It looks good.
The sound design is okay. The OST is kinda mediocre and sterile sounding save for like, three really good tracks, and I don't know why the grenade launcher sounds like a Star Wars rifle, but what do I know? Maybe they really sound like that and REmake's the idiot here.
I like the variety of zombie models and outfits, something REmake was terribly lacking in. Being able to tell clearly that they were once cooks, students, conductors, guards, and researchers does a lot more to illicit pity than a couple butlers and guys in lab coats. Continued in the comments.

+ Exploration is rewarded
+ Bosses that are challenging without being cheap (except for a few)
Cons:
- Some cheap boss designs
- No clear direction on where to go/what to do can be difficult for a new player playing alone.
- Lack of explanation for stats or bonuses
- Co-op can be a chore and requires a third party program "DSCM" by Wulf2K

As someone living in a small town with a bunch of delinquient friends, I could see aspects of myself and the people I know in the characters. Of course, this isn't a pre-requisite to enjoying the game - anyone dealing with a mental illness, be it their own or someone they love, can find someone and something to relate to in this world.
I strongly encourage anyone that's on the fence about this title to just pull the trigger and enjoy it, before Tumblr and other fan communities spoil everything of note for you.

This is essentially a visual novel with much more personal interaction in the flow of events, allowing for a lot more immersion as you explore to find clues to the city, your friends, and Mae. Literally nothing is given to you straightforward, you piece it together from Mae's thoughts and interactions gradually. It rewards lots of exploration every day, but isn't in a rush to get where it's going. If you want an organic story about flawed people with a spice of the possibly supernatural, give it a try. It has enough choices for two playthroughs, with the second one likely including a google to find everything you missed.

Well worth the play. The tag "story rich" should be particularly noted as it's more of an interactive story than a game. There are certain moments that require certain moments of puzzle solving or platforming to progress, and certain encounters or secrets can effect events later on, but there aren't any kind of fail states. The major appeal is very fascinating and relatable story and characters. There are minor continuity errors here and there, but nothing game breaking. I feel like there's possibilities for a sequel, and I hope there will be one, but there may not be. Philosophically, the ending still works even as a stand alone game.

A good single player game is a rare thing these days. 99% of the time I never finish a single player game. The plot either becomes dull, the gameplay repetitive, or the sense of progression stale, and yet somehow Shadow of Mordor has accomplished the feet of keeping me engaged right the way through the campaign.
The story is interesting, especially if one is familiar with the lore behind the Lord of the Rings, with surprisingly excellent voice acting and script writing and smooth animations. The stand out however is the Nemesis gameplay system. I cannot begin to describe how much more refreshing and engaging combat is when buttressed with such a reactive and impactful piece of design genius. Essentially, each enemy has the capability of rising up the ranks of Orc society depending on how often they kill you and rival Orcs. My amusement and wonder at one the game's ending sequences, where spoilers aside, a lowly grunt Orc I encountered fairly early on had risen to the rank of chieftain, was remarkable. What this sytem does is combine a deeply satisfying combat system with strategically rewarding aggressive 'diplomacy' (in a quintessentially Orcish fashion) and the finished package is fantastic.
The ending sets up the upcoming Shadow of War perfectly without leaving that sinking sensation of anticlimax and I have many many hours of fun left playing politics across the maps with the Nemesis system, upgrades, and collectibles. This is first game deserving of GOTY awards since, albeit for different reasons, The Last Of Us by Naughty Dog. A must buy, regardless of if there is a sale, but if there is, you can get this gem for £3!

Simply put, if you're considering this game, you probably have games like Neverwinter Nights and Baldurs Gate. Just replay those. Another play of those old stories are significantly better than this... mess.

In Shadow of Mordor you play as Talion, a ranger killed in action against Sauron's Black Hand. In death he does not find rest, but instead joins forces with the ancient Elf turned wraight, Celebrimbor.
Shadow of Mordor has amazingly enjoyable combat, so if you like fighting with tons of different options for taking down your enemies, this is the game for you. So many different styles of combat can be achieved with this game, such as stealth, swordfighting, archery, mounting beasts, or turning enemies against one another. The enemies all have their own little perks and can interact with Talion in unqiue ways depending on the situation. I went so long without hearing the same line being said - I was seriously impressed! It makes it seem like you're actually fighting against Sauron's army - none of the enemies appear to be clones like they do in other games.
The story is quite short and rushed, for instance Gollum makes an appearance but soon disappears never to be seen until the final moments of the game. None of the story missions feel especially connected, as many of them are simply tutorials for abilities that are locked until said mission is started. That's really the downside of the game - it limits your combative abilities until you actually play the story. They aren't even complex mechanics either, so I'm not sure why the developers did that.
Music in the game is nice, but not memorable by any means. Not really much else to say on that.
The game is open world, but you could easily divide the game into 'levels' thanks to the stronghold designs. There's also two different regions, which means the world is quite large and distinct.
There are two DLC campaigns, but if you get the GOTY edition (why wouldn't you?) you get EVERYTHING in one package. That said, the Lord of the Hunt campaign creates another separate world, introducing new monsters and moves. It isn't as good as the second campaign however. WIth the Bright Lord campaign, it really brings Talion's and Celebrimbor's story to a close and makes it seem more complete.
For those looking for a challenge, the game introudces Trials that you can complete. Two of them are required to beat for achievements, and they're quite challenging and fun.
Overall, while the game doesn't have much to do with LotR and doesn't really honor the lore, the game isn't played for the story but the combat.

Fortunately, Save/Load features are there, and there are always lots of other areas to explore.
It's not a game that drives me to finish it -- it's relaxing and interesting enough that I WILL come back to it and finish it. But not today  :)

The anime-as-hell presentation may turn off many people (me included), but this is a surprisingly inventive story-driven game filled with political intrigue. Like Princess Maker 2 (the only one in the series I've played) -- another anime-as-hell video game -- it has an interesting turn-based character-building system that is fun to poke around. Unlike PM2, however, the narrative is constrained within the short 40 weeks it is set in (basically 40 cycles of decision-making), and it is not afraid to murder the princess in many, many ways. It has an almost deterministic, flowchart-like narrative structure that might be a dealbreaker to some, but the writing is solid and there are enough branches and variations to allow for unique-enough playthroughs. In two different runs, I made a princess who's focused on studying military and royal intrigue but clueless of basic manners, and another who's a powerful, regal sorceress but pretty stupid and unfriendly (they both died different but equally terrible deaths). It's pretty fun to see how different builds tackle the same larger problem, having different options available to them.
My problem with it is that I didn't find this game to be the exploratory game I half-expected it to be. This isn't fully a game about exploration and experimentation. This is a game meant to be beaten and the objective is singular and simple: don't let the princess die. The princess can die (or sometimes survive) from the most seemingly arbitrary skill checks. It can be cool to get feedback for the kind of princess build you're aiming for, but sometimes there is just no way to foresee them. It's a bit weird to be grateful that the game is so short that a restart isn't such a big deal. Since things are largely deterministic, a path towards survival becomes clear a bit too easily after a few playthroughs anyway. Finding all the deaths and different ways to beat the game might be fun for completion's sake, but the core "fresh" experience is a rather short one (I'd say 4-6 hours).
If you're looking to burn a few hours on something that's like a visual novel, but a bit more involving -- this would be a really good choice. Just don't get this game expecting a mini Crusader Kings 2 or anything.

Dark Souls 1 is a hardcore RPG game, that was developed by FromSoftware and published by Namco Bandai Games. It has a refined combat system, decent graphics based on the time of its release, and rewarding gameplay.
I did not complete Dark Souls 1, but after purchasing the game I was determined that I would complete the game as I could prove to myself that I wasn't a noob when it came to this genre. After a days worth of hours sacraficed into this game, I still didn't believe that I would be able to complete the game, and the motivation to keep playing died due to its minimalistic story telling, and the shear difficulty of this game. Before you all try to murder me in a more savage way than any Dark Souls boss did, I would like to justify myself.
Sure this game is fantastic, and people that enjoy a strategic and punishing combat system will love the hell out of this game. Despite it being released in 2011, its graphics aren't outdated to any extent all thanks to DSfix.
The combat mechanics are some of the best that I have ever seen playing a game. You have to be strategic when it comes to battle, otherwise your a gonner, and you will remain a gonner unless you reflect on your combat methods, and try to find the most appropriate way to attack your enemy. Every enemy in this game has a unique fighting style, making every battle enjoyable until you die of course, as you then have to trek back across the badass world of Dark Souls fighting the same badass creatures that you had already spent excessive time slaughtering.
The sound effects of the game are decent, and the soundtrack is immersive and makes battling your foes that more intense.
The games combat and graphics were enough to keep me satisfied with the game for a reasonable amount of time, but the unforgiving difficulty ruined my experience entirely. Sure, this game was designed to be difficult, and the majority of people that have played this game have completed it, after many attempts and alot of dedication. I however don't have the fuse of these hardcore Dark souls warriors, and got fed up of retracing my footsteps only to get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me on a silver platter by the same creature that had KO'ed me previously.
I know, i've dissapointed the Dark Souls community by giving up so soon, but I would recommend this game to anyone who was questioning whether to buy it or not, as the experience that I had may have been irritating, but this was made acceptable by the rewarding feeling of defeating a boss after hours of dedication and the vast amount of customization that you can do to your character. I understand that this game was created to be difficult and to put the players skills to the test, and its very effective in doing so and has shaped the whole Dark Souls series, I just simply am not built to praise the sun.
I would have personally preferred the game if their was a saving function which would get rid of all the heartbreak when you die, but of course that would ruin the whole concept of Dark Souls.
Overall I loved the game, but the game didn't love me the same way.

Inventory Management and Backtracking: The Game. Resident Evil: Zero is a prequel to the popular survival horror series as the name suggests, and the game mechanics are more archaic and frustrating than the older entries' already infuriating systems. Whether that's an intentional, meta decision or just experimentation gone awry, I couldn't say for sure. The end result is a bad game either way.
 
  RE0 starts out strong. As S.T.A.R.S medic Rebecca Chambers, you're separated from your squad (as tends to happen) and find yourself searching a train for an escaped convict, Billy Coen. The train is a great introductory stage; essentially a long hallway with impressive environmental details and an ever-moving backdrop. You quickly find your liberated prisoner, and he's a real corny♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Billy's tribal tattoos, spiky hair, and cringy one liners are more than enough to get Rebecca's girl juices flowing, so the two partner up and you're introduced to the concept of playing in tandem with an AI partner. You can set the computer controlled character to follow you, stay put, attack enemies or be passive, and you can exchange items as long as they are on the same screen. The idea is novel and leads to the type of puzzles you would expect, and they each have minor differences and special equipment (Billy can push heavier objects, Rebecca can mix herbs, etc.). Judging by this first stage, things look great in the confined train as you pass objects through dumb waiters and separate to trigger time sensitive switches. As the scope of the game expands, everything quickly falls apart.
 
  Rebecca and Billy both have painfully small inventory slots, so neither of them can be the badly needed pack mule. Struggling with limited space is a staple of the genre, but Resident Evil: Zero pushes it to insufferable levels. The game goes crazy with multiple key items that need to be hauled, combined, and stored and those all eat up precious slots. Anything larger than a handgun (and some key items) take up multiple of your eight squares, plus the ammo needed... add a healing item and you are constantly fiddling and juggling and dropping and swapping and it's obnoxious. Previous games in the series gave you access to a storage box in save rooms that would magically transport items to other save rooms; video game-y? Sure, but it worked to alleviate the finicky nature of what you're doing to a degree. In the aptly named Resident Evil: Zero you just throw crap on the ground.
 
  The dropped objects are physically represented in the room, though you have to take the games' word for it sometimes when your ink ribbon is obscured by foreground objects and you walk in circles jamming 'A' trying to find it while the character remarks over and over about the vintage of the furniture. Even when you can see the items good luck picking up what you want when multiple items are next to each other. Another issue with the floor garbage is it multiplies the need to backtrack exponentially as your weapons, health, and ammo end up scattered all over the entire game as you drop them for key items and are subsequently blocked off, shuffled forward, or split up. It's an inelegant solution to a problem that had already been solved, and the game suffers for it.
 
  After the train the stages devolve from the familiar (another mansion...) to the boring (a sewage treatment plant?), and the story and characters go from cheesy to familiar to bad as well. It all culminates in a boss battle that frequently interjects little cutscenes to throw off your flow; a climax of the bad game design. Then Billy spouts a '90s action movie one-liner and your eyes and the credits roll. Resident Evil: Zero feels like a by-the-numbers Resident Evil game that doubles down on all the worst parts of the genre. It's a real... zero.

After about 17 hours I finished the campaign, and I enjoyed this game very much!
Let me give you all some pros and cons from my perspective:
Your mission is to survive and make your stand with others like you, gather supplies and look for shelter is the first thing that comes to mind, and also try to kill everything in a specific area to try and create a "safe zone", which is actually impossible since the zombies will eventually spawn there again. I saw a horde spawn right next to me right after I got out of the car once, I disliked this aspect of the game to say the truth, it killed the "sneaking" feeling of hunting down and intercepting enemies before they reach the area you just cleared.
A car is your best friend in this game, they are just ridiculously over powered. Once you unlock the vehicle delivery radio assistance you are pretty much invincible, that makes the game really fun because you can go out playing bowling simulator with zombies in the streets... But it's a huge con in my opinion, the game gets too easy. A fuel system would be a good idea to implement, and also a specialization system to turn the cars on, it feels really weird that every car in the city is open, with infinite gas and the keys just sitting there in the ignition...
When you die you die for real, and since there's not a manual save option in the game make sure to press f4 when you see you're not going to make it... When you die you switch to another survivor from your group which is friendly to you, or if you don't have any friends you just get a random guy. I died once and decided to restart the game, learned my lesson the hard way.
Once you progress enough in the game you can relocate your base, the best option is the Snyder Trucking Warehouse. You need at least 12 people in your group to move there, and once it's up and running you are going to feel untouchable, since you can have up to 8 outposts, and the consequence of that is a very big safe zone for you to chill during the zombie apocalypse.
Regarding the other survivor groups that appears during the game, the only thing that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off is the fact that you lose trust with them, if for example you approach them with a car, you get a penalty for "reckless driving" and they also can catch on fire if you throw a molotov near them, don't even think about using guns, unless you are alone, they will get in your way and get hit. This game is a beautiful tribute to the isometric RPGs of old.  It feels like the classics do and yet it's also something fresh.  It has plenty of its own combat nuances that make playing it after years of Infinity Engine games an exciting new challenge.  It also has a multi-faceted reputation system that does more for you in terms of roleplay and character reactivity than a simple alignment title ever could.
In terms of the story, this is a very long and complex but good narrative that is difficult to get into at first, due to the flood of worldbuilding that is presented, but once you get the hang of it, it all comes together beautifully and leaves you curious to know and see more about the world of Eora.  It's a very dark narrative, but not an over-the-top depressing one that leaves you unable to feel joy afterwards.  It's certainly not without humor and it has its share of lovable, memorable characters.
There is quite a bit of reading in dialogue, which can be challenging to some with focus issues, but if you're familiar with the walls of text in Baldur's Gate and could make it through those, these would likely be no problem for you.
Overall a wonderful game, especially for those who loved the Infinity Engine games and have been craving more like them for years.  I wholeheartedly recommend it.

One of the very best Early Access titles available, and easily in my top 3 survival sandbox games. I love the idea here, and the direction it's going. For that genuine deserted island survival experience you just can't beat Stranded Deep. The audio is masterful and immersive, very realistic, with the occasional chords of music at appropriate times. The lighting from the upgraded engine makes for the most beautiful sunsets and the most realistic water I've seen. Seldom have I felt more dread in a game than when diving out on a beautiful, sunlit reef when it suddenly drops out, and at your back is nothing but the black darkness of the deep ocean... you see the flicker of a huge dorsal fin out of the corner of your eye and hear the chords of music that let you know... you are being hunted. These features, combined with the survival and crafting elements, and a map editor that allows you to create your own custom world space, make for a truly immersive survival experience.
Some very minor improvements that I would like to see, to improve immersion: A chair to just sit in, by the fire, and watch the sun set or the moon rise. The ability to make time pass in real time. The sound of rain falling should reflect the type of roof it is falling on when inside a shelter. Caves. Fishing (there is spear fishing, but bait and tackle fishing would really be an impressive feature). An ultimate end-goal, or a story campaign, would be nice, but not necessary for the experience.
I've been checking in with the state of the game every couple weeks or so, and I can say that it is progressing and growing. Regardless of some of the negative reviews, the devs really are listening to the community and doing their best to please everyone, often straying from their original vision to appease people. It seems the devs are learning some key attributes of almost any online community:
1) Generally, many people are the most vocal when they have something negative to say. Conversely, those that are pleased often say nothing.
2) You can't possibly please everyone.
A good example of these things is the history of the crafting system in Stranded Deep. In earlier builds the crafting system was intuitive and had no actual in-game guide to tell you that a stick + a rock + some lashing = a crude hammer. You had to figure it out, and there was some satisfaction in that. And I found it more realistic. After all, why would our plane-crash survivor just happen to have the Webelos Field Guide To Deserted Island Survival in his back pocket? Despite the fact that there were numerous guides on the community hub, with all the recipes spelled out, many people found this crafting system too difficult to understand and demanded an in-game guide a'la other survival games. So it was done. But now all the people who liked the previous system, but said nothing, are loudly vocalizing their disapproval of the new system. Even evoking maudlin hyperbole that the game is ruined, the devs betrayed them, they have lost their way and sold out... etc. ad nauseum. (I should say here that I like different aspects of both the old and the new crafting systems. It is a means to an end, and not a make-it-or-break-it feature of the game.) So hopefully, lesson 1 and 2 here have been learned and the devs will remain faithful to what makes a game great; when the devs truly believe in it, and they make a game that they themselves would enjoy. You will never please everyone, but if, at the end of the day, you have remained true to yourself, you will have truly achieved something worthwhile.

The little side stories, the stuff you can find - or not, it doesn't matter, it's up to you - gives the whole game a sense of place. Depending on how you squint at it, you can read the whole thing in at least two very different ways, and there's nothing in the game itself that really says which is right. I loved this game dearly. It's setting and characters will feel familiar to anybody who grew up in rural America. This is it's strongest feature; its relevance. On the surface it is a touching story about one young woman's battle with the human condition, with lonliness, emptiness, and lack of purpose. But it says more about the condition of working class people in a society that values them less and less every year. While its gameplay may feel shallow to some; mindless platforming, minigames, and jumping through dialogue, but it works to put you in the mind of Mae, a character who is running from her feelings - from her lack of purpose. This feels like a new kind of game, one that values its characters above all else. The story is driven by the characters decisions, and it feels completely organic. I could say more, but I wont. I think that anyone who is a fan of adventure games should play this immediately, but I also think those who are not gamers should play it as well. This is a wonderful story and I wish there were 8 more like it. But there aren't. It is one of a kind.

While a small game, with Unity GameObjects practically showing their frayed C# code, Ninja Pizza Girl succeeded on a number of levels.
As a game, it imitates the style of classic Sonic games to an excellent degree. If you fall off a particularly difficult series of jumps, that's okay - you will end up on a lower platform that's just as fun, if not quite as fast. Levels are full of collectibles that you can be ranked on, and re-attempting levels for a faster speed is just about always fun.
Storywise, the game definitely surprised me. Simply, it's a game about bullying; the kind anyone may have experienced at any age. And, it's not heavy-handed about it either. The inclusion of "bully ninjas" as enemies slowly creeps into the game without forcing itself into the fun routine of delivering pizzas to odd customers. The story centers around Gemma's attitude towards herself and the neighbors she delivers to, as well as the antagonistic MegaCorp that competes its pizzas against her father's shop. Many of the elements of bullying are there, from the pointless need to impress, the total uncreativeness of the harrassers, and even the mood-destroying targeting of them.
In a Sonic game, it certainly felt aggravating to be cruising along as Sonic, leaping expertly between ramps and springs, only to suddenly run into one of Dr. Robotnik's robots and be stopped short and lose all the momentum you were building up. In Ninja Pizza Girl, this *sort of* ties in with the plot. Keeping up a steady pace in the game, across walljumps, tight platform jumping, and perfect fall-rolls feels great. But then, passing by a conspicuous cardboard box and being tripped out of NOWHERE by a STUPID F***ING ENEMY that you COULDN'T ever see, who then just LAUGHS at you...
It feels frustrating. It makes you want to stop where you are, attack them, or swear to yourself that you'll never get caught off guard again.
And that's how bullying feels.
Later levels in the game almost give you this sense of being *over*-wary; that you're no longer freely springing across rooftops, but CONSTANTLY on watch for anyone who might be out to get you, to the point that even correctly responding to each enemy slows you down. It's still fun in its own way, but it really impressed me how much the change in gameplay actually corresponded to the story being told.
It may help you to know that the game ends on a very positive note. I think it's a very worthwhile game, especially for someone who's had to go through these experiences or is still dealing with them.

No pants, no pizza. And with that statement, Ninja Pizza Girl reminds the player that the work of the pizza delivery guy/girl is a vocation potentially fraught with near nude shut-ins who can barely function behind every door. An early level demonstrates this point when a rather obese man greedily accepts the pizza from our teenage ninja hero in little more than some very well-worn once-white underwear. The fact that this is based on an actual event is more than a little disheartening, though it does make for an entertaining, if flawed game.
Inspiration can literally come from anywhere, I suppose, and this event has become supposition for what follows – a retro-future speed runner with some strong anti-bullying messaging thrown in.
It comes across as preachy, and the fact that the Australian Government helped pay for its development helps showcase where and how this game needs to be approached. Upon playing it, I kept getting the feeling that this is something that should be rolled out into schools, to have teens and tweens enjoying the relatively lacklustre gameplay and absorb its important message.
As a speedrunner, Ninja Pizza Girl is already entering very well worn territory. The idea is that the player, as the eponymous Ninja Pizza Girl must reach the end of the level in a relatively strict time frame. The only action the player can take apart from running is to jump, with the environment showcasing some rather bland parkour.
Like Mirror’s Edge, the game takes place in a dystopian future city and mostly on rooftops. The player can seamlessly slide under and jump over some obstacles, mostly avoid conflict with other ninjas for a conglomerate pizza rival, but the similarities stop there. Ninja Pizza Girl suffers from confusing level layouts, graphics that occasionally blend background and foreground elements, poor animation and a multitude of other minor issues.
Overall, Ninja Pizza Girl doesn’t feel strong enough to stand on its own against superior competitors. It's very short, repetitive, yet it has some great injections of humour between missions and plays well enough in short bursts. But it feels to much like a game built for educational rather than entertainment purposes and doesn’t stand well against the likes of Mirror’s Edge. Hard to recommend.

Dead Effect can be described as an old school, minimal bells and whistle linear FPS with an unimaginative plot and very sophomoric writing.  If you are an experienced FPS player you will recognize plot and play mechanics that have been inspired by or outright copied from such well-known predecessors as Quake 2, Half-life, System Shock 2 and Doom 3. so it has a very been-there-done-that feel.  All the corridors look the same.  All the zombie monsters look like familiar copies from Doom 3 such as the chain-saw zombie.   The weapons are your typical pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, mini-gun, high-tech cross bow, grenade types. The music oscillates between different versions of spooky sci-fi riffs and action soundtrack orchestral motiffs.  The controls are your basic W-A-S-D, space, 1-2-3-4 or scroll wheel (for weapons).  You do have controls for flashlight and crouch but these are basically not really needed.  You can't save during missions but you can pick up credits that can be used to revive yourself if you die.  Gold and credits can be picked up to purchase weapons and upgrades between missions.  You have two profile slots for a male and female protoganist but gameplay is identical regardless of who you pick.
So, you might think that on the basis of the above description I would tell you not to buy and play this game but you would be wrong.  For the price I paid ($4.99) you get the gaming version of snack food - something that satisfies that craving to just shoot stuff for 20 - 30 minutes without the need to learn complex controls, go through a steep learning curve or possess ridiculously high eye-hand coordination skills in order to make progress. It's not really a hard game but just hard enough (especially in the beginning) that you actually need to pay attention and employ some elementary strategy in order to finish the different missions.  It does also have some nice options - for example, you easily replay any mission level that you like plus there are stand-alone game maps where, on a timed basis, you can practice with different weapons and earn additonal credits and gold for new weapons and upgrades.  So, when you don't have time to FPS binge all night but you need a little distraction or break from whatever boring thing you are doing  Dead Effect fits that need.

I really wanted to like this game.  The style is spot on, the premise was interesting, and anything marketed as 'an innovative departure from the traditional point-and-click adventure genre' catches my attention immediately.
Having now played the game and having watched friends play through the bulk of it, I'm not quite sure if that quote was meant to be some sort of cruel joke or not.  Gods Will be Watching is not an adventure game.  It is a Crisis Management Simulator with a story attached, and retro point-and-click adventure game graphics and art that serve as a GUI for said Crisis Management Simulator.
Each level puts you in one room (Sometimes with one or two other rooms nearby) where you are given six or more things to manage in one turn, and one action that you are allowed to manage with.  In the first level you are put in charge of a hostage situation while your team tries to hack the mainframe of the building you are in.  There are four hostages, each with individual moods to manage, the hacking process itself which needs to be reinforced periodically otherwise you lose progress, and a group of armed guards right outside the room inching their way forward every turn.
With all these things progressively 'worsening' every turn and only one action per turn to use to address any of the six (or more, as you progress) factors, you are forced to make what the game is marketing as difficult, morally ambiguous decisions.
It is excruciatingly difficult, and you will never (Or very rarely) get through a level with all of your 'resources' in tact.  The game is designed that way, and you are meant to fail over and over again.  Levels can be anywhere from 45 minutes to an hour and a half long depending on how long you take to make decisions, but the game never moves beyond this basic tenet of creating a situation where you have to juggle eight chainsaws but you only have one hand, and then later you just become blind.
There's no adventuring anywhere near here, so when they say it's a 'drastic departure from point-and-click adventure' they could've actually said that it was a drastic departure from Microsoft Flight Simulator and that would've been just as true.
Misleading PR aside, what's especially annoying is the nature of this crisis simulator.  Sometimes, (And the game doesn't always tell you when.) it is heavily RNG dependent, meaning that you can lose the game 45 minutes into a mission because you got a bad roll behind the scenes and consequently got shot in the face.  There are no checkpoints in Gods, so you go back to the very beginning of the mission and have to roll the die again, after another 45 minutes.
I don't shy away from difficulty usually.  I love the Souls series because it is punishingly difficult and consequences to failure are dire, but it's never unfair with its difficulty.  Gods is unfair.
There are other times where you will have made a crucial mistake early on that doesn't outright screw you over, but slowly erodes your chances of winning until the very end of the mission an hour and a half later.  You fail and you restart, having to perfectly balance a host of rapidly changing factors for another hour and a half and hope you didn't screw up at all along the way.
Moral choices in the game thus become non-existent.  You think nothing of morals, and you start to view the game as a set of variables that need to be manipulated in such a way as to guarantee success as things start to erode.  I suppose you could say that the game forces you to be ruthless, but it is too effective.  Instead of worrying about the fate of the characters invovled, you look at them simply as bits in your poorly running machine, and if they take too much oil then you get rid of them.
The problem is, that's not a moral choice.  It's a mathematical one.  A clinical one.  You don't feel torn when you make these decisions because you care about the characters, you feel torn because you're not sure if this move is going to screw you over an hour later and make you painstakingly redo everything.  I would've gladly sacrificed everyone just to move onto the next mission successfully.
And that's the other problem.  Consequence, three quarters of the way into the game, does not exist.  I will avoid spoilers, but suffice it to say that things that happen in one mission don't seem to carry over with any kind of meaning to any subsequent mission.  To use a loose example, if you lose your special hat in one mission, you will magically have it in the next one with no explanation as to how.
Despite all of this, I don't think Gods Will Be Watching is necessarily a bad game.  It's a bad game for me, and a bad game for who it's being marketed to.  Some people will probably really enjoy it, but I think that group of people is relatively small.
They had a good vision for the game and they executed it without compromise.  And then I presume they realized that there's not a lot of money in an excrutiatingly difficult and unforgiving crisis management simulator that's partially RNG dependent and instead marketed the game as some sort of advanced point-and-click adventure game with a lot of ambiguous moral choices to make and consequences to follow.  Buyer Beware.

I never played Stranger's Wrath when it first came out. I always wanted to play this and Munch's Oddysee to see if they'd live up to the first two Oddworld games.
Having now played this game, I regret not doing so sooner. It mixes up third-person action platforming and first-person shooting in a way that I simply adore. The many types of ammo offer various ways of bagging the bad guys with either stealth (kind of) or just balls-out running and gunning. The bosses are fun too, sometimes even providing a bit of a challenge for the mind without making you stop and think on it for too long.
Personally, I would have liked the game to last just a teensy bit longer than it did, but at the same time it lasts long enough that you're satisfied without feeling it overstays its welcome.
I don't know if it's the HD version alone, but there were a few instances of some lapses in quality, such as blatantly mismatched/desynced subtitles, audio issues and, in a couple rare cases, graphical issues that were a bit annoying, but for the most part it felt like a solid experience.
In short, I really liked this game, if you like action adventure games, this might be right up your alley.
A minor note: I played the game on Normal (or at least thought so, since that's what I chose), but the game only gave me the Easy game completion achievement, so I dunno if I somehow picked Easy, but it would definitely explain the very forgiving difficulty.

First, let's list everything that sucks.

-No item chests.

-The "hookshot" item you'll have to carry around with you for 70% of the game.

-Rebecca's terrible defense stat.

-Boring and uninspired enemies.

-Annoying and cheap enemies. Especially the "Leech Man" that you'll encounter throughout the game.
-Unoriginal level design. With the notable exception of the train.

-A story that tries to make you bond with the characters, but fails.

-The absolute WORST dialogue since the original Resident Evil (1996).

Now that I got that out of the way, I want to recommend this game to fans of the classic Resident Evil titles. Because, despite all the cons listed above, this game is a pretty solid Resident Evil experience. It's not especially scary, given the fact that you almost always have a partner with you, but the core Resident Evil mechanics function as smoothly as ever.

Having two characters allowed Capcom to try new things with puzzle solving, and for the most part it works out nicely. Plus, it adds a new spin on item management. You have to think critically about who gets what item, and when. Weapons are particularly affected by this feature. Have to send Rebecca off on her own? Better give her the shotgun. You think you're about to face a boss? Better give Billy the shotgun instead, and consider leaving Rebecca behind.

All in all, this is a good Resident Evil game with some frustrating design choices that will occasionally irratate you. Not the best, but worth a playthrough. Play on easy if you want to ease the stress. No harm done.

Score, as a Resident Evil game: 7/10
Score, as a game in general: 6/10

I can appreciate the changes the developers made to keep this game feeling fresh but it ended up being even more frustrating than its predecessors.
Partner AI is awful - they miss enemies and are slow to react, wasting ammo and health. The other character is better used as a pack mule. These characters make the NPC characters in Outbreak seem super smart in comparison.
Fixed camera angels are even worse here, there are multiple places where the screen can transition multiple times, causing your character to run in the wrong direction because you, as the player, was accounting for the direction change in the previous camera angel. Yes, it's a problem with other RE games but here I ran into the issue a lot more often.
During different parts of the game, one character is taken away. If you're unprepared, then you have to reload and give the other character ammo/health instead.
In previous RE games, once you learn how an enemy works, it makes it easier to fight them effectively. This is not the case for this RE game. Most enemies have the ability to corner you and dodging hits is near impossible. Also, certain player attacks take way too much time. The molotov, for example, takes a long time to prep annd throw and they're easily attacked before it completes.
Too many places where the other games' stories in the series are poorly shoehorned and referenced, making for a very poor experience.
In my opinion, this game is worse than its predecessors in almost every way possible. Even the ability to drop/use items sucks because this was used in place of the item box. So there will be times where you have to, upon getting to a new area, drop everything and double back to bring all the other items with you.
It's RE0 just as you remember it.  If you liked RE0 and want to play it again, this is what you're after.

This game is certainly strange, but in a good way.
You will spend most of your time deciding which classes to take based on what skills you think will keep your princess breathing and keeping her mood in check to maximize skill gains. The rest is spent making fairly large (or small) decisions that change the course of the game, such as who you want to marry or whether or not to study magic.
If all you are looking for is a win, you might be saddened to learn that there's no randomness to be found (as far as I know), so a particular strategy for winning will forever and always work, assuming you make the same choices every time. The real meat here is exploring all the options available to the player and finding different ways for the game to play out.
This game certainly isn't for everyone, but if you enjoy visual-novel style games with a slow pace and/or finding new and exciting ways to die, it's worth looking into.

I recommend this game. It has a lot of good things going for it. However, personally I've found it's not the level it could be. I stopped playing Pillars of Eternity a while ago, not sure why I found the game a little tiring. But the things that are issues are fixed in Obsidian's other title, Tyranny, which has since come out. If these things aren't issues to you, do get Pillars of Eternity, because even with the problems it's definitely worth a buy.
PROS:
- GREAT Writing.
- Good story.
- Deep, nonlinear stats system - So well designed, in fact, that I've begun to dislike Dungeons & Dragons!
- Colorful world with huge depth and interesting characters.
- Better leveling system than most RPGs - quests grant XP instead of kills, so there's no grinding involved whatsoever.
- Combat system is fundamentally great
- While the story is linear, there are a lot of different ways to handle it "your way"
CONS (Neither are deal breakers but you might care. If you don't, buy it.)
- Six full RPG characters to control at once. Yikes. I like a decent level of micro, but as battles don't give XP, regular combat encounters get tiresome. Mages in particular are unnecessarily complicated to use.
* Tyranny fixes this, by having the same amount of individual character depth while reducing the active party size from 6 to 4.
- A LOT of inworld jargon and terminology that isn't very well explained, or is explained very slowly over time. There are references to characters and incidents and history everywhere. The world is very opaque from the get go.
* Tyranny fixes this. The world of Tyranny is as deep as Pillars of Eternity, but they included a mouse over function so key names and incidents were explained just from hovering above the words with the mouse.
CONCLUSION:
If you don't care about the cons, or if you prefer the setting and mood of Pillars of Eternity over Tyranny, buy Pillars of Eternity. Mechanics-wise, Tyranny is simply a streamlined, yet deep version of the same engine. I suggest that if you care about mechanics or prefer the evil Greek fantasy campaign of Tyranny, buy Tyranny.
Regardless, Obsidian is definitely worth supporting, and both titles are unique enough for both to be played. Buy and play both games if you have the gold.

TL:DR Pillars has some great story and writing and feels quite polished overall. Well worth trying even if your new to CRPGs like I was.
Full Version:
I havent played many CRPGs (Divinity: OS being the only one I've played)  so I was a bit uncertain as to whether I'd like Pillars going in, however I found it to be a really polished and enjoyable game. The writing, lore and story are great and I felt it's the games strong point and was good enough to keep me invested in the game throughout the 70 hours I played.
The real-time with pause combat system was a new experience for me and while I found it quite difficult at first once you get the hang of the basics, combat becomes a lot more fun. I found liberal use of the pause button and using the formation setting to be very helpful as well as knowing what classes to use to aggro and tie down enemies. I found some of the harder battles to be quite thrilling and theres a real feeling of satisfaction in beating a hard boss.
The game is quite polished as of now with a good UI and useful features like follower AI. It's good that the difficulty options are fairly customizable making it a good game for both CRPG veterans and newcomers alike. Also the amount of options when creating your character is great and would be a major plus for people who enjoy the roleplaying aspect of the game.
Overall its a fantastic game and I'm looking forward to the recently announced sequel.
Good points:
-great dialogue, writing and story and some great quests with various outcomes. The end of the game features a summary of how the various decisions you make in the game impact on Dyrwood after the conclusion of the story
-some good customization options when creating your character with the standard race and class, but also sub race and nation factions for example which impact your initial build
- the difficulty settings are quite flexible which makes the game accessible to experienced players or newcomers like myself.
-the White March DLC is a great addition featuring a new area called the White March north of Dyrwood, with new quests and storyline as well as new features that are implemented into the main game.
Bad points:
- learning the real time combat is a bit intimidating for a newcomer and I'd recommend consulting a guide. Though it is more enjoyable once you get the hang of it.
- the game did seem to be a bit too combat heavy at times, with quite a few areas just full of mobs of enemies to fight your way through. I found the game got a bit boring in these sections.

Stranger's Wrath is a charming and charistmatic game that is full of life and deserves to be played by everyone that is a fan of video games. Originally released on January 2005, the HD remaster has done wonders to the game and it looks as fresh and stylised as ever.

To start with, I'd say this game is segmented in to two parts (due to story reasons).
The first part introduces you to a Bounty Hunter, whom is simply known as "Stranger", and a series of Wild West towns. Your goal is to capture criminals, alive or dead, using a crossbow equipped with creatures which are used as ammunition. The gameplay follows a formula, you go to the "Bounty Office" to pick up a bounty, you proceed through a level picking up creatures for ammunition that all perform different functions, you attack enemies (either killing them or capturing them alive for a higher bounty) and then you face the boss, whom you must capture dead or alive.
The second half of the game is slightly different, playing more like a adventure first-person shooter game, whilst still using most of the same mechanics - it plays more similarly to a game such as Half-Life. There is a good reason for this, but I will not discuss it here due to spoilers.
Stranger's Wrath, like all Oddworld games, outshines itself in ingenuity, character, charisma and charm. It's near to impossible to hate any Oddworld games because they are so inherently strange and lovable.

Resident Evil 0 is another chapter who had its first debut on the Gamecube. This game used to be the very first experiment from Capcom aimed to test the potential of living a survival horror managing two characters instead of one.
The story takes place the day before the events that involved Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield horrorific nightmares in the mansion.
In this game we are asked to help Rebecca Chambers and Billy Cohen in their travel through zombies and monsters and to find their own safety.
The idea followed by Capcom is interesting: we manage 2 heroes at once, taking care of their inventory and health separately and combining their skills to solve puzzles and traps moving on their adventure.
I really liked the factor of removing the boxes where you could place your items in, however they introduced the option of discarding useless items placing them on the ground allowing you to retreive them in the future if needed. A cool feature that forced you to organize your inventory.
But where this feature forced you to organize your inventory, in reality it was used to hide the fact that this game is pretty short so they needed to make the player backtrack a lot to retreive items you could need in future situations.
The very bad side of the game, however, is the feeling of being thrown in areas that are the exact copy of the original Resident Evil but with a disposition of rooms and areas that are totally absurd [for example, after a train crash, you end up in the sewers under a mansion (no, not the same mansion) and after you climb the stairs you are in the HALL!].
The game is fun by itself anyway, but don't consider it an important part of the story line, is more like a filler but not really necessary.
The HD version improved the graphics just like they did in Resident Evil HD but in RE0 they added another mode named Wesker Mode where you can play the original campaign using Wesker and nuke down zombies and monsters with powerful skills.
In the end, i suggest this game considering is fun and will entertain you for sure, if you can afford it together with RE HD then it's a bingo.

I'm all for hard games.
As long as the game is based on skill or rules, not on luck.
This game is not one of those games.
I had been anticipating Gods Will be Watching for a while; it looked like an interesting premise. I'm a fan of narrative-driven games, and this one looked very promising.
However, the "normal" mode kills it. Completely.
And anyone who says the game is not luck-based is wrong; my first try of my first load of the game, I get the quintessential "game over" screen without having done a single thing (The data was blocked/corrupted). How can I lose a game without having even played it? A failure state is a requirement for a game, but interaction to achieve said failure state is also pretty much a given.
I restarted the game in "light" mode, taking away the "chance" mechanic (come on guys, even the developer says it's based on chance...). Even then, mechanics are uneven and the game is extremely unforgiving. Rules change every level... I made it to level 3, but then, I wondered "What's the point?".
I will most likely restart the game in narrative mode, so I can experience the story... because that's what drove me to this game in the first place.

Dead Effect is a mobile-ported zombie survival game (surprised to see one here on Steam) set in the enviroment of a spaceship, I will be breaking down the game by it's natural elements.
Story: Surprisingly, this mobile-ported game has a storyline attached to it, but I was not really expecting a storyline at all when I launched the campaign up. In short, the storyline is VERY linear and basic, and for the rest of this statement, the storyline was not good at all. Luckily the gameplay of this game makes it still an average game.
Gameplay: The gameplay of Dead Effect is simple and sweet, upgrading weapons you come across is nice when it comes to zombie survival games nowadays. Since there are zombies you face in the game, there are other variants you'll come across whilst blasting through the campaign. And what is also nice is that you get to upgrade yourself as well which comes in handy. What kinda bugs me since this was a mobile-ported game, there's no PC elements in the game, meaning there is no quicksave, quickload etc. Another gameplay mechanic I should mention is whenever you die you would have to decide to establish one of two options to move through the game, the first one is to restart, which does mean that you have to restart the whole chapter, while the other option is you can continue for a price of credits which is the currency in the game to buy weapons and its upgrades (luckily for your ownself upgrades there is no cost, but there is a catch). The price for continuing does change, I was playing through the game on Medium and I don't know if there is an increase of price when you die on higher difficulties. One last thing to mention, there are some extra gameplay modes in the game, there is New Game +, which is self-explanatory, another one is Survival, and lastly I saw Biohazard, not sure what that one would be.
I don't really know if there's any other things I can cover about this game, but overall for a measly price of only $8, I would recommend to you to buy this game when it's on sale, since the storyline sucks, which matters the most in a game in my opinion. Don't take this review I'm writing the wrong way, this game is an average joe, but again, buy it when it pops up on sale.

So I'm going to preface this by saying I don't have a ton of experience in the survival genre. That doesn't stop me from highly recommending Miscreated though. I know I don't have the insane amount of hours other people have put into the game but it's seriously a load of fun. The game is super intense and can really get your adreneline pumping. There's been plenty of incredibly stressful (in a good, fun way) situations.
One example of those situations was the first time I played the game. I met some guy and we eventually got a freshspawn group of 5 people and went to the airfield. We all had a little bit of loot, nothing spectacular though. Just a few pistols and melee weapons and some decent clothing. We're walking through the airfield when a sniper rifle rings out and one of our guys drops as he's talking to us mid sentence. Immediately we scramble for cover but another one of our guys gets lit up by an AR and there's only 3 of us left. We legit can't even spot our attackers because we weren't paying attention though. Another sniper shot rings out and then there's two of us left. Luckily, we spotted the guy and scramble into a pretty large tent. I got shot though so I'm about half health and bleeding out bad. I had to take off my clothes and bandage myself up.
So me and my last remaining buddy are sitting in a tent aiming at the opening. He tells me he's going to go grab the car we left just up the hill and that if he's not back in 10 minutes to run. So I set a gas can right in front of the tent opening and he leaves. My heart is racing and I'm literally sweating trying to survive, my pistol is aimed right at this gas can. Five minutes pass. Ten minutes pass. Fifteen. He's still not back and I know they got him. Just as I'm about to make a run for it a dude in military gear turns the corner to my tent.
BAM
Shot the gas cannister and it exploded killing the guy instantly. Instead of looting him though I bail and make a break for the woods. Now keep in mind I'm starving, naked, and at about half hp while dodging and weaving bullets until I finally make it out alive.
It was literally one of the most intense gaming moments of my life and it was fun as hell. And I've had plenty more like it. Do I recommend this game? Hell yes I do

This game is certainly strange, but in a good way.
You will spend most of your time deciding which classes to take based on what skills you think will keep your princess breathing and keeping her mood in check to maximize skill gains. The rest is spent making fairly large (or small) decisions that change the course of the game, such as who you want to marry or whether or not to study magic.
If all you are looking for is a win, you might be saddened to learn that there's no randomness to be found (as far as I know), so a particular strategy for winning will forever and always work, assuming you make the same choices every time. The real meat here is exploring all the options available to the player and finding different ways for the game to play out.
This game certainly isn't for everyone, but if you enjoy visual-novel style games with a slow pace and/or finding new and exciting ways to die, it's worth looking into.

I'll say this now, this is a hard game to explain. Trust me: Saying "You play a Princess and your goal is to live." is going to be one of the weirdest things you'll hear from a guy's mouth.
The game itself goes at your own pace, and is a lot of reading. Well, to the extent that you can skip dialogue, but you'll want  to read it because it may or may not come into play in decision you make in the game. The game itself has great replay value. The way you die feels like an ending, and even when I became Queen (twice so far) you feel like you could of done better. You can save at anytime, which was a huge plus for me as I work alot, and you could place the game in 1 minute, then go about your business. (I do not recommend this, because you might forget what's going on) If you do pick up this game, all I can suggest is: The first time you play, play it with one save file and play it up to your first death. (If you got to the end on your first time around, bravo! I've yet to meet anyone who lived their first time playing)

Long Live the Queen is a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure, novella game stylized in classic anime art.  The basic premise is that you play as a young princess who is soon to be thrust into the role of queen of a kingdom, and you have to make choices to deal with internal affairs, foreign politics, and even magical events - a the goal of surviving until the day you are coronated.
The Good:
-Artwork: Although I'm a little bored by the anime look, this game manages to do a nice job with adding details (likely because it's mostly static images and doesn't actually have to be animated to move).
-User Interface: The tutorial is super short because it CAN be.  The layout and general gameplay are very easy to pick up and play.
-The Premise: I hadn't seen a story idea in a game like this before and give kudos to the developers (Hanako Games) for thinking of it.
-Leveling Up: I like the idea of the emotion & education balancers in this game.  Being angry makes you better at learning various athleticly inclined skills, but isn't very suitabe for working on your public image.  Yes, I said 'idea'.  The problem isn't the system, but the overall game and how it's used.  See more in The Bad
-Politics: I actually feel like some excellent work was done in crafting certain characters (Banion especially comes to mind) responses to events and choices that you make.
The Neutral:
-Dialogue: Inane dialogue with this type of game is one of the reasons I will sometimes stay away, but this one manages to avoid the obnoxiousness and overly zealous attempts to be humorous and just simply provides a story.  The only reason I don't mark it as a positive point is due to the fact that it lacks complexity - this is not a game that will make you ponder life.
-Play Time: This game is not long, and most of your time will be spent replaying the game from scratch (unless if you heavily manage your savegames) to try to get a better or different outcome at some point in the story.  Once you manage to beat the game and get a positive ending..............you're done.
The Bad:
-Lots of choices, but no choices at all: While there are definitely lots of variables to manage in your skills and options to explore and plan for, I felt kneecapped on moving towards the end of the story.  The game is only 40 weeks long (i.e. 40 turns) and the writers for this title have a defined way to win.  I'd much rather the scope be expanded so that I can compare the events to my friends that play this game and not just die so early/easily.
-Sandbox Needed: Though we're talking about switching genres, I would be very interested in seeing this game be a simple, anime-style approach to the political maneuvering and family management of the Total War games.
Worth It?  Yes, you should buy this game and give it a shot; just don't pay full price.  $5 bucks or less is money well spent, but any more than that might leave you feeling a little cheated.  I'm still glad I gave teh developers some money as I look forward to seeing them revisit this type of game with more experience behind them.

Ghoul kid is a game where the player takes control of a ghost whom just wants some interaction with humans, not the Casper the friendly ghost type, more like a jigsaw type.
Your mission consists in scarying to death your intruders in form of waves, which consist in three types: children (takes two scares), the milf (takes 3-4 scares) and the coward dad (takes 3 scares), the enemy variety isn't there, the devs could had jeovah's witnesses, and more annoying stereotypes for more fun.
To scare people to death your ghost must possess the objects around the house (radio, tv, piano, blender, microwave, jackinthebox, etc...) the collection of objects is very constrained but the size of each house division can help you drain the souls faster.
The sound consists on a single track that can make you slowly descend into madness or shutdown the music.
The game has three modes: normal ( which tells your story - 10 waves ), trick or threat (10 waves on children that you have to scare to death) and Double Trouble (10 waves - i call it story 2).
Although the game isn't anything new or inovative, it still is a kind of fun, sure there are limitations in terms of object interaction, enemy design, lack of personality on the main character (yes i know it's a ghost but there are good ghosts), and repetion can become a turn off, but if you like the discount neightbors from hell vibe, and have a few time to spare and want some easy acheviements give it a shot, for me it waas simply not worth it.

This is basically a game about a girl who delivers pizza for her dad by parkouring through the city. The twist is that along the way she is bullied by other delivery ninjas, effectively killing her self-esteem.
I'm not saying the message of the game is bad, because it's not. Bullying is a serious issue. The game itself left a lot to be desired. The controls were wonky, the framerate was seriously all over the place (for a game that really doesn't look that amazing to begin with), and the levels just got frustrating the longer I played...not that it's even a long game to begin with.
I'd love to recommend this because it has a good message to it, but looking at it objectively from a gameplay standpoint, I cannot.

For the first 30 minutes or so the level design is basically fine. The game is 'preachy,' and even as someone who kinda agrees with most of what they're saying, the preachiness of the game was just so out of place and quite frankly random that it was kinda distracting. It's also kinda silly, because you spend most of the game kicking people in the face in a game opposed to bullying. Weird. Anyway, the real problem with the game is the level design after the first thirty minutes. It starts getting kinda obnoxious. Miss one jump and you're like, am I still okay, or am I now running back to get to where I started the level? You really have no way to tell. What the game needs is like a minimap if the level design is going to be this all-over-the-place. It's not the worst platformer out there, and the preachiness isn't that bad, but the platforming on some levels becomes more frustrating than fun.

"Ninja Pizza Girl is a serious game about bullying, emotional resilience – and pizza delivering ninjas! " - it's not a good game though.
The game is a mixture of runner and a platformer. You are a ninja pizza girl that scales the roofs in order to deliver the pizza within the time given. On the way you need to tackle time, obstacles and enemies. It's all accompanied by some sort of story presented in dialog between the main character and her friends.
The story is hard to follow. It's presented in a way that made me not really care. And while it might try to talk about bullying and other serious stuff - it couldn't make me care. In order to emphasis the emotional struggles of the main character a mechanic is introduced to take a tea in order to lighten up your mood. A bad mood is indicated by visual cue - everything starts to get darker and gloomy - it's an interesting thing - though found it more annoying than anything else.
The controls for a runner do not feel good. They feel a bit laggy and not very responsive. The level design is bad as well. The main path is unclear and it seems that falling at any point just forces you to take a different route so you don't feel all that challenged. The various uninspired pickups seem to be placed randomly or just without a sense. The enemies are very repetitive and with just a basic behaviour. Jumping, sliding, wall jumping does not feel good as well - with trampoline jumping being the biggest offender. Overall there's just no fun in playing the game.
The soundtrack is poor as well. It's a form of dub-step but not very energetic. The visuals look a bit like generic unity assets - a very bland sort of 3D models and environments.
On the good side though there doesn't seem to be any technical problems with it - but that's as much positivity I can muster for the game.
Overall I can't recommend it to anyone. The game is just no fun.

Note that I paid 4USD for the game, plus the sums of EULA subjugation and selling out beliefs about DRM and end-user rights. I doubt the review would be much different at full price, but I don't really agree with a person who thinks a USD/GBP/BTC has any value.

Months after purchasing "Gods Will Be Watching", I finally found some free time to  crawl through its chapters in their original difficulty. And the first thing I do upon completion, is to rewrite my earlier review for this game.
This is not a game about puzzles, while on the surface it looks like one, its nondeterministic results are enough set many patient solvers on fire.
This is not a game about morality, while we don't have canonical answers to many of its questions, their presence serve the ultimate goal of this game.
This is a game that ponder the worth of player decisions. And if you want to get metaphysical:
So before purchasing this game or choosing one of its many gameplay mode (some were added post-release), all you needed to ask yourself are these 2 questions:
1. Will I be OK that, after being tortured and torturing others, after losing not only to my own mistakes but also to random number generators, after going from deeply disturbed by its graphical content to constantly skipping the same content with blind eyes, that my blood-soaked sweat-stained decisions, are yet a mechanism to move its narrative forward?
2. Will I be OK that, with all the positivity I try to instill with my decisions, this game ultimately decides to cast a grim outlook on free will?
If you are ready for this taoist-esque afterthought, then maybe, you will enjoy playing "Gods Will Be Watching" in its normal (read: most unforgiving) difficulty.

I'm a little sad about giving this game a bad review because it looks like a lot of love went into it, but... short version, the gameplay is just not enjoyable.
The longer version:
Combat uses a strange pseudo-real-time system loosely inspired by the 4th edition of Dungeons and Dragons. You control up to six characters and constantly have to pause the game manually to assign actions or cancel actions to reassign new ones. With six characters using actions that have various use times and "recovery" times, this adds up to a level of micromanagement that turns fights into tedious chores.
This could have been mitigated by using fewer characters... if not for this game's bizarre experience system. Traditionally, RPGs will let you use whatever number of party members you choose, without penalty, by splitting EXP between characters present. If an encounter is worth 600 EXP, characters in a party of six would each gain 100 EXP, a party of three would see 200 EXP per member, etc. But in this game, where a group of six people would get a total of 600 EXP, a solo character would only get a total of 150; that's a -75% EXP penalty. It's still possible to play with one or two characters, but unlike with most traditional games, you will be severely punished for doing so. Also, solo characters will often talk (in both voiced content and dialogue choices) like they're in a party even if they're not.
Loading screens are also excessive. In part because of length, but also because of their frequency; entering a tiny one-room hut will require a loading screen to enter and another to exit. You'll have to go through two loading screens every time you want to talk to an NPC or shopkeeper that's in a house.
The game has "hidden" stashes of loot, which sounds like a lot of fun, except you generally can't see them unless you're in "Stealth/Scouting" mode, which halves your speed. Even if you're a knight in shining and clanky full plate armor, you'll be walking like a Rogue-type character on a secret mission even in the middle public streets, like an idiot... hoping that the secrets you find will actually be worth anything, because a surprisingly high number of them, despite being hidden, only contain near-worthless junk.
There were other, much smaller irritants present. Probably not worth listing, but let's just say this camel didn't need more straw on its back.
I'm sure there are people who love this game. But as a gamer of 30+ years, I found it to be too severely flawed and I feel that I must warn potential buyers of some of the more critical ones.
