After countless hours on the Xbox 360, I decided to re-buy the game on Steam to experience it on MAX graphics/frame-rates. And still to this day, the game is absolutely PHENOMENAL. The best way to describe it, is THE BEST SPLINTER CELL GAME EVER CREATED. Yes, I have played every game in the series and although Chaos Theory gets the most love, this game is light years ahead of it in every way.
To begin with, the game focuses on 3 ways to play:
Ghost - Avoiding all enemies and never being seen while still accomplishing your objective
Panther - Killing all enemies while never being seen
Assault - Guns blazing, there's no such thing as stealth
As for me, my preffered playstyle is Panther. Nothing is more satisfying then moving from cover to cover, stalking enemies, silently taking them down with the lethal Karambit expericing the beautiful stealth kills one by one. When using takedowns or kills, you will build an "Execute" meter. Once filled after the required amount of kills, you are able to "mark and execute" up to 3 enemies with the press of the button. This makes for some jaw-dropping moments of kill one enemy, then press "execute" button and take down 4 enemies like a bad-*bleep*.
Now depending on how you play each mission, you will earn a score at the end of each mission that rewards your playstyle. The reward is CASH. This cash you earn, can now be used to upgrade your weapons, suit/armor(depending on your playstyle, and gadgets. The way the game is set-up, it makes you want to play all missions in each and every playstyle which just expands the playability almost infinitely.
There's really no downside to this game in my eyes...The only issue I have, and it's very minor, but could be improved for the next game, is that there is no seemless way to move around an object that you are currently using as cover. In for instance, Deus Ex, you would hold the cover button to go around the object. However in this game, you have to line up the cover system to mark the next spot then press the button to move. When things get intense, it becomes a pain to try and line up the next spot on the cover you're already in.
TL;DR:
If you like Splinter Cell, or stealth games, buy this game instantly. It's the best Splinter Cell game ever made, hands down.

If you are looking for a survival game that recieves regular updates from a dev team that seem to genuinely care about the game look no farther from Miscreated.
The atmosphere, balance of loot, and combat mechanics of this game provide a very solid experience for any fan of the survival genre. As a long time DayZ player I find Miscreated to be a very good change of pace. The amazing map design and atmosphere the devs have created truly blows anything else out of the water from this genre. Guns, ammo, and everything else you need to survive in world of Miscreated is neither hard nor easy to acquire. You run into people everywhere on the map and the addition of base building gives another element to exploration and looting.
Combat mechanics are solid and responsive and getting a kill whether with a pistol, hatchet or AR feels like an accomplishment. I havent had an instance where I found myself blaming desync or cheap tactics. Dont expect the indepth bullet mechanics of DayZ but its better than H1Z1 which is a plus. If you want the full experience this game has to offer I definitely reccomend playing the game on First Person only servers. Where DayZ I feel is a smoother and better experience playing on 3rd person (though I do enjoy first person more because of balance), Miscreated however definitely shines playing in first. It really allows you to become immersed in the world and allows a better flow of gameplay because like I said, the map design and atmosphere is amazing, nearly every building being enterable and many having multiple floors allows one to set up ambushes or great overwatch positions.
Overall I would say Miscreated is a grossly underrated game that deserves much more recognition and praise then it gets. For such a fair price you wont find a better survival game out there.

Dead Effect is a story driven first-person corridor shooter set aboard a futuristic research vessel/station, where an accident suddenly turns the crew into homicidal zombies.  It is a very well made game enjoyable to play and satisfying to beat.  Essentially it is a free 2 play iOS port.  One of the few I have played that works well as a PC game.
You are part of an Elite unit awakened from hibernation to respond to an emergency aboard the vessel.  You can choose to take on the role of a male or female soldier the only difference being the starting weapons and the voice-overs.  Once armed you go up against a horde of zombie type enemies.  Your job 'as always' is to go from level to level and complete objectives in order to progress to the end boss.
Enemies consist of several types of zombie: crawler, zombie, scientist zombie, soldier zombie, spitters and grenade zombies, plus a few specials which I wont mention and spoil for you here.  Combat against the zombies is one of the strong points of the game.  While they are only effective in packs and at close quarters, the badder zombies can spit venom or throw grenades which can be deadly from range.  Furthermore even though the zombies close distance slowly their strength is in numbers, especially when moving through the vessels tight walkways.
As you move along the infested decks of the vessel you will be able to collect ammo and grenade refils, and credits from the (un)dead crew.  In addition you can collect datapads with snippets of story to help explain the events which unfolded before you awoke.  Killing enemies sometimes provides valuable item drops such as gold bars, credits (i.e. in-game cash), new weapon unlocks or weapon upgrades.  Gold bars seem to be largely a remnant of its free2play days, which I suspect were gained largely through some sort of microtransactions.  Thankfully though these do not exist in this PC version.  Gold bars can be used to buy a handful of ultra-powerful weapons or an auto-heal feature which seems redundant for most players except for casual gamers.  Credits allow you to purchase or upgrade combat weapons.
You start with a basic 1000 volt stungun which is good when you fighting lone enemies.  As you play you get access to better weapons.  Even though you can only carry two types of firearm (1-handed sidearm & a 2-handed assault weapon) and 1 batch of grenades during a level.  You can switch between several model types between levels.  This limitation is quite realistic even if you prefer the old skool method of carrying an arsenal into combat.
Weapons include different types of: handgun, assault rifle, shotgun, bows, energy weapons and a minigun. Melee lovers take note that there is a chainsaw weapon which you can get close and personal with the enemy but I found it to be the least satisfying of the weapons to play.  Whats even better about the guns is that they can be upgraded during play.  5 levels for each weapon that increase stats like: reload speed, magazine capacity, damage and accuracy.  New weapons can be purchased with the credits you collect.  By far the most satisfying weapons are the shotgun or the bow with exploding arrow heads! :)  You also get two special if limited abilties: Bullet time (slow-mo action) and Devastation (powerful strike eminating from the player).
The campaign consists of twelve levels ranging from short to long in terms of duration.  All levels though similar in the challenges and obstacles they provide are pretty well designed.  You will probably have to play through the game twice to complete the campaign achievements.  In addition there have been two modes added and play similarly to Killing Floor - Survival maps require you to not die for a number of minutes, while in Biohazard maps you must survive numerous waves of ever increasing difficultly.  There are around six maps for each mode.  These I found were adequate at best.  To be better coop is really needed here.
Overall I found the gameplay and aesthetics (graphics & sound) were pretty good, setting the right tone that will remind older gamers of Doom 3 or System Shock [if you have played either].  The story while pretty standard does its job in immersing you within the setting.  Graphics for a port are really well done bringing a claustraphobic feel as you move around the vessel. While voice-overs (there are three one for each marine character and the only other survivor a scientist who guides you) are quite good for an indie game.  I did discover a very few minor bugs which were not game-breakers but these were fixed during my time playing the game.
Rock, Paper, Shotgun wrote that Dead Effect fails in its ambition.  After playing through the game I found that what the game may lack in terms of ambition it more than makes up for in immersion, and quality implementation and delivery.  In conclusion Id say so many games that come through Early Access fail to deliver, Dead Effect does that and more.
For the price its an easy recommendation.  Looking forward to the sequel.

Really, really enjoyed this. Perfect? Nope. Inspired? Probably not. Hectic spraying and praying while walking backwards alot? Yup. A serviceable story with generally bearable acting? Sure, why not. Believable, claustrophobic environments with a tense atmosphere around every other corner? Absolutely.
I'm 50 years old. In other words, I'm way, way ancient. As I approach having played through the campaigns of about four dozen sci-fi/horror/shooter/stealth games stretching back decades--some of the AAA variety and others that less than 15 people in the west even know about (Kreed, anyone?)--I am slowly learning that all interactive entertainment exists in context. Anyone grousing about this game probably has no idea what a truly bad game is. Dear complainers: While it may appear to have the proper trappings (and do a lot of borrowing), Dead Effect ain't Dead Space (or Doom for that matter). But to our benefit, it also isn't Run Like Hell or Alien: Colonial Marines. This game exists as a competent, complete (as in finished), challenging, bloody, entertaining, intentionally goofy (at times), highly derivative, technically stable title with generally wider-than-average blood spray patterns. I mean, what else do you want in an indie?
Enter Dead Effect's playground with the proper context, and it will easily rise to meet your middling expectations. (And I mean that in the best, brain-splattery way possible. Reload.)
A more linear counter strike game, totally enjoyable though.

Visually I think this game is amazing. Really crisp colors, detailed designs, and cool character animations.
The plot is pretty typical - Infection aboard the ship and the crew has been turned into monsters. Nothing new, but hey who questions these kinds of thing. You have a gun and you know what to do.
The gameplay is simplistic, point n' click to shoot, navigate through the halls, look for little treasures and ammunition, get the achievements then onto the next one.
Honestly there's nothing very intense about the infected except when they're in huge masses, but that's because you know those shell counts are about to go down. I haven't felt any fear or panic like I had initially expected. I think something that contributes to that is you have the ability to move very fast (for a very short time) and they don't. So to get out of any situation is to simply put space between you and them and shoot. Even the mele weapon doesn't really give you the option to get up close and dirty.
I know there's an android/IOS app of this game, and that's one of the reasons I got it for Steam. But it still feels like an app game and not something played with a keyboard and mouse. It definitley needs to be fully converted with the playable freedoms of a PC game, and THEN I think this game will be phenomenal.
But right now, the app is free and this is $8. For some, it won't be a bang for their buck and I don't blame you.
I will recommend this in the hopes that it will be updated or reduxed altogether because it has some amazing potential that the Sci-Fi Horror genre needs.

You know how for 8-bit/16-bit retro games, there are indie developers who clearly don't know what they play like or feel like? In regards to 8-bit, there are too many colours. Or for 16-bit, the sprites aren't detailed enough. There's an inauthentic feeling that you can't shake.
That's the way I feel about this game. FMV games weren't trying to be bad. In fact, there were good FMV games. There were also just some that were hilariously bad, but they were hilarious because they didn't know better. There was an earnest attempt. A bad movie made by someone who thinks he's talented is better than a movie that's trying to take the
despite the person knowing they could do better. (Although I have doubts about that if this game is anything to go by.)
Some of the camera shots are just subpar or low quality. Like one scene has your character staring at a blank white wall longer than necessary. Hello? Get a painting or poster or something. There was one shot that had some weird switch between day/night in the middle of a scene, like it was filmed in a single day and they didn't want to wait the extra day to film it for continuity purposes.
The make up effects feel like they're not even trying, which you know, was quite evident they weren't. Like the acting. While I'm sure there weren't robots working on this production, but if you told me there were, I'd believe you. The game talks about "dynamic dialogue", but that's not how it'll come across with actors like these. With maybe the one M. Night Shyamalan joke being kinda funny (although they spoil that in the trailer for the game so you may as well not even play it if you've watched it), the rest of the writing is full of out of place and unfunny pop culture references like Twilight and Hunger Games that don't at all fit.
When you make me think that Family Guy of all things could handle crowbarring in references better, I think you've failed. What's more insulting to me is that there were no jokes making fun of the FMV format, let alone references to classic titles in the genre. Have any of these people even played Tex Murphy, let alone Phantasmagoria?
Oh, and hey guys, 1994 Mode was already done in Stay Dead Evolution, and it's more annoying than accurate. Stay Dead Evolution... now there's a bad game that wore the FMV concept proudly. SDE never tried to sell itself short with a "only kidding!" vibe that crap like this tries to. I certainly don't like Stay Dead, but I'd gladly say it's better than this.

Think of this game as a terraria campaign mode set in space. It's a fun game, but it could quickly become repetitive. There are many star systems and planets to visit, but there isn't really a need to go to all of them. There isn't really anything new and the planets all look similar and have similar lifeforms. It is very fun initially as you discover new creatures and vegetation, but you quickly realise there are only a limited number of them. I suggest going into this game with the mindset that this isn't a sandbox game like terraria, but rather a game which tells a story and you are playing a campaign mode. Overall, this game can provide tens of hours of fun, I suggest playing it with friends.

I'm a long time Street Fighter fan and started playing the game on the Super Nintendo when I was a little child around 11 years of age.
The game came as a package with the console and I was drooling over the cartridge's cover which looked so much cooler than the other variant sporting the Super Mario World cartridge, so I was making up stuff about what this game would be going to be like and who this Hulk-esque looking beast was.
My imagination was wrong, because even the imagination of a 11-year old boy could not fathom the awesomeness that was Street Fighter II: The World Warrior.
In Germany where I come from, there sadly was never an arcade culture, since our law sees every machine you throw money into as gambling and that is strictly prohibited to minors.
That still did not stop me to visit my friends and play the game with them, competing with each other and dreaming about how cool it would be if you could play with people from around world and visit tournaments and stuff.
Sooner or later my friends quit playing the game, either out of disinterest or because they felt it was too much effort to try keeping up with me.
Now I'm coming closer to the point I am trying to make.
See fighting games are pretty much worthless as single player experiences. You simply NEED to play these games with human competition, no matter how well-crafted the single player experience may be, in the end everything boils down to multiplayer.
When SFIV was finally released I first chose to ignore it, since I did not own a console at that time, but the thought that you could finally play this amazing game against other people from around the world was intriguing to say the least.
Couple of years later I saw the game in a Steam Sale and picked it up, had tons of fun with it, even though the Games For Windows Live-Online was garbage by my standards (I come from playing DotA, Blizzard titles and Dota 2, so my online standards are pretty damn high), it did the job good enough for me to keep playing and stay interested.
Now it has been 3 month since Super Street Fighter 4: AE2012 was ported to Steamworks and it completely broke online play for a lot of people. I personally have to set my computer to DMZ in my router in order to be able to play the game properly and it still lags horribly at least once a match, the menus start lagging as well and it's generally a pain in the butt playing the game.
When Ultra Street Fighter 4 hit the stores, I thought Capcom had been working on fixing these problem for the past couple of month and are now ready to patch it along with the upgrade.
Plot Twist:
Turns out they did not do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ despite their forum posts saying they were aware of the problem and working on it, they did not do anything and even had the nerve to post the same stuff that they already did with the AE transition, which was "We are aware of the problem and we are going to fix it".
I will try to come to an end here in my clumsy try to make a game review.
Bottom line for me is that if you are not living in Arcade America/Japan and you do not know anyone around you who regularly plays Ultra Street Fighter 4, then do not bother with this game since Capcom does not give a single fart about you and chances are that you will not be able to play this game with anyone else but yourself.
The game itself is well-designed maybe a bit buggy overall but it is a good entry to the Street Fighter series and tons of fun, ultimately I decide against recommending this game, since the online multiplayer is a major selling point, not only for me but for most people, and since it does not work like intended, I will refrain from telling anyone to buy it.
UPDATE:
As of the 03.30.2015, this game is actually playable online, to the same extend that GFWL was and XBox Live is.
Go ahead and buy it, if you're looking for a rather defensive but well-made Street Fighter game.
The game has its downsides of course, but it's still Street Fighter and a lot of fun to play.

The amount of hate this game is getting is absurd. To be fair, there should be a disclaimer: This game is built to make the player fail. You will fail. Repeatedly. Sometimes simply because RNG decides it so.
If that turns you away, then don't purchase this game. You are offered little to no direct instructions other than how to select commands, and you are presented with, at most, hints from other characters about how to proceed. The rest is completely up to you to figure out. And when you finally "get it", it will often be too late as half your party is either dead or about to die and the game over is seconds away. But every time you fail and restart (which, by the way, is incredibly smooth, putting you right back into the action by skipping any unneeded dialogue), you push forward with your newly found knowledge to beat the level. It could be as simple as memorizing the visual cues or realizing a pattern to how events sequence out. And it's not like you don't know what killed you. It is often extremely clear (I failed a chapter 1 minute in because I failed to light the campfire for the night, freezing everyone to death, with an accompanying message reminding me what I'm dumb). All this adds up to a "Eureka!" moment, when you finally get your own routine down to beat the level, where you understand how to keep that constantly rebelling hostage from attacking, and you are certain you can win.
...And then you fail an action that has an 80% chance of success, giving you a game over.
It's all very reminiscent of the difficulty of retro games, where the only way to succeed is by dying to the traps that you can't possibly avoid without already knowing they are there.
It does what a "choose your adventure" point and click like The Walking Dead series was supposed to do: Your moral choices aren't simply governed by how much you like a character (Let's be real, every "save this character" choice in TWD was ultimately inconsequential if you survived or not), but by the fact that choosing to be benevolent can doom your entire group. Knowing you are one unlucky dice roll away from death certainly skews most people's moral compass.
In multiple chapters you are presented with a survival challenge: Keep everyone in your group well-rested, fed, and happy, otherwise there will be deaths. Easy enough, right? So when oxygen is running out and the only way to survive is by getting passwords from your hostages who refuse to talk, do you beat their kid and threaten to blast his head off to break his mother into telling, or do you let him free to earn the trust of your captives? Or what about when your hunter is unable to come up with food for the day, and you have to choose between feeding your party's doctor or another member who offers purely moral support? Do you let the doctor go hungry and risk him dying/deserting, leaving your party without medical aid, or do you feed him and let someone else starve to death? Suddenly, moral choices become much more impactful.
For me, the combination of "You can't save everyone" with RNG elements and vague mechanics makes the game much more immersive than your standard survival game. You aren't given clear instructions, consequences need to be learned (the hard way), and often times you don't even know what the win state is.
Which brings me to chapter 2.  Everyone is whinging about it, so if you read the reviews you'll probably know a little about it.
All in all, this is an amazing game. The minimalistic graphics are awesome, the soundtrack is superb, the story is a little cheesy, yeah, but still enjoyable. If you are patient and aren't turned off by the fact you can fail simply because the game said ♥♥♥♥ you, pick this game up. Definitely worth at least a try.

I initially preorded the collector’s edition of Gods Will Be Watching with a friend because I’m a huge fan of another game Devolver Digital produced, Hotline Miami. I expected to pick it up for a few hours, beat it in a day, and never think much about it after that. I was wrong.
For one, this game is hard as hell. Even after the mercy update which added additional puzzle and narrative only modes that remove some of the chance, I spent honest to god hours trying to beat some of the chapters. The results were rewarding, don’t get me wrong, but every death sent me back to the beginning and with no checkpoint saving that meant every decision I made had the potential to send me down a different path within the level. There were many times that I would have ditched the damn thing, as I’m not a patient person and honestly, point and clicks rarely interest me. But this one did, because it isn’t really a point and click. It’s more of a resource managing survival simulator with a really killer soundtrack.
You follow the life of a man named Burden and direct him in seven different levels; a break in, a torture chamber, a laboratory, a desert. In every chapter, lives are in your hands, and there are often few repercussions for deciding to end those lives or choosing to save them. Do you inject a trusting pet with a poison to find a cure to save your whole team? Do you kill a child to get a security code that might save an entire planet? There’s nothing really stopping you from turning Burden into the most callous antihero you can imagine except that at the end of each level you can see how every other player did and what choices they made.
The game is also incredibly story driven, carefully constructing a gritty universe through simplistic (and gorgeous) pixel graphics and dialogue. The fun part is that while the end in pretty much the same no matter what you do, the small choices you make in early chapters will effect the rest of the game very quietly. I’ve rarely felt so haunted and confused as when I killed a teammate in Gods Will Be Watching, not because what happened was scary but because it didn’t matter.
I’m not going to go too much into that because, spoilers, but if you’re looking for something to lose sleep over for a few days this game will certainly help pass the time. As I type this the game is on sale for $5usd, but it's definitely worth the $20 I paid for the collector's edition.

I'm a bit mixed on this game, although it was certainly enjoyable enough that I would recommend it to the right kind of person.
The game is basically a stat oriented Visual Novel game, where you spend time studying 2 different subjects each week in order to help prevent and avoid future things that will cause your demise (which take the form of stat checks).  Overall the gameplay is rather basic, and there are many instances where you will see the possiblity for replay value to see what happens if you pass certian stat checks (although from some I saw it seems that the checks have no real effect even if you pass them). I will admit I've only seen one ending so far, so it is possible that some stat progressions may change some of the major events that I don't know about.
Stuff I enjoyed:
-The artwork in the game is adorable and fun (although there is no animation).
-The game also has a good sense of humor which lightens the feeling of getting into a dead end you can't get out of.
-The plot is well paced and fun.
Stuff I kind of disliked:
-Because of the nature of the game it heavily encourages save-stating and redoing to see if you have actually put yourself in a position you can't get out of (although the game does provide a dialoge skip feature if you press TAB).
-Some aspects of the game like how exactly mood affects stat growth and how outfits work aren't fully explain and will require a playthrough just to learn (but since you have no idea which stats might be good anyways you are going to be learning that too, so it isn't that big a deal).
-The game is very linear (there are some randomly placed events, but they don't seem all that important) so you know when major events will hit (which is nice in that it makes figuring out how to beat the game easier, but also makes the game super predictable, save for figuring out a different sequence of skill progressions to reach the ending in a different way).

I always thought of 'Resident Evil 0' as one of the lesser entries in the series. Not as bad as 'Outbreak', 'Outbreak - File #2', 'Survivor', or 'Dead Aim', but those are the only older entries it beats out. About the only thing this title has going for it is the classic-style gameplay, but even that has it's issues in this one.
#1. Classic Control Scheme Not Included:
R-Trigger - Ready Aim
L-Trigger - Switches Targets While Aiming
A Button - Confirms/Fires
B Button - Run/Cancel (Down+B = 180 Turn)
X Button - Switch Characters
Y Button - Status Menu
Z Bumper - Map
Remember playing this on your Gamecube in 2002 using the above controls? Well, the comparable X-Box control scheme is NOT present here. As a veteran of the originals, I ended up using "Classic Control Scheme D" and still had to make a custom controller wrapper that rotated the functions of B, X, and Y one step clockwise. This is the only way I've found to make the game play like 'Resident Evil - HD Remaster' does. And reload will still end up being R+X instead of R+B.
#2. No Item Boxes:
You must throw everything on the ground when you're not using it, or don't have room for something, then backtrack to pick it all back up again. Constantly. Unless you spend some sessions gathering your items to the central rooms, you'll be ripping your hair out by the finale. If you hated picking up your toys when you were younger, you're probably going to hate this too.
#3. Single-Player Cooperative:
Control two characters throughout the entire game by switching back and forth between them. This is the source of many player's frustrations with this title. The mechanic of switching characters makes certain areas of the game tedious and just plain not fun to play. Usually whenever sending items up and down a lift is involved. This mechanic is also the source of the greater-than-average (for the series) difficulty settings. The developers saddled you with an A.I. partner. At least they know how to fire a gun this time. (That's right, I'm lookin' at YOU, Ashley Graham.)
When all is said and done, 'Resident Evil 0' is not necessarilly a BAD entry in the series, it just doesn't hold a flickering candle to 'Resident Evil - HD Remaster', 'Resident Evil 2', 'Nemesis', or 'Code: Veronica X'. I'd say this one's mostly for veteran players and hardcore fans of the series.

A kind of nice experimental speedrunning game.
It feels nice to keep running while avoiding all the obstacles. The collectibles in this game don't do much (unless you're a completionist), so you can choose to just focus on fun parkour-like movement as you race across the rainy rooftops toward your pizza-addicted customer. Overall, the smooth running mechanics make this game enjoyable.
However, there are a few design flaws that disturb the running. For example, all the divekicks against enemies/planks bounce the character back instead of keeping their momentum. While this makes killing multiple enemies more fun, it takes away from the smooth forward running concept that makes this game fun.
The controls are simple enough and there is some reactionary skill to the game; walljumping and defeating ninjas. However, this becomes more of a mess later on when the game throws a multitude of hidden ninjas and a parade of mixed enemy types. I have to question who thought this was acceptable level design, as it went against what made the game entertaining.
The story is there. I did feel a bit empathetic towards the main character, Genny, learning to deal with other teenagers in a competitive environment. However, the plot quickly becomes quite predictable and generic towards the end with a 'evil corporations can be defeated with friendship' ending. Also kind of disappointed my finale glitched out and lacked any sound for how intense the level was.
tl;dr/conclusion: It was enjoyable as a short action game. However, there are many flaws with this game and may frusturate you at times (level design, generic plot/characters)

This is possibly the last game I will ever play. Unless they make a sequel of course.
Some bad bits:
- broken mechanics in some places (character occasionally gets stuck on corners, the "Race" level is incredibly easy to beat because the opponent gets stuck on stuff)
- in some levels the completion goals aren't stated explicitly or are contradicted (one level you're meant to be collecting stuff, but you actually get told by your brother character that you're delivering pizza when you fail it)
- performance is bearable but awful (probably built in unity)
- storyline starts amusing, but crosses the line into maudelin towards the end and undercuts it's own vibe with too much seriousness. It's hard to do that transition right, so I sympathise.
- some amusing glitches
- dialogue... functional but not lively
- fighting ninjas is more annoying than challenging
- last level makes absolutely no sense in the context of the game world
But the good stuff makes up for it:
- good polish to both level design, graphics and music
- good heart
- good core gameplay (the speedrunning)
- nice main character
- interesting dynamic between out-of-level 'perks' and in-level character performance
- nice to see a non-sexualised, somewhat realistic young woman in a videogame without going over the top and being 'edgy' or hardened
- nice message about bullying, even if the gameplay doesn't Entirely bring that element to a working strategy completion as a mechanic
- probably about the right length, but I think they could've done more levels using the same layout and had a more engaging, longer-playing title
- the speed-up mode (aka skrillex) is fun
- Speedrun worldwide leaderboards was a good idea, even if some of the scores are quite obviously cheaters
I hope the team do more stuff. It's hard to get this right, particularly as a first game. But they gave it a good shot, and it came off well compared to the original demo. I've played longer, more polished games, with greater budgets, by large studios, which were ultimately worse due to distributed focus and lack of individual artistic intent. The fact that this is a small team gives it both technical issues but also a feel which larger studios making similar works cannot do. I've also played speedrunners by smaller teams with more marketing ability, which were ultimately worse experiences (bittrip, for example).
Things I want to see in a sequel (and, I do hope they make a sequel):
* more coherent storyline
* less gloss (2d is fine!) and fewer glitches/performance issues
* Explorational, non-time-based missions in between 'run' levels, to gather recyclables. Currently the item-gathering mechanic works directly AGAINST the core mechanic (go fast). This would encourage both re-use of levels and learning about a level prior to a run so you can strategically work out the best run while not being on the clock and just having to fail repeatedly to get it "right".
* Crafting from multiple recyclables into (weird and wonderful) clothing, rather than just "buying them".
* Recyclables represented in-level as actual items, not dumb recycling symbols (it took a loooooong while for me to put those symbols and the clothing together in my head... did not make sense - obviously a hangover from the government-funding)
* Scrapping the Q-codes and replace with achievement-based feature-unlocks. In this one the purchasables felt weird and worked against world immersion.
* Better dialogue/less dialogue
* A kick button
* Working physics engine
* Maybe rename to parkour pizza girl? That's what this actually is.
* HUD options which show the relationship between off-level perks and their effects would be good.

Let me begin by sayin the first Soulsborne game I played was Bloodborne. My friend let me play it while I paying him a visit. I played for perhaps two hours, and I was terrible, but the gameplay sank its teeth in me. At the time, I did not own a PS4, so I looked for an alternative. I was aware that Bloodborne and Dark Souls were related. The same friend that let play Bloodborne was my roommate years ago, and I remembered that he played Demons Souls quite a bit, though I never played it myself. So I knew that all these games were part of the same family. Since Bloodborne was not availabe on PC, I looked for the next best thing: Dark Souls.
I have a fixation with doing things in order; if I start listening to a musician, I prefer to start with their first album. The same holds true for video games. If at all possible, I would like to start with the first game in a series. However, I do not own a PS3, and could not go back and play Demons Souls. Instead, I would have to forge ahead with Dark Souls.
I am not a skillful gamer. It took me years to get comfortable playing such titles as Oblivion and Skyrim, and by comparison to Dark Souls, these games are easy. But I have always gravitated to Tough But Fair gameplay. Thus, in recent times I finished Donkey Kong Country Returns, which is notorious for its difficulty. The difficulty though, was not punishing, in my opinion. I always felt that when I died, it was my fault, and not the game's. For me it was easy to persist to completion. Dark Soul's gameplay is in that same vein. With some notable exceptions among the boss fights, the combat is very fair, and in my opinion, is more of a matter of muscle memory than anything else. Once a player has the basic controls down, the game plays much smoother.
This last point leads me to a critique of the present Prepare to Die edition: it is nigh-unplayable with mouse and keyboard. The default M+K controls are very obtuse and not in line with modern PC gaming. In fact, a mod is almost required just to fix the janky mouse-camera control. It's hard to describe, but if you play without this mod, you will see that the camera moves in a very unexpected fashion. Therefore, I
advise that you buy a controller to play with this game. Not just any controller, though. Specifically, the only controller that works in
experience, is the
XBOX 360 controller. For my money, this is
to your enjoyment of the game on PC. Dark Souls simply isn't optimized for mouse and keyboard.
Another point for the PC release is the necessity of installing DSFix, a minor mod that, among other things, enables resolutions above 720p, and fixes a number of other small issues with the game. To me, it is almost unacceptable that the game is nearly unplayable in its default state. I run the game on a PC with Windows 10 installed, and the effort required just to play the game was almost enough to make me give up. I'm glad that I did not, though.
Once you begin the game with DSFix, and a functioning controller, it is an almost sublime experience. The visuals and aesthetic of the game are gorgeous. Character models are highly detailed and the environments are superb. If you can see a distant area, chances are you
visit it. This to me is unusual; most games include their views merely as decoration; in Dark Souls, it is likely to be a playable area. The game's dark fantasy/medieval atmosphere will not appeal to every one, but is right up my alley. It is something that has to be seen to be appreciated, and my poor descriptions will not do it justice.
On the matter of gameplay, I find this to have the greatest appeal. Dark Souls is not as difficult as you may believe it to be. However, the game punishes recklessness and hubris in many cases. But the punishment is not severe enough to dissuade progress. It encourages exploration when you "hit a wall" of difficulty, and finding an alternate path that may lead to greater joy. Precision is key to this game. One mis-timed parry could result in death. The complexity is intimidating. One must create a balance of mobility, attack strength, attack speed, and defense that a new player would find mind-boggling. I only began playing this about 3 months ago, and only now am I wrapping my head completely around its complexity. This does not mean that you will not enjoy yourself or progress. After a month, I beat the game. Imagine my joy! Another gameplay factor is the sense of accomplishment one gets after defeating a difficult enemy. For the most part, winning does require genuine skill and finesse. If you could track your skill increases (not in terms of levels, but skill as a player) you would be deeply satisfied. Some bosses are cheap and simply unfun to play against, but this do not even begin to tip the scales against the overall quality and fun of the game.
All in all, I have beat the story twice, up to New Game Plus, and am close to the end on NG++ and with a new character. I don't recall a game in recent memory that has captivated me the way Dark Souls has. I highly recommend this game to any gamer that appreciates the difficulty and skill required, but who also wants a mysterious story and environment that leaves more to speculation than solid elucidation.

This game is a throw back to the old Infinity Engine used on games such as Baldur's Gate... unfortunately it doesn't really enchance the experience much at all. There are many nitpicks and unless you really want a nostogia trip, then I wouldn't recommend playing this game.
First off the storyline appears expansive but it is a lie, the game railroads you via the areas you can visit and the quests/events you have to do. While you can do some things out of order, you'll soon enough always end out back on the same path. There is variance and the end does "change" based on what you do but as it is just narrated walls of texts, it isn't very meaningful, also many actions like wiping out all the NPCs in a town or village are ignored in the ending.
Secondly, the exploration is basic and not very rewarding, most of what you find is just caves with no point or maybe rarely an additional quest giver. This is made worse by the constant fog of war effect, apparently your character is incapable of ever seeing more than about 30 feet away but can see through solid walls rather well. Naturally as this is going for an Infinity Engine feel, everything is pre-rendered 2D with planes to make it feel 3D. In-game models (PC & NPCs) are infact 3D. The interface feels sluggish for moving around the map.
Third the combat system sucks bad, there is no default AI for any companion and so you either need to pause the game constantly to control each one or tell all to do the same thing. There is Party AI but it is disabled by default (why?), and even this had to be patched in to begin with. There is little foresight over how battles actually work and leads to oddly shifting between way to easy battles and then suddenly coming across a group of about 12 orges sat outside a cave. It just isn't well balanced and quickly becomes boring, it is more about how to exploit the battle system than to actually use strategy or tactics.
Fourth, The quests are a mixed basket. Most quests are quick and simple, but there is a couple that drags on too long. There are some quests that are simple but never supply you critical details and so you have to just move around until you randomly find the right place or force you to get to some arbitary point in the storyline before you can progress them. Some quests have entire areas dedicated to them but have little much else making them bland grindfests to eventually get to the quest objective (I.E. Raedric's Hold).
Fifth, There is one particular task which is to clear an area known as the endless paths of od nua... it is more endlessly boring, this area is almost a completely unconnected lore to the rest of the game with only a few things actually having any importance at all. It is suppose to be a challenge but really is just more of a grindfest to clear, there is a couple of bosses in this area but generally just kill everything and move on is the only point here. There is maybe a few encounters you can pass.
Penultimately, Events/Encounters are about the most interesting thing in this game. If I have to praise it for anything then that would be it, unsurprisingly this is the areas where storyline tends to work the best too. Most are pre-scripted events that trigger after certain conditions so unfortunately is lacking on the random side but else wise these tend to be well written and executed. Sometimes these do have a lack of options, such as not being able to call out obvious traps, when they are really obvious, fake messenger guy who sweats too much and is clearly lying...
Finally, The lore in this game sucks, like it really sucks. Mainly this is to do with the gods themselves, while lackluster and boring the game pulls a "plot twist" at the end that makes the barely average lore around the gods and some ancient civiliations just seem lame and terrible. Basically trying to achieve piece by constantly spawning wars, yeah... that is something in the plot you can never call out, the grand plan to make things "more peaceful" actually has only ever made everything more violent.

Pillars of Eternity was Kickstarted in 2012, with Obsidian promising a return to Infinity Engine-styled isometric RPGs with RTS-like combat. The first time I played it was in 1.0 before any of the expansions were released. The combat seemed to be pretty unintersting, as if they had complicated the IE-style "select all, attack" for easier encounters, and there seemed to be  far too much of it, with most areas being full of trash mobs.
Having finished it in 3.0 with both expansions, I'd say it's become a better game. Far from perfect, though.
There are still too many trash mobs to pad out content, even if the best fights are epic and difficult as all hell for a below-average cRPG player like me (played on Hard, Normal is still a bit too easy if you already have experience with this kind of games).
The third act is still very much rushed, and the end of Act 2 is still a terrible attempt at copying Dragon Age: Origins' Landsmeet (since unlike DA:O, your choices in this event have no effect on what happens at the end of it.) The stronghold still feels pretty tacked on, though improved. The performance is still awful for this kind of stuff, and loading times are pretty bad as well, getting worse the longer your playthrough becomes.
Still, it's an enjoyable game. It looks beautiful, having IE-style 2d art for each level, and a soundrack, which though somewhat different in a few tracks from the original IE games, is still good. When you get a good encounter, the combat feels much better, as you're using the wide array of abilites in each of your characters as best as you can in order to just get through the fight, instead of using them to kill trash faster.
You also have to have pretty good positioning of your characters, especially since the engagement system (which means when you're in melee with an enemy, either one of you leaving results in an attack of opportunity) restricts kiting, since trying to do it will result in dead companions. In the best fights I had quite a bit of tries to just find the best positioning for each character.
Character development is maybe still far from great: even though weak versions of other class abilities have been added as a choice to anyone (a possible test in multi-classing for the sequel), there are times when you're levelling up and you'll choose the least useless-sounding feat, but the abilities are pretty cool, casters having much more control than damage spells, making combat more intersting (though only when the encounters aren't padding, as i mentioned.)
The companions have some pretty fun banter and some of them interesting stories, and they sometimes liven up your average map painting/clearing simulator that is a game inspired by Baldur's Gate exploration. The story is interesting at first, dull in the middle and gets good as well towards the end, even though Act 3 and the accompanying city both feel unfinished (the second city was promised as a Kickstarter streatch goal, and they did deliver, though below expectations.
The base game itself is still just a decent/good game bar some bits (Raedric's Hold and the Adra Dragon), but the expansions are a major improvement. Less trash and harder encounters (if your steward tells you not to go to Cragholdt because you're too weak, then please don't trust me) make them worth by themselves, but the addition of soul-bound weaponry with a story and powers that you slowly unlock through combat is pretty cool, especially since the loot in the base game feels very much underwhelming without a lot of gear that feels unique or really powerful (hell, one of the first companions you meet already has what is probably one of the best armors he's going to get the entire game.) The areas you visit are also more interesting and visually striking.
This game was an enjoayble experience (I might have been too negative in this review), just not a really great one in case of the base game. I recommend it with the expansions.
Good old days RPG

What a game! Or maybe "what a world" would be more accurate. Pillars of Eternity certainly pulled me in from the start. Oldschool Infinity Engine -style isometric CRPGs are the type of game that has long been missing from modern gaming. Now they're back, and in what a spectacular fashion!
Get ready to lose yourself in the fantasy setting of Eora; a world full of juicy lore, masterfully written characters, and intriquing stories and plot. The writing is the highlight for me, because there's a lot of it, there's reactivity, there's philosophical stuff as well as political forces. The balance between reading and being involved in combat situations is a very nice fifty-fifty I'd estimate. My thorough playthrough of the game + both expansion took 130 hours.
Speaking of combat, oh what a treat this old style tactical party management in real-time with pause. It sure has a lot of variables and micromanagement like positioning characters, pausing at every second to issue new commands or use different abilities - which might deter many players more used to action RPGs or simply not interested in micromanagement in their RPG combat systems, but I certainly love it all. Good news to players who struggle with or dislike this sort of combat, there are multiple difficulty settings, especially the Story Mode, which lets you learn the combat mechanics without being constantly overwhelmed.
The art and environments are unlike any other, this is the hand crafted 3D into 2D style from the older CRPGs, but elevated into delicious levels of eyecandy. Top that with amazing spell and sound effects, good looking animations and the absolutely wonderful music and voice acting, and the experience is simply astounding.
I love the adventuring from area to area on the world map, which depends on what direction you decided to exit to, brings freedom and excitement to going into new areas. I love the unique items, quests and NPCs that one encounters, so much cool stuff to discover. I love the party NPC characters that you can have adventuring alongside you, very memorable personalities, they feel very alive and I certainly started to care about many of them very quickly.
There are so many details I could go into, so many things about this game I could gush about. But let me say it all in the simplest way I can: I've long held that my favorite game of all time is Baldur's Gate 1, this game is a worthy spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate 1, and I will go as far as to say, that Pillars of Eternity is now my new favorite game of all time.
Highly recommended for RPG fans, especially fans of oldschool CRPGs.

Don't let the low price, the simple visuals and the fact that it's a tablet port fool you.
I would have never imagined myself playing a shooter ported from tablets on PC and having so much fun. First of all, it's miles ahead of the portable version, almost a different game. The fact that there are no microtransactions help you enjoy this as a wholesome product, albeit with a little bit of fair grinding.
A good zombie game needs 2 things: good zombies and good weapons. While this is far from many AAA titles, the weapons in Dead Effect look and sound meaty enough to feel the punch of every shot, but don't expect spectecular quality of animations and sounds.
The zombies however are a whole other dimension, and are at the core of what makes Dead Effect so fun, as they should be. Despite the small scope of the game, it features quite a few types of enemies, each of which in its turn has its preset of behaviors, some of which are randomnly generated depending on difficulty. In other words: zombies are dangerous and unpredictable, and demand the best of your attention, reaction and situational awareness. The dodge funcion is in this game for a damn good reason. This, combined with the very much Doom3-inspired leveldesign, make up for a great immersive atmosphere of an ever-so-popular contaminated spaceship setting. There's even a small cheesy story that works well enough to glue the events together and give the player a sense of purpose in addition to a sense of place.
If I had to complain about Dead Effect, which would be stupid considering the price, I'd say some will find the grinding tiresome (althought there's not THAT much of it compared to other games of this type), and not much variety beyond the campaign and the survival modes. While admittedly true, these problems didn't stop me from finishing the game twice, and I'm sure I'll be going in for a third time on Hell difficulty where almost every zombie hit is deadly.
In conclusion, Dead Effect is easliy one of my best surprise purchases on Steam. It's like Doom 3 and Killing Floor had a baby that doesn't know much yet but already shows great potential for being its own thing. Big thing, hopefully.

Gods Will be watching is an example of the "sort by user review" ranking hurting the developers and the clientele. As of this writing, Gods has "Mixed" reviews. Well, if your post on Reddit has mixed reviews, your chances of getting to anybody's top page are shot. In many of the user reviews, people complain about the difficulty, and the lack of narrative. Well, the levels are harsh, but fair -- every scenario is easy once you know the trick(s), and/or do the math.
Personally this kind of "Oregon Trail"-like mathy survival sim turns me on. There's apparently a large number of people who bought this game who feel otherwise, polluting this excellent game's user reviews, and preventing new fans from discovering it. The discoverability of this game is shot, and finding hidden gems is something Steam will have to fix if they would like for other stranger, genre-bending games to come forward.

Sometimes I wish a neutral opinion can be given for a game. Because I like the art style for "Gods will be watching" and that the game is trying something different than other offerings. And I can see how for other people this might be an ejoyable game (as can be seen in the other reviews) however.....this to me is not a fun game to play. And when a game is not fun to play it pretty much becomes work, only without the salary as a reward.
To my fault I was expecting a point and click adventure or something aking to it, however this game sets you into a specific situation each level. And you have to 'work' at finding a way out of that situation by doing repetitive tasks (key word: repetitive) and if you fail after 10 minutes you can do the whole thing over again from the very beginning.
The Dark Souls comparison was made, however as opposed to that game, this one feels like the result is more based on luck than actually improving your skills into getting you further into the game. As such (to me) it wasn't satisfying when you cleared a level. It was more a sense of relief that I didn't have to do the same thing again...and again...and again.
The moral choices don't appear to matter much either, in one level I had people die on my watch only for them to reappear the next. Their characters are now glitching on the screen (that was funny) to show something is not 'right', but essentially their deaths apparantly didn't matter. Nor would your choices.
If you like puzzle games where the end result is gained by mostly (not all the time) luck as opposed to deducing what to do, then one could try "Gods will be Watching" for an original setting and a game which I find looks pretty cool. However if like me you were looking for something more than a puzzle game, then I would stay away.

Oh wow Undead Labs, how you've surprised me. What I honestly thought was a pretty standard, repetitive zombie-beater at first then turned into something so addictive and an absolute blast to play through. It's rare for a zombie game to deliver consistently (I'm looking at you Dead Island) but State of Decay does a great job. If you've ever been a fan of zombie games in general or in particular The Walking Dead TV series - you have to give this your time. You literally feel like a survivor - creating a base camp, finding survivors and materials, improving your skills and helping locate the source of the infection. Also - the added risk/reward scenarios resulting from the game's focus on permadeath and stamina/health penalties add to the survivor feel like you wouldn't believe.
Now I won't lie - it took a couple hours to get my head around the core mechanics - mission structure, building outposts, maintaining supplies, keeping morale high, character upgrades etc but once I had a firm grasp I couldn't stop.
The only downers overall I would say are repetition with certain missions and dialogue. The combat can also feel shallow at times but it has a pretty meaty feel which helps a lot (the shooting is also much stronger so this makes up for it).
There are not many games that have hooked me like State of Decay. And for the bargain price of £3.74 in the final day of the Summer Sale you could do far, far worse. The average player can get a good 20 hours out of this before hitting the final story mission with others playing for a lot longer. Buy it now and start surviving.

You want a quirky, story-driven western FPS with a nice mix of stealth... and whole lotta sass!
A very welcome change in the single-player FPS pool, placing you in the role of a Bounty Hunter bringing the local ruffians to justice. As expected from Oddworld Inhabitants (the legends behind Abe's Oddysee / Exoddus) the humour is dark, yet creatively surreal and playful. Whether it's an outlaw called 'Jo Mamma' or overheard chit-chat between outlaws of their love of oatmeal or inexplicable rashes, it's both silly and serious; the villains in particular have a lovable dumb charm to them.
What's clever is that you earn more moolah (the in-game currency) by bringing in enemies
... something a little harder to pull off than just breaking their jaw. It places a fun variety to levels; sneaking around and trying to pick off isolated targets one-by-one. You can set traps and lures... or if all else fails: Run in and fire an explosive bat at their head. It, by and large, lets you play it your way: But rewards taking effort to try and capture foes alive.
The other fun element is your bug-ridden crossbow. We forgo conventional weaponry to use local creatures; whether it's snarky chipmunks to lure enemies, web-spinning bolamites to snare them or fuzzles to preoccupy foes with a snarling dust bunny on their crotch. What's clever is that most of the bugs aren't directly lethal - so gunfights are a little more involved than just taking headshots and calling it a day. You "hunt" for ammo... but this is a tad misleading: You basically find a nest and milk it until you're fully stocked on that particular creature (and you can always go back). Annoyingly, they be so frequent that you seldom run short unless you get ridiculously trigger-happy... So it's not like you need to ration and carefully use your full range of critters, which I feel is a slightly missed opportunity.
The only thing not explained well is how to bounty bosses alive. You need to empty their
bar without killing them entirely: Which tends to require a consistent volley of charged zappflies and thudslugs (and maybe boombats to start if they have a plenty of HP to buffer it). The bar recharges, so you need to keep the hits coming.
The game's fun, but can get a little repetitive at times, partly where the outlaws aren't really driving the plot much more than giving you a new enemy to face. The story unfolds in the occasional leap, leaving the rest little more than filler. Whilst stealth is nicely supported, the routines for taking out enemies can become a little formulaic. It's still good fun though, and works out to being a decent challenge as you progress - even if it's a little linear.
So whilst it's not the game changer Abe's Odyssee was... it's still solidly enjoyable and good for a hearty number of laughs.

A bounty hunter looking to get an urgent medical procedure with his earnings sets out in a weird alien world in Oddworld: Stranger’s Wrath. This game features a bizarre wild-west setting with a variety of strange anthropomorphic characters.
The uniqueness of this game extends into its gameplay as what would normally be a typical stealth-action hybrid gets a few wacky changes, the first of which being your weapon. Rather than firing bolts, you load up your crossbow with wild animals that you capture with a particular electric animal. The captured animals are then shot at enemies or locations depending on the animal used and intent. For example, you get a sassy noisemaking squirrel that taunts enemies making for a perfect lure so you can launch a spider creature to tie them up in a web. The game also offers fauna equivalent to having a machine gun, grenade launcher, sniper rifle, and toxic gas cloud. Every animal also receives an upgrade at some point to make them even more useful against hardened enemies or groups. Stranger can also hold his own by shifting into third person to execute a variety of melee attacks and if the going gets too tough stranger can easily get away from combat by dropping on all fours and galloping away (yes, that’s as weird as it sounds).
Once you knock out an enemy, you have the option to “bounty” them by using a vacuum-like device that sucks them into compressed storage to be sold later at a bounty store. Like in the west, you can take your bounties dead or alive, with alive giving you more moolah (the game’s currency) to spend in stores for upgrades or specialized ammo. At first this is pretty neat although it does tend to get a bet repetitive having to knock out and bounty enemies over and overand you may instead opt to kill them and collect the cash they drop.
Stranger’s wrath does of course have a few problems here and there. Character voice acting is particularly bad and could have used some better choices in VA and a little less dependence on pitch change filters. Occasionally your camera will bug out but you can get around this by shifting into first person mode and back. The HD version of this game allows for turning up the detail but does so in a very un-optimized way yielding massive FPS drops at the highest levels of AF despite the game not looking much better than comparable titles that would run just fine at the same settings.
Despite all that, the crazy story and environment to this game really helped to keep it interesting and I found myself getting pulled back in despite the missions being a bit samey and sometimes frustrating. All in all, Oddworld: Stranger’s Wrath is a nice little hidden gem that’s worth trying out if you want to experience something really different for once.

I played this game a few times.  In the end, I think it is flawed in a lot of ways.  In order to play it well, you essentially are forced to play through multiple times and fail.  You need to learn what events happen when and plan accordingly.  I guess you could say that a game like Super Meat Boy is similar, in that you are forced to replay levels over and over in order to learn how to beat them, but the difference is that a skilled player has the ability to navigate an unplayed level with success.
This game doesn't seem to have any skill involved.  You just experiment until things go right.  There are ways to manipulate the bonuses in order to get skill points where you want them.  But it takes a few play throughs to learn what bonuses are associated with what moods, and what events take place that require you to have certain skills at certain times, and then by the time you figure it out, I really felt like I knew the story enough and I didn't care enough to play it again.
I did sink a fair number of hours into this game, and usually that is the sign of a game I enjoyed, but this one left me feeling annoyed that there was no payoff at the end.  I didn't get better, I just learned what happened when, and the experience is utterly forgettable.

Great classic RPG with interesting battle system, story, world and wonderful graphics.

TL;DR: Cheap and fun, but don't expect anything crazy.
For the price, this is a great game. It's very arcade-like, which is to say, there aren't a lot of frills. The campaign is fairly short, but if you want to collect all the upgrades and weapons, there's a decent amount of replayability.
It's rather refreshing in that the biggest threat is simply the number of enemies coming at you and they are almost never going to surprise you (they aren't stealthy zombies by any means, like in a "real" zombie scenario). Rarely (not never, mind you) was ammo an issue, and there's an upgrade you can buy that gives you absurdly powerful health regen, and at that point your only fear is getting swarmed because you literally can't kill the zombies fast enough, and you're incredibly slow moving yourself. I loved to hate the grenade zombie, which is exactly as terrifying as it sounds, because he's a zombie who can throw grenades that potentially one hit you, but he's fairly uncommon, easy to spot, and the ceilings have lots of underhangs for the grenades to bounce off and kill zombies for you, so he's not an unreasonable sort.
Anyways, despite being early access, all the features feel relatively polished. I'm not sure how I feel about the distinction between money (which is hidden in levels, but not dropped) and "gold bars" (which are only dropped randomly by enemies). I guess it's nice to have a second currency that you can only buy a limited number of things with, but I just don't know if its really necessary.

Gods Will Be Watching is a game made by sadistic people for sadistic people, so it is in this sense that I can say that I enjoyed this game. While its story is rather short (If you manage to perfectly run the game it would take 2 hours max) I still thought that the message behind it is rather excellent. You play as Sgt. Burden, and you spend your time as a member of E.D.U.K trying to stop Xenolifer and there plot to release a virus upon an innocent world. This sounds like it would be the grounds for an action packed, teeth gritting, and emotional ride. It is, just not in the sense you would imagine it. The first mission puts you in charge of a hostage situtation about to go wrong, while you micromanage hostages, your hacking progress and security, the guards inching closer and closer down the hall, and most importantly, your ethics. These situations are designed in a way that is brutally unforgiving, one that is designed to make sure you dont make it out of anything scot free. Do you really want to shoot a hostage and spray his brains all over his co-workers? If you dont, his friends may get to complacent and attempt to fight back, and his life will be as good as over anyway. Fear, compassion, brutality, calculation, all worked into a formula of sort to keep the hostages complacent. Then add 2 other things you have to keep an eye on in the form of a rescue team and the security of your hacking connection, and you'll find a situation getting more and more out of hand. You cant just scold and embrace people over and over, and you cant just shoot everyone in the head, you have to find a middle. However, the game is designed to throw so much stuff in your path, you will never find it. Thats the thing here, there is no perfection, sacrifice will either be of your choice, or the games. It will kill your friends, and you will watch and get frustrated, however the deeper narritive at play here will be something most indie titles lack. Im delving into spoiler territory here, but the final 2 missions are when this becomes most apparent. Everytime you lose, everytime you die, Burden does too. He gets frustrated with you, he knows what attacks Liam is going to throw and physically tells him much to his suprise. He is living the same hell you are, and thats when you find yourself thinking. Many people never gave the game enough chance to find this deeper narritive, and many don't care either way, but for people like me interested in the human psyche I cant stress enough how this game sticks with you. It deserves the time of day, just dont come to me if you punch through a monitor in rage.

Remember all the things you loved (or perhaps, hated) about FMV games back in the 90's?  Well, All Seeing Eye Games does and has packed "Press X to Not Die" full of them, along with a bit of self-referential humor and even some current industry tropes along the way.
Like the games from decades past that it undoubtedly draws upon, Press X to Not Die casts YOU as the protagonist in a world that has all of a sudden gone mad.  In true "Interactive Movie" style, the video scenes that follow as the story progresses are shot from your perspective and characters in the game address you directly.  At certain points, you will be presented with a situation that requires a button press (or combination thereof) within a specific time frame depending on the difficulty selected.  At other times, the player selects from a dialog tree or similar to keep things moving.  Though these interactions represent the entirety of the gameplay, the approach here is faithful to the FMV games of yore.  Additionally, the developers have done a fine job of interjecting humor (self-deprecating and otherwise) into the proceedings.
On the standard difficulty, I was able to get through the entirety of the game in just about a half an hour on the first go through with minimal deaths.  While I was a little surprised to have seen the ending that soon, the length of Press X to Not Die is commensurate with the price of admission.  There also exists the possibility of replaying the game several times, whether it be at a higher difficulty or to intentionally not press the required buttons or make different choices to see how the alternate video scenes play out.
In all, Press X to Not Die succeeds as a throwback to a genre that left the spotlight as quickly as it entered it over 20 years ago.  It also succeeds as a tongue in cheek reference regarding why those games had limited appeal and short shelf lives.  Regardless of which one is more prevalent, Press X to Not Die succeeds and is worthy of a purchase.

I don't know why people criticize this game so much.  I found it to be just as enjoyable as the original game and really had more fun.
You control two different characters (not at the same time) but your other characters can operate solo or team up with you and swapping characters is instantaneous at the push of a button.  I used one character as my zombie killer and the other as support and it worked very well.  There are areas you have to split up and it creates a little more tension that way which is good.  Inventory management is really not that bad as some say.  The ability to drop stuff and leave it actually makes is really easy and you can set up mini support stations that way, however once I moved to a completely new area i found my self having to make a few trips to carry the important stuff with me.  Puzzles are good, but not impossible.  They are not near as frustrating as RE and it is pretty easy to figure out what you need and where you need it item wise to progress though locked areas. Story is Blah, but adds some good background if you are interested in the RE story and more of where the T virus came from.
Recommend must play if you are any sort of fan of the RE series or zombies.

In the end its your by the numbers resident evil game but that’s not a bad thing at all because the classic resident evil formula works very well and playing as two characters at the same time is a cool twist to the formula.

This game has near universally good reviews, so I will likely be a minority on this opinion, but that's fine; it is just an opinion after all.
I hated this game.
Not just "Didn't enjoy it" downright "Would rather spend my time staring at the ceiling" hated it.
The game sells itself as though it has some dark grim story hidden just beneath the surface of a seemingly placid and gentle town, but I'm quickly realising than the gentle placid town is the story.
There is some darker stuff later on (Sorry for the spoilers) but as others have said "That's not the point"
The point really is everything else.
The whole motivation behind the game is displaying that feelings of discontenment and repressed frustration at the world are something everybody experiences, which I suppose might be a big eye opener if that wasn't already obvious to you.
I'm sure I'm just not the game's intended audience, it feels like it was made for a millenial from a small american town, an audience of just into adulthood gamers who are finally realising that life is complicated.
Unfortunately, these lessons are ones I've learned a while ago, and so what story the game has to tell is dreary and cliched.
I appreciate that others may enjoy the game, but this isn't the next undertale.
it's not a novel in video game form.
It's an after school special, it's "Saved By The Bell" in video game form.

Night in the Woods is a story rich platformer that focuses heavily on character development  and exploration.
The games shining achievement is most definitely the writing and character development. Infinite Fall has managed to make some of the most genuine and real writing i've seen. Every character is amazingly well written and developed, leading to relatable and unique personalities. Even side characters are memorable and leave lasting impressions. Infinite Fall is absolutely amazing at giving every character a turn in the spotlight and making sure no characters feel flat or left out.
The music is absolutely incredible, the songs are memorable and of amazingly high quality. This is one of the few games i'd recommend getting the sound track for, as nearly every track is downright amazing.
The world of Night in the Woods is absolutely beautiful and chock full of little touches scattered around. The art in this game complements the immense charm this game has, making the world feel even more real and recognizable. The game is extremely welcoming to heavy exploration leading to many hidden interactions and places which makes finding them so satisfying.
The story of Night in the Woods is memorable and paced well, the only complaint is that it felt rushed near the end.
Regardless of this it still manages to be extremely powerful in conveying it's messages. Not much more to say here without delving into spoiler territory.
This is definitely one of my favorites of 2017, and a must have for the genre.

At this time, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. After the 0.06 update, the engine has been completely changed, and the game as a whole has been diminished by it.
When you started a new game of Stranded Deep previously, it went like this: You wake up on a private jet, flying over the Pacific, amidst some turbulence. You get up from your seat and go up toward the cockpit to make yourself a martini, combining fruit, mix, and finally, setting the top aflame for an added flair, before drinking it and returning to your seat. Shortly after this, the turbulence get worse, and the starboard bulkhead of the plane is ripped open violently, your safety belt the only thing keeping you from being sucked out, as the plane crashes into the black ocean. With water having filled the cabin,you have to swim free of the plane, and, upon getting onto the sole liferaft, an explosion in the engine knocks you cold. You wake up to see an island you've never seen before, drifting slowly in the liferaft. When you get to shore, the tiny island you're on seems isolated from all the other tiny islands you can see off in the distance, and the reality of the situaiton sinks in: This tiny island isn't enough, but it's all you've got. To quote Mark Watney, "I'm gonna have to science the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this".
First thing's first, is there food? Well, there are some crabs scuttling about, palm trees with coconuts, and- ooh! potato plant. It's not a whole lot, but it'll help you survive for the time being. If we're going to be having fish and crab, we need fire, and that means would. You gather up some rocks, and what sticks you can find. Unfortunately, you only have just enough rocks to make the fire pit, OR you can make tools, so coconuts will have to suffice til you can get a proper cooking fire. You make an axe, which will allow you to chop down some trees, and a hammer to help with building. A couple of yucca plants provide you with rope enough to get moving on at least a basic shelter as the sun sets on your first day, after chopping down a couple trees, breaking the trunks into logs, then breaking the logs down into useable sticks. You spot the telltale dorsal fin of a shark off the eastern shore, and know that tomorrow, you'll need to venture out on your raft to find out what lies on that island in the distance.
Now it's like this: When you hit Start Game, you are taken to a 5x5 grid of tiles, each with a title, and an island on them, shot from overhead. Here, you'll pick which island you start on, complete with stats below the grid, so you can make an informed diecision. Once you pick your island, you appear in your raft, before a large island with a bunch of supplies on it. You don't see any other islands, but it doesn't really matter anyway, since this island has everything you need anyway. Your first day, you knock out a shelter, firpite with spit, and bed, using the crafting menu, along with an axe, hammer, spear, and a couple of fish traps that you place in the ocean. There are coconuts up in the trees, but they're so high up you'd break half the bones in your body trying to get to them. Better to focus on the multiple potato plants, and abundant fish life about, and leace the coconuts to themselves.
Gathering... is frustrating. You attempt to hack down some palms, and are ready to run and grab fallen coconuts, when you realize your axe can't actually hit the trees, you check the next most likely tree, and it can't be chopped down either.
You finally fina a sapling that allows you to chop it down, and it burst apart into two sticks. You decide to instead use driftwood, which has collected in piles of logs, so you use to axe break the logs appart into... logs, so that you can break the logs apart into sticks.
The game has been SIGNIFICANTLY reduced in scope, and playability with the new engine, and the new system pretty much cuts out all real impetous for exploration, which should be one of the cornerstones of the game. Instead, it has veered sharply into the territory of standard sandbox fare, shedding it's unique feel for a much more mundane one. Not really worth the buy at this point, as there are complete games that does as much or more at this point than the plans for Stranded Deep.
