You play a ghoul in a house. Various numbers of people enter the house per round, and your job is to possess objects and scare each of them till they reach a certain threshold and drop dead of shock. There is a timer so you have to do it fast, or
end up being the dead one. (That is, if ghouls can even die.)
The game is in 3D - using the keyboard with your left hand, you have to control how near/far your ghoul is, and using the mouse with your right hand, you control how high/low he is. This wouldn't be a problem, except for the "sliding" that occurs with each move. That is, if you stop pressing the left mouse button or the "left" command on the keyboard for instance, your ghoul doesn't immediately stop, but continues to move a bit more before he finally does. This lack of precision with the controls makes it hard to accurately control your ghoul, and becomes especially frustrating because there is a timer every round, so not having precise movement wastes the amount of time you have left.
Or at least, a point to all of this. Of course, scaring peeps is fun, but how about a bit of backstory as to why you became a ghoul, why you're haunting this house, what you hope to achieve, and so on. Just sayin'.
With that in mind, go give this game a try. The premise is pretty interesting, the graphics alright, and the objects you get to possess quite fun. (There's a grand piano, grandfather clock, and trophy bear among many others.)

The game is quite long - I clocked almost 70 hours and I haven't even completed the second DLC, so I estimate the main game to last for ~60 hours. I think it could be shorter - it was getting a little bit stale at the end - but that's a minor complaint. It was mostly due to fights becoming too easy/predictable. I played on HARD and at first the game was really challenging for me. I had to carefully position my team mates and use active pause a lot. If you like classic cRPGs – it’s for you. Heck, even if you haven’t played cRPG before – it’s one of the best games to start.

Length of Time Played: 7 Hours
Distance Played: Completed the Story on Hard Difficulty
Personal Grade: B-
Opinion of Each Aspect
Grading System - Outstanding, Excellent, Good, Acceptable, Poor, Horrendous, Abysmal
Gameplay: Excellent
Stability: Good
Story: Good
Controls: Acceptable
Graphics: Acceptable
Music: Poor
Sounds: Poor
Difficulty: Poor
Notes:
The gameplay is a typical FPS with plenty of narrow corridors and enough zombies to kill. Headshots tend to kill most in one hit with almost all the weapons. Body shots do next to nothing. You have many kinds of zombies to kill including some that will make you rip your hair out. You have a few abilities to help you in your mission. There are a few modes to pick from but they all are standard zombie FPS fare.
The story is so cliche and cheesy but it serves its purpose more or less. You are a soldier who has become surrounded by the undead and it is your job to prevent it from spreading. Your standard zombie survival plot.
The controls are good enough to deal with. You can remap the keys to whatever you want. Controller support is okish but I would recommend a keyboard & mouse for this. Nothing feels off really though using space bar for interacting seems a bit off.
The graphics are fine. Everything seemed easy to distinguish. The dark corridors do hide most textures but luckily, all items flash when you are near them.
Music wasn't exactly the top idea in mind in this game. Nothing stands out and it doesn't even provide any real atmosphere.
Sounds seem a little off. The gun sounds are a big culprit of this. They just don't sound convincing enough. Zombie moans are fine.
The difficulty is a tad too easy, even on hard. Your health means little since there are healing stations peppered throughout each level and there is more than enough ammo for you to miss several times.

This game hasn't been very well received, perhaps due to some failures in properly communicating the nature of the game prior to launch. People were expecting a very different kind of game and were thus disappointed when the finished game failed to meet their expectations. What initially might seem like a somewhat ordinary point-and-clicker is in reality a complex resource management simulation that could essentially be represented as an array of gauges steadily, or randomly, ticking away or being manipulated in some mystical way by you, the player.
Without a doubt this will be a huge turn-off for some, perhaps the majority of gamers. Being restricted to seven unforgiving, minimalist survival scenarios might not feel like something anyone in their right mind would enjoy. What I want to convey, though, is that there is a very unique charm to this game, very much unlike anything else out there. The pixel art is stellar. The music, ohh, the music is fantastic indeed. Perhaps most importantly, though, the hopeless atmosphere and the brutality of the story is what appeals to me the most. Having spent twenty minutes lying, begging and enduring pain in a torture chamber, clinging to dear life, the moment when your torturer pulls out a revolver, slides in a singular bullet and spins the cylinder is soul crushing. Every drop of the hammer makes your heart miss a beat because you actually have your all your previous progress through the level at stake. The fact that, in the original mode at least, there is that unforgiving element of pure chance somehow makes every decision have that much more weight.
Again, this is not for everyone. At this point, I'd suspect you'll already know if something like this is your cup of tea. Even if you're turned off by the randomness or the plain difficulty, I'd still dare recommend this game to most fans of adventure games. With recent patches the difficulty can be toned down, and while I don't suggest you do this if you can avoid it, there is now the possibility to experience the story with less frustration. If you're up for this kind of stuff definitely pick it up. If you're on the fence, I suggest waiting for a sale.

I finally finished Gods Will Be Watching (Deconstructeam﻿), a game that I backed on Indiegogo﻿ about a year ago. It took me a long time to complete this game, not because it was long (it wasn't), or because it was difficult (it was VERY difficult), but because I've been very tired, and this game is not at all "casual"…
This is the kind of game were EVERY decision may be life-or-death, and even seemingly trivial errors may result in failure. I found this constant pace of decision-making exhausting. Even when you "succeed" (when you complete a chapter), you probably failed to keep everyone alive, or to keep your ethics or morals intact. Taking the high ground is likely to result in EVERYBODY dying…
The gameplay is pretty simple. It's a point-and-click puzzle game, with most of the puzzles revolving around managing a group of people in various states of pending doom. For example, a hostage situation where you need to carefully manage the hostage's states of mind (if they get TOO upset they'll make a break for it, but if you don't keep them nervous ENOUGH, they'll attempt to overpower you) while simultaneously negotiating with/fighting off their rescuers, while simultaneously hacking a security system. Or researching an vaccine for an alien virus by doing potentially lethal experimentation on your party members while they simultaneously attempt to dig their way out a collapsed cave entrance before everybody suffocates to death.
A very satisfying game, and I'm glad that I played it.

Long Live the Queen is a game with dating-sim-like gameplay that has you making the right decisions and learning the right skills in order to survive your first year as a young princess waiting for coronation. This game is actually surprisingly tough, and you'll need either a lot of careful planning or a lot of luck to get through the game at all. There are many interesting ways to die before the coronation.
I played a lot of Magical Diary, another game by the same developer. While that game was objectively bad but still very enjoyable, this game is far better. The dialogue is much better, and much more focused on the politics and intrigue. Your choice of skills is incredibly important... not only how much you train them, but which other skills you choose to compliment them. On top of that, your mood has to be carefully managed, because that changes the rate of learning certain skills, so you may need to force mood changes in order to learn new skills.
Once you realize how this game works, it becomes a careful puzzle of figuring out which skills you'll need at which times in order to survive certain encounters, but the nice thing is that there are multiple ways of doing it. As an example, when you go to a gala, you may have friends and enemies waiting as the result of previous choices. Do you have the courtly graces to appear poised and mature, or will you lose everyone's faith? Can you sense the magic taking place that night? Will you be challenged to a duel, and if so, can you leave the fight alive?
The art style is usually pretty good, though some of the dress-up outfits are bizarre. The music is all piano, which fits this game pretty well. There aren't many different music tracks, but I found most of them pleasant and unintrusive. The control could be better.
I picked this game up, thinking that if I liked Magical Diary, then I could find something to enjoy in this game. I had definitely underestimated Long Live the Queen, and it took me by surprise. The premise of Press X To Not Die is that most people in the town have gone crazy and started attacking each other. It's an interesting twist on the zombie apocalypse scenario.
Pros:
I loved this game and was cracking up from start to finish. The humour is great and the dialogue is clever. The acting is cheesy which perfectly fits the style of the game. The characters were all interesting and crazy in their own unique way. Full disclosure, I do have a soft spot for FMV games.
Cons:
I played on normal and I did find the difficulty a little high and some of the key press combinations a bit tough. The death scenes were pretty entertaining so I didn't mind failing once, but I was stuck on the boss fight for a while which got a little frustrating. It's also only about 30 minutes of gameplay, although it does have some replayability and the price reflects the length (it's cheap!)
Conclusion:
It calls itself a B movie and that's exactly what it is - an intentionally cheesy and sometimes bizarre FMV game. Its offbeat humour and dialogue keeps it fresh and entertaining the whole way through. If that sounds like your kind of game, I'd snap it up. Also, it says it's early access but I didn't experience any bugs, anything unfinished etc. I'm guessing it's Early Access because there's only the one episode and it's designed to be episodic. Hopefully more episodes are coming!

I'm giving this game a "recommend" because it's trying something new (for the most part), and because I wouldn't give a "not recommend" to another developer unless they really deserved it.
But here are my major issues with the game:
1. It's missing some very basic things to make the combat feel more exciting.  When I'm punched in the face, why doesn't the camera shake?  Why doesn't the screen flash?  Why isn't there a loud cracking sound?  All of these things would be incredibly easy to add to the video footage, and they'd make combat feel much much better.  These same criticisms also apply when I punch someone else.
2. The story isn't interesting at all.  It's a basic zombie scenario.  If this wasn't a videogame, I would have lost interest immediately.  How about some mystery?  How about some dramatic conflict? Shawn of the Dead did the whole zombie comedy thing, but there was a ton of drama concerning the relationships between Shawn and his girlfriend, his best friend, and his step-dad.  These things kept me engaged, and they were completely absent here.
3. The QTE's shouldn't involve both mouse and keyboard.  I have pretty fast reflexes, and I played on "normal", but I messed up the QTE's that involved pressing a mouse button about 90% of the time.
4. The QTE's where you have to build up a meter by continually pressing a key were way too difficult.  The challenge should be to respond quickly, not to see if I can break my keyboard by jamming a single key at an incredibly high frequency.   I'm guessing these meter challenges feel better on gamepad.
So hopefully some of that stuff can be fixed by the time this game leaves Early Access.  I wish the developers good luck.

Owned the game since the first days it was launched. If I remember correctly, I also backed the kickstarter around 2012. It's a good game, and I've enjoyed it a lot, but it's not the kind of game I prefer nowadays, so I probably won't be playing it a lot more.
I really felt more inclined to post a review because of the recent wave of bad ones. I don't think Starbound deserves a negative rating. In its current state, it's easy to get 40-60 hours, more, out of it.
° Building is ludicrously easy and intuitive, and it almost feels like painting with blocks.
° Decoration has an enormous variety of furniture and although some of them are frivilous novelty sets (the kind you'd rather hide in a back-room than let guests ever see them) the majority are great options for whatever you're trying to build.
° Exploration, I can't speak for, as it's never really been my thing, but one of my friends tell me over and over how amazing it is.
° Combat's pretty fun, but weapons need more variety and uniqueness. Chucklefish should take some lessons from the more popular roguelikes, too.
° Monster generation has always been mediocre. This is one of the flaws of the game, but what exactly is wrong has changed since the earliest Beta releases to the modern release. Originally, they had the problem of overreliance on procedural generation of creatures with maximum visual strangeness and minimum mechanical variety. Creatures looked different but felt the same. Now, they have the problem of many of the "unique" pre-made creatures being identical across many worlds, and yet still most of them feel the same to fight.
° The atmosphere of the game is fantastic. You might say it's out-of-this-world. Somehow the very sprites bleed optimism and hope despite all odds, if that makes any kind of sense, even if it doesn't quite match the gameplay. The music is absolutely amazing, the art style is phenomenal, the lore is reasonably well-done, even the literal atmospheres of the orbital bodies you land on are amazing as well.
° Village and town generation is awful -- by my standards. Why are a bunch of space-faring species who have managed to colonize almost every star in the game stuck in hamlets with ten or twenty houses if you're lucky? There's precisely one species that has skyscrapers, and they're underwater! The sole evidence you'll find beyond such places that any kind of advanced civilization existed will be a number of scorched planets featuring apocalyptic remains of long-dead empires.
° The story's passable. You might find it good, or much worse. It's a bit railroady as far as most missions go, as they tend to tie into tech advancement. I didn't think it was very moving, but it takes a lot to move me.
Make of this as you will. Feel free to scream at me if you bought the game because of me and then didn't like it.

Not the longest nor the deepest of the episodes of this series, but certainly one of the more inventive. Back in the day, 0 introduced the concept of the leeches that could not only work together very intelligently, but also come together to form a new enemy with extra endurance and reach than the others. The hook shot was also another interesting addition, which offered new and more realistic ways to deal with problems in the environment, caused by the enemies, or due to the need to climb to higher surfaces to unlock places that either Rebecca or Billy cannot go. The ability to place items in random places when inventory space is needed are more realistic and intuitive features that would have made previous resident evil games a  little easier to handle.
The story  is well written, albeit brief and very confined to the most essential details. Expanded, they could have made a better narrative. As it is, the tale is well told and gives adventurers items of interest, if only a few. The voices for Rebecca and Billy are well cast and the main villain is pleasingly sinister, albeit underused.
0 is, overall, an atmospheric game that will entertain fans and newcomers alike, but it may seem a little too short. If you want a longer, more in depth experience, seek out Resident Evil 4 or 6. This title is stimulating while it lasts and Wesker mode offers some replay value, but you won't return after having completed all the difficulty levels.

Miscreated is an incredibly frustrating game. Unlike other titles in the ‘always alpha’ open world survival genre, it appears to have a lot of genuine promise. It is because of this that I’ve been bothered to write a load of words about it. The world is immersive, beautiful in parts and there are possibilities to build bases and fix up vehicles to drive around. It could be a great balance of challenge and exploration but it is held back by fundamental flaws in the gameplay that continue to be ignored by the developers.
You may find it encouraging seeing updates but these are just not addressing the major issues. I have had this view for a while and it has recently been echoed by the hosts of a decent server who could no longer justify its running cost. Their reason? “We are having too many issues with vehicles and items disappearing, and gameplay in general. The developers refuse to respond to our tickets”.
Simply put, there are so many recurring bugs and irritating features in the game that there is little incentive to invest time in your character. I will focus below on the main ones that bother me:
Death is a big problem and the punishment is dropping your inventory and possibly respawning on the other side of the map. It may take 10 minutes to run back to the spot where you died, while avoiding mutants and staving off hunger and thirst. Of course, it can be argued this is 'harsh but fair' and simply part of such a game. However, death can come through no fault of your own. When encountering a mutant, an inevitability while scavenging, the fight is almost always painfully glitchy. I have seen this on many different servers, so it is not a latency issue. The mutant could be facing the wrong way and still hit you, you could kill it in two direct hits or it’ll fail to die in ten. It is a coin flip whether I die or not in such an encounter. From my experience, guns appear to do little more damage than a melee weapon but ammunition is so rare that I don’t see the point in using them anyway. I regularly see mutants stuck on walls or bits of vegetation, being spooked by nothing, suddenly running off and then scampering back to attack. How this has not been sorted out by a competent team of developers is beyond me.
Crafting in Miscreated should be a good feature in a game of this type. You can create unique weapons, like the sawblade baseball bat. Despite having both a baseball bat and saw blade in my inventory, I was sadly unable to craft this item for reasons unknown. Crafting goes further with the possibility of constructing your own base. You will first need an axe or hatchet (to chop wood for lumber) and a box of nails in order to create a sign to claim some land. Finding key items like an axe/hatchet and nails can sometimes take an hour of scavenging and then losing them upon death is a major setback. Building a base should be fun but it isn’t. It requires endlessly swinging at trees and clearing your inventory as wood is too heavy. Dropping something is a risk as there's a 50:50 chance it will just disappear for good. Creating the numerous types of components out of lumber is a tedious exercise and could be easily simplified. Once you have made your section of wall or floor, you will likely find that placing it is no straightforward task. It is difficult to line up parts neatly and sometimes it is impossible to place due to a mischievous blade of grass, for example, in the way. Miscreated just needs to implement a simple yet creative building system and look to games like Rust or Conan for its basis.
Vehicles should’ve been a great addition to the game and yet finding all the parts to get them running, along with oil and fuel, can take a lifetime. It is very satisfying once you get a vehicle working but this only lasts until you get stuck on a small rock or fail to reverse up a gentle slope to free yourself. Fuel and oil can mysteriously drain fast, so you’re back to looking for heavy cans of gas in the surroundings. Botched vehicles can cause a lot of server issues, meaning more glitches and lag.
The hunger and thirst meters are fine to manage and the game is superior to similar survival titles, like Day Z, in most aspects. The graphics and the atmosphere created by the weather effects are great. This is what usually brings me back, along with the game being basically playable with a friend. However, the glitches and bugs, bizarre combat, harshness of death and mind-numbing crafting make this game impossible to recommend in its current state. The developers need to use their updates to fix the gameplay's fundamental problems. Sadly, I would not be surprised to re-read my comments in a year’s time and find the game to be exactly the same aside from a few superficial changes. I do sincerely hope the people behind Miscreated listen to the critcism and act on it, as this game could really be so much more.

Having played up to this point, about 83 hours of MIscreated I think I can safely give it a fair and honest review.
It's an early access title so let's get the BS out of the way first:
It isn't optimized all that well.
There is frequent frame stuttering and drops. (for me and a lot of others)
The player base  is relatively low.
Sometimes servers suck and you get canned, or you lose your gear, or you spawn beside a bunch of glitchy half loaded mutants or wolves and then instantly die.
Sometimes things get broken, but as of the time of writing (0.49 patch), most implemented mechanics are working and a lot of major hurdles have been addressed.
With that said, this game is far and away the best survival style game to come to early access, possibly ever. The base building leaves a lot to be desired for me, and a lot of people are complaining about floating bases (which ironically doesn't bother me either). But, where this game shines is in the sheer atmosphere. It feels desolate, and alone, but somehow also homey and lived in. The environment the Devs have created make the game enjoyable to play, even while running around lost in the forest for the first few hours until you establish patterns. When you meet another player in the world (which you do often enough as the map size is just right) it's tense. Will they be friendly? Will they not? If they are, they're usually great to help out. If not, the gunplay is satisfying, and challenging.
If you like survival games, and if you; like me, have been left♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in the wind with titles like Day Z and H1Z1, then you need to play this game.
It's not done, but it does have a multitude of working and mechanically stable weapons, glitchy but enjoyable vehicles which you have to piece together to fix, a good community who usually adhere to server rules (RP, PVE, PVP in zones, etc) and an extraordinarily active development team who is constantly updating (monthly) and hotfixing.
If you just want BR, maybe wait for PUBG to get  "better". But if you are down with the survival elements of hunting and crafting and looting, then get this now, and wait to see if BR is in the works for it as well. It's just plain fun to play.

This is precisely how to *NOT* make a game about killing zombies on a spaceship.
Never mind plot; even if the plot for this yarn was excellent (which it is not) I could not recommend it, because the gameplay is just plain awful.
Enter room.  Trigger zombies.  Shoot zombie heads until they're dead, or you're dead.  This sounded great, in a Painkiller-esque sort of way... until I actually played it.
There is hardly any mobility, because the fights are almost always inside very short corridors or other zones and your character cannot jump over stuff that an 80-year-old grandmother with the flu could.  Yes, that's right, kids, it is 2014, and somebody thought a FPS WITHOUT JUMPING OR ANY REAL USE OF THE THIRD DIMENSION WAS GOOD GAME DESIGN.
This is not even Quake; this is Doom, badly done, with modern-ish graphics.  It's not as fun as Doom, though.
Then let's talk about the guns and approach to game-balance.   Guns go bang.  Zombies get tougher.  Upgrade guns every level, so that guns still hurt zombies.
The magical upgrade system for guns between levels (because, gosh, pacing weapons availability throughout the story would take actual game-design skill) is lame and makes this feel like a title that was originally intending to be F2P, but failed to find an investor.  Especially the "gold" bit- that's a classic bit of F2P design (gold would normally cost Real Money, kids) but It is absolutely atrocious game design to need multiple resources in a SP campaign.  Seriously- if you don't want players to have gun X until Y point... don't give the players gun X.  Not real complicated.
But, to add insult to injury, the gun choices are perversely bad- not "so bad it's good", or "bad because it's part of a purposeful attempt to talk about an Idea" but bad out of sheer lazy programming and poor attention to detail.
Pistols might vary hugely in total DPS delievered per bullet fired... but the two pistols I've found thus far?  They have exactly as many starting bullets.  So, hmm, which one am I going to pick?  The one that will do 4000% damage for all shots fired, or the one that does 3000%?
Seriously?  Whoever designed this couldn't be bothered to get balance even roughly done, or differentiate weapons correctly?
The list of these kinds of good-god-why mistakes is terribly long.
How about a UI where it took many random button presses to figure out how to merely switch guns before a mission?  How about the game awarding upgrades to weapons I didn't even have equipped?
How about having a "grenade" button that, instead of instantly throwing a grenade, does the same thing as pressing the Select Grenade key?
How about a plot so lame and incoherently written that I could care less?
How about playing a female character, and hearing male breathing the first time I used the Sprint feature?
How about "crouching" so low you'd have to crawl IRL?
How about the transition from standing to crouching having absolutely zero purpose in the game at all?  No accuracy boost, no stealthiness, nothin'- it's just a gimpy way to move around.
Lastly... the graphics are really sub-par.  Each element is OK, in a boring, done-that-been-there fake-looking High Tech kind of way.  The zombies aren't terrible or exciting, although they really  don't make any sense at all- I'm on some high-tech spacecraft, there are no trees... so, uh, where did all those chainsaws come from???
That said, the environments and level designs are very lousy.  They aren't invested with any emotional involvement and  the vast majority of the locations look exactly the same; until I got to the D-Tox room, I was pretty much just staring at the same bland sci-fi-ish corridors over and over, with heavy use of colored lighting instead of genuine attempts to create interesting spaces.
Anyhow... if the gameplay wasn't terrible, I could have let the lousy use of art assets go; this wasn't a AAA title and I was expecting gameplay, not graphics, to be the show.  But for the record, it's not done well; the art assets are just fine, but the level designs are terrible and there is never a sense of Place about the vast majority of the ship, which makes the fact that gameplay consists mainly of doing the same encounters with the same zombie hordes, over and over again, that much more boring.
Could this game be fixed?  Somewhat.  Issues with the UI, the concepts of balance for the weapons, etc., could be addressed.  The major issues are with the level designs, not allowing jumping in general, and the lousy plot; these things aren't so easily addressed.  Anyhow, I hope that the developers read this and, should they get the opportunity to ever make another game, take this critique very seriously- I do not mind if your levels aren't AAA-looking in screenshots, but you'd darn well better build a game that's actually fun, if you want to avoid a diatribe like this one from Steam raters and reviewers alike.

Long Live The Queen is a cute little game that fits (if not follows, chronology isn't my strong point) the trend of Choose-Your-Own-Adventure indie games that seem to be coming out now. Much like Papers, Please or The Stanley Parable, this game is focused around a set dialog tree that is then hidden behind mechanics. Where for Papers, Please this was passport stamping, and for The Stanley Parable doors, in this game you train a princess in various skills that you think may be effective in helping her preserve the kingdom.
This said, where Papers, Please and The Stanley Parable really surpass this game is the simplicity of their mechanics. In the former you either stamp a passport or you don't, and in The Stanley Parable you generally choose to progress one way or the other. Long Live the Queen isn't as clear cut. The amount a skill is progressed is determined by the Princess's current mood and how much existing training is already in that area, and then your success is based off some hidden threshold. As a result it's not really clear how much leeway you have with any one choice, and so bar strict experimentation, it's very akin to stabbing in the dark and hoping you don't run into a literal dead end.
So while this game handles itself well in terms of setting and plot, it fails to achieve the very high standard set by the other two games mentioned above.
Now I like experimentation, so I didn't find reclicking through half an hour of text or reloading from any saved point and reattempting terribly tedious. Your mileage may vary though, so don't expect to just breeze through this game to a good ending without putting in any effort.
As a result, this game gets a 3.5/5 from me. It's pushing a solid 4 with its aesthetic, but I don't quite like Princesses that much.

Long Live The Queen is a game with a fantastic setup and promising mechanics. It sounds fun on paper, and the writing, art, and concepts for how the game works mechanically are all pretty great; in the end, though, I just found it frustrating to play. I'd still recommend getting it on sale if the theme, premise, setting, and art are all up your alley, because you'll definitely enjoy yourself at least somewhat... but I feel like the game could've been so much more if it had leaned more into the role-playing as opposed to the tired visual novel idea of playing the game over and over again, getting tons of Bad Ends, in order to get even one Good End.
On your first playthrough, planning out classes and trying to balance Elodie's mood seem like super interesting mechanics and if you're into the aesthetic of the game and the stuff you saw in, like, the Steam trailer and screenshots, you'll be thinking it's like the greatest game ever. The writing is great, the way taking classes shows you a brief overview of the progressively more advanced topics you're learning in a given subject is neat, and man, like everything about the presentation of the game itself is fantastic.
You notice as you play along that you're failing like every single skill check. You might even be like "aw man, I missed this Poisons check? Better bone up on Poisons" — only to find that you'll like never need Poisons again for the rest of the game. (Disclaimer: I have yet to complete a successful runthrough of the game, but have spent over three hours of time in the game according to Steam.) Then you'll die from something out of nowhere that you could've never seen coming and prepared for on your first time through.
"Okay," you think, "I'll give it another shot. This is clearly just a mechanics'd up visual novel, anyways, so I guess I should've expected hell of Bad Ends." On your subsequent playthroughs, you'll attempt to adjust your class schedules accordingly such as to allow you to pass checks for events that you now know are coming up from your previous playthroughs. Then, when you train for a key class, you'll get little-to-no skill points from it because you weren't watching your mood. Or worse yet, you were watching your mood and thought to make your princess as happy as possible because she starts the game all sad and depressed over the death of her mother, but as it turns out some class you wanted to take does barely anything or nothing at all for you because of the mood you're in. You search around the UI and try and find some sort of reasoning for which classes are affected by which moods — and it turns out that there is no such thing (although they [mostly] follow some sort of logic). Instead, you must either figure out which classes are affected by which moods on your own and write them down in a grid on a piece of paper... or just check the top-rated Steam guide for the game.
Basically, in the end, the game becomes more of an exercise in replaying the game over and over and learning from your failures, taking notes on what worked and what didn't, in order to come up with a plan to make a successful run through the game. If this sounds appealing to you, that's fine; I was hoping for a much more role-playing-oriented experience out of the game, myself. Again, I understand that it's a relatively short game once you have the path for "the right run" down, and the length of the experience comes from the act of replaying it over and over again, and also it's just a more mechanically-dense visual novel, when it comes down to it. These things are all fine, but it's just not quite what I hoped for given the promise of the game from the outset and the great writing the game has and such.
In summary, I feel like the game has a great setup, great art, great writing, average sound and music, and great mechanical premise... but just kind of crappy actual mechanics in the end. It's still worth playing if the theme and setting and stuff interests you, and even more so if you're willing to put up with the visual novel tropes that make several, several playthroughs a must if you want to see a non-death ending... but at the end of the day, I personally wound up finding the core gameplay systems to be frustrating and poorly thought-out.

Pillars of Eternity's story hinges on
in two major forms (minor spoilers):

Much like tabletop RPGs, your character's class, background, personality and actions are defined entirely by yourself, with a wide range of alternatives to choose from. These will affect your game experience in different ways, such as available dialog options, skills, character statistics, and of course the game's ending. However, your companions' tales are for you to discover (some in the form of quests). Several deific elements in the story not only contribute to the game's plot but also make for compelling folklore, which you're given the option to delve into by studying numerous books and texts throughout the game, should you wish to. It's worth mentioning that the game's important dialogue is nicely voiced over. This, alongside its masterful writing, terrific music and the beautiful environments and landscapes of Eora surely make for an enveloping experience. However, loading times are frequent and of great length, which considerably hurt the game's immersion.
Combat is fairly complex if you're not familiar with classic RPGs (especially infinity engine: Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale). While it may take you some time to understand combat mechanics, its information and explanation are available anytime during the game. Additionally, its core elements are explained in the form of tooltips, for example: if you were to mouse-over the word "Accuracy" in some skill's description, a small pop-up window would emerge, telling you all about how accuracy plays a role in combat (and possibly a numeric example). You can always pause and go over the combat log and there's also a "slow mode" if you feel it's all happening too fast (which I always did). I found the game's combat mechanics somewhat chaotic and overwhelming, given such a great amount of features like interrupts, vitality/health, damage types calculations, attack & defense rolls, engagement and much more happening concurrently at blazing-fast speeds. Particularly at higher difficulties, this can be a detriment to players.
Inventory management feels natural and practical, with separate item and equipment slots for each character, as well as a shared, unlimited stash. Much like in
, armor and weapons come in different "classes", like common, rare, exceptional and unique. These provide beneficial and sometimes harmful effects for the user, and can be further enhanced via enchantments. However, these improvements can only be stacked up to a certain limit, and cannot be reversed, so be careful. It's possible to craft your own potions and scrolls to aid your party in combat, an advantageous mechanic that felt terribly underexposed.
Pillars of Eternity can be as hard as you want it to, with four difficulties to choose from: Easy, Normal, Hard and Path of the Damned. Furthermore, there's also two game modes: Expert Mode (more realistic, spells' AoE is not displayed, no dialogue help options, etc.) and Trial of Iron (a.k.a. "permadeath"). As if that wasn't enough, the game will offer to crank up its difficulty if it considers your party is overleveled, which will assuredly result in a constant challenge during the whole game. Although I wasn't brave enough to try Expert Mode (let alone Trial of Iron), I did venture into the game on Path of the Damned difficulty, which proved absolutely brutal
, and that's not something you see in every RPG! If you're up for a real challenge, trust me: this game will not let you down.
Pillars of Eternity is a deep, enjoyable, beautifully crafted RPG. After more than 140 hours of gameplay I can assure you it'll be worth your while.

Dark Souls, this game, in many ways, has changed the way I see the world. A quote from a character in the game reads, "After all.. what is bravery without a dash of recklessness?". This reflects the entirety of the Dark Souls series, and it also reflects the way we should see the world. Why do we doubt ourselves? Well, I believe that our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate, rather our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond belief. "How does this relate to Dark Souls?" You may ask, my answer is very simple, it's your decision to decide what this game means to you.
All deep themes and meanings aside, this is a very quality game and series that should have its beauty appreciated. This is what makes it so great, you can choose. A game has never given me more freedom. The relationship I, along with many others have with this game, is a new approach never taken in a game. The game throws you into this world, you being as clueless as your character is, only telling you stories of the legends that once ruled this world. It's your choice to either claw your way from area to area, explore the unknown, and take huge risk, and trek your way all the way to the end, and find your own ending, and what that means to you. Or simply give up, and let the hollow land of Lordran corrupt you.
Notice how through all of this, I havent once said anything about the gameplay. Not once did I mention, "Hardest boss is _______" "Really hard game". This is because you need to find that out for yourself. Buy this game, get the DS Fix mod, grab a controller, whatever you have to do to make your life easier. Once you're ready to explore the hollow, dark, eerie, trechourous enviornment, enjoy yourself. Have fun with the game. Everyone's complaint with the game is that it's hard, and you just have to accept that you will die, a lot, over, and over again. Don't give up, it may seem impossible to get through the mentally challenging and frustrating experience that is this game, but it is well worth it. Once you beat the first game, it's all downhill from there. That's right, this is the hardest game in the series, so if you can get through this one, you can get through anything.
Thank you for your time, reading this long and drawn out review of this game, but shouldn't that just show how good of a game, and series it is? The rest is yours to fill in the blanks, goodbye now, and don't you dare go hollow

Dead Effect is an old school scifi horror FPS and I am having lots of fun playing it. I have not finished the game yet, but I have spent some hours playing it, so here are my thoughts on its pros and cons:
+ Good atmosphere
+ Nice graphics
+ Solid gameplay
+ Good sound effects and music
+ Collectibles and upgrades – you collect credits to buy / upgrade your weapons, gold to buy special weapons / autoheal ability, tablets to get more of the story and orbs to unlock another game / story information in the main menu – it is fun trying to get them all

This needs to be said first up, the recommendation for this game is a tentative one.
Dead Effect is a first-person zombie shooter, has a very Dead Space-y feel to it and a very linear story full of cliche. But, let's face it, you're not here for the story, you're here to paint the walls in zombie and that's what you'll end up doing with much gusto.
Pros:
~ Decent game considering the lowish price point, quite fun to play.
~ Gun combat is visceral and intense with horde based enemies, and grenades can be a lifesaver, just don't stand near them, they can kill you too.
~ Visual atmosphere is very reminiscent of Dead Space with the linear semi-claustrophobic levels.
~ Graphics are surprisingly good for an iOS port.
~ Controls are very smooth and easy to grasp, though I had to severely reduce the mouse sensitivity from standard to get it to a playable level.
~ Good variety of enemies.
~ Enemies pose a decent threat, even in normal mode (though, they can be a bit obnoxious at times).
~ You're never constantly short of ammo in normal mode, though you do need to be a semi-decent shot.
~ You rarely feel overpowered for area.
Cons:
~ Atmosphere is far too reliant on the music to create tension, often making it harder to hear if there are enemies nearby.
~ Game is DESPERATELY in need for a melee attack, most of my deaths so far have been from being swamped by enemies and I'm unable to break free and they chew my health up in about two seconds.
~ Firing from the hip is more accurate than ironsighting (for me at least).
~ Hit detection seems to be a little wonky. I had numerous incidents where standard zombies were taking three shotgun blasts directly to the head and it wasn't killing them or it was killing the ones behind them.
~ Speech volume is way too soft even at maximum, I almost had to turn the music off to be able to hear the voices with any clarity.
~ Combat gets very repetitive after a while; shoot zombies, find ammo, repeat.

I'll admit, the game is a little strange. You play as a guy named "The Stranger" who needs "moolah" (money) for an important operation. This game is Wild West themed, which means that the best way for you to make money is to collect bounties for cash. So you're a bounty hunter, collecting the biggest bad guys in the area. You get more money for capturing them alive than you do dead, and the best part is that even the minions can be cashed in.
You don't fire guns though. Instead, you are armed with a dual fire crossbow that uses live bait as it's ammo. There are spiders that act as your lasso, bats that act like grenades, bees that act like machine gun rounds, and much more. It's a pretty cool take on the western theme.
The world is filled with weird creatures instead of people too. You're some weird like guy that looks like no one else around, the major towns are filled with chicken people (they are really annyoing and have very cliche lines), there are weird native people that are like 2 feet tall, and then there are the bad guys which basically are all the same looking.
It's cheesy, weird, annoying at times, but somehow still fun. Definitely an older game. If you can stomach this kind of stuff, it might just be a game for you. My advice if you can't decide whether or not to buy it, find some videos or pictures online of the game and get this game for cheap (like $5).

Helpful information: The game will not run if you attempt to play it through steam, you have to use the launcher from the game’s folder.
It will also run like absolute garbage unless you turn off the Anti-Aliasing.
F1 and F5 are the default quick save and quick load keys.
Aside from a couple of issues the game is actually pretty fantastic. It manages to blend first and third person views near flawlessly, the whole “critters as ammo” gimmick is unique, well fleshed out, and makes using the double barreled crossbow exceptionally entertaining to use. And then there are the bosses. They did an outstanding job on the bosses and managed to stick with allowing you to choose whether to take them out lethally or non-lethally. And on top of that its story is actually good.
And the game practically oozes character. The mysterious stranger is everything you could want in a Clint Eastwood-esque bounty hunter and all of the locations feel well designed and are a joy to play in. It also seamlessly manages to combine a Western and Oddworld into something truly original and interesting. But there is also something else that this game has which you don’t really appreciate until its gone and that is a lack of “fluff.” Most games you get your upgrades and then there’s a sort of lull in the missions where they just kinda feel copy pasted and like they wanted to artificially pad out the campaign but I never really got that feeling with this game.
Then there are those issues I mentioned. Controlling the character can act up in some circumstances where he will either get stuck on a flat surface, rotating when climbing ropes is reversed from what you might expect, capturing enemies defaults to third person mode so you have to switch back to first person manually every time, and there is a mildly infuriating to control boat section somewhere in there as well.
But these are all minor complaints for an otherwise grand game that was highly enjoyable. Definitely buy it when it goes on sale.

At 2012, Obsidian Entertainment launched a Kickstarter project named Project Eternity. Their goals was to make a traditional RPG game which would become the spiritual successor of
and
, and their intention got sympathies and was later crowdfunded by over 77,000 backers. Their initial pledges of 1 million dollar was easily surpassed to the amount of 4 million dollars, and in 2015, the game
was finally released.
As I said above, Pillars of Eternity (will be written as “Pillars” from now on) is a traditional RPG which tried to bring back nostalgic feels of other classical games, such as Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale. Pillars uses game engine Unity 5, and is presented on isometric viewpoint which was pretty much similar to other Infinity Engine games. You couldn’t be able to change their camera angle and perspectives.
You could choose your character from 6 races available, they are Aumaua, Dwarves, Elves, Human, Godlike, and Orlans. You can also choose from 11 classes with each own unique skills and traits. But, your class doesn’t affect the kind of armor you could wear. It means that your wizard could use a heavy armor, but in cost of longer skill cooldown. Be wise for building your character to suit your own gameplay.
Pillars uses party-based mechanic; you could find various companions along the way and you could add them as your party member later. Every companion has their own unique backstories, and will react for your main character’s decisions, in good or bay ways.
Pillars is filled with various quests which can be finished, but the main quest is focused about a strange curse which called Hollowborn, where any newborn child in Drywood has no soul. On the other hand, your character was suddenly given a mysterious power; an ability to seek into other people’s souls. People called them a “Watcher”. The story later unfolds further and further, revealing what cause Hollowborn and the reason of your character had been chosen as a Watcher.
Pillars has similar gameplay as any old-school RPGs, using real time tactical combat. You could pause the game anytime and then give orders to your specifics party member which will be applied when you resume the game. The effectiveness of giving orders, the formation of party, and using the right kind of attack will dictate the result of combat. As combat happen, you could inspect how the combat was resolved through “combat log”, which is a helpful to giving the idea about what kind of attack that is effective for the enemies, and what kind of defense that is effective to protect the party.
There are two kind of vitality the characters have, they are
and
.  Endurance is a “short-term vitality”, it tells you how much vitality they have for surviving an encounter. When the endurance reaches zero, the character would be knocked down and couldn’t move or taking action until the combat ends. Endurance will be restored to a certain amount after the encounter ends. But, the game will be over when all of party members are knocked down.
On the other hand, health is a “long-term vitality”, it dictate how much vitality the characters have until they need a rest. Whenever the character receives damage, their health would be depleted as well. Once health reach zero, the characters would be knocked out and receive a Maimed status when the character revive at the end of combat. When the character was out of health during this Maimed status, they would die permanently. Unlike endurance, health couldn’t regenerate itself when it lost. The only means of regenerating health is by resting. Always look up for the health of your party to decide when the party needs a rest to restore their health or not.
About the rest system, Pillars is given a huge change compared to
. In
, party could rest whenever and wherever the player wants. It could be exploited with the players by resting after every encounter so their party was always on full health. Meanwhile, in Pillars, you need an item called “Camping Supplies” so that party would be able to rest in the outside the settlement. The amount of camping supplies you could bring is limited and varied based on the game difficulty. On the other meaning, your party could rest either in your Stronghold (will be explained later) or in the inn available in various settlement with certain prices. It makes the party management is getting more complex than before.
Drywood is a huge world with various places and dungeons to be explored, but it is also an unforgivable and dangerous world. Player could die easily when they meet an encounter without a proper preparation. The world in Pillars is majorly “deleveled”. You can’t beat every single enemy you meet with your current level, and the same goes for quests. If player have some difficulty to beat some enemies or finish the quest, it’s a wise move to retreat and come back later when player have better level and equipment. Save the game progress often, especially when you think you’re going to face some serious challenges.
Pillars has big replayability value. The game could be finished with various ways and scenarios. Most quests will give you several ways of how the quest will be resolved. Every way has its own consequences. The world will react differently for whatever you do, some will like it and some wouldn’t. Pillars is a heaven for players who likely to play heavily on the role-playing aspect.
Pillars has voice acting feature, but the game doesn’t use it fully. Voice acting will likely occur in certain interaction, such as main quests. The rest of game is heavily narrated by long text (although it isn’t as long and complex as
). Some people might hate this, but from my personal viewpoint, this kind of narration gives Obsidian chances to give us a reach, deep story. They were narrated brilliantly with full of details.
One interesting point of this game is its
system. As the main quest unfolds, you could get an abandoned keep called Caed Nua and using this place as base for your party. Caed Nua is upgradable and has various unique interactions and quests, such as bandit raid, adventurers and travelers who are looking for help, and bounty quests that offer certain rewards. You could finish them directly, ignoring them, or even asking for your companions who weren’t currently on your party to finish them.
And right below Caed Nua, you could find a huge labyrinth called "Endless Path of Od Nua", a mega-dungeon consist of 15 levels. You could encounter many high-leveled enemies which will push your ability to the limit to defeat them. There are also some minor quests and one unique quest regarding Od Nua which could only be finished with highest levels of character and grant you the unique rewards.
Finally, as the review was written, I already had a total 50 hour playtimes. So far, I had finished the Act I of main quests, finished all the quests I could found in Gilded Vale, the first settlement you could find in-game, and cleared the first 3 levels of Od Nua. One thing I cod say to this game: it’s an amazing experience. Obsidian succeeded to make a game with a deep, rich story, solid gameplay, and interactive world. It might sound cliche, but I haven’t found any major points that are lessening my enjoyment of playing this game. Pillars achieved its goal to bring out traditional RPG genre that everyone loves, especially from any experienced players, and reaches big enthusiasm from any newer players such as myself.
As a resurrection of older RPG genre, Obsidian succeeded to brings out a game with rich contents: a living, interactive world, a deep story, and solid gameplay.

I always assumed this game injected some sort of Rainbow Six-ish story into Counter-Strike, if you figured the same then you'd be wrong too! :P ...Instead the game simply leads you through 18 maps of CS each with a set of challenges. In general the challenges are nothing special, on Normal difficulty they keep engagements from seeming too repetitive, while on Expert they can potentially extend your playtime (for better or for worse). The only bummer thing about the difficulty levels is that they are tied to the campaign which you start, not the individual missions, so choose wisely. Unfortunately the game only lets you play as counter-terrorists, including terrorist challenges would have made it feel more complete. In it you get to assemble your own team but choices are shallow, consequenceless, and thus meaningless. The bots aren't impressive by far, but they get the job done. Oddly the game was surprisingly buggy on my Windows XP machine, but it worked perfectly on Windows 8. So that's it, classic counter-strike, against bots, plus challenges. It's a shame they hadn’t created a narrative to interestingly drive you through the maps, as I mistakenly imagined; or devised a more complicated and meaningful team building and progression system. As it turned out though, I just can't think of any reason to recommend it, other than if you're stuck on a craptop and really, really, need to scratch your classic CS itch.

Dark Souls is one of my favorite video game series of all time, if not my favorite.
Dark Souls 1 is, in my opinion, either the best in that series, or tied with Bloodborne. The combat, level design, atmosphere, scattered bits of lore, and metroidvania feel make it stand out as the best in its genre.
Combat feels slow, heavy and methodical. In order to succeed, you need to study your opponent, learn their patterns, and plan your attacks accordingly to exploit their weaknesses. Blocking and dodging are vital to your survival, as most enemies will hit hard when they hit you, meaning even that lowly hollow could pose a threat if you're completely careless.
Level design is brilliant. You will discover shortcuts linking two areas together in a logical manner, and the first time you have that feeling of "I know where I am, I was here just a while ago!" is incredible. The worlds are also, for the most part, brilliantly planned, so you're rarely thrown into completely BS scenarios (there are at most 3 encounters that actually feel unfair)
and of course, the multiplayer. Whether you prefer Jolly Co-operation or murder and mayhem, the multiplayer, seamlessly woven into the singleplayer experience, is one of a kind and incredibly entertaining.
Be sure to download DsFix and DSCM from the Nexus (also, a controller is highly recommended)
the port is admittedly very poor due to FromSoftware never planning to port the game over in the first place, and the multiplayer is basically broken without DSCM but with both mods it is an almost perfect experience.

Ninja pizza self esteem girl
So an interesting aspect of the game Ninja Pizza girl is that there is a stat that is tracked called self esteem.
It gets lowered apparently based on how you mess up in the game and there are enemies who affect it by intentionally causing you to make mistakes and then pointing and laughing and taunting after having done so.
There are other plot related things that affect it that I won’t go into detail about.
What was really interesting is that after it gets low it asks you to, before you continue doing deliveries to take some time and get something nice for the main character to help her feel better before continuing on. The first time I got this instruction I did so but, not seeing what this actually did ignored this the second time this happened.
As I continued to ignore the needs of my little avatar for this game it got more difficult. I attributed this difficulty to the normal difficulty curve of a game ramping up and began to get hard on myself for my failures. My character was slower and the screen started dim with color cues that made it more difficult to tell what the best thing to do was.
After an extremely difficult game I left the game but decided to poke my head back in the menu of stuff and decided on a whim to get some tea for the character. After I bought a few more things (with in game currency not for money) I noticed a message somewhere of the longs of feeling about as good as I can right now. so after playing some games, having a nice bath and taking some time with tea for a break apparently my character was feeling decently.
I decided to play a few more levels and was astonished by how bright the game was suddenly. Of course it was just as bright as it had been when I first started the game, but I had not noticed the gradual dimming of everything because I was so focused on blaming myself for being a little bit to slow or a little bit to uncoordinated for the jumps and tasks I was trying to perform.
I only played part way through this game and I’m sure it goes into more depth about this but it was a fascinating use of game mechanics to convey something very interesting and impactful and in a way that was much subtler then i’d give credit for most games doing that aren’t specifically built around the thing they are conveying. (of course I may be wrong in assuming this game isn’t built around mental health and coping which would just give even more credit for its subtly here.)
That is it. just me rambling about the design of this game.
edit: so I went to find a link to the game to include at the top and saw this text: “ Ninja Pizza Girl is a serious game about self-esteem, bullying and resilience — and pizza delivering ninjas!” so i guess that line about games that aren’t specifically about the thing is moot, but i still really like how they went about this and it didn’t produce any dissonance between the story and the gameplay.

surprisingly enjoyable.
it went from a generic, pathetically easy platformer that features all of the optimization problems of a trash unity game (my laptops integrated HD 520 with 128mb VRAM ran it better than my desktop running on a 1060), to one that's quite fun.
the whole story of the game itself is insanely generic, with comic bubbles and portraits portraying cheesy cutscenes, and yet, what i love the most of it is Gemma, the main character. it's odd, because what makes her so likeable aren't the cutscenes, but rather the gameplay itself. the reason for this is because as Gemma's emotional state deteriorates, the music, the color grading, and even the pace of the game all change.
the gameplay itself starts off pretty bland, pretty much refusing to change for the first two chapters, but for the rest of the game it felt like it changed with every delivery. the platforming remained unchanged, until the sudden introduction of moving platforms (which were very much needed), whereas changes are made until the end.
my biggest complaint is that there are some bad levels, most notably the one where you have to make a girl excited from delivering pizza that's just a pain to finish, but regardless, the last two chapters pretty much made up for it.
as i got this as part of a bundle, i didn't pay the 10 dollars for this game, and it probably wouldn't have been worth it either. regardless, it's a short and "cheap" unity platformer, but for it to succeed at telling a story through the gameplay instead of the lazy cutscenes, it just makes this so hard not to like.

Perhaps the most profoundly unsatisfying game I've played for a while.
It's a very interesting work, and tries some very interesting things - both in terms of the narrative and the gameplay - but it ultimately doesn't work out.  Extreme randomness in your decisions' outcome mean that if you feel any investment in the characters or storyline, the only way to get a desirable result is to replay the same sequences dozens of times.  On top of that, the narrative takes an ugly and self-indulgent turn at the end, one that breaks the fourth wall in a way that makes even the perseverance of getting desirable outcomes feel like a complete waste.
Although I can't reccommend this specific title, I hope all the same that devolver continues making games in this vein, and that they just learn from the mistakes of this outing; the implied potential here is huge.

SUMMARY: Its really fun and something no zombie and RPG fan should be without. I'm glad someone finally did a decent open-world zombie apocalypse RPG. (Red Dead Redemption's DLC doesnt count, although it was fun) However, the game seems a bit rough around the edges and unpolished. Ive encountered many minor-but-annoying graphical glitches such as clipping, pop-ins, twitching enemies, and weapons disappearing when wielded. I'm hoping that will be cleaned up in a patch or something. Overall, its a great game and I can see myself playing this one for hours.
MAIN:
Ok so where to start. This game is everything a single player zombie apocalypse RPG should be, although it is definitely not perfect. Ive been looking at it for a long time, but it was early access, and I generally don't buy e. a. games. I saw the e. a. tag was gone and it was extremely reduced for the summer sale, so I figured why the hell not.
You start the game as a guy named Marcus on a fishing trip in the remote wilderness with his buddy, but later you get the option to play as others in your group of survivors.
There are two aspects to this game, one is the open world run around doing random missions, story missions, collecting supplies and fighting zombies, the other (and what makes this game more than just an open world zombie-smash-fest) is managing your base's supplies and rooms and survivor's morale and trust. The base needs supplies such as food, ammo and medicine, which you can only get from raiding places. You can also build different areas inside your base, and upgrade them. Also, you can turn various outside areas into outposts which help you with the supplies, create safe zones, and set traps. Your survivors can go off on their own too, so you may have to rescue them. Random events happen, that can make survivors angry, or happy. The more stuff you bring back, the more you can ask for favors such as friends following you, radioing for certain supply caches, taking stuff out of the supply crate and so on (the mechanic in the game is your "reputation points").
Personally, I think it sucks that even if you were the one who braved the zombie hordes to bring back gear, once you put it in the base's supply chest, it costs MORE rep points to pull it out then you earned putting it in. I understand why the devs did it from a gameplay standpoint, but it only makes me want to put items I am probably not going to need in there.
Theres a LOT of stuff to do, just running around causes you to get random radio requests from your base. Things like clearing an infested house, helping a survivor (both strangers and ones in your group), hunting a dangerous type of zombie, raiding a certain building and many more. Helping people builds up trust, morale, and rep points, while ignoring requests for a certain amount of real-world time can fail the mission with negative consequences.
Thats another interesting fact. The game is run off of a real world timer. So say a character gets "hurt" (worse than just injured, their health permanently goes down until they rest and heal) or tired (max stamina goes down), you have to take them back to base and let them rest. Also, the in-game clock and date is the first day you start. So say you started playing on June 9th. Your diary would start that day as well.
The combat is simple to master and very fluid. It feels great to smash zombie heads with a lead pipe or other blunt object. There are various attacks you can do, as well as dodges(absolutely a must to master), finishing moves, and stealth kills. There is also many different types of firearms, with firing being relatively realistic. Not as much as a reality-based FPS army game, but more so then a typical 3rd person shooting game like GTA. The game also tries to be realistic with the sound of a shot drawing a crowd, so except for certain situations, sneaking up and bashing away seems a much better idea. The standard zombies are the running/jumping type for the most part, but generally go down easy as long as you arent swarmed. Not so for some of the rarer types, such as one bloated with poison gas and one that seems to act more like a werewolf.
Sound is a major part of the game. As your character walks, a little blue circle surrounds him/her getting bigger or smaller the more or less noise you make. The zombies are attracted to sound, so things like banging around while searching, driving a car (always fun to plow through a horde) and shooting draw them. The zombies also make noise, and it is very important to make sure you dont walk up on one lurching around where you cant see it by listening for the sounds it makes.
So, whats the bad points? Well. The graphics are glitchy as all hell for starters. Expect plently of pop-ins, clipping, disappearing weapons (even though your character still is rendered as if s/he is swinging away with it), enemies suddenly being on top of your car when you go to smash them and so on. The weirdest one I saw so far is a zombie laying down (some lay, then stand up and go after you when you alert them). I walked up and was about 5 feet away, and instead of getting to his feet, the zombie model laying on the ground did a jittery complete horizontal 360, and then suddenly disappeared, then popped-in standing and right in my character's face, where he bit me. Fun.
Another is it doesnt seem to be optimized very well. It jacks my core temp up by 20c or so no matter what graphics setting its on. And its not pushing my gpu/cpu very hard at all. Its not a big deal, though, just smacks of a rushed finish.
But even though its a bit glitchy and has rough edges, its still fun as hell. Anyone whose an RPG and zombie apocalypse fan should check this out.
