When considering what it is that distinguishes a survival horror game from an action or any other genre, things that come to mind for survival horror fans are usually locked camera angles which can often put the player at a viewing disadvantage, weak or limited combat abilities, low ammo supplies and adventure game exploration in a environment filled with dangerous enemies. What makes a survival horror game different from other genres is that while most games give the player great agency and power over the world, survival horror puts the player at a disadvantage and in a position of weakness. Under those parameters, Resident Evil Zero is undoubtedly a survival horror game.
If inconveniencing the player is part of what makes a game a survival horror game, then Resident Evil Zero may at times have too much of a good thing. While it is a staple of the classic Resident Evil franchise to give the player limited inventory and to juggle items, Zero goes a step further by flooding the player with a multitude of items while also providing no system of storage. The idea was to make item management more organic by forcing the player to pick up and put down items in the game world as necessary rather than being confined to chests. But the management of resources frequently crosses the line from being a source of tension to a source of tedium, and first time players can add whole hours to their play time as they trial and error which items they needed to take and which to leave behind.
Despite the two character co-op mechanic, this game brings nothing substantially new to the Resident Evil franchise or the survival horror genre. Many of the familiar enemies and settings seen in other games come back here and none of the features makes this game stand out compared to the other entries.  What it does bring is a solid entry into the genre and another hearty full length adventure for fans to sink their teeth into. One quality which stands out in this game versus the other classic Resident Evils is that while they have often been called survival horror, they usually ended up playing more like action games by the end. As early as Resident Evil 2 the games have been empowering the player more than the game advertises and even in the remake there is more bullets than there are enemies to kill by the end of the game. In Resident Evil Zero, especially on hard difficulty, there are truly more threats than there are resources to spare. Perhaps in trying to be how people remembered the classic Resident Evils were like rather than being how they really are, Resident Evil Zero is more survival horror than most of the other Resident Evils.
Playing Zero on hard, I was constantly on the verge of running out of ammo and I was truly worried that I might run out of supplies before I needed them. Zero will still empower the player in time for the end of the game, but first time players will be holding their breath for quite a while before that part arrives. Resident Evil Zero is not an accommodating game. Although released in 2002, this is a game with the design philosophy of 3D playstation 1 games. Many of the features and character control standards of modern AAA games are missing from this title, and it is a very real possibility to get permanently stuck. If you don't mind early 3D game mechanics however, and want to experience a survival horror challenge in what is clearly still a AAA game for its time, then I recommend Resident Evil Zero.
If you decide to play this game, I recommend that you play it on hard on your first playthrough. A big part of the survival horror experience is entering the unknown, and having to do the cost benefit analysis of risking using supplies versus future need for those supplies. This experience cannot be replicated on repeat playthroughs, and contributes greatly to the horror experience. Here is some spoiler free advice for newer players who might want to take on the challenge of playing this game for the first time on hard which will ensure a more smooth playing experience:
Having 20 save slots means that you can create backups to go back to in case you trap yourself in a corner. Going back 3 or even 4 saves is not as dreadful as it might seem since a great deal of play time is trial and error solution finding. A part that might have took you an hour to get through might take 20 minutes or less when you know what items you need and can save time on backtracking. Never put all your saves in one file or you might get irreversibly stuck.
Zombies are the low level mooks of this game, and despite what I said earlier, there are usually more handgun bullets than you need. The problem isn't just having ammo, its having the right ammo for the right enemies. Its usually not worth wasting a grenade on a zombie, there are bigger and badder things around the corner that will demand that firepower. A way to make handgun bullets more effective is to bring your partner character with you and have both of them equipped with handguns. Let Billy be the supporting AI since he has more health and shoots more agressively.
This is another flaw of this game. The game leads you to believe that gas is important enough to carry around with you, but it can only create molotovs and there is more of it than you need, which is usually placed around empty bottles in the first place. Any gas you don't immediately use you can almost always ditch. Another thing is that the molotovs are very poor weapons. The attack animation is too slow, the throw range is inconsistent and they don't do very much damage. They are most useful when you encounter leech monsters for the first time, who will often go through a transformation sequence. This gives you a window of time to throw 3-4 molotovs on them guaranteeing their death, but even then they might still get a good hit on you. It might be better to just avoid the leech monsters entirely if you can.
This always gets people. There is a weird gap after the first section of the game where you use the hookshot once, and then never need it again for the next map. You will need it multiple times in the next map following that one though and people will often leave it all the way back at the beginning of the previous map. Once that section is done though you can ditch it for good, unlike other key items it does not disappear after it no longer serves any use.
Good luck, have fun, and enjoy true survival horror!

Horror, quite possibly one of the most fun and difficult genres of gaming.  Originating back in the early 1990's on the Playstation One, the Resident Evil One (RE) in the series instantly became the icon for suspense, horror and mystery.  Like all great mysteries, answers to questions get overlooked leaving the player with a thirst un-quenched.  Resident Evil: Zero is that quintessential thirst quencher.  With it's complete fun integrated explanation of game play balanced with all the elements of the series storytelling.  The mystery uncloaked here is a prime example of a prequel meant to be played after having played thru RE:1 first, thus allowing for a  mystery, mystery then answer experience rather than a mystery, answer and mystery solved experience.
Warning: From here on out there are *SPOILERS* so read at your peril. XP
The mystery unveiled by the use of yet more mystery.  Lets quickly run through a brief overview of events to give us some feel for the game and story.  Starting out on  a train of the dead, that being a loose and relative thing, our heroine Rebecca Chambers after a lovely intro cut scene investigates.  Just like the first Resident Evil the player is left with a little to go on except micro-sandbox exploration.  Through the use of occasional scripted scenes a team member of STARS ( the police force Rebecca is on) dies from bites and loss of blood from super leeches and a new character/partner Billy Coen (the so called criminal) is introduced as well as the partner system.  Rebecca is attacked by a person made of leeches whom Billy heroically kills, saving Rebecca.  They team up exploring more of the train, while doing so Rebecca gets trapped after fixing a damaged circuit board on the roof of the train and Billy goes to find a tool to get her out.  On the search he gets attacked by a scorpion the size of a Buick, a mass of leech eggs hatch and our heroes have to stop a now run away train.  Managing to do so only to crash into an underground tunnel in a hillside, they somehow manage to survive.  After taking a minute to recover they proceed, only to discover they are in a mansion of the dead, note this one is different than the one in RE:1.  After several puzzles, zombies and a few new enemies we begin to paint a picture on how this whole chain of events came to be as well as reveal the Men behind the scenes and the role they played leading up to RE:1.  Prior to RE:1, and subsequently RE:0, a scientist discovered a means to immortality in the Progenitor virus and proceeded to experiment on how to make it viable.  Leeches where the key.  He the scientist is revealed to be alive, surprisingly because the two men mentioned earlier killed him.  Rebecca and Billy learn how all three villains got started, their dark experiments and after discovering the underground facility by way of a zip-line car and the Doctors revived form and world destructive plans.  They take on the doctor  kill him escape the self-destruction of the facility that then leads to Rebecca's Role in RE:1.  So, overall the game feels adequate to be a stand alone and also very satisfying as a prequel.  Note the partner system allows some choice on who plays what role in some sequences, while in other sequences it is character specific allowing for character development thru personal experiences thus shaping the story.  Flashbacks also play a small role enriching the experience to fill in any of the gaps literature found thru out the game failed to reveal or simply was missed while playing, for the player.
New and then kept for future games of the RE series was the partner system.  Though other games in the series had points when two characters would be together for short periods of time, they made both playable but never together.  Important to note also is that a player can switch between characters, single character to allow more complex puzzle solving and save time by switching between characters or have the second character (your choice) follow you, select how aggressive you want them to play burning thru ammo or being defensive and save it along with each respective inventory allows a great deal of freedom and customizablility, all showing the care, detail and standards to which this game was made.  In addition by having a secondary character carry a specific weapon you directly select what kind of weapon and ammo they use.  This intuitive function allows characters to be played with together or separately depending on how easy, challenging  the player wants to make it.   Having properly crafted this partner system the game also manages a decent blend of survival horror with it limited but numerous undead, finite ammo, payoffs of close quarters kills along with puzzles that really require as much as attention to detail as curiosity to truly discover all the secrets often with a worth while payoff.   The detective work to uncover the truth gives a rich lore and is a great driving force if not a the challenge of beating the game in general.   Overall, it's the blending of these elements, their timing and placement that keeps the game fresh and the player coming back for more.
Game play is just as good as the original if not slightly more spot on.  Combat is kept honest to the original, basically a 3 level system of up, middle and down attacks with a radial direction and again 3 levels of distance far, medium and close range.  The payoff of range and levels allows for a tactile application of selecting not just targets but relative parts of target Eg. a head shot at close range aimed squarely  and up at the target for max damage/kill shot or medium range with a grenade launcher for a multi kill and no self damage.   General movement controls give that traditional game play of the first RE through a bit wonky/clunky it serves to first add to the terror and suspense in any combat as well as♥♥♥♥♥♥off the unexperienced furthering the horror experience.
The re-release of this game brought with it updated graphics.  This is always a little bittersweet as it changes the visual feel of the game, though in this case it feels like someone cleaned off the screen allowing a more crisp view.   Hilariously though is that there are 3 levels of graphics in this game, game play graphics in HD, low res graphics of most of the cut scenes and one cut scene which they forgot to update at all making it the most entertaining.  Overall though it feels like a healthy mix of old and updated giving its own unique experience.
The music is identically the same.  Ambient eerie tonal tracks through out the environment help to create the horror without detracting from the immersion with out of place music.  The contrast of the safe rooms' tune emulates a breath of fresh air or a sigh of relief and acts as a synergistic amplifier between rest and tension outside the safe room.
Bonus or extra content considering the premise of the game seems a little out of place, primarily the costumes, which were earned/unlock in previous version of the game.  Rebecca's cheerleader costume in particular is one such case,  the is fully functional and moves relative to her movements, however.  The major drawbacks to every costume is it's absence in movie cut scene's losing some of its appeal.  The new Wesker mode makes Rebecca totally Smoken' hot and pay homage to RE 5's Jill mind control.  In addition Billy is now Wesker and comes with 2 unique abilities Death Vision a chargeable AOE with head shot ability and Super Speed. Yup no more walking or casual jogging, you can dash across rooms with ease, amazingly helpful for speed runs. There is more but I'm out of space
Simply, its a solid game made in an era when games had less graphics and were pushed to be engaging and with lasting depth that will always be memorable.

First off, this game is not for everyone this point cannot be  more emphasized. This game is very difficult and should not be played by those who don't have the patience to replay a stage over and over and over again. The difficulty might be an unattractive part of the game to some but for me and others who love this game it is one of the best parts of this game. This game is about survival, beating the odds, buckling down, making it by the skin of your teeth and how difficult it is to do so. The difficulty beautifully ties itself with the harsh realities of survival as each stage presents itself as an extreme situation where sacrifices must be made and even then in most cases you will lose. But you keep fighting, because thats what it takes, because thats what this game is about, because if it were easy, it wouldn't be worth doing and for those who fight and persevere, they will see the true significance of the story and its themes. And those who quit at the face of failure and difficulty won't, because they don't deserve to, they didn't do what this game demands: to have the will to fight and survive no matter the cost. A powerful game that shows that success is a road paved by failure and the refusal to give up.

The ability to drop items on the floor further turns in into a chore.
Most of the time you will controll one of the characters while the other one will be following you.You can toggle them following you and even shooting on and off in the menu.Problem here is that
or even help shove off monsters that grab you.At rare times when they decide to finally use their weapons they do it in the most inefficient way possible. I honestly didnt think parts of the story when your characters have to separate would become my favorite.
Boss fights in RE franchise are usually very thrilling and although quite simple for a player to figure out require at least some basic strategy to beat.Here they are only bullet sponges and not very good ones.You should check out the centipede one,that was hillarious!

I found the game very enjoyable, yet feel that it could have been beyond awesome.
Music is nice and fits the game, though it's not very diverse and might get boring after you listen to it for quite some time.
Visual part is beautiful. The art has a certain feel to it and its consistent.
The gameplay appeal, in my opinion, consists of two parts: the story and the mechanics.
Playing for the story is exploring all the different endings, branches of events and gaining ingame historical (or general-knowldege) remarks and notes. It's really fun and one can try to imagine the world as a whole. It's also inspiring.
Playing for the mechanics means for me trying to win (get coronated) with different "setups", building different characters. Winning as a magic-wielding, strong-willed princess or as a courteous and intriguing one is different and interesting for me.
But, the gameplay is about knowing what stats you need to survive (or get some other outcome you desire) some event and getting them. While there are multiple ways to get past something, they are usually still quite limited to get an RPG feeling to it. Sure, I do prefer some ways of dealing with stuff to other and can choose between them, but it's not like I can build a character that solves problems mostly through magic or abuses her political connections or whatnot.
While there are a lot of different skills to train, there is usually little sense in getting some of this and some of that. A princess that knows nothing about politics and history but is a trained warrior can do better than a princess that knows something about the other countries, has mild divination abilities and is an all-rounder. And even then, one could assume that beeing a great fighter pretty much allows you to fight off assassins, kill rebellious nobles in duels, have a great influence on your soldiers or make your way through to the coronation by trying to kill everything that poses a visible threat. No, you might actually fail some seemingly unrelated check about flowers because of some crazy circumstances you find the princess in and lose a fight. And you won't be offered a chance to kill that suspicious noble before he brings trouble.

So, while the game is immersing for me, I'd really like it to have more open-world type mechanics. It also kind of breaks some part of the RPG feeling when you can't use the abilities of your character to the extent of what you think you should. And not beeing able to predict some events before they happen doesn't help.

All in all, the game looks nice, feels nice, is inspiring for me and presents interesting challenges, but they are not the challenges I expected (worst-case scenario - you can't solve them until you stumble into them and you need to replay for that sometimes) and the gameplay doesn't allow the kind of variations that I like in RPGs. I expected it to be more like Princess Maker series, but it's a bit different. Still, I recommend it, since it is quite different from many games and I found it really enjoyable.

Long Live the Queen is a surprisingly addictive and challenging visual novel. You play as fourteen-year-old princess Elodine, whose mother, the queen of Nova, has just met an untimely end. As a result, Elodine will be crowned queen in one year. That is, if she can survive that long.
Survival is your top priority in this game and is much more difficult than it first appears. You will die. There are a total of eleven possible ways to die and plenty of opportunities to meet your demise. You could face anything from a civil war to assassinations to foreign invasions. My first death involved chocolate.
The gameplay is deceptively straightforward and simple to pick up. Each week you must decide which classes Elodine will take to increase the skills you want her to have. What skills she does or doesn’t have will determine her options during events and often the outcome of your choices. On top of this, her emotional state will affect how receptive she is to learning different skills, and bonuses or penalties are awarded accordingly. Learning skills she has a bonus for will help her learn those skills much faster, but penalties can actually make studying certain skills pointless until you change her mood. There are eight moods you must balance, each negating another mood, along with a hidden cruelty stat that can help or hurt you in the right circumstances.
Reaching the coronation is satisfying itself, but how you survived the year will lead to different endings. By the time my Elodine managed to become queen she was a cruel, power-hungry monarch. The ruthlessness that allowed her to survive had many consequences, not just on her but the people around her as well.
If you’re interested, there is a demo available at the Hanako Games website for Windows, Mac, and Linux which is long enough to give you a good idea of how the game plays. Save files from the demo will transfer to the full version, so you won’t lose your progress either.

Overall, this game is recommended for those who really love original RE series and not afraid to be challenged by legacy gameplay mechanics.

The leader of the clan said that we would all go to Brighmoor to scavenge. I got into a sedan with my friend and the leader and the other memebers followed in 4 more cars, kind like a convoy. About half way to Brightmoor we started to get shot at. The leader told us to get into some cover and he was then shot dead. When it was suggested to me in the Summer Sale as a similar game to Assassin's Creed and Batman: Arkham City, I have to say I was skeptical.
Now, 20+ hours into the game, I'm glad I got this game. I do not read The Hobbit or The Lord of the Rings, so I can only comment on the game and not the lore.
Graphics are great, even on low.
Combat system is similar enough to Batman: Arkham games, easy to learn and use while having its interesting twists with different combos using all three weapons. Best thing about this game is that it allows you the option of full frontal assault with the sword, sniping enemies from afar with the bow, or sneaking around stabbing enemies with the dagger - and there's no karma meter to hold you back from killing (a la Dishonored)!
Weapon customization system is good for flexible strategies versus different enemies, while simple enough to tailor to your likings. The legend forging missions are interesting, but I'd like to know more what those legends actually do - besides giving some carvings on your weapons and money.
The Uruk leader system is an interesting mechanic, and once you get Brand it's possible to manipulate the system to your benefits. The randomized weaknesses add an interesting gimmick to the captains and warchiefs and keep you on your toes. It can get repetitive hunting down a leader's domain or invades his event area to mess him up though.
I can certainly see why this game got Game Of The Year. It deserves the title.
To recap: Just get it. It's cheap, packs tons of content and has a lot of things to keep you interested.

I bought into this game hoping for a semblance of brillance that is Mirror's Edge on iOS. Despite being released years ago, that game conveyed the thrill and joy of parkouring with fluid animations, tight controls, and great level design.
Playing this game's earlier levels made me feel right at home, if not because the apparent 'inspirations' felt more familiar than they (legally) should.
However, the longer I played, the more I realised that the apparent resemblances were only superficial.
TL;DR - I liked what I see, but there's much to be improved upon.
I won't criticize the graphics fidelity of an indie title. They did what they could with the resources they had, and the results are good enough.
The animation quality however, is lacking. The half-second lag and imprecise character animations makes every action, from running to climbing, feel more robotic than organic. I also suspect that the animations are animated at 30fps instead of 60, since they look less silky smooth compared to the rain and camera panning.
The controls for basic actions - running, jumping, sliding and climbing are tight, which makes the game feel responsive. But others - combat, pole swinging and dive kicking barricades are less so. The contrast between the game's controls feels unpolished and a little disappointing, if not due to the better half casting a long shadow over the poorer half.
The level designs share the same criticisms as the controls. Overal level designs are great. especially the early ones.
Interesting objects litter the environment to offer visual clarity and variety. Collectibles sprawl across the multipath levels offering each level different ways to race through it. It's by the books old Sonic, new Mirror's Edge, good parkour level design.
However, the game tends to trips its protagonist metaphorically and literally in terms of enemy placements. Some enemies are positioned in problematic places, on edges or landing areas where the player can't act to defend or defeat them. Enemies hidden behind crates and electric boxes are particularly annoying because they're hard to identify from harmless level props when moving at speed.
Overall, I liked the game, and would recommend it to those with uncritical tastes longing for a serviceable side scrolling parkour game. This title screams 'indie' in the best and worst of ways - offering an unique experience (or re-experience) forlorn by mainstream gaming, with hints of lack of polish that distracts, but never disrupts the core gameplay.

First and foremost, SAVE OFTEN. I recommend creating multiple saves at different points of the game while you're successful because you
die. Long Live The Queen is a visual novel of sorts with an interesting concept. You're Elodie, a princess learning to be queen. You gotta start from scratch and take two classes a week to improve skills. Sounds good but the "strategy" required in this game is a little bit shallow.
Mood, no matter how good or bad, influences how effective Elodie will be at learning a skill. I thought that, because there was a Mood meter, you wanted to get her to the top of each emotion (ex: Cheerful vs Depressed) so that she could function at full capacity. However, no matter how negative or positive the mood is, one will benefit Elodie in learning certain skills that the other mood won't allow improvement for. Everything you pick has a ripple effect.
Doesn't sound so bad, yeah? What makes this a ridiculous mechanic is that there's no way of predicting what mood will affect skills you might need for upcoming events unless you look up a guide. Every action has consequences; you have to try to control
aspect and memorize events that are going to happen as they occur if you want Elodie to live. There aren't any tells and the events are always the same every gameplay so that helps in anticipating what will happen when you die. This game is good, don't get me wrong. It's just not as good as it could be, or not as good as it was during its developpement.
I started playing over 2 years ago and had to stop because the updates made it boring.
When I bought the game, it was near the end of the Koala version, which was before the Giraffe update (I know update names are weird). I started the game for the first time and I still remember how amazed I was at everything. The planet had many DIFFERENTS creatures, all with different attacks and different behavior. Some were passive, other hostiles and some were even friendly. If you were lucky, you could even find a mini-boss on every planet, which was a much stronger version of one of the monsters on the planet. Killing it usually yielded a very rare weapon, which you could keep for some time because of how good it was.
I also remember ranged weapons (exept the bow) not being obtainable before a long time, which made them much more valuable, both to the player and to the game itself. If you let someone think he has everything he needs and then later give even more, he will learn to appreciate both. However, if you throw everything at once at someone, he can't learn how to use or appreciate one thing before he have to get rid of it for an other.
But now, sadly, the game isn't what it used to be. For some aspects, it's better, but for a lot of core-gameplay ones, it's worst. Let me explain:
-> Monsters: Now they are all hostile (at the exception of 1 or 2 very rarely per planet). You get a couple that are re-used EVERYWHERE and some others that have a complete design that is used on every planet of the same type. Other than that, you might get a random one if you're lucky, otherwise it will be limited to something like 2-3 ground monsters, 2-3 flying monsters, 3-4 underground ones and a couple of fishes depending on the planet type. But other than birds, you will always see the exact same monster designs. They all use the same limited selection of attacks and none of them will see you as a friendly person, they all attack on sight.
-> World generation: Planets used to be all different. Sometimes you would find nothing at all. Other times you would find a rare temple or a couple of tiny underground structures. Now every planet is overflowing with life, dungeons, temples, mines and underground "treasures". That is unless you specifically pick a planet that doesn't have any life on it, which are made for building, which is silly. Finding an Avian ship used to be THE rare thing to do. Now you can find one pretty often if you pick the right type of planets. I think the developpers tried to make the world more filled with content but by doing so, they also killed the fun of exploration. In a couple hours you can easily see all dungeons and all villages.
-> Combat: I'm not a big fan of side-scrolling combat games but Starbound's is kind of good. That is one of the things that improved greatly with updates. There is a large selection of weapons, including the ones you can craft and the ones you will find. However the ones you find are completely randomly generated, which makes them pretty unique and the rng is sometimes a pain. That is why crafting your own weapons is often the way to go because their stats are pre-determined but the special attacks of crafted weapons are less impressive, so it's a trade-off. Then comes the ranged weapons. It really depends on your style  of gameplay but all in all, ranged weapons can be very good if you use them well. Most of them have a special attack and they all use "energy" as well as reload times and all that kind of stuff but NO AMMO. So yes combat is pretty good.
-> Base building/survival aspect: Well, this is a weird one. The game encourages you to settle on a planet and build a massive base and all that. However, the way your ship upgrades makes it so you don't actually need a base. Your ship can contain all the storage you need and it can take you anywhere you want. I personally never built a base because it didn't make sense to me.
-> Colonies (Spoiler(maybe?)): You have the option of building houses on planets and putting some colony items in them and colonist will come to the planet, live in your village/colony and give you quests and all that. You're supposed to build on lifeless planets from scratch and build your way up slowly, making money from the colonists and the quests they give. HOWEVER THERE'S A FLAW. You can simply buy a bunch of those things that turns an empty house into a colony house and slap them on existing village's houses. So you can basically turn an already existing NPC village in a colony and look like a big jerk. That part of the game is kinda funny but I do consider it as a flaw because it allows the player to somewhat break the game by forcing npcs into other npc's houses.
-> Story: Let's just say the build-up through all updates to finally complete with the official game launch was pretty clever. All the weird diagrams that had no sense or no meaning finally got revealed at launch and I was very impressed by the way they kept the secret throughout the updates. The story itself feels a bit too linear for a sandbox game however. It's like smashing openworld sanbox games with level progression games. It's not really a bad thing but it could be seen as the open world is your way to build up your equipment and the "missions" are the levels that progress the story, which you need to always upgrade your equipment to complete them.
-> Mod support: Workshop integration is very good and many mods are advailable to make the game better. However, some of those mods have access to too much stuff sometimes and it can break your game if you don't use the right mods. For example, one day I opened the game and my ship's interior had completely reseted. All storage gone, all crafting stations gone, everything but the ship upgrades were gone. So yes, there are good mods but just be cautious with them.
As I said, it's a pretty good game, buy it if you want, but I'll just say one thing: Chucklefish HAD something on Koala version. They HAD the core of it, the base to build up on, the variety to expand on. But they missed their opportunity. They went a different way, they wanted players to see everything too quickly and it killed it. They wanted to have more control over how creature looked and it killed the variety.
Sometimes you just have to let the game be discovered and let the players see the little details by themselves.

So first of all - Is Gods Will Be Watching a good game?
Yes.
Does it have good gameplay mechanics?
Yes
Is it fun?
Brutally so.
Does it have a good story?
Not a great narrative, but I saw myself getting into it.
Good character development?
If you spend time reading and paying attention to the game, I'd say yes. For instance, I got rather attached to Jack in a bros-to-the-end kind of fashion.
Moral Choices?
Only if you care about what's going on in the story and the game, or if you care about the characters.
For instance, in the classic level, you're faced with surviving in a hostile environment, but hunger is at an all time high. Do you carry on trying to survive, clinging onto any form of hope, or do you succumb to cannibalism, or even eat your own dog?
In another example (since people seemed to disagree), a soldier has a disability of having one leg and is slowing down the group significantly - Do the best for the group and put him down? Or fight on?
When I saw this game originally, I was absolutely amazed and didn't hesitate to buy it. Needless to say, I wasn't disappointed. It's an absolute beautiful, stressing, harsh and great experience, all at once. You play as Sgt Burden a hardened war hero known as a legend amongst his own, and you are faced with many survival situations - From taking a lead role in a hostage situation, to being tortured, or having to survive the harsh wilderness, moral choice over well being of yourself takes a lead role in this charming, pixelated art style game. Will you shoot the hostage in the leg to scare the others? will you fire at the guards to make them back up? Will you force on the suffering and possibly death of your friend so that you may live?
Gods Will Be Watching presents itself in a very good way, in a way that can be understood quickly, as long as you pay attention, I understood the gameplay mechanics very easily and found myself very quickly addicted to it. I was kind of shocked to see the amount of negative reviews this game got, so I knew I had to post this review to spread the truth of this.

State of Decay has some rough edges. There are some unpolished elements, some AI and glitch and design issues that could use some work. But with that disclaimer out of the way, it is essentially a hugely ambitious game that actuall pulls off so much of its goals that it makes up for its own flaws.
Sewing together so many gameplay elements isn't easy - there's combat, character development, base building, resource collection, resource management, territory control, missions, more missions, side missions, auto-generated missions, plot missions, and all sorts of things you can do that will eventually become a mission if you just happen to keep busy long enough that they become important.
So what, some of these many elements kind of get lost in the shuffle. I realized that if I just did my own thing, I never had to worry about resources. In fact, the biggest complaint over the radio was that I was always out of stockpile space. So, I ignored resources. And that's kind of the biggest problem with the game as well as its greatest success - it packs so much gameplay in, you simply don't have the time or the consciousness to DO everything. So I finished it in 24 hours, and it felt way to soon... after struggling for that many hours to reach the end, you relized that thtere as still so much left to do. So many things left to build, so many homes to try out, so many infestations left to clear... and I was left, in the end, wanting more.
Is it a perfect game? No. But its flaws are compensated, the acting is solid, the gameplay is balanced, and it all works together to keep you having fun. I'll be looking at the DLC very soon, because I WANT MORE State of Decay.

I would definitely recommend this game, and having bought it during the summer sale am extremely satisfied with the price that I paid for it. I've played a lot of zombie games and were extremely disappointed with them (like Dead Island, not a good game) since I'm used to older ones like the Resident Evil series where you spend more time sneaking and conserving ammo than blasting and smashing stuff non-stop.
Although it isn't for everyone, I really enjoy the grind aspect of the game where you have to constantly go out and rummage for resources to build up your home base. I could see how some people would get bored of this but for me it was just a part of the game that made me feel like I always had something to do. Although it isn't perfect, I think the combat system with melee weapons and guns is decent as well--you can pick many specializations and have to chose between melee or firearms, both which can be rewarding and you have the option to build your characters up different ways. Also, I did enjoy the fact that there isn't truly a main character in the game and you have to utilize different survivors that you pick up along the way--all which have a different set of skills to contribute to fighting or optimizing your base. While combat can be pretty easy and you'll often own tons of zombies, there's always a chance. Sometimes when I get careless I'll fire a gun without a suppressor, end up attracting a large amount of zombies with one special one in the mix and lose a character that I'm pretty fond of.  Cars are pretty fun too, always gotta love creaming zombies on the road! All these things make the game fairly immersive.
Now, I'll get to the bad parts of the game, which for me didn't really ruin the experience for me but they could be a deal breaker for some. Zombies can be pretty glitchy--they'll often get stuck on different things like rocks etc and can also sometimes glitch through walls. Driving can be kind of glitchy as youll sometimes run into obstacles on the ground like small rocks or stuff by the curb which will make your car flip over and eventually explode if you don't empty the contents of the truck. Sometimes the NPCs also act stupidly and wont help you out during fights. The story is also pretty weak, although in the game's defense the story is only a small part of this game.
There's a handful of other glitches that can ruin your fun but all in all, I would again highly recommend this game and the xpac Breakdown after you've completed the campaign.

Listen, man, it is the slightest bit of a grinder after a while but it definitely incentivises you to keep going and gives you room to get creative. This was an era before real micro transactions so you can work towards your desired stats and attributes nicely.
Map variation is moderate but the open world feel is pretty good for its time. It's actually fun to explore because there is definitely stuff to do along the way and different ways to do it.
The story is nice and engaging when it progresses, with a mystery-style uncovering of an unknown past type deal, but one you would like to find out. This is the underlying story that has a nice player world progression thinly draped over it for relatable feel to the ongoing storyline you create.
Combat is awesome. Yes, it's not a 1000 move list game but, you can change the way you fight by getting different skill points that actually make a difference the way you play. It is a mix of long range and melee combat and some interactive stuff as well, like the style that those tell-tale games use. Only in specific scenarios though and not often.
All in all, I don't play for long goes at a time but it's always nice to hop back on when I have the time. I recommend.

As an avid Resident Evil fan I'm honestly disappointed by this game, having played every RE title except Outbreak and handheld crap I needed this in my catalog, unfortunately it wasn't a fulfilling experience. Since this is my first time playing it, I can't say much about how good the remastering is, but the game looks good, so that's not a problem.
Firstly, the game isn't too bad, there are a lot of returning elements and joys from the old-school Resident Evils with a few new ideas.
What I liked: removing item boxes from the game was a weird move, but it adds to the survival aspect, you can't carry everything around, you must leave items behind and come back for them etc. The only problem with this is that you can only move your items one by one which is very annoying. In that aspect the item box wins. Outside of that the game sometimes nails how a survival horror game should play out and you can have a great time playing it.
And they actually made the alternate controlls feel better than the RE 1 Remaster, I liked that a lot.
Now the bad: The partner system was interesting at the first glance, I'm not against new mechanics, I think RE has proved with RE 4 that a franchise can bring in a lot of stuff in a new game and make something great while staying true to the franchise. But the partner system is one hell of a mess. Let's put it this way: your partner is close to useless. Sometimes you can shoot zombies together and it's working out, but they are too dumb and robotic. It's worse than RE 5 even, but in RE 5 you can at least play in co-op to eliminate the♥♥♥♥♥♥AI. The biggest problem: It just can't dodge anything. I mean I don't expect it to do anything when it's cornered, but when it's open space and all it has to do is follow me back in the room to create some space and it still gets grabbed by a zombie it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. When you bring it to a small room with multiple enemies (which isn't too rare) it's useless. I found myself just using it as a pack-horse and not bringing it to any fights.
So, the partner system is a great failure, the other thing is: enemies. Now don't get me wrong, the enemies are well-designed (except the monkeys, ♥♥♥♥ those) and the game has good variety. The problem is there are too many of them. Almost every room has at least 2-3 enemies, and with your partner being a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥multiple enemy encounters are a nightmare. I get that they wanted more enemies since you're not alone anymore, but when your other half is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and can't do anything by itself it feels like getting a tumour.
Also, the main characters have no chemistry between them, and one of them is as complex as making a toast, they were just threw together for the sake of it. Same as RE 5, shame.
These things together ruin the whole game, they just couldn't make the partner system work, while the game tries to compliment it. I'm honestly surprised this game sits at the same score as RE 1 on Steam, and that the negative reviews are just pummeled to the ground votewise. Overall, you may enjoy this, as it's not the most horrible game, but I can't recommend this.

In Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath, you will fill the boots of a strange, otherwise mysterious bounty hunter who tracks down villains and outlaws for "moolah" -- Wild West Wanted-Dead-or-Alive style. You'll explore a grand world of frontiers ranging from old Western towns, uninhabited wildernesses and some more modern type industrialized compounds. The game allows you to play in either third person or first person mode where third person view will be used mostly for exploration and first person mode for when it gets down to action and combat. The main character’s name is Stranger and he needs to raise money for a medical procedure he must undergo in order to survive. Stranger will go from town to town through forests and wildernesses, capturing outlaws and fighting his way through mob syndicates...all in the duty of the bounty assignments he receives from the local Bounty Store.
The only weapon Stranger carries is a modified crossbow strapped to his forearm. This is a mean weapon and its ammunition is actual living creatures and critters which he harvests from the environment. There are plenty of it crawling and bouncing around. This unique ammunition is also upgraded as the game progresses through its various levels which in turn is a good thing, a very good thing, because crime bosses become extremely difficult to take down later in the game, especially on hard difficulty settings. Other in-game role-playing elements include amour storage upgrades and knuckle dusters.
Doing bounty hunts might start to feel repetitive later on in the game and the pattern rather predictable, but the story takes a spin towards something different and totally unexpected. The story. That is essentially what distinguishes the guys at Oddworld Inhabitants from the rest. Their story telling technique.
The upgraded port of Stranger's Wrath, namely the HD version was first announced in 2010 for release on PC and PlayStation 3, developed by Just Add Water and is one of the more distinctive games released from the "old" generation. It's entertaining and fun, story rich, beautiful in HD and demonstrates the passion and love you get from the Oddworld Universe.
I recommend this game!

I'm going to save the bugs for last, and get down to the mechanics of the game first. This is the meat of the game, bugs may or may not be fixed in "hot-fixes".
This is a survival game, clearly inspired by Tom Hanks "Castaway". Although new purchasers wouldn't know this because they are still advertising content that no longer exists in the game, such as that plane crash intro - etc.
You start off on a raft with no paddles, they decided they weren't "needed" any further. You somehow dog paddle to shore (whilst standing), and begin "surviving". This consists of gathering sticks, rocks, lashing (gathered from their newly modeled Yucca Plants, from one of their "big content patches"), and coconuts.
You build a fire, because that's what you always do in survival games. Then focus on a shelter for the night, because we've been taught that night time is very dangerous. You head out and gather all the neat little materials, and get to building that shelter. This makes you realize that they are only cosmetic differences because there is no competing weather elements to contend with. So now you've seen 75% of the game-play & content.
Once daylight comes, and you realize there was no threat what-so-ever over the course of the night, you decide to build a raft so you can go explore other islands. You could however doggy paddle in the given raft, but that would be silly because the sound effect for the paddling would drive you insane before you left your home island's shore.
Upon watching the new island pop-in piece by piece like a stop-motion animation, you'll either be lucky and pass by a shipwreck or be unfortunate enough to contend with the pop-in later (assuming you care about finding the shipwreck). After scouting the new island for all of 1 minute you'll come to the realization that whether or not procedural generation is at play, all the islands contain the same resources, and thus it was pointless to waste your time going to this island, and a waste of your time building the raft you used to get there.
This is where the game fails; That moment you realize that there is nothing left to do. It's a defeating feeling because depending on your experience level, it may have taken you 2.1hrs to discover this, leaving you without a refund option. You now realize that there is no content in the game passed the 1hr mark. There is no survival mechanics minus infection, broken arm, food, hunger, oxygen. These are all easily negated/remedied/avoided. There is nothing that is a constant threat to your survival. All that time in the sun doesn't matter, the nights don't get cold, the wind don't bring in storms that threaten your very existence. Your biggest threat is falling from a tree due to the janky mechanics of tree climbing, rather than being eaten by a shark, of which I haven't even seen in 7hrs of game-play and 8 islands explored. Yes, depending on which version you have played, morphine probably fixed broken arms. But I can assure you that it might not in the next patch due to it breaking in the past.
The game is pretty to look at, minus the graphical glitches, and pop-in. It's a satisfying feeling to build a structure the first time, under the notion that you must do so before nightfall. But it's disheartening to see that structure floating in the sky-box the next time you login. It's disappointing to know that rebuilding one is inconsequential due to there being nothing in game to harm you or force the need of a structure.
It appears that the dev's are struck in a rut, and I wonder now if they haven't reached their coding limitations. The updates have consisted of cosmetic changes to systems that were in the game from day one. It's only when challenges are presented that we see their knowledge or lack there of come to light. We have seen this with the original crafting system, and we have seen their solution (however temporary, or however many promises are STILL being made to improve this). We have seen this when they removed the original raft, and motor, only to bring them back 8 months later. We have seen this when everyone was under the impression that they re-coded the engine, only to find that they simply upgraded to Unity 5 which left the game stagnant for nearly 2 months.
At best this is going to be a slow burn, at worse it'll be abandoned once they fail to find a way to "Jerry-rig" together a somewhat working game. That's a sad thought because the game came out with such strong potential. Those bugs in the early alpha releases were of no consequence because we simply didn't know what type of dev's we were dealing with. It's only now that we see their limitations, it's only a year later that we see the only mechanical forward progress has been by way of adding rafts back to the game. Every other change has been a removal, minus cosmetic building materials.
There simply isn't any confidence left that leads me to believe that this will ever be a true "survival game", but I'll happily update my review if that ever happens. Until that day comes though, I won't be updating this review again. They have added/removed so much content in such a short amount of time, it wouldn't even be fair to the dev's to keep making reviews. I only made this one because Sam pretty much challenged me to do so in the comments. But my question to Sam is, when are you going to update your Steam Store Page to reflect the changes in game? You were very direct with me about my "misinformation" and "dated" review, yet you continue to profit from advertising materials reflecting content that no longer exists in game.

While Pillar's of Eternity is a good game, and I bought it to support the genre, I do NOT recommend it to fellow CRPG fans on a tight budget. As many reviews suggest this game could be seen as a successor to Infinity engine games (ie Baldur's Gate), but only from a mechanical standpoint. Saying this game is the _spiritual_ successor to games like Baldur's Gate is an overstatement, and maybe even offensive..
With that in mind, I will anchor my review to two key Infinity engine games (Baldur's Gate 1 and 2) to show what is missing. There are lots of reviews highlighting what's good in this game, but I hope this comparison gives a better picture of what NOT to expect.
- To start with don't expect an immersive story. It's very difficult to justify and be part of the main quest. Without any spoilers, certain things happen to the PC, but it's absolutely not worth going through life dangering situations. Like, really.. This leaves you doing stuff because the journal says you should, not because you are interested.
- Characters are very shallow and predictable. Banter options are limited, Remember unforgettable party members from BG 1 or 2? Not gonna have them here.
- The main villian isn't interesting and doesn't feel like a real threat. Jon Irenicus (or also Sarevok for that matter) were scary mysterious figures. Both were real threats and hooked the player into the game. Same cannot be said for this game's villian.
- Quests aren't interesting or satisfying. Yes, there are different ways to solve almost every quest, and that is a fresh new take, but the actual content of most side quests is just meh. There has been way more focus on giving the player options, but the developers haven't seem to have thought as much about why you would want to be involved in the first place.
- Walls of text, everywhere. While the writing is impressive (and I thought hard whether I should even mention this bullet), everything is extremely wordy and sometimes reading all that text on a screen becomes so exhausting, it makes one think whether there is something as too much content.
- Worst of all, there are a crapload of features that are just Kickstarter bonuses and all of them come at the expense of immersion. And the only response to "why?" is "because money"..
For these reasons, I do NOT recommend this game,  unless you are a fellow fan of the genre or the game goes on a crazy discount.

Pillars of Eternity is a top-down dark fantasy RPG from Obsidian, and shares common themes with their other games including the realistic implications of fantasy elements, corrupt humans, and vivid dialogue. Harkening back to Baldur's Gate and Fallout, PofE feels like it came out of the 1990s/early 2000s. This isn't my preference as I think Bioware and others pushed RPGs into an objectively better format that leads to a more enriching experience. Still, PofE is the product of an artistic vision and it shows: this is an interesting, well-drawn world presented distinctively. The setting is unique in that this is set after the traditional medieval setting and in the renaissance - gunpowder has been discovered and is the biggest defense against magic. Alongside this, the study of souls is its own science, and gods are physical, real entities. Religious differences come not in denial of faith but in disagreement about their real place in society. Unfortunately, the story itself is less interesting. Witness and victim of events not understood, your character searches for answers, builds a team, establishes a stronghold, and essentially goes sight seeing. Your purpose is somewhat ill defined until very late in the story, and the main villain is not an engaging one. The weak story lets down the intriguing setup around it, but the world and certain characters are interesting enough to carry the experience for a long time. Recommended, but only if you enjoy detailed world building and dark subversions of fantasy over standard combat and a lacklustre story.

Pillars Of Eternity is NOT the spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate.
I have many complaints about Pillars Of Eternity (including its expansion The White March).
1) There should have been much more Voice Acting and Voice Over.
2) Too much reading.
3) Traditional Mage abilities split too much to the new classes (Chanter, Cipher, etc.).
4) and quite a few others...
Over $4 million was raised on Kickstarter for this game, and what we got was a disappointment.
Instead of spending money on building 15 levels to the "Endless Paths", that money should have went to more Voice Acting and Voice Over work.
I prefer to have one mage in my Party to cast Damage (e.g., Fireball, Missiles, etc.), Monster Summoning, Charm, and Drain Spells. In this game, you need three different NPCs (i.e. of different classes) to cast all these types of spells, which does not leave much room in your party for other classes.
All my other complaints about the game would seem minor. However, combined, it prevented me from getting "immersed" into the game and its story (which was so-so, maybe it would have been better with more Voice Over to read the endless amount of texts).
Also, the game is missing elements that made Baldur's Gate and Planescape Torment great games. Those games had towns/cities that felt more lively. Those games had better/richer ambient sounds (which helps with the "immersion" factor). Those games had "cheesy" romanceable NPCs (which adds to the "fantasy" element).
In contrast, Divinity Original Sin ENHANCED EDITION (DOSEE) was an excellent CRPG, which I would recommend getting instead.  Yes, it has a plot hole in the middle of the game, but DOSEE did so many things right (that Pillars Of Eternity did not) that I was easily able to overlook this flaw and continue to enjoy the game.

I find my opinions on this game extremely conflicting, and despite voting it down, there is a ton I absolutely love about this game.
So let's start with that.  Dark Souls is a ridiculously difficult RPG with real time action combat.  The gameplay is actually very fun, the setting is amazing, and the game oozes creativity.  If it sounds fun, it really is-- if you can keep your frustration in check.
This goes without saying, but if you aren't in the loop one of the main draws of this game is its difficult and downright punishing game play.
Overall, this should add up to things that I love.  The RPG elements drew me in.  I adored the difficulty in its own right.  But I can't recommend this game because of literally only one flaw in the game that I found to be downright gamebreaking.
The controls and glitches in relation to the Difficulty is just stupid.  I am all on board for the difficulty, but you can't  punish players for the inability of the devs to do thier jobs right.  For the most part, it handles well.  But there are instances where the controls are just stupid unprecise.  Moreover, and what was probably the straw that broke the camel's back, it needs an exterminator.  The bugs aren't always there, but when the game punishes you for the smallest mistake, there is nothing more mind numbingly frustrating than some bullcrap like that killing you for no reason.
And really, thats what did it for me.  I made it far and was having a massive ammount of fun throughout, but it is a stressfull game, and if punishment is going to be a cornerstone of the game, that punishment should only stem from the misplay of the player.  When a game punishes you for the crap it can't get together, that isn't fun.
I know I'm in the minority, so a lot of people can put up with the bullcrap.  But I can't. I can only take so much.

So, I thought this would be a cute game about delivering pizzas with parkour. Yes, it was that, for sure. The movement-based gameplay are cool, and the first time Gemma "got into the flow" (you'll see what I mean ingame) it felt really cool and I loved the way the music changed to push the gameplay along. In terms of mechanics and aesthetic, it feels like a three-way cross between Sonic, Mirror's Edge, and Blade Runner.
However, it also has a very powerful story. There are some really heartfelt scenes that, at least once, did bring tears to my eyes. It's not often do you see a game about how depression and bullying really suck, without ever sounding preachy or arrogant. (I found the scene with the transgender woman particularly touching.) The themes of self-esteem are entwined with a sort of health system, where Gemma literally gives up and you have to bring her back to her feel. You can also take care of her outside of missions by letting her make new clothes or buy video games, bubble bath, and other self-care items.
Additionally, the game has accessibility mechanics right down to its core, including control over game speed, timer duration, and even the harshness of the enemy ninjas you encounter. It even straight-up says that the difficulty settings are a "no-judgement zone".
It's a short little game, and took me less than three hours to finish one playthrough, but its mechanics are tight, the story is deep, and it's built from the ground up to be accessibile to everyone. Highly recommend you purchase it, even just to show your support for quality games like this.

Gods Will Be Watching can best be summed up by it's game over screen: the depiction of a ragged man, lost both literally and figuratively, as he fights against the harsh winds of a desert planet and he reflects upon past mistakes.
A few reviews criticise the random elements of the game and the game's general difficulty, but both of these factors really do work in the game's favour concerning it's story and gameplay's main themes. Like the main character, if you want to keep people alive and do the best to your ability you have to work hard and struggle against near impossible odds; even if life hands you cruel and random factors. A lot of sci-fi stories talk about near impossible odds and well known captains who have made miracles happen, and Gods Will Be Watching is one of the only stories to actually present these challenges.
The criticisms I hold against the game is that it never explains the main twist of the game, though I like the twist itself, and character deaths seem to matter little and so detract from the ethical dillemas. Aside from that I suggest getting this game if you want a real challenge and know that, if you do, the Gods will be watching as you struggle through their trials.

There's a lot of misconceptions regarding this game. Rather than a point & click adventure, it plays as more a time & resource management simulator crossed with a puzzle game
a running narrative. This means that while there's only really 6 puzzles to solve in the entire game each one will take you upwards of 2-3 hours to solve (on normal difficulty).
The game is rather difficult, but mostly fair. The reason it gets a lot of poor user reviews is that there's no solid 'solution' to each puzzle as each level has various RNG elements. This means you have to judge each playthrough by yourself rather than following along a gamefaq. Seemingly a lot of people can't deal with that, so they added in a mode which eliminates the RNG factor completely (but also diminishes the actual game part).
The presentation & soundtrack are fantastic, though there are several grammatical & spelling issues which I presume is due to it being made by a latino team (as the credits seem to be in Spanish or Portugese). The story while interesting takes a bit of a bizarre, philosophical almost mystical turn near the end. In my opinion, it doesn't answer a lot of questions thrown up earlier in the game & it would have been more fun if the protagonist Sgt. Burden was just a soilder with a talent for surviving the impossible rather than a hinted at deity type figure.
This criticism aside, it's a very unique game, I enjoyed my time with it & providing you're not expecting a genre of game that it isn't trying to be. If you're open minded about trying new game experiences out, this is well worth the money!

At first glance you might think this is some horrible anime garbage aimed at people who unironically use the word "kawaii" in everyday conversation. And... well, yeah, you'd be right. But if you can get over that, it's actually a horrendously addictive game which is half RPG and half time management game. You'll pick skills to focus on that sound like they're the sort of thing a successful princess needs to know, only to have the game throw skill checks at you for something completely unexpected and railroad you into failure. You'll go back and learn from your mistakes, focus on different skills, only to fail a completely different set of skillchecks and get railroaded into a new and exciting failure.
You'll lose a swordfight because you didn't train in athletics, you'll lose a magic fight because you didn't train in decoration, you'll naively eat poisoned chocolate because you didn't train in court manners and trade relationships, and every time you fail you'll feel compelled to start over, not make the same mistakes again, and instead make a completely different set of mistakes. And if you're really lucky or persistent, you might even manage to make it to your coronation without stumbling head first into a death which was obviously avoidable with the benefit of hindsight.

While doing so you have to make a LOT of choices. While nearly all skills you can learn are important and have individual impacts on your future decisions, some are more important than others depending on which "week" you are in. (On a sidenote, the game plays in weeks. You choose two classes, one morning and one evening class, which you'll attend all week long. To influence her learning curve, you must influence her mood with the correct weekend activities.) Each week might hold a certain event that... decides the fate of your queen. So-called "tests" of your skills unlock responses and reactions to such events, the right responses and reactions that is to say. However, important events have more than a single decision open for you... the tests pile up and become more difficult, which is ultimately why I failed to pass week 34.
All in all, it is fair to say that the game has a rather static story line which you can brilliantly influence and that it is a image-supported text-adventure-strategy genre.

LLTQ is a life-simulation/RPG game where you control a fledgling princess in a land rife with danger, and seek to train her skills and keep her alive until her coronation as Queen in 40 weeks. The characters and lore are well-written, and while at first the anime graphics and simple weekly events recap may lull you into a sense of security (no news is good news?), you soon realise, possibly after your first untimely death, that there are several hidden subplots lurking beneath the surface, and you have to account for them in future playthroughs or die horribly, again.
These sorts of games differ from graphic novel games in that there is always a progression of in-game time between turns, and most game decisions, and what options you have, are strongly based upon what kind of skills you have trained up till that point.
Each game turn (which represents a full week) takes the following format:
1. You get to choose her outfit (if any) -- they're unlocked by training skills to a certain point, and boost all skill checks (but not training) in that skill group for the rest of the week.
2. You get to choose two classes for her to take, which improve two of her skills by a certain amount. That amount is modified by any bonuses/penalties to that skill group for the week, which come from her prior knowledge already invested in that skill group, as well as modifiers from her dominant mood.
3. You then get a story phase, where every week the "main plotline" of the game continues, events occur and resolve, and your character does a bunch of skill checks and often picks an option or two in order to influence the outcome of the story. They are interconnected, so many events early on will influence things later. There is no randomness in this at all - if you train the exact same skills and pick the exact same options in two separate games, events will unfold in the exact same manner both times.
4. You then get a weekend phase, where you can pick one of various activities for her to spent her weekend at, to influence her mood. This phase is VERY important because once you figure out how the moods affect the skill bonuses/penalties, you will want to carefully balance her moods, mostly done via these weekend phases, in order to give her the right dominant mood for next week's training. There can be some story events that occur here as well, if you pick specially marked activities that may appear.
And then it repeats again, 39 more times, at the end of which you are crowned Queen (if you survive that long).
Because the game progresses in weekly instead of daily chunks, I found the game to be much shorter than others of its ilk, my first successful ending was disappointing because my initial reaction was "Nooo! That's it?! I want to see what happens to her next! She's just starting to come into her own and be a force to be reckoned with! I love her! Let me continue the story! Wah. :("
A lot of the depth of the game is in its side paths, and the branches you can take to successfully reach the end, rather than the length of the story and the actual success or failure. Even now that I know how the story ends, and I am at least dimly aware of all the subplots and what they lead to, I still want to see if I can take her through them at some point to view the story from those perspectives.
On the other hand, since each iteration of the game is so short, it actually has a bit of a rogue-like aspect to it, where you learn a little bit more each time you die (or win), and although you have to start over, it doesn't take all that long to get back to where you were before.
On a scale of 1-10, I would give it a 7.5:
---
Graphics (0-2): 1.5
It's typical anime graphics and I didn't enjoy that, though I didn't detest it either. However, some of the outfits she gets to wear are decidedly un-queenly and unrealistic. The graphics are static cardboards too, but that is the standard in life sim games and thus acceptable. She gets a different look for each of her 9 possible dominant moods, which was a nice touch.
Music (0-2): 1.5
The music seemed repetitive, but never got annoying. Also standard for life-sim games. A few more tracks would have been nice, though.
Story (0-2): 1.5
The story is awesome, and touching, especially since you can never see the entire story at once. The secret subplots going on in the background are very interesting when you realise their existence and look at them after a couple runs. There are little lore snippets written up for all the skills, for every 10 points you gain in each. You feel very connected to your character, and you feel yourself growing with her. There are lots of little awesome moments that don't influence the plot, but that your character can unlock by passing a skill check at a certain point anyway.
However! It is linear, comes to an abrupt end, and lacks much replayability. You can play your character a different way, to see a different path or outcome, but it still goes through the same series of events and you know how it's going to end each time. Not all life sim games run like that. I would have liked this scripted part of the story to be the first half of the game, with a second half dealing with after you become Queen where you have to deal with politics and events and manage your kingdom.
Gameplay (0-2): 1
It really, reeeeeally needs to be longer. There are games with similar sideways depth and branching options that also go on for much longer. At the least, break the weeks up into smaller chunks, and insert minor random events and evening activities in between. Time feels like it flies by and then is over too soon. Yes that lends itself to a rogue-like feel, but I don't think it's the best fit. There aren't enough opportunities to use many of the skills, and there is no reason to train many of them past a certain (unknown) point, or at all, because there are only one or two checks for that skill through the game, and often ones you can easily bypass anyway.
UI (0-2): 2
It's mouse-based, simple to navigate, and had nothing annoying about it. There is a clean save/load system as well. Mild problems include that the button to progress time was a small button on one screen and there's nothing on the main UI that points you to it before you know where it is. Also, the panels could be a bit more interconnected, I also often found myself wanting to look at my skills screen during the weekend phase, which is impossible.
---
Life sims are one of my favourite types of genres, and while I wouldn't consider this game the best one I've ever played (Academagia takes that cake as of now), it definitely ranks up there. In a sense, these life sim games are a digital evolution of the gamebook genre in the 90s and early 00s, similar to Lone Wolf, Fighting Fantasy, Fabled Lands, Tunnels and Trolls etc.
And between them, LLTQ matches up to Fighting Fantasy the best - something you won't complete on your first try, due to eclectic/unfair skill combinations/choices needed to complete a path, with some rather extravagant skill checks, skills that are only used once or twice anywhere in the story, and all in all a linear plot even though you have several ways to get there, but still a good read overall.

They unfortunately don't really know how to market themselves very well. That other game is Scheheraraze, and is on

For me, the part which captured my attention the most in RE0 is unquestionably the atmosphere. Capcom did a lovely job of bringing back that claustrophobic feeling of the original game (REmake), complete with the moody lighting & tight, purpose built spaces & environments. All the other RE games have failed in some way in this department for me (except perhaps 3 because Nemesis had me screaming like a little boy at times), REmake & Zero are both excellent at making the atmosphere the key focus throughout.
As for the negatives, the only major point for me is a story related issue, which granted, couldn't have been foreseen in '96. By the end of Zero, Rebecca has turned from a rookie to quite the survivor, yet when you see her later in the timeline (playing as Chris) in #1, she's a complete waste of space.
This next 'negative' isn't something I agree with, but it's a valid enough point that you should be at least aware of before starting the game - Item management. This game completely strips away the item boxes of other RE games & replaces it with you having the ability to leave items pretty much anywhere you like (there's a maximum number allowed for each room). If you don't mind a little micromanaging & back-tracking, this won't bother you in the least. If you're the type that likes to burn through sections of a game, or perhaps doesn't have a good track record of organisation lol, then it might become a problematic aspect (even though you can check where the items are by looking the map).

All things considered I enjoyed this every bit as much as the RE1 HD Remake. Of course, like everyone else, I had to adjust to the new item management system, which felt  a bit odd at first. But after an hour or so into the game I realized that it’s actually an improvement over the old design. Let me explain:
1) Let’s face it: The old item crate system was extremely unrealistic. Now you can drop your stuff wherever you please and will find it exactly where you dropped it – for me that’s a clear improvement.
2) Anyway: If you pick up stuff and drop it near typewriters, the game almost plays and feels like RE1 “real survival” mode, where item boxes aren’t linked.
3) The map has a mode that shows you exactly where all your items are. So even if you’re “untidy”, you will never have to roam around aimlessly searching for your grenade launcher!
4) Except the very first area, all areas are linked so you will also never have to leave an item behind for good (even if it may seem that way at first). Just bring the most important items when entering a new area and you won’t ever have to do any extensive backtracking.
Some people feel that six item slots are too few, especially as some items take two slots. I never had a problem with this – let me explain again:
1) You are most often in partner mode, that is you actually got 12 slots.
2) Even if every character carries a handgun and a big two-slot weapon (which you don’t have to do all the time), you will still have 2*3=6 free slots for other items! Now, if you let it sink in that the whole game area is basically a big item box, you’ll find that you really don’t have to constantly haul a lot of stuff around. Exceptions aside, I never actually carried health items with me and the same goes for extra ammo. 15 bullets in your handgun and 7 rounds in your shotgun will easily suffice for most excursions from your preferred typewriter area – finish your foray, then go back to heal, reload (and maybe save).
I'd now like to point out a few things in RE0 which are better than in RE1:
1) Graphics are even more detailed and atmospheric, in places they are absolutely stunning. The visual upgrade from RE1 to RE0  becomes especially apparent if you play both games in parallel.
2) The new partner system is refreshing: At times you run with your partner, which is then AI controlled, like in RE5/6, orders for general behaviour included. At other times you two go separate ways – which makes for a few nice puzzles where you have to “zapp” between them.  At still other times one partner gets “lost” and you have to go it alone until you eventually meet again. I feel this makes for a whole lot of additional variety over the "lone wolf only" system of RE1.
3) There were way too many health items in RE1 HD Remake, even in hard mode - my item crate used to look like a drugstore! I really like that there are much fewer herbs/sprays in RE0, which greatly contributes to the survival horror feel. (However, as a downside, RE0  has too much ammo. The “dancing around” zombies from RE1 to conserve ammo is never needed here, at least not on “normal”. Ink ribbon count is okay, though – I had about ten ink ribbons left on my first run. Edit: Playing on "hard" now, there's just enough ammo to get by - perfect!)
4) The endboss gauntlet in RE0 is much better and strategy-wise more satisfying than the tyrant fight of RE HD remake.
Now I made it sound like RE0 is actually the better game. But of course this is not true: RE1 will always be first choice on every list simply because it got the special "magic" that only the game which started it all can have. RE1 also has the better "mansion" and (all in all) better puzzles (though there are some memorable puzzles in RE0 too). RE1 has also a stronger story and better characters, but still: RE0 rounds out the backstory of RE1 quite nicely, and: you *will* get attached to Rebecca!
Because of the gameplay and the tied-together stories I feel that RE1 and RE0 belong together - I will now make it a habit of playing those two "back to back". Anyway, to make a long story short: For all fans of RE1 HD Remake, RE0 is a must – especially as nothing else out there will help us shorten the long wait for RE2 Remake.
