Wow, this game's on sale now? Welp...
In all honesty though, the game was worth its full price. ...Okay, that might be taking it too far considering the flaws I can see, but hear me out.
Shadow of Mordor was a great gaming experience the first time I played it. It has smooth graphics, great cinematic cutscenes with believable facial animations and voice acting, a simplistic movement system, and an easy-to-remember combat system. While yes, the movement system has its flaws and might not exactly be the most immersive, it lets the player pick where Talion should go and what to do there.
Combat is repetitive, I won't deny that, especially when you consider that it's basically comprised of "hitting a target enough to build up your combo meter to unleash your wraith abilities" and "pressing the correct button when prompted". But I think that flaw is part of the reason why the game was so interesting. Compare and contrast with comparatively input-heavy action games like Dark Souls or Nier: Automata for example; it's pretty clear that Shadow of Mordor might not be selling itself through its action segments. In fact, I find most of my time in stealth, picking out which target to attack first and consider whether I go for ranged, melee, or stealth takedowns. It's almost strategic rather than...action-y...in the way it's carried out.
The...Nemesis system, I believe it's called? Honestly, I can take it or leave it. It definitely expands the option of how you should take on your enemies, and at times it is really important if you want to know the weakness and strength of your targets, but really, all of them are generally weak to "hitting them 'til they're dead". The biggest strength the Nemesis system has is, in my opinion, is it lets you know how to take on an army and turn it into your own. You can actually do a near-Pacifist run on the game just by Branding the Captains and Warchiefs!
TL;DR go buy it and brainwash some orcs.

To start, I avoided looking or listening to people talk about this game for a long time for no reason, I was just blind from stress of my school life at the moment. Well now I regret not looking into this sooner. It actually relates to my age range and deals with really important topics such as mental illness, becoming an adult, and best friends. I suffer from severe depression, severe anxiety, and a general disconnection to a lot of things and the main character does as well. I will always be in a dark place, but certain games and movies pull me back into reality and bring up emotions that I don't always have access to. This is one of those games. And yes this all sounds cliche, but I say this with 100% sincerity, this game has changed my life. It has given me a more positive outlook on my life and my future. And since my completion of this game, whenever I feel down or have a hard time understanding something or someone, I think back to this game and it helps me get through my day. Now I'll actually talk about the game. All of the characters are amazing, in part to the fact that they feel like real people. The soundtrack is astounding and is currently available for purchase on Steam and the composer's Bandcamp. The art and style of the entire game is spectacular. It also has high replay value due to it having multiple routes and hidden stuff. If you are still unsure about the game, you should check out some let's plays on youtube and may I suggest you watch "Commander Holly and Ross" (the two are a part of Game Grumps) playthrough of the game. You should watch a little bit, then play the game yourself, and then watch their entire playthrough.
To conclude, this is a Masterpiece and will probably be the 2017 game of year for me.

From the moment the game launched I started recieving mixed emotions about this purchase.
I had eyed the game up over the past few Steam sales and had given it some opportunity to express itself via the plentiful youtube videos that are available. None of these videos reflect the experience I've had with this and I regret making the purchase as a PC player.
First thing I noticed when booting the game up for the first time is that the introductory videos promoting the games producers are not skipable which started my dismay. I had noticed that the videos were running kinda letterboxy so I figured my first stop is going to be the options menu to set resolution and ensure the graphical fidelity is cranked up to the max.
Here is when I noticed that the sliders for resolution do not go up to my monitors native resolution of 1440p and neither does the game allow any customisation of the options other than choosing your preset value (low, medium, high, ultra etc).
I figured that I'd give the game a shot in its max 1080p settings and have a little play about. Once the load scene had finished I hear some voices and an image starts to fade in but essentially never gets quite fully there. The contrast and saturation of colors in this game are dreadful and you cannot adjust anything barre the gamma in the options menu.
On a professionally color calibrated Asus ProArt monitor you do not expect to have to do any fiddling with these settings in the first instance.
In order to fix the issues I had faced I turned to google and found that by installing SweetFX and adding the line '-fullscreen' to my launcher settings for the game I could adjust the resolution and force differing calibration defaults.
Even with these the game still doesn't properly run at 1440 and neither does it fix the color. Suffice to say If I am at all to try and play this game with any real enjoyment I am going to have to fiddle even further with the settings which should not be the case for a game of its calibre.
I am extremely disappointed with my purchase.
As a PC gamer I expect that these issues crop up from time to time but from the lack of options available within the game and neither the compulsion to make this game work as expressed on numerous gaming sites I shall give up on this particular title. Let this review serve as a warning
Sincerely,

After a few years of waiting on this game I finally caved and bought it this past Christmas. While I can't say I would've ever recommended this in Early Access, I will now in its full release.
It's a great game. This is coming from someone, who by all accounts and purposes is a JRPG and FPS first fan. I tend to skip indie games and be wary of early access or crowdfunded games as it sets a very bad precedent in marketing and business models, and working in the creative industry you quite often see whimsical and far reaching promises that fail to deliver, especially when you have to deal with issues such as cross functionality between different teams, i.e: marketing and engineering, or scope-creep from outsiders.
Starbound is not that. It's a great game. Building off of Terraria's formula, this 8bit sandbox adventure game really does shine with its loads of content.
I've already sunk almost 50 hours into it and I'm just getting to the final mission (with no rush in beating it and minimal exploring, mostly base building)
That being said there are tons of items, procedural quests, biomes, worlds and stuff to explore.
It's a more grounded minecraft with a semi-functional plot and loads of fun to have in co-op modes with friends. I bought No Man's Sky on my PS4 thinking it would be fun after minimal interest or digging into that game, but, mostly on a whim to play with friends college who now live in different states. That game sucked♥♥♥♥♥ and its hilarious yet also ironic that a game a 1/3rd of the original MSRP of NMS put more time, money, effort, dedication and heart into delivering a wonderfully enjoyable game.
It's definitely not for everyone. A lot of people can get bored or find themselves feeling like its a chore/grind to do stuff, but part of the fun of this game is playing with close friends in a closed universe (or open to whomever) and adding a little bit of roleplay on your own. Explore worlds, feel like space pirates etc etc.
There aren't many cons, honestly, and if I look back I struggle to find anything that severely pisses me off, besides the unger aspect.
I can't recommend this game enough. I'm someone who can put 400+ hours into Battlefield 4, I put over 1500+ hours into 1.6/CZ/Source/DoDS/ and the like of those games before they started tracking hours played, and someone who has recently put in hundreds of hours into Bloodborne and hard action RPGs as such. Yet, with this indie game, Chucklefish Games has found a happy player and a new fan of their development team.
What's not to like a bout a sincere team that's focused on bringing a community funded game with real promises? Especially with good backlog and dev note updates, and enthusiasm that shows they see the importance and fun in making this game even better with more updates and content.
I paid $7.99 for this on sale and it's been one of the my best steam purchases in the past few years.

Ninja Pizza Girl is about bullying. Yep. Don't see those often. It's about a girl named Gemma, a teenage girl helping in her fathers pizza shop. Through-out the story, she starts to get bullied. Now I'm not going to spoil the game for you, but the end gets really intense.
Now the controls, discribed to the best of my ability, is similar to a beta indie motion controled phone game. The controls are a little wonky. But you get used to it.

The story. THE STORY! If you met me in real life, you would know that I LOVE story. If the story is bad, you better know the other two qualitys (above) are above satisfaction. This game knocked it out of the park. Between the factor of Gemma fighting bullys to how others are so nice to her,  This is a story you do not want to miss.
In the end, If I did spend 10$ on it, it would be worth it. So I just want to say, try it. If you dont like it, Steam would refund it. So just try it. For Disparity Games sake, Just try it. I know you will like it. I rate this a 8/10.

This game tries. It really does. Unfortunately, it aimed a bit too steep for the devs to deliver (pun intended).
- It would be a great platformer, if not for the slighly sludgy, confusing movement...
- The message would be meaningful, if the gameplay complimented it whatsoever...
- The visuals would be amazing, if they were not obviously using unity-default models...
- The graphics would be nice, if they were altered to be more stylized and had a focused aesthetic...
- The mechanics would be fantastic, if the difficulty curve were rounded a bit more and the platforming was better...
- The soundtrack would be incredible, if it didn't transition really aquardly between two completely different tracks all the time...
- The game would be great, if they focused just a bit more and put a few more months into it.
Pros:
- I like the fact that they tried to put across a positive message
- Good music
- I love the comic-style cutscenes
- I'm a sucker for parkour, and the parkour is ok
- A few good jokes and silly things (like first-person mode)
Cons:
- The enemies
- The absolutely terrible "combat"
- Dealing with the enemies via the combat.
- Lack of focus or pacing
- Obvious rough edges
- All-around sludgy feel and look
- No depth in the base mechanics
- The absolutely awful in-game playermodels and animations
- Bad UI
- No graphical options
Not great, not terrible.
It might be for you, but it's not for me.
To the devs: Please get a bigger team and PLEASE make a sequel. If this game got the polish and focus it deserves, it could become something incredible. At the moment, it's not a great game. But if you took this idea, started again from scratch, put a bunch more resources into it, and released it for double the price, it could be f**king amazing.

If you told me that one day I would fall in love with a game about pizza-delivering ninjas, I would probably call you a liar. But hey, here we are.
This was quite the surprise to me. I went into this game knowing absolutely nothing about it, other than that it was about it's namesake: pizza-delivery ninjas. I got so much more than I bargained for, and the true intentions of the game came to me like a slap in the face. I won't spoil it for you here, since I truly believe that this is a game that needs to be played to be believed,  but just know that, if you go in completely blind, you will probably end up crying. A lot.
PROS
-The very concept is ludicrous, and yet delightfully so. It never feels too out-of-place despite being completely irrational to the logic of the real world.
-The controls take some time to get used to, but once you do, they're very simple and easy to remember.
-This is one of the few modern-day games to feature unlockables such as a 'big head mode', 'motivational mode', and other such callbacks to old PS1&2-era games. It adds an extra bit of silliness without discarding the more serious nature the game takes on in the later half.
-The story is simple and easy for children to understand, and yet it treats the subject matter relatively maturely (considering the title, that's pretty damn impressive). It isn't nearly as juvenile as games like CoD that expect you to just kill everything in sight because "HEY GOTTA BE EDGY AND CONTROVERSIAL, RITE?!!"
CONS
-The dialogue is a bit stiff sometimes, and it far too often feels like people reading from a script rather than actual people speaking. This doesn't hold the more serious scenes back too much, but it can often feel uncanny.
-I hate to rip on the art because it grew on me, but it's...not great. Proporttions are off, characters feel like they're constantly off-model, and the expressions are, much like the dialogue, uncanny.
BEFORE YOU BUY
-This game is meant to be played by anyone of any age group. Don't expect any kind of violence aside from momentarliy knocking people out/being knocked out. If you want to sate your bloodlust go buy CoD or something.
-This game is really short. Like...REALLY, short. Like...90 minutes kind of short.
FINAL SCORE: 7.8/10

Thrust into a variety of life-threatening situations, Sgt. Burden has the tough job of not only getting himself, but those under his care through the situations by any and every means possible.  The game is divided into 7 chapters, each with it's own dillemma, resources, and time restraints that will challenge you, make you take notes, and question to what lengths you will go to complete the chapter.  For instance, in Chapter 1 you are responcible for maintaining hostages while your team retrieves data.  If one breaks and runs away, do you shoot the unarmed civillian increasing the chances the remainder revolts and attacks you, or do you let them run to saftey, and making the others not percieve you as a threat? Either are options, and there are no morals that you are judged by in game.  After each chapter, a Statistics screen shows your results compared to the community's.
The game is ment to be difficult, as the rules of each chapter are not always clearly presented.  There are also no mid-chapter saves, as the intention is for you to learn by trial and error.  I would recommend the "Original Light" difficulty for your first run through, and be aware there is a "Chapter Selection" feature if you would like to change the difficulty and play any reached chapter, allowing you to change difficulty on the fly if needed.
If you want a strangely intriguing plot, learning by trial and error, and bizzare survival scenarios, Gods Will Be Watching is worth the price of admission.
If you want a straight forward plot, clearly explained rules, and consistant experiance, you may want to look elsewhere.  Play the flash demo version to try it out and see if it grabs you:

A little bit puzzle game, a little bit resource management, and hugely infuriating and often utterly, unfairly difficult. But it's still great. My main problem with the game up to this point was that a lot of the events during the scenarios had very harsh stochastic elements -- so basically, no matter how well you had learned to beat the scenarios (through painful trial and error) you could be totally screwed over by the roll of a dice. This kind of thing can be OK occasionally, and add an element of risk to the game, but I reckon it was turned up way too high in the earlier versions. The latest patch includes a mode that removes a lot of the stochastic elements, which I think makes the game a lot better, but without lowering the difficulty TOO much. So, yeah, no worries there any more. Other than that, it's a pretty neat little game that looks fantastic and is set in a cool sci-fi universe. I think people will either love this or hate it -- no middle ground -- because the gameplay is pretty niche. There are a few other issues here and there (why do characters that died keep coming back to life??) But I really enjoyed it, even though the gameplay can be very tough, I still kept coming back.

Oddworld: Strangers Wrath is a third person shooter with elements of platforming and exploration.
The plot is relatively simple at first but gets progressively more complex and facinating the further you go on. You are the stranger, a lone bounty hunter who uses small animals as ammo in order to capture bounties. You are gathering all the money you can get your hands on in order to get an operation of some kind, one which will allow you to "survive". I wont spoil anything else about it, but the plot is well worth the price tag.
The gameplay is simple enough. You have a crossbow which can hold two types of ammo at any given time, each ammo type has a limited capacity of shots before you need to restock, and each one has a different function. Most are lethal, while some are none lethal, which is handy considering you get more money bringing in enemies alive. When you use the crossbow you enter a first person perspective and aim down the sights in order to bag'm and tag'm. However, when your outside of the third person perspective you go into a third person perspective where you can move much faster and do melee attacks, plus jump around and explore with impunity. To progress, you must go from town to town, completing all the bounty jobs in one town before you move onto the next, each one has an entirely unique level dedicated to them and different mechanics you must overcome in order to capture them. its much easier to kill them, but you get half the reward money. You can also buy upgrades in the town if you feel so inclined, or just punch the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the chicken people for a while.
Around the final quarter of the game, it changes drastically, i wont spoil why, but suffice to say there is no longer any real reason to not kill enemies anymore, and it stops being about the individual bounty heads your collecting and the entire focus shifts. Now, while i understand why this occurs in the game, this sudden shift of tone rubbed me the wrong way, as i was enjoying the whole "find and collect bounty" aspect of the game, but i would consider this a personal issue instead of an actual fault.
The game handles rather well, with only a few times i had to fight the camera (which happened maybe once or twice). The difficulty of the game does have a tendency to jump around however, one minute its very easy, the next its frustratingly hard. This can lead to some minor fits of rage, but rest assured these are only a minor aspect of the game and can be plowed through with skill, patience and a disregard for capturing the bounty alive.
Graphically speaking its an old game, but it still holds up quite nicely, it still has a certain charm to it and is very much of the PS2/XBOX era. The music in the game isn't particularly noticable, and when listened to on its own it has a few stand out tracks, but on the whole its not special, it does its job and doesn't distract or subtract anything, only adding to the overall tone.
Strangers Wrath is a classic and a very satisfying hybrid of first and third person action, i would recommend this to a fan of shooters or plateformers. fans of the wild west might enjoy the setting and plot of the game. really though, i would recommend this to anyone.

Resident Evil 0 is a survival horror video game by Capcom on Gamecube in 2002. In 2008, it was also ported to the Wii. I only played the first one when I was 10 years old with my brother. I won’t forget the horror feeling when zombie dog jumped from the tattered window. As a fan of Resident Evil series, I was very happy when I heard this port wise. Here are some reviews from my personal opinions.
First, story. RE0 is the prequel of all RE series. It talked about the story before the RE1. If you are the new fan of this series or old fan who forgot the plot of them, it is a good time to play it. As a famous horror game series over the world, the story of Resident Evil is one of its important selling points.
Second, sounds and pictures. Same with other old Resident Evil games, there are no sounds except cutscenes and Boss Fight. No sounds can render the horror feeling better than any music. About the picture, it has a qualitative improvement because it is a ported wise. Dusky scenes also improve the horror atmosphere.
Third, gameplay. As a third-person survival horror game, its gameplay remains largely the same previous works in the series. However, there are 2 differences. First is the “partner zapping” system. Player can choose one of two characters in any time and they have different abilities. Second, the dropped items can be showed on the game map and canceled the item boxes.
In conclusion, though it is a new port wise by Capcom again, as a fan of this series, I think it is okay and successful. If you are same with me, you should not miss it.

An excellent port of an excellent game. Classic survival horror in many respects.
While I agree that it's strange for the devs to have removed the item crate tradition, items can be easily stored in a location central to the area the player is in. Complaints that this removal ruins the game are greatly exaggerated. That said, it's not an easy game, so first time players should consider
mode at first. Very cool also that players can select either classic controls (woot!), or more modern controls for players unfamiliar with old survival horror.
The on-the-fly character swapping gameplay was a bold move when the game first came out, and offers a number of interesting scenarios throughout. Classic Resident Evil creepiness is intact in RE0, and the series had yet to become overly combat-heavy.
Highly recommended!

First off, I really like this game. I've completed both expansions and it's definitely grown on me over time. My first playthrough was as a death godlike cipher, which I didn't find nearly as fun as as an orlan wizard.
In my first playthrough I made the mistake of not having high enough perception and resolve (which you need for speech checks). As my wizard, I rectified that issue and dialogue became more enjoyable.
What I liked about the game:
It's text heavy with interesting lore and world, some interesting characters, good dialogue, and a decent plot (not groundbreaking, but it's good).
There are a variety of races to choose from, some of which are unique to the world and have different sub-types. You can also choose a culture in addition to race, which affects stats, and to a lesser degree, dialogue options. There are also quite a few classes, one of which is unique to the game. Classes and background (philosopher, slave, etc) also affect dialogue options to a small degree. All of these options make character building quite fun and interesting.
The combat can be fun if you aren't constantly getting swarmed with enemies
There are a lot of spells and abilities, some of which are pretty fun to use
Can level up abilities in Lore, Athletics, Survival, and Mechanics (lockpicking) which affect dialogue options and how you interact with the world
A lot of playtime (around 70 hours without expansions)
There's a fast mode (press D), if you want to traverse areas faster
The environments are beautiful
You acquire real estate early in the game
What I didn't like:
Too many spells, a good chunk which aren't worth using
The load times are quite long, even if you are just entering a house. This makes exploring cities tedious.
Too many enemies, especially at higher difficulties. Too much combat in general - there are diplomatic options, but not as much as, say, Planescape: Torment. This game is more like Icewind Dale with all the combat.
You have to camp or rest at an inn in order to regain health
There's a few tedious as ♥♥♥♥ dungeons. However, at least they're optional
All of the inns have the same music
You can only use so many spells before you have to rest
Endurance/Health relationship might take a bit to figure out
Companions don't take much convincing to follow you to uncertain death. Companions make more sense in Planescape: Torment and Tyranny, where companions most are manipulated or conscripted.
I know it seems like there are a lot of cons, but these are only the things that bothered me (and I'm a bit cynical) - they probably won't bother others, except for the load times. Everything considered, it's a great relaxing game to get immersed in, and it's definitely worth playing, especially if you've got time to kill.

THIS GAME IS GREAT. The RNG is assbutts but I really, REALLY love Gods Will Be Watching. The story and characters are really, really interesting, and the throwback to Ages Of Irving was a big plus. ( I loved that game, too! ) I'm really happy that Devolver Digital helped out Deconstructeam by publishing this, because wow. What a great bunch of guys. Without them, we wouldn't be able to play Gods Will Be Watching. From the amazing soundtrack that's absolutely impossible to get annoyed with to the impasses you find yourself standing at, deciding whether or not to threaten a child to have people give up passwords or injecting someone with a lethal antidote to make sure that it actually works, Gods Will Be Watching is certainly worth the amount of money that it asks for, if not a little more. ( Legend is a bunch of butts, though. Seriously. Screw Legend. I hate that chapter. )

If Christopher Nolan made a Blade Runner-esque thriller for a video game, it would be Gods Will Be Watching. What appears to be a standard point-and-click adventure game, is actually a story-driven (and a damn good one at that) turn-based strategy game with an emphasis on decision consequence, and ingenious level design. It's insanely difficult, but at the same time "fair". Each level cleverly advances the story to points that you'd think would be exclusively designated for cut-scenes. Aside from some crashing issues I had in the game's final level, no bugs were to be found. The overall game is probably at least 5 hours long, but much longer if you're going for the "cleanest" runs for each level. The ending leaves the story on a puzzling, yet reassuring note, that will leave you thinking about, days after your completion. Don't let Gods Will Be Watching slip away from you this year, as it's easily the best game released in 2014 so far this year...

Developed by the family team of Disparity games Ninja Pizza Girl is a free running game about delivering pizza in the shortest time possible while avoiding and combating the antagonistic Megacorp Pizza.
As a teacher one of the things that really struck me about the game was the open and strong anti-bullying message the game conveys and how well this has been realised into the relatively simple yet powerful story of the game.
Gameplay wise the game plays very similar to the excellent 2D Mirrors Edge game that was on iOS a few years back. Running and jumping your way through the levels timing jumps and rolling on landing is fluid and fun and the helpful arrow system always tells you where to go. As the game progresses opposing ninjas from Megacorp try to stop you at every turn and bully you into giving up should they trip or catch you mid move.
One of the most impressive things about Ninja Pizza Girl however is just how well the levels are designed. No matter how well you make a jump or how badly you miss you always eventually seem t end up in the same place…. The only other games I can think of that convey this sense of exploration and speed while making sure you always end up in the right place is the original Sonic the Hedgehog games and that really is saying something. Gameplay is overall tight and smooth with my only criticism being the ability to select between a roll and a slide when landing without the game deciding for you depending on distance fallen. Equally collision detection in some of the environment on later levels is a little wonky but I really am picking at straws.
Collectables as you race around the levels allow you to buy extra things such as costumes, and game play mods that while fun never really add to the game. There is the ability to play in a first person mode but due to the controls not changing just the viewpoint this is in fact and unplayable disaster best left alone.
The story mode is excellent and can be beaten in a bit under 2 hours depending on speed and you willingness to replay levels and the speed run mode will give you longer term playability. There are a few issues here in that the real focus is on the whole game and not individual levels. I think leader boards for different levels would have been nice plus in the speed run mode we really shouldn’t have to sit through cut scenes or faff around in option menus slowing us up. A great idea that should really be the bones of the game that is lessened a little by some less than perfect design choices.
But it really is a testament into how much I loved the game that I want to be able to replay the game without the cut scenes and see leader boards on each individual level. I know that during my time with the game I broke some of these individual world records and I am up for getting a lot more competitive.
Overall Ninja Pizza Girl is a strong indie title that delivers a strong anti-bullying message while giving an excellent game. At £6.99 it is a decent price for a few hours of gameplay and even more if you really want to push for those world records. I hope the game gets patched and tweaked going forward and if so I look forward to loads more parkour pizza.

A free runner/platformer designed for speed runs with a story about bullying, Ninja Pizza Girl is a really charming indie game.
The game has good level design that usually has several paths allowing you to clear a level in really fast time if you know the tricks, and still allow completion if you miss a tricky jump. Gemma is fast and able to jump very high, leading to nice freeflow parkour whenever things go perfectly right.
There are several unlockables which can be bought with the in-game collectibles, allowing for tricks like double jump and disabling the enemies, which can help in further exploring the levels and finding the perfect path.
At its best points, Ninja Pizza Girl is like a mixture between Mirror's Edge and precise platformers like Super Meat Boy. Excellent game.
Disclaimer: I backed this on Kickstarter, and completed the game on PS4. I played a little of the Steam version and it plays identically to the console version.

I've always been a fan of platformers but I've not come across many with as much heart as Ninja Pizza Girl.
The time challenges are great and take the replayability factor way up. The fantasy violence is unique, inspiring you in the split seconds in which they occur about bullying and the proper way to react - pick yourself up and keep going! And the music is some of the most awesome upbeat tempo I've had the pleasure of enjoying in an indie game for a long while.
Ninja Pizza Girl is a humorous game with a message of empowerment. I recommend it wholeheartedly and one day hope to taste a "Pizzariffic" pizza :)

Color me amused. I am not someone who considers themselves good enough to be a speedrunner. I never will and am at peace with that. I may have been as a youngster but not anymore. However, if I were to pick up a game and recommend it to them and players like me it'd be Ninja Pizza Girl. This may well be one of the more underappreciated games released in the past twelve months.
Ninja Pizza Girl is a game that I've had sitting on my wishlist since its release last September. That's really not saying much as I tend to have a wishlist containing every game that has trading cards that I don't own. And so it sat there until I was recently recommended the game by a regular Steamified reader. He suggested that I may want to feature it given the popularity of the genre among readers.  I didn't even know that the game was funded by the Queensland State Government, the state in which I live. I'm particularly critical of games that are from the place I call 'home'. This is because I don't want my personal cheerleading to persuade you to buy a game you'd be unhappy with. However, due to how much fun I actually did have with the game it's impossible not to recommend it to you.
If you look at the surface you're forgiven for thinking that it's just another side scrolling action platforming with parkour and ninja style stunts. Though that in itself sounds pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥ But it's been done before even with the female protagonist. But then you add pretty spectacular storytelling especially considering the genre. This isn't your normal female version of the Mario Bros. You see our girl Gemma is sixteen years old. Of course, it seems like she's dealing with all of the associated drama that a young woman at that age would be dealing with. She's forging her way into the world and standing up for her ideals while keeping her family and her father's pizza business above water.
On top of tackling the delicate issues of self-awareness and self-acceptance, Gemma's most merciless enemy in the ordeal are the other pizza ninjas. These are her peers who work for her father's competitors. They are out to get her in the way a traditional enemy in a video game is. However, they are also there to mock and scoff at every mistake that the player makes. As a result, the game deals with bullying in an articulate and well-developed manner rarely seen in video games. This is to be respected and appreciated. The results could have been anything but the success that it is.
The gameplay essentially is that of a traditional running platformer. Players who are familiar with the genre will be immediately at home with the game. Those who are new may struggle initially but the game is relatively simple to pick up. The key elements of the actual gameplay are its pace and its flow. You're going to be relying on free-flowing pace to get you through each level. Included in this are big jumps, soft landings (you need to time your landings with a press of a controller button) as you parkour and ninja throughout each of the game's levels.
The gameplay can be very challenging sometimes overly so. However, it never reaches the point of being too hard that the majority of players will be unable to advance. A few of the levels took me a few attempts to complete. I found myself getting stuck at some of the puzzles. However, the solution soon becomes apparent and it then becomes a basic learning of game mechanics before you advance. The good thing is that the same mechanics persist throughout the game and are plentiful following the initial learning. Hence, once skills are learned you will be putting them to use again and again.
I love the fact that the game utilizes a health bar system that is based upon Gemma's level of self-esteem. This works well with the overall themes of the game to effect gameplay in a decisive and well-measured manner.
The presentation in a word is slick. Graphically, the decisions behind the color palette were perfectly chosen and are representative of the type of color scheme that I would expect in a game about a teenaged girl. It perfectly blends with the self-esteem meter. The better you play and the higher Gemma's self-esteem the more vibrant the world becomes. Gemma will then ultimately get into the zone. Humorously, she leaves rainbow trails behind where she has run. However, when depression starts to play her mind and the color starts to drain from the world. The sound is very good but it is the graphical representation of the game where the game shines from a presentation perspective.
Ninja Pizza Girl delivers the Supreme version when it comes to Steamification. It has a set of five trading cards and twenty-eight Steam achievements. Further, it incorporates Steam leaderboards to provide a competitive edge to the game for those so inclined.
I wholeheartedly endorse Ninja Pizza Girl not only to fans of the genre but also to people seeking a deeper 'games as art' experience. You're going to get your monies worth within the content and it will leave you pondering the real world from the perspective of Gemma. Although not everyone is a teenaged girl I'd like to believe that everyone has a piece of Gemma's spirit inside them.

Oddworld: Strangers Wrath is quite a departure from the previous Oddworld games. No side scrolling or rescuing other inhabitants. Well, not in the same way at least.
In Strangers Wrath, you play as a bounty hunter and for most intents and purposes his name is stranger. Early on it is established he desires a surgery (to live). It is left ambiguous why exactly.
As a bounty hunter you have the ability to switch between first and third person camera views. In first person mode you have a crossbow; You have different sorts of ammunition used for various purposes. Some examples would be laying traps, stunning, doing heavy damage and immobilization. The thing is is that the ammunition is live. No no, actually alive. They are animals and insects you are firing. You even must hunt them yourself. Though you can buy them from the general store should you desire.
Your base ammo, the one that is always there (as in infinite) is zapflies which also have the ability to charge if you hold (as in stop firing) for a bit. Which gives you the ability to always deal some damage as well as stun should you completely run out of ammo.
Since you have a lot of options when it comes to ammo, you also have the ability to capture enemies alive as well as bounties. With the difference being more moolah (the actual name of the currency in game) To be spent at the store on ammo and more upgrades like faster regen for stamina, clip extenders and overall more stamina.
Stranger is rather impervious to damage (relatively) he actually can die very easily however he can literally just shake and the damage is taken away. With the exchange being stamina; So it's important to keep track of.
Now, the reason I don't outright recommend this game is after a narrative twist the game has a sudden difficulty spike I wasn't terribly fond of; suddenly favoring capturing enemies alive as the more effective option rather than the more difficult one with higher reward. Also your ammo bags have been reduced (if you got them) but now capturing enemies restores ammo. It's a weird switch that I don't think everyone will be okay with especially if you were really enjoying the game loop before the twist.

Don't be fooled by the cutesy anime style, this game is a lot tougher than it looks. Long Live The Queen is about Elodie, a newly-appointed queen of Nova. You're bound to get into some trouble during the story, facing against several assassination attempts, a duel of magic or metal, invasions, monsters, and so on. To overcome or even avoid these, you have to appoint Elodie's time to learn different subjects : Economy, Fighting, Magic, Military, History... and so on. The game changes greatly depending on how you raise Elodie, making the game replayable yet interesting.
However, there are some flaws that the game does have. The game is unhelpful with the "moods" and exactly how they impact Elodie's education; I had used a wiki for that. Some skill checks are also irrelvant to the success of an event, although some are reasonable. Lastly, there are certain skills that are really only there for a 100% clear.

A sort of mix between visual novel, RPG, and choose-your-own-adventure, Long Live the Queen is strangely absorbing at first. After a bit of playing it felt more like an adventure in save scumming, with most deaths being unavoidable without clairvoyance. The RPG aspects almost seem like a formality, since most skills are either only necessary to pass checks that don't seem to have any impact on the game, while others are used to avoid specific deaths that will always happen without an arbitrary number in a skill. Still, the plot is nice and interactive. I feel that more feedback that what I was doing was affecting the game would be nice. I also think that as a visual novel type game, there could be more of a visual aspect. There's fewer unique backgrounds and other things than there needs to be. Overall it's worth picking this up on a sale or at full price if you're a fan of such games.

Old school isometric RPG and spiritual sucessor of Baldur's Gate. You control up to 6 characters in real time, but can pause combat at any time to issue commands. Setting and classes are for the most part very original and combat somewhat challenging on the harder difficulties.
What's new is that you aquire a ruined stronghold, which you can rebuild and be the lord of. You can imprison people you defeat, give audiences, HAVE to defend it from time to time, and more.
The game lets you pick many approaches for situations, and remembers in which ways you have acted. Choices have consequences, sometimes very dire. Even simple dialogue choices. You gain points in traits such as benevolent, deceitful, aggressive and many more, depending on your behaviour, and people (and factions) will judge you based on them.
The story is somewhat obscure at the beginning, but picks up after a couple of hours and sparks enough curiosity to have one want to uncover the whole plot. It becomes more complex and interesting as it goes on. People claiming "bad story" after a few hours are simply ignorant. Epic stories take time to get on their way. They don't start with the endfight.
The AI is not exactly the smartest or fastest, so micromanagement is required (especially on the hardest difficulties). Then again, if you don't like to manage any parts of your combat in games, you're probably better off watching a movie.
TL;DR: Similar to Baldurs Gate, but with much more complexity in many things. Choices matter!

Serving as a prequel to the first game Resident Evil 0 sees STARS member Rebecca Chambers and convict Billy Coen join forces to try and survive the dangers ahead while uncovering Umbrella's plans.
As a throwback to old-school survival horror RE0 is a pretty competent albeit lazy and fiddly game that is quite fun to play.
-it really looks nice with overhauled 3d models, backgrounds and effects
-good soundtrack
-having two characters at your disposal, and being able to freely switch between them, is nice
-sheds some light on the events of the first Resident Evil
-some interesting puzzles
-being able to leave items anywhere is nice
-certain sections can be appropriately tense
-as in most RE games expect cheesy characters and plot
-per RE standards expect unskippable door animations between rooms
-while for the most part competent your companion's AI can sometimes hesitate too much
-somewhat forgettable bosses
-movies look a bit dated and low-res
-a couple annoying puzzles
-inventory management can be fiddly
Resident Evil 0's HD remaster is truly noticeable as the game looks great, the mechanics are still the same though (apart from a leaner control scheme) so you can expect a very old fashioned gameplay with all the pros and cons. To expand on that you'll find a pretty atmospheric and challenging survival horror experience with familiar puzzles, quite a few items to carry back and forth to solve them, very limited inventory space and a good amount of bioweapons that'll try to kill you.
The whole item management aspect is part of the old-school charm but can also feel unnecessary fiddly at times, especially when you find out there's a limit to how many items you can leave in each room or have to make a few trips to ensure you have all the items you need in the next area. Story and characters are also pretty shallow and don't really add too many interesting elements to the overarching narrative.
All things considered RE0 is still a worthwhile purchase if you're looking for more old-style survival horror and even more so if you missed it when it came out on Gamecube: it's not the strongest entry of the series but it's decent enough to warrant a playthrough.
If your a fan of the Resident Evil franchise like myself, then this game is right up your ally.

To conclude, this is a Masterpiece and will probably be the 2017 game of year for me.

All in all, Oddworld: Stranger's Wrath is a unique genre-bender that proves that other devs should take the risk once in awhile and break the standard format when it comes to making games. And the current sale price makes it a steal! Definitely worth adding to your library.

State of Decay offers a lot to do.  It's a big, open-world zombie survival game with unique NPC socialization, crafting, questing and looting systems.  Definitely kept me engaged throughout and there's great replay value with or without DLC.  Takes a hit in graphics, which feel muddy and not quite triple-A, and the controls, ported over from consoles, take some getting used to.  This isn't an action game like LFD2 or a hide-and-survive or run-and-gun like Day Z, it's more strategic, but does have action and survival elements.  It's just unique, has it's own flavor, and I think it's a lot of fun partly because of it's unique gameplay approaches.  Overall this is an amazing beginning to a franchise, and will probably rival series' like GTA and Saint's Row when it joins the next gen with visuals and physics.   It's a weird comment but I like State of Decay a lot.  I just think I am going to love State of Decay 2.

A masterpiece, spiritual successor of Baldur's Gate and Icewindale, 2D isometric RPG with real time combact and tactical pause.

Un capolavoro, secondo me erede spirituale dei Baldur's gate e Icewinddale da cui però si distacca per quanto riguarda le regole di D&D, qui liberamente interpretate, molto più approfondite e secondo me migliorate.
+ Fondali stupendi, level design sublime, tutto molto particolareggiato e curato, molto belle le animazioni di personaggi, mostri, magie ed elementi dei fondali.
+ Armi, magie, armature, oggetti unici a volontà e un sistema di craftaggio molto sviluppato.
+ Il background è molto bello, molto ben caratterizzato, sia per quel che riguarda i personaggi, il lore ecc...
+ Grande varietà di nemici e boss.
+ Il sistema di combattimento è solido e appagante, a livello di difficoltà "marcia della morte" il gruppo viene annientato se si lancia in battaglia senza un minimo di strategia, è sempre preferibile attirare i nemici, sfruttare il "fattore campo", eliminare prima i più deboli o quelli con abilità rognose ecc...le IA si comportano abbastanza bene, se un personaggio è ferito lo prenderanno di mira, cercheranno sempre di farvi fuori i maghi...niente di eccezionale ma convincente.
+ Le abilità sono tante, ben differenziate e incisive nel gameplay, con la campagna principale da quello che ho capito il level cap è bloccato al 12...pochetto...non si sbloccano molte abilità, ma con i DLC si arriva a livello 24...molto meglio.
+ La fortezza del protagonista è bellissima, piena di cose da fare, quest, strutture da costruire, relazioni diplomatiche...molto ben fatta, si può addirittura spedire in missione i PNG parchegiati...
+ Il comparto audio è molto valido con belle musiche, voci, sottofondo, effetti sonori...tutto molto bello.
+ Benchè piuttosto lineare le scelte influiscono notevolmente su trama e risvolti fornendo anche un discreto grado di rigiocabilità.
+ Gira tranquillamente su PC economici e datati.
- La trama principale non brilla certo per originalità, personalmente non mi è piaciuta tantissimo anche se non manca qualche colpo di scena e risvolto inaspettato. Le scelte compiute la influenzano certo, ma rimane piuttosto lineare, niente di epocale insomma. A qualcuno può comunque piacere.
- A volte le battaglie sono confusionarie, specialmente se ci sono elementi del fondale che nascondono i contendenti, il campo di battaglia zeppo di gente o ci sono molti effetti di magie in corso, è il prezzo da pagare per non avere una visuale ruotabile...
- Le due espansioni apportano migliorie al gioco davvero necessarie per godersi l'esperienza. Benchè la campagna principale sia sufficientemente lunga, io ne consiglio caldamente l'acquisto e non è che siano proprio economiche...

Don't buy it. First of all: Resident Evil HD Remaster was the first time I played the first Resident Evil game, and I was never a huge fan of the new ones, but I liked RE4, RE5 and Revelations 2. Resident Evil HD Remaster is a masterpiece if you ask me, so why don't I recommend RE Zero? Because they made TONS of MORONIC decisions.
First the puzzles. In RE1 the puzzles were unrealistic, but they made sense, you understood them and they fit the setting. In RE Zero the puzzles feel completely random, don't make any sense. It's like every time one of the developer said "we need a puzzle here" someone else took out his puzzlebook and just chose a random puzzle out of that.
Then whos ♥♥♥♥ing idea was to have 2 playable characters? Not only are both characters extremely boring, bland, and ♥♥♥♥ing cliche times 100, it also makes the gameplay extremely annoying. Inventory can be annoying in RE1, but it was fine. In RE Zero you have to manage two inventories now with the extremely clonky menus and long animations inbetween every action you do. And in gun fights your AI partner is a complete moron, which means you have to sometimes control both characters at the same time which can become really frustrating. Also if you don't pay attention for a second, your AI partner could waste your precious ammo for totally unneccessary reason.
One of the great things about RE1 was that combat wasn't a big challenge, it was always a decision if you want to do combat or try to dodge enemies, both approaches had benefits. In RE Zero you can't do that because of your AI partner, you have to kill almost every enemy you see. As you can see from my playtime, I didn't play for too long though, so maybe later in the game the level design gets better.
Another huge problem is that there are no item crates anymore, so you have to drop items on the floor and backtrack to pick them up again. Especially painful with the ink ribbons, which you have to always drop at the save point, next time drop another item to have space, pick the ink ribbon up, save, drop the ink ribbon, pick up the other dropped item.
This was also a bit of a problem in RE1, but this whole process was much faster with item crates and because of that it wasn't so ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. Every time you pick up an item there is a small animation and the game asks you if you want to pick it up first. Opening inventory and closing it always has a small delays, lots of small things like that make it extremely annoying.
RE1 is a 9.5/10 for me, I ♥♥♥♥ing love it. But this game is just annoying and a waste of time.

Game was fun, stealth is pretty good. Not super realistic in some instances (hidden behind an ATV even though there's a guy standing on the other side of it and looking right at me).
The upgrade system is pretty "meh", very few upgrades to most gear - clothing has only three upgrades in the same "branch" (i.e. three possible upgrads to the "stealth" armor) most of the time, with the best upgrade locked behind a bunch of lenghty missions.
The worst part is that most of the guns are useless and you have nowhere to put your money if you opt to take the "ghost" path (which rewards the most money and is the most difficult). On "ghost" you are not supposed to kill anyone so all those weapons you can buy are pretty much for show and are useless. Since you earn the most money on ghost you have a lot of it and nowhere to use it.
Also, a huge "con" to the game is the reason why I only have 0.2hrs played on steam - I had to download and use a no-cd crack to be able to play on a 21:9 monitor. The game has an option for 21:9 and shows the resolution correctly in the options, but it still chooses to display at 16:9 with black bars on the side. Basically, it pretends to have an option that does nothing.
Otherwise I had a blast with the game and, at this price, would recommend it to anyone interested in the stealth genre.
The story is quite interesting (even though it pretends to be urgent yet it throws a bunch of side missions at you), the gameplay is good, controls are good.

Finished the Main quest in Free weekend.
In Shadow of Mordor you play as a half dead ranger  named Talion who after being killed along with his family is possessed by the spirit of Celebrimor, the elf smith in LOTR 2nd age, who created most of the rings that are used to control middle earth's top leadership.  The two then seek to destroy the black hand, Sauron's top military leadership, and then fight Sauron himself.
Graphics: 5/10
This isn't crysis or Witcher 3, but the graphics are pretty good for a 3 year old game.  Games like 10 years older like half life 2 have better art direction.  Setting wise the maps are pretty confusing and poorly designed, with most of the map a series of rivers and terraced hills, with old ruins on top of these hills, which you just climb on and then jump on unsuspecting orcs.  Overall the game splits up into 2 parts, The beginnig which looks like gondor/mordor, at total gray wasteland where everything looks the same and pretty underwhelming,  The 2nd part is green with grass, which looks nicer but is also pretty much looks exactly the same through out the map.  Only differences are the certain fortresses that are in certain parts of the map.  This isn't skyrim or oblivion, where you would want to wish you were there.  Bad map design compared to the game it took its combat mechanics from arkham asylum.  In arkham asylum each map section had beautiful graphics and was a part of the arkham asylum's patient wings.  But in Shadow of mordor nothing separates Tolsig's crossing to other parts of the map.  This is just boring and bad map design.  Wraith vision is also very poorly done, with color scheme of blue orcs/slaves (nearly same color) to a gray background.  In arkham asylum, it was more distinctive to distinguish foe from friend and background.
Gameplay: 6/10 w/ controller? 5/10 for keyboard and mouse.
This game is basically batman arkham asylum in middle earth, with game mechanics that don't totally fit.  This game was probably designed for consoles rather than PC.  I played mostly with keyboard and mouse, but this game looks like a console port, where you should have a controller.  You mostly fight by properly left clicking the direction of your movement key and camera, but it was difficult to control.  Sometimes you would attack in a direction you wouldn't want to.  Jump and ledge grabbing in this game was also really clunky, and really frustrating to play on keyboard.  There are also no indication which ledges and buildings and objects you CAN grab and those which you CAN'T.  This is different from arkham asylum, where you had a easy to use grapple, and glide ability to escape form enemes.  In Shadow of mordor sometimes you try to climb up certain buildings, but you can't because you arent allowed to climb it.  Poor coding also means you can't jump off certain objects in certain directions, so if you are low health you are probably gonna die.  No glide from arkham asylum means you dont know the distance you are jumping and may miss a ledge grab.  This game is much worse than Arkham asylum, which I also played with Keyboard and mouse.
There are orc captains you have to assasinate or mind control to create an army against Sauron.  Each captain/warchief has strengths and weaknesses, which you can use against them.  MIndcontrol low level orcs to use against their leaders and use them to discover their strengths and weaknesses.  The game is hard in the beginning, if you dont have most abilities,  I would reccomend you do mostly main quest lines to level up until you get at least the mindcontrol abiility, and the execute ability before doing the rest of the game.  After these 2 abilities the game gets much easier.  Other than some very frustrating flaws and a final end boss fight consisting of mostly quick time events, the game has pretty good replayability, if you like assasinating/ stealth and planning games.  Warning: If you die alot to certain orc captains, they get really strong, and the game can become very frustrating.  If you are easily frustrated, refrain from playing this game.
Story: 2/10
If you like lord of the rings, especially the "the Hobbit" movie series, The story of this game is proabably enough.  If you wanted something deeper and less stupid, you will probably be disappointed in the character acting/reactions to events, and the boring and forgetting cast of friends in the game, with the cliche, dwarf, elf and human sidekicks.
Overall: 4/10
I wouldn't buy this game.  POORLY made game to cash in on the LOTR franchise.  Incredibly overrated by critics.  Silly to think of this game as GOTY material.

This is a game I can never get sick of. It has so much replay value, and since workshop support was added with the new DLC, you can always have a new experience.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward, you shoot enemies with your tears, pick up some items, and then shoot enemies with more powerful tears. Keep going till you've defeated one of the major bosses.
For someone just starting out with the game, I suggest you simply buy the whole package, with all the DLCs. If you're someone who likes to have concrete endings to stories, and wants to get every achievement, that's what you'll need to do.
Despite how good this game is though, it doesn't come without its flaws.
I dislike most that came with the Afterbirth+ DLC, except for the workshop support, and that we finally got an ending to the story.
Since the addition of booster packs, it seems like a lot less effort is being put into it. There are bugs and CTDs that were never there with the original mods. Not to mention, some of the sprites are a lot uglier than the originals.
One of the mods that was added with a booster pack is still receiving updates, so people simply install that version, negating the fact that an older version was already in the game.
Regardless, I'd give this game a solid 7/10. Maybe an 8 if some bugs were fixed.

Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a sweet middle ground between the Panther-like action of Conviction and the Ghost-like stealth of Chaos Theory. And, like the series’ Chaos Theory peak it can’t help but be compared to, Blacklist’s also packing a pair of multiplayer modes that could stand proudly on their own. Splinter Cell is back on the right shadowy track.

Long Live the Queen is a game that represents the nature of trial and error. Similar to the classic Princess Maker games that came out of Japan over a decade ago, I find that there is far more depth to this title. There are no random events in this game, as everything is scripted and outcomes are based on the decisions you make as you journey through the story. This does not mean the game is linear and lacks replayability by any means however, as there is a rather significant number of skills you can select to raise.
The flow of the game breaks down into three parts:
- At the start of the week, you select two classes for Elodie to take which will affect which skills increase. Skill increases have a bonus or penality modifier attached to them depending on Elodie's mood.
- At end of the week you decide what Elodie should do for the weekend. This is what affects her mood, and will therefore change the modifiers for skill increases the following week.
- After you decide what will affect Elodie's mood, a scripted event will take place. You are also often given choices to take which adds further variety. These events are where checks are done on Elodie's skill levels, which will determine how events in the story may progress, or potentially how you may be led into an ending.
This event-check system allows for a variety of replayability as one learns the cause and effect of the actions you have made in both developing Elodie, as well as the decisions you make within the kingdom. For some this may be seen as a negative. Without replaying the game several times you will not know the most effective route to take in developing Elodie, and you are likely to fail many times on the way toward her coronation.
The flaw with the skill system exists in that there are too many skills with too few reward. Unfortunately certain skills seem to exist simply to confuse the player and draw attention away from developing far more important ones. Some of the skills may only feature one or two checks within the entire game, while other skills are constantly relied upon, and thus deserve the player's attention more.
The visuals of the game are very simple, but incredibly clean. The artwork is well done and everything is discernable. The UI is simple and works, though unfortunately I personally dislike the use of the right-click. While convenient for bringing up the save/load menu quickly enough, I would have preferred it to act as a back button, however that is personal taste and not a strike against the game itself.
The music is simple midi, but relaxing to listen to. Designed to have a regal sense to it, I find it is appropriate.
The endings are where the game shines. There are many endings, most of them being bad ends. The severity of the deaths Elodie may happen upon would shock anyone who is not already familiar with this title, from being poisoned, to run through with a sword, to being taken out by magic. There are a variety of deaths awaiting Elodie if the player fails to consider the future and does not prepare the future queen for what is to come.
Long Live the Queen is a fun title that I do recommend playing through, however it is not without its flaws, specifically in regard to what I mentioned about skills above. I only recommend making the purchase at a more reasonable price point.

Dark Souls is by far my favorite series. Without a doubt an extremely enjoyable game and a game that will give you a sense of achievement at the end of it.
+Replay Value: There are many different ways you can play Dark Souls. There are enough different class systems to give you a different experience each time right form the start. There are a bunch of hidden secrets in the game that you may not find the first time you play through the game, so even if you play the same class there could still be more to find. The new game plus feature will also let you continue on with your current character against enemy's that are stronger than the previous playthrough.
+Difficulty: For some this may be a con, but for many others it is a pro. Dark Souls isn't exceptionally difficult like everyone says, but there is some difficulty. Some people can breeze through the game, and others will struggle boss after boss. No matter which side of the spectrum you're on though. Completing this game will more than likely leave you satisfied with your accomplishments.
+Bosses: Each boss is unique with different patterns of attacking and moving. There will be easy bosses and hard bosses for you to encounter throughout the game, and every time you defeat one you will feel like you've achieved something. In my personal opinion, I truly did feel great every time I beat a boss. I was always satisfied and when i defeated the final boss of the game, I felt the strong sense of achievement that I've brought up many times now.
+Storyline: The story to Dark Souls is very complex and buried in the game. In order to learn the storyline you have to seriously look for the clues to the story and find the pieces of the puzzle. If you're too lazy to do that there's always youtube to help you piece it together,
+/- Gameplay: I have mixed feelings about the gameplay. While I believe the combat system is solid there are definitely many issues with some of the features. The gameplay is solid with interesting systems of progression and covenants, but lacks in some other things. I'll go more indepth in the cons section.

-Hitboxes: Probably one of the biggest issues with this game is the hit boxes. They can work in your favor on occasion, but normally it works against you. You could be shooting an arrow around a corner or by a wall and it will catch onto the magical air that emits from the walls. Or enemies that grab at you will use telekensis to pull you into their grip.
-Mouse and Keyboard: Using a mouse and keyboard with this game is next to impossible. The amount of work you have to put in to just get it working decently is not worth the time and effort. I would highly recommend getting an xbox controller. You'll save yourself a lot of frustration.
-Framerate: Certain areas in the game can cause heavy framerate drops even on the highest end computers. Getting through these areas can be exceptionally annoying just because of how badly you will lag. Even outside of these areas, the frames are not very good. This is primarily just from how poor of a port this game is.
-Online: The online system has always been pretty bad. Invading people can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥with lag and hitboxes being♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. Trying to summon a friend you actually know and want to play with is harder than the entire game itself.
Overall, even with the bugs and issues the game is still worth playing. The amount of time you can put into this game makes it well worth $20.

Ok, I feel I have to step up and deliver my first and probably only review as I feel so strongly that people have really not given this game the chance it rightly deserves.
The Gods will be watching really brought back the nostalgic feeling of the old point and click style adventures some of you may remember from the early 90's, for me the music and graphics really sell the game. They are meant to be retro, this is good people!! the backing tracks are epic and will have you turn up the sound as you play this difficult (but by no means dark souls esque) as you try and try to save everyone and then decend into just trying to complete your objective at all costs.
You play Sergeant Burden a man who is resolute in his beliefs and weary of them at the same time. Undercover for months inflitrating a terrorist organisation that is trying to free people from galactic slavery.
As the story progresses the lines of morality are blurred until you are not sure who is right, or why it matters at all.
So for the gameplay, each scenario is pretty much stand alone but links the story together. In each there is an overarching objective to accomplish but with harsh contraints that mean you can't have your cake and eat it. Things will go wrong and its about learning what works and what doesn't (though there are multiple solutions). You have to manage the people under you and try (or not try) to get them out alive.
Once you learn that the game is not going to give you the win on a plate it makes it easier decide to take crazy actions from the start , that help you in the end!. It makes  for good play with a partner deciding what to do next, and dealing with the frustrations together.
There is about 6 chapters to get through, so it could be short if you are really good but the experience is worth it and hope these developers get more credit for a unique and stellar game experience.

Very different, unique game. Not for all (or even most) tastes. I'll start this review off with a series of cautions.
The biggest difficulty with Gods Will Be Watching is it is going to appeal to a very small audience. GWBW is a game where you aren't the all-conquering hero, where people will die through your actions, and where your only satisfaction will come from doing the best you can in the circumstances you draw. In other words, it's a lot like life, and asks deeper questions about why we game or what we expect to take away from a gaming experience, not to mention the 'heroic' avatars we play over and over in games that are so much ego food. GWBW has much more in common with your typical Jason Rohrer game than it does the average indie, let alone AAA title.
Furthermore, do not be fooled by anyone calling this a ' point-and-click adventure game'... it has almost nothing to do with that genre. This is a turn-based strategy game with very strict rules, although utterly unlike any other one out there in the minimalism of its style, substance, and execution.
GWBW itself consists of seven different scenarios, ranging from a hostage crisis, to enduring torture, to wilderness survival, and so on. This is not a 'happy game'. The scenarios are harrowing, to say the least, and many players are going to struggle with a game where they not only don't get to win, but can only hope to minimize loss.
The goal is simply to get through each scenario in any way the player can, with consequences that you can live with. This sets up a rapidly shifting moral boundary, as necessity will rapidly come to outweigh morality.
The game boils down to effectively managing all of the variables in these scenarios while trying to keep any of them from falling into a fail-state... which they inevitably will. The scenarios themselves, however--unlike the one-offs of a time/resource management game or a 'quest' game like Oregon Trail--are complex and intertwined. The player will not only need to work to understand those relationships, but also to recognize cues when the situation is tipping too far in any of multiple directions, and to plan and react accordingly.
This means, to pick one example:
-understanding what will cause a hostage's emotional state to improve/deteroriate
-monitoring the visual cues that indicate that hostage's emotional state
-planning in advance how to control/manipulate that hostage's emotional state
-having contingencies ready (in mind) if external circumstances interfere with that plan
-making hard decisions when all of this breaks down due to flawed planning or bad luck
To some players, the small element of luck/bad luck will be an exhiliarting thrill--an element that twists the story and changes possibilities, taking away control (similar to the great roguelikes) in order to generate emergent story. To others, taht same luck/bad luck will lead to exasperation or a feelign of malicious unfairness, and frequent reloads (especialy if they obsess about 'perfecting' each level). Buyer beware.
The most succinct thing I can say about this game to help you choose to buy it or not to buy it is: this game IS the choices you make. It's not about the story, or mastering each scenario, or working your way to a pay-off at the end (again, be warned, the ending is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of you if you're looking for validation there). It is about making choices without knowing if the choice you made is 'right' or 'wrong'.
The soundtrack and pixel art are bar none some of the best of the genre, and much of the dialogue is engaging (when it doesn't fall into tropes) and the debates about the ending will undoubtedly keep the Steam message boards raging for a long time.
Ignore them, play the free Ludum Dare version of the game, and form your own judgment. If you like that, give GWBW a try. It goes well with a nice glass of Chianti and any dog-eared copy of Sartre or Nietzsche.

I feel like this is "a sucessor" (not really "the" successor) to the Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale experience, and more. It is also a shout out to anyone who has played the tabletop games with some fresh "DM" style choices. It is also an attempt to implement a rules system gives racial bonuses while still basing everything off of stats, including their own kind of "saving throws." Basically, it is the kind of improvement I've been waiting for for years. Not "Neverwinter Nights" but this, something isometric with interesting rules, world, and creatures and a great story to boot.
Spoiler alert!
Negatives:
The biggest problem with this game is the conclusion, which has been revamped. The original ending was entirely predictable and ridiculously easy. The new ending (which I actually haven't completed yet) is more difficult, but still pretty predictable. This is basically on par with this being a good novel with a fairly predictable ending. It doesn't really diminish the bulk of the story, but it doesn't completely satisfy. Expect to be let down at the end.
Some would say it is the rules system is a negative, and that's mainly because it looks familiar, but it is farily unique. Maxing stats is not something that works too well in this game. If you max a stat, you will have less points to spend on defensive stats in other areas.  You can forgo defense for offense, or you can max defense.
So what's the problem? Almost any way you choose to spend your points is okay. So, this, in a way, means you have "less choice." Or "your choices don't matter."
POSITIVES
To me this rules system is fine, because the way you spend your points DOES affect the way your character achieves his success. He might kill a lot, but get knocked unconscious all the time. Or he might kill very few, and never get knocked out. The bottom line is that the way you spend your points can help you create a character that is really successful the way you want to play that character. And it takes a lot of experimenting to figure out how you want to do that. And there is always the challenge of party balance to consider. With the freedom to create your entire party, and retrain at any time, you have a lot of freedom. But you also have tons of formulas for success.
This doesn't even mention the fact that if you build a character that isn't very athletic, they might not be able to bend bars, or swim underwater a long way. Is your character the kind of guy or gal who can rescue someone from a burning building? Or find a trap? These are the "DM style" choices that are peppered throughout the game. These are narrative style scenarios where you are forced to make a decision, and then face the results of that choices. Also, throughout the game there are dialogue options which can be open to you based on your character stats, as well as dialogue options that will cause others to perceive you as cruel or clever or many others. All this plays richly into the role-playing narrative of the game, and makes you more a part of the story than most CRPGs.
The story itself is a positive, with an interesting take on "the afterlife" or "the soul" if you will, and what happens after death. This is the theme that permeates the entire story. It makes for a very interesting setting without the over abundance of creatures featured on the Sword Coast, and with the dizzying array of factions there. The story is more focused on the "colonies" in the wilderness, which makes for less distracting setting. Also, the keep allows for a whole new level of gameplay allowing army battles, and other major decisions to really become a part of the setting. I really do enjoy holding prisoners in my own dungeon.

Solid game. I began playing RPGs since the early Heroes of the Might and Magic days. I do look forward for some old-school-ish RPGs.
Things I liked:
+ Solid story line with vibrant background history of fan-sponsored NPCs. Really draws you in. Plenty of reading materials.
+ Solid battle mechanics. Logical and reaonable counters for each creature/weapon type.
+ OK Map desgin, great aesthetics.
+ Plenty of side quests and tasks.
Things I grew dislike the game as I progress through the main quest line. I spent over 50 hours and nearly finishing the main quest.
- Attribute check during conversations. This limits the choices severely, especially during late-game. When your character cannot grow on their primary attributes, you will run in problems that your character cannot pass EVERY attribute check. Then what's the point of putting them there? Don't tell me I should have known this before I create my character. I started this fresh like a new book. Can this system be improved? Certainly, can the skills contribute to the growth of attributes?
- Stat buff from artifacts/armors/jewels/etc... don't stack. Seriously? What is the rationale of this? And to add the confusion, some weapon buffs DO stack. Again Seriously? This is the first RPG I played have this kind of system, which really boggles my mind as why.
- The loading screens. I understand maybe it's the limitation of the engine. But for some smaller maps, like entering/exiting a house, can we not have a loading screen? It shows up too much till a point that you feel sick of it.
- The combat, although the mechanics/stat make it interesting for a while, the whole strategy doesn't change once you have a team that works, i.e. one or two tanks in the front and damager in the back thing.
- The monsters will not respawn. And no experience from comabat. This removes a great deal of replayability because the game becomes quite linear. And making travelling a chore in the late game.
I enjoyed immensely in the beginning. But the game grew more stale as it progresses and the fun gradually worn off due to the three minuses above. This is the kind of game that starts strong but finish feebly.
Do I recommend this game? Maybe. Since finishing the story is what it counts for RPGs, I have to lean slightly to a NO.
