Basically, it's like a spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate.  It's like the literally took the Infinity Engine, updated the graphics, and left everything else alone, including all the bad things.  Controls are slow and clunky as well as unintuitive.  Combat is fiddly and micro-managy in a bad way, and the game is filled with walls of uninteresting text that are a chore to read.  It's not fascinating, interesting text like in Planescape Torment where you couldn't stop reading, it's just very plain and boring stuff that they could've just shown in a few pictures with a lot more clarity and detail.
There's lots of statistics that are thrown at you with little to no hand holding, and there are a lot of superfluous stats and customizations that just allow you a chance to gimp yourself, and the class balance is really not that great.  The game system is kind of like a rehash of 2nd Edition Dungeons and Dragons, and overall, I'd say this game is definitely worth skipping if you're not sure about it.
I loved Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 back in the day, but it had its share of flaws, which this game copies wholesale while attempting to do nothing to correct.  I feel like the Dragon Age series has moved far beyond games like this, as well as more immersive action-adventure games like the recent Fallout and Mass Effect games.  Not to say that I wouldn't have liked an experience like this if it was more polished and had less filler to it, just that the way they presented everything in this game has really put me off.
The storyline is decent, and people who wouldn't mind playing Baldur's Gate 2.5 in a new setting with new characters would probably find this game worth a buy, but people who prefer more polished, streamlined controls and more modern trappings in their RPG's may want to stay away.

Ninja Pizza Girl is unique--from its Sonic the Hedgehog-meets-Mirror's Edge gameplay, to level paths accommodating gamers of different skill levels, to the..."realistic" depiction of a portly man answering the door in no pants.
7/10, would throw pizza over balcony screaming, "No pants. No pizza!" again.
In all seriousness, though, Ninja Pizza Girl's affirming messages and interesting premise really hit home when you encounter what could have been its most negative element--your fellow Ninja.
They emerge from the scenery to trip you, drop from the ceiling to slow you down, and chase you across the rooftops of NPG's future dystopia. They shove you to the ground, throw garbage at you, mock you, and record the humiliation with their phones to share on social media.
It's an eerie reflection of our modern world, and these Ninja are one of the only enemies in gaming I've truly hated...
I'm in a state of flow. Leaping across rooftops, dubstep occasionally kicking in to "wub" me along my merry way. And then...A horde of them. They swarm around me, shoving, laughing and taking pictures. Gemma slumps to the ground. By tapping the spacebar/[A] button, Gemma can rise up again, regaining her confidence and dashing through once more. However, the chunk of time this situation takes has almost certainly spelled out failure for this run.
And the funny thing is, the world of Ninja Pizza Girl is so fun to glide through I don't care about having to redo the level--I'm upset and frustrated because of HOW I lost. Because of what they did to her--and me. I want to lash out, taking out every Ninja in my way, but it doesn't provide any relief or satisfaction. Revenge feels...Empty.
So I do what Gemma loves to do:
I run.
I run past my would-be harassers, and in doing so gain a feeling better than any amount of enemy-stomping could have provided. Every enemy I slide through, jump over and dodge past give a sense of achievement better than a headshot, or a well-aimed kick to the face.
I--Gemma, is not like them. And in Ninja Pizza Girl, while in Early Access and a bit unpolished, I can finally express that through *gameplay.*
I'm not another man with a gun, shooting another man with a gun to somehow prove I'm a "hero" or "Murica." I'm a Ninja Pizza Girl, and in being different, I can rise above it all--and feel great doing it.

Please ignore the negative reviews based on how repetitive the gameplay is. Although the game is not a proper adventure considered each level consists in not more than one to three screens, is as repetitive as any other point and click game. the difference lays in the need of managing the "resources" to overcome every challenge and more often than not survive the situation your characters will be thrown into.
Gameplaywise the point and click is just what the developers decided fits best as a way to interact with the game and this is as far as the relation between this title and the point and click genre goes.
Regarding the narrative, it is really solid and I assure it will hook your chin and stick it in front of the screen as soon as you manage to pass the first level. And you will find yourself bonded to your comrades or your mission depending on who you are and how you feel you want to leave your mark in this thrilling story.
Failure is not an option, it is a certainty and you will have to try a bit hard to proceed through the game. But there is not only one good way to complete each level. You will find yourself struggle to decide if it is acceptable the way the events unfold according to your decision making or if a rerun of a given level is needed. To sooth the tension the authors provided a nice recap of your performance after each chapter in form of a statistic comparison of your choiches with the other players in the world over time.
On top of that there are beautifully designed pixel art, a matching soundtrack and the need to know, right after the first failure, how your main character  managed to find himself lost in the desert. (NOT A SPOILER, play it and you'll know what I mean)
In a few words the game is what it claims to be. A minimalistic survival thriller wrapped in a DERIVED FORM of the classic point and click gameplay. For all those who cannot figure out how it works from the various reviews posted here and there, I suggest to visit the official site where the original version of this game is freely playable from your browser:
this will help you to get a feel of the gameplay and atmosphere but is nothing like the full game.

The idea and gameplay is pretty good, unfortunately the execution in some areas is just terrible. The problem is the absolutely horrendous save system combined with the constant bugs can easily lead to frustration or game breaking scenarios.
This happened about 17 hours into the game with no survivor losses:
I was in the middle of a rescue mission which involves my survivor rescuing 2 other survivors: everything was going well, I decided to pause the game and do the laundry, came back in a few minutes and unpause the game. The "Loading" screen comes up for a few seconds and I'm back at my base...turns out my survivor and the other 2 I was rescuing all ended up dead...while I was paused...was not even able to recover their stash since it didnt show up ont he map, or the area I was in, so I lost some of my best weapons in the process.
Basically at this point I'm done enjoying the game because at any moment I can randomly lose things I've worked for while the game is paused, the enjoyment is gone and now it's just a chore to grind through until the story is over.
I understand that a lot of "random" events happen and the game continues to run when it's not being played, but to lose my character while the game is paused is absolutely ridiculous, especially since its permenant and unrecoverable. This was probably a bug rather than a mechanic but annoying none the less.
It's hard to believe that developers are still arrogant enough to think their games are flawless and implement a single-save, saving system, especially on a PC where manually backing up/recovering saves is easy to do ( which is something I constantly do now every time I pause the game), defeating the purpose of modifying/cheating through reloading saves.

Of all the zombie survival games to choose from I'm glad I had a chance to try this one. "How could it be fun if it's single player game?" was my initial take on this game. It's great to be pleasantly surprised from time to time. I'll try to be as general as possible as discovery was definitely something that shouldn't be spoiled.
I'd like to call this frantic survival game play like Left 4 Dead with open world/scavenging aspects of DayZ. Add in a ton of obective based missions and a few dynamic ones as well. For example, you radio in to a survivor to loot a location and on the way gets swarmed by a horde so you'll get a dynamically generated mission to rescue him/her so the scavenge mission can continue.
Things get overwhelming very quickly and you'll find yourself wanting for more time. The sense of urgency is really felt in this, much like in Left 4 Dead...it's one of the reasons I found it to be so successful.
Priorities shift constantly but the goal remains the same. The game keeps pushing you to a breaking point...eventually you'll end up choosing between a survivor or a potentially amazing cache or an opportunity to gain substantial influence. It's mostly about learning efficiency and expanding intelligently.
It certainly isn't without its flaws but it works overall and with the "expansions" you get a nice an extra map layout and endless survival mode. It isn't visually stunning or a mechanical masterpiece but its fun! Everything I want in a open world Walking Dead simulator and I'm totally fine with the fact that there's no multiplayer to ruin what's an otherwise well-sculpted game.

The Good Stuff:

The game itself looks really nice and well-drawn, enviroments are mostly beautiful (sometimes minimalistic, but eh, not a big deal) and its fun to lurk around, exploring rooftops and peeking in windows. Color pallet is different: ranging from bright city bathing in daylight to dark basements and graveyards. Animations are cool and not annoying to look at.

Its kinda shallow sometimes, but it fits the theme wonderfully. Some tracks are great, even worth listening without the game. And yeah, INSTRUMENTALS. Other in-game sounds (footsteps, jumping, leaves etc.) are lively and don't feel out of place at all.
There are quite a number of them and they are pretty fun. Especially that Demon Tower one, felt like Hyper Light Drifter  and had a nice progression system.
The Meh Stuff:
Don't know if its just my computer being not fit for the task, but my framerate sometimes tanked so much that the game felt choppy and slow. I also noticed some weird screen issues, seemed like the game were redrawing backgrounds every step i took in some locations. And LOADING SCREENS. Jeez, its 2017, PC can totally take on bigger things like actual open-world games in full 3D. Why would you ever put SO MUCH LOADING SCREENS IN YOUR GAME?

Many people noticed that the game delivers an obvious leftist message, flavored by communistic thought here and there, talking about beating up "fascist" and what not, pushing you into this whole "its okay to be gay" thingy, which I am personally not fond of. And its like a small american town, filled with old and conservative people. Strange, simply strange and out of place. Nevertheless, I understand that target audience is probably tumblr/buzzfeed kind of kids, I'm just putting it out there, so you know what to expect.
The Bad stuff:
Aside from minigames you have "jumping puzzles" which use a unique mechanic: jumping third time in a row will make your character go higher. Sounds simple and fun, is it? Let me assure you, the whole jumping thing is inconsistent and frustrating with standing ground just magically losing its "standing" capabilities, legdes shorter than they actually seem. Some jumps require almost pinpoint accurate timing and its not really about "challenge", its about trying over and over, going through several loading screens to get somewhere you need to get.
I don't know... There are some good moments and 3,5 funny jokes scattered through the storyline, but its not enought to cope with therrible hollowness that is everything else. Dialogues are plain and boring with practically no real thought put in them, characters just act like they are all silly children that can only say the most obvious things. And its not like its justified in any way. The story itself tries to spice things up with plot twists and characters speaking out about their "problems", but it ends up playing itself which is rather sad. Ending is goofed and there is nothing you can do about it. Not a thing.
5/10

When playing Gods Will Be Watch, It's important to remember that not every game is for every person, and that not every game fits neatly into the catagories we've created for games.
If you are interested in it because it is described as a point and click adventure, you should reconsider. On the surface this looks to be true, but under the hood sits a different beast. Instead we find a survival sim, ala Oregon Trail, with almost no forgiveness in it's computerized soul. There are strategies and ideas that work, but quite often you have to roll the dice and pray.
At any point, a single wrong decision or unlucky break at the wrong moment can send you screaming back to the begining of a chapter undoing half hour worth of work. The more mercenary you are, the more wiggle room you are given. Kindness may or may not be rewarded, and sometimes will be acts of futility or suicide. Soon it becomes a balance of risk and failure, of cost and rewards. You are forced to buy time more than once at the cost of your own flesh. People will die, and you never know who you really want to save.
Thrown into this mix are a set of metarules that neither the player nor the character know about until they are stumbled across. You'll stumble across them at the worst of moments, wasting time you never really have but serve as puzzle pieces to the larger narative.
That said, the question becomes: is it worth it a playthru?
My answer is a cautious 'yes' to those who like creative and harsh gameplay or those looking for a different experience.

Highlights: Unique Premise, Stylized Artwork, and Sufficiently Difficult.
I wasn't to sure what to expect when I went into trying out Gods Will Be Watching. I happened to come across it and thought the style of the game was appealing, so I preordered it. However, after playing it for multiple hours and understanding the core concept and design philosophy, I can say that this is truly a gem among adventure games.
Starting out the game, I was quickly introduced to the story and characters and then quickly placed into the first scenario. Without spoiling anything, I was tasked to, essentially, multimanage multiple situations in conjunction with completing the ultimate task at hand. It requires a lot (emphasis on LOT) of trial and error before you understand what exactly you need to do before accomplishing the goal. It took me around 20 times or so before I finally finished the first scenario, and that included a lower in difficulty at the half way mark.
Which brings me to my next point. This game is incredibly difficult and oftentimes unforgiving. This works in sync with the story since it always places the protaganist in seemingly impossible situations. You could be nearly complete with a scenario and then suddenly have everything go wrong at the press of a button. Despite this issue, albeit frustrating, the difficulty is what makes the game. Through trial and error, you will figure out strategies from past mistakes and rethink your approach to the situation. I believe this to be the core design philosophy of the developers, however, this idea can be muddled if you become infuriated with the constant failure. To quell this frustration a little, I'd advise starting with Easy unless you are brave enough and want to suffer through the game repeatedly.
Anyways, thats the jist of the game. It's difficult, but you defitinely feel a strong sense of relief after each scenario. Before you call the game off as bad, however, I advise really thinking about the game's design in conjunction with its storyline. I think if more players unlocks this "not-so-secret" secret, then they will feel a little more appreciative and connected to the game.
Advice for newcomers:
- Start at Easy difficulty so you will enjoy what the game has to offer the first time through.
- Take your time and really think through your options. Time progresses only when you do an action, therefore keep calm and breath through the situations.
- Expect things to go wrong. Since a lot of the game relies on chance and probability, make sure you have a backup plan before you go all in.
- Take extra time to read what the scenario instructions (if available) tell you to do.
- Guessing is inevitable.

After the success of the remaster of the remade Resident Evil, CAPCOM dove back into the archives and remastered Resident Evil 0 (which was developed on the same engine for the Gamecube).
One thing that can be said right off the bat is just how much a work of art the game really is. One of the beauties of this genre and franchise originally was the highly detailed static environments of the original mansion and subsequent environs. When given the level of time, adding on top of that would seem like a rare success but in this case CAPCOM's team emphasized this perfectly. From the train to the training facility and everything thereafter, the player is inundated with shadowplay, detail and an overall enjoyable atmospheric experience. There are some elements that actually look pixelated such as the fireplace in the training facility off the balcony, but they are so rare that they needn't be mentioned.
The sound mastery and soundtrack itself are, yet again, another original that was simply touched up and gained greater eminence because of it. The theme to the training facility might be my favorite track from all of the Resident Evils. It encapsulates that feeling of being trapped in a large, eery place with such perfection. You can hear it 100 times and it still retains, if builds upon, it's original quality. And like many of the franchises' best from pre-RE5, the rest of the soundtrack holds a similar quality that helps create the sensory immersion and atmosphere that made the original so great.
Gameplay wise, it is just as the original which really means not complicated in the least. Very straightforward, and for some, a little sluggish. But not too much so to where it isn't enjoyable even for those who are used to variations on the modern FPS.
The negative aspects of the game really only come from a previous memory of the game. For instance, the faces of Rebecca and Billy have been touched up in certain areas and definitely seem different from the game I remember as a kid. Same can be said with the in-menu faces above the item slots. Also, the FMVs during cutscenes do look slightly dated, but not to the point where it detracts from the story or the game itself.
While I may be a little biased I still give it a solid 8/10 for being shrewdly touched-up version of the original, which supplanted itself in my mind as a child as one of the best horror games ever created.

Admittedly, I had my reservations about this game, primarily because of the obvious title exploitation (Dead Space (or Dead anything) and Mass Effect), however, I am very pleased with my choice to give the game a chance.
If you like first-person shooters with lots of action and intense situations, zombie and/or space themes, and challenging gameplay, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are great - there is a lot of detail in the environment and zombie character models. The music and sounds go extremely well with creating a tense, adrenaline-filled atmosphere. Even though the gameplay is fairly slow in the beginning (zombies move pretty slow initially), the music really adds to the intensity of facing a horde of zombies while having a limited ammo count.
The controls are straightforward for your typical first-person shooter (you also can't jump, crouch, or sprint) and the learning curve is minimal to moderate; however, the zombie mobs can get challenging if you decide to go on a shooting frenzy vs. conserving your ammo. Making your shots count is crucial because zombies can rush you while you are reloading or after you've missed a shot.
Upgrading/purchasing weapons and equipment occurs between levels, and the game keeps you playing by implementing a random drop chance with every playthrough. There are a variety of weapons and upgrades, increasing the replayability value. When you die, you may respawn (vs. restarting the entire mission) for a percentage of your money.
Although the pacing of the action starts off slow, the atmosphere is so perfect with the music score, tight environments, and reasonable number of enemies per area. Taking the time to look down your sights and pick your shots can and will be very rewarding (you want to maximize your headshots if possible).
The levels are not too long, but remain really fun and action-packed.
Great for people who like gore, zombies, and first-person action.
Highly recommend!

Dead Effect is an Early Access game that is worth the time and the cheap price tag.  For me the look and the intensity of this game was quite enjoyable.
In the past I've been quite dismissive of Early Access titles and this has been based on a few notorious titles and the comments of famous YouTube personalities.  It's not a perfect or finished game, but this is one title you don't have to worry about.
The game environment reminds me of Doom 3, and likely takes some inspiration from it. I like the graphics and it runs just fine on my old computer.  The sound and music are really good and contribute to the overall experience.  The voice acting isn't so great, but it's passable.
At first the game feels really slow, because it is not possible to sprint or jump; you move at one speed.  The zombies don't move fast either, but when hordes of them are coming for you, the experience feels tense.  If you let a couple of zombies get too close you're finished.  A lack of quick save and check points adds to the tension; you really want to finish each episode in one go.  If you die continuation is possible, but it'll cost you some in-game cash (don't worry, no micro-transactions or in-game spending of real world cash).
The game does have an auto-heal option, but one must play long enough to earn the right to activate this feature. It'll become clear this isn't necessary by that time anyway.  I recommend never turning it on.
Included are 6 playable episodes, as well as 2 extra game modes, Survival and Biohazard.  Survival mode requires fighting for a specified time, and Biohazard requires defeating a fixed number of waves of zombies.  It's pretty clear from the most recent July 17th, 2014 update that these guys are hard at work.  Co-op and multiplayer options are expected to be included if the development team gets enough support and feedback.
For me the game was enjoyable.  I recommend it to someone looking for a gory, old school FPS experience.  Considering this game is made by a team of 5 guys, I have to say: GOOD JOB!

Shadow of Mordor is an open world third person action game based on the Lord of the Rings franchise, following the story of Talion who seeks revenge on Mordor.
The story in Shadow of Mordor takes a while before it gets interesting, but the further you come, the better the story gets. This together with the fantastic cinematic and voice acting, can make the game really immersive. You are free to choose how you approach missions, whether it's going all-in, playing it stealthy or using enemies against each other. While playing through the game, you'll notice the scenery in this game is gorgeous, there's 2 different worlds for you to explore and they look amazing. Thanks to Photo-Mode it's really easy to make great screenshots as well, this is an editor that pauses the game and enables you to apply filters, move the camera, change fov etc.
Shadow of Mordor introduces the Nemesis system. The Nemeses also known as Sauron's Army, are the Uruk and Olog leaders that are generated uniquely with each playthrough of the game. Each nemesis has their own personality and will rise or fall within their social structure as the game progresses. They are affected by Talion's actions, and each will react differently to Talion's actions in Mordor, be it fight, flight, or some other reaction. Resulting in enemies reacting differently when you meet them after they've already killed or almost killed you. Enemies also have unique fears/strengths to discover which will be important in battles.
Combat is really well done and comparable to the Batman series, it looks amazing and plays great. The combat in general is quite easy (making the game easier as well) but is just really satisfying. You will have 3 options for combat, either go in with your sword and slice through orcs and finish them with some brute finishing moves, stealth kill them through sneaking or keep your distance and snipe them with your bow. Next to combat, movement is really well done. Sneaking over buildings, climbing and hanging on the side of walls Assasins Creed style, everything feels great, smooth and just works. However controls can feel a bit wonky at times.
Throughout the game you'll earn points to upgrade your weapons and skills. From movement to combat abilities. Everything can be upgraded and it's really fun to discover all the new upgrades. This gives motivation to keep on playing even after the Story mode(Which has a decent length of 10-15 hours). Cause there will be enough to do in the world of Mordor. Even after finishing the main missions, there's tons of things to do like: Taking down warchiefs/captains, rescuing people, Doing challenges, finding collectables and more! After you're done with everything, there's DLC that adds more missions/outfits.
Some downsides of the game however, are for example: some missions can feel a bit unnecessary because of repetitivity, some battles are really anticlimactic and the game can be quite easy due to its easy combat at times. Side characters could've been used better as well, some of them are easy to forget.
Overall, i would highly recommend Shadow of Mordor. It's a great game with lots of content, a decent story, satisfying combat and great scenery! However, the game is more oriented towards stealth gameplay, so make sure you like that.

An exceptionally well-crafted game.  Some of the reviews here confuse me.  I would not say this game is a Witcher III, but it doesn't pretend to be, and it doesn't carry the same price tag. I'd buy the game for $25 or less (Champion Edition).
The game does drop you into the world, like most classic rpgs, but once you're there it pulls you in.  I suspect some reviewers don't read the storylines much, and if so, then of course, much of the flavor of the world is lost.  Some characters are narrated, but many are not, so reading is a requirement.  I'd play this game when you'd like a relaxing game with a beer or coffee, when you've had your fill of intense FPS games or even rpg games that requirement all hands on deck and 100% attention.  This is truly Baldur's Gate style - when game were just fun, and often their story, while subtle, sticks with you for quite some time.
NPCs: 8/10
The NPC character you find have decently interesting storylines, though I do wish they had a couple romance options, and it doesn't quite seem as dynamic as the Baldur's Gate conversations. That is, your responses don't seem to have as many or as dramatic of an effect on relationships in your party.  I do miss that.
Storyline: 8/10
The storyline, as mentioned above, doesn't necessarily start off incredibly deep, and the NPC storylines don't do a terrible amount to pull at your heartstrings, but they aren't dull as some reviewers have said.  That would be unfair to them.  It's a unique story with lots of interesting turns and plenty to discover and that keeps me interested in the next chapter.  More importantly, the world is teeming with interesting stories.  For instance, some of the stories connected with the keep are absolutely great, and your choices feel important.  Similarly, some of your choices in other stories can lead to unexpected allies or prisoners in your keep.  That is an exceptional aspect of this game and there are few other games like this.  Reminds me of table-top rpg games I've played for years.  And it's certainly not any worse than something like Divinity: Original Sin which I eventually got bored of and didn't finish the main storyline.
Graphics, Visual Design: 8/10
The graphic aren't exemplary.  The photos do an accurate job showing potential buyers what they'll get.  It's basically a prettier Baldur's Gate.  Or, to use a newer game, it's much like Divinity: Original Sin.  It's, perhaps, a touch less pretty, but it's got unique art design.  Again, you're not getting Witcher III, but nor should you be expecting that.
Gameplay: 8/10
Here's where I think some reviewers have totally lost their minds.  The game play is in some ways, what you'll expect - once again, like Baldur's Gate.  It's *certainly* not worse.  That's complete madness to say.  And in some ways, it's unique and wonderful; I find some features incredibly refreshing and superior to Divinity: Original Sin which seems to be a fan favorite.  The short instances that you occasionally find for grappling hooks, prybars, and lockpicks are beautifully rendered and the choice to provide a mini-Choose Your Own Adventure in those is beautiful!  It makes me feel like a kid again, making important choices and discovering new treasures or adventures.  Traps can be useful depending on the scenery.  Unfortunately you can only put down one so it's sometimes hard to lead enemies into them, but that's realistic.  Combat lacks the synergies of Dragon Age and Divinity, and in that respect resembles old-school D&D games most.  But the endurance and health mechanic is new and interesting, and gives a realistic feel.  The limited number of campfire rests makes the player reluctant to rest all the time, which leads to some nailbiting combat, but there are just the right amount of extra campfire supplies spread throughout maps to reward players that carefully push on and manage their spells and health.  I've been playing on the hardest difficult on my first playthrough (without Iron Man of course, though).  And it's been a perfect difficulty for a cautious player.  In the beginning I did have to retry quite a few battles as I was getting my characters leveled up to a sweet spot and I was learning the system, as well as acquiring loot.  But once I did that, I've been moving along at a good but challenging pace, occasionally turning my attention away when I realize that I'm in too deep.  This is the perfect balance between challenging and fun.
In all, the game has some very innovative aspects.  I haven't mentioned a number of other interesting features like the stronghold aspect (which is simple but highly engaging) or the balance between quick stories and deep dungeons, or the crafting (which is expensive at first, but overall balanced) or the interesting unique items you can find.  There's so much love put into this game that it would be unfair to rate it at anything below an 8.  But it would also be inaccurate to put it at a 9, alongside the likes of Witcher III.

Dark Souls changed the gaming world for me. Its unique atmosphere and playstyle is what caught me and I consider it an ideal gaming world. There are no other RPGs that have the vibe that Dark Souls has, and because it is so unique; I keep returning to it. With that written, I can say that I can spend 1000+ hours on playing this game without getting bored.
Ofcourse you die a LOT of times and thus it could not actually be considered ideal; However, the atmosphere really seals the deal. We all have our dark moments and Dark Souls is a great release.
I have played this game using my keyboard and mouse. Although it was not recommended by friends and reviews; I did manage to finish it (and I probably took longer than I could have with a controller). The controls take a bit of getting used to, and there are some moves that you might miss out on, like kicking.
These missing moves will not stop you from being capable of finishing the game and they will not stop you from enjoying the game (once you have gotten used to the controls).
The story of the game is kind of unclear. This could be because:
I didn't spend enough time on reading;
I spent too much time between dialogues.
Either way, I do think that I am not the only one. Why else would there be videos about Dark Souls lore? I definitely recommend keeping up with the story. A story of tragedy, a story of the 'light' against the dark. Prepare to cry, some say.
It indeed has a great lore.
Last but not least, the atmosphere and story are greatly complimented by awesome soundtracks. Once one has looked into the Dark Souls lore, one will understand how the music dramatically affects the game. This results in some soundtracks being filled with epicness and some soundtracks being filled with pain and sorrow.
This review is probably not complete, I can keep on praising Dark Souls. Praise the sun! My fellow sinners!

Correcting itself after the error from Splinter Cell Conviction, the Splinter Cell series returns to its most successful and compelling formula, of having you play as a black ops espionage focused third person stealth game with action elements.
The game combines a very adequate artificial intelligence with randomized spawns to make each playthrough, even each reloaded checkpoint, very different.  Each level primary routes, secondary routes, and then secret routes through which the player can monitor, track, and avoid or take-out hostiles.
It provides the player with the necessary tools to go with either a passive or aggressive stealth play-style, or an all-out assault play style more akin to a third person shooter, though surviving is much harder this way.
Weapons and gadgets can all be upgraded and equipped with different accessories or abilities to alter their function more to suit your approach.
The story is rather interesting, although some of the characters in it are noticeably hollow and lacking.  The best characters you'll come to find are Sam, the arms dealer you capture, and the primary villain.  I'd say it's a slightly more compelling story than some of the other entries in the Splinter Cell series, for instance Double Agent, and maybe one of the earlier titles, due to the fact that it paces itself exceptionally well and keeps itself from being bogged down by the more intricate details.  Though it doesn't keep itself as grounded as Chaos Theory or Pandora Tomorrow, sacrificing believability for a high-stakes hollywood-esque action thriller storyline.
Definitely a high note for the series as a whole, but lacking the innovation and proper espionage thrill to warrant it praise among the best.

Do you like zombies?  Well... who doesn't.  If you are looking for a survival game with zombies, this is probably the best one currently on the market.  Project Zomboid would be the only other one I'd recommend.  This one, you need to focus on finding supplies and managing a group of survivors.  You can upgrade your fort and even move to different locations (Though limited to their choices).  Plus, with the two DLC which are really good, it gives you variety to the game play as opposed to just the main mission.  It's a third person style game and you will eventually run out of supplies.  Only draw back is you only have 1 map in the main game and have only the story mode.  You need the dlc to play survival or get an additional map.

IMMERSIVE & UNIQUE
The best games know the difference between a movie and a video-game, State of Decay is one of those few. SoD is a framework of interlocking systems that determines the fate of a handful of survivors that you control. You choose a place to build your base, scavenge for supplies to keep it going, run over zombies with cars and trade with and help other surviving communities.
Everything is finite; from resources and vehicles to ammo and indeed the survivors themselves; the AI is intelligent and reacts to events believably; treat someone badly or overwork them, and they may leave your roof, losing a well loved survivor to the zombies demoralizes the rest (and you too). Vehicles are powerful tools to kill massive hordes of zombies with, but if they get destroyed, you may soon find yourself at the mercy of the hordes.
Sound also plays an important role in your affairs in zombieville; running is more dangerous than walking, sneaking is the safest and slowest; speeding along the road in a car brings out all the zombies from their hidey holes, cruising slowly is safer, but not ideal when you are enroute to save someone.
Weapons break in the middle of fights; ammo runs out all too soon and dodging and shoving away the undead is as important as slicing their arms off and bashing their brainless heads against the closest wall.
While the main game does have a story that explains the mechanics; its the DLC Breakdown that is the 'Real' SoD for me; in Breakdown; once you start finding the game too easy (or run out of resources on the map); you can choose to refresh the map, this comes at a cost though; each time the map is refreshed, the game becomes harder, throwing more zombies at you, more hordes and more specials.
An important fact to note is that the game has a small but dedicated modding community with quite a few mods that enhance the gameplay and visuals. Its no Skyrim, but its something.
State of Decay is not a storytelling benchmark, its not a polished title from a well known studio, neither is it a graphical beast that will bring your computer to its knees; its much more than those trivial things.

Resident Evil 0 is a lot of fun. It's more of the campy, gory, spooky good time we enjoy from the RE series and it offers a robust challenge. Lots of dying in this game. This is the last in the series that is essentially an action packed point-and-click adventure game and I appreciate the opportunity to play RE0 once again. Sure the puzzles are not necessarily realistic, but the whole series is always bordering on parody as it is. The level design isn't as strong as in previous titles of the series and some of the environments gave a strong sense of deja vu. The very worst thing about this game, though, is the inventory management. Holy f.ck! Each character can only hold six items and there was always a constant need to switch items between characters, leave items in a room and then have to hike all the way back for them once there was enough room in the inventory. Some items even took up two spots in the inventory. I understand this was a necessary feature for how some of the puzzles were designed, but... how dare they! There is a lot of back tracking in game simply because of the terrible inventory system. The main villain was laughably awful too. Everything he said was re-tarded and he looked like some androgynous NPC from a Final Fantasy game. Don't get me wrong, the puzzle solving, exploration, and blowing away monsters were a grand time and most of the game is spent doing these things. It took around 15 hours to finish the game for the first time. There's definitely incentive to re-play it too; and not just because it's a fun game in general either. After finishing the game for the first time, the ability to play as Wesker is unlocked. This is essentially easy mode. He has an attack that can clear a room faster than grandma's chili. It was a thrill to see groups of enemies all instantly drop dead in unison from a single blast. Boss battles became a breeze. Most only took around 3 blasts from Wesker to kill. There's another mode that wasn't as interesting to me where Rebecca and Billy need to find leech charms scattered throughout the mansion. RE0 still looks pretty good after all these years. Kudos to Capcom for the job they did polishing this game up, getting it ready for this HD release. The water animations stand out as the most impressive part of the presentation. Slime oozes from leeches, water from a filled sink splashes around dripping to the floor, and the rain beats down on top of the train all in convincing fashion, to give a few examples. Even a very simple cut-scene of water flowing from a pipe was impressive to watch. From a technical standpoint, the game ran flawlessly. The frame rate was consistently a rock solid 60fps and the game never crashed. RE0 won't win any converts to the series, but it's still a really good game that I highly recommend, even if it doesn't reach as high levels the series has previously reached.

I've had an amazing time with this game. Being a massive fan of the RE series, especially  the more 'classic' style games, this was the best thing I've played since, well, REmake HD to be honest. The partner mechanic mixed with the limited inventory system makes for some interesting tactical choices. I found myself unequipping the useless AI and using them as a pack mule, using my armed character to scout ahead and my then bringing in the unequipped character as a pack mule. Unfortunately when buddied up, the partner AI is prone to wasting ammo and running straight into the enemies arms and is one of the few cons i have against the game.
In regards to the inventory management, the ability to drop items is a mixed blessing. While I didnt suffer too much backtracking, I did have to cart myself all the way to an area I visited hours ago as I hadn't been able to bring my grenade launcher with me. With it being just before the final boss, it killed my momentum a little. That said, it does add more depth to the gameplay than the 'magic box' system favoured by the other classic titles and goes a long way to underlining the survival aspect of Survival Horror.
My playthrough took me 6 in game hours (according to my ranking at the end) or around 8-9 actual hours with deaths and reloads. I found that Normal was actually quite challening, more so than REmake HD. In fact Zero is up there with Code Veronica as personally what I believe to be the most challenging games in the series. With that in mind though the tougher than average difficulty really helped keep me invested in the game. If like me, its your first time playing this since the Gamecube days, then you arent going to have a lot of surplus ammo or healing items even by the end boss. I appreciated this personally, as I find with most RE games, the difficulty drops off sharply after the first half, by which point the 'magic box' has enough ammo and herbs in to last for another full playthough.
Graphically, I can't fault the presentation at all. While being less atmospheric that REmake, the environments still sing with the HD makeover. Character models, lighting and shadows are all very immersive too. With everything maxed my mid range PC never struggled to keep a 60hz refresh rate.
In terms of story, its probably one of the weaker of the series to be honest. It perhaps takes itself too seriously compared to the more 'B-Movie' values of the earlier installments. The story is serviceable but in all honesty, as a prequel it fails to tell us anything that would be integral to the understanding of the plot of the subsequent games. Dialog and cutscenes are actually quite sparse and it would have probably benefitted the game to have more interaction between the 2 playable characters. As it stands, they barely say a word to each other once their characters have been established.
There's plenty more I could say but the most important thing is I strongly reccomend the game. I actually enjoyed it a lot more than I did around 10+ years ago when I first played it. If you have the determination and the patience this is a great title thats more than worth the budget price.

Basically the same game that was released on the Gamecube back in 2002. The visuals have improved, in some places the difference are noticable, in others not so much. The game runs great on my PC, nice smooth framerate. Capcom threw in an additional set of alternate skins for the two main playable characters but nothing special.
I recommend this game to anyone who is an Resident Evil fan looking to replay this one, or maybe play for the first time since it was originally a Gamecube game. I'm not going to lie, the story for this game is weak and confusing. The inventory system while unique to the previous Resident Evil games can be annoying as hell. This certainly isn't as good as the Resident Evil 1 remake, but for $20 worth buying for any RE fan, or anyone who likes the older classic survival horror games.

The game is just as amazing as I remember from 2002, although I did not play it until 2007 when I was able to grasp the concept of inventory management and ammo conservation. Until I played it for myself I had watched my father play it, but when I did, oh boy was I glad I decided to play it myself. This is mostly due to the fact that my dad never beat the game and I wanted to see the ending.
Now as for the Remastered HD port here on PC, it is glorious. Runs 1080p 60fps everywhere except for 2 instances. Cutscenes which are capped at 30 fps, and room transitions, which I have had drop to as low as 19fps, but only for a split second. It isn't too big of an issue, but the fact it does it on my system is bothersome. That is with the game maxed out on a PC running an FX-8350 CPU and a GTX 980 graphics card. As you can see my PC blows the Recommended, and probably Max settings requirement out of the water. Like I said it isn't too big an issue to dock any points off, but the fact it happens is a little bothersome.
My rating for this game, is as it was for the GCN version, 10/10
Edit: So I should mention as well that the controls are vastly different than REmastered. Coming from Resident Evil to Zero took a little getting used to, at least for controller, I think Keyboard can be remapped to exactly REmastered. Also... holding B is how you run in Zero with a controller... X is the Status screen... they really should've switched those.

5 months ago, I wrote this review. But it's time to edit it as versions 1.3 and 1.4 improved greatly the game.
It's pretty rare when I install Early Access. And when I saw the video after buying a Groupees bundle, I was like: OMFG, IT LOOKS LIKE DOOM3! Being a huge fan of the series Doom (my first FPS was DOOM II), I didn't hesitate to activate the game.
If you want the cards, I stop you right now: it can take time to farm them - I don't know if it's still the case.
Back to the review, when I launched Dead Effect, I didn't know that it was first a game for tablets. And when I played the first minutes, I saw immediately some little problems but it's Early Access after all. But never did I feel like I was in a port of an iOS game. Developers managed to do a very decent port, listening to us, early access players: they added a run option very very helpful in 1.3.
Like I've said, it looks like Doom 3 and so, I'm not disappointed in graphics. It's dark enough to see your path (but not always the enemies) but the flashlight isn't really brightening the room. Remember that I had an hard time to find the flashlight icon? Well, it's no more the case. I can see it clearly, probably because of the change of design and the run icon.
I'm really feeling like I'm lost in space, though Dead Space will stay as number one in that feeling (I said Dead Space, not Dead Space 2 or 3). Weapons for now look good: the Stungun is powerful enough to kill an enemy. But the problem is the slow reload (even if you can buy upgrades after each mission). Ammo, like credits, are seen from far away thanks to big icons  (which I love) but tablets are difficult to spot - Doom 3 made me a PDA or documents searching lover. Anyway, now, all the tablets that you found can be read from the main menu.
Single player campaign is finished, they added more for Survival and Biohazard and I found myself in better shape with the run option AND the devastation power, new to 1.3. And I love the new weapon, the Deviant-Arc. Anyway, with all the weapons available (some can be bought with gold), you can really find your own style (even with the bow and the crossbow).
They also redid the main menu - removing mainly all leftovers from the mobile version (like game center) - in 1.4 and fixed some bugs. Like I said, they're listening to us.
Grenade zombies are less powerful (well, can't say that in Hell difficulty but at least in Easy and Medium, you don't die from one hit). The new ennemy, while not really a badass in Easy, is really doing damages and resistant in higher difficulty. I think that it's not even in the mobile version. I should try it because the APK for Android was in an Humble Bundle (got the PC on Groupees, remember).
And what's best? I can play a woman. Being a woman myself, I love playing as my gender.
Soundtrack is good, like the voice acting, it's very professionnal. And Wagner's laugh...
I'll tell you something: I enjoy it. Zombies in space? Yeah, seen and seen. But when you have a serious team, listening to players, behind that type of game, it can lead to a very good game. And for five bucks, even in Early Access,... well, it's worthy of your wallet. Besides, while co-op and multi are still absents, the developers have the intention to develop it. But like they said, they needed time. And I can wait a long time with them. I don't mind. Because they're listening to their customers, always answering you in the forums and thanking you for the bugs you found. Hey,zmetekvonsexistroj even took the time to thank me for the review in July :)

Awful, awful, awful. I liked everything that I heard and read about this game. The dark sci-fi setting, the decision-based point and click, the intense and dramatic music...and then I started playing. I figured, I'm a decent gamer, I'll try it on "original" difficulty. After twelve tries on the first task I gave up and switched to "easy" difficulty, figuring that I was much more interested in the storyline than the gameplay anyway. After six more tries on "easy" I finally made it through the first chapter. I was then introduced to chapter 2, where my character is being interrogated in violent fashion, I was soon informed that I would be performing the same torture sequence TWENTY TIMES! The game actually tells you that you have to survive, performing the same repetitive task, TWENTY TIMES in a row, each one taking about two minutes. And screw up once, you get to go back and do it all over again. The original writing wears itself out once you've read it four times, and can look forward to doing it two dozen more times before you get it right. I understand the idea of a game with consequences or where your character can die forcing you to try again, but the whole premise of this game is try the same task over and over and over and over again. Even on EASY DIFFICULTY. My patience wore out, having not even finished chapter two. This is a complete waste of money, do not buy this game unless you enjoy the idea of performing the same tedious thing over and over and over and over again. This game will appeal to the same kind of people that enjoy going to the dentist for a root canal. I seriously cannot stress enough how awful a game experience this "game" provides. If you're intrigued by the story, and I know that I was before playing it, then go on youtube and watch someone else play through the game for the story, then come back and thank me for sparing you the aggravation of actually dealing with this game. DO NOT BUY THIS "GAME".

In one chapter, you are just around a fire and need to keep everyone alive and the fire runing, and you need to care about their health. In another chapter, you are in a desert with a big team and need to care for water and ammunition, while moving around the desert.
I'm very curious how all this ends. I could go on playing 100 chapters of this! :)

An exceptionally well-crafted game.  Some of the reviews here confuse me.  I would not say this game is a Witcher III, but it doesn't pretend to be, and it doesn't carry the same price tag.  I would say I did buy the Champion Edition on sale for 66% off, and I have never regretted the purchase.  As you can see, I have quite a few hours in the game, so I've gotten my money's worth.  I'd buy the game for $25 or less (Champion Edition).
The game does drop you into the world, like most classic rpgs, but once you're there it pulls you in.  I suspect some reviewers don't read the storylines much, and if so, then of course, much of the flavor of the world is lost.  Some characters are narrated, but many are not, so reading is a requirement.  I'd play this game when you'd like a relaxing game with a beer or coffee, when you've had your fill of intense FPS games or even rpg games that requirement all hands on deck and 100% attention.  This is truly Baldur's Gate style - when game were just fun, and often their story, while subtle, sticks with you for quite some time.
NPCs: 8/10
The NPC character you find have decently interesting storylines, though I do wish they had a couple romance options, and it doesn't quite seem as dynamic as the Baldur's Gate conversations. That is, your responses don't seem to have as many or as dramatic of an effect on relationships in your party.  I do miss that.
Storyline: 8/10
The storyline, as mentioned above, doesn't necessarily start off incredibly deep, and the NPC storylines don't do a terrible amount to pull at your heartstrings, but they aren't dull as some reviewers have said.  That would be unfair to them.  It's a unique story with lots of interesting turns and plenty to discover and that keeps me interested in the next chapter.  More importantly, the world is teeming with interesting stories.  For instance, some of the stories connected with the keep are absolutely great, and your choices feel important.  Similarly, some of your choices in other stories can lead to unexpected allies or prisoners in your keep.  That is an exceptional aspect of this game and there are few other games like this.  Reminds me of table-top rpg games I've played for years.  And it's certainly not any worse than something like Divinity: Original Sin which I eventually got bored of and didn't finish the main storyline.
Graphics, Visual Design: 8/10
The graphic aren't exemplary.  The photos do an accurate job showing potential buyers what they'll get.  It's basically a prettier Baldur's Gate.  Or, to use a newer game, it's much like Divinity: Original Sin.  It's, perhaps, a touch less pretty, but it's got unique art design.  Again, you're not getting Witcher III, but nor should you be expecting that.
Gameplay: 8/10
Here's where I think some reviewers have totally lost their minds.  The game play is in some ways, what you'll expect - once again, like Baldur's Gate.  It's *certainly* not worse.  That's complete madness to say.  And in some ways, it's unique and wonderful; I find some features incredibly refreshing and superior to Divinity: Original Sin which seems to be a fan favorite.  The short instances that you occasionally find for grappling hooks, prybars, and lockpicks are beautifully rendered and the choice to provide a mini-Choose Your Own Adventure in those is beautiful!  It makes me feel like a kid again, making important choices and discovering new treasures or adventures.  Traps can be useful depending on the scenery.  Unfortunately you can only put down one so it's sometimes hard to lead enemies into them, but that's realistic.  Combat lacks the synergies of Dragon Age and Divinity, and in that respect resembles old-school D&D games most.  But the endurance and health mechanic is new and interesting, and gives a realistic feel.  The limited number of campfire rests makes the player reluctant to rest all the time, which leads to some nailbiting combat, but there are just the right amount of extra campfire supplies spread throughout maps to reward players that carefully push on and manage their spells and health.  I've been playing on the hardest difficult on my first playthrough (without Iron Man of course, though).  And it's been a perfect difficulty for a cautious player.  In the beginning I did have to retry quite a few battles as I was getting my characters leveled up to a sweet spot and I was learning the system, as well as acquiring loot.  But once I did that, I've been moving along at a good but challenging pace, occasionally turning my attention away when I realize that I'm in too deep.  This is the perfect balance between challenging and fun.
In all, the game has some very innovative aspects.  I haven't mentioned a number of other interesting features like the stronghold aspect (which is simple but highly engaging) or the balance between quick stories and deep dungeons, or the crafting (which is expensive at first, but overall balanced) or the interesting unique items you can find.  There's so much love put into this game that it would be unfair to rate it at anything below an 8.  But it would also be inaccurate to put it at a 9, alongside the likes of Witcher III.

It's hard to describe how good this game is. The graphics aren't something that will blow people away who are use to current games like The Witcher 3, Bloodborne, or Final Fantasy XV. The world itself is excellently crafted, but being a Obsidian game that is only expected. The story line is well polished and the side quests don't seem like some tedius things you have to go out of your way to do, or will bore you and not be worth your time, they flow nicely into the over all story of the game. The sound is also very well done, the music feels like it belongs and isn't something I just want to turn off. And the sounds over all adds to atmosphere of the game from it's dungeons to the wilderness.
Obsidian is known for great games such as Fallout New Vegas, and Neverwinter Nights 1 and 2. For $18 it is a steal, that will provide a very in depth old school role playing game that will last for hours upon hours.

A solid isometric, party-based RPG.  It tries to bridge a highly linear story with some more "open-world concepts" (like managing a keep and optional tasks) but that feels mostly tacked on, so while the ancillary activites are interesting they take urgency away from the main storyline.  Combat against particularly difficult enemies (dragons) or at the higher difficulty levels requires a lot of micro-management and highly optimized character builds (from among a very diverse set of charcter types), something that reduces immersion for me (the characters become more a collection of abilities than participants in a story) which is a shame because the characters are well-fleshed out, and the best part of the story.  Overall, I recommend the game to those with a familiarity with, and fondness for, this type of RPG, it may be a tough transition for folks coming from open-world, first-person RPGs (Skyrim) or JRPGs.  The ability to shift the difficulty down to allow for more focus on the story is welcome, however, and can ease this transition if you are the type of person who will allow yourself to do that.

Counter Strike: Condition Zero is a great game. For a game that was released on the GoldSrc engine the graphics are not that bad. Don't get me wrong they are still outdated but they were pretty impressive for its time. This game has basiclly everything the original Counter Strike had and much more. For starters there is the tour of duty mode which is a singeplayer campaign (NO STORY) where you go around famous counter strike map and have to complete objects such as defuse a bomb or rescue hostages. You will also be given mini challenges to complete in that mission (Challenges change depending on what difficulty you select) Along with that you can also download extra 3rd Party Campaigns made by players around the world. Now we move on to Counter Strike: Condition Zero Deleted Scenes and this is actually a seperate game that games with the base game and CS: CZDS is also a singleplayer campaign mode but unlike the tour of duty campaign mode this is actually more of a missions because your not playing clasic counter strike game modes but are rather faced with what appears to be Half-Life singleplayer with counter strike elements. And unlike classic counter strike you can't buys weapons instead you have to find and pick up weapons as you go alone and while it may stray far from the classic Counter Strike Formula you will find that it still actually feels like a actualy counter strike game while at the same time give a quite refreshing start to the game. In the end I would reccomend CS: CZ to old CS fans and even new comers as this is a great game and still has a large community to this day.

The plot is extremely minor and you won't know what's going on until very late in the game (There's a good quantity of foreshadowing though), and that hurt my interest in the game to get my full interest (Aside the Oddworld brand). The difficulty curve sometimes is out of place as some late bosses or areas can be taken down with ease but a few early ones or previous to those are overwhelming. The story is fairly simple. You are the stranger. An alien with a serious medical problem that is very expensive to fix. To fix it you need to get a LOT of money, and you do this by hunting down enemies Boba Fett style.
This is probably the best Bounty Hunter game ever made. Capturing crooks and using skill to take them alive rather than dead is one of those things you'll feel really good about. Mind you, the game drowns you in money, so you can easily get all the upgrades without capturing the crooks alive and all that. (Probably for the best.)

Play the game. It's a very solid port (I had no problems with it, but I've heard others have. So probably give it some research first.)

: I've been meaning to update this review to reflect the changes introduced by the game's extra difficulty options an I apologize for not having done so sooner. While I haven't spent a lot of time playing the new modes, all evidence points towards them providing acceptable alternatives which fix some of the issues highlighted below. I will leave my original review intact as the main difficulty hasn't changed any, and will hopefully have additional thoughts up eventually.
As I sit here and enter the same commands over and over again, I feel a certain autonomy take over. My mind has numbed to the plight of those whom I hold at the end of my gun. Empathy has long since ejected from the escape pods and crash landed onto a dead, sandy planet nearby. Common sense jettisoned eons ago. I shoot them in non-vital locations, I punch them repeatedly ‘til their faces look like the meat Rocky used to practice with. They beg me not to do anything crazy and I just don’t care. Oceans gush forth from blood stained eyes, the salty water providing no comfort or nourishment to parched souls. My finger is quivering above the trigger, its cold steel the only thing I know anymore. Lost to the hypnotic whir of densely packed computerized science equipment, I drift off in a daze in the midst of the situation. Why do I feel so disconnected from these horrific events? Have I always been this broken or has something made me this way? Why is it that, somewhere in the back of my mind, I feel like I have done this all before?
Oh, that’s right. Because I ♥♥♥♥ing have.
Gods Will Be Watching has been advertised as a game about choice, moral conundrums, and how far you’ll go for the sake of the mission. This is, unfortunately, not what the game turned out to be. Instead, it may be best to view it as a puzzle game, one in which you need to figure out the optimal pattern for shooting hostages in the leg, hacking the computer, and holding  off the oncoming SWAT team, all while keeping your hostages from losing their minds or getting a little too comfortable instead of fitting tetrominos together for a high score. It had all of the potential to be a memorable, stressfully worthwhile “experience” like Papers, Please. Unfortunately, the execution of its many parts fail to come together in any meaningful way, much like the game’s choices or lack thereof.
Despite flashing choice as though you were at an all-you-can-cry buffet of nerve testing conundrums a la The Walking Dead Season 1, there’s very little in the way of consequence to anything you do. Characters whom you watch violently expire from this godless universe will magically re-appear in the later chapters, which I will cover more later, even going so far as to having their ghost speak to you. Every situation has a set of conditions that must absolutely be met in order to progress or else you will be judged by the gods as unworthy and forced to redo the entire chapter. Failing to keep a specific person alive can doom you towards the end of a segment, mismanaging your various resources could lead to an instant ‘game over’, or the RNGods may decide that on this die roll that revolver will finally go off and plaster the wall with your brains.
The skill-based deaths and resets I could forgive to a degree, but the fact that die rolls can force you to lose 30 minutes of progress requiring you to do every painstaking move over again to try and progress is mind boggling. Even more so when you realize that there are no mid-chapter saves at all. The only saves that occur take place at the beginning of a chapter, so if you have to quit the game at all you will need to either finish that chapter first or be okay with your work vanishing. To call this a shortcoming is understating how frustrating the entire lack of saves thing really is. Almost every single chapter drags on needlessly and could have easily been cut in half with progress doubled to allow each scenario to only last 10-15 minutes instead of 30-45.
I audibly groaned when the torture sequence teased that it would last longer than 20 days. The desert scenario is almost entirely centered around RNG rolls and luck deciding you were worthy. At least some of the other chapters, such as the hostage scenario in chapter one, tie their mechanics to detailed animations that give you an idea of exactly where you stand with each element of the puzzle. The Russian Roulette segment can, and potentially will, send you back to the beginning of the chapter it appears in. I mean, I watched The Deer Hunter too and I didn’t think it would make for a good idea in a video game! Thematically, it’s cool, but leave it to cutscenes like Killer 7 did.
It’s a shame too, as the story presented could have made more of an impact if people could actually make it to the final chapters to see everything tie together. Players have been noticing a lot of inconsistencies and oddities, citing the game’s touting of choice as though it would matter and being disappointed that killing off a character in one chapter would leave them alive in the next. The story does, in fact, get around to explaining why this occurs but it happens so late in the game that I worry most players will have given up long before then. I get that the story uses the cycle of repeating the scenarios over and over again but it’s just not that fun. It’s like a Coen Brothers movie that misses its own point.
Gods Will Be Watching tested my patience, caused me to do things I wouldn’t have ordinarily considered doing, and made me live out the harsh life of Sgt. Burden, with us both wondering why the Gods insisted on punishing us so. In the end, the developers’ insistence on arbitrary difficulty through randomization under pressing time and resource limits and difficulty spikes really slaughters any momentum that could build up and may leave players feeling unsatisfied. I grew so frustrated by restarts that I ended up caving and playing on easy. Even then, the game was no cake walk. Perhaps the point of the game is to break me down and wear out my ability to give a damn. But somewhere deep within myself and Sgt. Burden, we found the will to continue on. Something driving us forward despite the odds. But not many others will, I fear. And for their sake, I hope the Gods are listening as well.

Gods Will Be Watching has a fantastic art style and a wonderful soundtrack, but where the game lets itself down is in the story and gameplay departments. (The story is good until the end)

Don't get me wrong here, I think GWBW is (for the most part) a good game to some degree, It offers an experience that many games fail to capture and create, a gritty and intense point 'n' click game that will have you on the edge of your seat and make your hands sweat and the thought of some of the decisions you will have to make, or at least, that is what I first thought.

( Before I continue, I am not saying the developers were lying about this, this is Gods Will Be Watching, not The War Z, but as I continue, you will see what I mean. )

All of that is merely and illusion, at first, you will be grinding your teeth like a madman, and twitching like a hyperactive 5 year old, but then you see the bigger picture, and you realize the fact that all those things simply aren't true anymore.

For Example, there are choices you will have to make, choices that at first seem important, but these choices don't even matter in the long run. ( i.e: ***SPOILERS*** There are multiple decisions in the game that can lead to the deaths of certain members of your posse, but in the next chapter, they can all be back and ready to go, even though the just died in the last chapter/ And yes I know about the ending, I will get to that later. ***SPOILERS***  )

The choices only matter for the chapter you are on, it no longer makes the game intense and nerve-racking, it turns the game into a resource management game, where you have to restart every time something goes wrong, it sucks out all the fun I had with the game.

The games has no checkpoints, great for all you hardcore gamers and dark souls elitists, but for me, it was just another sucker-punch to the gut every time I failed. And yes I realize 'that is the way the game is meant to be', but is it really, you could of at least put in a few save points, like when you get to the second stage in chapter 3. It can get frustrating having to play the same mission over and over again to get to the point you were last at.

Like this one time, I was 2 days away from escaping the planet in chapter 4, and everyone was fine, healthy and mostly happy, the campfire looked like it had one or two more days in it, ( The last day flame looks pretty big for what it is ) so I talked to everyone and cooked some food, but boy was I wrong, the next day the fire went cold, not to worry I thought, I'll just make a new one, so I got some wood and placed it one the campfire, now time to light it, but wait, no more bullets left, and Sgt. Burden being the mong he is said the fire couldn't be re-lit without bullets, so we all froze to death with one day left. Couldn't be re-lit, what was that bloody flame torch Donald has to repair the radio, and don't tell me it isn't a torch, 'cause it both looked and sounded like one, I would place my bets that it also tasted, smelt and felt like one too.

So fast-forward a few chapters and you get to chapter 7, the big bad boss of the game, what will the final chapter be? A combination of all that we have learn't from the other chapters, rolled into one hard-as-nails mega chapter. No, a prolonged game of Simon ♥♥♥♥ing Says, not joke, go to Youtube and watch it if you haven't already beat the game, I'll wait for you.

Yes the climax of the game is Simon Says. ***SPOILERS*** In this chapter, Burden starts to dribble story and exposition about how he has done this a million times, where Liam said the same thing I was thinking, 'Burden are you insane', this is the part where it only confirmed my suspicions, Burden was crazy and this was all some twisted perspective on the story, and that Burden was really Alexander or something, but much to my surprise, no. ***SPOILERS***

Now I am going to spoil the ending, look away now if you don't want it spoiled, don't say I didn't warn you. ***SPOILERS*** It turns out that Burden is stuck in some looping paradox, where he  replays the the events, or chapters if you will, over and over. Aside from this being the worst way anyone could possibly end anything, apart from maybe it was all a dream or some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it turns the game into a one big '♥♥♥♥ You!' to the player. It was like the nice men and women from Deconstructeam offered me a deal that was too good to refuse, then they quickly beat me with socks stuffed with the frozen tears of the last guy or girl.

After you beat Liam in a game of Simon Says, Burden spouts some more about what he is doing is the right thing, and if this is all meaningless if he is just going to do it again, but this time he finally beat Liam, and I thought he had broken the cycle, Burden says a few last words to Liam before choosing to cure the planet or to let Xenolifer do its thing, ( The endings are no different, it is just what direction the cure floats in ) and letting himself get carried away to the void of space and time.

I was genuinely sad at this, the music in the background was perfect and you could just imagine Burden's thoughts and feels, that maybe he had finally broken the cycle, and in some heart-breaking final stand of emotion, commit suicide. So I sat there, all depressed at the ending, I liked Burden, really I did, then all of a sudden, wormhole portal that continues the loop, ( from what I understand ) and Burden just floats into it, I was no longer sad, I was angry, come on he beat them, he won, but he still has to do all that again. It turned that '♥♥♥♥ You!' into  a massive flaming '♥♥♥♥ You!' with twisty nip-tassels.

If I have misunderstood the ending, and he really when into a black-hole and was atomically destroyed, then that makes it even sadder. ( But I doubt I did, seeing as it said epilogue and showed Burden in the desert waking up, the beginning of the cycle ) It would of been nice to have a small prologue of what came after and what happened to my team, but it is an indie game from a same indie company.

Now I know I am making it out the people at Deconstructeam to be evil villains, it is all part of the show, honestly the guys and girls at Deconstructeam, you have made a fantastic gem of a game, but it is just buried deep in an exterior of dirt, and I know you have put your blood, sweat and tears into creating this, and I get it can be crushing to hear someone slander your work off, with a bit of polishing, you have yourself a game a can truely be happy about being int he steam library. And yes I know, 'OMG JAKE I BET YOU COULDN'T DO BETTER,♥♥♥♥♥, your right, I can't, but if you saw a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ movie, in your opinion, but you couldn't make a better one, because you don't have the experience, knowledge or resources to do so, doesn't mean you can't be critical of it, your are going to say it was ♥♥♥♥♥♥, so don't give me that.

I am not saying the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ btw, it's great, I just can't recommend it because of a few flaws it has.

I was hoping for this deep, decisive survival game where my actions lead to meaningful consequence and the harshness causes gripping moral reflection in me...
What I got is a gory, strictly story driven resource management game where I min/max my way past the fail-states until I can figure out the patterns after dying 12 times.
Not disappointed with my purchase since I actually kinda like latter, but all of it is decidedly "meh"-worthy and it took me some time to readjust away from my expectations and try to get along with what I was eventually presented with. Eventually, I did like the atmosphere and I approve of the art, music and even the setting as the game's greatest merits. However, the systems and the story told simply don't play along nice.
Take Chapter 2 for instance. You're captured and are brutally tortured. The retort between your torturer who explains himself and the way you hold out by crafting an elaborate web of lies are actually pretty riveting... for the first 3 times.
Then the game falls flat and literally pulls out its own carpet out from under itself in this dialogue:
"There has to be a pattern to his torture. Most psychopats have."
"Yeah, if only I had a dozen lives to figure it out."
And you do! And its such a disappointment in its own way. Took me getting beaten to death twice to figure out begging actually works when you're in the bleeding posture, took me 6 drawn molars to realize I'm pretty safe lying after constructing a ruse by thinking twice.
I've now been killed thrice by getting ripped in half on the torture rack.
If that sounds extreme; don't worry. You'll get used to it. The game loses a lot of its charm and all investment you could have had for the plight of your characters, as you conquer its systems instead of enjoy the experience, which is the exact opposite of what I wanted. The survival horror is still present, but the game fails to marry it with the mechanics.
Now, this is a tough game. I recognize that. I'm not even punishing it for that and I'm not part of the conga-line of people that blame the game for being too hard or random. I'm the kind of guy that whips out a pen and paper whenever the game befuddles me and I can promise you that a lot of these actions aren't as random as you might think, or can be compensated for by mastering other factors.
And very rarely, yes, it is simply Russian Roulette - literally so in Chapter two torture scene where a seven bullet gun with one chamber loaded is placed against your head. Things like that are the only factors that are completely random (inside an otherwise predetermined routine mind you), but oddly enough this was the only situation that after neatly figuring out how to survive the entire jount and the most grizzly tortures on paper, that still managed to get a kick out of me and made me deeply empathize with what was on-screen. Didn't bat an eyelash being tore in two on the rack or getting an arm lobbed off since I know how to avoid that, but damn if that gun didn't made me turn away and close my eyes every frackin time. Its been a long time a game made me do that.
But do hostages that detailed truly add to the situation, or do they simply become faceless fickle systems you need to master? And why are their random failstates in a game I've learned to play as a spreadsheet system, even though those are sometimes the best moments? Should they be? Can I truly feel for characters I've seen die and resurrect more times than I care to count? (Even though I still really enjoy seeing these characters getting fleshed out under such bizarre circumstances.)
All of it is simply too disjointed.
I still think there are moments of brilliance though. The concept sounded really good on paper and some of the systems work brilliantly, even though not unified enough to create an end-product that I can recommend or understand.
If Gods Will Be Watching can be compared to a failed product other than a game, than it would be a wrongly crafted piece of jewelry where all the gemstones poke haphazardly out of an ugly clump of gold.
I just wish someone would take note of the design and not the result, to create the game that I would have liked Gods Will be Watching to be.
