This is a big disappointment. I was expecting this "HD REMASTER" to be a proper PC port, with decent mouse controls. Instead it lovingly recreates the old console controller experience. Playing this with the keyboard is awkward at best.
The slavishness of the console port is obvious at every turn, from it constantly reminding you not to turn off your computer while it's saving (as if people do that), to the clunky menu interactions. You can use the mouse for most things, but sometimes you can't, just to keep things nicely inconsistent.
Also recreated are the pointlessly long scene intercuts,  sluggish transition to and from character inventory and so on.,. I love to spend my time watching a door on a black background, just like it was 1997, back when some rubbish Capcom programmer found a way to pull data off the Playstation CD so ineptly that you could fill the entire console's RAM off the disc ten times over in the time they spent loading one backdrop. Why recreate a defect of an antique console on a modern PC with a perfectly good hard-drive? It's not cute, it's absurd. It's not suspenseful, it's boring.
The worst thing of all is the inability to stop playing the game whenever I want, without losing progress.
The lack of an ability to quit out and then simply resume at will is unacceptable in this era. Sure, the ribbons should still control actual saves (ability to reload after death or at will) but not being able to stop when I want and resume when I want just don't fit with the time I have to devote to this game.
The graphics are spruced up nicely, but this only highlights the archaic gameplay. Compared to the Wii port of RE4, which did a lot to make the controls enjoyable, this is awful. The only reason to play it is nostalgia.

Unresponsive controls, and very restricted set of control options. Inaccurate weapons, both via reticle and iron sights, and a very limited selection of them at that. Incredibly bad writing the developers actually somehow are delusional enough to think is any good. A supporting character you'll want to stab to death due to his self-importance, but can't and are stuck with.
3/10. Anybody who actually recommends this game has incredibly low standards, and their opinions regarding what makes a game good should be completely disregarded, because they clearly have standards so low, if it was a bar, it would be buried in the dirt.

Resident Evil 0 deserves more credit.
Of all the more traditional games in the series prior to Resident Evil 4's more action-y gameplay overhaul, 0 receives the most trash talk. It first appeared in 2002, well after all but the most ardent of fans were tired of the survival horror formula and ready for something new. Despite a few minor additions, Resident Evil 0 didn't offer that.
But that's precisely why this Resident Evil 0 HD re-release from Capcom is so useful. With distance from the atmosphere surrounding its release, it's a lot easier to view Resident Evil 0 for exactly what it is: a flawed but generally satisfying and, more importantly, smart take on Capcom's approach to horror.
And yet, aside from the very last area, I found Resident Evil 0's locales interesting enough to alleviate any frustration from backtracking. These are tightly-designed settings, paced perfectly to emphasize tension. I was rarely sent running in a direction I'd already been in without the area suddenly being invaded by a new nightmare creature, or without finding myself unexpectedly stalked by a returning foe. Even as the game advanced and I built up a healthy backpack of ammunition for my guns, I always felt just one or two bad rooms away from losing everything.
For as much as Resident Evil 0 embraces the series' classic gameplay, it also adopts the goofy, heavy-handed and poorly voice-acted storytelling of the franchise's earliest entries. If you're expecting serious drama from Rebecca and Billy, you're in for a disappointment, and don't even get me started on the game's hilariously ineffective villain. But if you love the cornier approach to survival horror, before everything took itself so seriously, it's a blast.
Removed from the moment in time when it debuted, Resident Evil 0 is just a really good classic RE game. It didn't set the standards for this style of game the way Resident Evil 1 did; it's not as ambitious or unblemished as Resident Evil 2. But it's far from the mess that history made it out to be. Whether you're a veteran who's played it before or a new fan who never tried out Resident Evil 0, it's good enough to deserve this second chance.

Comfy, cute and thought provoking little sidescrolling story game with minigames. It handles many topics that a lot of people have struggled with or are currently struggling with, making it very relatable. (mental health, adulthood, being lost or stuck in life, and more) Helps that the writing feels very sincere and is on point in general.
It's not all about being depressing though. There's other stuff to pace it out.
Don't recommend binging through this one, running around the town gets very repetitive and it's nice to have time to think about the different scenes.
It can be kind of difficult to see at a glance what is a platform you can land on and what isn't, which is annoying sometimes, but I think in the case of NITW the aesthetics are more important. The level of immersion and engagement would suffer from obvious visual clues and additional button prompts, etc.
Edit:
Second playthrough is recommended, even if you found a lot of the optional stuff on your first time (which is unlikely) just doing the different events is fresh enough. You also get new perspectives on characters.

Chicken Assassin – Master of Humiliation:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

McAllister is a chook, but not the usual sort that you greet happily when presented on your plate. No - McAllister is a chicken fighter who has a secret admirer (should we say, lover); the gorgeous Candy! At his last fight, Candy could not resist blowing a flying kiss to this magnificent specimen of a chook!  But therein lies the problem - Dr Pritzel, Candy’s partner, realised at that moment that there was a connection between McAllister and Candy. It is going to be a chook of a fight!
Chicken Assassin – Master of Humiliation is a fighting/clicker game where you play McAllister, the fighting chicken!
You will start the game at the fight club. The Mean McAllister will position himself in the middle of the screen and start dancing like a true boxer waiting for the first wave of enemies to come by. They will arrive from both directions, left and right. As you knock them out, they will drop souls and some items. These items will automatically be picked up but you will have to hover over the souls to acquire them. You can’t miss them, by the way; they are round and blue. Every ten waves, you will fight a boss until you reach the last one. For example, the fight club has 20 waves which means this level has two bosses to eliminate. As you level up, you will unlock new areas (every 10 levels reached), to fight in and you will have up to 40 waves of enemies to get rid of in the latest stages. You also have boss raids which are like side missions. However, you must have a specific number of items to enter them and they are significantly harder levels. Another point to take into consideration is that each time McAllister reaches another level of experience, his health will be fully regenerated. That could help you the beat a level or a side mission.
With the collected souls, you can upgrade McAllister’s battle expertise: attack, defence, critical hits and more. The resources upgrade is more towards how many souls he can gather, the lucky chest (random items), the black market and other things.
They are other ways to earn additional souls; you can exchange specific items on the black market or sell them from your inventory. Another way is via the rooster tales. The rooster tales are basically game achievements and you can score big numbers of souls when you achieve some of them.
Another fun part is the wardrobe where you can customize your favourite chook with hats, uniforms and other accessories. By the way, these item have additional value points which go towards McAllister: attack, defence, critical and health points. The right combination could see you through a level.

I found this game to be intriguing and rewarding, and definitely worth its price. The gameplay mechanics are primarily figuring out how to ideally manage scarce resources (there are no typical point-and-click adventure puzzles to speak of), and the story is integrated wonderfully with these mechanics; it was enough to draw me in and keep me going when the game had very nearly pushed me beyond the edge of despair, and the themes in the narrative often influenced my gameplay decisions. Likewise, my own experience mirrored the protagonist's closely enough that I found myself identifying with him easily, and when I finally triumphed against all odds I felt pretty good about myself.
The game requires quite a bit of trial and error - almost no mechanics are explained, and you are almost guaranteed to fail repeatedly. If you're easily discouraged, I would advise you to avoid this. I played this on Original difficulty, so I can't speak towards the experience on easy mode. My biggest gripe with this game is the fifth chapter: unlike every other chapter, it incorporates a big element of luck which compounds the difficulty and renders it into an exercise in frustration. It was enough to nearly make me stop playing, since the RNG could doom you from very early on and it's long enough to make restarting from the beginning (which you WILL do more than once) a giant pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ There is also a memory leak present in that chapter at the time of writing, which really doesn't really help.
Beyond that and an abundance of small typos, I can't really fault the game. It was interesting, it looks nice, and I was entirely distracted from the pointlessness of my life for the period of time that I was playing it. Would recommend, 8/10.

The amount of negative and quasi-positive feedback for Gods Will Be Watching is unprecedentedly large, for this being such an enjoyable game to me. Everything in the trailer tells me that this will be pixelated fun like Maniac Mansion and it will be hard like Dark Souls and I'll have to figure out the method to win every level like Dark Souls or The Fall. After playing this game I realize that is exactly what I got.
Yes, the game is hard. They will not spoon feed you the answers like so many point and click adventures. You have to figure out each chapter’s puzzle, which are different. Refreshingly different in fact, as there is little information you can take from one chapter to the next that will help you. I played the first chapter 10 times, before I understood I would need to stop trying to brute force my decisions and really think about each action I was taking. Once I figured that out I breezed through the remaining chapters, several of which I beat first try. And that is the secret to every chapter. Make every action count. I had to pull out my trusty notepad and map out a level, or jot down reactions to my actions on a first run through. I made sure to take every opportunity to take free actions that gave me more information about my situation.
Gods Will Be Watching is a refreshing change of pace that gives expert gamers a run for their money and forces you to learn how to play the game wel. If you are easily frustrated when you lose, then this game is not for you. Although if frustration and restarting a level emboldens you and forces you to become a better player, then this is one of the few games out there that does just that.

Good in almost every department -  writing, replayability, dialogue, art and graphics. Don't expect a mind-blowing experience, but expect a game that is surprisingly worth its price in my opinion (well, I did get it on sale). This game is also unique in that almost any character build is viable, granted you know how to play to that build's strength. And that is just beautiful, because that's how humans work. It's not like other RPGs where you *completely* gimp yourself by not dumping "this stat" or maxing "that stat". Some things are stronger than other for certain situations, but you can always adapt and overcome. Well done.
Cons
AI pathing is wack. On Path of the Damned (hardest difficulty), nothing will annoy you more than seeing your mage run around in circles to cast an ability on an enemy within spell range. Actually, everyone seems to like running around in circles when given simple commands, even enemies will stand around and watch their comrades fight me. This happens often enough for me to wonder why it wasn't fixed.
Load screens are frequent and load times are longer than open world games Bethesda games, even Wasteland 2. I also don't know why that is the case.

Dark Souls changed the gaming world for me. Its unique atmosphere and playstyle is what caught me and I consider it an ideal gaming world. There are no other RPGs that have the vibe that Dark Souls has, and because it is so unique; I keep returning to it. With that written, I can say that I can spend 1000+ hours on playing this game without getting bored.
Ofcourse you die a LOT of times and thus it could not actually be considered ideal; However, the atmosphere really seals the deal. We all have our dark moments and Dark Souls is a great release.
I have played this game using my keyboard and mouse. Although it was not recommended by friends and reviews; I did manage to finish it (and I probably took longer than I could have with a controller). The controls take a bit of getting used to, and there are some moves that you might miss out on, like kicking.
These missing moves will not stop you from being capable of finishing the game and they will not stop you from enjoying the game (once you have gotten used to the controls).
The story of the game is kind of unclear. This could be because:
I didn't spend enough time on reading;
I spent too much time between dialogues.
Either way, I do think that I am not the only one. Why else would there be videos about Dark Souls lore? I definitely recommend keeping up with the story. A story of tragedy, a story of the 'light' against the dark. Prepare to cry, some say.
It indeed has a great lore.
Last but not least, the atmosphere and story are greatly complimented by awesome soundtracks. Once one has looked into the Dark Souls lore, one will understand how the music dramatically affects the game. This results in some soundtracks being filled with epicness and some soundtracks being filled with pain and sorrow.
This review is probably not complete, I can keep on praising Dark Souls. Praise the sun! My fellow sinners!

There is also a lot of gear to pick from in Dark Souls. There is a big variety of weapons and armor sets (including the gear that bosses wear).

Writing this review since I think what one expect of the game, and what one gets are not the same thing, but I still think it's a good game. So, I'll split this into a few categories.
1 Main character.
This is not the Sam we know from previous titles. That's fine. There's been a lot of crying from Splinter Cell fans about Ironside not making the voice acting for Blacklist, and there's been some sighing about Sam seeming younger than previous titles. That's all fine. Sometimes, such things happens, in movies as well as in games. James Bond movies didn't sport the same actors either, and the actors interpeted James Bond differently as well. It doesn't have to be an issue unless you make it one. With that said, the new Sam is not a likeable person. He sort of tramples his team, and even though his calls are usually the right ones, it doesn't spell out team leader to me. He does however give off an air of competence, and uncompromising personalities are often likeable as long as you're not on the recieving end, which you as a player is not.
2 Story.
Meh. It's a predictable spy/terrorist/race against the clock story. There's nothing new to see here, and it doesn't have to be something new either. There's one plot wist in the whole game, as far as I am concerned, and it's "sort of" predictable as well. This is not what makes the game good, and if you're looking for a compelling and interesting story, look elsewhere.
3 Gameplay.
Let's make this clear, right off the bat. If you've read that Splinter Cell is a stealth game, and you're expecting stealth to be a necessity, you've been misinformed. Splinter Cell ->can<- be a stealth game, but doesn't have to be. It's true that you earn the highest score if you leave enemies undisturbed - that is, you're supposed to be a spy gathering information, and leave the fighting to the soldiers who swoop in after you've gotten what you came for. However, most of the unique mechanics in the game is focused on taking out enemies, rather than bypassing them. Much of your gear uses shock or gas to take out a target without injurying them. The controls are rather clunky, and ubisoft can't seem to be able to seperate keys for controls so jumping up to grab a pipe is the same key as hanging off a ledge, leading to the same problems as the assassin's creed franchise. Many of my rage moments with this game occured because I wanted Sam to do one thing, but the controls made him do something else.
4 Experience.
First time I played through Blacklist, I didn't get the sense that it was a stealth game. I saw it as a trial and error game with assassination elements. And if you are impatient, it will indeed be a trial and error game. My first impression of the game was thus that it's pretty bad. I couldn't easily forsee patrol routes, and didn't have neither time nor energy to memorize where hostiles were going. I was adamant that I shouldn't be seen during missions, and thus I restarted checkpoints and reran missions when they didn't go like I wanted to. My second playthrough was just as bad. I was focused on trying out the pure stealth approach, but again had no patience to learn patrol routes or think outside the box. It nearly ruined the game for me.
I'm on my third playthrough as I'm writing this, and I have finally understood what you're "supposed" to do. See, the game gets good only when you play it like it's an ironman game. That is; only when you never actively choose to reload does the game get fun. Only when you disallow yourself to reload checkpoints and only allow it once it autoloads because you died, does it become the game it's supposed to be. Your reasoning, while playing like that, will change. You will become more patient, because the costs of replaying is too great. You will be excited, because if someone spots you, you're going to have to fight, and fighting isn't always easy. You will start to utilize all of your gadgets, and you will cease thinking that a kill is necessarily bad. You will bypass enemies if you can, but if you can't, then you'll take them out.
The game becomes a lot better once you play it like that. I dare say that Ubisoft should have made that a feature. The ironman thing I mean. Make it a check box, and once tagged, you can only reload if you die and never otherwise. But that is not the case, so you as a player have to do it.
Game is recommended, but only if you stay away from the reloading demon.

This game is not for everyone. That should be made very clear. Play the prototype first, and it will at least help you get a better idea of what you're getting into. At first glance, the game looks like a point-and-click adventure, which it is definitely not. I haven't exactly decided what to call it yet, but go into the game with as few expectations as possible, and you may find yourself enjoying whatever this game is. It's a very unique experience at the very least.

I enjoyed God's Will Be Watching. There's a ton of bad reviews out there right now, but I think it mostly stems from a disconnect between what people were expecting and what the game is. If you know what you're buying, I think it's a pretty neat little experience. Here's what it is:
You play through 6 different scenarios in which you're shoved into tense life-or-death situations. Normal Mode is extremely hard, while Easy mode is....Well, it's significantly easier but still challenging in a few parts. The situations are basically all about resource management, but in a clever way. You're managing health, sanity, food, party members, etc...
The Good:
-The situations are difficult and even when you win a chapter you'll nearly always find yourself barely surviving.
-The story is pretty interesting. There's some twists but it's overall a pretty simple scifi story.
-I enjoyed the art and the music. It's a little subjective, of course, but I think it's well done.
-I played the game on easy mode, and it look me 8 hours. For a game that only costs $10, I feel that's a great length. But I know some people expect a longer game, so I'm noting it here. I imagine that playing on normal will take significantly longer due to more repetition. Additionally, there's some replay value because you'll want to try the game again on normal mode (if you played it in easy originally) and you'll want to see if you can survive using different techniques.
The Bad:
-There are definitely some parts of the game where randomness is a big factor. There's one scene with Russian roulette that plays out exactly like you'd expect- Basically you've got a 1 in 7 chance that you die immediately. There's a few other parts of the game where randomness is a factor but not nearly as bad (For example, randomness will determine which resources you find in a later chapter. You can conserve the resources and manage them carefully to boost your chances, but if you don't find anything for too long there's ultimately nothing you can do).
- No checkpoints. If you fail one chapter, you need to start the entire thing all over again. It's not a big deal for some of the shorter chapters, but some of them take closer to an hour to complete. This can make the deaths due to factors which feel out of your control much more frustrating. Additionally, there's no way to save mid-chapter. So if you need to take a break, you'll need to start the whole chapter over again.
-Decisions do not carry over from chapter to chapter. It's probably for the better in my opinion, since loosing certain characters early on would basically make later chapters impossible. But I know some people expected this, so I'm noting it here.
All in all, I enjoyed the game. It's a short experience with appealing art and music that challenges you in some interesting ways. It's not a grand adventure with moral dilemmas and far-reaching consequences. A few random elements and the inability to save inside a chapter hurt the experience, but I still feel it's worth the price of admission as long as that's what you're looking for.

It's like the Dark Souls of point and click adventure games. You will die, and fail. A lot. You will get frustrated and want to throw something at your monitor. But it does feel satisfying once you've finally completed a chapter after tons of trial and error. Plus you always have to manage a few things at once, so you may not be able to save everyone you want, you'll have to make sacrifices. It's a pretty good game.

Let's get this out of the way; this game is hard. Too hard, maybe, to the point that even on easy there are times when you feel like getting ahead is equal parts RNG luck and good planning on your part.
So if you cannot handle frustration, prefer your adventures to be relaxing or want games to be 100% "fair", this one's not for you.
However, if you can tolerate this, you will be rewarded with a very unusual gaming experience, the likes of which I have rarely, if ever played. To me, it is one of those games that tries to redefine what gaming can be, by leaving the tried & true concepts behind.
This game tries to force you out of your comfort zone by breaking a few conventions we take for granted
- there is no "perfect" path
- there is no "right" way to do things
- life isn't fair, and sometimes you're just out of luck, despite your best efforts.
Sometimes, tipping the odds in your favor and hope is all you can do
So the point where most games end (in a reload), is where Gods will be watching starts: When things are out of your control, can you still pull through, and live with the consequences?
In that, it blurs the line between gaming and real life and I like that, but I can also see why many people don`t
As with most experiments, the mixture isn't perfect right away, and the game could have done with just a little less frustration, but truly tough decisions, a surprisingly rich story, given the games minimalist design, and a thought provoking ending far outshone that problem in my books.
9 bucks well spent ;)

This is actually a really fun game once you get into it. UPDATE: I have now finished the game, so here's an updated review...
I only have 2 main complaints about the game. First, as I said above, it does a pretty bad job of telling you how to do stuff. You have to figure out a lot of things on your own (which I guess could be considered "realistic" in a zombie apocalypse).
The second is that it's really light on storyline missions. The side missions are pretty much constantly becoming available (kill this, deliver that, save this guy, clear that infestation, etc.), but they get a little repetitive toward the end of the game since the storyline missions are so sparse.
As for gameplay, you don't play as a single survivor. You play as all of them, and level up their skills separately. When one gets tired or injured, you can switch to another one. Your survivors can also die, get infected, or freak out and kill themselves (or others), but you can also find new survivors take in around the world.
Your home base (which can be moved to other locations if you want) has slots for building various structures like a med center, guard tower, crafting area, kitchen, etc. Each home location has different numbers of building slots, and require a different number of survivors to maintain.
Depending on the number of survivors and outposts, your base consumes resources each day (food, meds, ammo, building materials, fuel), so you always have to be on the lookout for more. On top of that you need to keep your survivors stocked with weapons, food, meds and ammo that they use while they're out killing zombies.
Overall, it's a really fun game that has a ton of potential. They just didn't quite live up to it with this one. Hopefully State of Decay 2 will be amazing.
If you can find it on sale, I do recommend trying this game out.

A very well done, Infinity Engine (i.e. Baldur's Gate and company) style game.  They really nailed the look and feel of the interface and graphics.  The game is pretty superb in all other areas but doesn't quite reach the level of Baldur's Gate 1 or 2 in my opinion.
They created their own world and lore, and while well done it, just didn't capture my imagination as much as the regular AD&D setting.  They also created their own rules system, and I think this is where it lacks the most.  I love a lot of things they did, but they really missed the mark with stealth and loot.  Stealth is just hard to pull off and was originally a group only ability.  This was changed in the expansions though.  The loot to me just wasn't very exciting.  Even late into the game I was still using some of the same equipment I found pretty early on.  Many, supposedly high end items I never even equiped as what I had was better, or was at least better for me.  I think the problems stems from the fact that equipment has certain enchanting rules and it just makes many items feel bland.  This was improved upon in the expansions but not a whole lot.
The difficulty of the base game seemed fairly easy to me.  I played on hard / expert and only had problems with some of the end game level battles.  Can't say the same for the expansions but that is for another review.
Anyway, those are some of the negatives.  Most of the rest is very good / great level so it is still a great game for those craving RPG's of the past.

Upon first glance at Chicken Assassin: Master of Humiliation on Steam, the game seemed like a 2D brawler games involving fowl in fisticuffs. If you read the description of the game, it would have you believe it is an “Epic Action RPG! Full of Sarcastic and Hilarious Characters…”. It is very difficult to tell that it is actually a clicker game, with no mention of this fact in the description or trailers. Let's see how it stacks up.

The gameplay of Chicken Assassin is very much as you would expect for a clicker game. As Mean McCallister, Chicken Assassin, you aggressively click-to-death each and every enemy that come storming in from off screen, clearing wave after wave of these baddies until you reach the boss of the level. And once you do reach the boss, you guessed it, you click it into submission. Defeating enemies provides you with items that you can use to give McCallister stat boosts to increase his battle effectiveness, and souls you use to purchase items and upgrades. You also unlock new outfits from time to time through collecting enough of certain item drops or beating certain enemies etc.
The upgrades available to you come in two forms; resource and character. Resource upgrades are focused on increasing the frequency that you obtain souls and the value they possess. This can be something on the level of directly increasing the numeric value per soul or something like purchasing little flame minions to gather souls while you are away (this is one of many portions of the game that seem very mobile gamey). The character upgrades give direct, permanent, stat boosts to Mean McCallister, like increased defense or increase critical chance percentage. You don’t really run into too many spots where you do not have enough souls to get upgrades, due to the “Rooster Tales”, the games achievements that award various amounts of souls as a reward for their completion. That being said, one extremely annoying feature that reeks of mobile game is the “Soul Limit” that you have to spend souls to increase. There were several times were I would earn a 500,000 soul reward only to receive 100,000 and the rest disappear into the ether because “I can’t carry that many souls”. It doesn’t even tell you your current souls limit, so you have no way of knowing if you are close to full or not.

After playing for an hour or so, you will quickly realize the pattern of gameplay. Since there is no way to heal outside of an upgrade that gives you a chance to heal after defeating an enemy or leveling up mid-game (instant full health), and the enemies usually get their attack(s) before you can react to them, you will click madly trying to stay alive whilst constantly bleeding health until the boss one-shots you and you have to restart the level. You will keep repeating the cycle of fight, die, re-equip, fight again over and over until you get lucky with the level up timing or are so over leveled you can murder anything in your path and beat the level. But, when you start the next level, it starts all over again, you get your teeth kicked in, so you die, re-equip, fight again etc. It is just the same thing over and over and over, and it gets boring extremely quickly.
While the sound effects are quite good for the game, the music is another beast all together. Mediocre at its best and irritatingly bad at worst. The main menu music (before you pay souls to unlock more music…in a game you paid for already) is a seemingly random assortment of drum beats and synths, with some weird pitched up vocals meandering around in the background that soon fades to almost out of tune piano chords. Most times you are better off playing with the music turned down.

The worst thing of all however is the blatant racist and sexist imagery the game uses for background characters and enemies. In the very first mission, there is an Asian man with thick round glasses with buck teeth and a rice hat betting on the game, with what looks like a black face caricature eating a fried chicken leg. In the riot scene you fight overweight women with picket signs that read “Free the Nipple”. Their title: “Angry Feminist”. It gets worse when you get to the “Borderlands” level in which you are fighting outside of a gigantic concrete wall where your enemies are “Vatos” and “Wetbacks”. In what way is this okay?!?! It’s astonishing that a game like this was greenlit on Steam, let alone has such high ratings. If these depictions were meant to be in jest (though still in poor taste), it should have been made more clear.

Final Opinion
Pros:
1.	Oil Painting ArtStyle is Cool
2.	Visual Effects are Well Done
3.	Lots of Customization Options
Cons:
1.	Grindy
2.	Gets Old Fast
3.	Bad Music
4.	Have to Unlock Features that Should Just Come with A Game You Paid For
5.	RACISM and SEXISM
Buyer beware, I would not recommend it but its your decsion.

Sound:		3/10
Content/Cost:	4/10
OVERALL:	3.4/10

Chicken Assassin – Master of Humiliation is a clicker game with RPG elements. Firstly, I’d like to mention this game really surprised me, I wasn’t expecting such a good game but it really is an awesome and addicting game.  The first time I started I kept on playing for 32 character levels and I only quit because I had to leave. I am a sucker for clicker games and this is right up my alley.
The game features nice looking almost borderlands-ish looking art-style and very gorgeous looking color scheme. The game has a “Noir” theme going on. Though it’s 2d but it’s one of the best looking unity game yet for me at least.  It’s nice and dark yet colorful and pleasing to the eyes. The game is locked at 60 FPS and there are no graphics options at all in-game. The options outside the game when you launch are there which is your usual Unity launcher menu with resolution and quality of graphics settings. There were no graphics glitches or errors for me the whole time I played.
I am going to have to say this game has an awesome soundtrack. All the levels I played had their own background music which to me really gave me that whole “noir” theme feeling the game is going for. There’s also cheesy sarcastic dialog voice overs when you start a new mission and I found them hilarious.
The gameplay is super addictive if you’re a fan of clicker games. Unlike a normal clicker game where you continue and keep clicking in one mode, this game has a story, RPG elements and levels. The game even counts how many times you clicked and that including clicking in menus as well. There's plenty of humor, references and sarcastic stuff in the game. Your main currency is souls which you can earn by killing enemies who then drop these blue souls which you can collect by hovering you mouse over them. You also have a “Soul Pot” I your main menu which you can keep clicking to earn more souls. Later in the game you can get upgrades and one of them is the “Soul Helper” upgrade which spawns a helper who will keep girding for souls. One thing which can be added is an offline farming feature because the can get pretty grind-y in the later levels.
There are quite a few levels and each level features different enemies, bosses, themes, music so there’s plenty of content in this game. When you start the game you’re pretty weak but grinding and upgrading your gear and gaining levels you start to get stronger and stronger. The enemies start coming towards you in waves and you have to click on them to cause damage. A health bar is displayed under each enemy while the bosses have huge health bars. The enemies will attack you and your only way to heal yourself is to have the upgrade ability “Chance to heal when you hit an enemy”. Every 10 waves you get a boss wave. The first few levels have 20 waves which means 2 boss battles and both these bosses are different. The first boss is the normal small boss and you need to kill this boss to unlock next level. The second boss is one of the many giant bosses. The later levels have more waves and bosses so you need to do 20 waves or more to unlock the next levels.
There’s a lot of items in the game, you can earn these items by either playing the game or through a chest that is in your main home screen. Of course to open this chest you need to spend some souls and later in the game you can upgrade the chest level and it’ll start giving higher level stuff. The price will be higher too so you might want to keep that in mind. Items include the levels’ theme stuff for example when you kill Agents enemy-type they will most likely drop ties or when you kill a mouse they will most likely drop cheese. These items can be used to purchase souls from the black market dealer who comes up every now and then and you’ll get a prompt at the bottom of the screen. He randomly wants a different item in different quantities each time and if you have that you can exchange those items for souls and xp.
There’s also equip-able items. You have 4 slots in which you can equip different items. Firs there’s the weapon slot where you can equip different weapons. Weapons can be a gun or a bat or a broken glass bottle, it doesn’t really make a difference other than stats. Other slot is the armor slot which is pretty self-explanatory. Third slot is the necklace slot and the last slot is the potion/drink slot where you can equip an item and it’ll give you bonus e.g. +2 ATK, +3HP. Other than these items you also have cosmetic items which get unlocked when you do certain things. E.G when you kill 10 constables you’ll unlock the constable hat etc. These costumes also give you boosts. There’s the head slot, the face slot (glasses, masks etc) and the clothes slot. All items effect ATK, DEF, CRIT and HP bonuses. All items have different stats so you can select the gear with HP if you like that playstyle more or you can pick the one with most ATK power.
There’s a lot of upgrades in this game. The upgrades are divided in 2 categories. The battle upgrades and the resources upgrades. Your regular increase HP, Attack, Defense upgrades, critical hit chance upgrade etc. are there, these and a few other ones like an attack bot companion attacks enemies are in the battle upgrades category. The resource upgrades include things like soul farming helpers, more xp earned from enemies, upgrade souls’ value, upgrade treasure chest level etc.
There’s also booster tales which are sort of like achievements/tasks, e.g. kill certain number of enemies to get 200 souls. You can visit the booster tales section and click on collect button to collect these souls. Keep in mind there is a maximum soul limit (this can be upgraded later) so don’t collect higher souls reward then your limit. E.g. if your limit is 10,000 maximum souls, don’t collect 50,000 souls reward. Leave it as is and you can collect it when you upgrade your maximum souls limit. There are no achievements in this game on Steam but I think this system can be used to make Steam achievements which is always a plus for any game.
Later in the game you also unlock boss raid mode. You have to pay a certain amount of a specific item to be able to join these boss raids.

Disciples III: Reincarnation follows in the footsteps of its predecessors in being one the all-around best-looking games of its kind as far as art direction and offering a unique blend of strategy and RPG mechanics. Unfortunately the inexperience of the development team makes this installment an ultimately unsatisfying experience.
The factions and rosters in Reincarnation are an almost direct copy-paste from Disciples 2, so if you've played that you already know the units and their roles.  The big change with this game is the introduction of hex grid-based battle maps, which offers a few new dimensions to combat, but not as many as you'd think or hope.  There's no bonus or penalties for flanking or attacking from behind, no accuracy penalties for moving, and only a few abilities that actually take advantage of unit proximity.  The only major change that the maps bring to the table are certain hexes that can amplify melee/ranged/magic damage, but because the maps are randomly generated, these don't even come into play in many battles.
The one big glaring issue with D3 is the lack of balance.  It seems almost like stats were applied to units randomly.  Low-level hero units are almost totally worthless, even weaker than regular T1 units, while some other starting units are stupidly overpowered.  Because of the aforementioned randomly generated maps, winning battles often comes down to being in the RNG's favor more than actual skill.  And speaking of the RNG, D3 continues the long series tradition of making the game "challenging" by loading the dice.  Expect enemies to get critical hits five or six times in a row while your units miss half of their swings.
What I've managed to see of the story is decent enough, and the voice acting is surprisingly competent, probably the best of the series (though that's a pretty low bar).  The design of the units and factions is excellent, building off the ones established in the second game, but it doesn't really do much that we haven't already seen.
If, like me, you're a long-time fan of the series, then it's worth it to pick this up just for the sake of nostalgia, since there are so few other games out there like it.  But overall, I can't recommend this to the general public.  Maybe some day someone who actually knows what they're doing will pick up this franchise, but that certainly didn't happen here.

As someone with 100% of achievements in this game and a considerable amount of hours, the only possible criticism I have towards the game is that there some of the challenges are stupid hard in comparison to the rest of the game (which is not easy by any means), but even then they are possible. Any major bugs that I rarely encountered have been patched (namely the void entrance portal not working after the hush fight).
I got the FIRST 100% achievement at around the 550 hour mark and didn't get the 1001% achievement until about 700 hours if that is any indication of how much time you can put into this game and still have more to do. I still play the game fairly regularly because I keep realizing that there are still things I can do even after total completion (getting 100% on all 3 files) and even if there wasn't, I would still play because I find the core gameplay very entertaining. The feeling of satisfaction you get from beating a certain run or challenge that has been kicking your♥♥♥♥♥for 4 days straight is incredibly satisfying and is the reason that this is the only game in my library that I have put real effort into getting 100%.
The variety in the gameplay is also a major point of attraction that keeps me coming back. This game has a good balance between RNG and skill. When you first start the game, you're probably gonna die over and over before even getting to the Mom fight. Once you have a ton of hours in the game and have learned what items are good and how to fight/dodge certain enemies, even challenges like Mom become a total joke. The ability to have runs where you barely scrape by and survive the final boss by half a heart and also have runs where you steamroll everything in the room and kill bosses in seconds is very fun to me.
The devs have added so much content since Rebirth's release and now there are workshop mods that only further increase the game's already insane replayablity. You simply cannot beat the amount of entertainement that you can get out of this game for its price tag.

The amount of negative reviews on here is ridiculous. This is a game that forces you to manage your time and manage it well; a mechanic that is just as refreshing as it is difficult. To fully enjoy this game you are going to have to put a few hours into it, something that the majority of these negative reviewers have not done.
Sure, the end product is completely different to what I expected. At first I hated what I was playing. It wasn't until I lost the first level for the millionth time that I realised just how rewarding it is to progress bit by bit until you manage to perfectly use the short supply of time that you have.

is a sci-fi point and click adventure game published by Devolver Digital, the same company that brought you Hotline Miami; another moral questioning game. The original idea of this game came from the 26th Ludum Dare based on Minimalism.
The writing on this game, in my opinion, is lacking. The whole was through was a confusing mess. No matter who was killed one chapter, the game threw them back into the next chapter with little to no explaination with only the ending giving
clarity. What the game does have going for it is the down to earth sections. The "lore" behind it was well planned and thought out, but it never did make up for the confusion of the story. It just seemed like average sci-fi story with a twisted dark side to it.
This is mainly where the flesh of the game is tainted. The game is broken up into 7 chapters. Each chapter is very different to the next, each one introducing a lot of new ideas and something you definitely haven't done before. It's exciting and fresh. Except when you have to redo it
again. This game is built around the idea of trial and error. So you will screw up. A lot. And this is where issues began. The chapters were mainly built on managing work and items. Who does what and what do we do with these items. Various chapters splash in specks of random. This is where the gameplay falls apart. You'll end up replaying chapters over and over again, failing each time to this random element. Frustrating gameplay doesn't equal having fun.
Devolver Digital has done it again! Made a visually appealing game out of something my SNES could run! Congratulations! But all jokes aside, this game is a looker. The different colors blend the pixels in well, and with each death lying there from my hands made my stomach churn with how it blended in well! The art team did a great job on this one.
The plinks and plonks of this game can really immerse you into the science fiction story. Each action seemed to be complimented with a gratifying audio sound. The music is easily compared to that of FTL, but less fast paced. It was lacking that sense of urgency on certain missions, but none the less blended in well.
Did this game fit in well with it's genre. Yes and no. Yes to the point and click adventure, and no to the moral choice gameplay. It is a dark game full of dark awful people, but aren't well all disgusting people? Well, no game. We are not. The game tends to put you into these hard choice moments,

This game is difficult. It's meant to be difficult. But I feel it's getting a lot of unecessary flak. One thing it isn't is random, or trial and error. Although clearly you are likely to fail numerous times before finding a solution, that's not the same thing.
Without spoiling anything, for the most part you are put in charge of controlling a group in some kind of life or death situation. The key thing is that most of the situations you're in are actually quite deterministic. While there are some random events of differing flavors throughout the various chapters, if you know how the mechanics of the situation work they are generally not a real threat.
All of the chapters are unique while still sticking to the basic outline. For me, the heart of the game is figuring out how these different systems work. You are thrown into completely disparate(sic) scenarios, from a data heist to managing a research team. Each situation, however grimdark, ultimately operates on a set of rules that can be understood. Ultimately, you are in control of everything that happens.

I don't know how to write a review, so here's an Apple pie recipe
Ingredients
Dough:
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
4 teaspoons sugar
1/4 teaspoon fine salt
14 tablespoons cold butter, diced
1 large egg, lightly beaten with 2 tablespoons cold water
Filling:
2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lemon juice
3 pounds baking apples like Golden Delicious, Cortland, or Mutsu
2/3 cup sugar, plus more for sprinkling on the pie
1/4 cup unsalted butter
1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon
Generous pinch of ground nutmeg
1 large egg, lightly beaten
Directions
Make the dough by hand. In a medium bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, and salt. Using your fingers, work the butter into the dry ingredients until it resembles yellow corn meal mixed with bean sized bits of butter. (If the flour/butter mixture gets warm, refrigerate it for 10 minutes before proceeding.) Add the egg and stir the dough together with a fork or by hand in the bowl. If the dough is dry, sprinkle up to a tablespoon more of cold water over the mixture.
Make the dough in a food processor. With the machine fitted with the metal blade, pulse the flour, sugar, and salt until combined. Add the butter and pulse until it resembles yellow corn meal mixed with bean size bits of butter, about 10 times. Add the egg and pulse 1 to 2 times; don't let the dough form into a ball in the machine. (If the dough is very dry add up to a tablespoon more of cold water.) Remove the bowl from the machine, remove the blade, and bring the dough together by hand.
Form the dough into a disk, wrap in plastic wrap and refrigerate until thoroughly chilled, at least 1 hour.
Make the filling. Put the lemon juice in a medium bowl. Peel, halve, and core the apples. Cut each half into 4 wedges. Toss the apple with the lemon juice. Add the sugar and toss to combine evenly.
In a large skillet, melt the butter over medium-high heat. Add the apples, and cook, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the mixture begins to simmer, about 2 minutes. Cover, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until the apples soften and release most of their juices, about 7 minutes.
Strain the apples in a colander over a medium bowl to catch all the juice. Shake the colander to get as much liquid as possible. Return the juices to the skillet, and simmer over medium heat until thickened and lightly caramelized, about 10 minutes.
In a medium bowl, toss the apples with the reduced juice and spices. Set aside to cool completely. (This filling can be made up to 2 days ahead and refrigerated or frozen for up to 6 months.)
Cut the dough in half. On a lightly floured surface, roll each half of dough into a disc about 11 to 12 inches wide. Layer the dough between pieces of parchment or wax paper on a baking sheet, and refrigerate for at least 10 minutes.
Place a rack in the lower third of the oven and preheat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Line the bottom of a 9-inch pie pan with one of the discs of dough, and trim it so it lays about 1/2 inch beyond the edge of the pan. Put the apple filling in the pan and mound it slightly in the center. Brush the top edges of the dough with the egg. Place the second disc of dough over the top. Fold the top layer of dough under the edge of the bottom layer and press the edges together to form a seal. Flute the edge as desired. Brush the surface of the dough with egg and then sprinkle with sugar. Pierce the top of the dough in several places to allow steam to escape while baking. Refrigerate for at least 15 minutes.
Bake the pie on a baking sheet until the crust is golden, about 50 minutes. Cool on a rack before serving. The pie keeps well at room temperature (covered) for 24 hours, or refrigerated for up to 4 days.
Cook's Note: You may freeze the uncooked pie, but don't brush it with egg or dust it with sugar beforehand. Place the pie in the freezer for 30 minutes, to harden it slightly, and then double wrap it with plastic wrap. Freeze for up to 6 months. When ready to bake, unwrap the pie and brush it with egg and sprinkle with sugar. HBake, from the frozen state, until golden brown, about 1 hour and 10 minutes

I admittedly did restore previous content to the game via mods, but I find it all very charming. I recommend Starbound. Why? Try it and see.

+ Huge playerbase, easy to find competition
++ Most system mechanics are intuitive and useful, Zangief has finally graduated from 2-8 matchups against zoners to 3-7 thanks to the Focus Attack
+ Varied cast of characters, everyone can find a favorite
+ Easiest fighting game available right now, great for newbies when combined with online tutorial resources
+ Great competitive balance, everyone is viable except for DeeJay
+ Rolento da bess
+ All the other pros of a 2D fighting game: competition, fun, showing off your e-peen with fancy combos, the works
+ Everyone is viable
- Ultra combos and Red Focus give me mixed feelings: one rewards players with a super move for taking damage (although it is harder to apply than normal supers for various reasons), and the other sees very little use outside of unique combos.
- Matchmaking is poor for a number of reasons: You aren't effectively sorted based on rank, and might play with people higher or lower than you when you don't want to; matchmaking is kinda like a 2-person lobby, so one person can boot the other to prevent rematches; connection isn't always great, and there are a number of glitches in the game (as of 8/14/2014) that contribute to bad connections: soon to be fixed, hopefully
Should you buy? I say yes, as there are ways to circumvent the self-DDoS glitches and secure good connections in matchmaking. Once the glitches are sorted out, you'll be left with one of the best fighting games ever and a huge community base to play it with. Much fun awaits.

Yeah, this game is actually quite good. I don't care either way about the anime art style, and there is an element of sameness sometimes when replaying it, but it's worth it just for the departure from the traditional computer RPG set-up. "Long Live The Queen" has the player as the Crown Princess of the kingdom of Something That I Can't Remember, and it follows said character through a bunch of encounters leading up to her coronation. It's important to note that isn't an action RPG -- while you train your character, essentially levelling up, and make decisions that affect the storyline, there's no fighting or gearing aspect beyond a fairly simple "wear this outfit to boost this skill" system.
The game is built around putting points into the Crown Princess's skill via her classes. Each day, she has morning and afternoon classes, and can gain points from each. How fast she learns certain topics depends on her mood, which is influenced by what else she's done recently. There are four separate scales, all of which can be influenced by her after school activities, that determine her mood and, thus, which classes she can learn from faster or slower. For example, when the Princess is feeling depressed, she has a boost to the number of points she can learn in one class in Animal Behavior. This works both ways, as some mood ratings act as penalties against classes, so you end up juggling the Princess's moods from week-to-week to build up ratings in the skills you want.
As you experience the encounters, there are some choice elements, but the vast majority of how you progress is built around skillchecks, and that's a big reason this game is pretty different from most of the RPG you see these days. It actually, in my opinion, feels a lot more like playing a pen-and-paper RPG than other games which share origins with dice-based games. The fact that skillchecks influence the storyline itself is quite cool, and frankly it's an idea that I'd like to see implemented in other games.
There are minor quibbles; the game does kill you a lot, and it's not always stuff you can reasonably see coming; one of your idiot friends will probably make fun of you for playing this game, and you'll be forced to hit him in the mouth with a bamboo stick; the replayability eventually frays a bit once you realize that the story has certain aspects that repeat no matter what route you take. But overall, this is a good game that's worth the buy at full price, despite it's flaws. The background story, and the lore of the kingdom and the version of magic that exists in this game are both interesting to read about. Did I mention the music? It's got a nice piano soundtrack, if that's your jam.
"Pinkhaired Crown Princess Skillcheck-Based RPG" has no business being this much fun, but it is.

Combining elements from a life simulation and visual novel, Long Live the Queen makes for an interesting change of pace from the usual action, platforming and rpg games. In spite of the uber-cute exterior, this is a fairly challenging game. You need to keep track of various skills, Elodie's moods (with can have a fairly heavy impact on a skill you're trying to boost), and the various events and characters you encounter. Also, you can expect to have Elodie die more times than South Park's Kenny and Star Trek's Red Shirt guy combined. Overall, LLtQ has a fair amount of replay value as you try for different outcomes and achievements (or to see how may ways poor Elly meets her untimely demise). Only you will determine if Elodie will become the beloved ruler of Nova or a severely depressed,traumatized and stressed out wreck with more emotional issues than Katawa Shoujo's Hanako Ikezawa.
As entertaining as the game is, LLtQ does have it's share of flaws. Most notably some parts of the skill check system. Some checks require skills you either will not have early on (Sense Magic for one) or at levels impossible to reach without the debug console. One example is  the weekend event in Week 8 requiring a nearly maxed Sense Magic or skill combinations at 120+ or higher (Lore,Conversation,Presence,Meditation). A slight rebalancing to lower the required levels somewhat and/or having Elodie able to learn Sense Magic without the crystal (natural/ inherited ability) would help here.
Another would be having a type of "Class System" which would give her more of a background. After all, she attended a boarding school for the children of the nobility and yet has no skills to show for it. Makes you wonder what she was doing there. One way to implement this would be similar to the "G.O.A.T" test from Fallout (series of questions to determine her background) or by selecting the type of school she attended / classes she was interested in or excelled at. Choose a Finishing school for Social and Dance Skills), Military (for Weapons,Military and Intrigue), Academic (Intellectual), Athletic (Agility/Athletics) or Artistic (Expression skills) for a small starting bonus (10-20 pts.).
Finally, this could use an expanded relationship system rather than just depend on the events in the game. A few Tokimeki Memorial / Sentimental Graffiti style date event and gift/letter exchanges with a chosen love interest (male or female) could add some more depth to the game as well.
Overall, in spite of the flaws mentioned, this is an enjoyable game and worth the $8-10 price tag

Before I begin my review I have to say that I really was looking forward to this game and that I, along with many people, thought this game would be something worth noting. It was not.
Pros:
*Decent looking story. I mean it's got it's originality.
*Great pixel art. I'm a sucker for it.
*Cool end-of-mission screeens. They can compare the actions you did on a level with everyone else who bought the game.
*Ok # of outcomes.
Cons:
*I can't connect with the characters due to their semi-bland personalities, fully bland jokes, and PLEASE SHUT THE FRONT DOOR dialogue. This makes testing my morality EXTREMELY easy.
*Runs ENTIRELY on luck. If a game were to have luck integrated into it (like Fallout's VATS system), then I'd hold my tongue. BUT to consider a mission successful based on percentages is pure bull.
I can tell how fun a game is based on whether I want to replay it and whether to increase the dificulty when I do so. This game says ITS REEAAAAAALLLLY RECCOMMENDED if you play it on "normal" dificulty to get the full experience, and then it kicks you in the balls with the borderline impossible gameplay. There are games out there where dying is constant and seemingly endless (Dark Souls), but this game determines your odds of success LITERALLY by a percentage and not by the skill of the gamer. If you play it on easy mode it makes a difference, but you're not enjoying the game the way the devs want you to.
tl;dr: The developers made promises it couldn't keep up to, it relies soley on percentages and not skill, the characters are bland. Not worth the price.

It's more like a visual novel or something than an actual videogame.

An unemployed troublemaker who just dropped out of college and seems to say everything wrong, the distant and tired owner of a local business trying to keep things together for her broken family, an insecure "bad boy" who can't sit still, and his smart but quiet boyfriend with a dark childhood walk out of a diner and find...well, I wouldn't want to spoil the surprise. If you can relate to any of those characters, even just a little, your experience with Night in the Woods will be that much better. Even if you can't, though, the game still boasts pretty visuals, some of the best music I've heard this year, waves of emotions, and an intriguing mystery.
The game itself is little more than an interactive visual novel, a delightfully story-rich experience, so if you're looking for serious platforming or anything like that, you're probably in the wrong place. Even your dialog choices don't really matter that much (Remember how I said one of the characters seems to always say the wrong thing? Yeah, that's you.) with the exception of which friends you decide to hang out with. That being said, if you like to explore every nook and cranny of virtual worlds, you'll be pleased to find plenty of bonus stuff to hunt down, ranging from comical flavor text to interesting lore and even lengthy scenes that you'd otherwise never see.
So, if you fancy a semi-comfy romp around a little town where everyone knows everybody by name, for better or for worse, pick up Night in the Woods. It's cute, it's happy, it's sad, it's unsettling, it's good.

Anime Princess Death Simulator.
Don't judge a book by its cover.
The game involves Princess Elodie (the playable protagonist) learning about the country she’s soon to rule called Nova. You have to guide Princess Elodie through different lessons while balancing her emotions and handing political, economical, foreign and inner affairs.
Oh, you also have to avoid untimely death and make it to Princess Elodie’s coronation, which is no easy task. (There’s a reason there’s an achievement for living through the year of training.)
There’s countless different ways you can go about for literally every event in the game. You can be an elegant and graceful queen; a military strategist who strikes fear into the other kingdoms; a powerful sorceress with a cute outfit; a cruel dictator ruling with an iron fist a la Marie Antoinette— your subjects can even cause a revolution against you if you choose this path!
While you may succeed in some areas, you’ll fail in others. You will have to make choices for the good of the people (such as having an arranged marriage) and others for your life, despite them not being the best or morally right thing to do.
You truly rule like Machiavelli wanted.

It's better to call this a visual novel with stat checks than a life sim ala Princess Maker, but that aside, the sharp writing and the ever present puzzle of how to piece together a win in your desired path are the real fun of this.
I do wish there was more art though.  Only Elodie has more than one facial expression, though since her mood is a key gameplay point, she is fortunately expressive enough to determine her mood at a glance (though the game still tells you her mood).  Everyone else haws the same frozen expression from start to finish.  Also would have liked more inserts during major story events, though the cutesy gorey death screens are a hilarious highlight.  And especially more backgrounds - that same shot of the castle gets old fast.  Aside from that, the art is genuinely good and much higher in quality than a lot of the more tryhard "otaku" games.
Because Elodie dies.  A lot.  You're basically thrust into a frilly pink Game of Thrones and if you think all you have to do is get married and smile pretty, you're going to eat a poisoned chocolate and croak or get an arrow in the gut or get torn apart by chains or one of the other sudden and brutal deaths.  Keeping a fifteen year old alive for a mere six months is harder than it looks when everyone and everything wants her cute pink curly head on a pike.
The overall storyline is very simple, the real highlights are how your choices play out in affecting the plot.  I'm particularly intrigued that in a girly princess game, where you'd expect romance to be played up, it's pretty much forgotten - the entire concept of marriage is played out for pure politics, as it historically would be. Elodie herself is usually marrying with an eye for how to solve a crisis or shore up a political weakness - as opposed to because she needs hot bishonen boyfriend to do everything for her.
I'd also add this game is freaking hard.  The only time I won was to become a bloodthirsty magical girl warrior - which had its own issues, but at least I finally saw fair Elodie crowned. Yet I keep playing because I know there are other ways to win, other paths to travel, and even other characters I've yet to meet!

To start off with something important to know; this game is challenging in many ways. It's not least because there are so many possible paths and you don't know how to handle each one until you've failed at it at least once - unless you're using a guide. I would recommend to NOT use a guide though, as experiencing each failure and mistake in this game for yourself is very satisfying. Even more satisfying is learning from them and eventually building up better and better strategies for getting all the achievements and/or endings you want.
The game is basically a visual novel with anime characters, and there's no sound except for the music (which I personally think is much too repetetive to enjoy). The art is well done, and the conversations are easy to understand and for the most part, well written, but cutscenes (or events  as one would more accurately call them) easily become boring after a while and fervently clicking them away because you've seen them somany times before becomes the norm quite early on. It's a bit of a shame since the story is quite good and it's genuinely interesting to see how your gameplay affects different events, and what becomes of the main character, Elodie, as well as her kingdom.
You choose yourself how you want Elodie to be - a cruel and war-hungry sorceress hunting animals on her weekends, a well-mannered and elegant history-buff charming nobles and peasants alike, or maybe a charismatic military leader aiming for peace and justice. There are two things that decide your fate: SKILLS and DECISIONS. An additional factor, MOOD, does not affect your story directly, but it affects how much you can improve different skills each week. These three factors affect each other; decisions (and events) affect your mood and skills, your mood affects your skills, and your skills affect your decisions. There are also two additional factors that linger in the background; cruelty and noble opinion. They seem small and insignificant at first, but they may eventually decide the difference between war and peace as well as who lives and who dies.
These mechanics are basically the core of the game. All you have to do is change how these factors affect each other and learn which changes will get you to the ending you want. It sounds quite simple, but there is a huge amount of changes you can make, and each one has the possibility of leading you onto a completely different path. Learning the possibilities of each little change takes a lot of time, but once again, the satisfaction of learning is great and it makes your victories even sweeter.
To finish this up I will say that even now, after 17 hours of playtime and multiple finished games, I can't say I have in any way mastered the game, that I know all about it or that I have found a way to "win" each time without effort, but playing and learning the game is immensely fun and I recommend it whole-heartedly.

People seem to have some trouble with crashes and the like, but I didn’t run into any. (Though it still is pretty un-optimized because running on high anti-aliasing drags the FPS down.) Overall though despite any flaws Stranger’s Wrath is a fun game.

I had great hopes and I was really hyped to finally play Gods Will Be Watching. I'll admit, I never played the free version that originated the full game and after playing this game I think I should have actually so that I knew what I was getting myself into. Be warned, this might contain SPOILERS!
On the Steam store page it says that Gods Will Be Watching is "An innovative departure from the traditional point and click adventure taking place in six intimate, tension-filled scenarios linked together through an epic narrative of interstellar espionage.". I have to agree to some extent, it is indeed an "innovative departure from the traditional point and click adventure" type of games but, the way I see it, the scenarios are not "linked together". So basicly the game is divided in several chapters and in each chapter there's a chance one of the characters from your "team" can die but on the other hand even if a character dies, let's say, in Chapter 3, it will still be alive in Chapter 4. This happened to me and I couldn't see a connection because as far as I know Chapter 1 takes place before the second chapter, the second before the third and so on, so I don't see a logical explanation for this, perhaps I'm missing something.
Putting that issue aside I can say that I think the game looks absolutely gorgeous and the sountrack is really good and does a great job in putting you in the right mood, atleast it did for me. One other thing that fascinates me in this game is the universe in which the game tooks place, from revolutionary organizations looking to end slavery to undercover operations being carried out by federations and empires that rule part of the galaxy. Overall the universe and the plot is plain great and that also creates another issue for me. It happens often in games that the world where the game takes place is rich and well designed, however some of these games only show you tiny fractions of the universe and I get really sad about that because there's a whole set of opportunities to explore in this world. For example, in Chapter 2 you have to endure torture during a few days and during your torture, your torturer talks with you and he speaks of a Sports League in which players compete but he then tells you that they win by actually killing the enemy team, or atleast that's what I understood. This is a great example of what I mentioned before, the game teases you with great things, yet it doesn't show you anything.
Of course this is very relative from one person to another, you can say I'm pretty much just ranting here but the ranting is just coming now.
When I got Gods Will Be Watching I was expecting a standard point and click game with a certain story that was told through a series of choices you made and each choice would lead to a different outcome on the storyline. In the end I was wrong. There's pretty much nothing like that in Gods Will Be Watching, if you don't follow a specific set of "parameters" you lose and you have to start the Chapter all over again. What infuriates me the most is that there's not even a specific path which you have to follow in order to complete a Chapter, most of them are pretty reliant on luck. Having looked for some guides and some walkthroughs on Youtube I saw that the same action could lead to totally different outcomes and sometimes even total failure. I can understand the fact that a game is hard when it doesn't rely on luck, which Gods Will Be Watching certainly does. People that think games like Dark Souls or Ninja Gaiden are hard would hate to play this, that I am sure, atleast in those games you can fight back and turn the tide when in this game you can't, sometimes it reaches a poin where there's nothing but defeat waiting for you, yet the game drags on.
I really want to like this game and I really want to finish it (I'm currently in Chapter 4), but the way you get (pardon the term) screwed over and over just makes me mad and feel like I shouldn't have bought it in the first place because of it's luck based nature. Like I said I don't mind a game that is hard to play and to master, but when a game is trying to tell you a story I just want to enjoy the story without having to worry and to go through all the hassle to find out how to beat a certain level. Some people might be okay with this but I'm totally not. I bought this expecting a narrative experience and I found myself in some sort of survival micro management game trying to make sure I wouldn't make a wrong move or else all my progress until that point would be lost.
I might return to it someday, hell, I might even play it again tomorrow, I honestly don't know. Probably I'll just watch some walkthrough/letsplay on Youtube to see how the game ends because that's what I'm most interested in. I can't really bother myself to spend hours on a single Chapter until the game decides not to shoot me in the face and I manage to get lucky and beat that chapter.
I often compare point and click adventure games to books/movies/tv shows because they present you with a linear storyline and you just experience it, and that's pretty much why I enjoy point and click adventure games, because they tell a story but in an interactive way, in a way a book or a movie can't tell because you're just watching/reading there's no physical input from you that affects when or how the story progresses, and I feel that's the problem with this game, I just can't enjoy the story because of it's luck based design. I really want to recommend Gods Will Be Watching but due to the flaws I've mentioned I think that if you're like me, you won't enjoy this. If you are looking for a game with a good story to enjoy, you probably won't like Gods Will Be Watching, you'll end up "suffering" while experiencing that story and I'm sure I'm not the only one who hates that.
After some tweaking I was able to finish the game on easy. Like I was told, on the last chapter the game finally explains to you, atleast in some way, why someone is alive despite their death on the previous chapter. After beating it, I can say for sure, this has an excellent plot and I find the ending quite remarkable.
Despite that, I honestly can’t recommend the game yet, I still think that it involves a great amount of trial and error and a huge deal of micro management. Please understand this, I don’t think Gods Will Be Watching is a bad game, I think it’s quite good actually. Do I think it stands as an innovative departure from the point and click adventure type of games? Yes. Do I think it stands out as a good narrative driven experience? Yes, but I don’t think the type of gameplay stands out for most people who are looking for a more “casual” narrative experience.
Concluding, the story, the plot, the soundtrack, the graphic style are amazing, however I feel like the type of gameplay that was introduced into the game doesn’t really help to appeal to a larger audience. Some people will love it and some people will hate it. Then there’s probably others like me who are in the middle ground.

I just can't recommend it. It is absolutely not the game described or aluded to in the trailer: it is a turn-based strategy game: not an adventure.  At best, it is an interesting story with beautiful presentation which requires unreasonable investment of patience from the player to progress.  At worst, it is a tedious, repetetive exercise in keeping counters above a threshold by performing limited actions.  In each chapter, there are basically only about eight actions you have available to you, all of which will add or subtract a predictable amount to some victory condition counters.  This game could easily be represented as a series of numbers and buttons, which is pretty damnable given how the game is positioned - and what I believed it to be.
The game is not centred around story, and nor are the choices really that affecting: the only choices you are really making are how best to juggle the variables to keep them within the tolerance levels.  As far as I can see, in the first chapter, the only choice you can make that affects anything fundamentally is if you kill hostages rather than let them live when they do make a run for it, your man who is assigned to keeping the incoming forces at bay will refuse to shoot because he is morally damaged.
If you like resource management, you will potentially find something to like in this as it is very, very hard.  If you like story, you likely won't, because it requires so much effort and frustration to get to the story that you will, like me, feel as though you have been cheated into playing a very different game than you were expecting.
An experiment that doesn't work, for me, at least.

Admittedly, I didn't think this game would be all that good at first. After reading some reviews I thought the controls would be clunky and it would be overly repetitive, and in a way, it kind of is but it's not at the same time. That may sound weird, but the repitition is kind of offset by the different environments you find yourself in. The day/night changes and the increasing difficulty as you progress.
The controls are a bit clunky but once you adapt to them, everything is a-ok. I have only been using the controller and the aiming is a bit♥♥♥♥♥♥at times so the mouse & key combination might be fine for that but I'm enjoying aiming being difficult, it kind of adds to it - seeing as how you're basically just some random people without much shooting experience, it works.
Part of the fun is the learning how to handle different things. I lost a favourite character fairly early in due to just not knowing what to expect on a mission. She got torn in half and I was upset for a good hour - death matters in this game, it really does and it will effect you on an emotional level. I swore revenge and stocked up and went in better prepared. That's a lesson you learn quickly in this game - always be prepared for the absolute worst. Carry as much as you can, but allow a bit of room for scavenging. If you're taking a car, put an extra weapon in the trunk and so on. Don't underestimate the value of molotovs; they will save your life in a pinch.
The story progresses quite nicely for a sandbox RPG and allows you to do things at your own pace. Whether you want to focus on building up your base or going straight for the missions, there's always room to move how you want it. It feels a lot like GTA with zombies and I wouldn't have it any other way. Great game. It has had me hooked for 2 days now and I don't want to stop playing... must survive... must thrive under pressure...

All in all, it's a very good game for a good price.
