This game when it first came out showed an immense amount of potential. Now this game only shows disappointment to me. The idea of surviving on islands in the Pacific is cool but the game suffers from lack of content and slow developement time. I was hoping the game would live up to being called a survival but I've never felt challenged on making sure I'm hydrated and not starving. You find a bucket, make a fire and a spear, spear whatever you desire (even crabs) and you eat your cooked crab and drink your distilled water. It feels like they have only added in waves and some new things and ways to craft. Why craft new items if the game is already easy, why not actually add in some more challenges to overcome or maybe do some new island types instead of expecting us to make them with the island creator?
I feel lied to as this game has only become more and more of a "creative survival" which I feel is the result to the developers wanting to finish the game as soon as possible so they've changed their plan to a more traditional, uninspiring, "crafting survival". There was once a period where people thought this game was abandoned and with good reason (there wasn't any updates for almost 2 months and no word from the developer). They take forever to update and none of it is meaningful. The game runs and looks worse from when it was first released. There hasn't been enough content added in 4 months of updates to even want me to check it out for more than an hour. At this rate, the game might take several years to make. Due to how long it takes for them to add anything, they could just be trying to work out some crafting ideas first and then focus on the core of the game (which i still would hope it's surviving) and that makes it seem like the game is going in a direction I didn't think nor wanted it to go in.
Regardless that doesn't make this product any better or anymore promising. I've lost hope on this game as it is forced to rely on its looks and ideas (ideas that seemed to have replaced the ones that was released with the game). I can only guess on where the game is going based on the past year and that is nowhere. I've waited a year to see what it has done and all there was to have been seen is money taken from me and now I can only hope the developers get their act together in 2016.

It retains or rather brings back the old school Chaos Theory/Pandora Tomorrow kind of mission structure where you can approach the missions however you like in terms of lethal or non lethal takedowns or completely evading the enemies entirely like a ghost. This is good because for the previous instalment (Splinter Cell: Conviction) the mission design was very linear and you didn't have an option other than to kill everyone. So that is definitely an improvement and what makes the game so brilliant. The campaign is quite neat; it has an interesting villain and lots of constant twists and turns throughout the narrative.
Even though it brings back the old school design it still has that feeling of triple A laziness and dumbed-down gameplay. The missions are still more linear than the classics like previously mentioned just not as much as Conviction. The game is really short as well, I got through it on normal difficulty in around 9 hours without rushing at all plus the multiplayer is dead as of 2016 since it's 3 years after release. The graphics are meh, the character models and faces for everyone but Sam Fisher (the protagonist) are disgustingly bland and have terrible textures. The voice actor for Sam Fisher has changed since the previous instalments from the beloved Michael Ironside (which is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to say the least) to a much more serious and monotone individual who also sounds younger than Ironside which is weird since it is set after all the others in the series...
All in all however, it is a really good game for £14.99 or around $20, I personally got it for £5 in a sale so I was happy with my purchase. If you want a 'modern-ish' stealth game that is not Dishonored/Dishonored 2 or Thief that have super powers and enhanced abilities to help you then this is a game that is absolutely perfect for you and you really can't go wrong with it. I would advise picking this up as a starting point (or Splinter Cell: Conviction) before the previous ones however, since this is the easiest to get into in terms of it's story and gameplay because the old ones are pretty hardcore stealth games that require a lot of practice and dedication to perfect the craft.

As you may already know, Resident Evil Zero (RE0) is a prequel to the very first Resident Evil (RE) game. If you remember the opening scene of the first RE, a Special Tactics and Rescue Service (S.T.A.R.S.) team consisting of Jill Valentine, Albert Wesker, Chris Redfield and Barry Burton (Alpha Team) are sent to find out what happened to Bravo Team, with whom they’ve lost contact. The mission of both teams was to investigate mysterious murders that have been happening on the outskirts of Raccoon City. They discover Bravo Team’s downed helicopter in the Racoon Forest, but no sign of survivors. Their search eventually leads them to the legendary mansion from the first game. In RE0, we get to find out what happened to Bravo Team as well as story elements that ties this game to future games. RE0 begins with an Umbrella owned train traveling en-route through the Raccoon Forest. It comes under attack by scary…”leeches”. These leeches seem to be under the control of an androgynous Final Fantasy-esque character who, for some reason, is accompanied by majestic opera music whenever he is on screen. We then cut to the Bravo Team helicopter which is en-route to the outskirts. For reasons unknown, their helicopter is damaged and they are forced to make an emergency landing in the forest. What happens next is for you to find out. I will say this - don’t set your expectations too high story wise. This is honestly B-grade SyFy channel plot material here. However it’s all about the good ol’ survival horror at the end of the day.
RE0 is a very polished remaster. The game runs buttery smooth in 1080p at 60fps (in 16:9 widescreen). Not only that but the game now has added support for 5.1 surround sound, which really amplifies the creepy ambiance. Also added are several new control schemes, so pick one that best suits you. Keep in mind though - this is the same GameCube game from back in the day, just with updated graphics (and sound). If you were hoping that Capcom went the extra mile to remove those tedious loading animations, you are going to be disappointed.
that you open a door (or climb stairs and ladders) you
be treated to a "movie" that shows the door opening (or the stairs being climbed etc). Mentally prepare yourself for this.
You control two main characters in the game - S.T.A.R.S. Rookie Rebecca Chambers and alleged criminal Billy Coen. These characters each have their unique traits. For example, Rebecca has the alchemist ability to mix herbs and Billy has the factory-man ability to move heavy boxes. Naturally, the game will present situations in which you need to determine the best character to use at a given time. The character that you choose to take control of is the “Main” character and the other becomes the “Partner” character (and CPU controlled). You can switch who you want as your Main and Partner at any time. You can give orders to your Partner character - such as to follow you, stay put and attack/don’t attack. Learn this mechanic. Also, I should warn you about Rebecca. Be very careful with her as she’s quite a fragile woman. If she even smells the bad breath of a zombie, her health is going to go down. Billy, on the other hand, being a former marine and all, is a tough guy and can take quite a beating before his health drops.
Having two characters to control means that you have two inventories to manage. Sadly, both characters’ inventories are very small and non-upgradeable. Therefore, a huge aspect of the game is item management. You will have to get used to abandoning items in order to make room for higher priority items, then backtracking for the items you left behind at a later time. Here’s a tip. In the mansion area, there’s a save point at the bottom of the stairs when you first get there (the main hall). You will be spending a considerable amount of time running in and out of this area. So you can use this area as a “hub”. A convenient place to leave items you don’t need at the moment. Speaking of save points, here’s an aspect of the game that will surely add to the tension - limited saves! You save by collecting ink ribbons and using them at Typewriters. If you save too much, you might run out of ribbons! So, save wisely.
Now, let’s talk about actually playing the game. All of the game’s locations are pre-rendered, with pre-assigned camera angles. Nothing new if you're an old school veteran but if experiencing this for the first time, get ready for some awkward situations in which you are shooting at things and you can’t even see the things you’re shooting at because they are off-screen. Also, if you’re accustomed to modern RE games, you might have the mindset that headshots are the way to go. This is not the case here. All you need to do is pump bullets into the enemy until they curl up dead on the floor. An exception to this is the shotgun. It is very simple and quite satisfying to obliterate zombie heads with the shotgun. Simply aim up, wait for your victim to walk within range and pull the trigger.
Now it would not be a RE game without special enemies and bosses. The theme of RE0 seems to be - wildlife. You’ve got Frogs, Scorpions, Rabid Dogs, Monkeys, Birds, Bats, Centipedes, Spiders and some weird Leech controlled zombies. Some of these wildlife are boss fights. You can’t avoid them. The rest of them are annoying as hell. Instead of fighting these things, your best bet is to probably avoid them and run the hell away. That’s another decision you will be making a lot - when to fight and when to run. Sometimes the Coward’s route is best.
So how are the boss fights? Well some are more fun than others. Also, almost all of them just happen at random, for no apparent reason. Sometimes you’re going your merry way and all of a sudden, there’s a boss. Oh well. That’s life. The good thing about this is that it adds an element of unpredictability that will keep you on your toes, which I like in a horror game. There is one in particular that annoyed the hell out of me though. The Bat fight. You see, the way the targeting system works in this game is you press the target button and it targets an enemy. Then you press it again and it switches to another. You can’t command the thing to target the enemy you want, as it just cycles through enemies until it gets to the one you want. So, this is the Bat fight. It starts off all well and good because it’s just me and Bat. However when the Bat gets hurt enough, it calls in some minion bats to help it out. So at this point, I’m really irritated because I’m trying to line up a shot on the main Bat but the minions keep getting in the way and my targeting system keeps targeting them instead of the main Bat. Then while that’s going on the main Bat swoops in casually, picks me up and flings me around the room. Thankfully, the other boss fights weren’t as frustrating as that one.
Now let’s talk about game length. I completed the game between 6-7hrs on Normal difficulty and was awarded a B-rank for my troubles. There is a bonus "Wesker Mode" that you unlock once you beat the game that allows you play as the man himself. Plus there’s a ton of replayabiliy if you want to get all of the achievements or a better rank. However looking at some of those achievements (going through the game without healing or saving?) I have a feeling only crazy people will attempt those. They are surely not for me. At the end of it all I did have a good time with this game. Once I got into the groove of things I enjoyed all the strategy involved with managing items & switching between characters to solve puzzles. The story as I mentioned before isn't stellar but RE games aren't known for having stellar plots anyway. I liked it for what it is and if you're a fan, you'll more than likely find it to be a worthy prequel. Whether all of that is worth the $20 asking price is up to you.

Princess Maker Lite.  At least, that's what I wanted Long Live The Queen to be.  It actually plays more like a visual novel with a character building game attached to it.  A friend of mine called it pattern recognition, but that isn't exactly accurate, either.  There's trial and error, certainly, but it isn't strictly linear, and there's usually more than one way around any given major event.  The game also contains plenty of secret side content you can only see if you trend and manage your skills carefully, so it isn't a matter of simply save scumming your way to all the unlocks like your average visual novel.  (Though I certainly suggest keeping saves up to a few weeks back for strictly non-exploratory playthroughs.  Playing without a save to fall back on can also be an entertaining experience.)

One of the major features of Long Live The Queen is all the varied ways you can get yourself killed.  In Princess Maker II, for example, you can constantly throw your daughter into the crucible and she'll (usually) be okay.  Death to Elodie, the Queen to be, usually comes swiftly and, at least for your first few playthroughs, often at unexpected times.  One way to avoid them is to avoid the obvious situations where your skills don't fit the situation, but it's never a guarantee the reaper won't show up.  The game is short enough, at 30-odd turns, to make death more entertaining than infuriating, and also adds extra pressure to focus on the skills necessary to get the kind of happy ending you want.

Unfortunately, the shortness is also why I can't suggest the game at full price.  It is a fun distraction with plenty of replayability, but what it offers can't really match the classics I was hoping it could recreate.  The Princess Maker series did have the benefit of corporate backing, however, and this is my sole disappointment.  You have little to lose by picking this title up on sale!

An unemployed troublemaker who just dropped out of college and seems to say everything wrong, the distant and tired owner of a local business trying to keep things together for her broken family, an insecure "bad boy" who can't sit still, and his smart but quiet boyfriend with a dark childhood walk out of a diner and find...well, I wouldn't want to spoil the surprise. If you can relate to any of those characters, even just a little, your experience with Night in the Woods will be that much better. Even if you can't, though, the game still boasts pretty visuals, some of the best music I've heard this year, waves of emotions, and an intriguing mystery.
The game itself is little more than an interactive visual novel, a delightfully story-rich experience, so if you're looking for serious platforming or anything like that, you're probably in the wrong place. Even your dialog choices don't really matter that much (Remember how I said one of the characters seems to always say the wrong thing? Yeah, that's you.) with the exception of which friends you decide to hang out with. That being said, if you like to explore every nook and cranny of virtual worlds, you'll be pleased to find plenty of bonus stuff to hunt down, ranging from comical flavor text to interesting lore and even lengthy scenes that you'd otherwise never see.
So, if you fancy a semi-comfy romp around a little town where everyone knows everybody by name, for better or for worse, pick up Night in the Woods. It's cute, it's happy, it's sad, it's unsettling, it's good.

The dev's not adding a checkpoint in the middle of chapters forces you to play with a level of unease that all your progress won't be saved (which it wont) if you make a mistake or neglect a certain part of the scenario for too long.
The funny thing is, you can make the game a whole ton easier in just about every scenario, but it runs against what most people play games with a hero for the main character, which is to get people out alive.
If you want the game to be easier, and secure your win without having to really try for it like most of the people giving the game a bad review, start "trimming" your staff.

What a wasted opportunity. The original flash game was an amazing mood piece. The unforgiving gameplay drove it. The dialogue was terse, the options few and you'd learn immediately the odds as you died over and over again. The point of the demo was not winning (there was barely any reward screen), but to instill in the player that dread of being barely alive and see your options dwindling, your mates losing their mind and hope slowly evaporate. Great stuff.
This sequel flips the concept disastrously on its head. The gameplay is just as unforgiving and random based, but you are required to win if you want to make sense of the plot. Besides being frustrating, it is extremely gimmicky. Oh really, the sarge gets locked in a room again for the fourth time? And as you repeat the chapter for the nth time you start to wonder. Why wouldn't the terrorist tie up the hostages? Why would a torturer ever put a live round in the revolver? Why can't the group multitask?
The link between the narrative and the underlying puzzle is so weak and feels so forced. It was okay in the demo because mood was god, but here it just doesn't work.
And the writing isn't very good either. Forget the typos.
You can't have a very tense torture scene and end it with the torturer saying "I had too many jalapeno". Really? A poop joke? Why not a benny hill music to go with it?
You can't have an undercover spy start its trasmissions by reporting its real name, its rank, its location and its mission. That's just poor espionage. That's  just you screaming at me "exposition tiiime".
You can't postpone explaining so much of the plot in a game where obstacles are so frustating. Why people come back to life? Why am I seeing ghosts? Why should I care if you keep not explaining it to me?
You can't have so few dialogues in a game whose sections you know will have to be repeated again and again.
Just skip it

I'm sure by now everybody has some opinion on the souls series. Some love it and some hate it, and that's perfectly fine, everyone's got their own opinions and now I'm gonna throw mine out there.
First things first, the port of this game is pretty terrible. Framerate issues plague a lot of areas even if you've got the reccomended specs and there aren't many customization options for the visuals. Luckily for us however, DSFix fixes this trashheap of a port, so download that and save yourself the hassle. I'd also reccomend playing this with a gamepad. I personally used a 360 controller and everything worked out fine.
Now onto the meat of this game, the gameplay.
Dark Souls is methodical and has a fairly steep learning curve for new players. It'll take time to get used to the mechanics that DS throws at you, so you'll likely die a lot in the first few hours of gameplay, which is
. Learning and overcoming the odds is a major part of why I still play Dark Souls to this day, because the game treats me like someone with a brain, and I respect that. There are viable strategies of play for all kinds of players: melee, ranged, magic, and any mix of those can be specialized so that you can play how you want to play. Using these skills, you'll explore an interconnected world that draws you into the experience really well (for the first two thirds of the game at least) and encounter different enemies and, eventually, bosses that'll test you in a lot of different ways. Dark Souls' difficulty is basically a meme at this point, and it isn't as soul crushingly difficult as a lot of people will tell you, that's just e-peen boosting. Everything DS challenges you with is fair and with a little skill and patience, most people can beat the game.
I'll mention story here too really quickly because I honestly don't think it's too important. On your first playthrough, you'll probably miss most of the story because it's tucked behind item descriptions, but really, most people will be having enough fun with the quality gameplay in front of them that they won't care anyway.
Overall, Dark Souls is challenging, but fair to new players and experienced ones alike. If you're interested in picking this one up, download DSfix and have some kind of gamepad ready to better your experience. I didn't want to give too much away writing this review, so all that's left for me to say is that you should buy Dark Souls if you're looking for a game that's well worth the time you put into it and treats you like an adult.

Yeah yeah, it's another zombie game - but it's kind of different. Here, instead of playing the immortal hero of save-die-reload, you instead guide a community of playable characters (some of them randomly-generated), all of whom get tired, sick, injured, and can die, and the game will still continue (and be winnable) as long as the community can supply and defend itself. And yup, there is no save feature - the game autosaves constantly, but there is no way to backtrack on your decisions, so you just have to live with the risk. Add to this the fact that the only way to keep your community alive is by scavenging items from the game world - and the only thing that respawns in the game are the zombies. Otherwise, search a house and you'll never find items there again. Blow up a car and you'll never be able to drive it again. Let a group of NPCs die and they'll stay dead. The whole world is open to you from the start, but get careless and you'll find yourself quickly ripped apart by zombies. While this might sound daunting and really hardcore, the main story game's difficulty is actually pretty moderate - nothing near DayZ levels of difficulty. The visuals and the writing in the game are passable at best, but somehow the whole package is pretty compelling and just works, thanks to an interesting gameplay concept. It was an enjoyable playthrough.
The Breakdown DLC is basically a sandbox mode, and is very worthy if you liked the campaign game and want more. Unlike the main story game and its moderate difficulty, Breakdown is ruthless and makes for a way tougher gameplay challenge, on par with some of the hardest survival games out there.

For a game of its age, it's looking pretty sharp with the HD update, leaping forward and distinguishing itself from the generation that saw it born.
Stranger's Wrath although being part of the large population of FPS, it has enough entretaining elements to distinguish itself from the rest. The hability to whimsily switch between 3rd and 1rst person, be it to turn tail and dodge some bullets or close in and knock some teeth or simply exlpore your surroundings, 3rd person forces a change in strategy as well as gameplay. As for 1rst person, it is pretty standard with only a few variations and some elements thrown in, such as in a pseudo-stealth combat (e.i. neutralize-don't-kill, hiding) however stealth as itself is overpowered but really REALLY situational (scripted settled foliage) and could be better, maybe system limitations couldn't handle line-of-sight detecting at the time. However most of the combat is done in 1rst person, even though you can get creative and trace and strategy mixing 1st/3rd person, 1rst person is more reliable.
As for the lore, even though it moves away from the style and tradition of the rest of the oddworld franchise, it still is rich and organic. A deep world to explore and an even deeper foreground as it forms part of the Oddworld universe, most of it deals with the themes of industrialization, explotation of natural resources and native kinship among others.
My only complains are that it has not much replay value unless you really love the world they present (as much as I did, it made me lose the count of my plays), and the inclompete universe as the story has stalled and no new game releases have added something new to said universe since the release of the original XBOX version. Nevertheless on a scale this game has a well deserved 4/5

While not perfect, this game seems to merit all its praise it has received over the past decade.
Pros
+ Combat, when all comes together, is very dynamic. Different small animals function as your ammunition with their own abilities. Third person melee and first person shooting blend a lot better than expected.
+ Platforming and movement can be enjoyable.
+ Simple, but rich story.
+ Excellent varying environments and soundtrack.
+ The game changes its style drastically about 2/3 the way through. To explain how would be a spoiler, but the "stealth" and non-lethal takedowns are let go in favor of a smashmouth approach.
+ Sense of humor typical to the Oddworld games.
+ Well balanced and rewarded careful strategy.
Cons
- Ear-bleeding-inducing voices. Almost all voices have been digitally altered to be a higher or lower register of a normal human... and altered quite poorly at that.
- Early game's focus on "stealth" is extrodinarily basic and hard to maintain. Almost all confrontations turn loud.
- To get a good reward, enemies need to be "bagged", requiring you to hold down control for about 3 seconds on EVERY enemy you knock out or kill. Can get repetitive and annoying.
- The late game ammo types, mechanics, and lethal approach were more enjoyable to me than the early game "tag and bag" playstyle. Depends what you're into, but this seemed to be the best avenue for combining your attacks.
- While there are plenty of ammo types, too many of them serve fairly similar functionalities.
- Many boss fights. Some uninspired and annoying.
While sometimes repetitive and a bit too slow paced, I enjoyed this retro first/third-person platformer/shooter/beat-'em-up thing. Try to avoid the "greatest game of all time" nostalgia filter reviews and enjoy the good this game has to offer that definitely overshadows its faults.

The devs have added so much content since Rebirth's release and now there are workshop mods that only further increase the game's already insane replayablity. You simply cannot beat the amount of entertainement that you can get out of this game for its price tag.

After finally finishing this after 100 goddamn hours, I think it honestly might be one of my favourite RPG's ever.
I always have faith in Obsidian. Their ability to create RPG's is unmatched. Or maybe I say that because Fallout: New Vegas showed just how utterly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bethesda are at it.
Anyway, if you've played old infinity engine games like Icewind Dale or Baldur's Gate, I can tell you that Pillars Of Eternity is a more refined version of those CRPG's with some mechanics to improve upon it, along with a more medieval, gritty world and lore. It also doesn't ultimately follow traditional DnD rules, but personally I liked the way it did things.
The story is basically that a crisis is happening that is leaving newborns without souls, and like all RPG's, you are majorly involved in this and you set out to uncover the answer. The story is honestly pretty deep and thought out. The ending was a bit anti-climatic, but the ending SCENE was good. The DLC was honestly even more climatic and tense than the main game, and I would highly recommend playing through it.
Mechanic wise, it's a huge improvement from older RPG's. The endurance system means no more losing party members every 10 minutes, as they just get knocked out in fights instead. (They still have max health and can die, it's just it takes a while to wear them down.)
Classes are set out to be proficient at pretty much most things, each having a different main proficiency though (like most RPG's). For example, fighters are good at taking damage, Beserkers are good at DEALING it, Paladins are good at attack and support, clerics are good at support spells, wizards, attack spells. It's all a really fun system and no class isn't fun to play.
The soundtrack is god-tier, the lore and world is incredibly interesting, the characters are pretty well done. This has genuinely been the only game in existence that made me warrant getting the collector's stuff BECAUSE I loved this♥♥♥♥♥♥so much.
Definitely recommend buying and playing. For how much content this has, it is truly worth more than it is. All I can say is that you shouldn't play it with the mindset that it will blow traditional CRPG's out of the water. You'll just dissappoint yourself. Play it and expect something you expect out of any other game.

This is a game that I really, really wanted to like. It's supposed to be a game about talking your way through tense, high stakes, dramatic scenarios by reading the characters' behaviors to gain the upper hand. It almost get, too. The problem is that the actions you take will do different things each time you play. Outcomes rely too much on hidden dice rolls for the punishing checkpoints to be bearable.
Some situations are explicitly RNG based. The game will even tell you "you have a 1 in X chance of failing this". If you do fail, you have to start the chapter over again (losing 10-20 minutes of progress). Other situations are balancing acts, where you essentially have to keep between 1 and 4 meters from getting too high or too low. Unfortunately, the actions that you choose from will impact each meter different amounts and in different directions each time you do them. Doing action X might lower all of the meters a little bit the first time, but the second time it might make one meter spike up and another meter dramatically fall. This is all interesting to poke at and explore the first few times, but after a while it becomes dull and frustrating.

This demonstration of the first level singlehandedly made me buy this game:
I DEFINITELY do not regret preordering this game. $9, took me 11 hours to complete and was unlike anything I've played before.
The game is pretty much a turn-based decision making game, where time progresses after each decision you make. The game is split into chapters and each chapter gives you a different situation, with a different goal and different factors to consider when making decisions. The first chapter, for example, requires you to survive long enough to hack into a computer system, while keeping your hostages calm (making sure you have at least 1 that is alive and in the main room) and dealing with guards outside that are usually creeping closer and closer to the room.
My favourite chapters are the ones where you had a lot of different actions you could choose from. The complexity of these chapters is overwhelming at first, but this is by design. You will likely fail each chapter the first time you play it and feel irritated because there just isn't a clear path forward; there are too many options to wrap your head around. But each time you play you learn a little more and when you retry it will be slightly easier. Eventually, you can solve a chapter reasonably easily, because you understand all the pieces of the chapter and how they work. It is very rewarding and the lack of checkpoints, which can seem irritating when you first start a chapter, turns out to be a great decision, as you guessing your way from checkpoint to checkpoint wouldn't feel like much of an achievement. They really aren't necessary once you learn the chapter.
Any complaint I can think up really doesn't detract much from the game and for its price there's nothing that should disuade you from getting it, if it sounds like the sort of game you would like.
If you think this sounds like your sort of game, but still aren't completely sure, check out the link to Polygon's attempt at level 1 at the top of this review!

I loved the Ludum Dare submission and put a few hours into trying to beat that. I happily paid for the pre-order just on how much I respected their work and their ambition. I'm happy with that payment even as I regret to say, the full game did not pan out well.
I get that it's not much of a point-and-click adventure...but there are ways to do resource-management-clicky games without the baffling design decisions made by Deconstructeam. There's a random-number-generator event in the second level that, no matter how well you've planned out your clicking strategy (which by this point, is dozens and dozens), one roll of the dice immediately kills you and sends you back to the beginning of a 15 minute long click fest. It's perhaps the dumbest, most bewildering design decision I've ever seen in a game (at least, in this decade). It's more fun to turn off the game and contemplate what exactly was going through the designers' minds when they thought that would be a worthwhile addition. I pity the game testers that had to sit through that part. But that assumes there were even any game testers, which I think is a questionable assumption given how clunky this game turned out to be. The sad part is, the problems are so endemic to the design that I don't see how a "bug patch" will fix them without completely changing the game.
That said, again, I'm happy with my pre-order purchase...indie games need support and hopefully GWBW will be a footstep for this studio to go on and create much better games in the future.

EDIT: So, I'm going to change up my review with the release of the free DLC.
Gods Will Be Watching is a non-traditional point and click game that utilizes a sort of resource management to guage how you handle high-stress, morally complicated and difficult scenarios.
Based on a flash game and funded on kickstarter, the game expands on the story present in the flash game of the same name.
GWBW is one of those rare games that makes up Devolver Digital's line of complicated, morally ambigous games revolving around difficult morality, and I absolutely love it for that reason.
The game is brutally difficult, and relies on trial and error gameplay to help you learn from your mistakes and helps to create that tension present in games like Dark Souls that give you a sense of true loss when you mess up a scenario that you were so invested in.
The scenarios are structured like puzzles more than they are a telltale game, which hides the morality of your choices through absolute pragmatism. For example, in the first scenario, your hostages fluctuate between two states: relaxed and tense. Relaxed hostages will assume that, while you're negotiating with the hostage rescue team and making sure your hacker is doing well, that you aren't paying attention and make a break for it. You can either shoot them or let them go, causing your hostages to tense up or relax, respectively. However, if they're too tense, they attack you, and they die in self defense.
In any other game, its a clear cut decision whether or not you want to spare a hostage. However, here, its all about resource. A hostage can be traded for benefits, or they can be killed to prevent them from attacking you. Your choice is dictated by circumstance and your abilities.
Also, you can see, Telltale style, how you stacked up to other players at the end of each scenario, which is a nice little addition.
If that seems too hard, (and in many cases, it is), the random elements can be turned off in the puzzle modes that have been added in an update, and if you want to experience the story, you can do so unhindered in narrative mode.
Bringing me to the story: it's fantastic. This is minimalist world building at its finest, and the story feels like a reward in itself. Finding out what happens after you save the world from genocide helped get me through the penultimate chapter, and the characters are lively, interesting and well written. Not to spoil anything, but the ending of the game deconstructs the very way we look at morality in video games, and the final boss is one you won't forget.
The music is one of the things I remember vividly as well. The way it subtly builds tension and creates an undeniable atmosphere for each scenario is uncanny, and is easily one of the strongest parts of the game.
TL;DR
A challenging game that isn't for everyone. The great story may be enough to hook you, however, and the unique take on the moral choice in games is something to behold.

So to start out I am not a LOTR fan in the slightest and this is why I have not really bothere buying this game until now. At £3.20 anything is worth a go right ?
24 Hours in and I can say that this is by far one of the best combat games I have played in a long time. If you are familiar with the batman arhkam trilogy fighting mechanics then you will feel right at home in middle earth. The store does feel stand alone and as someone with no knowledge of the LOTR lore / story the game does very well introducing you into the world without you feeling lost.
The nemisis system is something new and entertaining always giving you something to fight and kill and no battle is the same, if you search out 'worms' (basically like the riddler thugs that tell you where thr trophies are ) you have a good idea how to approach your foe. From stealth to ranged or to just all out combat most fights do feel different in some way and if you are not prepared you can die very quickly. Never be afraid to run if you are outnumbered. Although you will be taunted for it.
My only critisism of the game would be the upgrade tree. I am not that far into the game and I have all but 2 nodes maxed out. I would have liked a more expansive set of upgrades but with what the game gives you. The runes are a fantasic thing to also focus on and play around with as these can really help with the playstyle you incorporate. Changing the runes about can change the way you play really keeping the game fresh.
Finally the GFX. Performance on the pc (i7 6700k , gtx1080) is solid running at 1440p (or 1080p with steam link) with no issues in frame drops in large open world areas or when there is alot of action going on and you have 50+ enemies on the screen. Also playing this with the HD texture pack with the setting cranked up to 10 makes for a fluid, beautiful, seemless experiance. Note thought that ultra does not do anyhting if you do not go to the steam page and download the hd pack seperate. It does not come pre loaded with the base game or the GOTY
All in all I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a solid action adventure game. There is tonnes to do and even if you are not a LOTR fan dont dismiss this as a cash in on the franchise. You will be missing out.

State of decay focuses on the desperation and frustration of being overrun by a zombie apocalypse, every time you clear out one infestation of zombies it seems like two more crop up, you save one group of survivors only to discover there are others who need your help. It never ends; and that is exactly what I want. Playing State of Decay it feels like you're actually struggling to survive in a landscape that has been overrun by the walking dead.
I 100% recommend this game.

Ok so here's the thing:  I played this game months ago at a friend's house and it was cool.  One of the best early access titles I had played.  Good atmosphere with some challenge, despite having no threatening entities. Almost a year later I figure it must have improved a lot since then and I should buy it.
Wouldn't you know it? Of course you wouldn't, it's insane.  The game has gotten worse.  They have made negative progress in that time. It's not that they have done nothing, it's that they have actively worked to make their game worse. Not only was there pretty much nothing added, but features that used to be there are now missing. Crafting has been dumbed down but not at all improved, there is a completely pointless editor included now and for some reason islands are super close.  There are shipwrecks all over the place and you just find lots of loot.  The game not only makes you wonder things like "Why can't I hit this tree?", but also "Why am I violently ill from eating a potato?". The simplification and easy resources bring on a feeling of pointlessness which quickly fades into boredom.
Until this situation is fixed, DO NOT BUY.  They have not made good progress.  If you could see the progress of this game as a stock it would be in a massive down trend.

Stranger's Wrath HD is a great remastered game. It's not just a last gen game that has been upscaled for higher resolution, the character models have been remade from the ground up and the environment have more art assets, looking astonishing compared to the Original Xbox. The story is about a Steef named Stranger, set in the Oddworld universe, who is in desperate need for an operation, in which he became a bounty hunter to catch criminals to cash them in to meet his requirements to get it. Gameplay wise is a mixture between 3rd person platforming which also focus more on fighting and using agility, and a 1st person shooter in which you can switch views anytime seamlessly with a touch of a button/key. Instead of typical guns, you are equipped with a crossbow and you use live ammunition in which you can either buy in game or hunt for them. There are now a bit more features compared to its original release, such as unlocking concept art, new easter eggs, and select difficulties. Fan of Oddworld games and newcomers should definitely pick this game up!!!

In the almost-three and a half years between the original October 2013 Kickstarter and now, Infinite Fall released two smaller "supplemental games" which take place in the same universe. The first,
, a nostalgic dream of constellation-finding and storytelling around a campfire, and the second,
, a ghost story about an astronomer traveling through the woods of the Forest God, touch on themes similar to those of the full game. All of these games and stories come from a deep place and explore important and personal, yet oftentimes universal, topics. NITW looks at decaying towns and economic hardships, depression and mental health, growing up, making one's way through the world, and finding a purpose and meaning in life. It explores faith and belief, and having faith in people—and examines what that means.

I haven't beaten the game yet, so this will be going off what I have experienced thus far.
Night in the Woods is a game I was interested in since I first heard about sometime back in November. At first it simply drew me in because of the art style, there was an article that mentioned it I believe, and it posted a few screenshots. Once I saw its release date, and that it was up for pre-prder on Humble Bundle, I just HAD to get it.
The story is easily the best part of this game. It's the main focus as well, revolving around 3 specific characters, one of which you play as, and a few characters attached to them. Each has their own struggles, their own worries, wants and fears. It starts off simple enough, your character returns home after dropping out of college. But from there, the game delivers a multitude of amazing moments, be they hard hitting, depressing, or a pretty good laugh. And from what I've seen so far, the game only becomes increasingly more "real", targetting themes I've never seen a game take head-on. And yet, it does it in a way you don't really get the full impact of what you just experienced right away.
As I said, the art style is originally what drew me in. It's colorful, evem with it's somewhat limited palette, but it doesn't hinder the game as it takes place during the fall. The art only adds to the soul of the game, though it is also where my biggest gripe is so far, and it's more of a nitpick than a flaw. The game is on a 2D plane, with backdrops in the distance. As such, the characters do not move their heads, and the eyes are what help you keep track of who each character in the game is interacting with (even the random people you see walking around will follow you with their eyes). This, to me, detracts from some of the more heartfelt scenes, as I feel giving the characters the ability to look at the ground, or blink, or any other number of nuances would have them immensely more hard hitting. Though, this may be intentional to help kind of displace the importance of what the game is discussing.
The game uses very simple animations, with a simple run cycle, a jump cycle, birds flying, cars driving by, etc. This game is not an action game, by any stretch of the word. You do some crimes here and there, but you don't go from fight to fight, grinding or progressing like you do in a lot of other games. The sole focus is the characters, their relations to one another, and how the passage of time affects everything around them.
I love this game, hands down, and without a doubt recommend it wholeheartedly. Each character, even the supporting ones, are well written and feel like they have their own lives. It covers themes I think everybody needs to face up to at some point in their lives, yet does it in a way that it doesn't force you into a total feelstrip.
(As an added caveat, Greggory, one of the three main characters, is gay).

This gives me hope for the Resident Evil 2 Remake. Capcom is on the right track.
Update: For those concerning with more detail in this review, simply put the fact that it places Resident Evil right back in its roots; actual survival horror and not a third-person shooter in which enemies drop ammo. Nope, there is none of that here. It plays just like Resident Evil 1 Remake HD Remaster. You either conserve ammo and play it smart, or you can go guns blazing and suffer your imminent death whilst fighting with a knife as a last resort. The new mechanic of two character switching is easy to master and you can opt for either going into areas solo or together, though there are certain events in which you are required to go alone.
Graphics wise this game looks absolutely stunning especially for an HD remaster and, unlike the previous one, the background textures for this game is in very clear detail and doesn't look washed out which is a huge improvement. I have no problems playing it on max settings at 60 fps save for a few drops during the door transitions for some reason (?). However, I am having problems with getting it to play on full screen for now as it seems to crash almost constantly. Not sure if I'm the only one but for now I'm playing it windowed and hopefully Capcom fixes this with a patch soon, unless I'm the one being daft. I won't say much about the story other than the fact that it is classic Resident Evil cheesiness all over again, but hey that's what Resident Evil does best.
Overall it's a damn good Resident Evil game and if the Resident Evil 2 Remake heads in this direction with its own new gameplay mechanics and seamless integration for both scenarios A and B, Capcom will surely rise once again. Here's to the next true Resident Evil game!
